summary: Software architecture is about drawing boundaries and pointing source dependencies at policy, so that business rules stay independent of frameworks, databases and delivery mechanisms, and the system stays cheap to change.

unitSummaries.Part I: Design and architecture are one thing: the structure that keeps a system cheap to change, and it is worth fighting for.
unitSummaries.Part II: Each paradigm removes a power from the programmer: structured programming removes goto, OO removes indirect transfer of control, functional removes assignment.
unitSummaries.Part III: The SOLID principles say how to arrange functions and data into classes and how to connect them, so that modules tolerate change and are easy to understand.
unitSummaries.Part IV: Component cohesion principles say which classes to group; coupling principles say how components may depend on each other, with metrics for stability and abstraction.
unitSummaries.Part V-A: Good architecture keeps options open, separates by use case, layer and operation, and draws boundary lines by what changes for different reasons.
unitSummaries.Part V-B: Business rules sit at the centre; dependencies point inward; humble objects and partial boundaries keep the edges thin.
unitSummaries.Part V-C: The Main component, services and the test boundary are details at the outer edge; embedded systems need the same boundaries.
unitSummaries.Part VI: The database, the web and frameworks are details; a case study and a closing chapter show how architecture survives implementation.
unitSummaries.Whole book: How the ideas of Clean Architecture fit together, which to apply first, and what a careful reading leaves you able to do.

concepts.title: Design and architecture are one thing
concepts.question: Is there a real dividing line between software architecture and software design?

paragraphs: The author claims there is no difference between design and architecture. People use architecture for the high level and design for the low level, but he calls that usage nonsensical.

His evidence is the architect of his new house. The plans show the shape and room layout, and also every outlet, switch, water heater and foundation detail. Those small details support the big decisions and belong to one design.
Software works the same way: low-level details and high-level structure form one continuous fabric, a continuum of decisions with no clear dividing line.
card.example: A team lead says, 'Architecture is the boxes on the whiteboard; the method names are just design.' The author would answer that the boxes depend on the method-level choices and the choices depend on the boxes, so both are one structure.
card.rule: Treat high-level structure and low-level detail as one continuous design, not as two separate jobs.
card.limits: Our reading: the claim is about where the decisions sit, not about who makes them: people may still split work by level for convenience, and software architects have a special duty later in the unit.

concepts.title: The goal: minimal human effort
concepts.question: By what measure does the author judge whether a design is good?

paragraphs: The author states the goal of software architecture as minimizing the human resources needed to build and maintain the required system. That one sentence carries the proposition of the whole unit.
The measure of design quality follows from it: the effort needed to meet the customer's needs. If that effort is low and stays low over the whole lifetime of the system, the design is good.
If the effort grows with each new release, the design is bad. The measure is about the trend over time, not about how the first release felt.
card.example: Two teams ship a first release in a month. Team A needs three people for each later release; Team B needs one more person every release. By this measure Team A has the better design.
card.rule: Judge a design by how much effort each change costs over the system's whole life, not by how fast it started.
card.limits: Our reading: the measure speaks about effort to meet customer needs. It does not say how to make the effort small, and a low early cost does not count if it climbs later.

concepts.title: The signature of a mess
concepts.question: What pattern in staff, output and cost shows that a codebase has become a mess?

paragraphs: The case study uses real data from an anonymous company across eight releases. The engineering staff grows steadily, which looks like success, yet the growth of the code flattens toward an asymptote.

Cost per line of code climbs: a line cost 40 times more in release 8 than in release 1. Monthly payroll rises from a few hundred thousand dollars to 20 million, and the last 20 million bought almost nothing.
The author calls this the signature of a mess. Developers started near 100% productivity and fell toward zero, though nobody worked less: effort went into managing the mess.
card.example: A product team doubles its headcount in a year, but the number of features shipped per quarter stays the same and each estimate gets longer. That matches the signature.
card.rule: Rising headcount and cost with flat output is the signature of a mess, not of success.
card.limits: Our reading: the data show a pattern, not a cause: the author attributes it to haste and ignoring structure. Lines of code are a crude measure of output, so the pattern is a warning, not proof.

concepts.title: The Hare and the cleanup lie
concepts.question: Why does the author think developers who say 'we will clean it up later' end up in a mess?

paragraphs: The author retells the Tortoise and the Hare: the Hare, sure of its speed, naps. Developers are overconfident in the same way, believing 'we can clean it up later; we just have to get to market first'.
His argument has steps. Market pressure never abates, so there is never a calm time to clean up. So developers move on to the next feature, and the mess grows.
He adds that the belief is also a mistake of fact: making messes is always slower than staying clean, on any time scale.
card.example: A startup skips tests for the launch, promising to add them in the next sprint. The next sprint has a new customer deadline, and the tests are never written.
card.rule: The promise of cleaning up later fails because the pressure that caused the mess never goes away.
card.limits: Our reading: the author's claim is that messy code is slower at every time scale, not only that it is risky. It still rests on his experience and one experiment, so it is a strong claim rather than a proof.

concepts.title: The only way to go fast is to go well
concepts.question: What does the six-day experiment show, and why does the author reject a full rewrite?

paragraphs: Jason Gorman built a Roman-numeral converter six times over six days, each taking a little under 30 minutes. He used test-driven development (TDD) on the first, third and fifth days and not on the other three.
The TDD days were about 10% faster than the non-TDD days, and even the slowest TDD day beat the fastest non-TDD day. The author concludes that the only way to go fast is to go well.
For a failing product the answer is for developers to take responsibility for the mess. A rewrite from scratch is the Hare talking again: the same overconfidence would rebuild the same mess.
card.example: A team plans to throw away its tangled billing service and rewrite it in three months, with the same deadline habits. The author predicts the new service will end up as tangled as the old one.
card.rule: Cleanliness makes work faster even in the short run, so a rewrite without changed habits repeats the mess.
card.limits: Our reading: the experiment is small: one programmer, a simple task, six days, and a learning curve in the data. It supports the claim for that case; the author generalizes beyond it.

concepts.title: Behavior: the first value of software
concepts.question: What is the first value of software, and why is it not the whole of a programmer's job?

paragraphs: Every software system gives its stakeholders two values: behavior and structure. Behavior is the first. Programmers are hired to make machines behave in a way that makes or saves money for the stakeholders.

They do it by helping stakeholders write a functional specification or requirements document, then writing code that satisfies it. When the machine violates the requirements, programmers debug and fix it.
Many programmers think this is the entirety of the job. The author says they are sadly mistaken, because the other value is left out.
card.example: A developer's week is spent on a new checkout feature and three bug fixes. All of it is behavior work. The author would ask who, in that week, looked after the second value.
card.rule: Behavior, meaning meeting requirements and fixing bugs, is only one of the two values developers must keep high.
card.limits: The point is not that behavior is unimportant. Programmers must deliver it, and the author's complaint is that focusing on it to the exclusion of structure leaves the system eventually valueless.

concepts.title: Software must be soft
concepts.question: Why does the author say the second value of software lies in the word 'soft'?

paragraphs: The author reads the word 'software' as 'soft' plus 'ware'. Software was invented to be soft: a way to change the behavior of machines easily. Had we wanted behavior hard to change, we would have called it hardware.
So the second value is structure, the architecture: to fulfil its purpose software must be easy to change. When stakeholders change their minds about a feature, the change should be simple to make.
This word-play is the author's way of stating the purpose of software, not an etymological proof.
card.example: A store owner asks to add a loyalty discount to a working checkout. If the code lets a developer do this in an afternoon, the software is soft. If it takes a month, it has become hard in the author's sense.
card.rule: Software exists to make behavior easy to change, so ease of change is its second value.
card.limits: Our reading: soft does not mean sloppy or unfinished. It means the structure keeps change cheap. The word-play is the author's own way of stating software's purpose, so treat it as an argument by metaphor, not a proof.

concepts.title: Scope versus shape of a change
concepts.question: What does the author mean by the difficulty of a change depending on its scope and not its shape?

paragraphs: The author says the difficulty of a change should be proportional to its scope, not to its shape. Scope is how big the change is. Shape is how well it fits the structure the system already has. He admits he uses 'shape' unconventionally.
When difficulty follows shape, costs grow out of proportion to the size of requests. This is why year one is cheaper than year two, and year two than year three.

To stakeholders the requests look like a steady stream of similar scope. To developers they are jigsaw pieces to fit into an ever more complex puzzle. So architectures should be as shape agnostic as practical.
card.example: Two requests are each 'add one field to the report'. One touches a single file; the other touches forty because the data layout assumed a fixed format. Same scope, different shape.
card.rule: Aim for an architecture where the cost of a change tracks its size, not how awkwardly it fits.
card.limits: A shape-agnostic architecture is an aim 'as practical'. Some shapes will always be easier than others, and the author does not claim a system can be perfectly neutral.

concepts.title: Which value is greater: the extremes argument
concepts.question: How does the author prove that ease of change matters more than working today?

paragraphs: Business managers often say it is more important that the system works, and developers go along. The author calls this the wrong attitude and proves it by examining the extremes.
A program that works perfectly but cannot be changed will become useless. A program that does not work but is easy to change can be made to work and kept working, so it stays useful.

He admits that no program is truly impossible to change. But some systems are practically impossible to change because the cost of change exceeds its benefit, and many systems reach that point in some features.
card.example: A reporting tool computes figures correctly but nobody dares touch its code. When tax rules change, it becomes wrong and cannot be fixed. A broken but well-structured tool can be repaired.
card.rule: Ease of change outranks present function because a changeable system can be fixed, while an unchangeable one cannot.
card.limits: The argument uses extreme cases. The author concedes that no program is literally impossible to change, and that managers asked in the abstract may reasonably put working functionality first.

concepts.title: Urgent versus important
concepts.question: Which value of software is urgent, which is important, and what mistake follows?

paragraphs: The author borrows Eisenhower's matrix of importance versus urgency. Eisenhower said the urgent are not important and the important are never urgent. The author reads this as a great deal of truth, though some things are both.
Behavior is urgent but not always particularly important. Architecture is important but never particularly urgent.

Ranking the four couplets gives: urgent and important; not urgent and important; urgent and not important; not urgent and not important. Architecture holds the top two places, behavior the first and third. The mistake is raising position 3 to position 1.
card.example: A sales demo next week makes a flashy feature urgent, and it takes the whole sprint. The work that would keep later features cheap is important but has no deadline, so it waits.
card.rule: Do not let features that are urgent but not important push aside the architecture that is important.
card.limits: The author himself says some features are both urgent and important. The matrix asks you to separate those from merely urgent ones; it does not say behavior can be ignored.

concepts.title: Developers must assert architecture
concepts.question: Whose job is it to assert the importance of architecture, and why?

paragraphs: The author sees a dilemma: business managers are not equipped to evaluate the importance of architecture. That is what developers were hired to do.
His solution is that the development team is responsible for asserting the importance of architecture over the urgency of features.

This means a struggle. Marketing, sales, operations, management and developers all struggle for what they think is best. Developers must squabble with the other stakeholders as equals, because a developer is a stakeholder with a stake in the software to safeguard.
card.example: A manager asks to skip a refactoring to hit a date. The developer does not just comply or complain: she explains what the skipped work will cost on every later release, as a stakeholder defending her stake.
card.rule: Because only developers can judge architecture, they must argue for it as equal stakeholders.
card.limits: Our reading: the author describes a fight with other stakeholders as equals, not a refusal to deliver features. His advice presumes the developers actually know what the system needs.

concepts.title: The cost of putting architecture last
concepts.question: What does the author say happens if architecture comes last, and what is the architect's special duty?

paragraphs: The author says the challenge is doubly important for a software architect. Architects are by job description more focused on structure than on features, and they create an architecture that lets features be easily developed, modified and extended.
His warning is: if architecture comes last, the system becomes ever more costly to develop, and eventually change becomes practically impossible for part or all of it.
If that happens, the team did not fight hard enough for what it knew was necessary.
card.example: After three years of feature-first work, a product team finds that adding a payment method takes six months. By the author's words, they did not fight hard enough earlier.
card.rule: If architecture is left to last, change eventually becomes practically impossible, and the team is to blame for not fighting.
card.limits: Our reading: the warning concerns architecture put last over time. It does not forbid ever shipping a feature before structure is perfect; it condemns making structure always the lower priority.

concepts.title: Structured programming limits direct jumps
concepts.question: What does structured programming take away from the programmer, and what takes its place?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Unrestrained jumps with goto let control leap to any point in a program. Dijkstra showed in 1968 that this is harmful to program structure.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Replace the jumps with the familiar selection and loop constructs: if/then/else and do/while/until. The book summarises the paradigm as discipline imposed on direct transfer of control.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: control flow stays inside constructs whose shape is easy to see. Bad: a capability is gone, and the paradigm adds nothing new. Most modern languages no longer offer an unrestrained goto.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A routine where control can leap to a labelled line anywhere else, so the reader cannot tell how a line was reached.

card.rule: Structured programming replaces unrestrained jumps with if/then/else and do/while/until, which puts discipline on direct transfer of control.
card.limits: Our reading: it restricts jumps only; it does not make a design good in other ways.

concepts.title: Object-oriented programming limits indirect jumps
concepts.question: What did Dahl and Nygaard move to the heap, and what discipline does object-oriented programming impose?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In ALGOL, a function's local variables lived in a stack frame and vanished when the function returned. In 1966 Dahl and Nygaard saw that the frame could move to a heap.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The function becomes a constructor of a class, its locals become instance variables, and its nested functions become methods. Polymorphism follows from disciplined use of function pointers. The book's summary: discipline on indirect transfer of control.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: indirect calls through function pointers get a disciplined form. Bad: like the other paradigms, it removes a power and adds none.

card.rule: Object-oriented programming moved the call frame to a heap and imposes discipline on indirect transfer of control.
card.limits: The summary names indirect transfer, not data combined with functions and not modelling the real world; the book rejects those two as definitions.

concepts.title: Functional programming limits assignment
concepts.question: Which notion from lambda calculus underlies functional programming, and what does the paradigm restrict?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Church's lambda calculus rests on immutability: the value of a symbol does not change. The paradigm is the first of the three to be invented, before computer programming existed.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A functional language effectively has no assignment statement. The book summarises it as discipline imposed upon assignment.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: a program without assignment has no changing values to track. Bad: the paradigm removes a power. Our reading: the book develops the concurrency payoff later in Part II.

card.rule: Functional programming rests on immutability and imposes discipline upon assignment.
card.limits: Most functional languages do have some way to change a variable, but only under very strict discipline; no assignment means disciplined assignment, not none.

concepts.title: The paradigms only take powers away
concepts.question: What do the three paradigms have in common, and why does the book expect no fourth?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each paradigm removes a capability from the programmer and none adds a new one. Each imposes a discipline that is negative in intent, so the paradigms tell us what not to do more than what to do.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Together they remove goto statements, function pointers, and assignment. The book then asks whether anything is left to take away, and answers: probably not.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the pattern tells you what a paradigm is for. Bad: you get prohibitions, not new abilities. Our reading: the argument that no fourth paradigm exists is an inference from history, not a proof.

card.rule: Each paradigm takes a power away, and the book expects no further negative paradigm.
card.limits: Our reading: the claim covers negative paradigms only, those that remove capabilities; it does not say that no useful new style of programming can appear.

concepts.title: Each paradigm serves an architectural concern
concepts.question: Which architectural concern does each paradigm line up with?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Architecture has three big concerns: function, separation of components, and data management.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Polymorphism is the mechanism used to cross architectural boundaries. Functional programming is the paradigm tied to data management. Structured programming is the algorithmic foundation of our modules.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the history lesson maps onto the three concerns, which is why the book says it has everything to do with architecture. Our reading: this is the book's roadmap; later chapters develop each link.

card.rule: Structured programming serves function, polymorphism serves separation of components, and functional programming serves data management.
card.limits: The alignment is the book's overview, not a full theory; each link is developed in later chapters.

concepts.title: Dijkstra's goal of proof
concepts.question: Why did Dijkstra apply mathematical proof to programs, and what did he find about goto?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Programming is hard: a program of any complexity holds too many details for a human brain to manage unaided, and one overlooked detail produces programs that seem to work and then fail in surprising ways.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Dijkstra wanted a Euclidean hierarchy of postulates, theorems, corollaries and lemmas. Programmers would use proven structures and tie them together with code they proved correct.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: a decomposable module can be proved in small units, by divide and conquer. Bad: certain uses of goto stop a module from being broken down into smaller units, so those modules resist proof.

card.rule: Proof needs divide and conquer, and some uses of goto make a module impossible to decompose.
card.limits: Not every goto blocked decomposition; the book says some uses did not, and those matched the simple selection and loop constructs.

concepts.title: Three structures suffice
concepts.question: Which three control structures can build every program, and why did that matter to Dijkstra?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Dijkstra needed control structures that kept a module provable. The structures that did so had been identified two years earlier by Böhm and Jacopini.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Böhm and Jacopini proved that all programs can be built from three structures: sequence, selection and iteration. The structures that make a module provable are the same minimum set from which all programs can be built.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: nothing is lost by restricting yourself to these structures. The book calls the match remarkable and says it is how structured programming was born.

card.rule: Sequence, selection and iteration are enough to build every program, and they are exactly the structures that keep a module provable.
card.limits: The result is about control structures; it does not say that proofs of whole programs became practical, which the book denies later.

concepts.title: Proving each structure
concepts.question: How did Dijkstra prove sequence, selection and iteration correct?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To start a hierarchy of proofs, Dijkstra had to show how to prove each of the three structures correct.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Sequence: trace inputs to outputs by simple enumeration. Selection: enumerate each path; if both produce the right result, the proof stands. Iteration: use induction, proving the case for 1 by enumeration, then that N correct implies N + 1 correct, and prove the start and end criteria.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the approach was no different from any normal mathematical proof. Bad: the work was heavy, which the book returns to when it explains why the proofs never came.

card.rule: Prove sequence and selection by enumeration and iteration by induction.
card.limits: Our reading: enumeration works for sequence and selection; iteration needs induction because the number of repeats is not fixed.

concepts.title: The goto debate and its outcome
concepts.question: How did the argument over Dijkstra's goto letter end, and why are we all structured programmers now?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In March 1968 Dijkstra published a letter, Go To Statement Considered Harmful, in CACM. Letters poured into journals, and the battle lasted about a decade.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The argument petered out because Dijkstra had won. As languages evolved, goto all but disappeared, and most modern languages lack it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: structure is now the default. The book adds that we are structured programmers not necessarily by choice: our languages do not give us the option of undisciplined direct transfer. Even languages that keep goto often restrict its target.

card.rule: Dijkstra won the goto argument because languages dropped the keyword, so structured programming is now the default.
card.limits: Winning did not remove all transfer: named breaks and exceptions remain, as restricted forms.

concepts.title: Functional decomposition
concepts.question: What does structured programming make possible for large problems, and which disciplines grew from it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Structured programming lets a module be recursively decomposed into provable units, so a module can also be functionally decomposed.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Take a large problem statement and decompose it into high-level functions. Decompose each of those into lower-level functions, and so on without end.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: structured analysis and structured design became popular in the late 1970s and the 1980s, promoted by Yourdon, Constantine, DeMarco and Page-Jones. Our reading: the technique is a top-down breakdown, so it needs a clear statement of the problem first.

card.rule: Because structured modules split into smaller pieces, a large problem can be decomposed level by level into functions.
card.limits: The decomposition was meant to end in provable functions; the book says the proofs never came, and justifies decomposition later by testability.

concepts.title: The proofs never came
concepts.question: Did the proofs Dijkstra hoped for ever arrive, and what do programmers think of them now?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Dijkstra's plan was a Euclidean hierarchy of theorems that programmers could build on. The proofs never came and the hierarchy was never built.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Dijkstra's dream faded and died. Few of today's programmers believe that formal proofs are an appropriate way to produce high-quality software.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bad: the original goal failed, even though the control structures survived. Our reading: the failure concerns proving every little function, not the structures or the decomposition themselves.

card.rule: The Euclidean hierarchy of program proofs was never built, and few programmers now see formal proof as the way to quality.
card.limits: Our reading: the book rejects formal proof of every function as a practice; it does not reject the idea that software can be shown correct enough by other means.

concepts.title: Science is falsifiable, not provable
concepts.question: How does science earn trust without proof, and how does that differ from mathematics?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Science differs from mathematics: its laws cannot be proved correct. Measurements may match a law to many decimal places, but some later experiment could always show it wrong.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Science works by proving statements false. Statements that resist every effort to disprove them are deemed true enough for our purposes. Theories and laws are falsifiable but not provable.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Mathematics is the discipline of proving provable statements true; science is the discipline of proving provable statements false.

card.rule: Science proves statements false rather than true, and trusts those that survive every attempt to disprove them.
card.limits: Our reading: the standard is true enough for our purposes, not certainty; one failed experiment would overturn a law.

concepts.title: Tests show bugs, not their absence
concepts.question: What can a test show about a program, and what can it never show?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Dijkstra said testing shows the presence of bugs, not the absence of them. A test can prove a program incorrect; it cannot prove it correct.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: All tests can do, after enough effort, is let us deem a program correct enough for our purposes.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Tests for a leap-year check all pass, yet the function is wrong for 1900.
blocks.code:
def leap(y):
    return y % 4 == 0

print(leap(2024), leap(2023), leap(2000))
# True False True: all as expected
print(leap(1900))
# True, but 1900 was not a leap year

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bad: passing tests never proves correctness. Good: the standard is realistic, and it is the standard that science uses.

card.rule: Tests can disprove a program but never prove it, so the best we can say is that it is correct enough for our purposes.
card.limits: Our reading: a passing suite does not make a program provable; the claim holds for any number of tests.

concepts.title: Structured code gives falsifiable units
concepts.question: Why does structured programming still matter if the proofs never came?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A test can only try to disprove a program that is provable. A program that is not provable, for example through unrestrained goto, cannot be deemed correct however many tests it passes.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Structured programming forces a program to be decomposed recursively into small provable functions. Tests then try to prove each function incorrect, and if they fail we deem it correct enough.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: this ability to create falsifiable units is what makes structured programming valuable today, and why modern languages lack unrestrained goto. Bad: units are only falsifiable, never proven.

card.rule: Structured programming is valuable because it creates small provable units that tests can try to falsify.
card.limits: Our reading: falsifiable units are deemed correct enough, not proven; and non-provable code cannot even be deemed correct by tests.

concepts.title: Encapsulation was already in C
concepts.question: Does encapsulation define object-oriented programming, or did earlier languages already have it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Encapsulation is often cited as part of OO because OO languages make it easy to draw a line around a cohesive set of data and functions, so data is hidden and only some functions are known.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: C already did this. A header forward-declares the struct and its functions, the implementation file defines them, and users cannot see the members.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: users work through the header alone. Bad for the claim that OO defines encapsulation: this needs no OO language.

card.rule: Perfect encapsulation existed in C through headers that hide a struct's members, so encapsulation does not define OO.
card.limits: Our reading: the point is about hiding, not about OO being bad; and C only hides what is kept out of the header.

concepts.title: OO languages weakened encapsulation
concepts.question: How did C++ weaken the encapsulation that C had, and what does OO still rely on?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The C++ compiler needs to know the size of each class instance, so member variables must be declared in the class's header.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Clients of the header now know the members exist. The compiler blocks access, but renaming a member forces clients to recompile. Public, private and protected partly repair this, but they are a hack for a technical need.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bad: the once-perfect encapsulation of C is only partly kept.

card.rule: C++ had to reveal members in the header, so OO languages weakened the perfect encapsulation C had.
card.limits: Our reading: the compiler still blocks access to private members; what leaks is knowledge that the members exist.

concepts.title: Inheritance by field order
concepts.question: Did C programmers have inheritance before object-oriented languages, and what did OO add?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Inheritance is the redeclaration of a group of variables and functions in an enclosing scope. C programmers could do this by hand long before OO.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: If a second struct begins with the same fields as the first, in the same order, a pointer to the second can be cast to the first and used as one. C++ implements single inheritance this way.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: OO made masquerading significantly more convenient. Bad for the claim that OO invented inheritance: the trick predates it, and the book credits OO only with a half-point.

card.rule: Inheritance can be done by hand in C by repeating the first fields in the same order, so OO only made it more convenient.
card.limits: Our reading: the trick works only while the shared fields come first and in the same order.

concepts.title: Polymorphism is pointers to functions
concepts.question: How did C programs achieve polymorphism before OO, and what mechanism lies underneath it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The C copy program calls getchar and putchar without knowing which devices STDIN and STDOUT are. Their behaviour depends on the device, so the functions are polymorphic.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: UNIX requires every IO driver to provide open, close, read, write and seek with identical signatures. A FILE structure holds pointers to the five functions, each driver loads its own addresses, and getchar simply calls the function that STDIN points to for read.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The same trick in a few lines: one struct of function pointers, two drivers. The output is [screen a][screen b][log c].

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Polymorphism is an application of pointers to functions.

card.rule: Polymorphism is an application of pointers to functions: each device or object supplies its own functions behind one agreed shape.
card.limits: The mechanism is not an OO invention; what OO changed is how safe and convenient it is to use.

concepts.title: OO made polymorphism safe
concepts.question: What did OO languages change about polymorphism, and why does that matter?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Building polymorphism by hand with function pointers is driven by manual conventions: initialise the pointers, and call everything through them. A programmer who forgets either one causes a bug.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: An OO language removes the conventions. The language sets up the pointers and routes the calls, so polymorphism is safe and convenient. This is why the book says OO imposes discipline on indirect transfer of control.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the dangers go away with the conventions. Our reading: the gain is safety and convenience rather than new power, consistent with the book's view that paradigms remove, not add.

card.rule: OO languages remove the manual conventions of function pointers, so polymorphism becomes safe and convenient.
card.limits: Our reading: the conventions are removed for programs written in an OO language; hand-written function pointers in any language still need them.

concepts.title: Device independence and plugins
concepts.question: What does it mean for IO devices to be plugins to a program, and why was this wanted?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The copy program calls getchar and putchar, and its source code does not depend on the source code of any IO driver.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A new device, such as handwriting recognition in and speech synthesis out, needs no change to the copy program, not even recompilation, as long as its driver implements the five standard functions. The devices have become plugins.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: device independence. The plugin architecture has been built into almost every operating system.

card.rule: When a program calls only a standard set of functions, any device implementing them can be plugged in without changing the program.
card.limits: Our reading: plugging in works only while the new driver implements every standard function the program calls.

concepts.title: Dependency inversion
concepts.question: How does an interface let source code dependencies point against the flow of control?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In a typical calling tree, main calls high-level functions, which call mid-level ones, which call low-level ones. Every caller must name its callee's module (#include, import or using), so source dependencies follow the flow of control.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Put an interface between caller and callee. The caller calls through the interface, and the callee implements it. The callee's source depends on the interface, so the dependency points against the flow of control. This is dependency inversion.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: because OO languages give safe, convenient polymorphism, the architect controls the direction of source dependencies. Bad (our reading): an interface is a source-level device that adds a layer to read.

card.rule: Inserting an interface makes the callee depend on the caller's abstraction, so the source dependency points opposite to the flow of control.
card.limits: Our reading: inversion changes source dependencies only; the flow of control at run time is unchanged.

concepts.title: Plugins, independent deployability and developability
concepts.question: What follows when the UI and the database depend on the business rules?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: With ordinary dependencies the business rules depend on the UI and the database. The architect wants changes to those details not to disturb the rules.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Invert the dependencies so that the UI and the database depend on the business rules. The UI and the database become plugins to the rules, and the rules' source never mentions them. Compiled into separate components (jar, DLL, Gem files), they keep the same dependencies.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the business rules component does not depend on the UI or database components, so the rules can be deployed independently of them. Changes to the UI or database need not affect the rules.

card.rule: Point the source dependencies of the UI and database at the business rules, so the rules stay independent and the details become plugins.
card.limits: Our reading: this works for components whose dependencies really have been inverted; one remaining direct dependency on a detail breaks the independence.

concepts.title: Variables that do not vary
concepts.question: What is the key difference between a Java loop and a Clojure expression that print the same squares?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To see what functional programming is, compare two programs that print squares of integers. The point is not to teach Clojure, but to show a dramatic difference.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In Clojure, the first five squares come from this one expression, where range gives a never-ending list of integers. The variable x is initialised but never modified.
blocks.code: (take 5 (map (fn [x] (* x x)) (range)))

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The Java program uses mutable variables; the Clojure program uses none. The book's summary: variables in functional languages do not vary.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Java: the variables i and total change on every pass of the loop.

card.rule: A functional program computes with variables that are initialised but never modified, where an imperative loop changes them.
card.limits: Our reading: the point is about mutable variables, not syntax; a loop is not wrong, it is a user of changing state.

concepts.title: Mutable variables cause concurrency problems
concepts.question: Why does an architect care whether variables are mutable?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An architect wants systems to stay robust with multiple threads and multiple processors. Concurrent applications bring race conditions and concurrent update problems.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: All race conditions, deadlock conditions and concurrent update problems come from mutable variables. If no variable is ever updated, there is nothing to race over or update concurrently.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: with no mutable variables these problems cannot occur. Bad: immutability costs storage and processing power.

card.rule: All race conditions, deadlocks and concurrent update problems come from mutable variables, so removing mutation removes them.
card.limits: Our reading: the claim is about problems caused by mutation; it does not say that avoiding mutation is free.

concepts.title: Segregating mutable from immutable components
concepts.question: How can a system tolerate some mutable state safely, and where should most of the code live?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Because full immutability needs compromises, a common one is to split the application, or its services, into mutable and immutable components.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The immutable components work in a purely functional way and talk to components that do allow variable state to change. Those mutable components are protected by transactional memory, which treats variables like database records under a transaction or retry scheme. Clojure's atom is one example.
blocks.code:
(def counter (atom 0))
(swap! counter inc)
; counter is mutated only through swap!

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: well-structured applications keep non-mutating and mutating parts apart, and architects should push as much processing as possible into the immutable parts and drive as much code as possible out of the mutable ones. Bad: the mutable part still needs a protection scheme.

card.rule: Split the system into immutable components and a small, protected mutable part, and keep as much code as possible in the immutable side.
card.limits: Our reading: segregation shrinks the risk but does not remove it from the mutable part, which still needs protection.

concepts.title: Event sourcing stores events, not state
concepts.question: What does event sourcing store instead of state, and what does that make the application?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A bank application that keeps account balances mutates them on every deposit and withdrawal. Storage and processing power keep growing, so mutable state is needed less.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Store only the transactions, never the state. When a balance is needed, apply all the transactions from the beginning. A shortcut is to save the state every midnight and apply only the later transactions.
blocks.code:
def balance(events):
    total = 0
    for kind, amount in events:
        total += amount if kind == 'deposit' else -amount
    return total

events = [('deposit', 100), ('withdraw', 30), ('deposit', 5)]
print(balance(events))  # 75

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: nothing is ever updated or deleted, so the application is CR, not CRUD, and has no concurrent update problem. Bad: the store grows and needs a lot of room. With enough storage and processing power the application can be entirely immutable, and so entirely functional.

card.rule: Event sourcing stores the transactions and derives the state when needed, so the data store only ever grows.
card.limits: Our reading: the scheme costs a great deal of storage and processing, so it suits systems where both are plentiful.

concepts.title: One module, one actor
concepts.question: What does the Single Responsibility Principle say a module should answer to?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The name invites a reading that every module should do one thing. That guideline exists for functions, but it is not the SRP. The real force is that systems change to satisfy people, and different groups of people ask for different changes.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor. An actor is the group of people who require a given kind of change. A module is a source file or, where code is not kept in files, a cohesive set of functions and data. Cohesion is the force binding code that answers to one actor.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: a change asked for by one group touches only code written for that group. Bad: you must find out who each piece of code serves, which a count of methods or classes does not tell you. Reading the name alone leads to the wrong test.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A class whose methods are specified by different departments, each with its own manager and its own deadlines.

card.rule: Make each module answer to a single actor, the group that asks for its changes.
card.limits: The SRP is not the rule that a function does one thing; that is a separate habit for small functions. One actor may need many methods in one module without breaking the principle.

concepts.title: A shared helper links two actors
concepts.question: How can a change requested by one actor break something that a different actor relies on?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Careful developers avoid duplicating code, so two methods that need the same calculation share one function. If those methods answer to different actors, the shared function quietly links the actors together.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Payroll code and hours-report code both call regularHours(). Accounting asks to change how regular hours are counted. A developer edits the shared function, tests it, and accounting approves. Nobody tells HR, whose report now shows different numbers.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Both methods call the same helper, so one edit changes both results.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: no copy exists to drift out of date. Bad: a change made for one actor, even a well-tested one, silently alters what another actor receives, and only the first actor checks it.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A helper called by methods that different departments specified.

card.rule: Keep code that different actors depend on apart, so that a change for one cannot reach the other.
card.limits: Our reading: sharing is not wrong in itself. A function used by methods that answer to the same actor, or to actors who always want the same change, can be shared without this risk.

concepts.title: Many actors, one source file
concepts.question: Why do unrelated changes to one source file cause trouble when two developers make them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A source file with many methods attracts many editors. If its methods answer to different actors, each actor's requests land in the same file, and developers from different teams edit it at the same time.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Keep the code for each actor in its own source file. Two changes requested by different actors then touch different files and need no merge between them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: fewer collisions, and a bad merge no longer puts several departments at risk. Merge tools are good now, but none handles every case, so some risk always remains. Bad (our reading): more files to name and navigate.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A file that many teams edit in the same week, each for its own reasons.

card.rule: Put code that serves different actors into different source files so that their changes do not collide.
card.limits: Our reading: splitting files does not remove every merge: two developers serving the same actor can still collide, and the SRP does not replace merge tools or careful review.

concepts.title: Splitting the class: data, actor classes, facade
concepts.question: How can one Employee class be split so that three actors are no longer coupled?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Separating the code has a price: callers now have several classes to create and track. A split must remove the coupling between actors without making the system awkward to use.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Move the data into a plain structure with no methods. Give each actor its own class holding only that actor's functions. The classes do not know about each other. A facade creates them and delegates, so callers still see a single object.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Data, three actor classes and a thin facade.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: a change for one actor stays in one class, and the facade holds very little code. Bad: the developers now have several classes to instantiate and track, which the Facade pattern relieves.

blocks.label: Variant
blocks.text: Some developers prefer to keep the most important business rule next to the data. They leave the key method in the original Employee class and make that class the facade for the lesser functions.

card.rule: Separate data from functions, give each actor a class of its own and let a thin facade hide the extra classes.
card.limits: Our reading: a class per actor does not mean a class per function. And the facade must stay thin, since it holds almost no logic of its own.

concepts.title: Open for extension, closed for modification
concepts.question: How much old code should change when a new kind of report is requested for the same data?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Requirements keep growing. A web page that shows a financial summary must now also become a paginated, black-and-white printed report with headers, footers and negative numbers in parentheses. If such a small extension forces large changes, the architecture has failed at its basic job.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Open-Closed Principle says a software artifact should be open for extension but closed for modification: behaviour grows without editing the artifact. Here the work splits into two responsibilities: calculating the data to report, and presenting it as a web page or a printed report.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the ideal number of changed old lines is zero, since a new presenter is added beside the old one. Bad: the separation needs more classes and interfaces, and the diagrams grow more complex.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: A requirement changes the calculation itself, as that part is the one that must be modified.

card.rule: Separate calculating the data from presenting it, so that a new presentation extends the system instead of modifying it.
card.limits: Zero changed code is an ideal. A new report still needs new code, and a requirement that changes the calculation itself must modify the part that calculates.
card.example: The summary page scrolls and shows negative numbers in red. The printed version paginates and wraps negatives in parentheses. Both read the same figures from one calculation step.

concepts.title: A hierarchy of protection by level
concepts.question: Which way should a source code dependency point between a component to protect and one that changes more?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Parts of a system are not equally central. Business rules are the central concern. Controllers, presenters and views are peripheral concerns. A change in a peripheral part should not force a change in the central part.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: If component A should be protected from changes in component B, then B depends on A. Arrows between components point toward what we want to protect. In the report system the Interactor, which holds the business rules, is protected from everything; the Controller is protected from the Presenters, and the Presenters from the Views.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: changes to the Database, Controller, Presenters or Views have no impact on the Interactor. The result is a hierarchy of protection by level: the higher the level, the more protected. Bad (our reading): designers must decide levels deliberately, and lower levels end up depending on higher ones.

card.rule: Point source code dependencies from the component that changes more toward the component you want to protect.
card.limits: Protection is relative. A component can be peripheral to one component and central to another, as the Controller is peripheral to the Interactor but central to the Presenters.

concepts.title: Interfaces that point dependencies the right way
concepts.question: Why does the report design contain interfaces that look like needless complexity?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A reader may recoil at the number of classes in the report design. Much of that complexity exists to make sure that dependencies between components point in the correct direction. Without it, the business rules would depend on the database and the views.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Where a high-level component needs a service from a lower-level one, it owns an interface, and the lower-level class implements it. FinancialDataGateway sits between the report generator and the data mapper to invert the dependency that would run from the Interactor to the Database. The presenter and view interfaces do the same.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The policy side owns the interface; the database side implements it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the Interactor never mentions the Database, so database changes cannot reach it. Bad (our reading): extra interfaces and classes, and a reader has to follow one more step of indirection.

card.rule: Where a high-level policy needs a low-level service, give the policy an interface and let the low-level class implement it.
card.limits: Our reading: each interface costs indirection. The authors add them to control the direction of dependencies between components, so an interface that guards no such boundary adds cost without that protection.

concepts.title: Hiding internals behind a narrow interface
concepts.question: Why does a requester interface sit between the Controller and the Interactor?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Without a narrow interface, the Controller would reach the Interactor's internals, including the entities behind it. A transitive dependency exists when A depends on B and B depends on C, so A depends on C as well. Then changes to the Interactor's internals could reach the Controller.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The FinancialReportRequester interface exposes only what the Controller uses. The Controller depends on that interface and nothing behind it. This follows the principle that software entities should not depend on things they do not directly use.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the Interactor is protected from the Controller by the dependency direction, and the Controller is protected from the Interactor by the hiding. Bad (our reading): one more interface to design and keep in step with the real needs of the client.

card.rule: Give a client an interface that exposes only what it uses, so it has no transitive dependency on the internals behind it.
card.limits: Our reading: hiding is not free: each hiding interface is another type to maintain. It protects against changes behind the interface, not against changes to the interface itself.

concepts.title: Substitutability as the test for a subtype
concepts.question: When is one type safely substitutable for another?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Inheritance lets a subtype stand in for its base type, but programs written against the base type must keep working. Liskov's definition says: if replacing each object of one type by an object of another type leaves the behaviour of every program written for the first unchanged, the second is a subtype of the first.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Substitutability is judged from the user's side. A License class has calcFee(), which a Billing application calls. PersonalLicense and BusinessLicense compute the fee by different algorithms, but Billing's behaviour does not depend on which one it uses. Both are substitutable for License.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: users are insulated from the variety of subtypes. Bad (our reading): substitutability is a property of behaviour, not of syntax, so a compiler cannot check it and the designer must reason about what users rely on.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A user that has to ask which subtype it has been given.

card.rule: A type is a valid subtype only if programs written against the base type behave the same when it is substituted.
card.limits: Our reading: subtypes may differ in how they work, as the two fee algorithms do. The test is whether users written against the base type can tell the difference.

concepts.title: Why Square is not a proper Rectangle
concepts.question: Why is Square not a proper subtype of Rectangle, even though a square is a rectangle?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In geometry a square is a rectangle, so inheriting looks natural. But a Rectangle's width and height can be changed independently, while a Square's must change together. A user who believes it holds a Rectangle can be confused.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Write the test against the base type: set the width to 5, set the height to 2 and expect an area of 10. With a Square the area is 4, so the check fails. The only defence is for the user to detect a Square with an if statement, and then the user's behaviour depends on the types it uses.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The same test passes for Rectangle and fails for Square.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: a four-line test exposes the violation. Bad (our reading): a real-world is-a relationship misleads, since what counts is the behaviour that users of the base type rely on.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A user that checks whether the object it received is of a particular subtype.

card.rule: A real-world is-a relationship is not enough; a subtype must honour what users of the base type assume.
card.limits: Our reading: the example fails because Rectangle promises independent width and height. A base type that promises less would not expose the violation, so the check is always against what users rely on.

concepts.title: The LSP for interfaces and services
concepts.question: How does the LSP apply to interfaces and services, not only to classes?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Over the years the LSP has grown from a guide for inheritance into a broader principle about interfaces and their implementations. Users depend on a well-defined interface and on being able to swap one implementation for another.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The interface may be a Java-style interface implemented by several classes, several Ruby classes sharing the same method signatures, or a set of services answering the same REST interface. In each case every implementation must be substitutable for the others from the user's point of view.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: users can add or replace implementations without special cases. Bad (our reading): the contract must be well defined, and every implementer has to follow it closely. The best way to see the effect is to watch what happens to an architecture when it is broken.

card.rule: Any set of implementations behind one interface, from classes to remote services, must be substitutable for its users.
card.limits: Our reading: the LSP concerns implementations that claim to satisfy the same interface. Services with different interfaces owe each other no substitutability, but a user that treats them as alike must then add code of its own.

concepts.title: A taxi service that breaks the contract
concepts.question: What happens to an architecture when one service in a group breaks the shared interface?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A taxi aggregator dispatches a chosen driver with a PUT to the dispatch URI stored in the driver record, appending pickupAddress, pickupTime and destination. All companies must treat these fields alike. Acme's programmers abbreviated destination to dest.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The quick fix is an if statement on the URI, such as testing for acme.com. The architect refuses it: company names in code invite errors and security risks, and a merger could force more such statements. Instead a dispatch-command module is driven by configuration data keyed by the dispatch URI.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: no company names appear in the code. Bad: a significant and complex mechanism now exists only because one service's interface is not substitutable for the others.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A condition on a vendor's name or address inside the code that builds requests.

card.rule: A non-substitutable implementation forces special cases, and a good architect contains them in data-driven mechanisms and not in conditions on names.
card.limits: The mechanism contains the damage but does not undo it: the system still carries extra machinery because one interface differs.

concepts.title: Users that depend on operations they never call
concepts.question: Why does a user of one operation end up depending on operations it never calls?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Several users share one class, OPS, with operations op1, op2 and op3. User1 calls only op1. In a statically typed language like Java, User1's source code still depends on OPS, so a change to op2 forces User1 to be recompiled and redeployed though nothing it needs has changed.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Segregate the operations into interfaces, one for each user. User1 depends on U1Ops, which declares op1, and does not depend on OPS. A change to OPS that User1 does not use no longer forces User1 to be recompiled or redeployed.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Each user depends on a small interface of its own.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: each user depends only on what it calls. Bad (our reading): more interface declarations to write and name. How much the problem hurts depends on the language: statically typed languages need declarations that users import, and those create the dependencies.

card.rule: Split a broad class into interfaces for each kind of user, so that every user depends only on the operations it calls.
card.limits: The forced recompiling exists where source declarations create dependencies, as in Java. In Ruby or Python no such declarations exist, though the authors say the concern does not end with the language.

concepts.title: The ISP above the level of classes
concepts.question: Why can depending on something with unused features harm a whole system and not just its builds?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A language may remove the recompiling problem, which tempts one to treat the ISP as a language issue. The root concern remains: it is harmful to depend on modules that contain more than you need. At an architectural level the harm shows up as forced redeployments.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: System S includes framework F, whose authors have bound it to a particular database D. S depends on F, and F depends on D. D has features that F does not use and S does not care about. A change to those features can still force F, and so S, to be redeployed.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The lesson, in the authors' words, is that depending on something with baggage you do not need can cause troubles you did not expect. They return to the idea under the Common Reuse Principle in the chapter on component cohesion.

card.rule: Avoid depending on modules, frameworks or services that carry more than you need.
card.limits: Our reading: no dependency is free of baggage. The harm grows with how much unused, changing material comes along, so a stable platform facility worries less than a volatile framework tied to a database.

concepts.title: Depend on stable abstractions, not volatile concretions
concepts.question: Why should source code depend on interfaces and not on the concrete classes that implement them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A change to an interface forces a change to its implementations, but a change to an implementation seldom changes the interface. So interfaces are less volatile than implementations, and good designers work to reduce interface volatility by adding functionality without changing interfaces.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Dependency Inversion Principle says the most flexible systems are those in which source code dependencies refer only to abstractions, such as interfaces and abstract classes, not to concretions. A module should depend on a stable abstraction and avoid depending on volatile concrete classes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: changes to implementations do not reach the code that uses the abstraction. Bad: the abstraction is what everyone depends on, so it must be designed with care. Stable concrete facilities, like Java's String, are tolerated, since they change rarely and under tight control.

blocks.label: Do not use when
blocks.text: The concrete element is a stable part of the platform, not something under active development.

card.rule: Depend on stable abstractions and avoid depending on volatile concrete classes.
card.limits: Not every concrete dependency is a problem. A platform class like String changes so rarely that the authors tolerate it; the rule targets concrete elements that are under active development.

concepts.title: Four coding practices that follow
concepts.question: Which coding practices follow from avoiding dependence on volatile concretions?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A principle needs concrete habits. Concrete classes and concrete functions bring dependencies with them, whether code refers to them, extends them or overrides them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Four practices: refer to abstract interfaces, not volatile concrete classes; do not derive from volatile concrete classes; do not override concrete functions, but make the function abstract and give it several implementations; never mention the name of anything concrete and volatile.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: dependencies stay on stable abstractions. Bad: severe limits on how objects are created, which leads to the Abstract Factory, and a need to use inheritance with great care. In dynamically typed languages inheritance hurts less, yet it remains a dependency.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A subclass that overrides a method of a concrete class the team changes often.

card.rule: Refer to abstractions, do not extend or override volatile concrete code, and do not name volatile concrete classes.
card.limits: These practices target volatile concretions only. Extending a stable class or calling a stable concrete facility is not what they aim at.

concepts.title: Creating volatile objects through an Abstract Factory
concepts.question: How can code create an object without naming its concrete class?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In virtually all languages, creating an object requires a source code dependency on the concrete definition of that object. Following the rules about volatile concretions therefore needs special handling for the creation of such objects.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Abstract Factory: the Application holds a ServiceFactory interface with a makeSvc method. ServiceFactoryImpl implements it, creates a ConcreteImpl and returns it as a Service. Application never mentions ConcreteImpl. A curved line, an architectural boundary, separates the abstract side from the concrete side, and all source dependencies cross it toward the abstract side.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The Application knows two interfaces; the concrete class sits behind the factory.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: source dependencies are inverted against the flow of control, which gives the principle its name. Bad (our reading): an extra factory interface and class for each volatile product, and code that reads less directly than a plain new.

card.rule: Create volatile concrete objects through an abstract factory so that callers depend only on interfaces.
card.limits: Creating a stable concrete object, such as a String, needs no factory. And a concrete class must be named somewhere, since the factory's implementation has to create it.

concepts.title: Gathering the unavoidable violations
concepts.question: If every dependency must point at abstractions, where do the unavoidable concrete dependencies go?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Somewhere a class must name ServiceFactoryImpl and create it. The concrete component in the factory diagram therefore holds a dependency that violates the DIP. This is typical, and such violations cannot be entirely removed.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Gather the violations into a small number of concrete components and keep them apart from the rest of the system. Most systems have at least one, often called main, which is the function the operating system starts. Main creates the ServiceFactoryImpl and stores it in a global variable of the ServiceFactory type that the Application uses.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Only the start-up class names the concrete factory.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the rest of the system follows the DIP, and the violations sit in a place that is easy to find. Bad (our reading): the concrete component is still a wiring point that must be kept up to date. The authors say the curved line will return as the architectural boundaries of later chapters.

card.rule: Concentrate the unavoidable concrete dependencies in a few small components such as main, and keep them out of the rest.
card.limits: Confining the violations does not remove them: the concrete component still breaks the DIP. A system with such violations spread through its business rules has lost the benefit.

concepts.title: Components as units of deployment
concepts.question: What is a component, and what ability must a well-designed one keep however it is shipped?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A system is built from many pieces that must be shipped and kept up. Teams need a unit small enough to deploy on its own, and a name for it that holds in every language.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A component is the smallest entity that can be deployed as part of a system. In Java it is a jar file, in Ruby a gem file, in .Net a DLL. In compiled languages it is an aggregation of binary files, in interpreted languages an aggregation of source files. In all languages it is the granule of deployment.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Components can be linked into one executable, bundled into one archive such as a war file, or deployed separately as dynamically loaded plugins. Whichever way they are finally shipped, well-designed components keep the ability to be deployed on their own.

card.rule: A component is the unit of deployment, and a well-designed one stays independently deployable however it is finally shipped.
card.limits: Keeping the ability is not the same as using it: components may still be linked into one executable or one archive. The idea says what a component is, not which classes belong in one.

concepts.title: Fixed load addresses and library source
concepts.question: Why did early programs fix their own load address and carry their library functions as source?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the early years programmers controlled where their program sat in memory; one of the first lines was an origin statement naming the load address. Programs were not relocatable. Devices were slow and memory was expensive and limited.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Keep library functions as source, not binary. The programmer puts the library source together with the application source and compiles everything as a single program.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Compile time grows with the size of the function library. A large program could take hours to compile.

card.rule: When programs are not relocatable and libraries travel as source, every compile pays for the whole library.
card.limits: This describes early machines with slow devices and scarce memory. The book gives it as background that explains why later tools appeared, not as a design to copy.

concepts.title: Separate library binaries and split segments
concepts.question: What did compiling the library on its own fix, and what new problem did growth bring?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Source-included libraries made compiles slow. Applications and libraries both grew, yet each still had a fixed region of memory.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Compile the function library apart from the applications and load its binary at a known address. Create a symbol table for the library and compile that with the application. To run, load the library binary first and then the application.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: This works while the application fits in the space allotted to it. When the application outgrows that space it must be split into two address segments that jump around the library. When the library outgrows its bounds it takes space elsewhere, and programs and libraries fragment.

card.rule: Fixed addresses shorten compiles, but growth then forces fragmentation.
card.limits: The scheme helps only while each part stays inside its allotted range. The book calls the resulting situation unsustainable and uses it to lead to relocatable binaries.

concepts.title: Relocatable binaries and the linking loader
concepts.question: How did relocatable binaries let a loader place code anywhere and join separately compiled pieces?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Fixed addresses made programmers fragment programs by hand. The compiler knew the names of functions, but the binary held absolute addresses.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The compiler emits relocatable binary, flagged so that a smart loader knows which parts to change for the chosen address, usually by adding the starting address to memory references. It also emits function names as metadata: an external reference for a function the code calls, an external definition for one it defines. The loader links references to definitions once it knows where it loaded each piece.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The programmer tells the loader where to put the library and the application. The loader accepts several binary inputs and loads them one right after the other, relocating each as it goes. This is the linking loader.

card.rule: Emit relocatable code with named external references and definitions, and let a loader place and link the pieces.
card.limits: A linking loader worked well when relatively small programs were linked with relatively small libraries. As programs grew, resolving references became too slow.

concepts.title: Splitting linking from loading
concepts.question: Why did programmers move the slow linking work into a separate program, the linker?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the late 1960s and early 1970s programs grew more ambitious. A linking loader read dozens or hundreds of binary libraries from slow tape or disk and could take more than an hour to load one program.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Separate loading from linking. Put the slow part, the linking, into a separate application called the linker. Its output is a linked relocatable that a relocating loader can load very quickly.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Programmers prepare the executable once with the slow linker, then load it quickly at any time. In the 1980s the same idea served C programs of hundreds of thousands of lines.

card.rule: Do the slow linking once, ahead of time, so that loading is quick.
card.limits: Splitting the phases moved the cost; it did not remove it. As programs grew, the work before loading became the slow part.

concepts.title: Murphy's law of program size against Moore's law
concepts.question: Which two forces raced over compile and link times, and which one won by the mid-1990s?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Through the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s every speed-up was thwarted by programmers' ambitions and the size of the programs they wrote. Turnaround stayed near an hour.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The book names Murphy's law of program size: programs will grow to fill all available compile and link time. Moore's law pushed the other way: speed, memory and density double about every 18 months. Disks shrank and got faster, memory became cheap enough to cache disk data, and clock rates went from 1 MHz to 100 MHz.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: By the mid-1990s link time fell faster than programs grew. In many cases it dropped to seconds, and for small jobs a linking loader became feasible again.

card.rule: Build speed is a race between program growth and hardware speed, and in the mid-1990s hardware won.
card.limits: The race can go either way: from the 1960s to the 1980s growth won, and in the 1990s hardware won. The book gives no guarantee about the next round.

concepts.title: The component plugin architecture
concepts.question: What did cheap, fast linking at load time make possible for components?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Computers had become fast enough that linking could be done again at load time. This was the era of Active-X, shared libraries and the first .jar files.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Link several .jar files or shared libraries together when the program loads, in a matter of seconds, and run the result. Ship components as plugins to an existing application. These dynamically linked files, plugged together at runtime, are the software components of our architectures.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: It took 50 years, but a component plugin architecture can now be the casual default, where it was once a herculean effort.

card.rule: Dynamically linked files that plug together at runtime are the software components of our architectures.
card.limits: This tells how plugins became practical, not how to divide a system into components. The principles that follow address that question.

concepts.title: Reuse requires release
