concepts.question: Why must a reusable component be tracked through a release process with release numbers?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Reuse is now common: tools such as Maven, Leiningen and RVM exist because a vast number of reusable components and libraries have been created. People who reuse a component need to know when new releases come and what they change.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The granule of reuse is the granule of release. Track reusable components through a release process and give them release numbers.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Release numbers help check that all the reused components are compatible with each other. The need goes further: people who want to reuse a component cannot, and will not, do so without a release process.

card.rule: The granule of reuse is the granule of release: a reusable component needs a release process and release numbers.
card.limits: The principle says that a release process is needed, not what a release should contain. The book turns to later principles for that.

concepts.title: A cohesive group, and why the REP is weak
concepts.question: What does the REP imply about which classes go in a component, and why is it weak advice?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Classes in one component share a version number, release tracking and release documentation. That grouping has to make sense to the author and to the users.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The classes and modules in a component must belong to a cohesive group: there is some overarching theme or purpose that they all share, and they should be releasable together. A random hodgepodge breaks the principle.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The book calls this weak advice, because saying that a grouping should make sense does not say precisely what holds the classes together. Its strength is that violations are easy to detect: users see that the grouping does not make sense.

card.rule: Group classes that share a theme and can be released together; a grouping that does not make sense to users violates the REP.
card.limits: The REP cannot say precisely what glues classes together. Our reading: use it as a check on a grouping, and use the CCP and CRP to decide the grouping.

concepts.title: Common closure: group what changes together
concepts.question: Which classes belong in one component, and which in different ones, by the CCP?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Requirements change. If one change forces edits in many components, each of them has to be released, revalidated and redeployed.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Gather into components the classes that change for the same reasons and at the same times. Separate into different components the classes that change at different times and for different reasons. Just as a class should not hold several reasons to change, a component should not have multiple reasons to change.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: If two classes are so tightly bound, physically or conceptually, that they always change together, they belong in the same component. This minimizes the work of releasing, revalidating and redeploying the software.

card.rule: Put classes that change for the same reasons and at the same times into the same component.
card.limits: The CCP guides grouping by change, not by reuse. Tight binding that makes classes change together is the test; a loose resemblance is not.

concepts.title: Maintainability, closure and the CCP
concepts.question: Why does the CCP favour maintainability over reusability, and how is it tied to closure?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: For most applications maintainability matters more than reusability. When code must change, you would rather have all the changes in one component than spread across many.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Gather in one place the classes likely to change for the same reasons. Because 100% closure is not attainable, closure must be strategic: design classes closed against the most common kinds of change you expect or have met.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: If changes are confined to a single component, only that component is redeployed. Other components that do not depend on the changed one need not be revalidated or redeployed.

card.rule: Choose component boundaries so that the most likely changes land in as few components as possible.
card.limits: Closure can never be complete. The CCP protects against the changes you expect or have met, not against every change.

concepts.title: Common reuse: group what is reused together
concepts.question: Which classes does the CRP say belong in the same component?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A component has to be built so that the people who take it get a whole reusable unit. Grouping affects what users must depend on.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Classes and modules that tend to be reused together belong in the same component. Expect to see classes with many dependencies on each other, such as a container class and its iterators, which are reused together because they are tightly coupled.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Our reading: a user who needs the container gets its iterators in the same component. The CRP also says which classes not to keep together.

card.rule: Put classes that are reused together in the same component.
card.limits: The test is how classes are reused, not what they are called. Classes that are not tightly bound should not be grouped; that half of the CRP comes next.

concepts.title: Depending on a component means depending on all of it
concepts.question: Why does the CRP also say which classes must not share a component?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: When one component uses another, a dependency forms between the components, even if the user uses only one class of the used component. That does not weaken the dependency.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Make the classes in a component inseparable: it should be impossible to depend on some and not on the others. Classes that are not tightly bound to each other should not be in the same component.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Every time the used component changes, the using component will likely need corresponding changes. Mixed components cause more components to be redeployed than necessary and waste significant effort.

card.rule: Do not force users of a component to depend on classes they do not need.
card.limits: The advice concerns what users need. Tightly bound classes still belong together under the first half of the CRP.

concepts.title: The CRP and the ISP
concepts.question: How does the CRP relate to the Interface Segregation Principle, and what is the shared advice?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Depending on things you do not need burdens a design, in classes and in components.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The ISP advises us not to depend on classes that have methods we do not use. The CRP advises us not to depend on components that have classes we do not use.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: One question applies at both levels: what does my code actually use? Our reading: asking it before adding a dependency catches both kinds of excess.

card.rule: Do not depend on things you do not need, whether they are methods in a class or classes in a component.
card.limits: The shared advice does not say how to decide what is needed together. The first half of the CRP, classes reused together, covers that.

concepts.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
concepts.title: Inclusive and exclusive cohesion principles
concepts.question: Which cohesion principles make components larger, which makes them smaller, and what is the tension?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The three cohesion principles tend to fight each other, so satisfying one can cost another.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The REP and CCP are inclusive principles: both tend to make components larger. The CRP is an exclusive principle, driving components to be smaller. Good architects seek to resolve the tension between them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: An architect who focuses on the REP and CRP only will find that too many components are hit when simple changes are made. One who focuses too strongly on the CCP and REP will cause too many unneeded releases.

card.rule: The REP and CCP push components larger, the CRP pushes them smaller, and good cohesion balances all three.
card.limits: The tension tells what each choice costs, not where to stand. The best position depends on the concerns of the team now.

concepts.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
concepts.title: Where a project sits on the triangle changes over time
concepts.question: Why does the best position on the tension triangle change as a project matures?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Concerns change with time. Early in a project, developability is more important than reuse.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Find a position in the triangle that meets the team's current concerns, and know that these concerns will change. Early on, the CCP matters much more than the REP. Projects tend to start on the right-hand side of the triangle, where the only sacrifice is reuse. As the project matures and other projects draw from it, it slides to the left.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The component structure of a project can vary with time and maturity.

card.rule: Favour the CCP early; as other projects begin to reuse a project, the balance slides toward reuse.
card.limits: The slide is a tendency, not a law. The book says projects generally start on the right, and that the right balance today may not be right next year.

concepts.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
concepts.title: Cohesion is more than one function
concepts.question: How does the book's view of component cohesion differ from the old view, and why does the balance keep moving?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Cohesion was once taken to be simple: the attribute that a module performs one, and only one, function.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Treat component cohesion as a balance of the opposing forces of reusability and developability, which the REP, CCP and CRP describe. This is a more complex variety of cohesion.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Balancing these forces with the needs of the application is nontrivial, and the balance is almost always dynamic.

card.rule: Component cohesion is a balance between reusability and developability, and the balance keeps shifting.
card.limits: The conclusion gives no formula for the balance. It says what to weigh and expects the weights to change.

concepts.title: The morning after syndrome and the weekly build
concepts.question: Why do shared source files cause the morning after syndrome, and why does the weekly build fail as a project grows?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Many developers modify the same source files. Someone who stays later changes something you depend on, and the code that worked when you left no longer works next morning. This is the morning after syndrome.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: One long-standing answer from the telecommunications industry is the weekly build. All developers work on private copies of the code for four days and ignore each other, then integrate everything and build the system on Friday.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Developers live in isolation four days out of five, but pay a large integration penalty on Friday. As the project grows, integration spills into Saturday and creeps back toward Thursday, and the team moves to a biweekly build. Efficiency falls, risk rises and rapid feedback is lost.

card.rule: The weekly build postpones integration, and the postponed cost grows with the project until the schedule has to be lengthened again and again.
card.limits: The morning after syndrome is not too big a problem in relatively small projects with just a few developers. The trouble comes as the project and the team grow.

concepts.title: Releasable components and the acyclic rule
concepts.question: How does splitting work into released components avoid the morning after syndrome, and what must the dependencies avoid?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Teams need to work without being at the mercy of each other, and integration should come in small steps rather than one big event.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Partition the development environment into releasable components. When developers get a component working, they release it with a release number into a directory for other teams, and keep modifying it in their own private area. Everyone else uses the released version. The dependency structure of the components must have no cycles.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Teams decide when to adopt a new release and may stay on the old one, so no team is at the mercy of the others. Integration happens in small increments, with no single point when all developers must come together.

card.rule: Release components with numbers, let each team adopt releases when ready, and keep the dependency structure free of cycles.
card.limits: The process works only if the dependency structure has no cycles. If there are cycles, the morning after syndrome cannot be avoided.

concepts.title: Reading an acyclic component graph
concepts.question: In an acyclic component graph, how do you find who a release affects, what a test needs and the release order?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A component diagram is a directed graph: components are the nodes and dependencies are directed edges. With no cycles you can never follow the edges from a component back to itself, so the graph is a directed acyclic graph, or DAG.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: To find who a release affects, follow the dependency arrows backward. To release the whole system, go from the bottom up: components that depend on nothing first, and the top component, such as Main, last.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Releasing a top component affects no one, because nothing depends on it. The build order is clear because the dependencies are understood.

card.rule: In a DAG a release affects only what depends on it, and the system is released from the bottom up.
card.limits: The reading works only without cycles. With a cycle there probably is no correct build order.

concepts.title: The effect of a cycle
concepts.question: What goes wrong in releasing, testing and building when components depend on each other in a cycle?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A new requirement makes a class in one component use a class in another component that, directly or through others, already depends on the first. The graph is no longer acyclic.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In a cycle, every component depends on every other, directly or indirectly. The components in the cycle become, in effect, one large component, and the developers must all use exactly the same release of one another's components.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: All of the developers experience the morning after syndrome. A unit test of one component pulls in the other components and their libraries. Build problems grow geometrically with the number of modules, and there is probably no correct build order.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Running a simple unit test of one class needs many different libraries and much of everybody else's code.

card.rule: A cycle fuses the components in it into one large component that must be released, tested and built together.
card.limits: The effect is on releasing, testing and building. The book does not say a cycle changes what the code does.

concepts.title: Breaking a cycle: the DIP or a new component
concepts.question: How can a cycle between components be broken, and what does that say about the component structure?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A cycle must be broken to restore a DAG, and the structure changes as requirements change. The dependency structure has to be watched for cycles all the time.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: There are two main ways. First, apply the DIP: create an interface with the methods the using class needs, put it in the component of the user, and make the other component implement it. This inverts the dependency. Second, create a new component that both depend on and move the classes they both use into it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The second way means that the component structure grows: the book says the dependency structure jitters and grows as the application grows, and sometimes new components are created.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Before, entities depend on authorizer and authorizer depends back on entities. After, the interface lives in entities and authorizer implements it, so the dependency runs one way (compiled and run).

card.rule: Break a component cycle by inverting one dependency with an interface, or by moving what both need into a new component.
card.limits: The second way adds components, so the structure grows. The book expects cycles to appear again, so the structure needs watching over time.

concepts.title: The component structure grows; it is not designed first
concepts.question: Why can't the component dependency structure be designed from the top down at the start?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: We expect large-grained decompositions like components to be high-level functional decompositions. But component dependency diagrams say very little about the function of the application.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Treat the component dependency diagram as a map of the buildability and maintainability of the application. Early on there is no software to build or maintain, so no such map is needed. It grows as the system grows.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A structure designed before any classes would likely fail badly: little is known about common closure, no reusable elements are visible, and cycles are almost certain. The structure grows and evolves with the logical design.

card.rule: Let the component structure evolve with the system: it is a map of buildability and maintainability, not of function.
card.limits: The structure is not the first thing designed, but it cannot be ignored: as modules accumulate, the need to manage dependencies grows.

concepts.title: Isolating volatility
concepts.question: Why is the dependency graph shaped to keep volatile components away from stable, high-value ones?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some components change often and for capricious reasons, such as cosmetic changes to a GUI or the addition of reports. Other components hold high-level policies and ought to stay stable.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Shape the dependency graph to protect stable, high-value components from volatile components. Isolating volatility is an overriding concern of the dependency structure.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Cosmetic GUI changes do not touch the business rules. Adding or changing reports does not touch the highest-level policies.

card.rule: Arrange dependencies so that volatile components cannot force changes on stable, high-value ones.
card.limits: This is about the direction of dependencies. The stability metrics later in this part say how to measure it.

concepts.title: What stability means
concepts.question: What does stability mean for a component, and what makes a component hard to change?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Designs cannot be completely static; some volatility is needed if the design is to be maintained. Components shaped by the CCP are sensitive to some changes and immune to others, and some are meant to be volatile.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Stability is related to the amount of work needed to make a change, not to how often change happens. A penny standing on its edge does not change, yet it is not stable, because very little work topples it. The book sets aside size, complexity and clarity and looks at one factor: many other components depend on the component, which then needs a great deal of work to change.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A component with three dependents has three good reasons not to change. One that depends on nothing has no outside influence to make it change.

card.rule: A component is stable when changing it takes a lot of work, and many incoming dependencies make that work large.
card.limits: Size, complexity and clarity also make a component hard to change, but the book ignores them here. Stability does not mean that the component happens to change rarely.

concepts.title: Fan-in, fan-out and the instability metric
concepts.question: How do you compute a component's instability I from its incoming and outgoing dependencies?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To judge stability you need a number. The book counts the dependencies that enter and leave a component.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Fan-in is the number of classes outside the component that depend on classes inside it. Fan-out is the number of classes inside the component that depend on classes outside it. Instability is \( I = \frac{\text{Fan-out}}{\text{Fan-in} + \text{Fan-out}} \), a value from 0 to 1.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: I = 0 is maximally stable: the component has dependents and depends on nothing. I = 1 is maximally unstable: nothing depends on it and it depends on others. For fan-in 3 and fan-out 1, \( I = 1/4 \). In Java count import statements; in C++ count #include statements.

card.rule: I is fan-out divided by fan-in plus fan-out; 0 is maximally stable and 1 is maximally unstable.
card.limits: The metric counts dependencies, which is only one of the factors in how hard a component is to change. It counts classes on the other side of the boundary, not components.

concepts.title: Depend in the direction of stability
concepts.question: In which direction should dependencies run, and how do the I values compare along an arrow?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some components are designed to be volatile, and we expect them to change. If a component that is hard to change depends on one of them, the volatile one also becomes hard to change, though not a line of its source has changed.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Depend in the direction of stability. The I metric of a component should be larger than the I metrics of the components it depends on, so that I metrics decrease in the direction of dependency.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Components that are meant to be easy to change are not depended on by components that are harder to change. Not all components should be stable: if all were maximally stable, the system would be unchangeable.

card.rule: Each component should have a larger I than every component it depends on.
card.limits: A system of maximally stable components would be unchangeable, so the SDP asks for a mix of stable and unstable components, not for stability everywhere.

concepts.title: Fixing an SDP violation with the DIP
concepts.question: How is a stable component freed from depending on a flexible one, and why make a component of only interfaces?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A developer working in a stable component hangs a dependency on a component designed to be flexible. Now a change to the flexible component forces us to deal with the stable component and all its dependents.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Break the dependence with the DIP. Create an interface with all the methods the using class needs, put it in a new component, and make the class in the flexible component implement it. Both original components now depend on the new component, which is very stable (I = 0), and the flexible one keeps its instability (I = 1).

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: All dependencies now flow in the direction of decreasing I. The new component holds an interface and no executable code. This is a common and necessary tactic in statically typed languages such as Java and C#. In dynamically typed languages such as Ruby and Python these components do not exist, because inversion needs no declared interface.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The stable component's class U needs the services of class C in the flexible component. Both depend on an interface in a component of its own (compiled and run).

card.rule: To stop a stable component depending on a flexible one, put an interface in a separate stable component and make both depend on it.
card.limits: In dynamically typed languages inversion needs no declared or inherited interface, so no abstract component is needed.

concepts.title: High-level policy in stable, abstract components
concepts.question: Where does high-level policy go, and how can a maximally stable component stay flexible?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some software should not change often: it holds high-level architecture and policy decisions that we do not want to be volatile. Yet policy placed in a stable component is hard to change, which could make the whole architecture inflexible.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Put the software that encapsulates high-level policy in stable components (I = 0), and let unstable components (I = 1) hold only volatile software. Keep the stable components flexible by making them abstract: by the OCP, abstract classes can be extended without modification. The Stable Abstractions Principle says a component should be as abstract as it is stable.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A stable component should consist of interfaces and abstract classes so that it can be extended. An unstable component should be concrete, because its instability lets the concrete code be changed easily.

card.rule: A component should be as abstract as it is stable: stable components abstract, unstable ones concrete.
card.limits: The SAP pairs abstractness with stability. It does not ask for every component to be fully stable or fully abstract; the main sequence deals with degrees.

concepts.title: The SDP and SAP together are the DIP for components
concepts.question: How do the SDP and SAP together relate to the DIP, and what changes when the unit is a component?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The DIP is a principle about classes. The SDP and SAP are principles about components.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The SDP says dependencies should run in the direction of stability. The SAP says stability implies abstraction. Together, dependencies run in the direction of abstraction, so the two combined amount to the DIP for components.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The SDP and SAP combined deal with components rather than classes, and they allow a component to be partially abstract and partially stable.

card.rule: The SDP and SAP together are the DIP for components: dependencies run toward abstraction.
card.limits: The combination says nothing about how abstract or stable a given component must be. The metrics in the next ideas measure that.

concepts.title: Measuring abstractness: the A metric
concepts.question: How is the abstractness A of a component computed, and what do the values 0 and 1 mean?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: To check the SAP you need a number for how abstract a component is.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A is the ratio of interfaces and abstract classes to the total number of classes: \( A = N_a / N_c \), where \( N_c \) is the number of classes in the component and \( N_a \) is the number of abstract classes and interfaces.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A ranges from 0 to 1. A value of 0 means the component has no abstract classes at all. A value of 1 means it contains nothing but abstract classes.

card.rule: A is the number of abstract classes and interfaces divided by the number of classes; 0 means none are abstract and 1 means all are.
card.limits: A counts classes, not how much code they hold or how they are used. It measures abstractness only; stability is measured separately by I.

concepts.title: The main sequence
concepts.question: What is the main sequence, and which two positions on the graph of A against I does it join?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Components cannot all sit at the ideal positions, since many have degrees of abstraction and stability. So we need a line of reasonable positions.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Plot A on the vertical axis against I on the horizontal axis. Maximally stable and abstract components sit at the upper left, (0, 1). Maximally unstable and concrete ones sit at the lower right, (1, 0). The line joining those points is the main sequence, the points farthest from both zones of exclusion.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A component on the main sequence is not too abstract for its stability, nor too unstable for its abstractness. It is depended on to the extent that it is abstract, and it depends on others to the extent that it is concrete.

card.rule: Keep components on or near the line from (I = 1, A = 0) to (I = 0, A = 1): as abstract as they are stable.
card.limits: The main sequence is a line of good positions, not a law. The book accepts that some components of a large system are neither perfectly abstract nor perfectly stable.

concepts.title: The Zone of Pain
concepts.question: Why are stable, concrete components a problem, and when are they harmless?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A component near (0, 0) is highly stable and concrete. It is rigid: it cannot be extended because it is not abstract, and it is very hard to change because of its stability.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Treat the area around (0, 0) as a zone of exclusion, the Zone of Pain, and keep volatile components out of it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A database schema is notoriously volatile, extremely concrete and highly depended on, which is one reason the interface between object-oriented applications and databases is hard to manage and schema updates are painful. A concrete utility such as the String component is harmless there, because it is nonvolatile.

card.rule: Avoid volatile components that are both stable and concrete: they are rigid and painful to change.
card.limits: Only volatile components are a problem in the Zone of Pain. A nonvolatile component such as String is harmless there, since it is not likely to be changed.

concepts.title: The Zone of Uselessness
concepts.question: Why are components that are maximally abstract and have no dependents a problem?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A component near (1, 1) is maximally abstract, yet nothing depends on it. Such a component is useless.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Treat the area near (1, 1) as the Zone of Uselessness and keep components out of it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: What lives there is a kind of detritus: often leftover abstract classes that no one ever implemented, sitting unused in the code base.

card.rule: Avoid components that are abstract but unused; an abstraction that no one depends on or implements is useless.
card.limits: The zone is defined by abstractness together with a lack of dependents. Abstract components that others depend on and implement do not belong here.

concepts.title: Distance from the main sequence
concepts.question: How is the distance D computed, and how can it point to components worth reexamining?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If components should be on or near the main sequence, we need a number for how far each one is.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Distance is \( D = |A + I - 1| \), a value from 0 to 1. 0 means the component is directly on the main sequence; 1 means it is as far away as possible. Calculate D for each component, and reexamine and restructure any whose D is not near zero.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A design can also be analysed statistically: a conforming design has a mean and variance of D close to zero, and the variance can set control limits that pick out exceptional components. Plotting one component's D over releases shows drift, and a point past a control threshold, such as 0.1, is worth investigating.

card.rule: Compute D = |A + I - 1| for each component and examine those whose D is not near zero or rises past a threshold.
card.limits: D flags a component for a look; it does not say why. It also depends on A and I, which are themselves imperfect measures.

concepts.title: Metrics are measurements, not gods
concepts.question: How far does the book say the dependency management metrics can be trusted?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The metrics measure how well a design conforms to a pattern of dependency and abstraction that the author thinks is good.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use the stability, abstractness and distance metrics to measure conformance to that pattern. Treat the result as a measurement against an arbitrary standard.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A metric is not a god. The book calls these metrics imperfect at best, and hopes you find them useful.

card.rule: Treat the stability, abstractness and distance metrics as useful but imperfect measurements against a standard the author chose.
card.limits: The book does not claim that the pattern is the only good one, and it offers no proof for it.

concepts.title: Architecture is the shape given to a system
concepts.question: What is the shape of a system, and what is that shape for?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A system must be built, shipped, run and changed for years by people who come and go. Without a deliberate shape, each of those jobs gets harder as the code grows.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author defines architecture as the shape given to a system by those who build it. The shape lies in three things: how the system is divided into components, how the components are arranged, and how they communicate. Its purpose is to ease development, deployment, operation and maintenance.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the four jobs give a test for any design, namely how well each one goes. Bad (our reading): the definition names no favoured structure, so the shape has to be judged against the four jobs for the system at hand, which takes judgement.

card.rule: Architecture is the division, arrangement and communication of components, chosen to ease development, deployment, operation and maintenance.
card.limits: The definition says what the shape is for, not which shape to pick. A shape that helps one of the four jobs can hurt another.

concepts.title: Architecture serves the life cycle, not behavior
concepts.question: Does good architecture make a system work, and if not, what is it for?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Many people think architecture is what makes a system work properly. The author points to many systems with terrible architectures that work just fine.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author calls the architecture's role in behavior passive and cosmetic, not active or essential. Its primary purpose is to support the life cycle of the system: easy to understand, develop, maintain and deploy. The ultimate goal is to minimize lifetime cost and maximize programmer productivity.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: effort goes to the costs that last longest. Bad (our reading): the claim can be misread as permission to ignore behavior. The author still says the architecture must support proper behavior as one of its highest priorities.

card.rule: Judge an architecture by how well it supports the system's life cycle, not by whether the system works.
card.limits: Behavior remains a requirement. The claim is only that architecture rarely decides whether the code works, so a flawed shape shows up as cost.

concepts.title: Team structure pulls the shape
concepts.question: How do the size and number of teams change the architecture a system needs?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Development speed depends on how many people work in the code at once. A few people can coordinate in conversation; many teams need agreed boundaries.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A small team of five can work well on a monolith without well-defined components or interfaces. Five teams of seven each cannot progress unless the system is divided into well-defined components with reliably stable interfaces; the shape tends to become one component per team.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: each team can move on its own. Bad: the author says a component-per-team shape is unlikely to be best for deployment, operation and maintenance, yet teams driven only by schedule gravitate to it. Our reading: this is a trade between the four jobs.

card.rule: Choose the amount of structure for the teams that will build the system, and watch that the team split does not decide the whole shape.
card.limits: A shape fitted only to the development schedule may serve deployment, operation and maintenance badly, so the team split alone should not decide the design.

concepts.title: Deployment must be easy
concepts.question: Why must an architect think about deployment early, and what goes wrong if the team does not?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A system that is hard to deploy is less useful. Deployment is seldom considered during initial development, so the shape is set by other concerns.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The goal is a system that can be deployed with a single action. The author's story: a team picks micro-services early because the boundaries are firm and the interfaces stable. At deployment time the number of services is daunting, and configuring their connections and start-up timing becomes a big source of errors.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: considering deployment early keeps its cost in view while the shape is still cheap to change. Bad (our reading): the cost of a deployment-blind choice shows only late, when the choice is hard to change.

card.rule: Consider the cost of deploying the whole system, ideally in a single action, while the shape is still being chosen.
card.limits: Easy development is not the same as easy deployment. A structure that suits the first can make the second painful, so neither view alone tells you the shape is good.

concepts.title: Hardware is cheap, and architecture should reveal operation
concepts.question: Why is operation the cheapest job to fix, and what else should the architecture do for it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Operational difficulty looks frightening, but the cost equation matters: hardware is cheap and people are expensive.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The impact of architecture on operation is less dramatic than on development, deployment and maintenance. Almost any operational difficulty can be resolved by adding storage and servers. Beyond that, a good architecture communicates the operational needs of the system.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: effort goes first to the costs that hurt most, and the system's operation stays readable. Bad (our reading): the cost equation can be read as an excuse for a careless shape, which it is not.

card.rule: Spend architectural effort on development, deployment and maintenance first, and make the shape reveal what the system does.
card.limits: The cost equation leans away from operation, but it does not remove operation. If an operational limit cannot be bought with hardware, the architecture has to deal with it.

concepts.title: Maintenance costs spelunking and risk
concepts.question: What makes maintenance the most costly part of a system's life, and how does architecture reduce it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: New features and corrections never stop. Each one needs someone to find the place for it and to change it without breaking something else.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author names two main costs of maintenance. Spelunking is the cost of digging through existing software to find the best place and strategy for a feature or fix. Risk is the likelihood of inadvertent defects while making the change. A thought-through architecture separates the system into components, isolated by stable interfaces.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: isolated components illuminate the pathways for future features and greatly reduce the risk of inadvertent breakage. Bad (our reading): the benefit depends on the interfaces really being stable, which takes discipline to keep.

card.rule: Cut the cost of maintenance by dividing the system into components with stable interfaces, so features have visible homes and changes stay local.
card.limits: Stable interfaces help only while they stay stable. A boundary that changes with every feature does not isolate anything.

concepts.title: Structure keeps software soft
concepts.question: Why does the author rank the value of structure above the value of behavior?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Software was invented to change the behavior of machines quickly and easily. A system that is hard to change loses what software was for.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Software has two values: the value of its behavior and the value of its structure. The second is the greater of the two, because it is the value that makes software soft. To keep software soft, leave as many options open as possible, for as long as possible.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: attention goes to the property that preserves every future change. Bad: structure value is invisible in a demo, so it is easy to underfund. Our reading: the argument asks for a standing commitment, not a one-time effort.

card.rule: Protect the structure that keeps software soft by leaving as many options open as possible, for as long as possible.
card.limits: The author compares the two values, not their order in time: behavior still has to be delivered. Our reading: structure value is worth most where change is frequent.

concepts.title: Policy and details
concepts.question: Which parts of a system are policy, which are details, and what should the architect do about the difference?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Business rules need ways to reach people, other systems and programmers. Those routes are easy to confuse with the rules themselves.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author splits every system into policy and details. Policy embodies the business rules and procedures. Details let humans, other systems and programmers communicate with the policy without affecting its behavior at all: IO devices, databases, web systems, servers, frameworks and communication protocols. The architect shapes the system so the details are irrelevant to the policy.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the policy becomes the center of the design, and the details sit at its edge. Bad (our reading): the split relies on judging what truly does not affect the policy, and a wrong judgement puts a detail at the center.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A business rule that mentions a table name, a screen layout or a protocol.

card.rule: Treat business rules and procedures as policy and everything that only lets others reach them as detail, and shape the system so the policy is indifferent to the details.
card.limits: The test is whether a choice changes what the policy does. Our reading: a pricing regulation is policy even if it sits in a file, while a database brand is a detail.

concepts.title: Defer decisions about details
concepts.question: Why is it an advantage to postpone choices such as the database, the web server or a framework?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Choosing the database, web server and frameworks first feels like progress. Yet the high-level policy does not care which of them is used.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Develop the high-level policy without committing to the details around it. Not needed early: a database system, a web server, REST, a micro-services or SOA framework, a dependency injection framework. The longer you wait, the more information you have for each decision.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: each decision is made with more facts. Bad: the delay is real only if the policy is unaware of the detail; code that quietly depends on it turns the deferral into a pretence. Our reading: the discipline lives in the code, not in the plan.

card.rule: Develop the policy without committing to its details, so that each detail can be chosen as late as possible, with the most information.
card.limits: Some decisions cannot be deferred forever; there comes a point at which they must be made. Waiting helps only while the policy stays unaware of the detail.

concepts.title: Pretend the decision has not been made
concepts.question: What should an architect do when someone else has already chosen the database, web server or framework?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A company may have committed to a certain database, web server or framework before the architect arrives. The choice can feel final.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author's advice: a good architect pretends that the decision has not been made.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: a commitment becomes a choice that can be reversed if it proves wrong. Bad: it takes design discipline against the pull of a mandated tool. Our reading: the discipline also keeps the mandated tool from spreading through the policy.

card.rule: Treat a mandated tool as an undecided detail and keep the policy independent of it.
card.limits: Pretending is a design stance, not defiance: the mandated tool is still used. Our reading: where independence is costly and change is implausible, weigh that cost.

concepts.title: Device independence
concepts.question: What mistake did early programmers make with IO devices, and how was it fixed?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the 1960s programs used the instructions that controlled a particular device, such as a printer, card reader or card punch. At first this worked perfectly. Then data moved to magnetic tape, which was more secure, faster and easy to back up.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: All software written for cards had to be rewritten for tape, a big job. By the late 1960s the fix was device independence: operating systems abstracted IO devices into software functions that handled unit records that looked like cards. Programs called these services.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the same program could read and write cards or tape without any change; the author says the Open-Closed Principle was born, though not yet named. Bad: the lesson came through a costly rewrite, because the mistake was invisible while the programs worked.

card.rule: Make programs talk to an abstract device, so the real device can change without changing the program.
card.limits: The abstraction fits devices that behave like the abstract one. Our reading: a device with very different behavior may need a different abstraction.

concepts.title: Device independence pays off
concepts.question: How did device independence help in the junk mail printing job?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The author's company printed personalized form letters from client tapes. Printing on the expensive 360's single line printer took the machine for a very long time.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The programs were written to the operating system's IO abstractions, so the team told the operating system to use magnetic tape instead of the line printer. A full tape took about 10 minutes, and the tapes were mounted on offline printers. The policy was the formatting of name and address records; the detail was the device.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the author calls the value of device independence enormous, since programs could be written without knowing or caring which device would be used. Bad: the gain existed only because the programs had been written to the abstraction beforehand. Our reading: it could not be bought after the need arose without a rewrite.

card.rule: Keep the formatting policy free of the device, so the same program serves both test and production devices.
card.limits: The payoff needs the abstraction to be in place before the need. Without it, the change means the rewrite described in the earlier story.

concepts.title: Relative addresses hide the disk
concepts.question: How did a change of addressing scheme decouple the business rules from the physical disk?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A truckers' union accounting system hard-wired the disk's cylinders, heads and sectors into its code and indexes. A bigger disk would mean converting all the data and rewriting code everywhere, since the business rules knew the scheme in detail.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A more experienced colleague advised treating the disk as one huge linear array of sectors addressed by sequential integers. A small conversion routine sat between the records and the disk. The high-level policy became agnostic about the disk.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the decision about the disk drive structure was decoupled from the application. Bad: the hard-wired code and data had to be converted first.

card.rule: Hide the physical layout behind one translation point, so that only that point changes when the hardware does.
card.limits: A translation routine moves the knowledge of the hardware to one place; it does not remove it. That routine still has to change when the disk does.

concepts.title: The architecture shows its use cases
concepts.question: What is the most important thing architecture can do to support a system's behavior?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Architecture has little influence over behavior, because very few behavioral options can be left open. But influence is not everything.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The most important thing a good architecture can do to support behavior is to clarify and expose it, so the intent of the system is visible at the architectural level. A shopping cart application with a good architecture looks like a shopping cart application: the use cases are first-class elements visible at the top level.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: developers do not have to hunt for behaviors. Bad: the author leaves the full treatment to a later chapter, Screaming Architecture, so here the claim is only that behavior should be exposed, not how.

card.rule: Make the system's use cases visible as prominent elements named for what they do at the top of its structure.
card.limits: Visibility helps understanding; it does not make the use cases work. It also needs names that describe the function, not the technology.

concepts.title: Leave the form of operation open
concepts.question: Why should components not assume how they communicate, and what does that keep possible?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Operational needs differ: a system may need to serve 100,000 customers per second, or answer big data queries in milliseconds. The forms that meet such needs range from an array of small services on many servers, through lightweight threads sharing one process, to a few processes in isolated address spaces.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Which form to use is itself an option that a good architect leaves open. Components kept properly isolated, with no assumption about the means of communication between them, can be moved through the spectrum of threads, processes and services as the operational needs change over time.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the form can follow the real load. Bad: a system written as a monolith that depends on being one cannot easily be upgraded to multiple processes, threads or micro-services.

card.rule: Isolate components and do not assume how they communicate, so the system can move between monolith, threads, processes and services.
card.limits: Isolation costs design effort, and a system that will stay small may never use it. Our reading: weigh the chance of operational change before paying.

concepts.title: Conway's law and independent teams
concepts.question: What does Conway's law say, and how should the architecture answer it for a system built by many teams?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A system built by an organization with many teams and many concerns is developed by all of them at the same time.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Conway's law: any organization that designs a system will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure. So the architecture should partition the system into well-isolated, independently developable components, which can then be allocated to teams.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: teams can work on separate components. Bad: if the partition only copies the current teams, it inherits their accidents, as the earlier component-per-team warning shows. Our reading: choose the partition for the system first, then allocate the teams.

card.rule: Partition the system into well-isolated components that teams can develop independently.
card.limits: Conway's law describes a tendency, not a plan. A partition made only to fit today's teams may serve deployment, operation and maintenance badly.

concepts.title: Aim for immediate deployment
concepts.question: What does the author mean by immediate deployment, and what makes it possible?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Deployment grows costly when it depends on manual steps that must be done in the right order.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The goal is immediate deployment: a good architecture helps the system be deployed right after the build. It is reached through proper partitioning and isolation of the components, including the master components that tie the whole system together.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: shipping becomes routine and cheap. Bad: the master components are components too, and they must be designed with care. Our reading: the idea sets a target to approach, and the text gives no recipe.

card.rule: Make the build produce something deployable at once, with master components that start, integrate and supervise the isolated parts.
card.limits: Immediate deployment is a goal, not a guarantee. Some configuration may be unavoidable, and the text offers no recipe beyond partitioning and isolation.

concepts.title: Goals are indistinct and inconstant
concepts.question: What can an architect do when the use cases, constraints and teams are unknown and keep changing?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A good architecture must balance the use cases, operation, development and deployment. Yet most of the time the team does not know all the use cases or the operational constraints, team structure and deployment requirements.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Even if they were known, they will change as the system moves through its life cycle: the goals are indistinct and inconstant. All is not lost: some principles of architecture help balance the concerns even then, by partitioning the system into well-isolated components.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: change stays cheap whichever way the targets move. Bad: the author calls the balance pretty hard to achieve. Our reading: it also asks for some investment before the needs are known.

card.rule: When the targets are unknown and moving, use inexpensive principles that isolate components and keep options open.
card.limits: The principles do not tell you the targets. They only make it cheaper to move when the targets show themselves.

concepts.title: Separate layers by reasons to change
concepts.question: Which parts of a system change for different reasons, and how does that divide the system into layers?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The architect does not know every use case but does know the intent of the system, such as a shopping cart or an order processing system. The Single Responsibility Principle and the Common Closure Principle can then separate what changes for different reasons and collect what changes for the same reasons.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: User interfaces change for reasons unrelated to business rules. Business rules split into application-specific ones and application-independent ones, which change at different rates. The database, query language and schema are technical details. The result is decoupled horizontal layers: UI, application-specific rules, application-independent rules, database.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: each layer can change independently, while the use cases stay visible and clear. Bad: more parts to name and connect. Our reading: the cost is smaller when layers are drawn along real differences in what changes.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The mixed class has a screen, an input rule, an interest rule and a storage statement.

card.rule: Separate the user interface, application-specific rules, application-independent rules and database, because each changes for its own reasons.
card.limits: Layers are drawn from the system's intent, not from a fixed list. A tiny system may not need all four, and the horizontal split alone does not separate the use cases.

concepts.title: Use cases are vertical slices
concepts.question: How can the use cases be kept apart from each other down the whole height of the system?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Use cases change for different reasons too. Adding an order to an order entry system will almost certainly change at a different rate than deleting an order.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use cases are narrow vertical slices that cut through the horizontal layers. Each uses some UI, some application-specific rules, some application-independent rules and some database functionality. Keep the add-order and delete-order use cases separate in the UI, in the rules and in the database, down the vertical height of the system.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: new use cases can be added without interfering with old ones. Bad: parts that look alike must be kept apart, which asks for resistance to merging them.

card.rule: Cut the system into thin vertical use cases as well as horizontal layers, and keep each use case's parts apart from the others.
card.limits: Not every use case needs its own copy of every layer. Use cases that truly change together belong together, as the Common Closure Principle says.

concepts.title: Decoupling helps operations, if the mode fits
concepts.question: Why does decoupling for use cases also help operations, and what must be true for the benefit to appear?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Separating the aspects of the use cases means high-throughput parts are likely already apart from low-throughput ones. If the UI and the database are separated from the business rules, they can run on different servers, and the parts that need more bandwidth can be replicated.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: To gain the operational benefit the decoupling must have the appropriate mode. Components that run on separate servers cannot depend on sharing an address space; they must be independent services that communicate over a network.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the work done for use cases pays off for operation as well. Bad (our reading): the operational benefit is available only if the mode allows it; a module that assumes shared memory stays on one machine.

card.rule: Decouple for the use cases, then pick the decoupling mode that the operational need requires; services are one option, not the answer.
card.limits: Services are needed only when components must run apart on a network. Our reading: where one process is enough, source-level decoupling gives the same independence at lower cost.

concepts.title: Decoupling frees teams and deployments
concepts.question: What do strongly decoupled layers and use cases give to teams and to deployment?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The decoupling done for use cases and layers has side effects. Two of them are the third and fourth jobs of a good architecture: development and deployment.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: If the business rules do not know about the UI, a UI team cannot much affect a business-rules team. If use cases are decoupled, the addOrder team is not likely to interfere with the deleteOrder team. While layers and use cases stay decoupled, the architecture supports the organization of the teams, whether feature teams, component teams, layer teams or another variation.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: teams are free of one another, and deployment gains a high degree of flexibility; done well, layers and use cases can be hot-swapped in running systems. Bad: all of this depends on the decoupling being done well.

card.rule: Decouple layers and use cases well, and teams can be organized in any way and parts can be deployed on their own.
card.limits: The benefits hold only while the decoupling holds. A team structure that cuts across the decoupled parts still brings interference.

concepts.title: True and accidental duplication
concepts.question: How do you tell duplication that should be removed from duplication that should be left alone?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Duplication is generally a bad thing in software, and the urge to remove it is strong.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In true duplication every change to one instance necessitates the same change to every duplicate. In false or accidental duplication two similar sections of code evolve along different paths: they change at different rates and for different reasons. Return to them in a few years and they look very different, so they were never true duplicates.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: merging only true duplicates keeps the use cases and layers decoupled. Bad (our reading): telling the two kinds apart means judging how the code will change, which is a prediction.

card.rule: Before removing duplication, ask whether the copies must always change together; if they change at different rates or for different reasons, leave them apart.
card.limits: True duplication, where every change must be repeated everywhere, should still be removed. The rule does not excuse copying code that must stay identical.

concepts.title: Similar screens and records
concepts.question: What should you do when two screens, or a screen and a database record, look the same?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two use cases may have very similar screen structures, algorithms or queries, and the architects are tempted to share the code. In the same way, a database record may look like a screen view, which tempts passing the record straight up to the UI.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author judges both cases almost certainly accidental duplication. Resist unifying the use cases. Create a separate view model that looks like the record and copy the elements across.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: use cases and layers stay apart, and each can change on its own. Bad: some code looks copied, though the author judges it almost certainly accidental duplication.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The screen reads OrderView, never OrderRow, so a change to the table does not reach the UI.

card.rule: Create a view model and copy the fields across rather than passing a database record to the UI or merging look-alike use cases.
card.limits: The advice weighs a small cost of copying against the risk of coupling. Our reading: where the shapes truly must stay identical, sharing may be fine.

concepts.title: Three decoupling modes
concepts.question: At what three depths can layers and use cases be decoupled, and what does each depth control?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Decoupling is not one thing. Layers and use cases can be separated at different depths, and each depth controls a different kind of dependency.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Source level: control the dependencies between source modules so that a change in one forces no recompilation of others; all run in one address space and one executable, a monolith. Deployment level: control the dependencies between deployable units such as jar files or DLLs, so a change in one forces no rebuild or redeploy of others. Service level: reduce dependencies to data structures sent as network packets.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: from source to service, each mode gives more independence. Bad: the service level is expensive, in development time and in system resources, as the text's later discussion says.

card.rule: Name the mode before choosing a boundary: source level, deployment level or service level.
card.limits: The three modes are a spectrum, not a menu of three clean options. Components of one system may sit at different modes, and a service is often built from deployable units.

concepts.title: Which mode to start with
concepts.question: According to the author, which decoupling mode should a project start with, and why not simply use services?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: It is hard to know which mode is best during the early phases of a project, and as the project matures the optimal mode may change. A system that runs comfortably on one server might grow until some components ought to run on separate servers.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A popular solution is to decouple at the service level by default. The author objects: it is expensive in development time and system resources, and it encourages coarse-grained decoupling. His preference is to push the decoupling to the point where a service could be formed should it become necessary, but to leave the components in the same address space as long as possible.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good, according to the author: the option of a service stays open without paying for it early. Bad (our reading): this is the author's preference, and it depends on the team keeping the decoupling disciplined enough to form a service later.

card.rule: According to the author, decouple as if services were possible, but keep components in one address space until a real need says otherwise.
card.limits: This is the author's view of a contested point. Where the need for independent scaling or separate teams is known early, starting with services may be the better trade.

concepts.title: The mode can slide both ways
concepts.question: How should a system be able to change its decoupling mode over time, in either direction?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Needs change with time. A system may grow beyond one server, so the mode that suited one year may not suit the next.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A good architecture lets a system be born as a monolith deployed in a single file, grow into independently deployable units, and go all the way to independent services. Later it should allow the reverse, sliding back down to a monolith.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the system always uses the mode it needs. Bad: the author says that this is tricky and that a change of mode should not be seen as a trivial configuration option, though sometimes it is appropriate.

card.rule: Shape the code so that the decoupling mode can move up or down as needs change, without disturbing most of the source.
card.limits: Moving between modes is not free. The author calls it tricky and does not claim it can always be a configuration switch.

concepts.title: Premature decisions multiply effort
concepts.question: What do the stories of companies P and W show about deciding the architecture before the need is known?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Boundaries drawn early defer decisions and keep them from polluting the core business logic. What saps people-power is coupling, especially coupling to premature decisions about frameworks, databases, web servers, utility libraries and dependency injection.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Company P built a three-tier design for a server farm. Each domain object existed in three tiers, joined by serialized messages, so one new field meant three executables, four messages and eight handlers. Every system sold ran on one server. Company W adopted a full suite of domain services; adding a contact to a sales record meant calling several services and faking data.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the stories show what to avoid. Bad: the cost was person-hours spent in droves.

card.rule: Do not build for a need that may never come; draw boundaries to defer such decisions, and adopt heavy structures only when the need is real.
card.limits: The stories do not condemn tiers or services. They condemn adopting them before the need is known and enforcing them everywhere.

concepts.title: FitNesse: an interface in front of the data
concepts.question: How did the FitNesse authors keep the database decision open while building features?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The authors of FitNesse, a wiki for acceptance tests, had MySQL in the back of their minds but purposely delayed that decision by choosing a design that made it irrelevant.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: They put an interface named WikiPage between all data access and the data repository, with methods to find, fetch and save pages. First the methods were stubbed in a MockWikiPage. Then InMemoryPage kept pages in a hash table in RAM, which carried a year of features. Later FileSystemWikiPage wrote them to flat files.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: each implementation was replaced only when it stopped being enough, and no feature waited for a database. Bad: nothing could be saved until persistence was built, and the first version could not keep any work.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The business rules call only WikiPage, so each implementation can replace the last.

card.rule: Put an interface between the business rules and the data store, and start with the cheapest implementation that lets features move.
card.limits: An interface postpones the choice but does not make it. Sooner or later some implementation must keep real data, and a cheap one may not be enough.

concepts.title: What the boundary bought
concepts.question: What did the line between business rules and database save the FitNesse team, and what did it cost to keep MySQL possible?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: From the start the authors held a rule: users should have to download only one jar file. The author's name for it was Download and Go.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The line between the business rules and the database let the team delay the choice and implementation of the database for well over a year. It let them try the file system, and change direction when they saw a better solution, without blocking the original direction. A customer who wanted MySQL wrote a MySqlWikiPage derivative and had it working in a day.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: for 18 months there were no schema, query, database server, password or connection issues, and all tests ran fast. Our reading: the MySQL option cost little because it was only one more implementation of the interface.

card.rule: A boundary around the database lets you delay it, try cheaper options and still support the original choice later.
card.limits: FitNesse was a small program with simple data needs. Our reading: a system with heavy queries may find that cheap early implementations hide problems until late.

concepts.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?
concepts.title: Draw lines between what matters and what does not
concepts.question: Between which parts of a system should a boundary line be drawn, and why is the database one of them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Many of us were taught that the database is inextricably connected to the business rules, and some were told that the database embodies them. The author says this idea is misguided.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: You draw lines between things that matter and things that do not. The GUI does not matter to the business rules, the database does not matter to the GUI, and the database does not matter to the business rules, so each pair gets a line. The database is a tool the business rules use indirectly.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the business rules need not know the schema, the query language or any other detail of the database, and the database can be put behind an interface.

card.rule: Draw a boundary between each part and the parts that do not matter to it, starting with the GUI, the database and the business rules.
card.limits: The lines express what depends on what, not what is unimportant to the product. The database is vital to the product, though not to the rules.

concepts.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?
concepts.title: The boundary points toward the business rules
concepts.question: Where does the boundary go between business rules and database, and which way do the dependencies point across it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The business rules must load and save data, yet should not depend on the database that does so.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The BusinessRules use a DatabaseInterface to load and save data, and DatabaseAccess implements the interface and directs the actual Database. The DatabaseInterface classes live in the BusinessRules component and the DatabaseAccess classes in the Database component. The arrows cross the boundary toward BusinessRules: the Database component knows them, and they do not know it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the Database component can be replaced by Oracle, MySQL, Couch, Datomic or flat files, and the rules can be written and tested before the choice. Bad: the direction feels backward, until you recall that the Database component holds the code that translates the rules' calls into the query language.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The interface sits with the rules; the implementation sits on the other side of the line.

card.rule: Put the interface the rules need inside the rules' component, and let the database component depend on it.
card.limits: The arrow shows source-code dependency, not the flow of data or of control. Data and calls still go from the rules to the database at runtime.

concepts.title: The IO is irrelevant
concepts.question: Why does the author say that input and output are irrelevant to the system, and which way does the GUI boundary point?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A system is often judged by what people see of it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author's principle: the IO is irrelevant. In a video game the screen, mouse, buttons and sounds dominate the experience, but behind them is a model of data structures and functions that does not need the interface. A boundary separates the GUI from the business rules, and the GUI depends on the rules, so any other interface could replace it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: any interface can be swapped in for the one first built. Bad: customers who equate the system with its screens may find the boundary strange. Our reading: it helps to show them a working screen early, built as a replaceable plugin.

card.rule: Treat the input and output as a replaceable layer around the business rules, and let the GUI depend on the rules, not the reverse.
card.limits: Irrelevant means the rules do not depend on the IO, not that the IO is unimportant. Users judge the product by its interface, and it needs real care.

concepts.title: Plugin architecture
concepts.question: What pattern do the database and GUI boundaries create, and what can be plugged in?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The decisions about the database and the GUI are two cases of a general pattern. It is the same pattern used by systems that allow third-party plugins.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The core business rules are kept separate from, and independent of, the components that are optional or can take many forms. With the UI as a plugin, web, client/server, SOA or console interfaces can be plugged in; with the database as a plugin, SQL, NoSQL or file-based storage can be.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: components can be replaced when needed. Bad (our reading): replacement is not free.

card.rule: Keep the core business rules independent, and attach every optional or varied component to them as a plugin.
card.limits: A plugin structure makes a replacement possible and practical, not free. Rules shaped around the first interface may still need rework for a very different one.

concepts.title: Plugins are protected by an asymmetry
concepts.question: Why does a plugin relationship protect one side from the other, and why does the author want that asymmetry in our systems?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two teams in different companies and countries produce ReSharper and Visual Studio. It is hard to imagine two teams that are more separate. Which team can damage the other, and which is immune?

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The dependency structure tells: the source code of ReSharper depends on the source code of Visual Studio. The author wants this deeply asymmetric relationship in our own systems, with certain modules immune to others.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the business rules do not break when someone changes the format of a web page or the schema of the database, Bad: the immune side can disable the plugin, so the plugin owner must live with that.

card.rule: Make the modules you want to protect not depend on the modules that change, so changes cannot propagate to them.
card.limits: The protection runs one way. The plugin remains exposed to the core's changes, so the core's owners carry a duty not to break plugins needlessly.

concepts.title: Boundaries follow the axis of change
concepts.question: Where should a boundary be drawn, and which principle tells us so?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A system has many possible places for a line. A boundary drawn where nothing differs on its two sides protects nothing.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Boundaries are drawn where there is an axis of change: the components on one side change at different rates, and for different reasons, than the components on the other. GUIs change at different times and rates than business rules, and business rules change at different times and for different reasons than dependency injection frameworks.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: each boundary has a reason that can be checked against how the code changes. Bad (our reading): finding the axes needs knowledge of how the system and its environment change, which the team may lack early on.

card.rule: Draw a boundary wherever the parts on its two sides change at different times and for different reasons.
card.limits: A boundary has a price. Where two parts change together, a line between them adds cost and gives no protection.

concepts.title: Crossing a boundary inside a monolith
concepts.question: How can a call cross a boundary inside a monolith while the source dependencies still point toward the higher level?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: At runtime a boundary crossing is a function on one side calling a function on the other and passing data. The trick is to manage the source code dependencies, since a changed module may force changes, recompilation and redeployment of others.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The simplest boundary is a disciplined segregation of functions and data within one address space: the source-level mode, deployed as one executable, the monolith.
