When a high-level client must call a lower-level service, dynamic polymorphism inverts the dependency against the flow of control: the client calls f() through a Service interface that ServiceImpl implements, and Data is defined on the calling side.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: teams work apart and high-level components stay independent of lower-level details; calls are cheap, so crossings can be chatty. Bad: without OO or an equivalent form of polymorphism, the only tool is pointers to functions, which most architects find too risky, so they give up partitioning.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Control flows from Client to ServiceImpl, while the source dependency points from ServiceImpl up to Service.

card.rule: Where control flows to a lower-level service, put an interface on the higher level's side so the source dependency points up.
card.limits: The inversion needs polymorphism. Without polymorphism, only function pointers remain.

concepts.title: Deployable units and threads
concepts.question: How is a boundary drawn with deployable units, and where do threads fit?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A boundary can take a stronger physical form than a disciplined layout in one executable, and the team must not confuse it with ways of organizing execution.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The simplest physical form is a dynamically linked library: a .NET DLL, Java jar, Ruby Gem or UNIX shared library. Deployment involves no compilation; components arrive in binary form and are gathered in a WAR file or a directory. This is the deployment-level mode. Threads are not boundaries or units of deployment, but a way to organize the schedule and order of execution.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: components can be deployed apart, while communication stays cheap, with only a one-time cost for dynamic linking or loading, and still can be chatty. Bad: the components remain close to a monolith, with the same processor, address space and segregation strategies.

card.rule: Use dynamically linked, independently deployable units for a boundary; do not treat threads as boundaries.
card.limits: Deployment-level units share an address space and are still close to monoliths. A thread says nothing about where components are separated.

concepts.title: Local processes are stronger boundaries
concepts.question: What does a local process add to a boundary, and what stays the same about the dependencies?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A stronger physical boundary separates not only the code but the memory in which it runs.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A local process is typically created from the command line or an equivalent system call. Local processes run on the same processor, or the same set of processors, but in separate address spaces, and memory protection generally prevents sharing. They usually communicate through sockets or operating system facilities such as mailboxes or message queues. Source code dependencies still point toward the higher-level process.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: lower-level processes are plugins to higher-level ones. Bad: communication involves operating system calls, data marshaling and decoding, and context switches, which are moderately expensive, so chattiness should be carefully limited.

card.rule: Use a local process for a stronger boundary, keep dependencies pointing to the higher level, and limit chatter across it.
card.limits: A local process still runs on the same machine, so its boundary is weaker than a service's. Each process may itself be a monolith or a set of deployment components.

concepts.title: Services and the mixture of boundaries
concepts.question: What makes a service the strongest boundary, and why do real systems mix several kinds of boundary?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each step from a monolith to a deployable unit to a local process adds independence. The service is the last step, and its price is paid in time.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A service is a process that does not depend on its physical location, and it assumes all communication takes place over the network. The same rules apply as for local processes: lower-level services plug in to higher-level ones, and the higher-level source holds no physical knowledge, such as a URI, of a lower-level service.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: it is the strongest boundary. Bad: communication across it is very slow compared to function calls.

card.rule: Treat a service as the strongest and slowest boundary: keep the same dependency rule, hold no physical addresses in higher-level source, and avoid chatter.
card.limits: A system rarely uses only one kind of boundary. A service may be built from local processes, each a monolith or a set of deployable units.

concepts.title: Policy, level and dependencies
concepts.question: How do policies group into components, and in which direction should dependencies between the components run?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A program is a detailed description of the policy by which inputs are transformed into outputs.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Regroup policies by how they change: those that change for the same reasons and at the same times are at the same level and share a component; the others are at different levels and belong apart. The components form a directed acyclic graph. A strict definition of level is the distance from the inputs and outputs; the farther away, the higher.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the direction of each dependency can be decided by level. In a good architecture low-level components depend on high-level components. Bad: levels have to be worked out from how the code changes, and the policies that handle input and output are the lowest level of all.

card.rule: Group policies by how they change, measure level by distance from the inputs and outputs, and make low-level components depend on high-level ones.
card.limits: Level is about distance from input and output, not about importance as judged by users. Dependencies are compile-time, source-code dependencies, not the flow of data.

concepts.title: The encryption program
concepts.question: In the encryption example, why do source dependencies not follow the data flow, and what does the better design do?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A simple encryption program reads characters from an input device, translates them using a table, and writes them to an output device. The data flows from reader to translator to writer, but the source dependencies need not follow it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Translate is farthest from the inputs and outputs, so it is the highest level. Source dependencies should be decoupled from data flow and coupled to level. The incorrect design has the high-level encrypt function call readChar and writeChar directly. The better one puts Encrypt and the CharReader and CharWriter interfaces in one unit, with all dependencies crossing its border pointing inward.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the encryption policy is reusable in a wide range of contexts, and a change to the input and output is unlikely to affect it. Bad (our reading): it takes more types than the direct version, since each device sits behind an interface.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The Encrypt class names only the two interfaces; the console classes name them in turn.

card.rule: Let source dependencies follow the level of the policy, not the direction of the data flow.
card.limits: The data flow does not change: it still runs from reader to writer. Only the direction of the compile-time dependencies is chosen by level.

concepts.title: An Entity binds critical rules to critical data
concepts.question: What makes a business rule critical, and what does an Entity hold?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some rules make or save the business money whether or not a computer runs them, such as a bank's interest charge on a loan. Such a rule needs data to work on, such as a balance, a rate and a payment schedule, and the rule and its data change together.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Call the rule a Critical Business Rule and its data Critical Business Data. Bind the two together in one separate software module, an Entity. The Entity holds the data or has very easy access to it, and its interface is the set of functions that implement the rules.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the Entity stands alone as a representative of the business, with no concern for databases, user interfaces or third-party frameworks, so it could serve the business in any system. Our reading: a rule that makes sense only inside an automated workflow does not belong here.

card.rule: Put each rule that would make or save money even without a computer, together with its data, in a separate Entity that knows nothing of databases, screens or frameworks.
card.limits: An Entity holds a small set of critical rules. Rules that exist only because the system is automated do not belong in it.

concepts.title: A use case holds rules that exist only because of automation
concepts.question: How does a use case differ from an Entity rule, and what does it describe?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some rules make or save money by shaping how an automated system runs, and would never be used in a manual shop. A bank may refuse any payment estimate until contact details are verified and the credit score is 500 or higher.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A use case describes how an automated system is used: the input the user provides, the output returned to the user, and the processing steps between them. It holds application-specific business rules and refers to Entities for the critical rules. It names the data going in and out but not how the screen looks.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the rules of the application sit in one place apart from the Entities. Our reading: a rule that could belong to either place is a prompt to ask whether it would still exist if no computer were involved.

card.rule: Put rules that exist only because the system is automated into use cases that describe input, output and processing steps, and leave the user interface out of them.
card.limits: A use case is not the screen flow: it names the data in and out, not how it looks. Rules that hold with or without a computer stay in Entities.

concepts.title: Use cases direct the Entities and depend on them, never the reverse
concepts.question: Which way does the dependency run between use cases and Entities, and why?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Entities are general and can be used by many applications. Use cases are specific to one application and sit close to its inputs and outputs. If a general rule depended on a specific one, every application would be tied to the details of one.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use cases hold the rules that say how and when Entities are invoked: they control the dance of the Entities. Entities have no knowledge of the use cases. Use cases know the Entities. This follows the Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level concepts know nothing of lower-level ones.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the Entities stay usable by many applications. The book calls use cases lower level because each is specific to one application. Our reading: an Entity change can still reach every use case that depends on it.

card.rule: Use cases depend on Entities and direct them, and Entities never refer to use cases.
card.limits: In the book, higher level means more general and farther from the system's inputs and outputs. It does not mean larger or more important.

concepts.title: Requests and responses are plain structures that depend on nothing
concepts.question: What kind of data structures should a use case take in and hand back, and why?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A use case needs input and produces output, but it must have no inkling of how that data reaches the user or any other component. It must not know about HTML or SQL.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The use case accepts a simple request data structure as input and returns a simple response data structure as output. These do not derive from framework interfaces such as HttpRequest and HttpResponse. They know nothing of the web or of any user interface in place.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the use case stays free of the delivery mechanism. Our reading: data may need to be copied between a framework's types and these plain structures.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The use case takes a plain request and returns a plain response. Nothing in it names a web type (run: prints 50.0).

card.rule: Give a use case plain request and response structures that carry no framework types, so it knows nothing about how data is delivered.
card.limits: Plain does not mean empty: the structures carry exactly the data the use case needs, in a form no framework dictates.

concepts.title: Keep Entities out of the request and response models
concepts.question: Why should request and response models not hold Entity objects, even though they share data?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Entities and request and response models share much data, so reusing the Entity as the carrier looks tempting and saves a class. But the two exist for very different purposes.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Keep two separate sets of objects. The Entity serves the Critical Business Rules. The request and response models serve one use case's exchange with the outside. The author says they change for very different reasons over time, so tying them together violates the Common Closure Principle and the Single Responsibility Principle.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: each side can change for its own reasons without dragging the other. Bad, if they are tied together: both principles are broken. Our reading: keeping them apart costs some extra classes and copying.

card.rule: Do not let request or response models hold Entity objects: they change for different reasons, so keep them separate even when they share data.
card.limits: Our reading: sharing field names is not sharing a class. Two objects may carry similar data and still be separate, if they change for different reasons.

concepts.title: The architecture should scream the system's use cases
concepts.question: Should the top-level structure of a codebase announce the system's purpose or its frameworks?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A newcomer forms a first impression from the top-level directories and the highest-level package. If the names announce a framework, the framework seems to be the architecture. If they announce the system's purpose, the use cases are.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author, following Jacobson, says software architectures are structures that support the use cases of the system. The plans of a house or a library show what the building is for, and the architecture of an application should do the same for its use cases. A health care system should look like one. Architectures should not be supplied by frameworks.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the structure tells readers what the system is for. Bad, if the architecture is based on frameworks: according to the author it cannot be based on the use cases.

card.rule: Let the top-level structure announce what the system is for, its use cases, rather than which framework it uses.
card.limits: The point is what the structure announces, not a ban on frameworks. Frameworks may appear below the top level; the concern is that they must not supply the architecture.

concepts.title: A good architecture lets tool decisions wait
concepts.question: Why does the author want decisions about frameworks, databases and web servers delayed?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An architect's first concern is that a building is usable, not what it is made of. A house plan lets the owner choose brick, stone or cedar later, once the plans ensure the use cases are met. Software teams feel the pull to commit to tools before that.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A good architecture is centred on use cases so that the architect can describe the supporting structures without committing to frameworks, tools and environments. Frameworks are options to be left open. It should be unnecessary to decide on Rails, Spring, Hibernate, Tomcat or MySQL until much later in the project.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: decisions about frameworks, databases and web servers can be deferred and delayed. Our reading: the decoupling takes design effort early, in return for choices that stay open.

card.rule: Centre the architecture on use cases so that framework, database and web-server choices stay open options, to be decided late.
card.limits: Delay is not refusal: a choice is eventually made. Our reading: a platform that is mandated from the start is already decided, and leaves little to defer.

concepts.title: The web is a delivery mechanism, an IO device
concepts.question: Does delivering a system over the web decide its architecture?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Delivering over the web tempts a team to let the web shape packages, flow and data. But the web is only one way of getting data into and out of a system.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author answers no. The web is a delivery mechanism, an IO device, and the application architecture should treat it as one. That the application is delivered over the web is a detail that should not dominate the system structure, and the decision to use the web is one to defer.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the same architecture can deliver a console app, a web app, a thick client or a web service without undue complication or change to the fundamental architecture. Our reading: the web part must be written as a thin outer piece, which takes design care.

card.rule: Treat the web as an IO device: a delivery detail whose choice can wait and that must not dominate the system's structure.
card.limits: A detail is not unimportant: the web still needs good code and care. The claim is only that it should not set the system's structure.

concepts.section: Frameworks Are Tools, Not Ways of Life
concepts.title: Treat a framework as a tool, with skepticism
concepts.question: How should you treat a framework when its authors and followers urge you to let it do everything?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Frameworks can be powerful and useful. Their authors believe deeply in them, and examples and books about them are written from the point of view of a true believer who assumes the framework should do everything.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author says to take another stance: look at each framework with a jaded eye, and view it skeptically. Ask how you should use it and how you should protect yourself from it. Develop a strategy that prevents the framework from taking over the architecture and keeps the emphasis on use cases.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the framework stays a tool and the architecture stays based on use cases. Our reading: you give up some of the convenience that comes from letting a framework do everything.

card.rule: Use a framework as a tool, with skepticism, and plan how to protect a use-case architecture from it.
card.limits: Skeptical does not mean refusing frameworks: the author says they can be very powerful and very useful. The point is to keep them from taking over.

concepts.title: With use cases at the centre, rules can be tested alone
concepts.question: What can be tested without a web server or a database when the architecture is about use cases?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If the rules can be exercised only through the web server and the database, every test needs them running. Our reading: such tests are slower to run and mix the rules with their surroundings.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: When the architecture is about use cases and the frameworks are kept at arm's length, all the use cases can be unit-tested without any framework in place. The Entity objects are plain old objects with no dependencies on frameworks or databases. The use case objects coordinate the Entity objects. All of them together are testable in situ, without framework complications.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: no web server needs to be running and no database needs to be connected to run these tests.

card.rule: Keep Entities plain and have use cases coordinate them, so that all of them can be tested together without a web server, a database or any other framework.
card.limits: Our reading: testing without frameworks leaves the framework-facing code to other tests. The edges still need checks of their own.

concepts.title: Source code dependencies point only inward
concepts.question: In which direction may source code dependencies point, and what may inner code name?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Hexagonal architecture, DCI and BCE all aim at separation of concerns by layers, each with a layer for business rules and a layer for user and system interfaces. They want a system that is independent of frameworks, the UI, the database and any external agency, and that is testable.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Dependency Rule: source code dependencies must point only inward, toward higher-level policies. The outer circles are mechanisms and the inner circles are policies. Nothing in an inner circle may know anything about something in an outer circle, so the name of anything declared in an outer circle, such as a function, class or variable, must not appear in inner code.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the five properties the family of architectures aims for, namely independence of frameworks, UI, database and external agencies, plus testability. Our reading: inner code can never call outward directly, which the next ideas address.

card.rule: Source code dependencies point only inward, so nothing in an inner circle may mention a name or a data format declared in an outer circle.
card.limits: The rule limits what code may name, not which way data or control flows. Control can still travel outward, by means the next ideas show.

concepts.title: The four circles hold different kinds of code
concepts.question: What does each of the four circles hold, and does the rule need exactly four?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Different code changes for different reasons. Business rules should be least affected by outside change, application steps change when the application does, and delivery formats and tools sit at the edge.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Entities hold enterprise-wide Critical Business Rules, or the application's business objects if there is no enterprise. Use cases hold application-specific rules and orchestrate the data to and from the Entities. Interface adapters convert data between the inner form and the form for the database or web; MVC and all SQL live there. Frameworks and drivers hold the database, the web framework and glue code.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the web is a detail and the database is a detail, kept on the outside where they can do little harm. The circles are schematic: there may be more than four, but the Dependency Rule always applies.

card.rule: Place enterprise rules in Entities, application rules in use cases, converters and SQL in interface adapters, and tools and glue in frameworks and drivers.
card.limits: The four circles are schematic, so more may be needed. What cannot be given up is that source code dependencies always point inward.

concepts.title: Inversion lets control flow outward while dependencies point inward
concepts.question: How can control flow outward while source code dependencies still point inward?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A controller calls a use case, and the use case must hand its result to a presenter in an outer circle. Control goes in and then out, yet the rule forbids the inner circle from naming the outer one.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use the Dependency Inversion Principle. The use case calls an interface declared in its own circle, shown in the book as the use case output port, and the presenter in the outer circle implements it. In a language like Java, interfaces and inheritance are arranged so that the source code dependency opposes the flow of control at just the right points.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the Dependency Rule holds, however the control flows. Our reading: each crossing needs an interface and a class that implements it.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The use case knows only OutputPort; the presenter implements it (run: prints Total: 7).

card.rule: When control must go from an inner circle to an outer one, have the inner circle call an interface it owns and let the outer circle implement it.
card.limits: Inversion is applied at just the right points of a boundary, not everywhere: a call that already points inward needs no interface.

concepts.title: Only simple data structures cross a boundary
concepts.question: What kind of data may cross a boundary?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Data has to cross boundaries, and the easy way is to pass what you already hold, such as an Entity or the result of a database query. That drags a dependency across the line.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Pass isolated, simple data structures: basic structs, simple data transfer objects, arguments in a function call, a hashmap or a constructed object. Do not cheat by passing Entity objects or database rows. No structure may carry a dependency that violates the Dependency Rule.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: nothing crossing the line ties an inner circle to an outer one. The book's example: a row structure returned by a database framework must not be passed inward, since that would force an inner circle to know something about an outer one.

card.rule: Pass only simple, isolated data structures across a boundary, never Entity objects or database rows.
card.limits: Simple does not mean one shape: structs, DTOs, arguments and hashmaps are all fine. What counts is that the structure carries no dependency that breaks the rule.

concepts.title: A request travels through the typical web and database scenario
concepts.question: Which component handles the request at each step of the typical scenario, from controller to view?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A web request must enter the system, reach the business rules and come back as a page, without the rules naming the web, the database or the page.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Controller packages the user's input into a plain old Java object and passes it through the InputBoundary to the UseCaseInteractor. The interactor controls the Entities, then builds OutputData, another plain object, and passes it through the OutputBoundary interface to the Presenter. The Presenter repackages it as the ViewModel, which the View uses.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: all dependencies cross the boundary lines pointing inward, as the Dependency Rule asks. Our reading: one request touches several small types, which is the price of the isolation.

card.rule: The Controller passes plain input through the InputBoundary to the interactor, which passes OutputData through the OutputBoundary to the Presenter, whose ViewModel the View displays, with every dependency pointing inward.
card.limits: This is one typical scenario for a web-based Java system using a database. Our reading: other systems may arrange the same roles in other shapes.

concepts.title: Split hard-to-test behaviour from testable behaviour
concepts.question: How does splitting a behaviour into a humble part and a testable part help testing?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some behaviour is hard to test, such as a GUI, because tests cannot easily see the screen and check what is shown. Yet most of what surrounds it is easy to test.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Split the behaviours into two modules or classes. One is humble: it holds the hard-to-test behaviours stripped down to their barest essence. The other holds all the testable behaviours that were stripped out of the humble object. The pattern was first identified to help unit testers, and presenters are a form of it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the hard-to-test part shrinks to almost nothing and the rest can be unit tested. Our reading: one behaviour becomes two modules, and the humble one is still untested by unit tests.

card.rule: Split hard-to-test behaviour into a humble module stripped to its barest essence, and move everything testable into a second module.
card.limits: Our reading: the humble object shrinks the hard-to-test part but does not remove it, and it still needs checks of another kind.

concepts.title: The Presenter prepares everything so the View stays humble
concepts.question: What does the Presenter put in the View Model so that the View has nothing left to decide?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The View must put data on the screen but is hard to test, so any decision it takes goes untested. Whatever the application controls on screen must be settled before the View touches it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Presenter is the testable object: it takes data from the application, formats it and places it in the View Model, a simple structure of strings, booleans and enums. The View is the humble object and only moves that data to the screen. A Date becomes a string; a Currency becomes a formatted string plus a flag that turns it red if it is negative.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the Presenter can be unit tested with no screen, and the View has nothing left but loading data into the screen. Our reading: the View Model must carry every on-screen detail, so it grows with the screen.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The Presenter turns a date and a balance into strings and a red flag (run: prints 13 Oct 2026 1,234.50 True).

card.rule: Have the Presenter turn every on-screen value into a string, boolean or enum in the View Model, so the View only moves data to the screen.
card.limits: The View Model holds what the application has some control over on the screen. Even so, the View itself is still not covered by unit tests.

concepts.title: Database gateways keep SQL out of the use cases
concepts.question: Where does SQL go when use cases need stored data, and which side is the humble object?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Use cases need stored data, but SQL is not allowed in the use cases layer. They still need a way to ask for exactly the data they require.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Between the use case interactors and the database sit database gateways: polymorphic interfaces with a method for every create, read, update or delete operation the application needs. A UserGateway might have a method named getLastNamesOfUsersWhoLoggedInAfter that takes a Date and returns a list of last names. Classes in the database layer implement the gateways, using SQL or whatever the database interface is. That implementation is the humble object.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the SQL stays in the database layer, and each interactor asks for data by a method named for the need. Our reading: one method per operation can mean many narrow methods.

card.rule: Let use cases call gateway interfaces with one method per database operation, and put the SQL in the humble implementation in the database layer.
card.limits: The interactor is not the humble object: it holds application-specific business rules. Only the gateway implementation is humble.

concepts.title: An ORM is really a data mapper in the database layer
concepts.question: Why does the author say there is no such thing as an object relational mapper, and where does the tool belong?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Tools such as Hibernate are called ORMs, but the name suggests that objects are being stored. The author asks what an object is, from the point of view of its users, and what a data structure is.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Objects are not data structures from their users' point of view: users cannot see the data, which is private, and see only public methods, so an object is a set of operations. A data structure is a set of public data variables with no implied behaviour. Such tools load data into data structures from relational tables, and would be better named data mappers. They belong in the database layer.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the mapping tool sits as a detail in the database layer, out of the use cases. Our reading: this is the author's naming opinion, and the tool is still widely called an ORM.

card.rule: Treat an ORM as a data mapper that loads relational rows into data structures, and keep it in the database layer behind the gateways.
card.limits: Our reading: the point is about what the tool does and where it goes, not a ban on the word. Other schools use ORM without this objection.

concepts.title: At a service boundary, humble modules format and listen
concepts.question: How does the Humble Object pattern create a boundary with external services?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: An application may call other services or provide services itself. Each service has its own message format, which the application's rules should not have to know.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: On the output side, the application loads data into simple data structures and passes them across the boundary to modules that format the data properly and send it to the external service. On the input side, service listeners receive data from the service interface and format it into a simple data structure the application can use, which then crosses the service boundary.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: formatting and transport stay in modules at the edge, and only simple structures cross. Our reading: each service needs a pair of small modules, one for each direction.

card.rule: At a service boundary, pass simple data structures across and let humble modules on the outside format and send, or listen and format.
card.limits: Our reading: gateways, presenters and listeners are one pattern in different places. The pattern does not design the service protocol itself.

concepts.title: Skip the last step: build the boundary but deploy it as one
concepts.question: What does a team save, and what does it risk, when it builds a boundary but deploys both sides as one component?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A full boundary needs reciprocal polymorphic boundary interfaces, input and output data structures, and the dependency management to isolate the sides into independently compilable and deployable components. That is a lot of work to build and to maintain, yet an architect may think, I might need it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Do all the work to create independently compilable and deployable components, then keep them together in the same component. The reciprocal interfaces and the input and output structures are there, but everything is compiled and deployed as a single component.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: no version number tracking and no release management burden for several components. Bad: it needs the same code and preparatory design as a full boundary, and the separation can weaken over time, making it a chore to re-separate.

card.rule: To hold a place for a boundary, build every interface and structure of a full boundary but compile and deploy both sides as one component.
card.limits: The saving is in administration, not in code or design effort. Without a real boundary the separation can erode.

concepts.title: A Strategy interface holds a place for a boundary, in one direction
concepts.question: How does a Strategy interface hold the place for a boundary, and what does it leave unprotected?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Reciprocal interfaces keep isolation in both directions, which is expensive in setup and in maintenance. A cheaper placeholder guards only one direction.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use the traditional Strategy pattern. A ServiceBoundary interface is used by clients and implemented by ServiceImpl classes. The dependency inversion needed to isolate the Client from ServiceImpl is in place.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: cheaper than a full boundary, with the Client isolated from ServiceImpl. Bad: without reciprocal interfaces, nothing prevents a backchannel (our gloss: a direct path around the interface) except the diligence and discipline of developers, so the separation can degrade rapidly.

card.rule: A Strategy interface gives a one-dimensional boundary: it isolates clients from the implementation in one direction and relies on discipline for the rest.
card.limits: It guards one direction only. Whatever the structure does not enforce is left to the diligence and discipline of the developers and architects.

concepts.title: A Facade is the simplest boundary and gives up inversion
concepts.question: What does the Facade boundary give up compared with the Strategy boundary?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Even a one-dimensional boundary costs an interface and its inversion. A cheaper placeholder defines the boundary in one place.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The Facade pattern: a Facade class lists all the services as methods and deploys the service calls to classes that the client is not supposed to access. The boundary is simply the Facade class. Even the dependency inversion is sacrificed.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bad: the Client has a transitive dependency on all the service classes. In static languages a change to the source of one service class forces the Client to recompile, and backchannels are easy to create. Good: it is the simplest of the partial boundaries.

card.rule: A Facade is the simplest partial boundary: one class lists the services, but clients still depend, transitively, on every service class behind it.
card.limits: Hiding the service classes behind a Facade does not remove the dependency: in static languages the client still recompiles when they change.

concepts.title: UI, rules and storage are not the only components
concepts.question: What does Hunt the Wumpus show about splitting a game into a UI, rules and storage?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: It is easy to think of a system as three components: a UI, business rules and a database. For simple systems that is enough, but most systems have more.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Take a text game, Hunt the Wumpus, with commands such as GO EAST. To support several human languages, decouple the text UI from the game rules behind a language-independent API, and let the UI translate. Give the store, which may be flash, the cloud or RAM, its own API too. With dependencies managed, any number of UI components can reuse the same game rules, which neither know nor care which language is in use.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: UI languages and storage can vary without touching the rules.

card.rule: Give each part that varies, such as the UI language or the data store, its own component behind an API the rules define, so that many variants can reuse the same rules.
card.limits: Our reading: each split adds an API and components, so it pays only where the variation or the change is real.

concepts.title: Each axis of change may be a boundary whose API belongs to its user
concepts.question: How does a second axis of change add a boundary, and who owns each boundary's API?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Language is not the only axis along which the UI can change. The way the text is carried could vary too: a shell window, text messages, a chat application.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Each axis of change is a potential architectural boundary. Put an API across it, here to isolate the language from the communication mechanism. The API is defined and owned by the user, not the implementer: GameRules defines the API that Language implements, and Language defines the API that TextDelivery implements.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: variants such as English, Spanish and SMS plug in as implementations of abstract API components. Source code dependencies point toward the component that owns the API.

card.rule: Treat each axis of change as a potential boundary with an API that the using component defines and the used component implements.
card.limits: The example does not say every axis needs a full boundary. The chapter's conclusion warns that fully implemented boundaries are expensive.

concepts.title: Components divide the flow into streams that meet at the rules
concepts.question: Why do the streams of data flow meet at GameRules, and can there be more than two?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Once the API components are drawn, the arrows show how the components relate. They record source code dependencies and not data flow, which can mislead a reader.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Draw the dependency arrows so that they all point up, which puts the component with the highest-level policies, GameRules, at the top. The structure divides the flow of data into two streams, one concerned with communicating with the user and one with data persistence, and both meet at GameRules. Add a network component for multiplayer play and there are three streams, all controlled by GameRules.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the highest-level policy sits on top and each stream hangs below it. As systems grow more complex, the author says the component structure may split into many such streams.

card.rule: Orient dependency arrows toward the highest-level policy: each independent concern forms a stream that meets at that policy, and there can be more than two.
card.limits: The arrows show source code dependencies, not the direction in which data flows.

concepts.title: Inside the rules, policies sit at different levels
concepts.question: Do all streams end in one top component, and how can a higher-level policy sit above the rules?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: It is tempting to think that all the streams meet in a single component at the top. The reality, the author says, is more complex.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Inside GameRules, part of the rules deals with map mechanics: how the caverns connect, which objects sit in which cavern, how the player moves and which events follow. A higher-level policy knows the player's health and the cost or benefit of an event. The lower-level mechanics declare events such as FoundFood or FellInPit to it, and it manages the player's state and decides whether the player wins or loses.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the higher-level policy owns the state, and the mechanics only report events. Our reading: whether such a line is a boundary depends on how the two sides are deployed.

card.rule: Inside one component, look for policies at different levels: the lower level declares events and the higher level decides what they mean.
card.limits: Our reading: policies at different levels need not be separate boundaries. A line between them is an architectural boundary only where the cost is worth paying.

concepts.title: Build a boundary where building becomes cheaper than ignoring
concepts.question: When should an architect pay for a boundary, and how does that decision change over time?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Fully implemented boundaries are expensive. Yet boundaries that are ignored are very expensive to add later, even with comprehensive test suites and refactoring discipline. YAGNI has wisdom, since over-engineering is often much worse than under-engineering.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The architect must guess intelligently: weigh the costs and decide which boundaries to implement fully, which partially, and which to ignore. The goal is to implement a boundary right at the inflection point where the cost of implementing becomes less than the cost of ignoring.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: boundaries exist where they pay for themselves. Bad: the author calls the answer dissatisfying, since there is no formula; it takes a watchful eye.

card.rule: Weigh the cost of each boundary against the cost of ignoring it, aiming to build it where building becomes cheaper than ignoring.
card.limits: The advice is a judgement and not a formula. The author endorses neither building every boundary at the start nor ignoring them all.

concepts.title: Main is the ultimate detail
concepts.question: Where does Main sit in a system, and what is its job?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some code has to create the concrete parts of a system and start them running. That code is full of detail, and it must not pull the high-level policy down into the detail.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author calls the Main component the ultimate detail: the lowest-level policy and the initial entry point of the system. Nothing except the operating system depends on it. Its job is to create the Factories, Strategies and other global facilities, then hand control to the high-level abstract parts of the system.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: all the untidy start-up work sits in one outermost place. Bad: by the author's description Main is the dirtiest of all the dirty components. Our reading: so everything else has to stay out of its reach.

card.rule: Main is the lowest-level, outermost policy: it builds the concrete parts, hands control to the high-level policy, and nothing depends on it.
card.limits: Running first does not make Main high-level. It is the lowest-level policy because it holds the most detail and nothing else is allowed to depend on it.

concepts.title: Main wires dependencies and hides the dirty class names
concepts.question: Where may a dependency injection framework work, and how does Main pass dependencies on?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Choosing and creating the concrete parts is untidy work. If a framework does the wiring, its machinery must not spread through the code that uses the parts.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Dependencies should be injected into Main, by a dependency injection framework if one is used. Once they are inside Main, Main distributes them in the ordinary way, without the framework. In the Wumpus example Main also names a game class with a string and gets it from a factory, so changes to that class do not make Main recompile or redeploy.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The factory call takes a class name as text, so Main holds no compile-time link to the class.
blocks.code: Game game = GameFactory.makeGame("app.game.GameFacade", new Main());

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the framework is confined to Main, and the rest of the code receives its dependencies in the usual way. Bad: Main carries the untidy detail, such as lists of strings that the author does not want the main body of code to know about.

card.rule: Let a dependency injection framework, if you use one, work only in Main, and have Main pass the dependencies on by ordinary means.
card.limits: The framework's job ends inside Main. Naming a class by string keeps Main from recompiling when that class changes; it does not remove the need to build the object somewhere.

concepts.title: Main is a plugin: one per configuration
concepts.question: How does treating Main as a plugin make configuration easier?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: One application often has to run with different settings: in different environments, for different customers or in different places. Mixing those settings into the policy would make every variation a change to the policy.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Think of Main as a plugin to the application, sitting behind an architectural boundary. It sets up the initial conditions and configurations, gathers the outside resources, and hands control to the high-level policy. Because it is a plugin, a system can have many Main components, one for each configuration.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the author says the configuration problem becomes a lot easier to solve. Bad: Our reading: every extra Main is another outermost component to maintain, a cost the book does not discuss.

card.rule: Treat Main as a plugin behind a boundary and keep one Main for each configuration.
card.limits: The claim is that configuration becomes easier, not that it disappears. Each Main still contains its own untidy detail, and the high-level policy is the part that stays the same.

concepts.title: Using services does not make an architecture
concepts.question: Does building a system from services mean it has an architecture?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Service-oriented and microservice designs are popular, and many teams treat the split into services as the architecture. The author tests that belief.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author calls it patently untrue that using services is by its nature an architecture. A system's architecture is defined by the boundaries that separate high-level policy from low-level detail and follow the Dependency Rule. Services that only separate application behaviors are little more than expensive function calls and are not necessarily architecturally significant.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: a service split can be judged by the question the author asks of any design, whether it draws a boundary that follows the Dependency Rule. Our reading: a system can have many services and little architecture, and pay the cost of a call across a process for each one.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: Services whose only purpose is to separate behaviors, with no high-level policy kept apart from low-level detail.

card.rule: A service is architecturally significant only when it sits on a boundary that separates high-level policy from low-level detail and follows the Dependency Rule.
card.limits: The point is about what defines architecture, not about whether services are worth building. The author does not say services should be avoided, and he agrees some of them are architecturally significant.

concepts.title: A service is a function call across a process boundary
concepts.question: How is a service like a function call, and which calls count as architecture?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Services feel like a different kind of thing from the functions inside a program, so they seem to carry architecture by their nature. The author offers a comparison to test that.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: In a monolithic or component-based system, the architecture is defined by certain function calls: those that cross architectural boundaries and follow the Dependency Rule. Most other functions only separate one behavior from another. Services are likewise function calls across process or platform boundaries, and only some of them are architecturally significant.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the test for a service becomes the test for any function call, whether it crosses an architectural boundary in line with the Dependency Rule. Bad: Our reading: the comparison says what counts but leaves you to find the boundary-crossing services yourself.

card.rule: Treat a service as a function call across a process or platform boundary, and ask whether it crosses an architectural boundary.
card.limits: The comparison is about what counts as architecture. It does not say that a service costs no more than a local call, or that services have no use.

concepts.title: The decoupling fallacy
concepts.question: Are services strongly decoupled because they run in separate processes?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Each service runs in its own process, maybe on its own processor, so it cannot touch another service's variables, and its interface has to be well defined. This is the case for services being strongly decoupled.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author grants some truth but not much. Services are decoupled at the level of individual variables, but they are strongly coupled by the data they share. If a new field is added to a record passed between services, every service that operates on that field must change and must agree on its meaning, so the services are coupled to the record and indirectly to each other. Well-defined interfaces are no truer of services than of functions.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: it shows where to look for coupling, namely shared data, not variables. Bad for the believer: the author calls the benefit something of an illusion.

card.rule: Services are decoupled only at the level of variables; the data they share still couples them.
card.limits: The author concedes the part that is true: services are decoupled at the level of individual variables. His claim is that this is a small part of what decoupling needs.

concepts.title: The fallacy of independent development and deployment
concepts.question: Can services be developed and deployed independently by separate teams?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The belief is that a dedicated team can own each service, and that systems of dozens, hundreds or thousands of services can be built by a similar number of independent teams.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author says there is some truth in this, but only some. First, large enterprise systems can be built from monoliths and component-based systems too, so services are not the only way to scale. Second, because of the decoupling fallacy, services cannot always be developed, deployed and operated independently: to the extent that they are coupled by data or behavior, the work has to be coordinated.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the claim is cut to its true size. Bad: the more the services share, the less the teams can work on their own.

card.rule: Independence of teams holds only to the extent the services are not coupled by data or behavior, and services are not the only way to scale.
card.limits: A team can own a service; the author does not deny it. His claim is that independence is partial and that other structures scale too.

concepts.title: The kitty problem: one feature touches every service
concepts.question: What happens to a service-based taxi system when a new feature cuts across all its services?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A taxi aggregator is built from many micro-services, each owned by a small team. After a year of happy work, marketing announces kitten delivery: a nearby taxi collects a kitten from a collection point and delivers it. Some drivers may be allergic, so they must never be picked for the service, and some customers will have allergies too.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The services form a chain. TaxiUI handles customers' orders. TaxiFinder checks the taxi suppliers' inventories and leaves candidate taxis in a short-term record attached to the user. TaxiSelector picks a taxi by the user's criteria. TaxiDispatcher orders it. The kitten feature changes all of them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bad: the services are all coupled and cannot be independently developed, deployed and maintained. Good: the example shows the two fallacies at work in one story.

card.rule: If a new feature forces every service in a chain to change, the services are coupled and cannot be developed, deployed or maintained independently.
card.limits: Our reading: the example shows a feature that touches every service. A change to one service's internals, such as how TaxiDispatcher contacts a supplier, need not spread this way.

concepts.title: Cross-cutting concerns defeat functional decompositions
concepts.question: What is a cross-cutting concern, and which structures suffer from it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Teams cut a system into pieces by function, one piece per behavior. New features rarely respect those cuts.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author says the kitty problem is the problem of cross-cutting concerns: features that cut across all the functional behaviors. Structures that cut a system up by function, like the chain of taxi services, are very vulnerable to such features.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bad: a feature of this kind touches every piece, however well each piece is built.

blocks.label: Smell
blocks.text: A planned feature that needs a change in every piece of the system.

card.rule: A feature that cuts across all behaviors forces changes through a system that is cut up by function, so design for that case.
card.limits: The problem is not limited to services, and it is not a reason to avoid services. The next ideas show the author's fix.

concepts.title: Objects absorb the kitty feature
concepts.question: How would a component-based design take in a feature that cuts across the whole taxi system?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The taxi system needs a kitten feature that touches finding, selecting and dispatching. In a component-based system the same pressure applies, so the answer has to come from the design of the classes.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Careful use of the SOLID principles would give a set of classes that can be extended polymorphically for new features. The logic specific to rides is pulled out of the original base classes into a Rides component, and the kitten feature goes into a Kittens component. Both components override the abstract base classes with a pattern such as Template Method or Strategy, and both follow the Dependency Rule: they depend on the base classes, not the reverse.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: most of the original logic stays in the base classes, and each feature lives in its own component. Bad: Our reading: the base classes must offer the right places for extension, so they have to be designed with that in mind.

card.rule: Put each feature in its own component that overrides abstract base classes, with dependencies pointing at the base classes.
card.limits: This is the component-based answer, not a free one: the user interface still has to change, and the base classes must offer a place for each extension, such as a Template Method or a Strategy.

concepts.title: Services can be built from components too
concepts.question: Can a service itself be given a component structure so new features arrive without changing it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If a service is built as a small monolith, every new feature means editing and redeploying it. The object-oriented answer for programs ought to work for services as well.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Yes: services do not need to be little monoliths. They can be designed with the SOLID principles and given a component structure, so that new components are added without changing the existing ones. In Java, think of a service as a set of abstract classes in one or more jar files; each new feature or extension is another jar with classes that extend those abstract classes.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: each service keeps its own internal design, and new features live in derivative classes within their own components. Bad: Our reading: each service must be designed with this structure from the start.

card.rule: Give every service an internal component structure, so a new feature is a component the service loads, not a change to the service.
card.limits: Jar files are the Java form of the idea. The rule is the component structure that lets a feature be added without editing the old components, not the file type.

concepts.title: Architectural boundaries run through services
concepts.question: Where do architectural boundaries fall: between services or through them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Cross-cutting concerns hit every significant system. A structure that puts the boundaries between services leaves each feature to cross all of them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Architectural boundaries do not fall between services. They run through the services, dividing them into components. To handle cross-cutting concerns, a service needs an internal component architecture that follows the Dependency Rule. The components inside the services, not the services, define the architecture.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the architecture is defined by boundaries within the system and the dependencies that cross them, not by the physical means of communication and execution. Bad: Our reading: a team that stops at drawing service edges has not yet drawn the boundaries that matter.

card.rule: Draw the architectural boundaries inside services, as component boundaries that follow the Dependency Rule.
card.limits: Whether a service gets such boundaries depends on its design. The claim is that the edges of services alone do not decide the architecture.

concepts.title: Tests are components of the system
concepts.question: Are tests part of the system, and how do they depend on the rest?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: There is much confusion about tests: are they part of the system, and do unit, integration and acceptance tests differ? The author leaves that debate aside because for architecture it does not matter.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Tests are part of the system and take part in the architecture like every other part. From an architectural point of view all tests are the same: the tiny tests made by TDD and large acceptance tests are architecturally equivalent. Tests follow the Dependency Rule: they are detailed and concrete and always depend inward on the code under test. Nothing in the system depends on the tests.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: no need to settle the debate over kinds of tests before placing them in the architecture. Our reading: because tests count as system components, their design has architectural cost.

card.rule: Treat every test as an outer component that depends inward on the code it checks, with nothing in the system depending on it.
card.limits: The claim is about architectural equivalence, not about speed, scope or cost. The author does not say all kinds of tests are the same in those ways.

concepts.title: Tests are the most isolated component
concepts.question: In what ways are tests isolated, and does that put them outside the system?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Tests are not needed to run the system and are rarely deployed to production, so it is tempting to treat them as outside the system.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Tests are independently deployable: most of the time they are deployed in test systems, not production. So even where independent deployment is not otherwise needed, the tests are deployed on their own. They are the most isolated system component, not necessary for operation. Their role is to support development, not operation, and they are no less a system component for that.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the tests stay out of production. Bad (our reading): the isolation tempts people to leave tests out of the design, which the next ideas show is costly.

card.rule: Tests are the most isolated component: independently deployed, not needed for operation, and still part of the system.
card.limits: Isolation describes how the tests are used, not whether they matter to the design. Not being needed for operation does not make them less of a component.

concepts.title: The Fragile Tests Problem
concepts.question: What is the Fragile Tests Problem, and what does it do to the system?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Tests are isolated and rarely deployed, so developers often think they fall outside the design of the system.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Tests that are not well integrated into the design tend to be fragile and make the system rigid. The cause is coupling: tests strongly coupled to the system change with it. A trivial change to a common component can break hundreds or thousands of tests, which is the Fragile Tests Problem. A suite that starts at the login screen and navigates the page structure to check business rules breaks whenever the login page or navigation changes. Developers who know a simple change will break a thousand tests resist the change.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bad: the fragile tests make the system rigid. Good: naming the problem points to its cause, coupling to what changes.

card.rule: Tests coupled to volatile parts of the system become fragile and make the system rigid, so the coupling of tests must be designed.
card.limits: The cause is coupling to what changes, not the size of the suite. Thousands of tests break only when they are coupled to the component that changed.

concepts.title: Do not depend on volatile things
concepts.question: Which rule of design tells you how to test business rules?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Tests that go through the GUI break whenever the GUI changes, and the GUI changes often.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author states the first rule of software design: do not depend on volatile things. GUIs are volatile, so test suites that operate the system through the GUI must be fragile. The solution is to make business rules testable without using the GUI.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: tests of business rules do not break when the GUI changes. Bad: Our reading: checking the GUI itself still needs some other kind of test.

card.rule: Do not depend on volatile things: test the business rules without going through the GUI.
card.limits: The rule names what to avoid, not how to avoid it. The next idea gives the author's tool, a separate API for tests.

concepts.title: A testing API with superpowers
concepts.question: What is the testing API for, and what powers does it have?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Tests need to verify the business rules without the GUI, without logging in each time, without slow resources such as databases, and from states that are hard to reach.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Create a specific API that tests use to verify all the business rules. It has superpowers: it can avoid security constraints, bypass expensive resources such as databases, and force the system into particular testable states. It is built on what the user interface uses, with extra powers. Its purpose is to decouple the tests from the application, and not only from the UI: the structure of the tests should be decoupled from the structure of the application.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: tests reach every rule without the GUI and without setup steps. Bad: Our reading: it is one more API to build and keep in step with the application.

card.rule: Give tests their own API, built on what the UI uses, with the powers to skip security, skip expensive resources and force states.
card.limits: The testing API widens what a test can do. It does not replace what the UI uses; it is built on top of it.

concepts.title: Structural coupling between tests and code
concepts.question: Why can one test class per production class hurt both the tests and the code?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A tidy-looking habit is to give each production class a test class and each production method a test method. It mirrors the code, so it feels organised.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author calls structural coupling one of the strongest and most insidious forms of test coupling. A suite with a test class per production class and a set of test methods per production method is deeply coupled to the structure of the application. When a method or class changes, many tests must change, so the tests are fragile and the production code is rigid. The testing API hides the application's structure from the tests, so each side can be refactored without affecting the other.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: production code and tests can evolve separately. Bad: strong structural coupling blocks that separate evolution.

card.rule: Do not mirror the structure of the application in the tests; let the testing API hide that structure so both can change.
card.limits: The warning is about the one-to-one mirroring of classes and methods, not about having unit tests. Tests that target behaviour through the testing API are what the author recommends.

concepts.title: Firmware is defined by dependencies, not storage
concepts.question: What makes code firmware rather than software?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Hardware keeps evolving, so parts become obsolete while the features of a product keep growing. Code tied to a particular piece of hardware will not outlive it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Software can have a long useful life, but firmware becomes obsolete as hardware evolves. The author argues that common definitions of firmware, based on storing code in ROM or flash, are wrong or obsolete. Code is firmware because of what it depends on and how hard it is to change as hardware evolves. He adds that software can be destroyed from within by unmanaged dependencies on firmware and hardware, and he wants less firmware and more software.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the test for any module becomes what it depends on. Bad: code that is polluted with hardware details is denied a long useful life, and the author gives a message processor tied to UART details as an example.

card.rule: Code is firmware because of what it depends on and how hard it is to change as hardware evolves, not because of where it is stored.
card.limits: The author has nothing against firmware or firmware engineers. His claim is that too much code becomes firmware that need not be.

concepts.title: Passing the App-titude test is not enough
concepts.question: What does getting an app to work prove, and what does it leave undone?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Most of the emphasis in embedded work is on getting the code to work, not on structuring it for a long useful life. Some code is also written with an obsession for speed.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Kent Beck describes three activities: first make it work, then make it right, then make it fast. Making it work is what the author calls the App-titude test. Making it right means refactoring so you and others can understand and evolve the code. Making it fast means refactoring for needed performance. Programmers who stop at working code do their products and employers a disservice.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: a working app is necessary, since you are out of business if it does not work. Bad: an app that only passes the test has no clean architecture, and in the author's example nothing but the target can run its tests.

card.rule: Making it work is the first of three steps; passing the App-titude test does not make an architecture clean.
card.limits: Beck's order does not say to skip the first step: working code is necessary. The claim is that it is not sufficient.

concepts.title: The target-hardware bottleneck
concepts.question: What is the target-hardware bottleneck, and what causes it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Embedded engineers face special concerns: limited memory, real-time deadlines, limited IO and sensors. Often the hardware is developed alongside the code, so there may be nowhere to run it, and when the hardware arrives it may have defects.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: One special embedded problem is the target-hardware bottleneck. When code is structured without clean architecture principles, you can often test it only on the target. If the target is the only place for testing, the bottleneck slows you down. The author grants that embedded is special but not so special that the principles of his book do not apply.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bad: development slows when the target is missing or faulty. Good: the principles of the book can remove the bottleneck.

card.rule: If code can be tested only on the target hardware, the target-hardware bottleneck slows development, so structure the code to be tested elsewhere.
card.limits: The special concerns of embedded work are real. The claim is that they do not make the book's principles inapplicable, not that the concerns disappear.

concepts.title: Software and firmware must not be intermingled
concepts.question: What goes wrong when software and firmware are intermingled?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The line between hardware and the rest of the system is a given, but nothing stops knowledge of the hardware from seeping into all the code. The line between software and firmware is fuzzier.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Think of three layers: software, firmware and hardware. The author calls the intermingling of software and firmware an anti-pattern. Code with this anti-pattern resists change, and changes are dangerous and often cause unintended consequences. Even minor changes need full regression tests of the whole system. Your job is to firm up the line between software and firmware.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bad: mixed code is hard to change safely. Good: a firm line limits the damage of a change to one side.

card.rule: Keep a firm line between software and firmware; intermingling resists change and makes even small changes risky.
card.limits: The hardware-to-code line is a given once the hardware is defined. The work is on the fuzzier line between software and firmware.

concepts.title: The hardware abstraction layer
concepts.question: What is the hardware abstraction layer, and whose needs shape its API?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Firmware offers what the hardware can do, such as storing bytes in flash. The software above it needs something else, such as storing a name with a value.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The boundary between software and firmware is the hardware abstraction layer (HAL). The idea is not new: PCs have had it since before Windows. The HAL exists for the software above it, so its API is tailored to that software's needs. The software does not care whether name and value pairs go to flash, a disk, the cloud or core memory. The HAL does not reveal how it provides its service.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the flash is a detail hidden from the software, and a successful HAL gives a seam where a substitute can be put in for off-target testing. Bad: Our reading: the software now relies on the HAL's API, so that API needs careful design.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The first call mirrors the hardware; the second says what the product needs.

card.rule: Shape the HAL's API to the services the software needs, and hide how the hardware provides them.
card.limits: A HAL that only mirrors the hardware, with bytes and bit numbers, still leaks hardware detail. Its worth comes from being written from the software's point of view.

concepts.title: The processor is a detail
concepts.question: How do you keep vendor C extensions from tying code to one processor?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Vendor toolchains add keywords, headers and what look like global variables to reach registers, IO ports and timers. That code looks like C but is not, and it will not compile for another processor or maybe another compiler.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Limit which files may know about the C extensions. Do not use the vendor header acmetypes.h directly: use the standard stdint.h, and if the target compiler lacks it, write one for target builds that wraps the vendor header. Confine direct use of device registers to a few places in the firmware. A processor abstraction layer (PAL) can isolate these low-level functions.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the rest of the code stays portable. Bad: anything that knows about the registers becomes firmware and is bound to the silicon.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: Only the target-build stdint.h knows the vendor header.

card.rule: Let only a few firmware files know the vendor's C extensions and headers, and use standard types everywhere else.
card.limits: Some firmware has to use the extensions: that is why the chip was chosen. The rule is to limit which files know them, not to ban them.

concepts.title: The operating system is a detail
concepts.question: Why treat the operating system as a detail, and what does an OSAL give?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In bare-metal systems a HAL may be enough. Systems that use a real-time operating system, or an embedded Linux or Windows, add another thing for the code to become addicted to.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Treat the operating system as a detail and protect against OS dependencies. The OS is a layer between software and firmware. Using it directly is risky: the RTOS supplier may be bought and raise royalties or lower quality, or your needs may outgrow it. A clean embedded architecture isolates software from the OS through an operating system abstraction layer (OSAL). Sometimes it is as simple as changing the name of a function; sometimes it wraps several functions.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: moving to another RTOS means writing a new OSAL to a defined interface, not modifying complex existing code. Bad: the layer can look like code bloat.

card.rule: Isolate the software from the operating system through an OSAL, so a change of OS means writing a new OSAL.
card.limits: A HAL alone may be enough in bare-metal systems. The OSAL is needed when an operating system sits between the software and the firmware.

concepts.title: Program to interfaces; keep headers lean
concepts.question: What belongs in a header file that serves as an interface?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A layered design depends on modules that interact through interfaces. In C, the header file is the natural place for an interface, and it is easy to clutter.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: When modules interact through an interface, one service provider can be substituted for another. A rule of thumb is to use header files as interface definitions. Limit their contents to function declarations and the constants and struct names the functions need. Leave data structures, constants and typedefs that only the implementation needs out of the header, because they lead to unwanted dependencies. Limit the visibility of implementation details, and expect them to change.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: fewer places know the details, so fewer places have to be tracked down when they change. Bad: Our reading: the implementation needs its own private header or source file for what the interface leaves out.

blocks.label: Before and after
blocks.text: The header keeps only what callers need.

card.rule: Use a header as an interface, and put in it only the function declarations and the constants and struct names those functions need.
card.limits: A header can hold a constant or struct that callers need to use the functions. The rule keeps out what only the implementation needs.

concepts.title: Replace repeated conditional compilation
concepts.question: How can a HAL remove repeated conditional compilation for different targets?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Embedded C and C++ programs often use conditional compilation to switch code on or off for different targets or operating systems. The same test can end up repeated thousands of times.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: The author tells of a telecom application that mentioned #ifdef BOARD_V2 thousands of times. Repeating it violates the Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY) principle.
