With a HAL, the hardware type becomes a detail hidden under the HAL, which presents interfaces. Instead of conditional compilation, the software can be connected to the hardware through those interfaces.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Good: the software no longer carries the hardware type. Bad: Our reading: the HAL and its interfaces must exist first.

card.rule: Hide the hardware type under a HAL, and connect the software to the hardware through its interfaces instead of repeating target conditionals.
card.limits: The claim is about repetition of the hardware-type test. It presupposes that the HAL interfaces exist.

concepts.title: The database is a detail; the data model is not
concepts.question: Why does the author call the database a detail while calling the data model architecturally significant?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A system must store its data somewhere, and the storage product is easy to treat as the foundation of the design. Yet the database is a piece of software, a utility that gives access to the data.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Tell two things apart: the data model, the structure you give to data inside the application, and the database, the utility that stores and retrieves it. The model belongs to the architecture. The utility is a low-level mechanism, a detail.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The author compares the database to a doorknob in the architecture of a house. A good architect does not let low-level mechanisms pollute the system architecture. He expects the claim to provoke, and calls it fighting words.

card.rule: Give the structure of the data a place in the architecture, and keep the database product out of it.
card.limits: The claim is about where the database sits in the design, not about whether databases work well.

concepts.title: Keep rows and tables out of the use cases
concepts.question: Why does the author call it an architectural error to pass database rows and tables around as objects?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Many data access frameworks let rows and tables travel through the system as objects, which is convenient. The use cases of the application should neither know nor care about rows within tables.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Restrict knowledge of the tabular structure of the data to the lowest-level utility functions in the outer circles of the architecture. Everything nearer the core handles data in the application's own form.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Letting rows and tables travel couples the use cases, the business rules and in some cases even the UI to the relational structure of the data. The author calls this an architectural error.

card.rule: Only the lowest-level utility functions in the outer circles may know that data is arranged in rows and tables.
card.limits: The rule hides the relational structure from the inner circles; it does not ask the outer utility code to avoid tables.

concepts.section: Why Are Database Systems So Prevalent?
concepts.title: Disks are slow, so data access systems arose
concepts.question: In the author's account, why did databases come to dominate, and how do file systems differ from them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A disk read means moving the head to the right track, waiting for the sector to rotate under it and reading the whole sector, often 4K, into RAM. That takes milliseconds, a million times the cycle time of most processors. Disks are slow.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: To cope with the delay, programmers need indexes, caches, optimised queries and a regular way of representing data. This became a data access and management system, of two kinds. File systems are document based. Database systems are content based.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: File systems store and retrieve whole documents by name and help little with searching their content. Databases find records by their content and are poor at storing opaque documents. Both arrange data on disk for efficient access and bring the data they need into RAM.

card.rule: Databases and file systems exist to hide the slowness of disks: files hold documents by name, databases find records by content.
card.limits: This explains why databases became prevalent, not that they are essential to the architecture; the author goes on to call them a detail.

concepts.section: What If There Were No Disk?
concepts.title: With no disk, data would not be tables
concepts.question: If all disks were replaced by RAM, how would programmers organise data, and what does that say about databases?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Disks are a dying breed, being replaced by RAM, just as tape drives, floppy drives and CDs went before them. Programmers have known no other form of long-term storage for decades, which makes tables and files feel natural.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Ask how you would organise data if it all lived in RAM. You would use linked lists, trees, hash tables, stacks and queues, reached by pointers or references, because that is what programmers do. You already do this today.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Programmers would not leave the data as files or tables. The author concludes that the form data takes on the disk surface is not an architectural concern.

card.rule: Programmers reorganise data into their own structures in RAM, so the form it takes on disk is not what the design is about.
card.limits: The prediction that disks are fading is the author's, and a reader may weigh it. The conclusion concerns architecture, not any one storage medium.

concepts.title: The database is a bucket of bits
concepts.question: In what sense is the database only a mechanism between the disk and RAM, and what follows for the architect?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Data must survive power-down, so it is kept on disk. Treating the stored form as the design lets a storage choice decide the shape of the system.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: See the database as a mechanism that moves data back and forth between the surface of the disk and RAM, a big bucket of bits for long-term storage. Design for the data as the program uses it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Architecturally we should not care about the form data takes on a rotating magnetic disk. The author goes further: we should not acknowledge that the disk exists at all.

card.rule: The database only moves bits between disk and RAM, so the architecture should not acknowledge the disk.
card.limits: The author's wording is strong and applies to the architecture. Code at the outer edge must of course deal with the disk and the database.

concepts.title: Storage performance is encapsulated, not architectural
concepts.question: Is performance an architectural concern for data storage, and where does the author place it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Data has to get into and out of the data store quickly, and it is tempting to let speed concerns shape the whole design. That need is real, and it is a low-level concern.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Address the speed of data storage with low-level data access mechanisms, encapsulated and kept separate from the business rules.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: For data storage the concern can be entirely encapsulated and separated from the business rules. The author says it has nothing whatsoever to do with the overall architecture of the system.

card.rule: Handle the speed of data storage with low-level access mechanisms, apart from the business rules.
card.limits: The claim covers data storage. It does not say that speed is unimportant to the product.

concepts.title: A real requirement can lack an engineering reason
concepts.question: Why does the author say he was wrong to keep the relational database out of his product, though right on engineering?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the late 1980s the author's team built a network management system for T1 lines and kept its data in random access files, as trees and linked lists, because the data had few content-based relationships. A marketing manager and a hardware engineer pushed for a relational database.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Separate the engineering question from the market one. On engineering the author was right to resist putting an RDBMS into the architectural core. Yet customers expected a relational database, which had become a check-box item on purchasers' lists, with no engineering rationale.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The need was irrational, external and baseless, but no less real. The RDBMS went into the system, the hardware engineer was promoted over the author to software manager, and the author says he was wrong, though not for engineering reasons.

card.rule: A customer expectation is a real requirement even if it has no engineering rationale.
card.limits: Our reading: this is one story of one product; it shows that expectations are real, not that they decide where a detail sits in the architecture.

concepts.title: Bolt the detail on the side with a narrow channel
concepts.question: What does the author say he should have done in the T1 story to satisfy customers and keep the core clean?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Customers expect a relational database. The core is better served by random access files, trees and linked lists. Both pulls are real, and giving in fully to either costs something.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Bolt an RDBMS on the side of the system. Provide a narrow and safe data access channel to it, and keep the random access files in the core of the system.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The customers get the relational database they expect, and the core stays as designed. The author says this is what he should have done; instead he quit and became a consultant.

card.rule: Meet an outside demand for a detail by attaching it at the side through a narrow channel, not by moving it into the core.
card.limits: Our reading: the author gives this as hindsight about one product, and describes the channel only as narrow and safe.

concepts.title: The web is one swing of a long pendulum
concepts.question: Why does the author say the web changed nothing, or at least should not have?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the 1990s the web seemed to change everything, and old client-server designs looked out of date. But the industry has swung since the 1960s between putting computing power in central servers and putting it out at the terminals.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: See the web as one swing of this pendulum. First the browsers were stupid and the power sat in server farms; then applets moved into browsers; dynamic content moved back to servers; Ajax and JavaScript pushed processing back to browsers; Node now pulls JavaScript onto the server.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: We cannot seem to decide where we want the computer power, and the swings will continue. As architects we look at the long term, and treat the swings as short-term issues to push away from the central core of the business rules.

card.rule: Treat the web as one swing in a long pendulum, and keep such swings away from the business rules.
card.limits: Our reading: the author's history is a sketch. It supports keeping the core separate, not the claim that web work is easy.

concepts.title: Decouple business rules from the UI before marketing asks
concepts.question: What should the architect at company Q have done, before marketing demanded a web-like interface?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Marketing can order a sudden change of the UI. Company Q changed its desktop finance GUI to look and behave like a browser, users disliked it, and Q gradually removed the feel. Company A's phone upgrade changed the look and feel of every app.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Decouple the business rules from the UI beforehand, so that a UI change leaves the rules alone. Isolate the two from each other before anyone asks.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The author does not know whether Q's architects had done this, and does not know what difficulties A's change caused. He would have lobbied hard for isolation, because you never know what marketing will do next.

card.rule: Isolate the business rules from the GUI before a marketing change forces the question.
card.limits: Q and A are cautionary stories; the author does not claim to know how their architects had designed the systems.

concepts.title: The web is a GUI, and a GUI is an IO device
concepts.question: How does the author argue that the web is a detail, and where does he say device independence stops?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: In the 1960s we learned the value of writing applications that are device independent. The web is full of JavaScript validation and drag-and-drop calls, so it is easy to argue that such independence is impractical for a GUI.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Argue in three steps: the GUI is a detail, the web is a GUI, so the web is a detail. Treat the web as an IO device and put it behind a boundary that keeps it separate from the core business logic.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: To some extent the objection is true. The exchange between the application and the GUI is chatty in ways specific to the kind of GUI, so abstracting it the way UNIX abstracts devices seems unlikely to be possible.

card.rule: The GUI is a detail, the web is a GUI, so keep the web behind a boundary like an IO device.
card.limits: The chatty exchange between a particular GUI and the application cannot be abstracted like a device, so the boundary has to be drawn elsewhere.

concepts.title: Pass input and output data structures between UI and use case
concepts.question: Which boundary between UI and application can be abstracted, and how do use cases operate the UI device-independently?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The chatty exchange between a particular GUI and the application cannot be abstracted. Yet the business logic is a suite of use cases, each performing some function on behalf of a user.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Describe each use case by its input data, the processing performed and its output data. Put the input and the output into data structures, and use them as the input values and output values of the process that executes the use case.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The use case then operates the IO device of the UI in a device-independent manner. The author says this abstraction is not easy and will probably take several iterations, but it is possible, and often necessary.

card.rule: Give each use case plain data structures for its input and output, so it does not know which UI it serves.
card.limits: The author warns the abstraction is not easy and will likely need several iterations to get right.

concepts.title: A framework solves its author's problems
concepts.question: Why do framework authors, however kind, not have your best interests at heart?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Frameworks have become popular and many are free, powerful and useful. Most authors offer them free, wanting to help the community, which is laudable.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Remember whom the framework was written for. The author knows his own problems and those of coworkers and friends, and writes the framework to solve those, not yours. The author does not know you or your problems.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Your problems probably overlap with the author's quite a bit; if they did not, frameworks would not be popular. To the extent that they overlap, a framework can be very useful indeed.

card.rule: A framework solves its author's problems, so use it where yours overlap.
card.limits: The author calls frameworks generally a good thing; the warning is about trust, not about avoiding them.

concepts.title: The commitment to a framework runs one way
concepts.question: Why does the author call your relationship with a framework author asymmetric?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Framework documentation advises you to wrap your architecture around the framework: derive from its base classes and import its facilities into your business objects, coupling your application to the framework as tightly as possible.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Look at who carries the risk. You make a huge commitment to the framework, while the author makes no commitment to you. For the author, coupling to his own framework is no risk, because he has absolute control over it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The author wants you coupled because it is then very hard for you to break away. The author calls it a one-directional marriage: you take on all the risk and burden and the framework author takes on nothing.

card.rule: Coupling your code to a framework is a one-way commitment: the risk is all yours.
card.limits: The warning is about commitment and control. The author has already said that the motives of framework authors are laudable.

concepts.title: The risks of letting a framework into the core
concepts.question: What risks does the author list for coupling business objects to a framework?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: A framework may help with early features of your application, which makes it attractive to inherit its code into your business objects, including your Entities.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Weigh the risks. The framework's own architecture is often not clean: frameworks tend to violate the Dependency Rule, which says source dependencies point inward toward higher-level policy. As the product matures it may outgrow the framework. A new and better framework may come along that you wish you could switch to.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Once a framework is in the innermost circle it does not come out. The author compares this to a wedding ring on your finger, and says that the framework will fight you more and more as time passes.

card.rule: Inheriting a framework into your Entities invites a lasting cost: it will not come out when the product outgrows it.
card.limits: The risks are the author's own list ('just a few'). He does not claim every framework will cause all of them.

concepts.title: Do not marry the framework: derive proxies
concepts.question: What does the author tell you to do instead of coupling core code to a framework?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Frameworks are useful, but their authors want your business objects derived from their base classes, and that puts the framework into your innermost circle.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use the framework, but do not couple to it. Keep it at arm's length as a detail in one of the outer circles. If it wants your business objects to derive from its base classes, say no and derive proxies instead, kept in components that plug in to your business rules and follow the Dependency Rule.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Your business objects do not know about the framework. You may use Spring to wire dependencies, but you should not sprinkle autowiring annotations throughout your business objects. Spring is injected into your Main component.

card.rule: Do not marry the framework: keep it in the outer circles and derive proxies, not business objects.
card.limits: Some frameworks cannot be avoided, as the next idea shows. The advice is about keeping them out of the core.

concepts.title: Marry a framework only by decision
concepts.question: When must you marry a framework, and how should that decision be made?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Some frameworks cannot be avoided. You will probably end up married to some of them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Treat marrying a framework as a decision, not a drift. You will be stuck with it for the rest of the life cycle of the application, for better or for worse. Try not to marry right away: date it for a while, and keep it behind an architectural boundary as long as possible.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The author says this is not a commitment to enter into lightly. Perhaps you can get the milk without buying the cow.

card.rule: Marrying a framework is acceptable only as a deliberate decision, taken as late as possible.
card.limits: The advice to keep a framework behind a boundary is given 'if at all possible'; the author does not say it always is.

concepts.title: Actors are the sources of change
concepts.question: Who are the actors of the video-sales system, and why does the author partition the system by them?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The site sells videos to individuals and businesses. Individuals usually view and buy; businesses often have people who buy videos that others will watch. Authors supply the video files and descriptions, and administrators manage series and prices.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: First identify the actors and use cases. By the Single Responsibility Principle, the four main actors are the four primary sources of change. Partition the system so that a change for one actor does not affect any other.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Each new feature or change serves one actor, so each actor's code can change without touching the others.

card.rule: Treat each actor as a source of change, and partition so that a change for one actor does not reach another.
card.limits: Our reading: the actors are four in this case study. A fuller analysis could find more.

concepts.title: Unify similar use cases with an abstract one
concepts.question: What is an abstract use case, and why does the author draw one for the catalog?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Two use cases, View Catalog as Viewer and View Catalog as Purchaser, are very similar. Drawing them separately would hide how alike they are.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Recognise the similarity early and unify it in an abstract use case, which sets a general policy that another use case flesh out. Both concrete use cases inherit from the abstract View Catalog.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The abstraction records the shared policy once. The author drew it so that the similarity is unified early in the analysis.

card.rule: When two use cases are alike, unify the likeness in an abstract use case that sets general policy.
card.limits: Our reading: an abstraction is worth drawing only when the likeness is strong enough to unify.

concepts.title: Partition views, presenters, interactors and controllers by actor
concepts.question: How does the preliminary component architecture divide the code, and what is each component?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: With actors and use cases known, the author can draw a preliminary component architecture. It must keep each actor's changes apart from the others.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use the usual partitioning into views, presenters, interactors and controllers, and break each category up by its actor. The double lines in the drawing are architectural boundaries. Each component is a potential jar or dll file holding the views, presenters, interactors and controllers allocated to it.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: A change for one actor lands in that actor's components. The partition is only preliminary, and the author describes how some parts are likely to be coded.

card.rule: Split views, presenters, interactors and controllers by actor; each group is a potential deployable component.
card.limits: The drawing is a preliminary architecture, not a final deployment plan.

concepts.title: Keep deployment groupings open
concepts.question: How can the components be grouped into deliverables, and why does the author keep the options open?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The author would not necessarily deliver every component as its own jar or dll. Yet he wants to build independent deliverables, and the system will change over time.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Break the compile and build environment up by component, and reserve the right to combine the deliverables into fewer. One grouping gives five jar files: views, presenters, interactors, controllers and utilities. The components most likely to change can be deployed independently of each other.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Keeping the options open lets you adapt the way you deploy as the system changes over time.

card.rule: Build components separately but decide later how many deliverables to ship.
card.limits: Fewer files cost the ability to deploy parts independently; the source structure is unchanged by the choice.

concepts.title: Two dimensions of separation: actors and the Dependency Rule
concepts.question: Which two dimensions of separation does the case-study architecture use, and which way do its dependencies point?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Control flows from controllers, which receive the input, to interactors, which process it into a result, to presenters, which format it, and finally to views, which display it. Yet most arrows in the figure point the other way.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Follow the Dependency Rule: all dependencies cross boundaries in one direction, toward components containing higher-level policy. Using relationships, drawn with open arrows, point with the flow of control. Inheritance relationships, drawn with closed arrows, point against it. This applies the Open-Closed Principle so that changes to low-level details do not ripple up to high-level policy.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The architecture has two dimensions of separation: actors, by the Single Responsibility Principle, and the Dependency Rule. The goal of both is to separate components that change for different reasons and at different rates.

card.rule: Separate by actor and by the Dependency Rule, so that components that change for different reasons and rates stay apart.
card.limits: Our reading: the figure is only described in words here, so the individual arrows must be taken from the author's description.

concepts.title: Package by layer groups code by technical function
concepts.question: How does package by layer organise code, and what are its limits?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Many books, tutorials and courses start with a layered design, and Martin Fowler calls it a good way to get started. It gets something running quickly without much complexity.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Slice the code horizontally by what it does technically: web code, business logic and persistence. In a strict layered architecture each layer depends only on the next adjacent lower layer. In Java a layer is typically a package, so all dependencies between packages point downward. The orders example has a controller, a service interface and implementation, and a repository interface and implementation.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Once the software grows, three large buckets of code are not enough and further modularising is needed. The chapter's author adds that the structure says nothing about the business domain, and that there is another huge problem, which comes later.

card.rule: Package by layer sorts code by technical function: quick to start, but silent about the domain.
card.limits: The chapter's author calls it the simplest approach and says it suits a start, not a large system.

concepts.title: Package by feature slices vertically by concept
concepts.question: How does package by feature differ from package by layer, and what does it gain?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Teams that find problems with horizontal layering often switch to vertical layering. They want the top-level organisation to say what the system is about.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Slice the code vertically by related features, domain concepts or aggregate roots. In typical implementations all the types go into a single Java package named for the concept. The interfaces and classes are the same as before, so it is a simple refactoring from package by layer.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The top level now says that the code base has to do with orders, not with the web, services and repositories. It is also potentially easier to find all the code to change when a use case such as view orders changes. The chapter's author still thinks both styles are suboptimal.

card.rule: Package by feature puts all the types of one concept in one package, so the packages name the domain.
card.limits: According to the chapter's author, both package by layer and package by feature are suboptimal.

concepts.title: The outside depends on the inside
concepts.question: What is the major rule of ports and adapters, and how does the orders example follow it?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Approaches such as ports and adapters, hexagonal architecture and boundaries-controllers-entities all aim to keep business and domain code independent of technical details such as frameworks and databases.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Compose the code base of an inside, the domain, and an outside, the infrastructure: UIs, databases and third-party integrations. The major rule is that the outside depends on the inside, never the other way around. In the view orders example the domain package is the inside, the other packages are the outside, and dependencies flow toward the inside.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: The domain stays free of technical detail. The diagram in the chapter is a simplified version: it omits interactors and the objects that marshal data across the dependency boundaries.

card.rule: In ports and adapters, the outside depends on the inside and never the reverse.
card.limits: The chapter's author calls his diagram simplified; a full version has interactors and marshalling objects.

concepts.title: A downward arrow does not stop a layer being skipped
concepts.question: How can a layered design be bypassed even when every arrow points downward, and why is enforcement hard?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Strict layering gives a clean acyclic dependency graph, and rules are meant to keep it so. But one can cheat by adding undesirable dependencies and still keep a clean, acyclic graph. Between packages, the interfaces have to be public so that other packages can see them.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A newcomer adds a new orders use case to the existing controller and injects the repository implementation into it. The arrows still point downward, but the controller now bypasses the service. This is a relaxed layered architecture, where layers may skip their neighbours. A guideline such as web controllers should not access repositories directly is needed.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Bypassing the business logic is often undesirable, for example when that logic ensures authorised access to individual records. Discipline and code reviews are fallible, as are build-time static analysis tools, and both give a longer feedback loop than is wanted. Left unchecked, the code base can become a big ball of mud.

card.rule: Downward arrows are not enough: without enforcement a layer can skip the one beneath it.
card.limits: Static analysis tools are crude but can do the trick. The chapter's author's point is that they are fallible, not useless.

concepts.title: Package by component bundles logic and persistence behind one interface
concepts.question: What is package by component, and how does it differ from the earlier styles?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The chapter's author wants the compiler, not discipline or after-the-fact tools, to enforce the architecture if at all possible. A layered design with a package per layer does not allow it.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Bundle all the responsibilities of one coarse-grained component into a single Java package: business logic and persistence together, with the UI kept separate, as ports and adapters treat the web as another delivery mechanism. His definition: a component is a grouping of related functionality behind a nice clean interface, inside an execution environment.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: To work with orders there is one place to go, the orders component. Inside it, business logic is still separate from persistence, but that is an implementation detail consumers need not know. It resembles a separate orders service in a micro-services or service-oriented design, but the decoupling mode differs.

card.rule: Bundle business logic and persistence behind one clean interface in a single package, with the UI kept apart.
card.limits: This is the chapter's author's own view, and his definition of a component differs from the book's earlier unit-of-deployment definition.

concepts.section: The Devil Is in the Implementation Details
concepts.title: Overusing public hides the architecture
concepts.question: How can overuse of the public modifier undo an architectural style?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The four approaches look like different architectural styles, but that view unravels fast if the implementation details are wrong. Developers use the public keyword by instinct, and it is in their muscle memory.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Notice what making every type public does: it means you are not using the language's facilities for encapsulation. Nothing then stops someone writing code that instantiates a concrete implementation class directly, violating the intended style.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: This habit appears whatever style the code base is aiming at: horizontal layers, vertical layers, ports and adapters or something else. The example is Java, but the chapter's author says the principles apply to other languages too.

card.rule: Do not mark every type public: access modifiers are what make a chosen style real.
card.limits: The example is Java, whose modifiers the author calls imperfect; the point is the use of whatever encapsulation the language offers.

concepts.title: Packages organise only; modifiers encapsulate
concepts.question: When all types are public, what are packages reduced to, and how do modifiers restore the styles?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: If every type is public, packages are only an organisation mechanism, like folders, not a means of encapsulation. Public types can be used from anywhere, so the packages can be ignored.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Use packages for encapsulation by making every type package protected unless something outside needs it. In package by layer the service and repository interfaces must be public and their implementations can be package protected. In ports and adapters the same holds for the interfaces. In package by component only the component interface is public.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: When all types are public, the four styles have identical arrows: conceptually different but syntactically the same, four ways to describe a traditional horizontal layered architecture. With package by component, code outside the package cannot use the repository directly, so the compiler enforces the principle. The fewer public types, the fewer potential dependencies.

card.rule: Packages encapsulate only when types are made package protected, otherwise the four styles are the same code.
card.limits: Java's access modifiers are not perfect: they cannot restrict access by package and subpackage, and reflection can cheat.

concepts.title: Module systems and source trees as other decoupling modes
concepts.question: Beyond access modifiers, how else can dependencies be decoupled, and what is the Périphérique trade-off?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: Access modifiers are not the only way to decouple source dependencies, but each way has costs.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: A module system such as OSGi or the Java 9 module system distinguishes public types from published types: a module can mark all its types public and publish only a few. Or split the code into source trees built as separate modules in Maven, Gradle or MSBuild: domain, web and persistence, where web and persistence depend at compile time on the domain, which knows nothing of them.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Repeating this for every component is idealistic, because of real performance, complexity and maintenance issues. A simpler form uses two trees, domain and infrastructure, but then infrastructure code in one area, such as a web controller, can call infrastructure in another, such as a repository, without going through the domain, especially if modifiers are forgotten.

card.rule: Compile-time separation of source trees and module systems can decouple more than modifiers, at a cost in complexity.
card.limits: The author calls the full split an idealistic solution; weigh the real costs for your team.

concepts.title: Design intentions survive only in the implementation
concepts.question: What does the closing chapter say a design needs beyond the principles in the rest of the book?

blocks.label: Forces
blocks.text: The best design intentions can be destroyed in a flash if the intricacies of the implementation strategy are ignored.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Think about how to map the desired design on to code structures, how to organise that code, and which decoupling modes to apply at run time and compile time. Use the compiler to help enforce the chosen architectural style.

blocks.label: Consequences
blocks.text: Leave options open where applicable but be pragmatic, taking into account the size of the team, their skill level and the complexity of the solution, with the time and budget available. The devil is in the implementation details.

card.rule: A design is kept only if you map it onto code structures and let the compiler help enforce it.
card.limits: The advice is pragmatic: how much structure to build depends on the team, the problem and the budget.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: One goal behind every chapter
concepts.question: What single measure does the book apply to every design choice, from a function to a boundary?

paragraphs: Every part of the book answers to one goal: keep the effort needed to build and maintain a system as small as possible over its whole life. A design is judged by what it does to the cost of the next change, not by how quickly the first release shipped.

Software has two values. Behavior is what the system does today. Structure is how easily that behavior can be changed. The authors argue that structure is the greater value: a system that works but cannot be changed becomes useless when requirements move, while one that is easy to change can be made to work.
The paradigms, the SOLID principles, the component rules and the boundary rules are then one effort at different scales: each is a way to keep structure soft.
card.rule: Judge any design choice by what it does to the cost of future changes, since ease of change is the second and greater value of software.
card.limits: Our reading: this is the authors' position, argued from extreme cases rather than measured. It does not make behavior unimportant: the system must still work, and the structure exists to serve that behavior over time.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: One move at every scale: point at the policy
concepts.question: What single rule about the direction of source dependencies recurs from classes up to whole architectures?

paragraphs: One move recurs at every scale of the book: arrange source dependencies so that they point toward the code you most want to protect, the higher-level policy. Between two classes, an interface does it. The code that changes more should depend on the code you want to protect.

Between components, each should depend on components more stable than itself, where stable means hard to change because many others depend on it. Between the circles of the Clean Architecture, source dependencies point only inward, so nothing in an inner circle may name anything declared in an outer one.
Control may still flow the other way. A use case calls a presenter at run time, yet the use case owns an interface that the presenter implements, so the source dependency opposes the flow of control.
card.rule: Make the code that changes more depend on the code you want to protect, and use an interface owned by the protected side when control must flow the other way.
card.limits: Some dependencies on concrete, volatile code cannot be removed. The book says to gather them in a few small components, such as main, and keep them out of the rest of the system.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Group by reason to change at three scales
concepts.question: How does the single-responsibility idea reappear for components and for whole architectures?

paragraphs: The Single Responsibility Principle says to gather code that answers to one actor and separate code that answers to different actors. The book restates it twice. For components it becomes the Common Closure Principle: classes that change for the same reasons and at the same times belong in one component.

For architecture it becomes the axis of change: a boundary belongs wherever the parts on its two sides change at different rates and for different reasons. At each scale the test is the same: who asks for this change, and what else must move with it?
This is why look-alike code is not always duplication. If two copies change for different reasons, merging them links the groups that use them, so a change for one can break the other.
card.rule: Keep together what changes for the same reason and apart what changes for different reasons, whether the unit is a class, a component or a boundary.
card.limits: Our reading: the Common Closure Principle is one of three cohesion forces. The reuse principles pull components the other way, and the best balance shifts as a project matures.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Policy first, details later
concepts.question: Which parts of a system does the book call details, and why can decisions about them wait?

paragraphs: The book splits a system into policy, the business rules that carry its value, and details, which only let people, machines and programmers reach that policy. Its list of details is longer than many expect: IO devices, the database, the web, frameworks, the operating system and the processor. None of them changes what the rules do.

Because the policy does not depend on any detail, choosing among them can wait, and a later choice is better informed. You can even try several databases or delivery mechanisms against the same working rules before committing.
A detail is not the same as the data model. The structure of the data has a place in the architecture; the product that moves bits on and off a disk does not.
card.rule: Treat the database, the web, frameworks and the operating system as details behind boundaries, and delay choosing them for as long as the policy allows.
card.limits: Delay is a default, not a ban. Some commitments are hard to avoid, such as a language's standard library, and the book accepts them when they are made as deliberate decisions.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Boundaries cost money: build where it pays
concepts.question: How does the book decide which boundaries to build fully, build partly or ignore?

paragraphs: A full boundary is costly: interfaces on both sides, input and output data structures, and the dependency management to compile and deploy each side alone. An ignored boundary is costly too, because adding one late is expensive. The book offers judgement, not a formula: weigh the cost of building against the cost of ignoring, and review the decision as the system evolves.

Between nothing and everything lie partial boundaries. One, called skip the last step, keeps every interface and data structure of a full boundary but deploys both sides as one component. A strategy interface isolates clients in one direction only. A facade lists the services in one class but leaves clients depending on all of them. Each trades protection for lower cost.

Services do not remove the need for this judgement. A service matters architecturally only when it sits on a boundary that separates high-level policy from low-level detail and follows the Dependency Rule.
card.rule: Build a boundary at the point where building it becomes cheaper than ignoring it, hold places for likely ones with partial forms, and review the decision often.
card.limits: No formula decides it: the authors say the architect must guess the future intelligently and will sometimes guess wrong. They also say that over-engineering is often worse than under-engineering.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Triage a change request
concepts.question: In what order should you ask the book's questions when a real change request arrives?

paragraphs: Our reading: the book gives no checklist for a change request, but its parts suggest an order of questions. First ask who is asking, because the actor tells you which module or component should absorb the change. Second ask what level the change belongs to: a business rule, a use case, or a detail such as a screen, a database or a framework.

Third, check the direction of dependencies. A change to a detail should not force edits in the rules, and nothing in an inner circle should name something from an outer one. Fourth, only if friction keeps appearing, ask whether a boundary is now cheaper to build than to ignore.

If the change reaches code that serves another actor, or reaches inward through a dependency, restructure before you add the feature. When you do draw lines, the book names the GUI, the database and the business rules as the first to separate.
card.rule: On a change request, ask who is asking, what level the change belongs to and which way dependencies run, and consider a new boundary only when friction appears.
card.limits: This order is our reading, not the authors' procedure. For a brand-new system the book starts instead from the use cases and keeps tool decisions open.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Testability as evidence of sound structure
concepts.question: Why does the book treat testability as a sign that a design is sound?

paragraphs: Tests cannot prove a program correct; they can only fail to find a bug. The authors take this from science, where a theory is trusted because it survives every attempt to disprove it. So they prize structure that yields small units a test can try to falsify, from a single function up to a component or a service.

That is why testing keeps returning in the later chapters. The Humble Object pattern splits behavior that is hard to test from behavior that is easy to test. Business rules kept free of the web, the database and frameworks can be tested alone. Tests are themselves the most isolated component: they depend inward on the code, and nothing depends on them.
The reverse also holds. Tests that drive the system through a volatile part, such as the GUI, break whenever that part changes, and a system whose changes break a thousand tests becomes rigid.
card.rule: Shape the system so that its rules can be tested alone, with tests as outermost components that depend on the code and are not depended on.
card.limits: A passing suite shows only that no test found a bug, so the book calls code correct enough for its purposes, not proven correct.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: What a finished reading leaves you able to do
concepts.question: After reading the whole book, what should you be able to do and argue in your own team?

paragraphs: Our wording of the book's message: architecture exists to keep a system cheap to change, and it does so by separating policy from details with boundaries and by pointing source dependencies toward the policy. A finished reading leaves you able to say this in a sentence and to apply its tests to code you have never seen.

It also leaves a duty. Business managers are not equipped to judge architecture, so developers must assert its importance over the urgency of features. Urgent but unimportant features should not push aside the important structure.

Finally, hold the tools lightly. Treat a framework as a tool, used with skepticism. Treat the stability and distance metrics as measurements against a standard the author chose. And map design intentions onto code structures, because intentions alone do not survive the implementation.
card.rule: After a full reading you should be able to state the book's aim in a sentence, apply its tests to unfamiliar code and argue for architecture against feature pressure.
card.limits: Our reading: the book is one author's view, and its metric thresholds come from his experience. Check each rule against your own system and note where it does not fit.

questions.q: A colleague says architecture means the high-level structure and design means the low-level detail. What would the author of this unit say about that split?
options: Both words name one continuum of decisions, with no clear dividing line
It is right: architects decide the shape and designers fill in the details
Architecture is a subset of design that only senior staff may touch
Design comes first and architecture is added once the details are fixed
optionExplain: Right: he says there is no difference at all and the decisions form one continuum.
This is the common usage, which feels natural, but the author calls it nonsensical.
It sounds like a way to keep both words, but the author does not rank one under the other or reserve it for seniors.
It sounds like a sensible order of work, but he sees no first and second stage.
questions.explain: The author asserts there is no difference between the two. The card next shows how he argues for it.
questions.rule: Treat high-level structure and low-level detail as one continuous design, not as two separate jobs.

questions.q: The author says low-level details and high-level structure form one continuous ____ that defines the shape of the system.
questions.explain: He calls them a continuous fabric: you cannot have one without the other.
questions.rule: High-level structure and low-level detail are one whole.

questions.q: A team lists decisions it has made. Which of them count as part of the system's design in the author's sense? Select all that apply.
options: Splitting the system into a web part and a data part
Choosing how a single function validates its input
Only the decisions made by the most senior engineer
Only the decisions above the level of individual classes
optionExplain: Right: it is a high-level decision and part of the design.
Right: low-level details belong to the same whole, as the outlets and switches belong to the house plans.
Who decides does not change what the decision is part of; the author's claim is about levels, not seniority.
This restates the usual split between architecture and design that the author rejects.
questions.explain: The author counts the high-level and the low-level decisions as parts of one design, as the house plans hold both layout and switches.
questions.rule: Every level of decision belongs to the same design.

questions.q: A reader says: 'So the author thinks a house, and a program, have no architecture at all.' What is wrong with this reading?
options: Nothing is wrong: the author says the word architecture should be dropped from software altogether
He says only large programs have an architecture, while a house has only a design and no architecture
The house has an architecture of shape and layout; he denies only that it is separate from the details
He says the architecture is nothing but the details, so the high-level shape of a building does not matter at all
optionExplain: This misreads a denial of a difference as a denial of the thing; he asks 'Does this home have an architecture? Of course it does'.
The size of a system is not the point he makes.
Right: the house has an architecture of shape, appearance and layout; what he rejects is the idea that it is divorced from the low-level details.
He says both levels are parts of one whole, so the high-level shape still matters.
questions.explain: The author affirms that the home has an architecture (its shape, outward appearance, elevations and layout). His target is the idea that this level is divorced from the details.
questions.teaches: The author does not deny that a house has an architecture of shape and layout; he denies that this high-level view is divorced from the low-level details.
questions.rule: Reject the separation, not the existence of the high level.

questions.q: A company keeps a boxes-and-arrows diagram owned by senior staff and treats class-level code as a separate matter that is not checked against the diagram. What does the author's view predict?
options: Nothing in particular: the levels are independent, so changes in the details cannot affect the diagram
The diagram will become more accurate as the code grows, because the details are filled in later on
The code will always match the diagram, since senior staff made it and the juniors only follow it
The diagram will stop describing the real system, since the details are part of the same structure
optionExplain: This assumes the separation the author denies.
More unchecked detail gives more room to differ, not less.
Seniority does not make code follow a drawing.
Right: if the details are part of the same whole as the high-level shape, the details change what the system really is.
questions.explain: Since low-level details and high-level decisions are parts of the same whole, decisions made at the bottom can change the system's real structure whatever the diagram says.
questions.rule: Levels of a design affect each other.

questions.q: A restaurant designer's plan shows the dining room and kitchen layout, and also where every burner, drain and fridge outlet goes. A critic says the burner positions are not real design. Which answer follows the author's way of arguing?
options: The critic is right: only the layout counts as design, and burner positions are mere implementation work
Both belong to the design, as the plans show, so the critic's split does not hold
Burner positions should be left to the cooks, who are the experts on how a kitchen is really used
Designers should drop the burner positions from the plan, since they belong to a much later stage
optionExplain: This repeats the split between levels the author rejects.
Right: the author looks at what a real architect produces and finds both levels in the same plans.
Who knows best is a different question; the author's point is that the details belong to the design.
Removing details would not make them stop mattering; the author says the details support the high-level decisions.
questions.explain: The author tests the claim by looking at the plans a practising architect produces. They hold the layout and the small details together, so the split between them falls.
questions.teaches: The architect's drawings also show which switches control which lights and the size and placement of the water heater and the sump pump: small details that support the high-level decisions.
questions.rule: Check a label against what practitioners actually produce.

questions.q: Someone asks how you could tell whether a software design is good. Which test seems the most useful?
options: How quickly the first release was shipped to the market and how much it earned in its first year
Whether it uses the newest technology and the most fashionable frameworks of the time
How much effort each customer need costs, now and as the system ages
How many developers have been hired and how fast the headcount has grown over the years
optionExplain: Speed at the start is easy to see, but it says nothing about later releases.
New tools can be used well or badly; they do not measure design.
Right: effort per need over the system's life is the measure the author uses.
More hires may mean more effort needed, which is the opposite of good.
questions.explain: Good design shows in the effort needed to keep meeting needs. The card next gives the author's wording.
questions.rule: Judge a design by how much effort each change costs over the system's whole life, not by how fast it started.

questions.q: The author says the goal of software architecture is to ____ the human resources required to build and maintain the required system.
questions.explain: The goal is to minimize the human resources needed to build and maintain the system.
questions.rule: The goal is minimal human effort over the system's life.

questions.q: Team X needed 3, 4, 6 and 9 person-months for four releases of similar size. Team Y needed 5, 5, 5 and 5. Which verdict fits the author's measure of design quality?
options: Team Y, because its effort stays level while X's effort grows each release
Team X, because its first release was cheaper than the first release of Team Y
They are equal, because both teams finished all four releases within the same year
Neither, because person-months say nothing about design quality in either team
optionExplain: Right: effort that stays flat over releases is the author's sign of good design, and growth is the sign of bad.
The first release is cheap, but the author judges by the trend: growth with each release is the sign of bad design.
Finishing is not the measure; the effort required to finish is.
The author says the measure of design quality is exactly the effort to meet the customer's needs.
questions.explain: The author says design is good if the effort is low and stays low, and bad if it grows with each release. Team X's effort grows.
questions.rule: Compare the trend of effort per release, not the first release.

questions.q: True or false: A design whose first release cost very little effort is good by the author's measure even if the effort grows with every later release.
questions.explain: The author's measure covers the whole lifetime of the system. Effort that grows with each new release marks the design as bad whatever the first release cost.
questions.rule: A cheap start does not make a design good.

questions.q: An engineering staff grows steadily over eight releases. By the author's measure, what does that growth alone tell you about the design?
options: That the design is good, since a growing staff shows that the company is a success
That the design is bad, since more people always mean more mistakes in the code
That the design is neutral, since staff size is not a design matter at all
Nothing yet: growth must be read against output and cost per release
optionExplain: The author invites this reading ('must be an indication of significant success!') and then shows it can be wrong.
Staff growth alone does not show a bad design either; the verdict needs the other curves.
Staff size is exactly what the measure of effort counts, so it is not irrelevant.
Right: growth looks like success, but the case study reads it together with code growth and cost to show the opposite.
questions.explain: The author first presents the staff curve as seemingly good news, then shows output and cost, which reveal a failing design. One curve is not a verdict.
questions.teaches: Growth in staff can look like success while hiding a failing design; it must be read against output and cost per release.
questions.rule: Read effort against output before judging.

questions.q: A mobile game studio had record profit this year, but the effort for each update has tripled over three years. What does the author's reasoning say about its prospects?
options: It is safe, because high profit today shows that the design works and will go on working
The trend threatens the profit: rising effort can drain it and push the company to collapse
It is neutral, because profit and design quality are unrelated matters in a company
It should immediately double its staff so that output can keep pace with the growing cost
optionExplain: The author warns that it does not matter how profitable the company is at the moment.
Right: he says such curves will catastrophically drain profit from the business model and can drive a company into a stall or collapse.
The author ties profit to design through the effort needed per release.
More staff is what the case study company did, and its costs exploded.
questions.explain: The author says it does not matter how profitable a company is today: curves of rising effort and cost will catastrophically drain the profit.
questions.teaches: Current profitability does not excuse a rising-effort trend; the author says such curves will drain the profit and may drive the company into a stall or collapse.
questions.rule: Profit today does not cancel a rising cost trend.

questions.q: A company's engineering staff has grown every release, yet the amount of code shipped per release is levelling off. What is the most likely cause?
options: The staff are mostly idle because the work has run out and nobody is assigning new tasks
The customers have stopped asking for new features, so output has levelled off by itself
Much of the extra effort goes into handling the problems of the existing code
Code is a poor measure of output, so nothing in the charts shows that anything is wrong
optionExplain: The author notes everyone is working hard, so idleness is not the explanation.
Nothing in the case study suggests that demand fell; the problem lies in the cost of meeting it.
Right: the author says effort is diverted from features to managing the mess.
Lines of code are crude, but the author reads the pattern as a warning sign, not a measuring error.
questions.explain: The author's case study shows hard-working people whose output falls because of the mess they work in. The card next gives the data.
questions.rule: Rising headcount and cost with flat output is the signature of a mess, not of success.

questions.q: Match each measure in the case study with what happened to it over the eight releases.
pairs: 40 times higher in release 8 than in release 1
A few hundred thousand dollars at release 1, 20 million by release 8
questions.explain: Staff and payroll rose, while code growth flattened and the cost of each line rose 40-fold. That mix is the author's signature of a mess.
questions.rule: More people and more money, less new code.

questions.q: A mobile app team grew from 6 to 24 developers over six releases. Features shipped per release fell from 10 to 8, and developers say most days go to working around old code. Which reading fits the author's account?
options: The team is healthy, because growth in staff and in cost always shows that the product is a success
The team lacks motivation, so the remedy is to replace the managers and push developers harder
The measure of lines of code is unreliable, so no conclusion about the design is possible at all
It matches the signature of a mess: rising cost, flat output and effort diverted from features
optionExplain: The author shows that growth in staff can come with a collapse in productivity.
He stresses that nobody has decreased their effort; the cause is the mess, not motivation.
The data are rough, but the pattern matches the one the author warns about, so it deserves action.
Right: rising headcount, flat output and effort spent on the existing code match the case study.
questions.explain: The team matches the author's pattern: staff up, output flat, and developers spending effort on the mess rather than on features.
questions.rule: Staff up, output flat, effort diverted: suspect a mess.

questions.q: According to the author, which circumstances together mean you can bank on riding this curve to its ugly end? Select all that apply.
options: Systems thrown together in a hurry
The number of programmers as the sole driver of output
Little or no thought given to code cleanliness or design structure
Frequent changes of management and low pay
optionExplain: Right: the author names hurried construction.
Right: he names headcount as the sole driver of output.
Right: he names neglect of cleanliness and structure.
The text does not tie the curve to management turnover or pay.
questions.explain: The author names the conditions of the mess: haste, headcount as the only lever, and no thought to cleanliness or structure.
questions.teaches: The author names the conditions that produce the signature: hurried construction, headcount as the only driver of output, and little thought for code cleanliness or design structure.
questions.rule: Haste plus headcount without structure produces the curve.

questions.q: A manager argues: 'The staff doubled, so output must have doubled; the lines-of-code chart must be wrong.' Which step fails, judging by the case study?
options: The step from more staff to more output: here staff grew while code growth flattened
The chart is certainly right because the author drew it from real data, so the manager is mistaken
The manager should have looked at payroll first, since payroll shows the output of a team
Doubling the staff halves the cost per line, so the lines-of-code chart must be wrong
optionExplain: Right: the step assumes output follows headcount, while the case study shows the two parting ways.
The author's data come from a real company, but the point is the pattern, not who drew it.
Looking at payroll alone would show cost, but not whether it bought output.
The case study shows cost per line rising, not falling.
questions.explain: The case study exists to show that output does not follow headcount when the design is a mess. The manager assumes it does.
questions.rule: Headcount is not output.

questions.q: A manager studying a failing product looks only at the payroll chart and approves a hiring plan because the money is being spent anyway. What does the case study recommend instead?
options: Ask the developers to work overtime until the output curve catches up with the payroll
Ignore the payroll curve, since only the output of the team matters to an executive
Read the payroll curve against the output curve: that shows what the spending buys
Wait for the revenue figures before looking at any other chart or taking any action
optionExplain: The author notes that overtime and heroics did not stop the decline.
Cost matters: it is half of the comparison.
Right: the payroll chart alone is scary, but set beside lines of code per release it shows the last 20 million bought almost nothing.
The author hopes revenue outpaces cost, but his point is that these two curves already show the need for action.
questions.explain: The author sets the payroll curve beside the output curve; only together do they show that the last 20 million bought almost nothing.
questions.teaches: Charts should be read together: the payroll curve alone is cause for concern, but set against the output curve it shows how little the money bought.
questions.rule: Compare cost with output, not cost alone.

questions.q: A team ships a messy first version, promising to clean it up after launch. What does experience most often bring?
options: A calm period after launch in which the cleanup is finally done properly and at leisure
Faster work from then on, since the mess is already paid for and costs nothing more
A rewrite that the managers approve straight away once the first release has shipped
The cleanup is postponed again and again because the next deadline always arrives
optionExplain: This is the hope behind the promise, but the author says the market does not give calm periods.
Messy code feels fast at first, but the author says it is slower on every time scale.
A rewrite is a different plan, and the author doubts it works.
Right: the author says things never do get cleaned up later, because market pressures never abate.
questions.explain: The author argues that the cleanup promise fails because the pressure that caused the mess never lets up. The card next gives his steps.
questions.rule: The promise of cleaning up later fails because the pressure that caused the mess never goes away.

questions.q: Put the author's argument against 'we can clean it up later' in order.
items: Developers say they will clean up later, once they have reached the market first
Market pressure does not abate after launch, so competitors stay close behind
The developers must finish the next feature, and the next, so they never switch modes
The mess builds and productivity keeps heading towards zero
questions.explain: The promise is followed by unrelenting pressure, then by no time to switch modes, and finally by the growing mess.
questions.rule: Later never comes while the pressure stays.

questions.q: A founder says: 'We will write the tests after the next funding round, when things calm down.' Which part of the author's argument speaks to this plan?
options: The funding round will bring a calm period after launch in which cleaning is easy and quick
The pressure will not abate after the round, so the next demand will crowd the tests out again
Messy code is faster in the short term, so the plan to add tests after the round is sound
Tests are a design matter that belongs to the architects, so developers need not plan time for them
optionExplain: This is the hope the author calls a lie: he says market pressures never abate.
Right: the author's reason is that the pressure carries on, so cleanup is always postponed.
He says the opposite: making messes is always slower than staying clean.
The author treats clean code and structure as one concern for all developers, not a task for a few.
questions.explain: After the round there will be new customers, new deadlines and competitors, which push the cleanup aside once more.
questions.rule: Expect the pressure to continue, not to end.

questions.q: Getting to market first, the author says, only means you now have a horde of ____ on your tail, and you must keep running as fast as you can.
questions.explain: A lead only brings pursuit by a horde of competitors, so the pressure goes on and the cleanup is postponed.
questions.teaches: Getting to market first only brings a horde of competitors close behind, which keeps the pressure on and the cleanup postponed.
questions.rule: A lead brings pursuit, not rest.

questions.q: Which statement is the author's own claim about the speed of messy code?
options: Messy code is faster at first and slower later, so it is a fair trade-off
Messy code is slower only in teams that have a bad process
Messy code is always slower than staying clean, on any time scale
Messy code is faster for small programs and slower for large ones
optionExplain: He calls exactly this idea the bigger lie developers buy into.
He does not tie the claim to a team's process.
Right: he says that making messes is always slower than staying clean, no matter which time scale is used.
He does not split his claim by size; he says on any time scale.
questions.explain: The 'bigger lie' is that mess makes you fast now and slow later. He asserts it is slower always.
questions.rule: Mess is slower, not just later-slower.

questions.q: A cook leaves pots unwashed through a busy week, planning to scrub them all once service quietens down, though every night is as busy as the last. Which false belief of the Hare does this show?
options: That one can switch from making a mess to cleaning it up whenever one chooses
That cooking fast always produces better food than cooking carefully does
That customers prefer a dirty kitchen because the food then arrives sooner
That the cook does not work hard enough to keep up with the orders
optionExplain: Right: the developers' overconfidence is in their ability to switch modes from making messes to cleaning them up later, and they never do.
The author's concern is not about quality of output but about the habit of postponing.
This has nothing to do with the author's argument.
The author says that developers work hard; the fault is not laziness.
questions.explain: The overconfident belief is that one can change from mess-making to cleanup at will. Because the pressure stays, the change never comes.
questions.teaches: The Hare's overconfidence takes a specific form: believing one can switch from making messes to cleaning them up at will, when in fact the developers never switch modes.
questions.rule: Do not rely on a later switch to cleanup mode.

questions.q: A programmer builds the same small program six times, using a disciplined test-first method on three of the days. What would you expect from the times?
options: The disciplined days will be slower, since the extra discipline adds work to every task and delays the finish
The first day will be the fastest, whatever the method, because the programmer is least tired then
There will be no difference between the days at all, because the task and the tests are the same each day
The disciplined days will be a little faster, and even the slowest beats the fastest of the others
optionExplain: It feels natural that extra discipline costs time, but this is the belief the experiment challenges.
The author reports a learning curve, so later days were quicker.
The author reports a difference, not a tie.
Right: the author reports the disciplined days about 10% faster, with the slowest beating the fastest of the others.
questions.explain: The result is a surprise to many, which is why the author uses it. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Cleanliness makes work faster even in the short run, so a rewrite without changed habits repeats the mess.

questions.q: In Jason Gorman's experiment, the cleanliness discipline used on the first, third and fifth days was ____.
questions.explain: He used test-driven development (TDD) on days one, three and five, and no such discipline on the other days.
questions.rule: Three days with TDD, three without.

questions.q: Another programmer repeats the experiment. The fastest non-TDD day took 24 minutes and the slowest TDD day took 27 minutes. Does this match the pattern the author reports?
options: Yes, since the TDD days are about 10% faster on average, which is within the normal noise
No, since even the slowest TDD day beat the fastest non-TDD day in the report
Yes, since the learning curve explains it: later days are faster whatever method is used
No, since TDD days must always take exactly the same time as the days without it
optionExplain: An average gap does not settle it: the author reports that every TDD day beat every non-TDD day.
Right: in the original result the slowest TDD day was faster than the fastest non-TDD day, and here it is not.
A learning curve is in the data, but the claim concerns the ranking of days.
The author does not say the TDD days took equal times.
questions.explain: The author stresses that even the slowest TDD day was quicker than the fastest non-TDD day. The repeat breaks that pattern.
questions.rule: Check the ranking, not only the average.

questions.q: Which of these patterns does the author point out in the six-day results? Select all that apply.
options: Work on later days was completed more quickly than on earlier days
The TDD days were about 10% faster than the non-TDD days
The non-TDD days were about 10% faster than the TDD days
Each day's work took about a quarter of an hour
optionExplain: Right: he says to notice the learning curve, with later days quicker.
Right: he says the TDD days were about 10% faster.
This reverses the author's finding.
Each day took a little less than 30 minutes, so this misstates the time.
questions.explain: The author draws attention to two patterns: a learning curve across the days and an advantage of about 10% for the TDD days.
questions.teaches: Besides the TDD effect, the results show a learning curve: work on the later days was completed more quickly than on the earlier days.
questions.rule: Separate the learning curve from the method effect.

questions.q: True or false: The author calls the wish to start over from scratch the Hare talking again.
questions.explain: He says the same overconfidence that led to the mess would drive the redesign into the same mess, so starting over is not the way out.
questions.rule: A rewrite with the same habits repeats the mess.

questions.q: A government agency's tangled permit system keeps failing. Officials plan a ground-up replacement with the same contractors under the same deadline pressure. What does the author's conclusion recommend instead?
options: Proceed with the replacement, since new code written from scratch is always cleaner than the old
Hire more contractors to finish faster, since the deadline pressure is the real cause of the failures
Recognize the organization's own overconfidence and take the quality of the structure seriously
Drop the permit system entirely, since a system that keeps failing is not worth repairing
optionExplain: The author expects the redesign to end in the same mess when the habits stay.
More headcount is what the case study company did, with its costs exploding.
Right: his conclusion says that in every case the best option is to recognize and avoid your own overconfidence and take architecture quality seriously.
The author does not propose giving up the system.
questions.explain: The author's conclusion is not to start again but to change the attitude, by recognizing overconfidence and taking structure seriously.
questions.teaches: The author's conclusion for a failing organization: recognize and avoid its own overconfidence, and take the quality of its software architecture seriously.
questions.rule: Change the attitude before the code.

questions.q: A developer says: 'My whole job is to make the machine meet the requirements and fix the bugs.' How would the author respond?
options: That is the whole job, and nothing more is expected of a developer once the bugs are fixed
That is a job only for the first release, after which developers have nothing further to deliver
That is a manager's job, not a developer's, since requirements belong to the business side
That is one value of two; he is sadly mistaken to take it as the entirety of the job
optionExplain: This is the belief the author says many programmers hold, and he rejects it.
The author does not restrict behavior to a stage of the project.
He assigns behavior to programmers, not only to managers.
Right: behavior is the first value, but he says those who think it is everything are sadly mistaken.
questions.explain: The author names behavior as the first of two values. The card next shows what the second is to be.
questions.rule: Behavior, meaning meeting requirements and fixing bugs, is only one of the two values developers must keep high.

questions.q: According to the author, why are programmers hired?
options: To make machines behave in a way that makes or saves money for stakeholders
To pick the tools and frameworks for the business, since developers know them best
To produce as much code as possible, since output is what the stakeholders pay for
To write the requirements document alone, because only developers understand the machines
optionExplain: Right: programmers are hired to make machines behave in ways that make or save money for the stakeholders.
Tools are not mentioned as the reason for hiring.
The author's measure is behavior that makes or saves money, not volume of code.
The author says programmers help the stakeholders to write it; they do not write it alone.
questions.explain: Behavior is what makes or saves the stakeholders money, and the code is written to satisfy the requirements.
questions.rule: Behavior is the first value.

questions.q: Sort each piece of work by whether it serves the first value, behavior, or the other value (structure).

items.t: Fixing a crash a customer reported
Implementing a line of the requirements document
