Helping the stakeholders write the functional specification
Keeping the system easy to change when stakeholders change their minds
Making sure a later request costs only as much as its size
Arranging the code so that new requests of similar scope do not get harder each year

questions.explain: Behavior covers the specification, the requirements and the bug fixes. Structure concerns how easily the system changes later.
questions.rule: Behavior: what the machine does. Structure: how easily that can change.

questions.q: True or false: The author says that meeting requirements and fixing bugs is unimportant work for a programmer.
questions.explain: The author calls behavior the first value and says programmers must deliver it. His complaint is that those who think it is the entirety of the job are sadly mistaken.
questions.rule: Behavior matters, but it is not the whole job.

questions.q: A bridge-inspection firm's app has every requested feature working, but nobody looks after its structure and each change takes longer than the last. Which statement fits the author's warning?
options: The firm has done its job, since every requirement is met and nothing more is asked of developers
The firm has focused on structure and neglected behavior, which leaves the system worthless in time
The firm has focused on the lesser value and neglected structure, which can leave it valueless
The firm has no problem as long as bugs are fixed quickly whenever a user reports one
optionExplain: This is the view of the many programmers whom the author calls sadly mistaken.
In the firm every feature works, so behavior is not what is neglected.
Right: the author warns that developers often focus on the lesser of the two values, leaving the system eventually valueless.
Fixing bugs is part of behavior; it does not address the growing cost of change.
questions.explain: The author warns of focusing on one value to the exclusion of the other, and calls behavior the lesser of the two.
questions.teaches: The author calls behavior the lesser of the two values and warns that developers who focus on it to the exclusion of structure leave the system eventually valueless.
questions.rule: Do not trade the greater value for the lesser.

questions.q: If we had wanted the behavior of machines to be hard to change, the author says we would have called it ____.
questions.explain: The author's word-play: software was meant to be soft, so hard-to-change behavior would be hardware. The card next gives the point behind it.
questions.rule: Software exists to make behavior easy to change, so ease of change is its second value.

questions.q: True or false: In the author's account, software was intended to be a way to change the behavior of machines easily.
questions.explain: He says software was invented to be soft, meaning a way to change the behavior of machines easily.
questions.rule: Software is meant to be easy to change.

questions.q: The owner of an online shop changes her mind and wants a different shipping rule. In which case is the software doing what the author says it should?
options: The change is made, but only by rewriting the checkout part of the shop software
The change needs a meeting of all the teams and then a month of testing before release
The change is refused because it was not part of the first specification of the shop
The change is simple and easy to make
optionExplain: Having to rewrite a part for a small change is also a sign the structure is hard.
A heavy process for a small request is the opposite of soft.
Refusing changes treats the software like hardware.
Right: the author says that when stakeholders change their minds about a feature, the change should be simple and easy to make.
questions.explain: The author says a stakeholder's change of mind should be simple and easy to make.
questions.rule: A changed mind should cost little.

questions.q: Match each part of the author's word-play on 'software' with what he takes it to mean.
pairs: Easy to change: the second value
The name for behavior that is hard to change
questions.explain: The author splits the word: 'ware' is the product and 'soft' is the quality of being easy to change, which is the second value.
questions.teaches: In the word 'software', 'ware' means 'product', so 'soft' names the second value, the part that makes the product easy to change.
questions.rule: Soft names the second value.

questions.q: Stakeholders ask for a change to a feature, and it proves very hard to make. What does the author's account imply about the software?
options: It is working as intended, since hard problems take time to solve in any craft
It is failing at what software was meant to be: a way to change behavior easily
It is perfectly good, because the old feature still works exactly as it did before
It is hardware, so the change should be refused and a new product bought instead
optionExplain: Hard problems take time, but the author's purpose for software is ease of change.
Right: to fulfil its purpose, software must be soft, that is, easy to change.
A working old feature is the first value; the author's point is about the second.
It behaves like hard ware in the author's sense, but that is a fault, not a reason to refuse.
questions.explain: Because softness is software's purpose, a feature that is hard to change shows the second value has been lost.
questions.rule: Hard-to-change behavior defeats software's purpose.

questions.q: A catering firm changes its menu every season. Its ordering software needs a full new version of the whole system for each menu change. How does the author's view treat this?
options: As normal, since menus are business matters that no software can be expected to follow
As a fault of the caterer, who should change the menu less often to suit the software
As a failure of the software, since a stakeholder's changed mind is the normal case to absorb
As proof that ordering systems must be built as hardware, since they cannot be soft
optionExplain: Menus belong to the business, but the author expects the software to absorb such changes.
The author puts the burden on the software, not on the stakeholders who change their minds.
Right: he treats a stakeholder's change of mind as the normal case, and says it should be simple and easy to make.
The author's word-play warns against hardware-like behavior in software.
questions.explain: The author expects stakeholders to change their minds about features and demands that the change be simple. A full new version for each menu change fails that test.
questions.teaches: Costs grow out of proportion to the size of the requested changes: the first year of development is much cheaper than the second, and the second much cheaper than the third.
questions.rule: Design for changed minds.

questions.q: Two change requests are the same size, yet one takes a day and the other a month. What best explains the difference?
options: How well each request fits the existing structure of the system
One request was far more urgent than the other, so the team rushed it
The developers worked at different speeds on the two requests
One request came from a more senior stakeholder, so it got more attention
optionExplain: Right: the author blames a mismatch between the shape of the request and the shape of the system.
Urgency affects priority, not the work needed.
People differ, but a month against a day points to something in the system.
Seniority changes who asks, not how hard the change is.
questions.explain: The author's term for what you have just guessed is shape. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Aim for an architecture where the cost of a change tracks its size, not how awkwardly it fits.

questions.q: The author says the difficulty of making a change should be proportional only to the ____ of the change, and not to its shape.
questions.explain: Difficulty should follow scope, how big the change is, and not shape.
questions.rule: Cost follows scope, not shape.

questions.q: Request A: add a tax field to invoices; it takes an hour. Request B: add the same field to credit notes; it takes three weeks because credit notes were built on a different structure. How does the author's idea describe B?
options: B has a larger scope than A, because credit notes are bigger documents than invoices
B shows that the developers on A were more skilled than the developers who worked on B
B shows that credit notes are not important enough to deserve a cheap change
B has the same scope but a different shape, and its cost follows shape: weak architecture
optionExplain: The two requests add the same field, so their scope is the same.
Skill is not what separates the two jobs in the example.
Importance is not the author's point here.
Right: the scope is the same but the request fits the system badly, and cost that follows shape is the author's problem.
questions.explain: The two requests have the same scope. The extra cost of B comes from how awkwardly it fits the existing structure.
questions.rule: Same scope, different cost: look at shape.

questions.q: Why does the author want architectures to be as shape agnostic as practical?
options: Because every shape of request costs exactly the same, whatever the architecture prefers
Because the more an architecture prefers one shape, the harder new features are to fit
Because shape is a matter of taste and best ignored when a system is designed
Because scope never matters in software, and only the form of a request counts
optionExplain: He asks for cost in proportion to scope, not for identical cost, and he says as practical.
Right: the author says the more the architecture prefers one shape over another, the harder the new features are to fit.
He treats shape as a main cause of rising costs.
He says difficulty should be proportional to scope, so it does matter.
questions.explain: An architecture that favors one shape makes requests of other shapes ever harder, so he asks it to be agnostic.
questions.teaches: An architecture that prefers one shape over another makes features of other shapes ever harder to fit, so the more it favors one shape the worse it handles new requests.
questions.rule: Do not favor one shape.

questions.q: True or false: If an architecture were perfectly shape agnostic, the author says every change would cost the same.
questions.explain: He asks that difficulty be proportional to the scope of the change. Bigger changes still cost more; what shape agnostic removes is the extra cost of poor fit.
questions.rule: Shape agnostic removes the fit penalty, not the size cost.

questions.q: A warehouse's shelving fits only pallet-sized boxes. When an odd-shaped product arrives, staff wedge and rearrange boxes to squeeze it in, and each such product takes longer than the last. Which part of the author's account does this match?
options: Stakeholders asking for more each year, until the staff can no longer meet their demands
The scope of a change being larger than expected, so the staff must work extra hours
Developers feeling forced to jam square pegs into round holes when the shape does not match
The Hare's overconfidence about speed, which leads staff to rush each odd product through
optionExplain: The stream of requests is described by the author as of roughly similar scope.
Scope would mean the size of the request; here the trouble is in the fit.
Right: the author says developers feel as if they must jam square pegs into round holes when the shape of the system does not match the request.
Overconfidence is a separate point in the case study.
questions.explain: The shelving prefers one shape; products of another shape are harder and harder to fit, as in the author's metaphor.
questions.teaches: The feeling of jamming square pegs into round holes is the developers' sign that the shape of the system does not match the shape of the request.
questions.rule: Square pegs signal a shape mismatch.

questions.q: Which would you rather inherit: a program that works perfectly but cannot be changed, or one that does not work but is easy to change?
options: The perfect one, because it works today and today is what the business is paying for
Both are worth the same, since each has one fault and one virtue
Neither, because both are useless to anyone who needs software that keeps pace with requirements
The easy-to-change one, because it can be made to work and kept working as requirements change
optionExplain: It feels safer, but it will fail when requirements change and cannot be repaired.
Their futures differ greatly: one can be repaired and the other cannot.
The changeable program can be fixed, so it is not useless.
Right: the author argues that the changeable program remains useful.
questions.explain: This is the author's own pair of extremes. The card next gives his reasoning.
questions.rule: Ease of change outranks present function because a changeable system can be fixed, while an unchangeable one cannot.

questions.q: The author tests the managers' claim with the simple logical tool of examining the ____.
questions.explain: He examines the extremes: a program that works but cannot change, and one that does not work but can change.
questions.rule: Test a claim at its extremes.

questions.q: Program P works perfectly today, but its code is so tangled that the team will not touch it. A new law alters one rule next quarter. What does the author's argument predict?
options: P will stop working and cannot be made to work again, so it becomes useless
P keeps working, because it worked before and a working program needs no changes
P will be fixed quickly because the new rule is small and the team knows the code
P will gain value because the law favors programs that have been stable for years
optionExplain: Right: it won't work when requirements change, and nobody can make it work.
The author says a perfect but unchangeable program will not work when requirements change.
A small rule does not help if the structure cannot be changed.
The law adds a new requirement, which an unchangeable program cannot meet.
questions.explain: P is the author's first extreme: working but unchangeable. When the requirement changes it fails and cannot be repaired.
questions.rule: Unchangeable means useless once things change.

questions.q: A manager says that current functionality matters more than any later flexibility. According to the author, how will that manager react when a requested change is quoted at an unaffordable cost?
options: Calmly, because current functionality came first and the manager already said so
By dropping the request without comment, since the manager never valued flexibility
Furious that the system was allowed to reach the point where the change was impractical
By blaming the stakeholders who asked for the change, since they should have asked earlier
optionExplain: It is the stance in the abstract; the author expects it to break when the quote arrives.
The author expects anger, not quiet acceptance.
Right: he says managers will likely be furious that you allowed the system to get to that point.
The author puts the blame on the developers who let the system reach that state.
questions.explain: The manager's ranking of function over flexibility meets the real cost of a change, and the author expects fury at developers.
questions.teaches: Managers who rank present functionality above later flexibility are likely to be furious when a change is quoted at an unaffordable cost, because the system was allowed to reach that point.
questions.rule: The abstract preference changes when the quote arrives.

questions.q: True or false: The author admits there is no such thing as a program impossible to change; his point is about systems practically impossible to change.
questions.explain: He admits there is no such thing as a program impossible to change. His point is about systems that are practically impossible to change because the cost of change exceeds the benefit.
questions.rule: Practically impossible is enough.

questions.q: A sensor's firmware is burned onto a chip, and its requirements will stay fixed for its whole life. How does the author's argument apply to it?
options: It condemns the firmware, because all software must be easy to change whatever its use
It shows that working programs are less useful than broken ones in every case
It proves the firmware must be rewritten as hardware, since software is meant to be soft
The harm arrives when requirements change, so for fixed requirements the unchangeable program is not made useless
optionExplain: The author's case is about the moment requirements change; if they never do, that case does not arise.
The argument compares changeable and unchangeable programs, not working and broken ones in general.
Firmware is not hardware in the word-play, and the argument does not call for rewriting.
Right: he says the unchangeable program 'won't work when the requirements change', so the argument bites where change is expected.
questions.explain: The author's first extreme fails only when the requirements change. The case of fixed requirements marks where the argument stops applying.
questions.teaches: The author's case against the unchangeable program is stated for the moment requirements change: it 'won't work when the requirements change'.
questions.rule: The argument bites where change is expected.

questions.q: A manager says the feature due on Friday is urgent. Does that make it more important than the long-term structure of the system?
options: Yes: urgent things are by definition the important ones, so Friday's feature ranks above structure
No: urgency and importance differ, and structure is important though seldom urgent
Yes: only what a customer can see can be important, so structure never competes with features
No: structure is never important to the business, only the features that customers see are
optionExplain: This merges two ideas that Eisenhower's matrix separates.
Right: the author reads the matrix this way: urgent and important are different measures.
Customers see features, but visibility is not the same as importance.
The author says the opposite: structure is the important value.
questions.explain: The author uses Eisenhower's matrix to separate urgency from importance. The card next gives his ranking.
questions.rule: Do not let features that are urgent but not important push aside the architecture that is important.

questions.q: Put the author's four couplets in his order of priority, highest first.
items: Urgent and important
Not urgent and important
Urgent and not important
Not urgent and not important
questions.explain: The author ranks them in this order, so architecture (important) holds the top two places and behavior the first and third.
questions.rule: Important beats urgent.

questions.q: Sort each task into the box the author's reading of the matrix suggests: usually urgent but not important, or important but not urgent.

items.t: Adding a banner to the home page for tomorrow's promotion
Matching a minor competitor feature by the end of the week
Changing module boundaries so later features cost less
Keeping the structure free of any preferred shape of request
Moving a button because a manager wants it today
Separating pricing rules from the rest of the code so they can change alone

questions.explain: Features usually bring the deadlines (urgent), while structure is what keeps all later work cheap (important) but seldom has a date.
questions.rule: Features press, structure matters.

questions.q: When business managers and developers raise position 3 to position 1, what exactly do they fail to do?
options: Decide which team should write the feature, since the wrong team will make it urgent
Estimate the number of lines of code in each feature, so that urgency can be measured
Separate the features that are only urgent from those that are both urgent and important
Find out whether the stakeholders agree with each other about which features come first
optionExplain: Team assignment does not come into his argument.
Estimating size is not the mistake the author names.
Right: the author says they fail to separate the merely urgent features from those that are truly urgent and important.
Agreement among stakeholders is not the failure he describes.
questions.explain: The failure lies in treating every urgent feature as if it were also important. That leads to ignoring the important architecture in favor of unimportant features.
questions.teaches: The mistake comes from failing to separate features that are merely urgent from those that are both urgent and important, which leads to ignoring architecture in favor of unimportant features.
questions.rule: Separate merely urgent from truly important.

questions.q: A lead argues: 'Architecture is not urgent, so it can wait until the features are done.' Which step is faulty by the author's ranking?
options: Treating a lack of urgency as a lack of priority: important but not urgent still outranks urgent but not important
Architecture is urgent because the features are, so it cannot wait until the features are done
Features are never done, so nothing can be ranked and the lead's claim cannot be tested at all
Architecture comes last because it is neither urgent nor important by the author's ranking
optionExplain: Right: not urgent and important ranks second, above urgent but unimportant, so absence of urgency does not lower the priority.
The author says architecture is important but never particularly urgent.
Whether features are ever done is not the author's point here.
The author calls architecture important, so it is not in the last position.
questions.explain: The faulty step moves from 'not urgent' to 'lower priority'. In the author's ranking important ranks above urgent when the urgent is not important.
questions.rule: Lack of urgency does not lower importance.

questions.q: A hospital IT team must patch a flaw that attackers are exploiting today, and also has a long-term plan to restructure old code. Which statement fits the author's reading of the matrix?
options: The patch cannot be important, since it is urgent and the matrix says the two never meet
Neither task can be ranked, since they belong to different parts of the organization
The restructuring is urgent, since it is important and the matrix says these always go together
The patch can be urgent and important; the matrix says these usually part ways, not always
optionExplain: The author says some things are both urgent and important.
He gives a full ranking of the four couplets.
The author calls architecture important but never particularly urgent.
Right: he calls Eisenhower's saying true to a great degree, but says urgent things are rarely, and important things seldom, of the other kind.
questions.explain: The author softens the saying: the urgent are rarely of great importance and the important seldom of great urgency, and some things are both.
questions.teaches: The author softens Eisenhower's wording: urgent things are rarely (not never) of great importance, and important things are seldom of great urgency.
questions.rule: Urgency and importance usually part ways, not always.

questions.q: Business managers are not equipped to judge how much the architecture of a system matters. Who should speak up for it?
options: The managers, once they have been trained in architecture by the development team
The development team, whom the company hired for that judgment
The customers, who see the results and so can tell good structure from bad
Nobody, since architecture shows itself in time without anyone having to speak for it
optionExplain: Training is not the author's answer; he says judging architecture is why developers were hired.
Right: the author says it is the responsibility of the development team to assert the importance of architecture.
Customers see behavior, not structure.
Waiting is the road to the costs the unit describes.
questions.explain: The author puts the duty on the people who can judge. The card next gives his reasoning.
questions.rule: Because only developers can judge architecture, they must argue for it as equal stakeholders.

questions.q: The author reminds developers that as a software developer you are a ____ with a stake in the software that you need to safeguard.
questions.explain: A developer is a stakeholder and may squabble with the other stakeholders as an equal.
questions.rule: Developers are stakeholders too.

questions.q: A product owner asks the team to skip planned restructuring so that a feature meets a sales date. What does the author's advice suggest the developer do?
options: Comply silently, since the managers decide the priorities and the developers carry them out
Refuse to build any feature until the planned restructuring is finished in full
Argue as an equal stakeholder that the importance of architecture outweighs this urgency
Wait until the managers understand architecture themselves before raising any objection
optionExplain: Silent compliance leaves the judgment to people not equipped for it.
The author asks for a struggle among equals, not a strike.
Right: it is the team's responsibility to assert the importance of architecture over the urgency of features.
The managers are not equipped to evaluate it, so waiting for them fails.
questions.explain: The developer is the one equipped to judge architecture and is a stakeholder, so she must argue the case against the urgency of the feature.
questions.rule: Explain the cost, as an equal.

questions.q: How does the author describe the place of this struggle in a developer's work?
options: It is a regrettable distraction from real work that good developers should avoid
It is a task for architects alone, so ordinary developers can leave it to them
It is a sign that the company is badly run and the developers should look elsewhere
It is a big part of why developers were hired, and effective teams tackle it head on
optionExplain: The author does not treat it as a distraction.
He says the challenge is doubly important for architects, but it is every developer's part and duty.
He says it is always a struggle for every team, which shows it is normal.
Right: he says it is part of the role and duty of developers, and effective teams tackle the struggle head on.
questions.explain: The author calls fighting for the architecture part of the role and duty of a developer, and a big part of why you were hired.
questions.teaches: Fighting for the architecture is a big part of why developers were hired, and effective teams tackle the struggle head on.
questions.rule: The fight is part of the job.

questions.q: True or false: The author's solution is for developers to refuse to build features until the architecture is perfect.
questions.explain: The author asks developers to assert the importance of architecture over the urgency of features, in a struggle among equals. He does not call for a refusal to deliver.
questions.rule: Assert and argue; do not stop.

questions.q: A new developer sees marketing, sales and developers arguing hard over priorities and concludes that the company is dysfunctional. How does the author's view treat this?
options: As the normal way things are done: each team struggles for what it believes best
As dysfunction, since stakeholders who are doing their jobs well ought to agree at once
As proof that developers should stay out of priorities and leave them to marketing and sales
As a problem for the managers alone, which developers should watch from a distance
optionExplain: Right: he says it is always a struggle, and every team struggles for what it believes best for the company.
The author expects friction rather than harmony.
He says the opposite: developers should join the struggle.
He says developers must take part as stakeholders.
questions.explain: The author says that this is always the way these things are done: every team struggles for what it believes best.
questions.teaches: The author treats a struggle between stakeholders as the normal way these things are done, not as a sign of dysfunction.
questions.rule: A struggle among stakeholders is normal.

questions.q: A team regularly puts architecture behind new features. What do you expect in the end?
options: The features will pay for a later cleanup, since each one brings in more income than the last
The architecture will fix itself with time, as the team learns the system and tidies it as it goes
Change becomes practically impossible for part or all of the system
Costs fall as the team learns the system, since later features reuse earlier work
optionExplain: The author says things never do get cleaned up later.
Structure does not improve without work.
Right: he says costs rise and eventually change becomes practically impossible for part or all of the system.
The case study shows costs rising, not falling.
questions.explain: The author warns of rising cost ending in change that is practically impossible. The card next gives his wording.
questions.rule: If architecture is left to last, change eventually becomes practically impossible, and the team is to blame for not fighting.

questions.q: True or false: The author says software architects are by job description more focused on the structure of the system than on its features and functions.
questions.explain: He says architects, by virtue of their job description, focus more on structure and create an architecture that allows features to be easily developed, modified and extended.
questions.rule: Architects focus on structure.

questions.q: After years of feature-first work, a retailer finds that adding a delivery option to one product line takes a year, while other lines change easily. Which part of the author's warning does this match?
options: Architecture coming first, which makes change easy in every product line of the retailer
Architects focusing too little on structure because they spend their time on features
Costs falling in proportion to the scope of change, as the retailer's developers learn the code
Change becoming practically impossible for part of the system
optionExplain: The retailer put features first, which is the opposite.
The scenario does not tell us what the architects focused on.
Here cost has risen far beyond the scope of the change.
Right: the author warns that change can become practically impossible for part or all of the system.
questions.explain: Only one product line has become practically impossible to change, which is the 'part' in the author's phrase 'part or all'.
questions.rule: Decay may start in one corner.

questions.q: Besides fighting for it, what does the author say taking architecture seriously requires? Select all that apply.
options: Knowing what good software architecture is
Knowing which attributes of an architecture minimize effort and maximize productivity
Hiring the largest possible team
Starting the system over from scratch
optionExplain: Right: the author says you need to know what good architecture is.
Right: you also need to know which attributes lead to minimal effort and maximal productivity.
More staff is what the case study company did, with costs exploding.
The author doubts that starting over helps.
questions.explain: The conclusion says that to take architecture seriously you must know what good architecture is and which of its attributes lead to low effort and high productivity. The book exists to describe them.
questions.teaches: Taking architecture seriously requires knowing what good architecture is; the author says the book exists to describe good clean architectures and designs so developers can build systems with long profitable lifetimes.
questions.rule: To fight for it, know what good looks like.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, if architecture comes last and change becomes impractical, the development team did not fight hard enough.
questions.explain: He says that in this case the software development team did not fight hard enough for what they knew was necessary.
questions.rule: The team that knew carries the duty.

questions.q: A city council tells its planner to postpone water-main replacement in favor of ribbon-cutting projects. Years later mains fail in some districts. Applying the author's logic about who carries responsibility, who is most at fault?
options: The council, which cannot be expected to know the condition of the pipes beneath the streets
The planner, who knew what was necessary and did not fight hard enough
The residents, who did not protest when the water-main work was put off
Nobody, because the pressure for visible projects was urgent and could not be resisted
optionExplain: The author reasons that those not equipped to evaluate are not the ones expected to carry the duty.
Right: the author blames the team that knew what was necessary and did not fight hard enough.
Residents are not the party with the knowledge in the author's logic.
Urgency is the very pressure the author asks the knowing party to resist.
questions.explain: The author blames the development team because it knew what was necessary. Responsibility follows knowledge of what the system needs.
questions.teaches: Responsibility follows knowledge: the author blames the team because it knew what was necessary, not the managers who were not equipped to evaluate it.
questions.rule: Whoever knows carries the duty to fight.

questions.q: Which language feature did Dijkstra show to be harmful to program structure?
options: Recursive function calls
Local variables in functions
Unrestrained jumps with goto
Comments between statements
optionExplain: Recursion is a plausible suspect because it is hard to trace, but Dijkstra's target was the jump.
Locals can cause confusion, yet they were not his target.
Right: goto lets control jump anywhere. The card next shows what replaced it.
Comments do not change control flow at all.
questions.explain: Dijkstra's 1968 argument was about goto. The next card shows what replaced it.
questions.rule: Structured programming begins with goto.

questions.q: True or false: Structured programming gave programmers a new capability that earlier languages lacked.
questions.explain: It did the opposite: it removed unrestrained jumps. The book stresses that each paradigm takes something away.
questions.rule: Structured programming subtracts; it does not add.

questions.q: A legacy shipping script uses goto to skip a step when stock is zero and to repeat a check until a counter reaches ten. Select the constructs that replace those jumps in a structured version.
options: An if/then/else around the step that may be skipped
A do/while loop that repeats the check
A function pointer chosen at run time for each step
A global flag that each step sets before jumping
optionExplain: Right: selection covers the skip.
Right: iteration covers the repeat.
This is indirect transfer, the concern of a different paradigm, and it replaces nothing here.
A flag still needs a jump to act on it, so unrestrained transfer remains.
questions.explain: The book names selection and iteration constructs as the replacements for jumps.
questions.rule: Skip with if, repeat with a loop.
questions.hint: Which two constructs does the card name?

questions.q: Some readers point to named breaks in Java, or to exceptions, as goto in disguise. What does the book say about them?
options: They are not the unrestricted transfers of older Fortran or COBOL
They break the paradigm, so Java cannot count as structured programming
They are identical to goto and should be avoided in all new code
They only count as structured when used inside a loop or a function
optionExplain: Right: they are constrained, so they fit the discipline.
It sounds consistent with a ban on goto, but the book says these constructs are restricted.
They look alike, but identical is too strong: the target is limited.
The book draws no such condition about loops.
questions.explain: The book separates restricted transfers from the free jumps of older languages.
questions.rule: Restricted jumps are not the target.
questions.teaches: Named breaks and exceptions are restricted transfers of control, unlike the utterly unrestricted jumps of Fortran or COBOL.

questions.q: True or false: A team deletes the goto keyword from its C code base but adds a macro that jumps to any label in the program. The discipline of structured programming is still in force.
questions.explain: The discipline concerns direct transfer of control. A macro that jumps anywhere restores the unrestrained jump under another name.
questions.rule: Judge the freedom to jump, not the keyword.

questions.q: A language keeps the goto keyword but only allows jumps to labels inside the current function. How does this compare to the old languages the book describes?
options: It is the same as the old languages, because any use of goto is an unrestrained transfer
It is less restricted, because keeping the keyword means nothing was really taken away
It cannot be compared, because scope rules belong to a different paradigm altogether
It is more restricted, since such languages often limit the target to the current function
optionExplain: A keyword can look decisive, but the reach of the jump matters, and here it is limited.
Keeping the word suggests nothing was removed, but the scope limit removes power.
Scope rules are one way of limiting jumps, so the comparison holds.
Right: the keyword alone does not decide how unrestrained the transfer is.
questions.explain: The book notes that many languages with a goto keyword limit its target to the function scope.
questions.rule: Reach matters, not the keyword.
questions.teaches: Even languages that still support the goto keyword often restrict its target to the scope of the current function.

questions.q: In 1966 two programmers noticed that something in ALGOL could be moved from the stack to the heap. What was it?
options: The compiler's table of names
The stack frame of a function call
The machine instructions of the program
The global variables of the program
optionExplain: A plausible guess about compilers, but the discovery concerned running programs.
Right: its locals could then outlive the call. The card next shows what grew from this.
Instructions are code, not call-time data.
Globals already outlive any call.
questions.explain: The call stack frame moved to the heap. The card next explains what that made possible.
questions.rule: The frame moved; classes followed.

questions.q: True or false: In the discovery by Dahl and Nygaard, the function became a constructor of a class and its local variables became instance variables.
questions.explain: Right: constructor, instance variables and methods are the three mappings.
questions.rule: Function becomes constructor, locals become instance variables.

questions.q: A function in an old language builds a report from local variables, but they vanish when it returns. Which change from the 1966 discovery lets them outlive the call?
options: Turn the locals into globals and call the function once
Keep the call's frame on a heap so the locals persist
Replace the return statement with a jump to a label
Pass every local in as an argument on each call
optionExplain: Globals persist, but that discards the idea of per-call state the discovery kept.
Right: the frame outlives the call, and the function becomes a constructor.
Jumps change control flow, not the lifetime of the locals.
This moves the data around without giving the function any state of its own.
questions.explain: A heap-allocated frame lets locals live past the return.
questions.rule: Heap frame, lasting locals.

questions.q: Dahl and Nygaard's discovery dates from 1966 and Dijkstra's goto letter from 1968. Which paradigm was adopted first?
options: Object-oriented programming, because it was discovered first
Functional programming, because it is the oldest idea
All three together, in the early 1970s
Structured programming, though it was discovered second
optionExplain: Discovery order feels like adoption order, but the book separates them.
It was invented first of all, but it has only recently begun to be adopted.
The book describes them arriving one after another.
Right: structured programming was the first adopted but not the first invented.
questions.explain: Adoption order and invention order differ for the first two paradigms.
questions.rule: Adopted first is not invented first.
questions.teaches: Structured programming was adopted first although object-oriented programming was discovered two years earlier.

questions.q: A student summarises the 1966 discovery. Select the two mistakes.
options: The stack frame of a function call moved to a heap
The function became a constructor of a class
The local variables became the methods of the class
The nested functions became instance variables
optionExplain: Correct as stated.
Correct as stated.
Mistake: locals became instance variables.
Mistake: nested functions became methods.
questions.explain: Locals map to instance variables and nested functions map to methods.
questions.rule: Locals to instance variables, nested functions to methods.

questions.q: A C programmer stores pointers to functions in a struct, fills them in once at start-up, and calls everything through them. Which part of the book's history does this repeat by hand?
options: Polymorphism, from disciplined use of function pointers
The move of the function call stack frame to a heap
The removal of goto from the language by Dijkstra's rule
The ban on assignment found in the lambda calculus
optionExplain: Right: it is the mechanism OO languages later made routine.
That change is about where locals live, not how calls are routed.
That belongs to structured programming.
That belongs to functional programming.
questions.explain: Calling through stored function pointers is indirect transfer of control, which OO disciplines.
questions.rule: Function pointers by convention become polymorphism by language.
questions.teaches: Polymorphism arises when function pointers are used in a disciplined way, so a hand-built table of them in C is the same mechanism without language support.

questions.q: Which of the three paradigms was invented first?
options: Structured programming, because it is the simplest
Object-oriented programming, because of the early ALGOL work in 1966
Functional programming, which predates computer programming
None; all three were invented in the same year
optionExplain: It was adopted first, but simplicity says nothing about the date.
OO came in 1966, long after the first idea.
Right: its roots are in the 1930s. The card next gives the details.
They were years apart.
questions.explain: Functional programming is the oldest idea of the three. The card next shows its core notion.
questions.rule: The oldest paradigm is functional.

questions.q: True or false: A foundational notion of lambda calculus is that the values of symbols do not change.
questions.explain: Right: immutability is the foundational notion, and it leads to a language with no assignment.
questions.rule: Immutability is the foundation.

questions.q: A language lets a variable be set once and then read many times; changing it later requires a special guarded operation. Which paradigm's discipline does this show?
options: Structured programming, discipline on direct transfer
Object-oriented programming, discipline on indirect transfer
None of the three; the rule is a matter of style
Functional programming, discipline upon assignment
optionExplain: That paradigm concerns jumps, not changing values.
That concerns calls through pointers, not values.
The book names exactly this kind of restriction as the third paradigm.
Right: assignment is allowed only under strict rules.
questions.explain: The restriction falls on assignment, which is functional programming's concern.
questions.rule: Guarded change means discipline on assignment.

questions.q: Functional programming was the first paradigm to be invented, but it has only ____ begun to be adopted.
questions.explain: The book gives functional programming the earliest invention and the latest adoption.
questions.rule: Oldest idea, newest adoption.
questions.teaches: Functional programming, though invented first, has only recently begun to be adopted.

questions.q: True or false: A language is not functional in the book's sense if it offers any way at all to change a variable's value.
questions.explain: Most functional languages do offer some way to change a variable, but only under very strict discipline.
questions.rule: Disciplined assignment still counts.

questions.q: A hardware team believes that unchanging values are a recent fashion linked to multi-core processors. What does the book's history say?
options: It began with Java in the 1990s, alongside object-oriented programming
It comes from the 1936 lambda calculus, which LISP of 1958 builds on
It began in 1968 with Dijkstra's letter on the goto statement
It began with C++ in the 1980s, as classes were added to C
optionExplain: Java is a mutable-variable language; the idea is far older.
Right: the idea is older than computer programming itself.
That letter concerned goto.
The book ties it to lambda calculus instead.
questions.explain: The book traces immutability to Church in 1936 and to LISP, invented by McCarthy in 1958.
questions.rule: Immutability is older than programming.
questions.teaches: Church invented lambda calculus in 1936 and McCarthy built LISP on it in 1958, so immutability is older than computer programming itself.

questions.q: A new programming paradigm is announced. Which description would fit all the paradigms the book discusses so far?
options: It adds a capability earlier languages lacked
It speeds up programs by changing the hardware they run on
It removes a capability the programmer used to have
It replaces every earlier paradigm entirely
optionExplain: Paradigms sound like advances, yet each one subtracts.
Hardware is not the subject of the paradigms.
Right: each paradigm takes something away. The card next explains.
The three coexist in modern practice.
questions.explain: All three paradigms subtract. The card next puts the pattern in one line.
questions.rule: Paradigms subtract.

questions.q: Match each paradigm to the capability it removes.
questions.explain: The book lists the three together as goto statements, function pointers and assignment.
questions.rule: Goto, function pointers, assignment.

questions.q: Which of these changes to a language would the book count as paradigm-like, in the sense of the three paradigms?
options: A rule that forbids a variable to be altered once it is set
A compiler that builds large programs in half the usual time
A library that adds a hundred extra sorting routines for speed
A debugger that lets you step backwards through a program run
optionExplain: Right: it removes a capability to impose discipline.
Faster building adds speed, not a restriction.
A library adds features, which is the opposite of the pattern.
Tooling adds ability and removes nothing.
questions.explain: Only the rule removes something from the programmer.
questions.rule: A paradigm restricts.

questions.q: What evidence does the book give that no further negative paradigm is likely to appear?
options: Computer scientists proved that exactly three restrictions can exist
Hardware limits make any further restriction on programmers impossible
All three date from 1958 to 1968, and none has been added since
Every language in use today applies exactly three paradigms at once
optionExplain: A proof sounds convincing, but the book offers no proof.
The book does not argue from hardware.
Right: a short burst of discovery followed by a long silence.
That describes practice, not why there are no more.
questions.explain: The book's evidence is historical: discovery clustered in 1958 to 1968.
questions.rule: A decade of discovery, then none.
questions.teaches: The three paradigms were all discovered within the ten years between 1958 and 1968, and no new one has been added in the decades since.

questions.q: A colleague describes the three paradigms. Select the two statements that go against the book.
options: Each paradigm adds a capability while it removes another
Together they remove goto, function pointers and assignment
New paradigms have appeared steadily in every decade since 1968
The paradigms tell us more about what not to do than what to do
optionExplain: Against the book: none of them adds any capability.
As the book states.
Against the book: none has been added since.
As the book states.
questions.explain: The book says paradigms only subtract, and that none has been added since the 1960s.
questions.rule: Subtract only; none since 1968.

questions.q: A manager says software advances as quickly as hardware. What does the book's closing remark on the paradigms say in reply?
options: The rules of software are the same as in 1946; only tools changed
The manager is right, because each new decade added a new paradigm
Software has stood still because its tools have never improved
Software advances only when the underlying hardware advances too
optionExplain: Right: the essence of software has not changed since 1946.
The book says no paradigm was added after 1968.
The book allows that tools have changed; its claim is about the essence.
The book separates the two.
questions.explain: The book's conclusion says software is not a rapidly advancing technology.
questions.rule: Tools change, essence stays.
questions.teaches: The rules of software are the same as in 1946, when Turing wrote the first code to run on an electronic computer; tools and hardware have changed but the essence has not.

questions.q: An architect must let a user interface and the business rules be developed apart. Which mechanism would you expect the book to name for crossing that boundary?
options: Goto statements
Assignment to shared variables
A longer list of comments
Polymorphism
optionExplain: A jump across a boundary would tie the two sides together.
Shared mutable data joins the sides rather than separating them.
Comments do not enforce a boundary.
Right: it is the book's mechanism for crossing boundaries. The card next shows the full map.
questions.explain: Polymorphism is how the book crosses boundaries. The card shows how the other two paradigms fit.
questions.rule: Polymorphism crosses boundaries.

questions.q: Match each paradigm to the architectural concern it serves.
questions.explain: Each of the three paradigms lines up with one big concern of architecture.
questions.rule: Three paradigms, three concerns.

questions.q: A team's bug reports all involve two threads updating one account balance at the same time. Which paradigm's discipline does the book point to for this concern?
options: Structured programming, which governs the algorithms inside modules
Functional programming, the paradigm tied to data management
Object-oriented programming, which handles crossing boundaries
None, because the book treats concurrency as unrelated to paradigms
optionExplain: It shapes the logic inside a function, not who may change data.
Right: the concern is data management.
Boundaries are a separate concern from concurrent updates.
The book later ties concurrency to mutable variables.
questions.explain: Concurrent updates are a data management problem.
questions.rule: Data management belongs to functional discipline.

questions.q: How does the book describe the part functional programming plays in architecture?
options: It decides how components are packaged and released together
It imposes discipline on the location of and access to data
It replaces polymorphism at the architectural boundaries
It removes the need for any algorithms inside modules
optionExplain: Packaging is a different matter.
Right: the concern is where data lives and who may touch it.
The two have different jobs in the book's map.
Algorithms remain; they are the job of structured programming.
questions.explain: The book words it as discipline on the location of and access to data.
questions.rule: Functional discipline guards data.
questions.teaches: Functional programming serves architecture by imposing discipline on where data is located and on who can access it.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's map, polymorphism is the algorithmic foundation of a module, and structured programming is the mechanism for crossing boundaries.
questions.explain: The roles are the other way round: structured programming is the foundation of a module's algorithms and polymorphism crosses boundaries.
questions.rule: Algorithm inside, polymorphism across.

questions.q: A bank splits its software into a payments part and a reporting part that must change independently. Which mechanism does the book name for crossing that boundary, and what does it give the architect?
options: Goto statements, which let control cross the boundary wherever it needs to
Shared variables, which let both parts read the same data at will
Structured loops, which repeat calls across the boundary again
Polymorphism, which lets the architect point dependencies either way
optionExplain: Free jumps tie the parts together.
Shared mutable data couples the parts.
Loops structure an algorithm inside a module.
Right: dependencies need not follow the flow of control.
questions.explain: The book later explains that polymorphism gives control over the direction of source dependencies.
questions.rule: Polymorphism frees the direction of dependency.
questions.teaches: Used at a boundary, polymorphism lets the architect point the source code dependency either way, whatever the flow of control.

questions.q: Dijkstra wanted programmers to build programs the way mathematicians build theory. What was the main reason?
options: Programs hold too many details for a mind to manage unaided
Mathematicians write faster than programmers do
Computers could not run programs that were untested
Programming languages already contained a proof engine
optionExplain: Right: proof was his way to tame the details. The card next explains.
Speed was not his point.
Testing is not the issue in his argument.
No such engine is mentioned.
questions.explain: Complexity was the problem he set out to solve. The card next shows his plan.
questions.rule: Proof tames detail.

questions.q: True or false: Dijkstra found that certain uses of goto prevent a module from being recursively decomposed into smaller units.
questions.explain: Right: without decomposition, divide and conquer cannot be used for proofs.
questions.rule: Some goto blocks decomposition.

questions.q: A proof engineer wants to prove a payroll routine correct by proving each small part and combining them. What must be true of the routine for this plan to work?
options: It must be short enough to be read in a single sitting
It must avoid every function call so that nothing is hidden
It can be split recursively into smaller and smaller units
It must run faster than the equivalent hand-written loop
optionExplain: Length is not the condition; decomposability is.
Calls are not the obstacle in the book.
Right: divide and conquer needs recursive decomposition.
Speed does not matter for the proof.
questions.explain: Decomposition into provable units is what the plan needs.
questions.rule: Provable means decomposable.

questions.q: Were all uses of goto equally an obstacle to proof?
options: Yes: any use of goto at all defeats recursive decomposition of a module
No: only goto that jumped out of a function body was a problem
Yes, but the problem was solved by adding more comments
No: the good uses matched selection and iteration, like if and while
optionExplain: That is the plain reading, but the book says other uses did not have the problem.
The book draws no such line about location.
Comments do not restore provability.
Right: modules using only those structures could be subdivided into provable units.
questions.explain: Dijkstra noticed that the harmless uses corresponded to selection and iteration.
questions.rule: Good gotos look like if and while.
questions.teaches: Some uses of goto did not block decomposition: they corresponded to simple selection and iteration constructs such as if/then/else and do/while.

questions.q: A module built only from if/then/else and do/while constructs can be recursively ____ into provable units.
questions.explain: Right: these structures keep the module decomposable, which is what the proof method needs.
questions.rule: Use only these constructs and the pieces stay provable.

questions.q: A student starting to prove programs expects even simple algorithms to be easy to prove. What did Dijkstra find when he first tried to demonstrate basic proofs?
options: He found it easy, since simple algorithms leave no room for error
He found it quite challenging, even for simple algorithms
He found it impossible, so he dropped proof for testing
He found it straightforward once goto was removed
optionExplain: Small size feels safe, but the book says otherwise.
Right: the first proofs were hard won.
He did not drop proof at that point.
Removing goto made proof possible, not easy.
questions.explain: Before the hierarchy could grow, the technique for basic proofs had to be shown.
questions.rule: Even basic proofs were hard.
questions.teaches: Dijkstra found it quite challenging to demonstrate the technique of writing basic proofs, even for simple algorithms.

questions.q: Böhm and Jacopini proved that every program can be built from a small set of structures. How many structures?
options: One
Five
Three
Twelve
optionExplain: A single structure would be too weak to branch or repeat.
More feels safer, but three suffice.
Right: sequence, selection and iteration. The card next names them.
A large set is not needed.
questions.explain: Three structures are enough. The card next names them.
questions.rule: Three structures build every program.

questions.q: Put these in the order Dijkstra's argument reaches them.
items: Some goto uses block decomposition into provable units
Good uses match if/then/else and do/while
These structures with sequence were identified by Böhm and Jacopini
The provable structures equal the minimum set that builds every program
questions.explain: Dijkstra moved from the obstacle, to the harmless structures, to the earlier proof that three structures suffice, and then to the match.
questions.rule: Obstacle, harmless set, minimum set, match.

questions.q: A scheduling program needs to run steps in order, choose between two routes, and repeat a check until it passes. Which structures cover this need?
options: Sequence, selection and iteration
Sequence and goto, which jump between the steps
Selection and recursion, with nothing for ordered steps
Iteration and polymorphism, with no way to choose
optionExplain: Right: they correspond to ordered steps, a choice, and a repeat.
Goto is the structure the paradigm removes.
Order of steps is missing.
Polymorphism is a different paradigm's concern.
questions.explain: Order, choice and repeat map to sequence, selection and iteration.
questions.rule: Order, choice, repeat.

questions.q: The book calls the match between provable structures and the minimum buildable set remarkable. What does the match show?
options: Provable programs run faster than programs that are full of jumps
Goto can be proven correct if enough effort is spent on it
Restricting programs to these structures loses no expressive power
Any program built only from these structures is then bound to be correct
optionExplain: Speed is not part of the claim.
The book says some uses of goto block proof.
Right: they are also the set from which all programs can be built.
Using the structures makes a module provable, not correct.
questions.explain: A restriction that costs nothing makes the paradigm attractive.
questions.rule: Restriction without loss.
questions.teaches: Because the provable structures are also the minimum set that builds every program, giving up unrestrained goto costs no expressive power.

questions.q: True or false: A language offering only sequence, selection and iteration can still express every program.
questions.explain: Böhm and Jacopini proved that all programs can be constructed from those three structures.
questions.rule: Three structures reach every program.

questions.q: A trainer lists the ingredients of all software as sequence, selection and iteration, and says one more is needed for polymorphic calls. Which ingredient does the book add to the three structures?
options: Indirection
Assignment
Recursion
Encapsulation
optionExplain: Right: indirect transfer through pointers is the fourth element.
Assignment is what the functional paradigm disciplines, but the book does not list it as an ingredient.
Recursion is not on the book's list.
The book argues that encapsulation does not define OO.
questions.explain: The book's closing says software is composed of sequence, selection, iteration and indirection.
questions.rule: Add indirection to the three.
questions.teaches: Software is composed of sequence, selection, iteration and indirection, and nothing more.

questions.q: To prove that a loop does the right thing for any number of repeats, which kind of argument does the book say Dijkstra used?
options: Enumeration of every possible run
Measurement against many examples
A single trace of one example run
Induction
optionExplain: Enumeration cannot cover an unbounded number of repeats.
That is the scientific method, not a proof.
One run shows one case only.
Right: case 1, then N implies N + 1. The card next gives the whole scheme.
questions.explain: Loops need induction. The card next shows the scheme for all three structures.
questions.rule: Loops need induction.

questions.q: Match each structure to the proof technique the book describes.
pairs: Induction plus start and end criteria
questions.explain: Sequence and selection use enumeration; iteration needs induction.
questions.rule: Enumerate, enumerate, induct.

questions.q: Consider the Python function below. Following the book's method for selection, what must be shown to prove it returns the absolute value?
options: That the function gave correct results when run on one negative and one positive number
That the negative path returns -n and the other returns n, each correct
That the function is short, with fewer than ten lines of code in it
That the condition n < 0 is written without any use of a goto
optionExplain: Two runs are tests, not a proof of every path.
Right: each path is enumerated.
Length has no bearing on correctness.
Having no goto allows the proof but is not the proof.
questions.explain: Selection is proved by enumerating each path.
questions.rule: Prove every path of a selection.

questions.q: In an induction proof of a loop, what else must be proved besides the step from N to N + 1?
options: That the loop does not run more than once on any input
The starting and ending criteria of the iteration
That the loop body contains a jump
That the loop is faster than a recursive version
optionExplain: A loop may run many times.
Right: the book says these are proved by enumeration.
A jump would block the proof.
Speed is not part of correctness.
questions.explain: Induction needs a base case, the step, and the boundary conditions.
questions.rule: Prove the start and end too.
questions.teaches: An iteration proof also needs its starting and ending criteria, which the book proves by enumeration.

questions.q: True or false: If the induction step shows that N correct implies N + 1 correct, and case 1 is shown correct, the loop is correct for every number of repeats.
questions.explain: That is the structure of the book's induction proof, together with the start and end criteria.
questions.rule: Base case plus step covers all repeats.

questions.q: A colleague says the proofs for sequence, selection and iteration were too laborious to count as real proofs. How does the book classify them?
options: Not real proofs at all, only tests dressed up with a formal look to them
Proofs, but of no use for building a hierarchy of theorems
Proofs that were short and easy to repeat for any program
Laborious, but still proofs, and they made the hierarchy seem reachable
optionExplain: The book says they were proofs.
The book says they made the hierarchy seem reachable.
The book calls them laborious and complex.
Right: the effort did not make them any less of a proof.
questions.explain: The book separates how hard the proofs were from whether they were proofs.
questions.rule: Hard work is still proof.
questions.teaches: The proofs of the three structures were laborious and complex but real proofs, and with them the idea of building a Euclidean hierarchy of theorems seemed reachable.

questions.q: How does the book say the public argument over Dijkstra's 1968 letter ended?
options: It faded after about a decade because Dijkstra had won
It ended when Dijkstra withdrew the letter
It ended in a draw, with both views taught today
It never ended, because the letter is still being disputed today
optionExplain: Right: goto retreated from languages. The card next tells how.
He did not withdraw it.
The book says one side won.
The book says it petered out.
questions.explain: Dijkstra's side won. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: Dijkstra won.

questions.q: True or false: The goto debate sparked by Dijkstra's letter lasted about a decade before it petered out.
questions.explain: Right: letters in journals, for and against, went on for about ten years.
questions.rule: A decade of argument, then silence.

questions.q: A team chooses a modern language for a new project and finds it has no goto at all. In the book's words, what does that make them?
options: Rebels against the paradigm they were taught
Unstructured, since structure requires a deliberate decision
Structured programmers, though not necessarily by choice
Functional programmers, as the language lacks jumps
optionExplain: The language, not the team, made the choice.
The book says discipline can come from the language.
Right: the language leaves no option of undisciplined jumps.
Removing jumps is the structured paradigm's concern.
questions.explain: The language enforces the discipline for everyone.
questions.rule: Languages made us structured.
questions.hint: Who made the choice, the team or the language?

questions.q: What did the book say happened to goto as languages evolved?
options: It was replaced by a safer keyword called jump
It was kept in every language but hidden by tools
It became more popular as languages grew richer in features
It moved ever rearward until it all but disappeared
optionExplain: No replacement keyword is described.
The book says it largely disappeared.
The opposite happened.
Right: most modern languages do not have it.
questions.explain: Languages dropped goto, and LISP never had it.
questions.rule: Goto retreated.
questions.teaches: As computer languages evolved, goto moved ever rearward until it all but disappeared, and LISP never had it.

questions.q: Named breaks and exceptions are ____ transfers of control, not the unrestricted jumps of older languages.
questions.explain: Right: they are constrained, so the discipline stands.
questions.rule: Restricted is not unrestricted.

questions.q: An engineer expects that a proposal to remove a long-used language feature will be met with general agreement. Which part of the goto story cuts against this?
options: The journals refused to print any letters on the matter, so no debate took place
The letters were split between intensely negative and strongly supportive
Every letter backed Dijkstra, though some took years to arrive
The matter was settled within a week by a ruling of an editor
optionExplain: Letters were printed and written in large numbers.
Right: the response was mixed and sharp.
Some letters were intensely negative.
The battle lasted about a decade.
questions.explain: Strong feelings on both sides drove a decade-long argument.
questions.rule: Expect a fight over removed features.
questions.teaches: Letters answering Dijkstra were not all polite: some were intensely negative and others voiced strong support.

questions.q: A team receives a large problem statement. Which method does the book connect to structured programming?
options: Write one large routine first and divide it into smaller parts afterwards
Create a class for each real-world object in the problem first
Break it into high-level functions, then break each into lower ones
Copy a proven design from another system and then adapt it to fit
optionExplain: Dividing afterwards ignores the top-down method.
Modelling the world is a different approach.
Right: that is functional decomposition. The card next explains why it works.
Copying is not described as a method here.
questions.explain: The method is a top-down breakdown into functions. The card next shows why structured code allows it.
questions.rule: Break the problem into functions, level by level.

questions.q: Structured programming allows modules to be recursively decomposed into ____ units.
questions.explain: Right: provable units, which is why modules can be functionally decomposed.
questions.rule: Provable units allow decomposition.

questions.q: An airline wants a booking system. Following functional decomposition, what is the first step?
options: Split it into a few high-level functions, such as search, reserve and ticket
Draw the database tables for seats and flights, then add the functions
Write the lowest-level seat-numbering code first and then build everything upwards
Pick a framework and let it dictate the structure of the system
optionExplain: Right: top-down, level by level.
Tables describe data, not the functions that decompose the problem.
That is bottom-up, the reverse of the method.
A framework choice is not a decomposition.
questions.explain: Functional decomposition starts from the whole and divides.
questions.rule: Start with the whole problem and divide.

questions.q: What did the disciplines of structured analysis and structured design aim to let programmers do?
options: Replace testing altogether with careful reviews of the design diagrams at every stage
Hide data inside objects so that clients cannot see it at all
Break large systems into modules and components, then into tiny provable functions
Move the stack frame to a heap so that locals live longer
optionExplain: Testing is not described as replaced.
Hiding data is encapsulation, a separate topic.
Right: that was the goal of the method.
That is the object-oriented discovery.
questions.explain: These disciplines applied decomposition to whole systems.
questions.rule: Systems break down into modules, then tiny functions.
questions.teaches: Structured analysis and design aimed to break large proposed systems into modules and components, and those into tiny provable functions.

questions.q: Select the two statements that the book supports about functional decomposition.
options: Decomposition runs from high-level functions to lower-level ones
Each decomposed function may jump with goto between levels
Decomposition can continue level after level without a fixed limit
Decomposition must stop after three levels
optionExplain: Supported: it is top-down.
Not supported: unrestrained jumps are what block decomposition.
Supported: the book says it can go on ad infinitum.
Not supported: the book sets no such limit.
questions.explain: Decomposition runs top-down and can be repeated at every level.
questions.rule: Top-down, level after level.

questions.q: A city office splits improve transport into bus, rail and cycling, and then splits bus into routes and timetables. Which feature of functional decomposition does this show?
options: Each level is broken into lower-level parts, again and again
Each part is merged back into a single department once it is done
Each part reuses the same route in a loop until it is done
Each part hides its data from all of the other parts
optionExplain: Right: the same top-down breakdown.
Merging is the opposite of decomposition.
Looping is iteration, not decomposition.
Hiding data is encapsulation.
questions.explain: The book describes decomposition continuing level after level.
questions.rule: Break down level by level.
questions.teaches: Each function produced by the decomposition can itself be written using the restricted control structures of structured programming.

questions.q: Decades after Dijkstra's proposal, how does the book say programmers regard formal proofs for producing quality software?
options: Most of them require a proof for each function
All of them use proofs for safety-critical code only
They have not heard of Dijkstra's idea about proving programs
Few of them believe formal proofs are an appropriate way
optionExplain: A strict rule sounds responsible, but the book says the opposite.
The book makes no such claim.
The idea is well known; it simply did not catch on.
Right: the dream faded. The card next tells the story.
questions.explain: Proofs did not catch on. The card next shows what happened to the hierarchy.
questions.rule: Formal proof faded.

questions.q: True or false: The Euclidean hierarchy of theorems that Dijkstra imagined was eventually built by programmers.
questions.explain: The book says the proofs never came and the hierarchy was never built.
questions.rule: The hierarchy was never built.

questions.q: A project lead says no function ships without a formal Euclidean-style proof. Using the book's history, how likely is it that programmers at large would accept this rule?
options: Likely: the rule follows directly from the structured programming paradigm
Unlikely: few believe that formal proofs are the way to quality software
Certain: Dijkstra proved that the rule is necessary for all code
Impossible: nobody is able to write a proof of a real program function
optionExplain: Structured programming made proof possible, but did not make proof popular.
Right: the practice never won over programmers.
Dijkstra never established such a rule.
Proofs could be written; they were laborious.
questions.explain: The practice did not spread.
questions.rule: Possible is not popular.

questions.q: Programmers at large did not see the benefits of the ____ process of formally proving each little function.
questions.explain: The book's explanation is effort without visible benefit.
questions.rule: Laborious, with no benefit seen.
questions.teaches: Programmers at large never saw the benefit of the laborious process of formally proving each and every little function correct.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, a Euclidean-style mathematical proof is not the only strategy for showing something correct: the scientific method is another.
questions.explain: The book says another highly successful strategy is the scientific method.
questions.rule: Proof is not the only strategy.

questions.q: A medicine is accepted after many trials rather than by a mathematical argument. Which strategy named in the book does this resemble?
options: A Euclidean hierarchy of theorems
The scientific method
Induction on the number of loops
Polymorphic dispatch
optionExplain: That is Dijkstra's proof style, the one that faded.
Right: it relies on evidence rather than formal proof.
That is a proof technique for iteration.
That is unrelated to ways of showing correctness.
questions.explain: The book names the scientific method as another highly successful strategy.
questions.rule: Evidence is a strategy too.
questions.teaches: The book names the scientific method as another highly successful strategy for showing something correct, besides Euclidean-style proof.

questions.q: Newton's second law, F = ma, is relied on every day. Which description fits how the book says science treats it?
options: It was proved correct once and for all by repeated experiment
It is a mathematical theorem derived from a small set of axioms
It is only a guess that engineers must keep re-checking each year
It has survived every attempt to disprove it but is not proved
optionExplain: Many measurements feel like proof, but they cannot be one.
Laws of science are not theorems in this sense.
Trust rests on failed attempts to disprove, not on guessing.
Right: laws are falsifiable, not provable. The card next explains.
questions.explain: Science cannot prove its laws, only fail to disprove them. The card next shows the idea.
questions.rule: Laws are falsifiable, not provable.

questions.q: True or false: Scientific theories and laws are falsifiable but not provable.
questions.explain: Right: no number of experiments proves a law, but one could show it wrong.
questions.rule: Falsifiable, not provable.

questions.q: A lab has seen a thousand white swans in a region and nothing else. What is the status of the claim that all swans in the region are white, under the book's view of science?
options: Not proved; deemed true enough until a counterexample shows it false
Proved, since the sample of a thousand swans is large enough
Meaningless until the lab has examined every swan that is alive today
False, because no claim in science can be regarded as true
optionExplain: Right: failure to falsify earns trust, not proof.
A large sample suggests proof but cannot supply it.
A complete survey is not the standard the book describes.
The book says survivors are deemed true enough.
questions.explain: A single counterexample would overturn it; none has, so it stands.
questions.rule: No counterexample yet means true enough.

questions.q: Does the book say every statement can be proved or disproved?
options: Yes, every statement can be settled if enough effort is made
Yes, though only mathematics is able to settle them all
No: 'This is a lie' is neither true nor false
No, because most statements are far too long to check properly
optionExplain: Effort cannot settle a statement that is neither true nor false.
Mathematics proves provable statements, not all of them.
Right: some statements fall outside proof altogether.
Length is not the obstacle.
questions.explain: The book gives the liar-style statement as the simplest unprovable example.
questions.rule: Not every statement is provable.
questions.teaches: Not every statement is provable: 'This is a lie' is neither true nor false, and the book offers it as one of the simplest unprovable examples.

questions.q: Sort each description under mathematics or science, as the book distinguishes them.

items.t: Proves provable statements true
Builds a Euclidean hierarchy of theorems
Proves provable statements false
Accepts laws that survive every attempt to disprove them

questions.explain: Mathematics proves provable statements true; science proves provable statements false.
questions.rule: Math proves true; science proves false.

questions.q: A pharmacist says a drug is proven safe because ten trials found no harm. How should this be restated using the book's standard?
options: It is certainly safe, so further trials would be pointless
It is unsafe until a formal proof of safety is written
It is neither safe nor unsafe, like the statement 'This is a lie'
No trial has shown it unsafe, so it is deemed safe enough
optionExplain: Certainty is what science does not claim.
Science does not require a proof of safety.
That statement is a special case of an unprovable claim.
Right: failure to falsify is what the evidence gives.
questions.explain: We bet our lives on laws that cannot be proved, such as F = ma every time we get into a car.
questions.rule: Trust is earned by surviving attempts to refute.
questions.teaches: We bet our lives daily on laws that cannot be proved, such as F = ma when we ride in a car, and we accept them as true enough for our purposes.

questions.q: True or false: A program that passes thousands of tests has been proven correct.
