questions.explain: Passing tests means no bug was found yet. The card next shows why that is not a proof.
questions.rule: Tests cannot prove correctness.

questions.q: Testing shows the presence, not the ____, of bugs.
questions.explain: Right: a failing test reveals a bug, but passing tests cannot show that none exists.
questions.rule: Presence, not absence.

questions.q: A developer writes three tests for the function below, using 2024, 2023 and 2000, and all pass. What do the results show?
options: The function is correct for every year, since all tests passed
No bug found yet; the function is not thereby proven correct
The function is wrong, since tests must fail in order to count
The tests are wrong, because 2000 should return False here
optionExplain: Passing three tests feels convincing but covers three years.
Right: the function still fails for 1900.
A passing test is not a failure of the function.
2000 is a leap year, so True is right.
questions.explain: Three passing cases cannot prove the rest of the cases.
questions.rule: Passing tests prove nothing about untested cases.

questions.q: What does the book say about the nature of software development?
options: It is a mathematical endeavour, so proof is the way to settle its correctness
It is an art, and so correctness has no real meaning in it
It is not a mathematical endeavour, although it uses mathematical constructs
It is an engineering craft with no connection to science at all
optionExplain: It manipulates mathematical constructs, which makes this tempting.
The book does not say correctness is meaningless.
Right: it is more like a science.
The book says it is like a science.
questions.explain: Software behaves like a science: correctness is shown by failing to disprove.
questions.rule: Software is like a science.
questions.teaches: Software development is not a mathematical endeavour although it manipulates mathematical constructs; it is like a science.

questions.q: True or false: A test suite that fails to find a bug after years of effort lets us deem the program correct enough for our purposes, not proven correct.
questions.explain: It only lets us deem the program correct enough for our purposes; tests show the presence of bugs, never their absence.
questions.rule: Failing to disprove is the best we get.

questions.q: A regulator asks for a certificate that a piece of flight software contains no bugs, based on its test results. What is the best reply from the book's position?
options: Tests show bugs but not their absence, so we can only deem it correct enough
Provide many more tests, since enough tests will in the end prove it correct
Provide a Euclidean proof of every function in the software as well
Decline, since software of this kind cannot be tested at all
optionExplain: Right: testing cannot give a no-bugs certificate.
Any number of tests still cannot prove correctness.
The book says that approach never took hold.
Testing is useful, just not conclusive.
questions.explain: The right standard is correctness shown by failing, despite our best efforts, to prove incorrectness.
questions.rule: No test can certify the absence of bugs.
questions.teaches: We show correctness by failing to prove incorrectness despite our best efforts; that is the realistic standard for software.

questions.q: The formal proofs did not arrive. What does the book say is the lasting value of structured programming?
options: It lets programmers write formal proofs for every function they write
It makes programs run faster than jump-based code
It creates small units that tests can try to prove wrong
It removes the need for tests altogether
optionExplain: That is the hope that faded.
Speed is not the book's argument.
Right: falsifiable units. The card next shows how.
The units depend on tests to be trusted.
questions.explain: The value lies in falsifiable units. The card next explains the link.
questions.rule: Structured code is testable code.

questions.q: True or false: Tests can deem a program correct enough regardless of whether the program is provable.
questions.explain: A program that is not provable, due to unrestrained goto for example, cannot be deemed correct no matter how many tests are applied.
questions.rule: Only provable programs can be deemed correct by tests.

questions.q: A team splits a 2,000-line routine full of jumps into small functions, each built from sequence, selection and iteration. What does the split buy them according to the book?
options: Small provable units that tests can try to falsify
A guarantee that the whole system is then free of bugs
Freedom from writing any tests
A proof of the routine, done once by the compiler
optionExplain: Right: units that can be tested and deemed correct enough.
Falsifiable units give no guarantee.
The units need tests to be trusted.
Compilers are not described as proving anything.
questions.explain: The split makes tests meaningful.
questions.rule: Small provable units are what tests can attack.

questions.q: How far up does the book say falsifiability applies?
options: Only at the level of single functions, since larger units cannot be tested
Only to code written in a language that has no goto at all
Only to the tests, and not to the program under test
At every level, from the smallest function to the largest component
optionExplain: The book carries the idea upward.
The book's claim is about every level.
The units under test are what must be falsifiable.
Right: software is like a science at every level.
questions.explain: The same logic of falsifiability governs components and services.
questions.rule: Falsifiability applies at every level.
questions.teaches: At every level, from the smallest function to the largest component, software is driven by falsifiability.

questions.q: Match each contributor to what it gives in the book's account.
pairs: Attempts to prove those units incorrect
questions.explain: Structure creates the units, tests try to refute them, and surviving the tests earns the verdict.
questions.rule: Structure first, then refutation.

questions.q: An architect designs services so that each one can be tested alone and its tests can show failures. Which idea from the book does the architect apply, and at what level?
options: Provability, with a Euclidean proof written for each service
Falsifiability, with structured-programming-like disciplines at a higher level
Polymorphism, by replacing the services with tables of function pointers at run time
Immutability, by forbidding every assignment in the services
optionExplain: The book says formal proof did not take hold.
Right: the same logic, one level up.
That addresses a different concern.
That is the functional paradigm's discipline.
questions.explain: Architects define modules, components and services that are easily falsifiable (testable), and functional decomposition remains a best practice at the architectural level.
questions.rule: Design for falsifiability at every level.
questions.teaches: Software architects define easily falsifiable (testable) modules, components and services, using restrictive disciplines similar to structured programming at a much higher level.

questions.q: A C header contains only the line struct Point; with no fields listed, while the fields appear in point.c. Can code that includes the header read a point's x field?
options: Yes, through a pointer to the struct that the header declares
No, because the fields are not visible outside point.c
Yes, if the code is compiled in the same build
Only if the program uses classes
optionExplain: A pointer feels like access, but the layout is unknown.
Right: it is an incomplete type there. The card next explains.
A shared build does not expose the fields.
C has no classes, and the hiding works anyway.
questions.explain: The compiler refuses field access outside point.c. The card next shows the idea.
questions.rule: Hide fields in the implementation file.

questions.q: True or false: Perfect encapsulation was possible in C before any object-oriented language existed.
questions.explain: Right: headers with forward declarations hid the implementation completely.
questions.rule: C had perfect encapsulation.

questions.q: Which line of this program fails to compile, and why?
options: The makePoint line, because it returns a pointer to an incomplete struct
The include line, because headers are not allowed to declare structs
No line fails; C lets any code read any field of any struct
The printf line, because the field x of struct Point is hidden here
optionExplain: Returning a pointer to an incomplete struct is fine.
Headers may forward-declare structs.
That is true only if the fields are in the header.
Right: only point.c knows the fields.
questions.explain: The compiler stops access to members that the header does not reveal.
questions.rule: Fields in the .c file are hidden from users.

questions.q: Users of the C header can call the declared functions but have ____ knowledge of how either the data structure or the functions are implemented.
questions.explain: Both the struct and the function bodies are hidden.
questions.rule: Users see declarations, not details.
questions.teaches: Users of the C header have no knowledge of the implementation of either the data structure or the functions, so both are hidden.

questions.q: True or false: If the team moves the full definition of struct Point, with its x and y fields, from point.c into point.h, callers still cannot read the x field.
questions.explain: Whatever the header shows, callers can use, so the encapsulation is gone.
questions.rule: Encapsulation depends on what the header reveals.

questions.q: A tutor says a language counts as object-oriented only if it provides encapsulation. Given the C example, how does the book score OO on encapsulation?
options: No point: C already had perfect encapsulation without OO
Full marks: OO invented encapsulation
A half point: OO improved on C
It cannot be scored, since encapsulation has no agreed definition here
optionExplain: Right: it cannot be what defines OO.
The C example predates OO languages.
The book says OO weakened it, as the next idea shows.
The book defines it as a line around cohesive data and functions.
questions.explain: The book gives OO no point for encapsulation.
questions.rule: No point for encapsulation.
questions.teaches: The book awards OO no point for encapsulation, since C had it perfectly before OO.

questions.q: A C++ client includes a header that lists a class's private members x and y. What does the client learn?
options: Nothing at all, because private members are completely invisible to clients
Their current values, because the header is a public file
That the members exist, though the compiler stops it using them
Only their types, never their names, since names stay hidden
optionExplain: Private blocks use, but the declarations are still in the file.
Declarations do not carry values.
Right: knowledge leaks even without access. The card next shows why.
Names are also visible in the header.
questions.explain: The header shows the members. The card next explains why C++ needs this.
questions.rule: Visible declarations leak knowledge.

questions.q: True or false: In C++ the compiler needs to see a class's member variables in its header, because it needs the size of each instance.
questions.explain: Right: that technical need forced the members into the header.
questions.rule: The size of instances forces members into the header.

questions.q: A teammate renames the private field x to px in point.h. What must happen to the files that include this header?
options: Nothing, since private members are hidden from clients
Only point.cc needs recompiling
They must be rewritten to use the new name
They must be recompiled, since the header they depend on changed
optionExplain: Hidden from use is not hidden from the header file.
Clients that include the header also depend on it.
They cannot use a private name at all.
Right: clients depend on the member declarations.
questions.explain: A change in the header ripples to every file that includes it.
questions.rule: A changed header forces recompilation.

questions.q: Java and C# abolished the header and ____ split altogether, so a class's declaration and definition cannot be separated.
questions.explain: Without the split, nothing is hidden by file structure.
questions.rule: No split, less hiding.
questions.teaches: Java and C# abolished the header and implementation split altogether, making it impossible to separate a class's declaration from its definition.

questions.q: True or false: A C opaque struct gives weaker encapsulation than a C++ class whose private fields are listed in its header.
questions.explain: The C user cannot learn that the fields exist, whereas the C++ client can see them even though it cannot use them.
questions.rule: Not seeing beats not touching.

questions.q: Smalltalk, Python, JavaScript, Lua and Ruby have little or no enforced encapsulation. What does this say about whether OO depends on strong encapsulation?
options: It does; those languages are not really object-oriented, whatever they claim
It does not; OO relies on programmers not to circumvent encapsulation
It does; their programmers enforce it by hand using header files
It says nothing, since those languages are not compiled like C
optionExplain: The book counts them as OO languages.
Right: these languages are OO without enforcement.
These languages have no header split to use.
Compilation is not the point.
questions.explain: Enforcement is weak in many OO languages, so strong encapsulation cannot be part of the definition.
questions.rule: OO needs well-behaved programmers, not strong walls.
questions.teaches: Many OO languages, such as Smalltalk, Python, JavaScript, Lua and Ruby, have little or no enforced encapsulation, so OO relies on programmers not circumventing it.

questions.q: In C, struct B begins with exactly the fields of struct A, in the same order, followed by extra fields. What can you do with a pointer to a B?
options: Nothing: C does not allow a struct to stand in for another
Call A's functions with no cast at all
Cast it to a pointer to A and use the B as if it were an A
Convert it into an A by copying all of the extra fields away
optionExplain: C allows the cast, which is how the trick works.
C needs an explicit cast.
Right: the shared prefix lets B masquerade as A. The card next shows it.
No copying is needed.
questions.explain: The shared prefix is what makes the cast work. The card next shows the trick.
questions.rule: Same first fields, same order.

questions.q: True or false: C programmers could masquerade one data structure as another before there were object-oriented languages.
questions.explain: Right: the book calls this a common practice before OO.
questions.rule: The trick predates OO.

questions.q: What does this C program print?
options: Nothing: it fails to compile
optionExplain: Right: x + y is 2.0 + 5.0 through the Shape view of the Label.
That would be y alone.
That would be x alone.
The explicit cast makes it compile.
questions.explain: The Label starts with the same two fields as the Shape, so the cast reads them correctly.
questions.rule: A matching prefix makes the view valid.

questions.q: In the book's C example the programmer had to cast the derived struct to the base struct. What happens in a real OO language?
options: The cast is still written by hand
The cast is forbidden
The upcast is implicit
The base struct is copied into the derived one
optionExplain: That is the C way.
Upcasting is allowed and automatic.
Right: the language does the conversion for you.
No copy is involved.
questions.explain: OO made the masquerading much more convenient.
questions.rule: OO makes upcasting implicit.
questions.teaches: In a real OO language the upcast from derived to base is implicit, whereas the C programmer had to write the cast by hand.

questions.q: The book awards OO no point for encapsulation and perhaps a ____ for inheritance.
questions.explain: OO made inheritance more convenient but added little to what C could do.
questions.rule: OO scores badly on both so far.

questions.q: A programmer wants one struct to masquerade as two unrelated structs using the field-order trick. How does the book view this?
options: It is exactly as easy as single inheritance, since the same trick applies twice
It is much harder, which is why multiple inheritance is hard by trickery
It is impossible in every language, so it cannot be done
It needs a heap-allocated stack frame for each of the structs
optionExplain: Right: the trick suits single inheritance.
The book says it is considerably more difficult.
The book says difficult, not impossible.
That belongs to the 1966 discovery.
questions.explain: A shared prefix can match only one other struct's layout at the start.
questions.rule: The trick fits single inheritance only.
questions.teaches: Multiple inheritance is considerably more difficult to achieve by the field-order trick, which is why true inheritance is more convenient.

questions.q: The C function getchar reads input without knowing which device it reads from. How can one function work with many devices?
options: getchar contains a separate branch of code for each of the known devices
The compiler rewrites getchar again for each device it meets
The operating system copies the device itself into the program
Each device supplies its own functions, and getchar calls through them
optionExplain: That would break whenever a new device appeared.
Compilers do not do this.
No such copying happens.
Right: the call is routed through pointers. The card next shows the details.
questions.explain: The routing goes through pointers to functions. The card next shows the pointers.
questions.rule: Route calls through function pointers.

questions.q: Polymorphism is an application of pointers to ____.
questions.explain: Right: the book says polymorphism is an application of pointers to functions.
questions.rule: Polymorphism is pointers to functions.

questions.q: What does this C program print?
options: [screen a][screen b][screen c]
[screen a][screen b][log c]
[log a][log b][log c]
[screen abc]
optionExplain: The second struct holds toLog, not toScreen.
Right: each emit call goes through the pointer in the struct it is given.
The first struct holds toScreen.
put is called once per character, with its own brackets.
questions.explain: emit has no idea which function it calls; the struct decides.
questions.rule: The struct picks the behaviour.

questions.q: In C++, where do the pointers used for virtual function calls live, and who loads them?
options: In a global table, filled in by the linker before the program starts
In a vtable, loaded by the constructors of the derivatives
In the object's local variables, set by the caller of each method
In the compiler, which inlines every call to a virtual function
optionExplain: The linker is not described as filling it.
Right: the same trick, built into the language.
The table belongs to the class mechanism, not the caller.
Inlining would remove the indirection.
questions.explain: The vtable is the hand-built FILE structure made automatic.
questions.rule: A vtable is a table of function pointers.
questions.teaches: In C++, every virtual function has a pointer in a table called a vtable, and constructors of derivatives load their versions of the functions into the table of the object being created.

questions.q: A student describes UNIX IO drivers. Select the two mistakes.
options: Every driver provides open, close, read, write and seek
The signatures of those functions must be identical for every driver
Each driver may choose its own signature for read
getchar contains separate code for each device
optionExplain: Correct as stated.
Correct as stated.
Mistake: identical signatures are what let one caller serve every driver.
Mistake: getchar only calls through the pointer.
questions.explain: A standard set of identical signatures plus a call through a pointer is the whole mechanism.
questions.rule: Same signatures, call through the pointer.

questions.q: A historian says polymorphism was invented with OO languages in the 1960s. What does the book reply?
options: The historian is right; nothing earlier was polymorphic in any way
Polymorphism dates from the lambda calculus of 1936, not from OO
Polymorphism first appeared with Java in the 1990s, not in the 1960s
Pointers to functions gave polymorphism from the late 1940s onward
optionExplain: The C copy program was polymorphic long before.
Lambda calculus is the root of the functional paradigm.
Java came much later.
Right: OO added nothing to the mechanism itself.
questions.explain: The book dates the practice to the late 1940s.
questions.rule: OO provided nothing new here.
questions.teaches: Programmers have used pointers to functions to achieve polymorphic behaviour since Von Neumann architectures were first implemented in the late 1940s.

questions.q: A C team builds polymorphism by hand with function pointers. What is the main risk?
options: It relies on conventions, and a forgotten one causes a hard bug
Function pointers run slower than direct calls on every machine
C does not allow pointers to functions to be declared at all
Pointers to functions cannot be stored inside structures in C programs
optionExplain: Right: that is the danger. The card next explains.
Speed is not the book's concern.
C allows them; that is the point.
They can, and the FILE structure does just that.
questions.explain: The danger is human, not technical. The card next shows what removes it.
questions.rule: Conventions are the weak point.

questions.q: True or false: OO languages did not create indirect calls; pointers to functions already allowed them, and OO made them safe and convenient.
questions.explain: The mechanism existed in pointers to functions; OO made it safe and convenient.
questions.rule: OO added safety, not the mechanism.

questions.q: Which of these is a convention a C programmer must follow for hand-built polymorphism and an OO language enforces instead?
options: Choosing meaningful names for the functions in the struct and the driver
Writing a comment above each struct that holds pointers
Setting each pointer before the first call and calling through it
Compiling with the highest warning level that the compiler offers
optionExplain: Naming is good practice but not a polymorphism convention.
Comments are not what the pointers need.
Right: both are conventions the OO language handles.
That is tooling, not a convention of the mechanism.
questions.explain: Initialisation and calling through the pointer are the two conventions named.
questions.rule: The language keeps the conventions for you.

questions.q: Using an OO language makes polymorphism ____, a power that old C programmers could only dream of.
questions.explain: Safety and ease turn a dangerous trick into an everyday tool.
questions.rule: Trivial polymorphism is a large power.
questions.teaches: Using an OO language makes polymorphism trivial, an enormous power that old C programmers could only dream of.

questions.q: What does this fragment most likely do when it runs?
options: It prints x to the screen, as the structure's author intended
It fails to compile because the field put has not been given a function
It does nothing and returns normally from the main function
It typically crashes, since it calls a pointer that was never set
optionExplain: Nothing was set to print anything.
The compiler accepts a null function pointer.
Calling a null pointer is not a silent no-op.
Right: the forgotten convention shows up at run time.
questions.explain: A missing initialisation is exactly the bug the conventions try to prevent.
questions.rule: A forgotten convention becomes a crash.

questions.q: A security reviewer worries that indirect calls through stored pointers are dangerous. How does the book answer for code written in an OO language?
options: The danger is real, so OO code must avoid polymorphism altogether
OO languages eliminate the conventions, and so the dangers
The danger only affects C and does not affect other languages
The danger is removed by testing every single pointer by hand
optionExplain: The book builds on polymorphism.
Right: the language does the risky parts.
The point is conventions, not the language name.
Hand testing keeps the conventions alive.
questions.explain: Bugs from a forgotten convention are devilishly hard to track down, so removing the convention matters.
questions.rule: Remove the convention, remove the danger.
questions.teaches: A bug from a forgotten convention of hand-built function pointers can be devilishly hard to track down and eliminate.

questions.q: A new input device is invented. What would you expect the copy program to need in order to read from it?
options: A rewrite of its input code for the new device's behaviour
A recompile with the new device's name written in the source
Nothing, if the driver provides the standard functions
A new copy program written for each separate device
optionExplain: That is how device-dependent programs behaved.
The source does not mention devices.
Right: it needs no change, not even recompiling. The card next explains.
One program serves all devices.
questions.explain: The program does not know its devices. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The program stays unchanged.

questions.q: True or false: Using a speech synthesizer as the output device would require recompiling the copy program.
questions.explain: The copy program does not depend on the source of the drivers, so nothing changes, not even a recompile.
questions.rule: No change and no recompile.

questions.q: A report tool writes through five standard functions. A new e-ink display driver implements the same five. What must be changed in the report tool?
options: Nothing: the driver is plugged in
The output code, to add an e-ink branch
The tool's name, to reflect the new display
The five functions, to add a sixth for e-ink
optionExplain: Right: the tool only calls the standard functions.
A branch per device is device-dependent design.
Names do not matter to the mechanism.
The standard set is what makes devices interchangeable.
questions.explain: The same shape of driver is all the tool needs.
questions.rule: Same functions, no change.

questions.q: Programs written for decks of punched cards had to be rewritten when customers moved to magnetic ____.
questions.explain: A program that did the same job with another device had to be rewritten, which was very inconvenient.
questions.rule: Device-dependent programs get rewritten.
questions.teaches: Device independence was learned in the late 1950s: programs written for punched card decks had to be rewritten when customers moved to magnetic tape.

questions.q: True or false: If a new device driver leaves out one of the five standard functions that the copy program calls, the copy program can still use the device.
questions.explain: The plugin promise was conditional: the program relies on the driver implementing the standard functions.
questions.rule: A plugin must honour the whole contract.

questions.q: The plugin idea was built into almost every operating system, yet few programmers used it in their own programs before OO. Why?
options: Operating systems forbade user programs from using plugins
Programs never needed to change devices
Using pointers to functions was dangerous
Plugins only worked for IO devices on UNIX
optionExplain: The book gives no such rule.
They did: cards became tape.
Right: OO made it safe to use anywhere, for anything.
OO lets the idea apply anywhere.
questions.explain: OO allows the plugin architecture to be used anywhere, for anything.
questions.rule: Safe polymorphism spreads plugins everywhere.
questions.teaches: Most programmers did not extend the plugin idea to their own programs because function pointers were dangerous; OO allows it anywhere, for anything.

questions.q: In a conventional calling tree, in which direction do source code dependencies point compared with the flow of control?
options: The same direction: callers must name the modules they call
The opposite direction, since callees must depend on their callers
No direction, since dependencies exist only at run time
It varies, as the architect chooses freely
optionExplain: Right: the dependency follows the call. The card next shows how to reverse it.
Callees need not name their callers.
Source dependencies exist at compile time.
Without polymorphism the architect has few options.
questions.explain: Without polymorphism the dependency follows the call. The card next shows the reversal.
questions.rule: Source dependencies follow calls unless inverted.

questions.q: True or false: In the Java code below, OrderService mentions SqlStore by name.
questions.explain: OrderService mentions only the Store interface; SqlStore mentions the interface too, since it implements it.
questions.rule: The caller names only the interface.

questions.q: In the code below, which source code dependencies exist?
options: OrderService depends on SqlStore, since it saves through one
Store depends on OrderService, since the service owns the interface
SqlStore depends on OrderService, since it saves the orders
OrderService depends on Store, and SqlStore depends on Store
optionExplain: The service never names SqlStore.
The interface knows neither class.
SqlStore never mentions the service.
Right: both point at the interface.
questions.explain: Both classes point at the interface; the call at run time goes from OrderService to SqlStore.
questions.rule: Both sides depend on the interface.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's picture of dependency inversion, the interface still exists at run time as an object that forwards every call.
questions.explain: The interface is a source code contrivance: at run time it does not exist and the caller reaches the callee, albeit indirectly.
questions.rule: The interface lives in the source, not at run time.
questions.teaches: The interface is a source code contrivance: at run time it does not exist and the caller reaches the callee, albeit indirectly.

questions.q: A MemoryStore that implements Store is added and handed to an OrderService. The source of OrderService needs ____ change.
questions.explain: OrderService depends only on the Store interface, so any implementation can be passed in.
questions.rule: New details need no change to the policy.

questions.q: A mobile app's business rules call the database module directly. How can the architect make the database depend on the business rules instead?
options: Move the business rules into the database module and drop the interface
Define an interface in the rules and have the database implement it
Make the database module call the business rules through goto jumps
Remove the interface, so the rules call the database directly
optionExplain: That ties the rules to the database even more.
Right: the database now points at the policy.
That is the opposite of structured discipline.
That keeps the dependency pointing at the detail.
questions.explain: Any source code dependency, wherever it is, can be turned around by inserting an interface between the two sides.
questions.rule: Insert an interface to turn a dependency around.
questions.teaches: Any source code dependency, no matter where it is, can be inverted by inserting an interface between the modules.

questions.q: A team compiles its UI, business rules and database into three jar files. Which dependency arrangement lets the rules jar stay unchanged when the UI changes?
options: The rules depend on both the UI and the database components
The UI and database depend on the rules; the rules depend on neither
All three components depend on one another in both directions at once
The database depends on the UI, and the rules depend on the database
optionExplain: Then a UI change touches the rules.
Right: details point at policy. The card next explains.
Mutual dependency spreads every change.
The rules would still depend on the database, so a database change would reach them.
questions.explain: The rules must not name the details. The card next shows what that buys.
questions.rule: Details depend on policy.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Only the changed component needs redeploying
Different teams can develop components separately
A detail that depends on the business rules
questions.explain: The book defines both terms in the same short passage.
questions.rule: Deploy and develop independently.

questions.q: The marketing team redesigns the web user interface. In the inverted design, what has to be redeployed?
options: The UI and the business rules, which are linked together
The UI and the database, since both are details
All three components, to be safe
Only the UI component
optionExplain: They are separate components with dependencies pointing inward.
The database component is unaffected.
The point of the design is to avoid that.
Right: only the component whose source changed.
questions.explain: When the source in a component changes, only that component needs redeploying.
questions.rule: Redeploy only what changed.

questions.q: How does the book connect independent deployability to independent developability?
options: Components that deploy independently can also be developed by separate teams
They are the same property under two different names, used loosely
Independent developability must exist before anything can be deployed at all
Developability depends on using the same language across teams
optionExplain: Right: one leads to the other.
The book gives them different meanings.
The book's order is the other way round.
Language is not mentioned.
questions.explain: The book moves from deployment to development in one step.
questions.rule: Deployable apart means developable apart.
questions.teaches: If the modules of a system can be deployed independently, they can be developed independently by different teams.

questions.q: True or false: A database component that depends on an interface defined by the business rules is a plugin to the rules.
questions.explain: The detail points at the policy, which is what makes it a plugin.
questions.rule: A plugin depends on what it plugs into.

questions.q: A company's reporting module, owned by team B, imports code from the payments module of team A, so the two teams must ship together. From the book's view, what would an architect gain by gaining control of those dependencies?
options: A guarantee that the two teams no longer need to talk to each other at all
A way to merge both modules into one program that is released together
High-level policy independent of low-level details that become plugins
A faster build, since the two modules would then share a single language
optionExplain: The book says independence, not silence.
Merging removes the independence.
Right: this is what the book says OO is about for an architect.
Build speed is not the point.
questions.explain: For an architect, OO is the ability to gain absolute control over every source code dependency through polymorphism.
questions.rule: Control the dependencies and the teams decouple.
questions.teaches: To the architect, OO is the ability, through polymorphism, to gain absolute control over every source code dependency in the system and so create a plugin architecture.

questions.q: In a Java loop that prints the squares of 0 to 24, which variable changes state while the program runs?
options: The println method
The number 25 in the condition
The class name
The loop control variable
optionExplain: A method does not change state like that.
A constant does not change.
Names are fixed.
Right: it changes on every pass. The card next contrasts this with Clojure.
questions.explain: The loop control variable is a mutable variable. The card next shows a program without one.
questions.rule: A loop counter mutates.

questions.q: True or false: In the Clojure squares program, the variable x is modified on each pass.
questions.explain: In the Clojure program variables like x are initialised but never modified.
questions.rule: Variables do not vary.

questions.q: The number of mutable variables in the Java code below is ____.
questions.explain: Both total and i are updated as the loop runs, so both are mutable.
questions.rule: Count the variables that get updated.

questions.q: The Clojure program starts from an endless list of integers. Why does it still finish?
options: The list is cut down to size by the compiler before the program runs
No element is evaluated until accessed, so few elements are created
Endless lists silently stop at the largest integer the machine holds
range secretly returns only 25 numbers, so the list is not endless
optionExplain: The compiler does not trim the list.
Right: take asks for a few, and only those are made.
The book gives a different reason.
range returns a never-ending list.
questions.explain: Elements of a never-ending list come into being only when accessed.
questions.rule: Evaluation waits for access.
questions.teaches: No element of an endless list is evaluated until it is accessed, so only the elements actually requested are ever created.

questions.q: True or false: If take were removed so that println received the whole endless list of squares, the program would still finish.
questions.explain: Nothing would limit how many elements are accessed, so the program would keep producing them.
questions.rule: Laziness needs a limit.

questions.q: The shell pipeline below prints the first five squares from a long stream of numbers. Which stage plays the role of take in the book's Clojure example?
options: seq, which produces the long stream of numbers to be squared
awk, which squares each value that passes through
head -5, which keeps only the first few of the stream
The pipe, which joins the stages into one program
optionExplain: seq plays the role of range.
awk plays the role of map.
Right: it limits how much is consumed.
The pipe carries values; it does not limit them.
questions.explain: The book reads the Clojure expression from the innermost call outward.
questions.rule: Read from the innermost call outward.
questions.teaches: The Clojure expression is read from the innermost call outward: range produces the list, map squares it, take keeps the first elements and println prints them.

questions.q: Two threads each add 10 to a shared balance of 100. Both read the balance before either writes it back. What final value is possible?
optionExplain: Right: both wrote 100 + 10, so one deposit is lost. The card next explains the cause.
That would need one thread to read the other's result.
Both threads wrote back a larger value.
Nothing subtracts from the balance.
questions.explain: A lost update arises because the balance is mutable. The card next states the general point.
questions.rule: Shared mutable state invites lost updates.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, all race conditions, deadlocks and concurrent update problems are due to mutable variables.
questions.explain: Right: with no mutable variables they cannot happen.
questions.rule: Mutation is the root cause.

questions.q: Threads in a service exchange only values that are not changed after creation, and no shared variable is updated. What does the book support?
options: Race conditions remain possible on the values that the two threads share
Lost updates remain possible when two threads write at the same moment
None of the race, deadlock or concurrent update problems can occur
Concurrent update problems remain possible between the threads of the service
optionExplain: A race needs a variable that is updated.
Nothing is written back.
Right: they need something to be updated.
They require updates.
questions.explain: Without updates there is nothing to race over.
questions.rule: No updates, no races.

questions.q: Is immutability practicable for a real system?
options: Yes, with compromises, because machines lack infinite resources
Yes, with no compromise at all, on any real machine we have today
No, since every real system needs mutable variables somewhere in it
No, since concurrency itself needs mutable locks to be used safely
optionExplain: Right: the answer is nuanced.
That is true only with infinite resources.
The book says compromises can make it practicable.
Locks are what the problems come from.
questions.explain: With infinite storage and speed the answer would be plainly yes.
questions.rule: Practicable with compromises.
questions.teaches: Immutability is practicable with infinite storage and infinite processor speed, and with certain compromises when those resources are limited.

questions.q: Which schedule of two threads adding 10 to a balance of 100 loses a deposit?
options: A reads 100, A writes 110, B reads 110, B writes 120
A reads 100, A writes 110, B reads 110, B writes 110
B reads 100, B writes 110, A reads 110, A writes 120
A reads 100, B reads 100, A writes 110, B writes 110
optionExplain: This schedule never overlaps and gives 120.
B would write 120 if it added to what it read.
This also runs one after the other and gives 120.
Right: the second write overwrites the first, so the final value is 110.
questions.explain: A lost update needs both reads to happen before either write.
questions.rule: Interleaved read-then-write loses updates.

questions.q: Select the problems that cannot occur in a system in which no variable is ever updated.
options: Race conditions
Deadlocks, which need mutable locks
Concurrent update problems
A slow algorithm that takes too long to finish
A program that uses more memory than it should
optionExplain: They need updated variables.
Without mutable locks there is nothing to hold.
Nothing is updated, so nothing is updated concurrently.
Speed is a separate matter from mutation.
Memory use is unrelated to the three problems.
questions.explain: The three problems named in the book all need mutation.
questions.rule: The three problems all need something to change.
questions.teaches: You cannot have deadlocks without mutable locks, which is why a system with no mutable variables is free of them.

questions.q: A system must keep some state that changes. Where should most of its processing sit, in the book's view?
options: In the mutable components, which hold all the data
In components that do not mutate variables
Spread evenly, so no component is overloaded
In whichever component was written first
optionExplain: That keeps the risky part large.
Right: push work towards the immutable side. The card next explains.
Even spreading ignores the segregation.
History has no part in the design.
questions.explain: Most processing belongs where nothing is mutated. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Push work to the immutable side.

questions.q: Match each term to its description.
pairs: Splitting the system into mutable and immutable components
Treating variables like database records with transaction or retry
A special variable mutated only under conditions enforced by swap!
questions.explain: The three terms build on each other.
questions.rule: Split, protect, enforce.

questions.q: An inventory service has 40 functions: 35 only compute results from their inputs and 5 update stock counts. What does the book advise?
options: Spread the stock counts evenly across all of the 40 functions in it
Keep the 5 in a small protected mutable part; keep the 35 immutable
Move the 35 into the mutable component so that everything sits in one place
Replace the 5 with global variables, to make them faster to reach
optionExplain: That scatters mutation everywhere.
Right: segregate, then shrink the mutable part.
That grows the risky part.
Globals add mutation without protection.
questions.explain: Drive code out of the mutable components and protect what remains.
questions.rule: Shrink the mutable part.

questions.q: swap! reads the counter value, passes it to inc, and then locks and compares. What happens if the value changed in the meantime?
options: The new value is stored anyway, over the other thread's change
The program stops with an error that the caller must handle
The other thread's change is undone and its value restored
The lock is released and the swap is retried from the start
optionExplain: That would be a lost update.
The strategy retries.
swap! does not undo changes.
Right: this is compare and swap.
questions.explain: The compare step detects that the value moved on.
questions.rule: Compare, swap, or retry.
questions.teaches: swap! uses compare and swap: it reads the value, computes the new one, locks and compares with the value it read, stores it if unchanged and otherwise releases the lock and retries from the beginning.

questions.q: A counter holds 5. Thread A begins swap! with inc and reads 5. Thread B completes a swap! with inc, making the counter 6. Then A reaches its compare step, fails, and retries. The counter then holds ____.
questions.explain: A's compare sees 6 where it read 5, so it retries from the beginning, reads 6 and stores 7. Both increments take effect.
questions.rule: A failed compare means a retry.

questions.q: A banking service moves money by updating two separate atoms, one per account, and the two balances depend on each other. Does the atom facility fully safeguard this?
options: No: an atom cannot fully safeguard dependent variables; more is needed
Yes: applying swap! to each atom in turn is enough to make the pair safe
Yes: atoms only fail when a program uses a single shared variable
No: atoms are not usable in banking, or in any similar field
optionExplain: Right: the book names this limit.
Each atom is safe alone, but the pair is not.
The limit is for several dependent variables.
The book says atoms are adequate for simple applications.
questions.explain: Safety for one variable does not extend to two that depend on each other.
questions.rule: One atom is safe; dependent atoms are not.
questions.teaches: The atom facility cannot completely safeguard against concurrent updates and deadlocks when multiple dependent variables come into play.

questions.q: A bank stores every deposit and withdrawal and does not store a balance. How is a balance obtained?
options: By reading the balance from the last transaction only
By asking the customer to report it
By adding up the transactions for the account
The system cannot give a balance without storing it
optionExplain: The last transaction does not hold the total.
The system must compute it.
Right: the state is derived. The card next gives the name of the idea.
Computing from events is possible.
questions.explain: State is derived from events. The card next names the scheme.
questions.rule: Derive state from events.

questions.q: In an event-sourced application the data store is not CRUD; it only has create and read, which makes it ____.
questions.explain: Right: only creating and reading happen, since nothing is updated or deleted.
questions.rule: Create and read only.

questions.q: The function below keeps only events and stores no balance. For the list shown, it returns ____.
questions.explain: 100 - 30 + 5 = 75: the balance is a function of the events.
questions.rule: Balance equals the sum of the events.
questions.code:
def balance(events):
    total = 0
    for kind, amount in events:
        total += amount if kind == 'deposit' else -amount
    return total

events = [('deposit', 100), ('withdraw', 30), ('deposit', 5)]
print(balance(events))  # 75

questions.q: True or false: The book says event sourcing has to keep working forever, which is why old transactions must eventually be deleted.
questions.explain: The scheme need only work for the reasonable lifetime of the application, and nothing is ever deleted.
questions.rule: Work for the lifetime, not forever.
questions.teaches: Event sourcing does not have to work forever, only for the reasonable lifetime of the application, which today's storage and processing power can cover.

questions.q: Which everyday system does the book say works exactly the way event sourcing does?
options: A spreadsheet that overwrites cells
A text editor's undo buffer
A compiler's symbol table
Your source code control system
optionExplain: Overwriting is the mutation event sourcing avoids.
The book names source control.
A symbol table is mutable state.
Right: it stores the changes and rebuilds the state; nothing is overwritten.
questions.explain: Source control keeps history and derives the current state.
questions.rule: Source control is event sourcing.
questions.teaches: A source code control system works precisely the way event sourcing does: it keeps the history of changes and derives the current state from it.

questions.q: True or false: The Single Responsibility Principle says that every class should contain only one method.
questions.explain: The principle concerns who asks for changes, not how many methods a class has. A class with ten methods that all serve one group can follow it. The card next shows the wording the authors settle on.
questions.rule: The SRP counts actors, not methods.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is the final form of the SRP?
options: A module should do one thing and do it well
A module should contain only one public method, so that each class stays small and focused
A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor
A module should have exactly one author in the team
optionExplain: This is the popular reading of the name, and the authors say it is a different guideline, meant for functions.
It sounds strict and measurable, but the principle says nothing about counting methods.
Right: an actor is the group of people who require a given change, so the module answers to a single such group.
It mixes up who writes the code with who asks for changes to it.
questions.explain: The authors move from reason to change, to user or stakeholder, and settle on actor, because several people can want the same change and form one group.
questions.rule: One module, one actor.
questions.hint: The final wording uses a word the authors coined for a group of people.

questions.rule: Ask who requests the change, not how many methods exist.
questions.q: True or false: A class with eleven methods that all answer to the same actor can follow the SRP.
questions.explain: The SRP is checked by asking who requests changes, not by counting methods. Eleven methods serving one group can follow it, while two methods for two departments may not.

questions.q: Sort each action: does it apply the SRP, or the separate guideline that a function should do one thing?
groups: The SRP (module answers to one actor)

items.t: Split a 200-line function into several short functions
Move pay rules requested by accounting away from reports requested by HR
Extract a helper that only validates a date
Separate code the DBAs specify from code the finance team specifies
Rename a function so that its name matches its single job
Give marketing code and compliance code separate source files

questions.explain: The SRP separates code by the group that asks for changes. Shrinking a function so that it does one thing is a different habit that the authors call useful at the lowest level.
questions.rule: Actors split modules; one-thing splits functions.

questions.q: A ReportGenerator class has campaignSummary(), specified by the marketing team, and monthlyRevenue(), specified by the finance team. What does the SRP say about it?
options: It answers to two actors, so the two methods should live apart
It is fine because it has only two methods
It breaks the SRP only if the two methods also share a database table or a helper function
It is fine because both methods produce reports
optionExplain: Right: marketing and finance can each ask for changes, and one module serves both.
A small method count does not decide the matter.
Sharing data may add risk, but the violation is already there when two actors depend on one module.
Similar output makes the methods look related, but the SRP asks who requests their changes.
questions.explain: Two departments with separate bosses and separate deadlines are two actors. Keeping their code apart stops one team's request from reaching the other's.
questions.rule: Different departments usually mean different actors.

questions.q: A company ships one deployable package that holds code for its billing actor and for its shipping actor, so every release redeploys both. Using the logic of the SRP at the scale of components, what would the authors suggest?
options: Keep one package, since fewer releases are easier to manage and to test as a whole
Split it by layer, putting all interfaces in one package
Merge the two actors so that one team owns both
Split it so that code for each actor sits together, apart from the other's
optionExplain: This favours release convenience, but the SRP's logic favours separating by reason to change.
Splitting by layer groups code by kind, not by the reason it changes.
Merging actors is not a design option the authors offer; it moves the problem into the org chart.
Right: the SRP reappears at the component level as the Common Closure Principle, grouping what changes for the same reason.
questions.explain: The authors say the SRP reappears at the level of components as the Common Closure Principle, and at the architectural level as the axis of change that draws boundaries.
questions.rule: Group together what changes for the same reason, at any scale.
questions.teaches: The SRP's logic scales up: at the component level it becomes the Common Closure Principle, and at the architecture level an axis of change creates boundaries.

questions.q: Two methods in one class, written for different departments, call the same helper. One department asks for a change in how the helper counts hours. What is the main risk?
options: The other department's method changes behaviour without anyone asking for it
The helper becomes slower for every caller, because two methods now compete to call the same code
The class no longer compiles because of the shared call
The helper cannot be tested separately from the class
optionExplain: Right: the helper is one piece of code, so any edit reaches every caller.
Speed is rarely the issue; the problem concerns who relies on the result.
Sharing a helper compiles without trouble.
A helper can usually be tested on its own.
questions.explain: An edit to shared code reaches every caller, including callers that serve other people. The card next shows how this played out in the payroll example.
questions.rule: Shared code carries one actor's change to the others.
A shared function is a hidden link between its callers' actors.
questions.q: In the payroll example, HR's report went wrong because the edit to the shared ____ function also changed what reportHours() returned.
questions.explain: The developer changed regularHours() for accounting without noticing that reportHours() called it too. HR had no chance to check the result.

questions.rule: Trace every caller of a function before editing it.
questions.q: Accounting asks for the regular-hours cap to drop from 40 to 38, and a developer edits only the shared helper as shown. Then new Employee().reportHours(45) returns the text regular=____ .
questions.explain: The report calls regularHours(), so it returns regular=38 (and calculatePay for a rate of 10 gives 380). HR never asked for this.

questions.rule: Safe means every dependent actor was considered.
questions.q: True or false: If the accounting team validates a change to a shared function and all tests pass, the change is safe for every actor that calls the function.
questions.explain: The check covered only the actor who asked for the change. The other actor who depends on the code never had a chance to look at it, so passing tests and one approval prove little.

questions.q: Two methods of an InvoicePrinter, both specified by the finance team, share a roundCents() helper. A colleague proposes copying the helper into each method to be safe. What is the best response?
options: Agree, because shared helpers always cause the problem described in this chapter, whoever uses them
Move the helper to a class that HR also uses
Agree, because duplicated code is easier to read
Keep the shared helper, because both callers answer to the same actor
optionExplain: The chapter's problem comes from actors who differ, not from sharing itself.
This would introduce a second actor into the shared code, the very risk to avoid.
Readability is not the reason the chapter gives, and copies add a cost of their own.
Right: with one actor, a shared helper does not carry one group's change to another.
questions.explain: The risk comes from two actors depending on one function. Where one actor owns both callers, sharing is safe and avoids true duplication.
questions.rule: Share code among callers of one actor; separate it between actors.
questions.hint: Count the actors, not the callers.

questions.q: A date helper shared by two teams is changed for one team. Weeks later the other team's invoices show wrong dates. What does the book's story suggest about how the problem comes to light?
options: Late: the affected team does not know of the change, and the problem is found eventually, after damage
Early: the first team's tests will have caught it, because shared code is exercised by every team that calls it
Never: wrong dates are small, so the second team will not notice them in its invoices
At once: the compiler reports every caller whose result changes when a helper is edited
optionExplain: Right: in the story the COO's team did not know of the change, and the problem was discovered only eventually.
The first team's tests checked its own use of the code, as in the story, where accounting was satisfied.
In the story the wrong numbers did matter: they cost the COO's budget millions of dollars.
Compilers check types, not meaning, so a changed result raises no warning.
questions.explain: In the payroll story the HR people kept using the reports, which now held wrong numbers, until the problem was eventually discovered, after the bad data had cost millions.
questions.rule: Damage from a shared change surfaces late and costs much.
questions.teaches: The harm can be large and found late: in the book's story the problem was discovered only eventually, after the bad data had cost the COO's budget millions of dollars.

questions.q: Two developers from different teams edit the same large class at once, one for a database schema change and one for a report format change. What is the likely result?
options: The version control system blocks one developer
The compiler rejects the second change
Both changes are applied cleanly, so no further step or review is needed
Their edits collide and must be merged, which carries risk
optionExplain: Most systems allow concurrent edits and rely on merging afterwards.
Compilers do not arbitrate between editors.
Sometimes they merge cleanly, but the chance of a collision is the problem.
Right: concurrent edits to one file can conflict, and merging them is a risky task.
questions.explain: Concurrent edits to one file need a merge, and merges can go wrong. The card next shows how the SRP lowers the odds.
questions.rule: One file with many editors invites merges.

questions.q: In the Employee example, which two requests collide in a merge?
options: A tax change from accounting and a salary change from HR, both made to the payroll code on the same day
A schema change from the DBAs and a format change to the hours report from HR
Two format changes requested by HR on the same day
A bug fix and a code comment from the same developer
optionExplain: The example does not use these two requests.
Right: one concerns saving data and the other concerns reporting, but both land in the Employee class.
Both come from one actor, which is not the case the chapter describes.
A single developer does not merge with themselves.
questions.explain: The DBAs and HR clerks each change the Employee class for their own reasons. The merge puts both the CTO and the COO at risk.
questions.rule: Different actors editing one file means merges.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, even good merge tools leave some risk in merges.
questions.explain: The authors say tools are good nowadays, but no tool can deal with every merge case, so there is always some risk. Separating the code is the way to avoid the situation.
questions.rule: Avoid the merge; do not rely on the tool.

questions.q: Employee is split so that the saving code and the hours-report code sit in two different source files. The DBAs change the saving code and HR changes the report format on the same day. What follows?
options: A merge is needed, because both files are in the same repository
Both developers must wait for each other to finish
The edits land in different files, so these two changes need no merge
The schema change breaks the report, because both teams read the same database
optionExplain: A repository holding both files does not cause a merge between them.
Nothing forces a wait when the files differ.
Right: each actor's change stays within the file written for that actor.
The question is about editing collisions, not about shared data.
questions.explain: Collisions need edits to the same file. With one file per actor, edits requested by different actors stay apart.
questions.rule: Different actors, different files, no merge.
Separate the code of different actors.
questions.q: Describe in one or two sentences what you would do about the 4,000-line OrderProcessor that the pricing, shipping and audit groups all edit, and why.
questions.a: Move each group's code into separate classes (and source files), one per actor, so that edits requested by different groups no longer land in the same file and no longer need merging.

questions.q: Two teams' bug fixes keep undoing each other in one file, though no merge conflict is reported. Which diagnosis fits the chapter?
options: The same cause: several people change one source file for different reasons, so the code of different actors should be separated
A tooling fault, because without any conflict report the file itself cannot have a design problem, whatever its history
A matter unrelated to the SRP, since only reported merge conflicts count as symptoms of it
A sign that the file needs more reviewers, so that each change is checked by a third person
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the many symptoms all involve multiple people changing the same source file for different reasons.
Missing conflict reports hide the problem; they do not show that the file is sound.
The authors list merges as one symptom among many, so other symptoms count too.
Review is useful, but it leaves several actors changing one file for different reasons.
questions.explain: The chapter presents merges as one symptom and notes that others exist. All of them come from several people changing one source file for different reasons, so the cure stays the same.
questions.rule: Many symptoms, one cause: one file serving several actors.
questions.teaches: Merges are only one symptom; the authors say all the symptoms involve multiple people changing the same source file for different reasons, so one remedy fits them all.

questions.q: An Employee class mixes pay rules, hours reports and database saving. Which change removes the coupling between the teams that request them?
options: Rename the class so that its name describes all three jobs it performs
Move each group of methods into a class of its own
Add comments that mark each method's owner
Make every method static
optionExplain: A better name documents the mix and leaves the coupling in place.
Right: separate classes break the link between the three actors' code.
Comments help readers but leave one file for all three teams.
Static methods do not separate the code that different teams depend on.
questions.explain: Separating code by actor removes the shared home. The card next shows the structure the authors use.
questions.rule: Separate the code of different actors into different classes.

questions.q: In the split design, what does EmployeeFacade do?
options: It holds the pay, report and save algorithms itself, so callers need only one class
It stores the employee data in a database
It creates the actor classes and delegates calls to them
It decides which actor may change the code
optionExplain: A facade holding all three algorithms would put the actors back together.
Saving belongs to one of the actor classes.
Right: it contains very little code and gives callers one object to deal with.
Governance is not a job for the facade.
questions.explain: The facade fixes the downside of the split, which is that callers must create and track three classes.
questions.rule: A facade instantiates and delegates.

questions.q: Put the steps of the authors' first solution in order.
items: Pull the fields out into a data structure that has no methods
Place each actor's functions in a class of its own that works on that data
Add a thin facade that creates those classes and delegates to them
questions.explain: The data comes first so that all three classes can share access to it. Each class holds one actor's code, and the facade is added last to ease the use of the three classes.
questions.rule: Data, then actor classes, then a facade.

questions.q: Compare two ways to give callers one entry point: a new EmployeeFacade, and keeping the original Employee class as the facade. Which statement is accurate?
options: The second keeps the key business rule next to the data; the first puts every rule in a separate class
The first violates the SRP because it adds a class that all three actors share, while the second does not violate it
The second removes the need for the data structure, because the original Employee class holds the data itself and so needs no other holder
The first needs the actor classes to know each other
optionExplain: Right: the authors note that some developers prefer the second, keeping the key method in Employee and delegating the lesser ones.
Both leave the actor classes separate; neither violates the SRP on that point.
Both designs still rely on the shared data.
In both designs the three classes do not know about each other.
questions.explain: The two designs differ in where the most important rule lives, not in whether the actors are separated.
questions.rule: Pick the facade style by where the key rule should live.
A request from one actor touches one class.
questions.q: True or false: After the split, a request from accounting to change the overtime rules would be made in the class that calculates pay, not in EmployeeFacade.
questions.explain: Only the class that calculates pay serves accounting, so only that class changes. The facade only creates the actor classes and delegates to them.

questions.q: A colleague objects that the split leaves each class with a single function. The pay class needs rounding, overtime and tax-table helpers. What happens?
options: Each actor class holds many private methods, forming a scope that outsiders cannot see into
The helpers must move to the facade, which then holds the shared logic of all three actors
The helpers must move into the data structure so that all three classes can reach them without knowing each other, which suits a structure
The split fails, because one class cannot hold more than a single public function
optionExplain: Right: the number of functions to calculate pay is large, and the family of private methods forms a scope.
A facade that holds the logic would couple the three actors again; it should contain very little code.
The data structure has no methods, so helpers cannot move there.
Nothing limits a class to one function; the objection mistakes the split for one function per class.
questions.explain: The authors answer the objection by noting that each class holds many functions. Each family of methods is a scope, and outside it no one knows its private members exist.
questions.rule: One class per actor, with many private methods inside.
questions.teaches: Each actor class keeps a whole family of functions; that family is a scope, and outside it nobody knows the private members exist.

questions.q: A system shows a financial summary on a web page, and stakeholders now ask for the same data as a printed report. In a good architecture, how much existing code changes?
options: All of the web page code, rewritten for printing
The calculation code, to add print settings
As little as possible, ideally none
Half, since the two reports share half their features
optionExplain: A rewrite of the page code is the failure that a good architecture should avoid.
The figures are the same, so the calculation has no reason to change.
Right: new presentation code is written beside the old and the rest stays as it is.
The goal is to reduce changes to a minimum, not to share the burden.
questions.explain: A good architecture keeps the changed code to a bare minimum. The card next names the principle behind this.
questions.rule: A small extension should not force large changes.
Extend; do not modify.
questions.q: The Open-Closed Principle says that a software artifact should be open for ____ but closed for modification.
questions.explain: New behaviour is added without editing the artifact. The authors call this the most fundamental reason that we study software architecture.

questions.q: A weather app shows forecasts as text, and the team is asked to add a voice read-out. Which design follows the OCP?
options: Add a voice presenter that reads the existing forecast data; leave the calculation alone
Copy the whole app and change the output of the copy
Rewrite the forecast code to produce spoken text only
Add an isVoice flag and if branches inside the forecast calculation, so one code path serves both
optionExplain: Right: the new behaviour is an extension and the old code stays closed to modification.
Two copies must now be kept in step.
This breaks the text display the app already has.
Branches in the calculation mix presentation into it and modify code that did not need to change.
questions.explain: Calculation and presentation change for different reasons. A new presenter extends the system while the calculation stays closed.
questions.rule: Add a new presenter beside the old ones.
Closed means unrelated parts need no edits when you extend.
questions.q: True or false: The OCP means that the part that calculates the data may not be edited even when its own rules change.
questions.explain: The aim is new behaviour without modifying unrelated parts. A change to the calculation itself is a modification of the part that calculates, and the principle does not forbid it.

questions.q: Later, stakeholders ask that negative numbers on the web page be blue instead of red. In the separated design, which part changes?
options: The calculation of the reported data
The printed report presenter
All parts, because they share the same data
Only the web presentation
optionExplain: The figures are unchanged, so the calculation stays as it is.
The printed report has its own format and is not affected.
Sharing data does not make every part change for a colour request.
Right: colour is a presentation matter for that view alone.
questions.explain: Each responsibility changes for its own reasons. A request about web colours reaches only the web presentation.
questions.rule: A change should land in the one part that owns the reason for it.

questions.q: An online shop sends order confirmations by email, and push notifications are requested next. An architect first separates the confirmation content from the delivery channel. Why does this come first?
options: Separate classes always run faster than a single class, so the split makes both channels send their mail more quickly
Content and channel change for different reasons, so a new channel extends the system without modifying it
Email must be removed before push notifications are added
The content can then be written in a different language
optionExplain: Speed is not the reason for the separation.
Right: the OCP depends on first separating what changes for different reasons (the SRP) and then arranging the dependencies.
Removing email is not needed to add another channel.
Language choice is unrelated to the separation.
questions.explain: The authors reach an extendible design by two steps: separate the things that change for different reasons, then organise the dependencies between them.
questions.rule: Separate by reason to change, then arrange the dependencies.
questions.teaches: The OCP is reached in two steps: apply the SRP to separate what changes for different reasons, then organise the dependencies between the parts, using the Dependency Inversion Principle.

questions.q: True or false: To protect component A from changes in component B, B should depend on A.
questions.explain: A dependency carries change from the depended-on component to the dependent one, so B depending on A keeps A safe. The card next gives the rule and an example.
questions.rule: Dependencies carry change from the target to the source.

questions.q: In the report example, which component is the most protected from change?
options: The Interactor
The Database component
The Presenters
The Views
optionExplain: Right: it holds the highest-level policies, so changes elsewhere should not reach it.
It is a detail that the central rules are protected from.
They sit above the Views but below the Controller and the Interactor.
They are among the lowest-level concepts and the least protected.
questions.explain: The Interactor contains the business rules, the central concern of the application. Everything else deals with peripheral concerns.
questions.rule: Business rules sit at the top of the protection hierarchy.

questions.q: A mobile banking app has account rules (limits, balances), screens, and a client that talks to the bank's server. To protect the account rules from changes to the screens and the client, which dependencies should exist?
options: The screens depend on the client, which depends on the rules
The account rules depend on the screens and the client
All three depend on each other for flexibility
The screens and the client depend on the account rules
optionExplain: This can chain, but it makes the screens depend on the client, a link that this goal does not call for.
This reverses the arrows and exposes the rules to every change in the screens and the client.
Mutual dependencies leave no component protected.
Right: the components to protect are the ones depended on, so change flows toward the less protected ones.
questions.explain: The account rules are the component to protect, so the other components must depend on it and not the reverse.
questions.rule: The protected component is the one that others depend on.

questions.q: Match each component of the report system to how it is protected.
pairs: Highest level, protected from changes in all the others
Peripheral to the Interactor but central to the Presenters
Higher than the Views, lower than the Controller
questions.explain: Level follows how central the concern is. The same component can be peripheral to one neighbour and central to another, which is why the protection forms a hierarchy.
questions.rule: Level is relative to the neighbour.
Swapping a peripheral detail leaves the policy alone.
questions.q: True or false: Replacing the relational database with a document store requires changes to the Interactor.
questions.explain: The Database component depends on the Interactor and not the reverse, so a change of storage reaches only the Database side. The Interactor is the most protected component.

questions.q: A team's component graph shows the Presenters depending on the Controller and the Controller depending on the Presenters. What does this imply?
options: Both are well protected, because each component knows exactly what the other does
Neither can be protected from the other, so the relationship should run one way
The Presenters have become the highest-level component
The Interactor must be moved between them
optionExplain: Mutual knowledge exposes each to the other's changes.
Right: each double line between components should be crossed in one direction only.
Neither is higher than the other when each depends on the other.
Adding a third component does not resolve the cycle between these two.
questions.explain: A two-way relationship means a change in either one can reach the other. Protection needs a clear direction.
questions.rule: Component relationships cross each boundary in one direction.
questions.teaches: Each boundary between components should be crossed in one direction only; a two-way relationship leaves neither component protected from the other.

questions.q: A report generator needs figures from a database. Which structure keeps the generator unaffected by changes to the database code?
options: The generator calls the database classes directly
The generator copies the database queries into its own code
The database class owns an interface that the generator implements and calls
The generator owns an interface that the database-side class implements
optionExplain: Direct calls make the generator depend on the database classes it names.
Copying binds the generator to the database even more tightly.
This makes the generator depend on the database side.
Right: the source dependency then points from the database side to the generator.
questions.explain: When the policy owns the interface, the detail depends on the policy. The card next shows how the authors apply this in the report system.
questions.rule: The policy owns the interface; the detail implements it.
A gateway inverts a dependency on a detail.
questions.q: FinancialDataGateway exists to ____ the dependency that would otherwise point from the Interactor component to the Database component.
questions.explain: The data mapper implements the gateway, so the dependency points toward the Interactor. The presenter and view interfaces do the same.

questions.q: In a diagram, ReportGenerator (business rules) has an arrow to MySqlReportDao, a class in the database component. A colleague says this is fine because the generator calls only one method. What is the flaw?
options: One method is too few calls to justify a separate Dao class, so the generator should call the database directly instead
The source dependency points from the policy to the detail, so database changes reach the rules
The Dao class has the wrong name
The Dao should depend on the Controller instead
optionExplain: The count of methods is not the issue.
Right: the arrow should be inverted with an interface owned by the policy side.
Naming does not change the direction of a dependency.
The Controller is not the component that the rules should serve.
questions.explain: A dependency carries change from the depended-on class to the depending one, however few calls it involves.
questions.rule: Judge the arrow direction, not the number of calls.
Own the interface on the policy side.
questions.q: In a mobile app, OrderLogic calls HttpOrderClient directly to submit orders. How would you apply the chapter's idea?
questions.explain: The interface belongs to the side that needs the service. The implementation on the detail side then points toward the policy.
options: Merge OrderLogic and HttpOrderClient into one class, so that no boundary is left to cross
Define an OrderSender interface in the HTTP client component and have OrderLogic use it from there
Define an OrderSender interface in the order-logic component and make HttpOrderClient implement it
Make HttpOrderClient static so that OrderLogic does not need an instance of the client
