optionExplain: Merging removes the boundary and exposes the rules to every network change.
The interface sits in the detail's component, so the logic still depends on that component.
Right: OrderLogic then depends on an interface it owns, and the HTTP code depends on the logic component.
Static access still names the concrete class in the logic's source.

questions.q: True or false: The data format behind load() changes, as in the code shown, and ReportGateway stays the same; ReportGenerator must then be edited.
questions.explain: The generator depends on ReportGateway, which is unchanged. Only the class that implements it, DbReportGateway, knows the format.
questions.rule: A detail's change stays on the detail's side.

questions.q: In the report system at run time, the Interactor asks for data and the database component supplies it. Which statement describes the control flow and the source code dependencies?
options: Control flows from the Interactor into the database component, while the source dependency points back to the Interactor
Both control flow and source dependencies run from the Interactor to the Database, because the Interactor calls it at run time
Control flows toward the Interactor and so do the source dependencies
Control and source dependencies point nowhere in particular
optionExplain: Right: the interface lets the two directions differ.
That would be the plain design, without the gateway interface.
Control flows from the Interactor to the data supplier in this run.
Both have a direction, and here they oppose each other.
questions.explain: At run time the Interactor calls the implementation, so control crosses into the database component. In the source, the implementation names the interface, so the dependency points back.
questions.rule: Source dependencies need not follow the flow of control.
questions.teaches: The direction of a source code dependency can be the opposite of the flow of control at run time, and an interface owned by the caller is what makes the two differ.

questions.q: A Controller calls an Interactor class that exposes entities and helpers. A developer changes one entity's internals. What is the likely effect on the Controller?
options: Nothing, because the Controller never calls the entities directly and so cannot be affected by them
It may need to change, because it can reach the entity through the Interactor
It is protected because the Controller is higher level
It must be rewritten in a different language
optionExplain: An indirect path still carries change to the Controller.
Right: reaching internals creates a transitive dependency on them.
The Controller is lower than the Interactor in the hierarchy.
Language has no part in this.
questions.explain: A client that can reach internals is exposed to changes in them. The card next shows how the authors close that path.
questions.rule: What a client can reach, it depends on.
A chain of dependencies is still a dependency.
questions.q: A chain in which A depends on B and B depends on C is called a ____ dependency.
questions.explain: A transitive dependency is a chain. The authors say it violates the principle that software entities should not depend on things they do not directly use.

questions.q: Sort each purpose: does it belong to FinancialDataGateway, which inverts a dependency, or to FinancialReportRequester, which hides internals?

items.t: Stops the business rules from depending on the database
Keeps the Controller from depending on the entities
Lets a lower-level class implement an interface owned by a higher-level one
Narrows what the Controller can see of the Interactor

questions.explain: Both are interfaces, but they serve different purposes: one flips the direction of a dependency on a detail, and the other shrinks what a client can reach.
questions.rule: One interface flips a direction; the other narrows a view.

questions.q: A checkout screen class uses a PaymentProcessor object that exposes card parsing, fraud scoring and ledger classes, though the screen needs only pay(). What should the architect do?
options: Let the screen call all four parts directly so that nothing is hidden from the screen
Move the screen into the PaymentProcessor class
Give the screen an interface with pay() only, implemented by the processor
Rename PaymentProcessor so that its role is clear
optionExplain: More access means more dependencies for the screen.
Merging the screen into it removes the boundary altogether.
Right: the screen then has no dependency on the parsing, scoring or ledger classes.
A name does not narrow what the screen can reach.
questions.explain: The screen should depend only on what it uses. A narrow interface keeps the other classes behind it out of its dependencies.
questions.rule: Expose to each client what it uses and no more.

questions.q: Suppose the requester interface is removed and the Controller refers to the Interactor class directly. A change is then made to a financial entity. What is the likely effect?
options: The Controller may now be affected by a change it has no interest in
None, as the Interactor was already hiding the entities from every other component
The Database component must be rewritten
The Views stop working
optionExplain: Right: the Controller has a transitive dependency on the entities again.
With the interface removed, nothing hides them.
The Database component is not involved in this path.
Nothing connects the Views to this change.
questions.explain: The interface is what cuts the chain from the Controller to the entities. Without it, the chain returns.
questions.rule: Remove the hiding interface and the chain returns.

questions.q: A web client library exposes 200 classes, and your app uses three of them. Applying the same principle, what is the main risk of depending on the whole library?
options: The library cannot be used with static types
The three classes you use will run more slowly
You will have to learn all 200 classes before you can use even three of them safely
Changes to the 197 unused classes can still force you to change or redeploy
optionExplain: Nothing in the situation suggests this.
The principle is about change, not speed.
Learning effort is a cost, but not the one the principle names.
Right: depending on a module that holds more than you need exposes you to its unrelated changes.
questions.explain: The reasoning that applies to the Controller and the Interactor also applies between systems. The authors note they will meet the idea again in the ISP and the Common Reuse Principle.
questions.rule: Do not depend on things you do not directly use.
questions.teaches: The rule that entities should not depend on things they do not use applies between separately built systems too, not only between classes in one design.

questions.q: Billing calls calcFee() on a License. PersonalLicense and BusinessLicense compute fees in different ways, and Billing needs no changes for either. What does this suggest?
options: The design is poor, since different algorithms mean different types
Billing must be using a hidden type check
Both subtypes can stand in for License without upsetting Billing
The License class should be deleted
optionExplain: Different algorithms are fine if users cannot tell the difference.
The example says Billing's behaviour does not depend on the subtype.
Right: Billing treats them alike, so each is a valid substitute.
Nothing in the example calls for removing the base class.
questions.explain: A user that behaves the same whichever subtype it has is the sign of a proper subtype. The card next gives Liskov's definition.
questions.rule: Same user behaviour means valid substitution.
Subtype means programs cannot tell the difference.
questions.q: If replacing T objects with S objects leaves the behaviour of programs defined in terms of T unchanged, then S is a ____ of T.
questions.explain: This is the substitution property in Liskov's definition. It speaks about the behaviour of programs and not about declarations.

questions.q: A developer says: Dog extends Animal and the code compiles, so Dog is a valid subtype of Animal in the LSP sense. What is the flaw?
options: Compiling shows only that the types fit, not that programs behave the same with a Dog
Dog must be a final class to be a subtype
Animal should be an interface, not a class
Compilers reject inheritance between real-world categories such as dogs and animals, so the code could not have compiled
optionExplain: Right: substitutability concerns behaviour, which a compiler does not check.
Finality has no bearing on substitutability.
Whether Animal is a class or an interface is not the point.
Compilers accept it; that is not the flaw.
questions.explain: Behaviour decides. A compiling class can still break a user's assumptions.
questions.rule: Compiling is not the same as substitutable.

questions.q: Sort each situation: does it satisfy the LSP, or violate it?

items.t: Two license classes compute fees differently, and Billing is unchanged
A user must test which subtype it holds before using it
A subclass changes an internal algorithm and users see the same results
Callers add an if statement to handle one special subtype

questions.explain: The first and third leave user behaviour unchanged. In the second and fourth, the user has to know the concrete type, so the types are not substitutable.
questions.rule: If users must know the subtype, it is not substitutable.

questions.q: A Payment base type has charge(). Checkout code charges any Payment. A new GiftCardPayment charges successfully but throws an unexpected exception when the balance is too low, which checkout does not handle. Is it a valid subtype?
options: No, because gift cards are not real money
Yes, because it implements charge()
Yes, because exceptions are a normal part of Java and callers should expect them
No, because checkout's behaviour changes when it is substituted
optionExplain: The domain question is irrelevant to substitutability.
Having the method is not enough.
Exceptions are normal, but this one is unexpected by the users of the base type.
Right: by Liskov's definition, programs written for Payment must behave the same.
questions.explain: Checkout was written against Payment and now crashes. It would need extra handling that depends on the subtype.
questions.rule: Judge by what happens to the user.

questions.q: A game has a Weapon type with attack(), and the combat code calls attack() on any Weapon. A Crossbow subtype is added and satisfies the LSP. What must change in the combat code?
options: Add a branch for Crossbow in the combat code, since it is a new type of weapon
Nothing, because the combat code only uses the Weapon type
Recompile the combat code against a new base class
Rewrite attack() in every other weapon
optionExplain: A branch on the subtype is what the LSP is meant to avoid.
Right: substitutability lets a new subtype be added without modifying its users.
A new base class is not part of the situation.
Other weapons are not affected.
questions.explain: Because users cannot tell the subtypes apart, a new subtype extends the system without any change to them. This is how substitutability supports the open-closed goal.
questions.rule: Substitutable subtypes extend a system without changing users.
questions.teaches: Substitutability is what lets a new subtype be added without modifying its users, so the LSP supports the open-closed goal when inheritance is used.

questions.q: In geometry every square is a rectangle. In code, Square extends Rectangle and keeps its two sides equal. A user sets the width to 5, the height to 2 and reads the area. What is the likely problem?
options: The area may not be 10 as the user expects
The user cannot call setH on a Square
The area is always correct since a square is a rectangle
The code fails to compile because the sides differ
optionExplain: Right: a Square keeps the sides equal, so the second setter changes both.
A Square inherits both setters, so the calls are allowed.
Real-world classification does not decide how the code behaves.
The code compiles; the trouble shows at run time.
questions.explain: A Square cannot keep a width of 5 and a height of 2 at once. The card next shows the standard test.
questions.rule: Is-a in the real world is not is-a in behaviour.
Square and Rectangle is the standard LSP violation.
questions.q: The authors call the canonical violation of the LSP the square and ____ problem.
questions.explain: Square fails to be a proper subtype of Rectangle because the height and width of a Rectangle can change independently, while those of a Square must change together.

questions.q: What does the program print?
optionExplain: The Square does not give 10, because its second setter changes both sides.
The Square's second setter overwrites the first, so its sides are not 5.
The plain Rectangle keeps its two sides independent, so its area is 10.
Right: Rectangle gives 5 times 2, while Square ends up with both sides equal to 2.
questions.explain: For the Rectangle the area is 5 times 2. For the Square, setW(5) sets both sides to 5, and setH(2) sets both to 2, so the area is 4.
questions.rule: Test substitutability by running the base type's expectations.
A type check in the user signals a broken substitution.
questions.q: True or false: Adding an if statement to the user that detects a Square shows that Square is substitutable for Rectangle.
questions.explain: The need for that mechanism is the violation. A user whose behaviour depends on the subtype it holds shows that the types are not substitutable.

questions.q: A FileStore has write(). A ReadOnlyFileStore extends it and throws an exception from write(). Code that writes through the FileStore type now fails when it receives the read-only one. What is the verdict?
options: It is a proper subtype, because it inherits all the methods
ReadOnlyFileStore is not a proper subtype, because FileStore users cannot treat it alike
It is a proper subtype if the exception is documented
It is a proper subtype because read-only files are still files, and users can tell them apart
optionExplain: Inheriting methods does not make behaviour match.
Right: it breaks what users of the base type assume, as Square does.
Documentation helps readers but does not restore substitutability for existing users.
The real-world class says nothing about how callers behave.
questions.explain: Code written for FileStore expects write() to work. The subtype changes that, so the same fault as the Square appears in a new domain.
questions.rule: A subtype that removes a capability users rely on is not substitutable.

questions.q: A Square works correctly for a dashboard that only calls setSize(side, side) on rectangles. Later, another program sets width and height separately and breaks. By Liskov's definition, was Square a proper subtype of Rectangle all along?
options: Yes, because the first program worked
Yes, because the second program is badly written
No, because the definition covers all programs written in terms of the base type
Yes, until the second program was written, since only then did the difference show
optionExplain: One working program is not what the definition asks for.
The second program uses Rectangle as promised, so it is not at fault.
Right: one program that notices the difference is enough to break the property.
The definition does not depend on when programs are written.
questions.explain: The definition quantifies over all programs defined in terms of the base type. A subtype that works for one user and fails for another is still not a proper subtype.
questions.rule: Substitutability is judged against every possible user.
questions.teaches: Liskov's definition quantifies over all programs written for the base type, so a subtype that passes for some users and fails for one is still not a proper subtype.

questions.q: True or false: The LSP also covers users that depend on a well-defined interface and on swapping its implementations, including services.
questions.explain: The principle goes beyond classes connected by inheritance: it covers any users who depend on a well-defined interface and on the substitutability of its implementations. The card next lists the forms of interface that the authors name.
questions.rule: The LSP follows the user's dependence on an interface.

questions.q: Which of these does the book name as an interface to which the LSP applies?
options: Only abstract classes in statically typed languages
Only classes that share the same constructor
Only interfaces that have exactly one implementation, so that users are never confused
A set of services that all respond to the same REST interface
optionExplain: The authors list several forms, and Java interfaces are only one.
Constructors are not what the authors discuss.
With one implementation there is nothing to substitute.
Right: the authors list this among the forms of interface.
questions.explain: The authors name Java-style interfaces, Ruby classes sharing method signatures and services answering a REST interface.
questions.rule: Interfaces take many forms; the LSP covers all of them.

questions.q: Which situations call for the LSP to be considered? Select all that apply.
options: Three Ruby classes with the same method signatures used by one caller
Several payment gateways that expose the same HTTP interface to one client
One Java interface with two implementing classes used by a billing module
A single concrete class with no alternatives and one user
Two unrelated modules that no user ever treats as alike
optionExplain: Right: callers rely on the shared signatures and on the classes behaving alike.
Right: the client depends on a well-defined interface and on swapping gateways.
Right: the module relies on substituting one implementation for another.
There is no interface and no swap, so nothing needs to be substitutable.
Without a shared user relying on both alike, substitutability does not arise.
questions.explain: In each of the first three, a user depends on an interface and expects any implementation to stand in for another. The last two lack that dependence.
questions.rule: If a user swaps implementations, the LSP applies.
questions.hint: Look for a user that treats several implementations alike.

questions.rule: From inheritance to interfaces of every kind.
questions.q: Sort each statement: does it describe the early view of the LSP, or the later view?

items.t: Guides the use of inheritance
Covers services answering the same REST interface
Concerns subtypes of a base class
Concerns users who rely on swapping implementations of an interface

questions.explain: In the early years of object orientation the LSP guided inheritance. Over time it grew into a broader principle about interfaces and their implementations.

questions.q: A system uses three cloud storage services through one StorageService interface that many clients call. A fourth vendor's service returns errors in a different format. What is the likely cost, by the LSP's logic?
options: None, since the interface name is the same
The clients, or a layer between them, need special handling for the fourth vendor
The three existing vendors must adopt the new format and retest all of their services
The fourth vendor's service will refuse all requests
optionExplain: A shared name does not make the behaviour substitutable.
Right: the lack of substitutability pushes extra mechanism into the system.
Nothing forces the first three to change.
The service works; the trouble lies in how users must treat it.
questions.explain: Whenever one implementation breaks the shared contract, someone has to add special handling. That is the architectural cost of a violation.
questions.rule: A broken contract costs extra mechanism.

questions.q: In Python, classes Basket and Wishlist both define total(items), and callers add the totals. Basket returns a number, but Wishlist returns a string. No interface is declared anywhere. What does the LSP say?
options: Nothing, since Python has no declared interfaces
Basket should be converted to return a string as well, and the callers adjusted to match
Wishlist is not substitutable for Basket, even though no interface is written down
The principle applies only after the code is compiled
optionExplain: Callers still rely on a shared behaviour even without declarations.
Changing the compliant class is not the fix suggested by the principle.
Right: the shared signature creates a contract that callers rely on.
The principle concerns behaviour, not compilation.
questions.explain: Our reading: in a dynamically typed language the interface is implicit but real. Callers still assume that the classes behave alike.
questions.rule: An implicit interface carries the same obligations.
questions.teaches: Liskov's definition says that S is a subtype of T if programs written in terms of T behave the same when an object of type S is substituted for one of type T.

questions.q: A taxi aggregator sends the same dispatch fields to every company's service. One company calls a field dest instead of destination. Where would handling this be most harmful?
options: In a configuration table keyed by each company's dispatch address
In an if statement on the company name inside the dispatch code
In a note to the company asking them to comply
In a test that fails when the field names differ
optionExplain: A table keeps company knowledge in data, not in code logic.
Right: company names in logic invite errors and spread with every merger.
Asking is harmless, though it may not work.
A failing test reports the problem without spreading it.
questions.explain: Special cases written into the code multiply as companies change. The card next shows what the architect does instead.
questions.rule: Keep vendor knowledge out of the logic.

questions.q: Why does the architect in the book reject an if statement testing for acme.com?
options: It would make the system run too slowly
It would change the REST interface that every other taxi company has to follow, and break their dispatch
Company names in the code invite errors, and mergers would force more such statements
The if statement is not allowed in Java
optionExplain: Speed is not the reason given.
The if statement does not alter the shared REST interface; the objection is that company names in the code invite errors.
Right: the authors warn about errors and about a merged company needing a further case.
The statement is valid code; the objection is about design.
questions.explain: The authors ask what happens if Acme buys Purple Taxi and keeps both brands: would another if be needed for purple? The architect avoids the problem.
questions.rule: Names in code do not scale with change.

questions.q: Put the story's events in order.
items: The aggregator defines a common dispatch format for all taxi companies
Acme's programmers abbreviate one field name
A special case for Acme becomes necessary
The architect adds a configuration-driven dispatch command module
questions.explain: The common format comes first, then the deviation, then the need for a special case, and last the architect's way of containing it.
questions.rule: A deviation forces a special case; contain it in data.
Special cases grow with every change in the market.
questions.q: True or false: Testing whether the dispatch URI contains purple would be a sound way to handle the second company, since it matches how Acme is handled.
questions.explain: It repeats the fault of putting names in code, and each rebrand or merger would need another change. The architect's table holds the differences as data.

questions.q: A payments app calls five bank APIs through one adapter interface. Bank four needs dates as day/month/year while the others use ISO dates. Following the book's approach, what is the best design?
options: A format table keyed by bank, read by a single request-building module
An if on the bank's name in the payment code
Ask every user to enter dates in the format of bank four, whatever bank they use
Drop bank four from the supported list
optionExplain: Right: differences live in data, and the logic stays free of bank names.
This puts a company name in logic, the approach the architect rejects.
Changing user input pushes the problem onto people.
Dropping a customer is a business decision and not a design solution.
questions.explain: The configuration approach holds each bank's quirks as data, so a new difference becomes a new row instead of a new branch.
questions.rule: Put differences between vendors in data.

questions.q: Suppose Acme buys Purple Taxi and both brands keep separate websites, but the systems are unified. With the book's configuration table keyed by dispatch URI, what must be done for the Purple drivers?
options: Add a new if statement for purple to the dispatch code, as was done for Acme, next to the existing one
Rewrite the dispatch command module
Ask the drivers to change their URIs
Change rows in the configuration data so that purple URIs use the Acme format
optionExplain: This is the very statement the architect set out to avoid.
The module reads its data from the table, so it does not need rewriting.
The URIs belong to the companies' systems and are not the aggregator's to change.
Right: the mechanism copes with the merger by changes to data.
questions.explain: Because the table is keyed by the dispatch URI, a merger needs only data changes. The code stays free of company names.
questions.rule: Key the mechanism on the interface address, not on names in code.
questions.teaches: In the book's configuration table one row gives Acme.com its own dispatch format with dest, and a catch-all row *.* gives every other URI the standard format with destination.

questions.q: In Java, User1 calls only op1 of a class Ops that also has op2 and op3. Someone edits op2. What is the likely effect on User1?
options: None, because User1 never calls op2 and so cannot depend on it in any way
User1 stops compiling because op2 is missing
User1 must be recompiled and redeployed, though nothing it uses changed
User1 is rewritten automatically by the compiler
optionExplain: Not calling an operation does not remove the dependency on its class.
The operation still exists; only its body changed.
Right: its source depends on the class that holds op2.
Compilers do not rewrite source code.
questions.explain: User1 depends on the whole class and not just on the operation it calls. The card next shows how the authors cut that dependency.
questions.rule: A user depends on the whole class it names.
One interface for each kind of user.
questions.q: Segregating OPS gives each user its own ____, so User1 no longer depends on op2 and op3.
questions.explain: User1 then depends on U1Ops, which declares only op1. A change to op2 in OPS no longer reaches User1's source.

questions.q: With the interfaces shown, a developer edits only the body of op2 in Ops. What must User1 do?
options: Nothing, since its source depends only on U1Ops, which is unchanged
Be redeployed, since op2 and User1 are part of the same system and ship together
Wait for the compiler to confirm that op1 is unchanged
Be recompiled, because it uses Ops
optionExplain: Right: the change does not reach any declaration that User1 imports.
Being in the same system does not create a source dependency.
There is nothing to wait for.
User1 names U1Ops, not Ops.
questions.explain: User1's source mentions only U1Ops and its op1. The edit to op2 touches neither.
questions.rule: Depend on a small interface and unrelated edits stay unrelated.

questions.q: Sort each case: does it force recompiling and redeployment through a source dependency, or does it avoid that problem?

items.t: A Java user that imports the OPS class
A Ruby user that calls op1 on any object it receives
A Python user whose called methods are inferred at run time
Statically typed code with a declaration naming the OPS class

questions.explain: Statically typed languages need declarations that users import, which create source dependencies. In Ruby and Python the declarations are inferred at run time, so no such dependency exists in the source.
questions.rule: Declarations in source create the dependencies.

questions.q: A Java class UserService has createUser(), deleteUser() and exportAll(). The signup screen calls only createUser(), the admin tool only deleteUser(), and a batch job only exportAll(). How do you apply the ISP?
options: Merge all three operations into one method with a mode flag that each caller sets to pick its job
Make exportAll() private
Rename UserService to describe all its jobs
Give each caller an interface with only its operation; UserService implements all three
optionExplain: A mode flag makes every user depend on all the modes.
The batch job needs it, so this breaks a user.
A name does not change what the callers depend on.
Right: each caller depends on a small interface and ignores the rest.
questions.explain: Three kinds of user get three small interfaces. A change to one operation then reaches only the user that calls it.
questions.rule: Match each interface to one kind of user.

questions.q: A team moves a service from Java to Python. Which coupling cost shrinks most in the move?
options: The need for users to depend on operations they do not call, which Python removes as well
Forced recompiling of users when an unrelated operation changes
The effort of choosing good names for operations
The risk that two developers edit the same file
optionExplain: The dependency exists in ideas, though in Python it no longer leads to forced recompiling.
Right: dynamic typing removes the source declarations that cause it.
Naming remains a task in either language.
Merges depend on files and actors, not on typing.
questions.explain: Dynamically typed languages infer what they need at run time, so no declarations create source dependencies. The authors give this as the primary reason such systems are more flexible and less tightly coupled.
questions.rule: Typing discipline decides whether declarations create dependencies.
questions.teaches: Dynamically typed systems avoid forced recompiling because their declarations are inferred at run time, which the authors give as the main reason such systems are more loosely coupled.

questions.q: A system uses a framework that is bound to a particular database, and the framework uses few of the database's features. What risk remains for the system?
options: Changes or failures in unused database features can still force redeployment or failures
The database will refuse queries from the framework
The system will need a second framework to run
None, because the system never calls the database itself, only the framework does, and the framework is unchanged
optionExplain: Right: the chain from the system to the database carries them.
Nothing in the situation points to refused queries.
A second framework is not implied.
The framework depends on the database, and the system depends on the framework.
questions.explain: Unused features can still change or fail, and the dependency chain carries the effect upward. The card next shows the chain.
questions.rule: What your dependencies depend on is also yours.
Unneeded dependencies are a liability.
questions.q: The root concern behind the ISP is that it is harmful to depend on modules that contain more than you ____.
questions.explain: This is true for source code dependencies and also at a higher, architectural level, where it shows up as redeployments and failures.

questions.rule: The harm outlives the language.
questions.q: True or false: Because dynamic typing removes forced recompiling, depending on more than you need is harmless in a Python system.
questions.explain: Dynamic typing removes the recompiling effect but not the architectural harm: a framework bound to a database can still pass on changes and failures.

questions.q: A mobile app imports a full analytics SDK (ads, crash reports, experiments) only to log crashes. A bug in the ads part crashes the app at start-up. Which action best fits the principle?
options: Add error handling around the whole SDK call
Wait for the vendor to publish a fix
Import a second SDK to run beside the first one and share the load
Depend on a narrower module that offers only crash logging
optionExplain: This treats a symptom while the app still carries the baggage.
This leaves the app exposed to the next failure in a part it never uses.
A second SDK adds more baggage.
Right: the app should not depend on things it does not need.
questions.explain: The problem came from a feature the app did not use. Choosing a narrower dependency removes the path for that failure.
questions.rule: Depend on the smallest thing that does the job.

questions.q: System S depends on framework F, which depends on database D. D ships a change to a feature that F does not use. What does the dependency chain imply?
options: S is untouched, because F absorbs the change and shields S from the database
S may need redeploying, even though nothing S cares about has changed
D must be rewritten to match S
S must switch to another database at once
optionExplain: The chain does not absorb changes automatically.
Right: the change can force F, and so S, to be redeployed.
D is not rewritten for S.
Nothing demands a switch of database.
questions.explain: S depends on F, F depends on D, so a change in D reaches S, whether or not any of the three uses the changed feature.
questions.rule: Change travels along the chain of dependencies.

questions.q: Your app uses a PDF library that bundles an unused image engine. The engine has a defect. What does the chapter's reasoning predict?
options: Only code that calls the image engine directly can be affected by the defect in it
The defect stays harmless to the app, because the app never calls the image engine and does not use any of its features
Failures matter only in so far as they force the app to be recompiled and rebuilt
A failure in the unused engine can still cause failures in the library and in your app
optionExplain: It sounds precise, but the chain of dependencies carries a failure upward, not only to direct callers.
Not calling a feature feels like protection, but the app still depends on the module that carries it.
Recompiling is one effect of the ISP's concern; a failure at run time is another, and it needs no rebuild.
Right: a failure of one of the features within a dependency may cause failures in what depends on it.
questions.explain: The authors say a failure in one of the features of the database D may cause failures in the framework F and in the system S, whether or not they use the feature. The same chain holds for a library and its bundled engine.
questions.rule: Failures travel along the chain of dependencies.
questions.teaches: A failure in a feature that a dependency carries, even one nobody uses, may cause failures in the modules that depend on it, and not only force redeployments.

questions.q: Which change is more likely to ripple outward to other code: editing the inside of an implementation, or adding a method to its interface?
options: Editing the inside of an implementation
Neither, since both stay inside one file
Both are equally likely to ripple
Adding a method to its interface
optionExplain: Internal edits seldom reach the interface or its users.
An interface is shared by many implementations and users.
They differ: one touches a shared contract, the other does not.
Right: every implementation of that interface must change too.
questions.explain: An interface change reaches every implementation, while most implementation changes leave the interface alone. The card next draws the conclusion.
questions.rule: Interfaces are less volatile than implementations.
Avoid the volatile concrete, not the stable concrete.
questions.q: Interfaces are less ____ than implementations, because a change to an interface forces its implementations to change.
questions.explain: Changes to concrete implementations do not often require changes to the interfaces they implement, so interfaces change less.

questions.q: Sort each dependency: is it a tolerable concrete dependency, or one to avoid under the DIP?

items.t: The Java String class
An operating system facility that changes rarely
A payment provider client class the team rewrites each sprint
A pricing engine class under heavy development

questions.explain: The test is volatility. Platform classes are stable and tightly controlled, while classes the team is actively developing change often.
questions.rule: Judge a concrete class by how often it changes.

questions.q: A report module imports CsvWriter directly, a class the team keeps rewriting. How do you apply the DIP?
options: Copy CsvWriter into the report module
Define a Writer interface the report module owns, and have CsvWriter implement it
Make CsvWriter a subclass of the report module so that the module controls its changes and its timing
Leave it, since CsvWriter has only one user
optionExplain: A copy is still a volatile concrete class in the module.
Right: the module then depends on a stable abstraction, and CsvWriter depends on the module.
Inheriting from the module puts the detail above the policy.
A single user does not make a volatile class stable.
questions.explain: The abstraction is stable and owned by the policy side. The volatile class moves behind it.
questions.rule: Introduce an interface and let the volatile class implement it.

questions.q: An argument says: interfaces are no more stable than classes, since both are only source files. What is wrong with this?
options: Source files are rarely changed after their release, so both kinds of file are equally stable in practice, whatever they contain
Classes are stable and interfaces are not
A change to an interface forces every implementation to change; most implementation changes leave it alone
Interfaces are changed by a different team
optionExplain: Files do change; that is not the flaw.
This reverses the point.
Right: that asymmetry makes interfaces the less volatile of the two.
Who changes them is not the argument.
questions.explain: The authors add that good designers work hard to add functionality to implementations without changing interfaces.
questions.rule: Stability follows from how many things must change with it.

questions.q: A Python function imports the module pricing_engine and calls its quote() function. The module implements quote() and is rewritten every month. Does the DIP concern this dependency?
options: Yes: a concrete module is one that implements the called functions, and this one is volatile
No, because modules are not classes and the rule is only about classes in static languages and Python programs
No, because Python has no interfaces
Yes, but only if the module is compiled
optionExplain: Right: in dynamic languages, any module in which the called functions are implemented counts as concrete.
The rule covers any concrete module.
The authors apply the rule to dynamic languages too.
Compilation is not the criterion.
questions.explain: The rule is the same in both kinds of language. What differs is how to recognise a concrete module.
questions.rule: Concrete means the called functions live there.
questions.teaches: In dynamically typed languages, a concrete module is any module in which the called functions are implemented, and the DIP still applies to the volatile ones.

questions.q: A subclass overrides a method of a base class that the team changes every week. What problem does this create?
options: The override runs more slowly than the original, because it adds a layer of calls on every invocation
The override inherits the base method's dependencies and stays tied to a volatile class
The subclass can no longer be compiled
The base class becomes immutable
optionExplain: Speed is not the concern.
Right: overriding does not remove a method's dependencies.
The code compiles.
Overriding does not change the base class.
questions.explain: The subclass stays tied to a class that changes often. The card next gives the authors' advice.
questions.rule: Inheriting from a volatile class means depending on it.
Abstract the function; do not override it.
questions.q: For a concrete function that subclasses want to change, the authors advise making the function ____ and creating multiple implementations.
questions.explain: An abstract function declares what is needed and leaves the how to separate implementations, so the dependencies are managed behind an abstraction.

questions.q: A team's Shipper class is volatile. Which actions follow the four practices? Select all that apply.
options: Declare a Carrier interface and write callers against it
Subclass Shipper and override its calculateRate method
Make calculateRate abstract and write two implementations
Write new Shipper() in every caller
Keep the name Shipper out of the callers' source
optionExplain: Right: callers refer to an abstract interface.
This derives from a volatile class and overrides a concrete function.
Right: this is the authors' advice for a function that varies.
Each caller then names a volatile concrete class.
Right: callers should not mention the name of a volatile concrete class.
questions.explain: The three right options refer to abstractions and keep the volatile name out of callers. The others derive from, override or name the volatile class.
questions.rule: Abstract, do not extend, do not name.

questions.q: Which practices does the SalePriceCalc code shown break most directly?
options: None, because the code compiles, and compiling shows that the dependencies are managed
Only the practice of referring to abstract interfaces, since the subclass should have implemented an interface
Do not derive from volatile concrete classes, and do not override concrete functions
Only the practice of overriding, because deriving from a class is safe if the subclass adds no new fields
optionExplain: Compiling shows only that the syntax is valid; the dependency on a volatile class remains.
The code does lack an interface, but the sharper breaks are the deriving and the overriding.
Right: SalePriceCalc derives from a volatile class and overrides its concrete method.
Deriving from a volatile concrete class is itself one of the practices, whether or not fields are added.
questions.explain: The subclass extends a class that changes often and overrides total(). It inherits the dependencies of the method it overrides.
questions.rule: Extending and overriding a volatile class both bind you to it.

questions.q: The same design is written in a dynamically typed language. How does the warning about inheritance change?
options: It is less of a problem, but inheritance remains a dependency, so caution is wise
It becomes stronger, because inheritance is more rigid in dynamic languages than in static ones
It stays exactly the same in every respect
It disappears, because dynamic languages have no inheritance
optionExplain: Right: this is how the authors put it.
The authors say it is a bigger problem in static languages.
The authors say the problem is smaller in dynamic languages.
Inheritance exists in many dynamic languages.
questions.explain: In statically typed languages inheritance is the strongest and most rigid of the source code relationships. In dynamic languages it is less of a problem, but it is still a dependency.
questions.rule: Caution remains wise in both kinds of language.

questions.q: A teammate overrides send() of a concrete Mailer class so that mail goes through another provider. The original send() imports an SMTP library. Does the override remove the dependency on the SMTP library?
options: Yes, because the new method replaces the old one, so the library is no longer needed
Yes, as long as the new method does not call super
No, but only on the first release
No, because the subclass inherits the dependencies of the method it overrides
optionExplain: The subclass still inherits from the class that imports the library.
Avoiding super does not detach the subclass from its base class.
Nothing in the situation changes with releases.
Right: overriding hides the old behaviour without removing the dependencies.
questions.explain: Overriding a concrete function does not eliminate its dependencies. The cure is to make the function abstract and provide several implementations.
questions.rule: An override inherits the dependencies of what it overrides.
questions.teaches: Overriding a concrete function does not remove its dependencies; the subclass inherits them, which is why the authors advise making the function abstract instead.

questions.q: A class needs a new instance of a volatile implementation but must not mention the implementation's name. Which structure helps?
options: It copies the implementation's source into itself
It creates the instance with new and hides the call in a helper method of the same class
It asks a factory interface for the instance; another class implements that factory
It reads the class name from a comment
optionExplain: A copy is as concrete as the original.
The helper's class still names the concrete class in the same code.
Right: only the factory implementation names the concrete class.
Comments are not executable.
questions.explain: The name has to appear somewhere, and the trick is to put it where the policy does not depend on it. The card next shows the pattern.
questions.rule: Put the concrete name behind an interface.
Only the factory implementation names the concrete class.
questions.q: In the Abstract Factory structure, the class ____ implements makeSvc and creates the ConcreteImpl.
questions.explain: The implementation of the factory sits on the concrete side of the boundary and does the creating. The Application only knows the interfaces.

questions.q: Which names appear in the source of the Application class?
options: Service and ServiceFactory only
Service, ServiceFactory and ConcreteImpl
ServiceFactoryImpl and ConcreteImpl only
Service and ConcreteImpl only
optionExplain: Right: the Application works with the two interfaces.
ConcreteImpl is named only in the factory implementation.
These are on the concrete side.
The Application reaches the factory through its interface.
questions.explain: Application declares a ServiceFactory field and calls makeSvc to obtain a Service. It never mentions the concrete classes.
questions.rule: Check the names in a class to see its dependencies.

questions.q: Put the run-time sequence in order, from the first action to the last.
items: The start-up code stores a ServiceFactoryImpl where the Application can reach it
The Application calls makeSvc on the ServiceFactory interface
ServiceFactoryImpl creates a ConcreteImpl and returns it as a Service
The Application calls run on the Service
questions.explain: At run time control moves from the Application into the factory implementation and then into the concrete class, while the source dependencies point toward the abstract side.
questions.rule: Control crosses the boundary; the source dependencies point back.

questions.q: A class builds a StringBuilder for a message and also creates a RemoteOrderApi client that the team rewrites every sprint. Which creation needs an abstract factory?
options: The StringBuilder, since it is created more often
Both, because every creation needs a factory
Neither, since the class owns both objects
Only the RemoteOrderApi client
optionExplain: Frequency does not decide it; volatility does.
A stable platform class is tolerated as a concrete dependency.
Ownership does not remove the source dependency on the volatile class.
Right: it is volatile and concrete, while StringBuilder belongs to the stable platform.
questions.explain: The DIP targets volatile concretions. A stable platform class can be created directly, while the volatile client goes behind a factory.
questions.rule: Use factories for volatile concrete objects.

questions.q: In an online shop, one component holds OrderPolicy and the interfaces PaymentGateway and ShippingGateway. A second component holds StripeClient and DhlClient, which implement them. Which description matches the factory diagram's boundary?
options: The second component is the abstract side, because it holds the classes that do the real work, and the first depends on it
The first component is the abstract side with the business rules, and the second depends on it
Neither component is on the abstract side, since both contain classes
Both components depend on each other equally across the line
optionExplain: This reverses the roles.
Right: source dependencies cross the boundary toward the abstract side.
The first holds the rules and the interfaces, so it is the abstract side.
All dependencies cross the line in one direction.
questions.explain: The curved line divides the system into an abstract component, with the high-level business rules, and a concrete component, with the details those rules use.
questions.rule: The abstract side holds the rules and is depended on.
questions.teaches: The boundary divides the system into two components: an abstract one holding the high-level business rules, and a concrete one holding the implementation details that the rules manipulate.

questions.q: In a system whose business rules depend only on interfaces, where should the line that creates the concrete factory live?
options: In the start-up code, apart from the business rules
In every class that needs a service
Inside the business rules, next to the place where the service is used
In a comment, so that it is never executed
optionExplain: Right: the concrete wiring is kept in one small place.
Spreading it multiplies the violations.
This would make the rules depend on a concrete class.
The system needs the line to run.
questions.explain: Somebody has to create the concrete objects. The card next shows where the authors put that code.
questions.rule: Wire the concrete parts at the edge.
Main is the usual home of the wiring.
questions.q: Most systems contain at least one concrete component that creates the factory, often called ____.
questions.explain: It is called main because it contains the main function. It creates the ServiceFactoryImpl and places it in a global variable of the ServiceFactory type.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, DIP violations cannot be entirely removed from a system, but they can be gathered into a few concrete components.
questions.explain: The violations cannot be entirely removed, but they can be gathered into a small number of concrete components and kept apart from the rest of the system.
questions.rule: Confine the violations; you cannot erase them.

questions.q: A developer writes new StripeGateway() inside the OrderPolicy class, saying it is only one place. What is the flaw?
options: Stripe is not a good payment provider
OrderPolicy should create all of its objects with factories that it holds itself, including this one
One new call is too small to matter
The concrete dependency now sits in the business rules, not in a concrete component
optionExplain: The choice of provider is not the issue.
A factory inside the policy would still need a concrete creator somewhere.
The size of the call is not the argument; its location is.
Right: the policy now depends on a volatile class, which the wiring code should hold instead.
questions.explain: The aim is that the business rules depend only on abstractions. The creation belongs with the other wiring, in the concrete component.
questions.rule: Keep concrete creation out of the policy.

questions.q: A team replaces StripeGateway with AdyenGateway. In a design where main does the wiring, which parts change?
options: All the business rules, since they all use payments and must be told about the new provider
The new gateway class and the wiring in main; the rules stay as they are
The gateway interface and every caller
Nothing, since main is generated automatically
optionExplain: The rules use the gateway interface and do not name Stripe.
Right: the rules depend on the interface, which is unchanged.
Swapping the vendor does not change the interface.
Main is ordinary code and needs the new line.
questions.explain: The change is confined to the concrete side. This is the payoff of gathering the violations in one place.
questions.rule: Swapping a detail edits the wiring and the detail.

questions.q: A mobile app has an Application subclass that builds the object graph at start-up and does nothing else. How does it relate to the chapter's main?
options: It is unrelated, because main exists only in command-line programs and not on mobile platforms
It is a business rule and should depend only on interfaces
It plays the same role: a concrete component that connects the concrete parts
It breaks the DIP and should be removed
optionExplain: The role of the concrete component appears in any program.
It does the opposite: it creates the concrete objects.
Right: the role matters, not the name.
It confines the violations, and the system needs it.
questions.explain: A concrete component is defined by its job, which is creating and connecting the concrete parts. Many platforms have their own name for it.
questions.rule: Look for the role, not the name.
questions.teaches: The concrete component is defined by its job of wiring the concrete parts together, so any start-up module that builds the object graph plays the role of main.

questions.q: In a Java project, which of these is the closest match for the smallest piece deployed as part of the system?
options: A single method
A package declaration
A jar file
The build script
optionExplain: A method is far too small to be shipped by itself.
A package declaration is a line of source, not something deployed.
Right: in Java the unit of deployment is the jar file.
The build script produces the deployable pieces; it is not one.
questions.explain: In Java the smallest deployable unit is the jar file. The card next names the same unit in other languages.
questions.rule: Components are what get deployed.

questions.q: Match each language to what a component is in it.
questions.explain: Java, Ruby and .Net each have a named archive, and in interpreted languages a component is an aggregation of source files. In all of them it is the granule of deployment.
questions.rule: Whatever the file type, a component is what gets deployed.

questions.q: A Python team installs a bundle of .py files on servers as one unit. By the book, what is that bundle?
options: A component, since in interpreted languages it is an aggregation of source files
Not a component, since only compiled binaries can be components
Not a component, since components exist only in Java
A component only after it has been compiled
optionExplain: Right: for interpreted languages the book says a component is an aggregation of source files.
Binary files are the compiled-language case; interpreted languages use source files.
The book lists Ruby and .Net as well as Java.
Interpreted languages have components too, with no compile step.
questions.explain: The deployable bundle is the component, in a compiled or an interpreted language.
questions.rule: The deployable unit is the component.

questions.q: True or false: A team links all its components into one executable today. By the book, this means they were not well designed.
questions.explain: Components can be linked into one executable, bundled into an archive or deployed as plugins. Good design means keeping the ability to deploy independently, not using it today.
questions.rule: Keep the ability; the shipping form can vary.

questions.q: A colleague makes four claims about components. Which claims are wrong by the book? Select all that apply.
options: Components are always deployed as separate plugins
In a compiled language a component is an aggregation of binary files
Several components may be linked into a single executable
Only Java has components
optionExplain: Wrong: they can also be linked into one executable or bundled in an archive.
Right as stated: compiled languages use binary files.
Right as stated: linking into one executable is one allowed form.
Wrong: the book names gems in Ruby and DLLs in .Net.
questions.explain: Components appear in every language and can be shipped in several forms. The two wrong claims make shipping form or language a requirement.
questions.rule: A component is not tied to one language or one packaging.

questions.q: A component is built to stay independently deployable, even though it ships inside a war file today. What else does the book say follows?
options: It must be dropped into a folder as a separate plugin
It may not depend on any other component
It needs no release numbers
It is also independently developable
optionExplain: Plugin form is one option, not a consequence of the ability.
The book does not rule out dependencies; later principles manage them.
Release numbers are the topic of a later principle and are not removed by this ability.
Right: the book ties deployability and developability together.
questions.explain: A component that can be deployed independently can also be developed independently.
questions.rule: Independent deployability brings independent developability.
questions.teaches: Because a well-designed component can be deployed independently, it can also be developed independently.

questions.q: Early programs were compiled together with all their library functions as one body of source. What was the main cost?
options: The program could not call library functions
Compile time grew with the size of the library
Library code ran slower than application code
The library had to be rewritten for each program
optionExplain: Calls worked; the library source was part of the program.
Right: every compile had to process the whole library again.
Once compiled, the library code ran like any other code.
The same library source was reused, not rewritten.
questions.explain: Including library source in every build makes every build slower as the library grows. The card next explains the setting.
questions.rule: Libraries in source make every compile pay.

questions.q: In the early days, a program began with an origin statement that declared the address at which it was to be ____.
questions.explain: The origin statement fixed the load address, because programs were not relocatable.
questions.rule: The programmer chose the load address.

questions.q: A 1960s compiler needs several passes over the source, but memory cannot hold it all. What happens to compile time as the library grows?
options: The source stays cached in memory between passes, so compile time stays flat however large the library
The source is re-read from slow devices on each pass, so a bigger library compiles longer
Library code is skipped on later passes, so its size costs nothing
The library is loaded at a fixed binary address, so compile time drops
optionExplain: Memory was too limited to keep the source resident.
Right: slow devices plus several passes make size cost time.
Nothing in the book lets the compiler skip library source in this scheme.
That is the later fix of separate compilation, not this setting.
questions.explain: Limited memory forced repeated reads from slow devices, so compile time followed library size.
questions.rule: Size of the source set drives compile time.

questions.q: True or false: Adding more functions to a source-included library in this era made compiles faster, since more code could be reused.
questions.explain: More library source means more to read and compile on every build. Reuse did not shorten the compile.
questions.rule: More library source, longer compile.

questions.q: Match each early practice or condition to its consequence.
pairs: The programmer chose the load address
questions.explain: Each condition in the setting led to the next cost: fixed addresses, source libraries, repeated slow reads, and long compiles.
questions.rule: Each condition of the era added to compile time.

questions.q: Why was a compile in that era slow, even with a correct compiler? Pick the reason the book gives.
options: The compiler wrote its output to tape one character at a time, which took hours on large programs
Library source had to be typed in again for each program
The loader had to link hundreds of libraries first
Several passes over source that memory could not hold, re-read from slow devices
optionExplain: The book does not describe character-at-a-time output.
Library source was copied as decks, not typed in; see the footnote about decks on a shelf.
Linking loaders came later and are a different cost.
Right: several passes plus slow, limited storage.
questions.explain: Compilers needed several passes, memory could not hold the source, so it was re-read from slow devices.
questions.rule: Passes plus slow storage cost time.
questions.teaches: Compilers needed several passes over the source, and memory was too limited to hold it, so the source was read in again several times from slow devices.

questions.q: True or false: If a library is compiled separately and loaded at a fixed address, applications can grow without limit.
questions.explain: An application must fit in the space left for it. The card next shows what happens when it does not.
questions.rule: A fixed layout cannot absorb growth.

questions.q: To shorten compile times, what did programmers do with the function library?
options: Compiled it separately and loaded the binary at a known address
Rewrote it in a lower-level language
Copied its source into each application deck
Kept it on tape and read it for every call
optionExplain: Right: separate compilation and a known load address.
The book does not mention rewriting it.
That is the source-included practice the change replaced.
Reading per call would be slow and is not the described fix.
questions.explain: Compiling the library separately removed it from every application compile.
questions.rule: Compile the library once, load it at a known address.

questions.q: Put the steps of the separate-library scheme in the order the book gives.
items: Compile the library on its own and build its symbol table
Compile the application together with the library's symbol table
Load the library binary at its known address
Load the application into the memory left over
questions.explain: The symbol table lets the application compile without the library source. At run time the library binary is loaded first and the application after it.
questions.rule: Library first, application after.

questions.q: A library binary sits at a known address with a fixed gap below it for the application. The application outgrows the gap. What does the book say the programmer must do?
options: Move the library source back into the application
Delete rarely used functions from the library
Split the application into two address segments that jump around the library
Load the application at the same addresses as the library
optionExplain: That returns to the slow source-included scheme.
The book does not suggest cutting the library.
Right: two address segments, jumping around the library.
Two programs cannot occupy the same addresses.
questions.explain: The fixed layout leaves no room to grow, so the application is cut in two around the library.
questions.rule: A fixed layout turns growth into splitting.
questions.hint: Look at the layout of the memory, not at the compiler.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's example, once the library exceeds its bounds, nothing else in memory has to move or be split.
questions.explain: The library needs more space elsewhere, so programs and libraries fragment further as memory grows.
questions.rule: Growth of one part fragments the others.

questions.q: Why could the function library stay loaded in memory for days on those old machines?
options: The library was flashed into read-only chips
The loader reloaded it every few seconds
The application kept a private copy
Core memory kept its contents when the power was off
optionExplain: The book does not mention read-only chips.
Nothing in the text describes periodic reloading.
The library was loaded once and shared; private copies are not described.
Right: the footnote says core memory was not erased at power down.
questions.explain: Most of those machines used core memory, which kept its contents, so the library could be left loaded.
questions.rule: Persistent memory let the library be loaded once.
questions.teaches: Most of those old machines used core memory, which was not erased when the power went down, so the function library was often left loaded for days.

questions.q: A compiler emits code with absolute addresses. What would let one binary be loaded at any address chosen later?
options: A larger memory
Flags telling a loader which parts to change once the address is chosen
A separate copy of the source for each address at which it might be loaded
A symbol table that the programmer keeps on paper and applies by hand at load time
optionExplain: More memory does not stop addresses being absolute.
Right: flags tell a loader what to adjust.
That multiplies work and is the problem to avoid.
A paper table does not change the binary.
questions.explain: Marking the address-dependent parts lets a loader adjust them. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Flag what must change, then let the loader change it.

questions.q: When a program calls a library function, the compiler emits the function name as an external ____.
questions.explain: A call is an external reference. A function the code defines is emitted as an external definition.
questions.rule: Call is reference; definition is definition.

questions.q: Binary A calls parse(). Binary B defines parse(). The loader puts B at 5000 and A at 9000. How is the call connected?
options: A's compiler copies B's source text into A so that parse() becomes local to A
The programmer edits the call by hand to use address 5000 after seeing where B went
The loader links A's external reference to B's external definition after placing B
A is loaded again at 5000 so both share the address
optionExplain: Copying source is the older practice relocatability replaced.
Hand editing is the old fixed-address burden.
Right: names are matched after placement.
Two binaries cannot share addresses.
questions.explain: References and definitions are matched by name, after the loader has chosen addresses.
questions.rule: Match names after placing the pieces.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A function name the code calls
A function name the code defines
Marks a place to adjust for the chosen address
Places binaries and joins references to definitions
questions.explain: The compiler supplies the names and flags; the loader uses them to place and join the binaries.
questions.rule: Compiler marks, loader acts.

questions.q: True or false: As programs grew to need hundreds of binaries read from tape, the linking loader stayed fast enough.
questions.explain: Resolving the references meant reading all those binaries from slow devices, so loading could take more than an hour.
questions.rule: A fix has a size limit.

questions.q: A team's tool loads many small compiled modules at start-up. Which benefit of the 1960s loaders does this mirror?
options: Only the functions the program needs have to be loaded
The compiler no longer needs a symbol table
Every module must sit at the same address
The loader never touches the memory references
optionExplain: Right: because the loader took several binary inputs, programmers could load just what they needed.
The symbol-table topic belongs to the earlier scheme.
Several binaries were placed one after another, not at the same address.
Relocation does change memory references.
questions.explain: Loading several binaries one after another let programmers choose only the functions they needed.
questions.rule: Load only what the program needs.
questions.teaches: Because the loader accepted several binary inputs and loaded them one after another, programmers could load only the functions they needed.

questions.q: Loading a big program takes an hour because resolving references means reading hundreds of binaries from slow media. Which change attacks that cost?
options: Buy a larger tape so that more libraries fit on one reel
Merge all the libraries into one source file and compile it with the program
Resolve the references in an earlier, separate step and load the result
Skip relocation entirely
optionExplain: A larger tape does not remove the reads.
That returns to compiling the library with every program.
Right: do the slow part once, ahead of time.
Without relocation the load address is fixed again.
questions.explain: Moving the slow resolving step out of the load path makes loading fast. The card next names the step.
questions.rule: Do slow work ahead of time.

questions.q: The program that took over the slow reference-resolving work from the loader is called the ____.
questions.explain: The linker does the slow part, and its output is a linked relocatable.
questions.rule: Linking and loading are separate phases.

questions.q: A test harness loads 300 compiled modules at start and spends 20 minutes resolving them. By the book's historical fix, what should change?
options: Compile the modules into a single source file so that nothing is left to resolve
Resolve the references once in a linker, then load the linked output
Fix each module's load address by hand
Split the harness into two address segments
optionExplain: That brings back the slow, source-based compile.
Right: link ahead of time, load fast.
Hand-chosen addresses are the pre-relocation burden.
Segment splitting was a symptom of fixed layouts.
questions.explain: The slow resolving step is done once by a linker, and the quick loader runs every time.
questions.rule: Link once, load many times.

questions.q: Put the 1980s C build steps in order.
items: Compile each .c file into an .o file
Feed the .o files into the linker
The linker creates the executable
Load the executable quickly
questions.explain: Source modules were compiled to .o files, linked into an executable, and then loaded quickly.
questions.rule: Compile, link, then load.

questions.q: In the 1980s programs of hundreds of thousands of lines used the linker. What was the turnaround like?
options: Turnaround fell to a matter of seconds because loading was already fast
Loading became the bottleneck again
Turnaround no longer depended on the size of the program being built
Loading stayed fast, but compile and link could take an hour or more
optionExplain: That happened only by the mid-1990s.
Loading was the part the split had made fast.
Program size still drove the time.
Right: the slow work moved to compile and link.
questions.explain: The split made loading fast but left compile-link time as the bottleneck.
questions.rule: The cost moved; it did not vanish.

questions.q: A mobile team finds its release build slow while app start-up is quick. Which statement matches the book's 1980s lesson?
options: Linking is the fastest build step, so a slow build must come from compiling alone
Start-up time must be slow if the build is slow, since both read the same files
Compiling each module is quick, but compiling all and then linking takes long
Build time is independent of the number of modules
optionExplain: The book says linking took even more time than compiling.
The split made loading fast while building stayed slow.
Right: this is the pattern the book describes.
More modules meant more build time.
questions.explain: Compiling one module was relatively fast; compiling all of them took a while, and the linker then took even more time.
questions.rule: Quick loading does not mean a quick build.
questions.teaches: In the 1980s compiling each individual module was relatively fast, but compiling all the modules took a while and the linker then took even more time.

questions.q: Tools got faster for decades, yet build turnaround stayed near an hour. What best explains this?
options: Programs grew to use up the extra speed
Developers declined to use the faster tools
Linkers had not yet been invented
Compilers were made slower on purpose
optionExplain: Right: growth consumed the gains.
Nothing in the text says tools were refused.
Linkers existed from the early 1970s.
No such motive is described.
questions.explain: Faster tools were matched by larger programs. The card next names this pattern.
questions.rule: Growth can eat speed gains.

questions.q: Murphy's law of program size says programs will grow to fill all available compile and ____ time.
questions.explain: The law covers compile and link time together.
questions.rule: Programs grow to fill the time available.

questions.q: A game studio's builds take 30 minutes. New machines are twice as fast, but the studio then doubles its code. By Murphy's law of program size, what happens to build time?
options: It halves, because the new machines are twice as fast
It doubles, because the code has doubled in size
It drops to seconds, because hardware outpaces growth
About the same: growth fills the time gained
optionExplain: That assumes the code stays the same size.
Twice the speed and twice the code roughly cancel.
Seconds came only when hardware outpaced growth, as in the mid-1990s.
Right: the gain is consumed by growth.
questions.explain: Speed doubled and code doubled, so the time to build is about unchanged.
questions.rule: Faster machines plus bigger programs can cancel out.

questions.q: Which statement is Moore's law as the book gives it?
options: Programs grow to fill all available compile and link time
Computer speed, memory and density double every 18 months
Linking must take under a minute for a program to be built at all
Memory costs fall by half every year as production scales up
optionExplain: That is Murphy's law of program size.
Right: that is the book's statement.
The book states no such limit.
The book states no such price rule.
questions.explain: Murphy's law is about programs growing; Moore's law is about hardware doubling.
questions.rule: Murphy: programs grow. Moore: hardware doubles.

questions.q: True or false: By the mid-1990s the time spent linking had begun to shrink faster than programs grew.
questions.explain: Hardware speed had overtaken ambition, and in many cases link time fell to seconds. This made linking at load time feasible again for small jobs.
questions.rule: Hardware won the race in the mid-1990s.

questions.q: A team plans its build system on the belief that machines will keep doubling in speed every 18 months. What caution does the book add?
options: Moore's law never applied to linking or loading at all
Murphy's law stops applying once programs become large enough
Disks stop getting faster after the mid-1990s because they shrink
The doubling held until about 2000, then stopped for clock rates
optionExplain: The book uses the law to explain falling link times.
Murphy's law is what the book calls the growth pull; it does not stop.
The book does not claim that.
Right: the book's footnote says the law stopped cold for clock rates.
questions.explain: The doubling held from the 1950s to 2000, but then, at least for clock rates, it stopped.
questions.rule: Do not rely on hardware doubling for ever.
questions.teaches: Moore's law held from the 1950s to 2000, but then, at least for clock rates, it stopped cold.

questions.q: A user adds a feature to a desktop game by copying one file into a folder. Which idea makes that possible?
options: The game links separately built pieces when it loads
The game is compiled with all features in source
The game fixes its pieces at hand-chosen addresses
The game reruns a weekly build
optionExplain: Right: pieces linked at load time.
That would need a rebuild for each feature.
That is the early practice that blocked this.
A weekly build integrates source, not plugins.
questions.explain: Linking at load time lets a new file join the program. The card next names this style.
questions.rule: Link pieces at load time.

questions.q: True or false: By the book, dynamically linked files that can be plugged together at runtime are the software components of our architectures.
questions.explain: That is how the chapter closes: the plugged-together files are the components.
questions.rule: Components are the runtime-pluggable files.

questions.q: A reporting tool lets customers drop a new exporter .jar into a folder. What does the book call this style?
options: A weekly build
A linking loader of the kind used in the 1960s
A component plugin architecture
A fixed-address segment layout
optionExplain: A weekly build is an integration schedule.
Linking loaders are from the 1960s and were not run on jars.
Right: components plugged in as separate files.
Fixed-address layouts are the early memory practice.
questions.explain: Dropping a separately built file in to extend an application is the plugin style.
questions.rule: Extend by adding a component.

questions.q: Put these steps of the history in order.
items: Programs fixed at hand-chosen addresses with library source
Relocatable binaries and the linking loader
A separate linker produces a linked relocatable
Link time shrinks and plugin components become the casual default
questions.explain: The history runs from fixed addresses, to relocation, to a separate linker, and then to fast linking and plugins.
questions.rule: Each step answered the cost of the one before.

questions.q: True or false: Plugin architecture became practical because programs stopped growing.
questions.explain: Programs kept growing; hardware improved faster, so link time fell to seconds.
questions.rule: Hardware speed made load-time linking practical.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a plugin component that the book gives?
options: A weekly build of Minecraft
A Minecraft source deck on a shelf
A Minecraft program fixed at a chosen address
A Minecraft mod delivered as a .jar in a certain folder
optionExplain: Not a plugin example in the text.
Source decks belong to the early era.
Fixed addresses belong to the early era.
Right: the book names mods and Resharper in Visual Studio.
questions.explain: The book names a Minecraft mod (a custom .jar in a certain folder) and Resharper in Visual Studio (DLLs) as plugins.
questions.rule: A plugin is a file added to a host.
questions.teaches: A Minecraft mod is added by placing a custom .jar in a certain folder, and Resharper plugs into Visual Studio by including the appropriate DLLs.

questions.q: Teams want to reuse a company's logging library. What must its owners provide before teams will rely on it?
options: A promise never to change it
A release process with numbered releases
Its source copied into every project
Daily builds sent to every user
optionExplain: A frozen library is not what the book asks for.
Right: reusers need to track versions.
Copying source is the early practice, not tracked reuse.
Constant builds do not tell users what changed.
questions.explain: Reusers need to know which version they have and when a new one comes. The card next states the principle.
questions.rule: Reuse needs release tracking.

questions.q: The granule of reuse is the granule of ____.
questions.explain: This is the statement of the REP: what is reused is what is released.
questions.rule: Reuse unit equals release unit.

questions.q: Team B uses Team A's library. A releases 3.0 with documented changes. B reads the notes and stays on 2.4 for now. Is that acceptable by the book?
options: No, users must adopt every release at once to stay compatible
No, only the owners may choose which release is used
Yes, users decide whether and when to integrate a release
Yes, but only when no release notes exist
optionExplain: The book describes users who keep the old release.
Users choose; owners inform.
Right: informed choice is the point of a release process.
