Notes are what make the choice informed.
questions.explain: Release numbers and notes let users choose when to move. Staying on an old release is a normal, informed decision.
questions.rule: Releases let users decide when to upgrade.

questions.q: True or false: The only reason the REP asks for release numbers is to check that reused components are compatible with each other.
questions.explain: Compatibility is one reason. The other is that developers need to know when new releases come and what changes they bring.
questions.rule: Release numbers serve compatibility and information.

questions.q: True or false: People will reuse a component that has no release process, as long as it is shared widely.
questions.explain: The book says people who want to reuse components cannot, and will not, do so unless they are tracked through a release process with release numbers.
questions.rule: No release process, no reuse.

questions.q: A mobile SDK vendor replaces the old SDK on its site with no notes. What does the REP say is missing?
options: Release notes and notices so users can choose when to upgrade
A larger set of classes in the SDK so that more users are served
A way to force users onto the new version as soon as it is out
Source code for every user so that they can check changes themselves
optionExplain: Right: the release process must produce them.
Size is not the issue.
The book wants users to be able to stay on the old release.
Source access is not part of the principle.
questions.explain: The release process must produce the appropriate notifications and release documentation so that users can make informed decisions.
questions.rule: Releases need notice and notes.
questions.teaches: The release process must produce the appropriate notifications and release documentation so that users can make informed decisions about when and whether to integrate a new release.

questions.q: A jar holds an XML parser, a payroll calculator and a PDF printer under one version number. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing, because a jar can hold any classes that the authors choose
Its version number is too high
Its classes share no theme, so one release means little
It should be released without a version number
optionExplain: A jar can hold anything, but the version then says nothing useful.
The number is not the issue.
Right: no common purpose.
Release tracking is what the REP asks for.
questions.explain: Unrelated classes under one release number do not make sense together. The card next names the principle.
questions.rule: A release needs a theme.

questions.q: True or false: By the REP, a component may be a random collection of classes as long as it has a version number.
questions.explain: The REP requires a cohesive group with an overarching theme or purpose, not a random hodgepodge.
questions.rule: Cohesive, not random.

questions.q: Which grouping best satisfies the REP?
options: A component holding the date parser and invoice printing
A date component holding the parser, formatters and time-zone tables
One component holding every class in the company
A component whose classes were picked alphabetically
optionExplain: Invoice printing has a different purpose.
Right: one theme, releasable together.
No theme joins everything in a company.
Alphabetical order is not a purpose.
questions.explain: Classes with one shared purpose make a release that users can understand.
questions.rule: Choose classes by shared purpose.

questions.q: The book calls the REP weak advice. What is the weakness?
options: It applies to Java components and not to other languages
It makes release numbers harder to assign to the classes of a component
It forbids grouping classes at all
It only says the grouping should make sense, without saying why
optionExplain: The book states it for components in general.
The REP is about release numbers.
It asks for grouping, not against it.
Right: this is the book's complaint.
questions.explain: The principle's wording leaves the glue unspecified, so it is hard to apply precisely.
questions.rule: Weak to apply, easy to violate.

questions.q: If you violate the REP, your ____ will know, because the grouping does not make sense to them.
questions.explain: Violations are easy to detect: the people who use the component see that its grouping makes no sense.
questions.rule: Users can see a bad grouping.

questions.q: How does the book say the CCP and CRP relate to the weak REP?
options: They define it strongly, but in a negative sense
They replace it with a stricter rule
They contradict it
They apply only to classes, not components
optionExplain: Right: they say what does not belong.
The book keeps the REP and adds to it.
They define the REP rather than contradict it.
Both are component principles.
questions.explain: The CCP and CRP strongly define the REP by saying what to separate and what not to keep together.
questions.rule: The later principles sharpen the REP.
questions.teaches: The CCP and CRP strongly define the REP, but in a negative sense.

questions.q: A tax rules class and a tax report layout class change together every year. Where should they live?
options: In separate components, one per kind of class
In the component that changes least
In separate components, so each stays small
In the same component
optionExplain: Splitting them forces two releases for one change.
Placing them with unrelated code spreads the change.
Small size is not the goal of the CCP.
Right: they change for the same reason.
questions.explain: Classes that change together should be released together. The card next names this the CCP.
questions.rule: Same change, same component.

questions.q: The CCP says to gather into one component the classes that change for the same reasons and at the same ____.
questions.explain: Reasons and times are the two tests of the principle.
questions.rule: Same reasons and same times.

questions.q: Discount rules and a coupon parser change with every promotion; a label printer changes with the courier. How does the CCP group them?
options: All three together, as they are all part of one shop's order flow
Discount rules and coupon parser together; label printer apart
Each in a component of its own
The coupon parser with the label printer
optionExplain: The printer changes for another reason.
Right: group by reason for change.
Separating the two promotion classes needs two releases per promotion.
They change for different reasons.
questions.explain: Two classes share a reason to change, and the third has a different one.
questions.rule: Group by shared reason to change.

questions.q: Sort each reason for grouping two classes by whether it comes from the CCP.

items.t: The classes change for the same requirement changes
Users take the two classes together
The classes share a release number
The classes change at the same times
Their names are similar

questions.explain: The CCP looks at what makes classes change. Joint use is the CRP, a shared number follows from grouping, and similar names are not a reason.
questions.rule: CCP: change. CRP: use.

questions.q: True or false: A requirement change that touches classes in five components needs all five to be released, revalidated and redeployed.
questions.explain: Each changed component has to be released, which is the work the CCP tries to confine to few components.
questions.rule: Scattered changes multiply releases.

questions.q: In your own words: why does the CCP keep the number of components touched by one requirement change low?
questions.a: Classes that change for the same reasons and at the same times sit in the same component, so one change lands in few components and only those need to be released, revalidated and redeployed.
questions.rule: Group by change to confine change.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the SRP and the CCP?
options: The same rule one level up: classes into components, by reasons to change
The SRP applies to components and the CCP applies to classes, for the same purpose
The SRP is about reuse and the CCP about change
They give opposite advice
optionExplain: Right: the same idea at two sizes.
The levels are the other way round.
Both are about change.
They agree.
questions.explain: The SRP tells us to separate methods into different classes if they change for different reasons; the CCP does the same with classes and components.
questions.rule: Same rule, one level up.
questions.teaches: The SRP tells us to separate methods into different classes if they change for different reasons; the CCP tells us to separate classes into different components if they change for different reasons.

questions.q: A change request touches code in one component only. Which statement about the other components is true?
options: All components must be redeployed
They need testing only if they are larger than the changed component
Those that do not depend on it need not be redeployed
They must be recompiled but need no testing
optionExplain: Only the changed component and its dependents are affected.
Size is not the test.
Right: the change is confined.
Revalidation follows dependency.
questions.explain: Confined changes confine the release work. The card next names the principle behind this.
questions.rule: Confine changes to few components.

questions.q: True or false: By the book, for most applications maintainability is more important than reusability.
questions.explain: The book says so when it explains why the CCP gathers classes that change together.
questions.rule: Maintainability usually outweighs reuse.

questions.q: A payroll app's tax rules change yearly; report styles rarely change. Where should the closure effort go?
options: Spread tax code over every component to share the load
Make each class closed against every possible change
Group classes by size
Group the tax classes so yearly changes hit one component
optionExplain: Spreading multiplies the release work.
Complete closure is not attainable.
Size says nothing about change.
Right: protect against the likely change.
questions.explain: Closure is strategic: aim it at the changes you expect, such as yearly tax rules.
questions.rule: Aim closure at likely changes.

questions.q: A designer wants every class completely closed. The book says complete closure is not attainable, so closure must be ____.
questions.explain: Closure is aimed at the most common kinds of change that are expected or have been met.
questions.rule: Closure is strategic, not total.

questions.q: True or false: A component grouped by the CCP is closed against every possible change.
questions.explain: It is closed against the kinds of change the designers expect or have met. Other changes can still spread.
questions.rule: The CCP protects only against anticipated change.

questions.q: In what sense does the CCP use the word closure?
options: As the closing of a release, after which no further change is allowed
As the end of a project, when all of its components are frozen
In the OCP's sense: classes closed to the same changes are gathered
As a rule against any modification of the classes in a component
optionExplain: Closure here is not about releases ending.
It has nothing to do with project ends.
Right: the CCP applies the OCP idea to components.
The OCP allows extension, so closure is not a ban on change.
questions.explain: The CCP gathers into a component those classes that are closed to the same types of change, so a requirement change touches few components.
questions.rule: Gather classes closed to the same changes.
questions.teaches: The CCP addresses closure in the OCP sense: it gathers into the same component the classes that are closed to the same types of changes.

questions.q: A stack class is shipped in one jar and its iterator in another, and users of the stack need the iterator too. What is the issue?
options: Classes reused together are split across components
The iterator is too big
The stack has too many users
The two jars share a release number
optionExplain: Right: they should travel together.
Size is not the issue.
Many users are not a flaw.
A shared number would help, not hurt.
questions.explain: Users must take both jars to use one idea. The card next states the CRP.
questions.rule: Put the reused-together classes together.

questions.q: A simple example of classes reused together is a container class and its associated ____.
questions.explain: The container and iterators are tightly coupled and reused together.
questions.rule: Tightly coupled classes are reused together.

questions.q: A charting library has Chart, Axis and Legend classes that every user takes together, and a CSV importer few use. How does the CRP group Chart, Axis and Legend?
options: In the same component
In three separate components
With the CSV importer
Each with the application that uses it
optionExplain: Right: they are reused together.
Users would then need three dependencies for one idea.
The importer is used by few of them.
Components are shared, not per application.
questions.explain: Classes that users take together form one reusable unit.
questions.rule: Group by joint use.

questions.q: Sort each observation by the principle it argues from.

items.t: Users import the container and its iterators together
Two classes change for the same requirement
Classes collaborate inside one reusable abstraction
Classes are edited together in each release

questions.explain: The CRP argues from how classes are reused. The CCP argues from how they change.
questions.rule: CRP follows use; CCP follows change.

questions.q: True or false: A component built by the CRP is expected to hold classes that have nothing to do with each other.
questions.explain: The CRP groups classes that are reused together, so they are tightly bound and have many dependencies on each other.
questions.rule: Expect strong ties inside.

questions.q: A team extracts a Money class into a shared component alone. Users also need its Currency and Rounding classes. What does the CRP say?
options: Money should stay alone, because each class is a unit that can be reused alone
Currency and Rounding should be left to each user to write or copy for themselves
Reuse of single classes works the same as reuse of groups, so nothing changes
Money collaborates with them as one abstraction, so they belong together
optionExplain: Classes are seldom reused in isolation.
Users would then depend on separate pieces.
The CRP says reusable classes collaborate.
Right: they form one abstraction.
questions.explain: Classes are seldom reused in isolation; reusable classes usually collaborate with others in the same abstraction.
questions.rule: Reuse goes with collaborators.
questions.teaches: Classes are seldom reused in isolation: reusable classes typically collaborate with other classes that are part of the reusable abstraction.

questions.q: Your service uses one small class from a large utility jar. A new release changes other classes in the jar. What is likely?
options: Nothing, since you use one class
Only users of the other classes are affected
You may still need to recompile, revalidate and redeploy
You must rewrite your class
optionExplain: Using one class does not weaken the dependency.
Dependency is by component.
Right: the dependency is on the whole component.
No rewrite is implied.
questions.explain: The dependency is on the component, so its releases reach you. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: Depend on a whole, pay for a whole.

questions.q: Even if a component uses only one class of another, that does not weaken the ____ between the components.
questions.explain: The using component still depends on the used component.
questions.rule: One class used, whole component depended on.

questions.q: A mobile app imports a common-tools component only for a string helper. The component also holds a chart engine. Which principle is at issue?
options: The CRP: the app depends on a component with classes it does not use
The REP: the helper has no release number of its own to rely on
The CCP: the chart engine changes too slowly to be kept with the helper
None: unused classes are harmless
optionExplain: Right: unneeded classes in the dependency.
The issue is unneeded classes, not numbers.
The issue is not the rate of change.
Releases of the chart engine still reach the app.
questions.explain: The app must follow releases of a component full of classes it never uses.
questions.rule: Unneeded classes still cost.

questions.q: Which situation best shows the cost the CRP warns about?
options: A change in the string helper forces the apps that use the helper to rebuild
A new chart class is added, and no one who uses the string helper notices
A release number is skipped between two consecutive releases of the component
A chart engine change forces helper-only apps to rebuild and revalidate
optionExplain: That is the normal case of using a changed class.
Unused additions do not reach those who do not depend on them.
Skipped numbers are unrelated.
Right: unrelated change reaches users.
questions.explain: The cost is a change in classes users never need reaching them anyway.
questions.rule: Unrelated changes reach every user.

questions.q: True or false: Moving the string helper into a component of its own removes the app's dependence on chart engine releases.
questions.explain: The app then depends only on the helper component, which no longer carries classes it does not use.
questions.rule: Split so users need only their part.

questions.q: A vendor's new release changes only classes your team does not call. Is your team's work finished?
options: Yes, as long as your team uses none of the changed classes in its code
No, you will likely still need to recompile, revalidate and redeploy
Yes, if the vendor's release number is unchanged
No, you must rewrite all of your classes to match the new release
optionExplain: Not using changed classes does not release you.
Right: even without needed changes.
A new release is a new release.
A rewrite is not implied.
questions.explain: Even when no change to the using component is necessary, it will likely need recompiling, revalidating and redeploying.
questions.rule: Dependency means following releases.
questions.teaches: Even if no change is necessary to the using component, it will likely still need to be recompiled, revalidated and redeployed, even though it does not care about the change.

questions.q: Which one-line advice covers both classes with unused methods and components with unused classes?
options: Depend on abstractions
Gather what changes together
Release what you reuse
Do not depend on things you do not need
optionExplain: That is the dependency inversion idea.
That is the CCP.
That is the REP.
Right: it covers both levels.
questions.explain: The same advice works at the level of methods and of classes. The card next names the principles.
questions.rule: Avoid dependency on the unneeded.

questions.q: Match each principle to its advice.
pairs: Do not depend on classes with methods you do not use
Do not depend on components with classes you do not use
The granule of reuse is the granule of release
questions.explain: The ISP and CRP are the same advice at two levels; the CCP and REP address other forces.
questions.rule: Four principles, four pieces of advice.

questions.q: A service imports an auth component for one password-check class. The component also holds OAuth, LDAP and SAML classes the service does not use. Which fix follows from the CRP?
options: Separate the password check from the classes the service does not use
Add more classes so that the component is complete for every kind of user
Copy the source into the service
Ignore it, since the classes are unused
optionExplain: Right: shrink the dependency.
More classes add more to depend on.
Copying source loses release tracking.
Unused classes still bring releases.
questions.explain: The CRP advises not depending on components that carry classes you do not use.
questions.rule: Split off what is not needed together.

questions.q: Which pair puts the ISP and CRP at the right level?
options: ISP: components and their classes; CRP: classes and their methods
Both work between methods and variables, inside a single class or module
ISP: classes and their methods; CRP: components and their classes
Both: modules and packages only
optionExplain: That reverses them.
Neither is about variables.
Right: the same idea one level up.
The CRP is explicitly about components.
questions.explain: The ISP works inside a class; the CRP works at the component level.
questions.rule: Same idea at two levels.

questions.q: True or false: A class that uses every method of an interface, but one of five classes in an imported component, is flagged by the CRP and not by the ISP.
questions.explain: The interface is fully used, so the ISP has nothing to say. Four of the five classes in the component are unused, which is the CRP's concern.
questions.rule: Check each level on its own.

questions.q: Which statement about the CRP and ISP does the book make?
options: The CRP is the opposite of the ISP and contradicts it on every point
The CRP is the generic form of the ISP, for components
The CRP replaces the ISP in object-oriented code, which makes it obsolete
The ISP is a special case of the CCP applied to methods instead of classes
optionExplain: They agree.
Right: that is the book's statement.
Both stand.
The book links the ISP to the CRP.
questions.explain: The book calls the CRP the generic version of the ISP, and reduces both to one sound bite.
questions.rule: CRP generalises ISP.
questions.teaches: The CRP is the generic version of the ISP, and both can be reduced to one sound bite: do not depend on things you do not need.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: A team wants fewer, larger components for easy release and few components touched per change. Which principle pushes back?
options: The CCP, which wants fewer releases of the larger components
The REP, which wants release numbers
The CRP, which wants only classes used together
The SRP, which forbids classes
optionExplain: The CCP agrees with grouping.
The REP also favours grouping.
Right: the CRP pulls the other way.
The SRP does not forbid classes.
questions.explain: Larger components bring in classes that users may not need. The card next names the tension.
questions.rule: Grouping and splitting pull apart.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: Sort each effect by the kind of principle that causes it.

items.t: Pulls classes that change together into one component
Pushes out classes users do not need
Puts reusable classes under one release
Keeps users from depending on unused classes

questions.explain: The REP and CCP include classes; the CRP excludes them.
questions.rule: REP and CCP include; CRP excludes.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: An architect focuses only on the REP and CRP. What does the book say goes wrong?
options: Too many components are hit when simple changes are made
Too many unneeded releases are produced
Components cannot be reused
Components become too large to release
optionExplain: Right: the CCP is neglected.
That is the cost of neglecting the CRP.
Reuse is what the REP and CRP serve.
Large size comes from CCP and REP.
questions.explain: Neglecting the CCP spreads changes across components.
questions.rule: Neglect the CCP: changes spread.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: True or false: Focusing on the CCP and REP alone leads to too many components being touched by a simple change.
questions.explain: That is the cost of neglecting the CCP. Focusing on the CCP and REP leads to too many unneeded releases.
questions.rule: Neglect the CRP: unneeded releases.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: True or false: Ignoring the CRP completely tends to shrink components to single classes.
questions.explain: The CRP is the exclusive principle. Without it, the REP and CCP make components larger, and users get releases they do not need.
questions.rule: Without the CRP, bloat.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: A team's design leans toward the edge joining the REP and CRP on the tension triangle. What does that edge describe?
options: The cost of abandoning the REP, which sits at one end of the edge
The cost of abandoning the CRP
The cost of abandoning the CCP, at the opposite vertex
The benefit of keeping all three principles at once
optionExplain: The REP is at one end of this edge.
The CRP is at one end of this edge.
Right: edges name the cost of the opposite vertex.
Edges describe costs.
questions.explain: Each edge describes the cost of giving up the principle on the vertex opposite to it.
questions.rule: An edge costs the opposite vertex.
questions.teaches: Each edge of the tension diagram describes the cost of abandoning the principle on the opposite vertex.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: A new library is used by one team and changes weekly. Which concern should drive its grouping now?
options: Reuse by many outside teams who will adopt it in the future
Developability: keeping weekly changes in few components
Long release cycles
Making components tiny for others
optionExplain: No outside teams use it yet.
Right: development comes first.
Long cycles do not suit weekly change.
Others are not yet the audience.
questions.explain: Early on, ease of change matters most. The card next explains the slide over time.
questions.rule: Early: ease of change.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: Early in a project, the CCP matters more than the REP, because developability matters more than ____.
questions.explain: The book says developability is more important than reuse early on.
questions.rule: Early on, developability over reuse.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: An internal framework once used by one app is adopted by six other teams. Which shift fits the book?
options: The CCP matters more than before, because more teams now change it
Release numbers stop mattering
The project moves to the right on the triangle
Reuse matters more, so the balance slides toward REP and CRP
optionExplain: That was the early stage.
Reuse needs release numbers more.
The slide goes the other way.
Right: other projects begin to draw on it.
questions.explain: As other projects draw from a project, reuse becomes more important.
questions.rule: Adoption shifts the balance.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: True or false: The component structure of a project depends mainly on what it does, so it stays the same as it matures.
questions.explain: The book says the structure has more to do with how the project is developed and used than with what it does, and it varies with maturity.
questions.rule: Structure follows use and maturity.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: Projects tend to start on the right-hand side of the triangle, where the only sacrifice is ____.
questions.explain: Early on, the CCP matters more than the REP, and only reuse suffers.
questions.rule: Start right; slide left.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: Two projects do the same job: one internal, one a public library. Why may their component structures differ?
options: Structure follows how a project is developed and used
A structure is fixed by the job
Public projects ignore the CCP because their users are outside the team
Internal projects need no components
optionExplain: Right: the book's claim.
The book denies this.
No such claim is made.
No such claim is made.
questions.explain: How the project is developed and used shapes its structure.
questions.rule: Use shapes structure.
questions.teaches: The component structure of a project has more to do with the way the project is developed and used than with what the project actually does.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: Which is the old, simpler view of cohesion that the three component principles go beyond?
options: A module has the fewest possible classes
A module is released once a year
A module depends on nothing
A module performs one, and only one, function
optionExplain: Size is not the old view.
Release frequency is unrelated.
Independence is not the definition.
Right: the single-function view.
questions.explain: The old view looked at what a module does. The card next gives the richer view.
questions.rule: Cohesion once meant one function.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: The three component cohesion principles balance the opposing forces of reusability and ____.
questions.explain: The book names these two opposing forces in its conclusion.
questions.rule: Reusability against developability.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: A component does one function, but changes for six unrelated reasons and ships classes most users do not use. Is it cohesive by the three principles?
options: Yes, because it does one function
No: it fails the CCP and CRP despite doing one function
Yes, because it has a release number
Unknown: the principles do not apply to a component of this kind
optionExplain: That is the old view.
Right: cohesion is more than one function.
A number does not make it cohesive.
The principles apply.
questions.explain: Many reasons to change and unused classes violate the CCP and CRP.
questions.rule: One function is not enough.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: True or false: When a project moves from heavy development to wide reuse, its component composition stays fixed.
questions.explain: The book expects the composition to jitter and evolve as the focus changes.
questions.rule: Expect the grouping to evolve.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: In your own words, why might a grouping of classes that is right today be wrong next year?
questions.a: Because the balance between developability and reusability changes as the project matures, so the grouping that fits today's concerns may not fit later ones.
questions.rule: The balance is dynamic.

questions.section: The Tension Diagram for Component Cohesion
questions.q: A team sees its component boundaries shift each release. What does the book suggest this means?
options: The team has broken the REP by changing its component boundaries
The CRP should be dropped because it keeps splitting components
The design is finished and the boundaries have settled for good
Normal: the focus moves from developability to reusability
optionExplain: Nothing says so.
The CRP is one of three forces.
The design is still moving.
Right: composition jitters and evolves.
questions.explain: The composition of components will likely jitter and evolve as the focus changes.
questions.rule: Jitter is expected.
questions.teaches: The composition of components will likely jitter and evolve with time as the focus of the project changes from developability to reusability.

questions.q: Which project is most exposed to code that works at night and fails the next morning?
options: A large team modifying the same source files
One developer working alone
A team with no shared source files
A codebase that is frozen
optionExplain: Right: others change what you depend on.
A lone developer has no one changing the code under them.
Without shared files, nobody else can alter what you rely on.
A frozen codebase does not change overnight.
questions.explain: The syndrome needs several people changing the same files. The card next describes it and a common answer.
questions.rule: Shared files plus many editors invite surprises.

questions.q: In the weekly build, developers work on private copies for four days and integrate on ____.
questions.explain: The weekly build puts all integration at the end of the week.
questions.rule: Integrate once a week.

questions.q: A team has used a weekly build for a year, and integration now spills into Saturday. By the book, what comes next?
options: Integration time shrinks as the team learns the codebase
The team moves to daily builds at no extra integration cost
Integration starts earlier, on Thursday
Nothing changes, since weekends are not part of the schedule
optionExplain: The book says integration burden grows with project size.
The book does not describe a free move to daily builds.
Right: the start of integration creeps toward mid-week.
Weekend spill is a symptom that pushes the schedule.
questions.explain: As integration grows, it eats more of the week, so integration begins earlier and the cycle is lengthened.
questions.rule: Integration cost creeps into the schedule.

questions.q: Which statements about the weekly build are wrong by the book? Select all that apply.
options: It lets developers work in isolation for most of the week
Its integration penalty stays the same as the project grows
Lengthening the build schedule lowers project risk
Integration and testing get harder as the schedule lengthens
optionExplain: Correct as stated: four days of isolation out of five.
Wrong: the burden grows with project size.
Wrong: lengthening the schedule increases project risks.
Correct as stated: they become increasingly hard and feedback is lost.
questions.explain: The weekly build trades isolation for a growing integration penalty and higher risk.
questions.rule: The penalty and the risk both grow.

questions.q: True or false: As integration takes a growing share of each cycle, the team's efficiency falls and it loses rapid feedback.
questions.explain: The duty cycle of development versus integration decreases, so efficiency does too.
questions.rule: More integration time means less efficiency.

questions.q: A 60-developer team edits the same files daily. Which outcome does the book call not uncommon?
options: The team builds a stable version each night, since the code is shared
Weeks pass without a stable build as everyone chases others' changes
Nobody notices changes made by others
The team stops changing code and waits
optionExplain: The point of the example is that stable builds become rare.
Right: this is the nightmare the book describes for large projects.
People notice when their code breaks.
The book says developers keep changing and changing their code.
questions.explain: In large projects it is not uncommon for weeks to pass without a stable build, because everyone chases the last change someone else made.
questions.rule: Shared files at scale mean no stable build.
questions.teaches: As a project and its team grow, it is not uncommon for weeks to go by without the team being able to build a stable version, as everyone keeps changing code to make it work with the last changes that someone else made.

questions.q: Team A's component is used by Team B, and A wants to keep changing it. How can B stay stable meanwhile?
options: B edits A's working copy directly
A freezes the component until B has finished
B uses A's released version while A works on a private copy
Both teams integrate at the end of the week
optionExplain: Shared editing is the source of the syndrome.
Freezing blocks A for no gain.
Right: release separates the stable from the changing.
That is the weekly build, with its growing penalty.
questions.explain: A released version gives B something stable to build on. The card next names the practice.
questions.rule: Use released versions, not working copies.

questions.q: Put the steps of releasing a component in the order the book gives.
items: The team gets its component working
The team gives it a release number
The team moves it into a directory for other teams
The team keeps modifying it in its private area
questions.explain: A component is released only once it works, and further work continues privately while others use the release.
questions.rule: Work, number, publish, continue privately.

questions.q: Team B finds that Team A's release 5 breaks its tests, so B keeps using release 4 for now. Is the process working as intended?
options: Yes, no team is at the mercy of the others
No, B must adopt every release at once
No, A must stop work until B adapts
Yes, but only if A withdraws release 5
optionExplain: Right: each team decides when to adapt.
That would recreate the single integration point.
A continues in its private area.
Withdrawing is not needed; B simply stays on release 4.
questions.explain: Each team can decide for itself when to adapt to new releases.
questions.rule: Teams adopt releases at their own pace.

questions.q: True or false: With released components, all developers must come together at one point in time to integrate everything they are doing.
questions.explain: Integration happens in small increments. That single point is the weekly build's Friday.
questions.rule: Small increments replace one big integration.

questions.q: The released components end up depending on each other in a cycle. What does the book say about the morning after syndrome?
options: It cannot be avoided
It disappears, because releases are numbered
It affects only the newest component
It is cured by a longer build schedule
optionExplain: Right: cycles defeat the release scheme.
Numbers do not help if releases are tied together by a cycle.
A cycle ties several components, not one.
A longer schedule is the weekly build's failing path.
questions.explain: With cycles in the dependency structure the syndrome cannot be avoided.
questions.rule: No cycles, or no relief.

questions.q: A company wants to assign ownership of its codebase. What does the book say a component can be?
options: A single class owned by the whole company
A branch that every developer must merge into daily
A unit of work for one developer or a team
A directory with no release numbers
optionExplain: Components are larger than a class and owned by developers or teams.
Daily merging is the integration burden.
Right: the unit of work and of release.
Release numbers are part of the scheme.
questions.explain: Components become units of work for one developer or a team, who release them for others.
questions.rule: A component is a unit of ownership.
questions.teaches: The components become units of work that can be the responsibility of a single developer or a team of developers.

questions.q: Component P depends on Q and R. Who decides whether to adopt a new release of Q?
options: The developers of Q only
The developers of P, which depends on Q
The developers of R
No one, since releases are automatic
optionExplain: Q's developers release it; the users of Q adopt it.
Right: dependents choose when to adopt.
R is another dependency of P and unaffected by Q's release.
The book describes a decision by the dependent teams.
questions.explain: Dependents decide when to take a new release of what they use. The card next shows how to find them.
questions.rule: Dependents choose.

questions.q: To find who is affected by a release, follow the dependency arrows ____.
questions.explain: You trace from the released component back to the components that depend on it.
questions.rule: Follow arrows backward.

questions.q: UI depends on Logic. Logic and Reports each depend on Data. Data is released. Which components are affected?
options: Logic and Reports only
Data only
UI only
Logic and Reports, and UI through Logic
optionExplain: It is natural to stop at direct dependents, but UI depends on Logic.
Data is the component being released.
UI is affected only because Logic is.
Right: following the arrows backward reaches UI as well.
questions.explain: Following the arrows backward from Data reaches Logic and Reports directly, and UI through Logic.
questions.rule: Impact reaches indirect dependents.

questions.q: Web depends on Services, Services on Domain, and Domain on Storage. In what order is the system released?
items: Storage
Domain
Services
Web
questions.explain: Release goes from the bottom up: what depends on nothing first, the top component last.
questions.rule: Bottom up.

questions.q: True or false: Releasing a top-level component that nothing depends on affects no other component.
questions.explain: No component knows about it or cares when it changes, so the impact of the release is small.
questions.rule: No dependents, no impact.

questions.q: A team wants to unit test Checkout, which depends on Pricing and Inventory, in an acyclic graph. What must the test build include?
options: Checkout with the Pricing and Inventory versions it uses
The whole system, built and integrated in advance of each test
Every component that depends on Checkout
Checkout alone, with nothing else
optionExplain: Right: only what it depends on.
That is the cost of cycles, not of a DAG.
Dependents of Checkout are not needed to test it.
Checkout needs the components it depends on.
questions.explain: Developers build their version of the component with the versions of its dependencies they use. No other component need be involved.
questions.rule: Test with your dependencies only.
questions.teaches: To test a component in an acyclic graph, developers build their version of it with the versions of the components it depends on that they currently use; no other component need be involved, so there are few variables to consider.

questions.q: You want to unit test one class, but must include many libraries and much of other teams' code. What is the likely cause?
options: Too few comments in the code
Too many release numbers
A missing weekly build
Cycles in the component dependency graph
optionExplain: Comments do not decide what a test must include.
Numbers do not pull in other code.
A weekly build does not remove dependencies.
Right: cycles make isolation hard.
questions.explain: When components depend on each other in a loop, none can be isolated. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Cycles prevent isolation.

questions.q: True or false: In a cycle, the components in it must in effect all use exactly the same release of one another's components.
questions.explain: That is why the book says they have become one large component.
questions.rule: A cycle ties releases together.

questions.q: Billing depends on Customers, Customers on Reports, and Reports on Billing. How do the three behave?
options: As three independent components
As one large component that must be released, tested and built together
As a stable chain with Billing at the bottom
As a chain that can be built in any order, one at a time
optionExplain: Each depends on another in the loop, so none is independent.
Right: the cycle fuses them.
There is no bottom in a loop.
A loop probably has no correct build order.
questions.explain: Every member of the cycle depends on the others, so they behave as one.
questions.rule: A loop is one unit.

questions.q: A cycle ties three components together. Which problems does the book say follow? Select all that apply.
options: The developers all experience the morning after syndrome
A unit test of one component pulls in the others
Release numbers can no longer be assigned
The code stops compiling by itself
There probably is no correct build order
optionExplain: Right: they must all use exactly the same release of one another's components.
Right: testing one needs the others built and integrated.
Wrong: numbers can still be assigned; the trouble is that releases are tied together.
Wrong: the book does not say a cycle breaks compilation by itself.
Right: the book says there probably is no correct order.
questions.explain: A cycle fuses the components into one large component, which hurts releasing, testing and building.
questions.rule: Cycles tie releases, tests and builds together.

questions.q: True or false: A correct build order can be worked out even when the component graph has cycles.
questions.explain: In a graph with cycles there probably is no correct order, which is part of why cycles are harmful.
questions.rule: Cycles can leave no valid build order.

questions.q: Why can a missing build order be especially nasty in a language like Java?
options: Java has no compiler, so everything is built at run time
Java forbids packages from depending on each other
Java builds all components in parallel without regard to order
Java reads declarations from compiled binaries
optionExplain: Java is compiled.
Packages are allowed.
Parallel builds are not described.
Right: this is the book's remark.
questions.explain: Languages like Java that read declarations from compiled binaries are hit hard when there is probably no correct order.
questions.rule: Binary-reading languages need an order.
questions.teaches: Because there is probably no correct build order, cycles can cause very nasty problems in languages like Java that read their declarations from compiled binary files.

questions.q: Two components depend on each other. Which change breaks the cycle?
options: Put an interface in one and have the other implement it
Rename the classes that cross the boundary between the two
Give each component its own release number
Have each component call the other through a script
optionExplain: Right: inverting one dependency removes the loop.
Names do not change who depends on whom.
Numbers do not remove a dependency.
Calling by script is still a dependency.
questions.explain: Replacing one dependency with an interface the other side implements breaks the loop. The card next names the principle.
questions.rule: Invert one dependency.

questions.q: The two ways to break a cycle are to apply the Dependency Inversion Principle, or to create a new ____ that both depend on.
questions.explain: The new component holds the classes both sides need.
questions.rule: Invert, or extract a shared component.

questions.q: Orders calls Pricing, and Pricing calls back into an Orders class. Using the DIP, which change breaks the cycle?
options: Define the interface inside Orders and make Pricing depend on that interface
Merge the two components and keep both names
Put the needed interface in Pricing; the Orders class implements it
Move both components into Main
optionExplain: That keeps Pricing depending on Orders.
That would remove the cycle only by erasing the components and is not one of the two ways.
Right: Orders then depends on Pricing, and Pricing no longer depends on Orders.
Main depends on everything; moving into it does not remove the loop.
questions.explain: The interface goes where the dependency should point, in Pricing, and the Orders class implements it.
questions.rule: Put the interface on the side that should be depended on.

questions.q: Two components both need the same helper class, which creates a cycle. Which way fits best?
options: Make an interface for the helper in each component
Merge the two components
Copy the helper into both
Move the helper into a new component that both depend on
optionExplain: That would not remove what both depend on.
The book gives two ways; merging is not one.
Copying adds duplicates.
Right: this is the second way.
questions.explain: When both need the same classes, a new component holding them breaks the loop.
questions.rule: Shared need, shared component.

questions.q: True or false: Once a component structure has been made acyclic, it can be left alone as the application grows.
questions.explain: The structure jitters and grows as requirements change, so it must be monitored for new cycles.
questions.rule: Keep watching for cycles.

questions.q: A colleague says some cycles cannot be broken, so teams must live with them. What does the book say?
options: The colleague is right for large systems
Only the DIP can do it, and only in Java
It is possible to break any cycle of components and reinstate a DAG
Cycles are harmless if the team is small enough
optionExplain: The book names two ways with no size limit.
The second way needs no interface.
Right: the book states it is possible.
The book says cycles cannot be avoided without breaking them.
questions.explain: The book says it is always possible to break a cycle of components and reinstate the dependency graph as a DAG.
questions.rule: Any cycle can be broken.
questions.teaches: It is always possible to break a cycle of components and reinstate the dependency graph as a DAG.

questions.q: What does a component dependency diagram best describe?
options: How buildable and maintainable the application is
What the application does, function by function
Which team owns which feature
The order in which users meet screens
optionExplain: Right: it is a map of building and maintaining.
A functional breakdown is what many expect, but the book says the diagram is not that.
Ownership is not what the diagram shows.
Screens are not components.
questions.explain: The diagram shows how parts depend on each other, so it helps with building and maintaining. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Components map the build, not the function.

questions.q: True or false: The component dependency structure is one of the first things designed in a system.
questions.explain: The book says it is not designed first; it evolves as the system grows and changes.
questions.rule: The structure evolves.

questions.q: A start-up has written ten classes. A consultant demands a complete component diagram of 20 components today. What is the book's objection?
options: Little exists to build or maintain, so the structure is not yet known
A component diagram cannot show dependencies, only the features of an application
Twenty components is too many for any system
Components are chosen by marketing
optionExplain: Right: the structure grows with the code.
The diagram shows dependencies.
The book gives no limit on count.
Nothing links components to marketing.
questions.explain: Too early, nothing needs a build and maintenance map, and the grouping rests on knowledge that does not exist yet.
questions.rule: Design the map when there is something to map.

questions.q: Put these influences on the component structure in the order the book describes them arriving.
items: The SRP and CCP gather classes that change together
The CRP begins to shape components as reusable elements appear
The ADP is applied as cycles appear and the graph jitters and grows
questions.explain: First changes are localised, then reuse matters, then cycles must be broken.
questions.rule: Change, then reuse, then cycles.

questions.q: True or false: Designing the component structure before any classes would likely fail badly.
questions.explain: Common closure and reusable elements would be unknown, and cycles would be almost certain.
questions.rule: Structure follows classes.

questions.q: When does the need for a build-and-maintenance map first appear in a project?
options: Before any code exists
As modules accumulate in early implementation
Only after the first release
Only when reuse begins
optionExplain: With no software there is nothing to build or maintain.
Right: at the growing stage.
The need arises earlier than release.
Reuse is a later concern.
questions.explain: As more modules accumulate early on, managing dependencies becomes necessary to avoid the morning after syndrome.
questions.rule: Dependency management grows with the code.
questions.teaches: As more and more modules accumulate in the early stages of implementation and design, there is a growing need to manage the dependencies so that the project can be developed without the morning after syndrome.

questions.q: A company restyles its screens monthly, and its pricing rules rarely change. How should the dependencies run?
options: Pricing rules depend on the screens
Both depend on each other
Neither may depend on the other
Screens depend on the pricing rules, not the reverse
optionExplain: Then each restyling would reach the pricing rules.
A mutual dependency exposes pricing to every restyle.
Screens need pricing results, so a dependency is needed one way.
Right: volatile code depends on stable code.
questions.explain: Keeping the volatile part dependent on the stable part protects the stable one. The card next gives the aim.
questions.rule: Volatile depends on stable.

questions.q: One of the overriding concerns of the dependency structure is the isolation of ____.
questions.explain: The structure keeps frequent, capricious changes from reaching stable components.
questions.rule: Isolate volatility.

questions.q: Report layouts change weekly, yet a highest-level policy class imports a report class. What is the problem?
options: Reports are too abstract to be depended on by a policy
The policy class is too small
A volatile component can force changes on the policy
The report class has too many comments
optionExplain: Abstractness is not the issue here.
Size is not the issue.
Right: that is the dependency to avoid.
Comments are irrelevant.
questions.explain: A policy that depends on a volatile report class will be disturbed by report changes.
questions.rule: Do not let policy depend on volatile code.

questions.q: Sort each component by how the dependency graph should treat it.
groups: Volatile: keep others from depending on it

items.t: GUI cosmetics
Report formats
Business rules
Highest-level policies

questions.explain: Cosmetic GUI work and reports are named as volatile; business rules and policies are named as the things to protect.
questions.rule: Protect policy; isolate cosmetics.

questions.q: True or false: If the business rules component imports the GUI component, a restyling of the GUI can reach the business rules.
questions.explain: A component inherits the changes of what it depends on, which is why volatility must be isolated.
questions.rule: You inherit the volatility you depend on.

questions.q: Who shapes the component dependency graph, and for what purpose?
options: The compiler, to speed builds and shorten link times
Product owners, to match features
The linker, to reduce file size
Architects, to protect stable high-value components
optionExplain: Compilers do not design structure.
Features do not decide component dependencies.
Linkers resolve references.
Right: that is the book's statement.
questions.explain: The graph is created and molded by architects, with that aim.
questions.rule: Architects mould the graph.
questions.teaches: The component dependency graph is created and molded by architects to protect stable high-value components from volatile components.

questions.q: A coin stands on its edge and has not moved for days. By the book's meaning, is it stable?
options: Yes, since it has not changed
No: very little work would topple it
Yes, since it is balanced
Only if it is heavy
optionExplain: Not changing is not the same as being hard to change.
Right: stability is about the work needed to move it.
Balance on an edge takes almost no effort to undo.
Weight helps, but the example shows the idea without it.
questions.explain: Stability is the work needed to move something, not how often it moves. The card next applies this to software.
questions.rule: Stable means hard to move.

questions.q: Stability is related to the amount of ____ required to make a change.
questions.explain: The book defines stability by the work a change needs, not by frequency.
questions.rule: Stability: work to change.

questions.q: A date library is imported by 40 components and imports nothing. A prototype imports five libraries and nothing imports it. Which is more stable, and why?
options: The prototype: it has many sources of change
The date library: its many dependents make any change costly
The prototype: no one depends on it
Neither: both change at some time
optionExplain: Many outgoing dependencies make a component unstable, not stable.
Right: incoming dependencies create the cost of change.
No dependents makes change easy, which is not stable.
Stability is about effort, and the two differ.
questions.explain: A component with many incoming dependencies needs a great deal of work to reconcile any change.
questions.rule: Many dependents, much work.

questions.q: True or false: By the book, a component with many incoming dependencies is hard to change, whether or not it has ever been edited.
questions.explain: Stability is about the work needed to change a component. Many dependents make that work large, whatever the component's history.
questions.rule: Effort, not history.

questions.q: True or false: When ten more components start depending on a utility component, it becomes less stable.
questions.explain: More dependents make changing it more work, so it becomes more stable.
questions.rule: Dependents raise stability.

questions.q: Component X has three dependents and depends on nothing. What does the book call it?
options: Irresponsible and dependent
Responsible and dependent
Responsible and independent
Irresponsible and independent
optionExplain: That describes a component with no dependents and some dependencies.
It depends on nothing, so it is independent.
Right: it answers to dependents and has no outside influences.
It has dependents, so it is responsible.
questions.explain: Having dependents makes a component responsible to them. Depending on nothing makes it independent.
questions.rule: Dependents: responsible. No dependencies: independent.
questions.teaches: A component with dependents is responsible to them, and one that depends on nothing is independent; one with no dependents but with dependencies is irresponsible and dependent.

questions.q: A component is used by nine outside classes and uses none outside itself. How stable is it likely to be?
options: Maximally unstable
Neither, since it is used
Stable only if it is small
Maximally stable
optionExplain: Instability needs outgoing dependencies.
Being used makes it stable.
The count of dependents is what matters.
Right: many dependents and no dependencies.
questions.explain: Many dependents hold it in place and nothing pushes it to change. The card next gives the metric.
questions.rule: Dependents add stability.

questions.q: A component with no incoming dependencies and some outgoing ones has an instability I equal to ____.
questions.explain: With fan-in 0 the ratio is fan-out over fan-out, which is 1.
questions.rule: No dependents, I is 1.

questions.q: A component has fan-in 4 and fan-out 12. What is I?
optionExplain: That swaps the roles and gives 4 / 16.
That divides fan-out by fan-in without adding the denominator.
That divides fan-in by fan-out.
questions.explain: I = fan-out / (fan-in + fan-out) = 12 / 16 = 0.75.
questions.rule: I = out / (in + out).

questions.q: Order these components from the lowest I to the highest I.
items: Fan-in 8, fan-out 0
Fan-in 6, fan-out 2
Fan-in 2, fan-out 6
Fan-in 0, fan-out 3
questions.explain: Their I values are 0, 0.25, 0.75 and 1. More incoming dependencies lower I, and more outgoing ones raise it.
questions.rule: Out raises I; in lowers it.

questions.q: A component has fan-in 3 and fan-out 1. Two more outside classes start depending on it. What happens to I?
options: It falls from 0.25 to about 0.17
It rises to 0.5
It stays at 0.25
It falls to 0
optionExplain: Right: 1 / (5 + 1) is about 0.17.
That is what fewer dependents would do.
Fan-in changed, so I changes.
Fan-out is still 1, so I is above 0.
questions.explain: More incoming dependencies make the component more stable, so I falls.
questions.rule: More dependents, lower I.

questions.q: A student reports I = 0.25 for a component with fan-in 2 and fan-out 6. What went wrong?
options: She divided fan-in, not fan-out, by the total
She forgot to add fan-out to the denominator
She counted components instead of classes
She should have used the average of the two counts
optionExplain: Right: 2 / 8 is 0.25, while the correct value is 6 / 8 = 0.75.
That slip would give 6 / 2 = 3, not 0.25.
Counting components would change the numbers, but not by this pattern; the book counts classes.
The book gives no averaging rule.
questions.explain: I is fan-out divided by the sum of fan-in and fan-out, so the correct value is 0.75.
questions.rule: Fan-out goes on top.

questions.q: A tool reports Ca = 6 and Ce = 2 for a component. Using the book's current names, what follow?
options: Fan-in 6, fan-out 2, I = 0.25
Fan-in 2, fan-out 6, I = 0.75
Fan-in 6, fan-out 2, I = 0.75
Fan-in 2, fan-out 6, I = 0.25
optionExplain: Right: Ca is fan-in, Ce is fan-out, and I = 2 / 8.
That swaps Ca and Ce.
The pairing is right, but 2 / 8 is 0.25, not 0.75.
The sums fit but the pairing is swapped.
questions.explain: The book's earlier names were afferent coupling (Ca) for fan-in and efferent coupling (Ce) for fan-out.
questions.rule: Ca is fan-in; Ce is fan-out.
questions.teaches: In earlier publications the author called fan-in afferent coupling (Ca) and fan-out efferent coupling (Ce).

questions.q: A flexible UI component is imported by a core component that many others depend on. What is the likely problem?
options: The core becomes easier to change
The UI becomes more abstract
The UI becomes hard to change because of the core's dependents
Nothing: the UI source is unchanged
optionExplain: The core is not made easier by depending on something volatile.
Abstractness is unrelated.
Right: the dependency makes the UI costly to change.
The source is unchanged, but the cost of change has grown.
questions.explain: A dependency from a hard-to-change component makes the depended-on one harder to change. The card next states the SDP.
questions.rule: Dependents harden what they depend on.

questions.q: The SDP says that I metrics should ____ in the direction of dependency.
questions.explain: Dependencies point toward lower I, toward more stable components.
questions.rule: I decreases along the arrow.

questions.q: Component A has I = 0.3 and depends on component B with I = 0.6. Does this arrow obey the SDP?
options: Yes, because A is more stable than B
No: A's I should be larger than B's
Yes, because B is more unstable
It cannot be told without the fan-in
optionExplain: That is the reason it breaks the rule.
Right: A is more stable than what it depends on.
B being more unstable is the problem.
The I values are given and settle the matter.
questions.explain: A stable component depends on a more unstable one, so I increases along the arrow.
questions.rule: I must fall along an arrow.

questions.q: Which of these dependencies violate the SDP? Select all that apply.
options: P (I = 0.9) depends on Q (I = 0.2)
R (I = 0.1) depends on S (I = 0.7)
V (I = 0.6) depends on W (I = 0.3)
X (I = 0.4) depends on Y (I = 0.8)
optionExplain: Fine: P is less stable than Q.
Violation: R is more stable than S.
Fine: V is less stable than W.
Violation: X is more stable than Y.
questions.explain: The SDP wants the depending component to have the larger I.
questions.rule: Check that I falls along every arrow.

questions.q: Every component in a system is made maximally stable. What results?
options: The system would be perfectly flexible
The system would have no dependencies
The system would be fully abstract
The system would be unchangeable
optionExplain: Maximal stability means high cost of change.
Stable components are depended on, so dependencies exist.
Abstractness is a separate matter.
Right: the book says so.
questions.explain: If nothing can change cheaply, the system cannot change.
questions.rule: A mix is needed.

questions.q: A chain of components each depends on the next. Which order of I values obeys the SDP, from the first component to the last?
items: App (I = 0.9)
Service (I = 0.6)
Domain (I = 0.3)
Core (I = 0)
questions.explain: Each component depends on the next one, whose I must be smaller. So I decreases along the chain.
questions.rule: I falls along the chain.

questions.q: In a diagram with unstable components on top, how do you spot an SDP violation?
options: Any arrow that points down
Any horizontal arrow
Any arrow that points up
Any arrow leaving the top component
optionExplain: Downward arrows are the intended direction.
The convention does not make horizontal arrows violations.
Right: the convention puts changeable components above stable ones.
Arrows leaving the top follow the rule.
questions.explain: Putting unstable components at the top makes any upward arrow a violation.
questions.rule: Draw unstable on top; arrows should point down.
questions.teaches: Putting the unstable components at the top of the diagram is a useful convention, because any arrow that points up violates the SDP.

questions.q: A heavily used core component imports a class from a frequently changing component. Which change removes the problem?
options: Make the core depend on an interface the changing class implements
Move the changing class into the core so that the core controls it
Add release numbers to the changing component
Let the changing component import the core's tests to detect breaks
optionExplain: Right: invert the dependency.
That makes the core change as often as the class.
Numbers do not change who depends on whom.
Tests are unrelated.
questions.explain: Putting an interface between them lets both depend on something stable. The card next shows the layout.
questions.rule: Depend on an interface.

questions.q: A component that holds only interfaces and no executable code is an ____ component.
questions.explain: The book calls it an abstract component, and it is very stable.
questions.rule: Interfaces only: abstract component.

questions.q: Core (I = 0.1) calls Exporter in Plugins (I = 0.9). You add an interface IExporter. Which structure has I falling along every arrow?
options: Core depends on Plugins directly, calling Exporter without an interface
IExporter sits in Plugins and Core depends on Plugins to reach it
IExporter's component depends on Plugins to find the implementations
IExporter in its own component, with Core and Plugins depending on it
optionExplain: That keeps the stable core depending on the unstable plugin.
Core still depends on the volatile Plugins component.
The interface component would then be unstable.
Right: both depend on the stable interface component.
questions.explain: The interface component has no outgoing dependencies, so its I is 0 and both sides can depend on it.
questions.rule: Put the interface where everyone can lean on it.

questions.q: Why do abstract components not appear in Ruby or Python designs?
options: Those languages forbid components
Inversion there needs no declared or inherited interface
Those languages have no inheritance
Abstract classes are too slow in dynamically typed languages
optionExplain: Components exist in every language.
Right: the book's reason.
The point is about declared interfaces, not about inheritance as such.
Speed is not discussed.
questions.explain: In dynamically typed languages, nothing has to be declared, so there is no interface component to depend on.
questions.rule: Typing decides whether interface components are needed.

questions.q: True or false: In the fixed design, the interface component has I = 0 and the flexible component keeps I = 1.
questions.explain: The interface component has no outgoing dependencies, so its I is 0. The flexible component keeps its instability, which it needs.
questions.rule: All arrows now run toward lower I.

questions.q: Why is a component made only of interfaces a good thing for volatile components to depend on?
options: It contains no code that can fail
It is always the smallest component
It makes the volatile components stable
It is very stable, so depending on it follows the SDP
optionExplain: Failure is not the point of the book's argument.
Size is not the argument.
The volatile components stay unstable; that is intended.
Right: abstract components are very stable.
questions.explain: Abstract components are very stable, so less stable components can depend on them without breaking the SDP.
questions.rule: Depend on the stable abstraction.
questions.teaches: Abstract components are very stable and are therefore ideal targets for less stable components to depend on.

questions.q: Your core business policy sits in a component that dozens of others depend on. How can it stay open to new behaviour?
options: Make it consist of interfaces and abstract classes that others extend
Fill it with concrete classes that are edited when needed
Duplicate it into each dependent
Mark it unstable so that it can be edited freely
optionExplain: Right: extend rather than modify.
Editing a stable component is costly.
Duplicates multiply the cost of change.
Making it unstable would defeat its role.
questions.explain: Abstractions can be extended without editing the stable component. The card next states the SAP.
questions.rule: Stable means abstract.

questions.q: The SAP says a component should be as abstract as it is ____.
questions.explain: Stable components should be abstract, so their stability does not prevent extension.
questions.rule: Abstract as stable.

questions.q: A component with I = 0 holds only concrete classes. By the SAP, what is the concern and the remedy?
options: It is stable and concrete, which is ideal for high-level policy
Make it unstable by adding dependencies that pull it toward change
Stable but concrete: add abstractions so it can be extended
Delete its dependents so that the component becomes easier to edit
optionExplain: The SAP wants stability matched by abstractness.
Adding dependencies to hide the problem undermines its role.
Right: add abstraction to a stable component.
Dependents are why it is stable and needed.
questions.explain: A stable concrete component is hard to change and cannot be extended.
questions.rule: Match stability with abstraction.

questions.q: True or false: An unstable component (I = 1) that holds only interfaces follows the SAP.
questions.explain: The SAP asks unstable components to be concrete, since their instability lets concrete code be changed easily. Abstractness belongs with stability.
questions.rule: Unstable: concrete.

questions.q: By the ____ (open closed principle), classes can be extended without modification, which is why abstract classes keep a stable component flexible.
questions.explain: The OCP tells us it is possible and desirable to create classes that can be extended without modification, and abstract classes conform to it.
questions.rule: OCP keeps stable code open.

questions.q: A team fears that putting policy in a stable component will freeze its architecture. What does the book answer?
options: Stable components should be rewritten in full with every release
Policy belongs in unstable components, where it can be edited
If abstract, it can be extended without freezing the architecture
Stability does not limit change, since stable code is easy to edit
optionExplain: That would make them unstable.
The book puts policy in stable components.
Right: extensible stable components are flexible.
Stability does make concrete code hard to change.
questions.explain: Stable components that are extensible are flexible and do not overly constrain the architecture.
questions.rule: Stable and abstract is flexible.
questions.teaches: Stable components that are extensible are flexible and do not overly constrain the architecture.

questions.q: Dependencies should point toward stable things, and stable things should be abstract. What follows?
options: Dependencies point toward abstract things
Dependencies point toward concrete things that change often
Dependencies point in both directions
Dependencies are not needed
optionExplain: Right: stable leads to abstract.
Concrete things are not the stable ones in this scheme.
A cycle would follow, which the ADP forbids.
Dependencies remain.
questions.explain: Chaining the two rules gives a direction toward abstraction. The card next names it.
questions.rule: Toward stable is toward abstract.

questions.q: Match each principle to its advice.
pairs: Dependencies run in the direction of stability
A component should be as abstract as it is stable
Dependencies run in the direction of abstraction
No cycles in the component graph
questions.explain: The first two combine into the DIP for components, and the ADP is a separate rule about cycles.
questions.rule: Each principle has its own advice.

questions.q: Component X is abstract and stable (I = 0, A = 1). Component Y is concrete and unstable (I = 1, A = 0). Which arrow fits the SDP and SAP?
options: Y depends on X
X depends on Y
X and Y depend on each other
Neither should depend on the other
optionExplain: Right: toward stability and abstraction.
That points toward the concrete and unstable.
A cycle breaks the ADP.
Y needs the services of X, so a dependency is expected.
questions.explain: Dependencies run toward the stable, abstract component.
questions.rule: Point arrows toward the stable abstraction.

questions.q: True or false: A component may be partly abstract and partly stable.
questions.explain: The SDP and SAP combined allow degrees of both in a component.
questions.rule: Components come in degrees.

questions.q: True or false: When the SDP and the SAP are both followed, a dependency between two components tends to point toward the more abstract one.
questions.explain: The SDP points dependencies toward stability and the SAP ties stability to abstraction, so dependencies run toward abstraction.
questions.rule: Dependencies run toward abstraction.

questions.q: How does the component-level version differ from the DIP?
options: The DIP applies to components and the SDP and SAP apply to classes
A class is abstract or it is not; a component can be partly abstract
There is no difference, since both say the same thing about classes
The DIP forbids interfaces, which the SDP and SAP require
optionExplain: That reverses them.
Right: degrees rather than a binary.
The book states a difference.
The DIP relies on interfaces.
questions.explain: With classes there are no shades of gray; with components there are.
questions.rule: Degrees for components.
questions.teaches: With classes there are no shades of gray: either a class is abstract or it is not, which is why the DIP deals in whole abstractions while the SDP and SAP can describe a component that is only partly abstract.

questions.q: A component has 10 classes, 4 of them interfaces or abstract classes. What fraction is abstract?
optionExplain: That is the concrete fraction.
That is the count, not a ratio.
That is 10 / 4.
Right: 4 / 10.
questions.explain: Abstractness is the share of classes that are abstract. The card next gives the metric.
questions.rule: Abstract share of the classes.

questions.q: A component with no abstract classes at all has A equal to ____.
questions.explain: With Na = 0 the ratio is 0.
questions.rule: No abstract classes, A = 0.

questions.q: A component has 8 classes, of which 2 are abstract or interfaces. What is A?
optionExplain: That is the concrete share, 6 / 8.
That inverts the ratio.
Right: 2 / 8.
That divides by 10, which is not the class count.
questions.rule: A = Na / Nc.

questions.q: True or false: A component with 3 interfaces and 1 concrete class has A = 0.75.
questions.explain: A is the abstract count divided by the total number of classes: 3 / 4 = 0.75.
questions.rule: Ratio, not count.

questions.q: A team deletes every concrete class from a component with 2 interfaces and 6 concrete classes. What is the new A?
optionExplain: That was the old value.
That assumes half were removed.
That would need one concrete class left.
Right: 2 / 2.
questions.explain: With only the two interfaces left, every class is abstract.
questions.rule: All abstract gives A = 1.

questions.q: A component holds only abstract classes, and one of them derives from an abstract class in another component. Is it maximally stable?
options: Yes, since A = 1
No: its dependency lowers its stability even though A = 1
Yes, since abstract classes never depend on anything
No, since A = 1 means it is unstable
optionExplain: A = 1 says nothing about dependencies.
Right: abstractness and stability are separate measures.
An abstract class can derive from another.
A = 1 says nothing about instability.
questions.explain: A derived abstraction is maximally abstract but has a dependency, so it is not maximally stable.
questions.rule: A and I are separate.
questions.teaches: It is common for one abstract class to derive from another, so a component can be maximally abstract yet not maximally stable, because its dependency decreases its stability.

questions.q: On a graph with abstractness vertical and instability horizontal, which corner holds the ideal stable and abstract component?
options: Lower left
Upper left
Upper right
Lower right
optionExplain: Low I with low A is stable and concrete.
Right: low I, high A.
High I with high A is unstable and abstract.
High I and low A is the other ideal, unstable and concrete.
questions.explain: Stable means low I and abstract means high A, which puts it at the upper left. The card next names the line.
questions.rule: Stable and abstract: upper left.

questions.q: The line that joins (0, 1) and (1, 0) on the A/I graph is called the main ____.
questions.explain: The main sequence joins the two ideal endpoints.
questions.rule: Main sequence joins the endpoints.

questions.q: A component has I = 0.5. At what A does it sit on the main sequence?
optionExplain: That is the unstable-concrete end, which needs I = 1.
That is the stable-abstract end, which needs I = 0.
That would be on the line only at I = 0.75.
Right: A = 1 - I.
questions.explain: The line runs from (I = 0, A = 1) to (I = 1, A = 0), so A + I = 1.
questions.rule: On the line, A + I = 1.

questions.q: Sort each (I, A) position by whether it lies on the main sequence.
questions.explain: Points on the line satisfy A + I = 1. The others sum to 0.4, 1.6 and 0.7.
questions.rule: Sum to 1.

questions.q: A component sits on the main sequence at I = 0.3 and A = 0.7. Many new components then depend on it, so I falls to 0.1, and A stays 0.7. What happens?
options: It stays on the main sequence
It moves to the zone of uselessness
It leaves the line unless its abstractness rises
It becomes more abstract by itself as its dependents grow
optionExplain: The sum is now 0.8, not 1.
The zone of uselessness is near high A with high I.
Right: at I = 0.1 the line needs A = 0.9.
Abstractness does not change when dependents are added.
questions.explain: More dependents lower I, so the abstractness must rise to stay on the line.
questions.rule: As stability grows, abstraction must grow.

questions.q: In a large system most components sit at the endpoints, but a few fit neither. Where do the few do best?
options: In the zone of pain
In the zone of uselessness
On or close to the main sequence
optionExplain: The zone of pain is to be avoided.
(0, 0) is the zone of pain.
The zone of uselessness is to be avoided.
Right: the book says so.
questions.explain: Good architects put most components at the endpoints, and the rest have the best characteristics on or near the line.
questions.rule: Endpoints, or near the line.
questions.teaches: Good architects strive to put the majority of components at the two endpoints of the main sequence; the small fraction that is neither perfectly abstract nor perfectly stable does best on or close to it.

questions.q: A component used by dozens of others holds only concrete classes and must change often. What is the cost?
options: It is easy to change because it is concrete
It is hard to extend and hard to change
It is easy to extend because it is used
There is no cost
optionExplain: Concrete code that many depend on is hard to change.
Right: rigid on both counts.
Being used does not make it extensible.
The cost is the pain the book describes.
