questions.explain: Many dependents make it hard to change, and concrete code cannot be extended. The card next names the zone.
questions.rule: Stable and concrete is rigid.

questions.q: True or false: A highly stable, concrete component is rigid because it cannot be extended and is hard to change.
questions.explain: That is the book's description of the area around (0, 0).
questions.rule: Stable plus concrete is rigid.

questions.q: A shared database schema changes monthly, is concrete and is used by dozens of components. Where does it sit, and why does it hurt?
options: In the Zone of Uselessness: abstract and unused
On the main sequence: balanced
In the Zone of Pain: volatile, concrete and highly depended on
Nowhere: schemas are not components
optionExplain: It is concrete and heavily used, the opposite.
It is concrete and stable, not balanced.
Right: this is the book's own example of the zone.
The book uses it as an example of what sits in the zone.
questions.explain: Volatile, extremely concrete and highly depended on, schemas make updates painful.
questions.rule: Volatile and rigid hurts.

questions.q: A String component is concrete and used everywhere. Why is it not a problem?
options: It is nonvolatile, so it is unlikely to be changed
It is abstract, so its stability cannot make it rigid
It has no dependents
It sits on the main sequence
optionExplain: Right: only volatile components are problematic here.
Its classes are concrete.
It is used everywhere.
A concrete, much-used component sits near (0, 0), not on the line.
questions.explain: Nonvolatile components are harmless in the zone since they are not likely to be changed.
questions.rule: Only the volatile ones hurt.

questions.q: The more volatile a component in the Zone of Pain, the more ____ it is.
questions.explain: Volatility sets the level of pain, which is why only volatile components are a problem there.
questions.rule: Pain grows with volatility.

questions.q: The book sees volatility as what kind of addition to the A/I graph?
options: A new principle that replaces the SDP in later chapters
A colour code with no meaning
A third axis, shown only at its most painful plane
A second main sequence
optionExplain: The graph extends the existing principles.
The book gives it a role.
Right: volatility is the third axis.
No second line is described.
questions.explain: Volatility can be considered a third axis, and the figure shows the most painful plane.
questions.rule: Volatility is a third axis.
questions.teaches: Volatility can be considered a third axis of the A/I graph; the figure of the zones shows only the most painful plane, where volatility is highest.

questions.q: A module has interfaces only, and no one implements or uses them. How does the book describe such a thing?
options: A well-designed abstraction
Useless detritus left in the code base
A stable core
A reusable library
optionExplain: Design needs a user.
Right: abstract but unused.
A stable core has dependents.
Reuse needs users.
questions.explain: An abstraction with no dependents serves nobody. The card next names the zone.
questions.rule: Unused abstractions are useless.

questions.q: A maximally abstract component with no dependents sits in the Zone of ____.
questions.explain: Near (1, 1), the book calls it the Zone of Uselessness.
questions.rule: Abstract and unused: uselessness.

questions.q: A component has I = 0.95 and A = 0.9. What does the book suggest about it?
options: It is on the main sequence, with abstraction matching stability
It is in the Zone of Pain
It is ideal for volatile policy
In the Zone of Uselessness, likely full of unused abstractions
optionExplain: The sum is far from 1.
The zone of pain is at (0, 0).
Nothing depends on it, so it protects no policy.
Right: high I and high A.
questions.explain: Near (1, 1), the component is abstract with few dependents.
questions.rule: High A with high I is wasted.

questions.q: Match each position on the graph of I and A to what the book calls it.
questions.explain: Two corners are zones of exclusion and the other two are the good endpoints.
questions.rule: Two corners to avoid, two to aim for.

questions.q: True or false: When leftover abstract classes get implementations and users, their component moves away from the corner at (1, 1).
questions.explain: Dependents make the component more stable, so I falls and it moves toward the main sequence.
questions.rule: Use rescues abstractions.

questions.q: What can you infer about a component deep in the Zone of Uselessness?
options: It likely holds a significant fraction of such unused entities
It must be very stable, since it is abstract and many depend on it
It must be the most reused component
It must have no classes
optionExplain: Right: that is the book's inference.
High I means it is unstable.
It has few dependents.
A is high, so it has classes.
questions.explain: A component deep in the zone must hold a significant fraction of such entities, which is undesirable.
questions.rule: Deep in the zone means mostly detritus.
questions.teaches: A component positioned deep within the Zone of Uselessness must contain a significant fraction of unused abstract entities, and the presence of such entities is undesirable.

questions.q: A component has A = 0.5 and I = 0.5. Is it on the main sequence?
options: No, since A is not 1
No, since I is not 0
Only if it has dependents
Yes, since A + I = 1
optionExplain: The endpoints have A = 1 or 0, but the line has points between.
The same applies to I.
Dependents are already counted in I.
Right: the line is A + I = 1.
questions.explain: Any pair with A + I = 1 is on the line. The card next turns this into a distance.
questions.rule: A + I = 1 on the line.

questions.q: With D = |A + I - 1|, a component directly on the main sequence has D equal to ____.
questions.explain: On the line, A + I - 1 is 0.
questions.rule: On the line, D = 0.

questions.q: A component has A = 0.25 and I = 0.5. What is D?
optionExplain: That forgets to subtract 1.
That is the value of I.
That is the largest D possible.
questions.explain: A + I - 1 = -0.25, and the absolute value is 0.25.

questions.q: Order these (A, I) positions from the smallest D to the largest D.
questions.explain: Their D values are 0, 0.1, 0.7 and 0.8.
questions.rule: Compute before comparing.

questions.q: A component's D over four releases is 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.12, with a control threshold of 0.1. What does the book suggest?
options: Ignore it, since D is still small and far below its maximum of 1
Restructure the first release
Raise the threshold
Find out why the last release crossed the threshold
optionExplain: The point of a threshold is to prompt attention.
The earlier releases were within limits.
Moving the threshold hides the signal.
Right: crossing the threshold calls for a look.
questions.explain: A point past the control limit is worth investigating.
questions.rule: Watch the trend and the threshold.

questions.q: A component lies well over one standard deviation from the mean D of its design. What can you say about it?
options: Very abstract with few dependents, or very concrete with many
It is exactly on the main sequence, so it needs no further attention
It has no classes
It is always a mistake
optionExplain: Right: that is the book's description.
On the line D would be near zero.
A component must hold classes.
The book says such components are worth examining, not that they are wrong.
questions.explain: Aberrant components fall into one of the two zone-like cases.
questions.rule: Outliers are worth examining.
questions.teaches: Components more than one standard deviation from the mean D are aberrant and are either very abstract with few dependents or very concrete with many dependents.

questions.q: A tool reports D = 0.4 for your component. How should you treat that number?
options: As proof that the design is wrong and has to be restructured at once
As proof that the design is right
As a measurement against a chosen standard, worth a closer look
As meaningless
optionExplain: The metrics are imperfect, so one value is not proof.
A large value is not a pass.
Right: a prompt to look, not a verdict.
The book hopes the metrics are useful.
questions.explain: The metric points to places to look. The card next gives the book's own caution.
questions.rule: A number prompts a look.

questions.q: True or false: By the book, the dependency management metrics are perfect measures of design quality.
questions.explain: The book calls them imperfect at best, a measurement against an arbitrary standard.
questions.rule: The metrics are imperfect.

questions.q: A build fails whenever D passes 0.1. A reviewer finds a sound component at 0.15 for a good reason. What fits the book?
options: Restructure it at once to bring D back under the limit
Remove the metric
Raise D for every component
Examine it, since the metric is imperfect
optionExplain: The number alone does not settle it.
The book finds the metrics useful.
Moving numbers hides the issue.
Right: judgement stays with people.
questions.explain: A metric is not a god; it flags, and a person decides.
questions.rule: People judge; metrics flag.

questions.q: The metrics measure conformance to a pattern of dependency and abstraction that the author thinks is ____.
questions.explain: The book says the metrics measure a design against a pattern the author considers good, which is an arbitrary standard and not a proof.
questions.rule: A standard, not a proof.

questions.q: True or false: A team that restructures every component whose D is above zero is using the metric as the book intends.
questions.explain: The book calls the metrics imperfect measurements against an arbitrary standard, to flag components worth examining, not rules to satisfy exactly.
questions.rule: Do not treat metrics as absolute.

questions.q: What does the pattern behind the metrics reflect, according to the book?
options: Experience that some dependencies are good and others bad
A mathematical proof about components and their dependencies
A rule of the compiler
The preferences of tool vendors
optionExplain: Right: experience.
The book offers no proof.
The compiler does not enforce it.
Vendors are not mentioned.
questions.explain: The metrics measure conformance to a pattern the author considers good, grounded in experience.
questions.rule: The standard comes from experience.
questions.teaches: The pattern behind the dependency management metrics reflects experience that certain dependencies are good and others are bad.

questions.q: A manager says, 'Our architecture is the list of frameworks we chose.' Which description is closer to the author's definition?
options: The tools and frameworks the team agreed to use
The diagram drawn at the start of the project and then filed away
How the system is divided into components, arranged and connected
The documentation that explains the system to new hires and auditors
optionExplain: A common habit, but a framework list says nothing about how the parts are divided or connected.
A diagram can record a shape, but the shape is what the builders actually give the system.
Right: the definition is about structure, not about tools.
Documentation describes the system; the shape is a property of the system itself.
questions.explain: The author defines architecture by structure: components, their arrangement and their communication. The card next gives the full definition.
questions.rule: Architecture is the division, arrangement and communication of components, chosen to ease development, deployment, operation and maintenance.

questions.q: The architecture of a software system is the ____ given to that system by those who build it.
questions.explain: The author's definition starts from the shape the builders give the system, and then says where that shape lies.
questions.rule: The shape is made by the builders.

questions.q: What does the author say a software architect should do about writing code?
options: Keep taking programming tasks, so as to feel the problems created for the other programmers
Step back from code to concentrate on higher-level issues
Write all the core code personally, so that the shape stays consistent and nobody else can damage it
Review designs only, since coding slows down decision making
optionExplain: Right: the author says architects cannot do their job properly without experiencing the problems they create.
The author calls this a lie and says architects do not pull back from code.
Architects may write less code than other programmers, but the argument is about feeling the effects, not owning the code.
This is the pulling-back view the author rejects.
questions.explain: The author insists that architects remain programmers, because only then do they live with the consequences of their own shape.
questions.rule: An architect who stops coding loses sight of the problems the shape causes.
questions.teaches: Software architects stay programmers: they may write less code than others, but they continue to take programming tasks so that they experience the problems they create for the team.

questions.q: Match each complaint to the job that the system's shape has failed to support.
pairs: A release needs forty manual steps
Adding a field means hunting through the whole code base
Traffic doubles and the response times fall apart
Five teams keep overwriting each other's files
questions.explain: Each complaint points at one of the four jobs the shape is meant to ease. The author's definition lets you name the failed job before choosing a remedy.
questions.rule: Architecture is the division, arrangement and communication of components, chosen to ease development, deployment, operation and maintenance.

questions.q: Which of these are named in the author's definition of the shape? Select all that apply.
options: The programming language the components are written in
The division of the system into components
The brand of server that hosts the system
The arrangement of those components
The ways in which the components communicate
optionExplain: A language is a detail the components may use; it is not part of the three things named.
It is the first of the three things the shape lies in.
Hosting is a detail, not part of the shape the definition names.
It is the second.
It is the third.
questions.explain: Division, arrangement and communication make up the shape. Languages and servers are details the shape can leave open.
questions.rule: Architecture is the division, arrangement and communication of components, chosen to ease development, deployment, operation and maintenance.

questions.q: A mobile team ships weekly, runs on millions of phones and keeps adding features. The lead wants one strategy for shaping the app for all four jobs. Which strategy does the author give?
options: Settle the framework, database and release process on day one
Copy the structure of the largest team into the app, since that team knows the work best
Add as many layers as the language allows
Leave as many options open as possible, for as long as possible
optionExplain: Early commitment is the opposite of what the author recommends.
A component per team is a pull the author warns about, not a strategy.
Layers are tools for decoupling; the strategy is about keeping decisions open.
Right: the author names this as the strategy behind the facilitation of all four jobs.
questions.explain: The shape serves the four jobs best when decisions that do not need to be made yet are kept open.
questions.rule: Keep decisions open as long as you can.
questions.teaches: The strategy behind the shape is to leave as many options open as possible, for as long as possible.

questions.q: True or false: A system with a terrible architecture cannot work properly in production.
questions.explain: Many badly structured systems run well. Their pain shows up elsewhere. The card next says where.
questions.rule: Judge an architecture by how well it supports the system's life cycle, not by whether the system works.

questions.q: The author says the primary purpose of architecture is to support the ____ of the system.
questions.explain: The author puts the life cycle first and treats the architecture's role in behavior as passive.
questions.rule: Architecture serves the life cycle.

questions.q: The author says that many badly structured systems work fine. According to the author, where do their troubles lie?
options: In operation, where they fail under load
In deployment, maintenance and ongoing development
In their user interface, which is hard to learn
In the programming language, which limits what can be done
optionExplain: The author says the troubles are not in operation.
Right: these systems run, but they are costly to ship, change and extend.
The user interface is not the point of the argument.
Language is not the author's explanation.
questions.explain: A system can work and still cost a fortune to deploy, maintain and develop; that is where bad architecture bites.
questions.rule: Bad architecture hurts the life cycle, not necessarily the run.
questions.teaches: The troubles of a badly architected system that works lie not in its operation but in its deployment, maintenance and ongoing development.

questions.q: Sort each complaint: is it mainly a behavior defect, or a life-cycle cost that the shape of the system affects?

items.t: The invoice total is wrong when a discount code is used
A new developer needs three weeks to find where to add a field
The release script must be run by hand in a fixed order
The export button writes an empty file
A small change in billing keeps breaking shipping
The login page rejects a valid password

questions.explain: Defects in what the system does are behavior problems. Cost in understanding, changing and releasing it is where the shape matters.
questions.rule: Judge an architecture by how well it supports the system's life cycle, not by whether the system works.

questions.q: A system passes every behavior test, yet its architecture is poor. What does the author's view predict over the coming years?
options: The tests will begin to fail within a year, because a poor shape slowly corrupts the behavior
Cost will rise in deployment, maintenance and development while the tests stay green
Nothing will change, since a system that works today will keep costing the same to change
The system will stop working once it has more users
optionExplain: Poor shape does not make correct behavior fail.
Right: the tests check behavior, and the life-cycle costs are exactly what they do not measure.
Working today does not protect the cost of tomorrow's changes.
Operation is the cheapest problem to fix, usually with more hardware.
questions.explain: Passing tests say little about life-cycle cost. The effects of a poor shape show up in effort and risk, not in test results.
questions.rule: Green tests do not mean cheap changes.

questions.q: A mobile app crashes at startup on one phone model. A colleague blames the architecture. Which reading fits the author's view better?
options: It proves the architecture is wrong and calls for a redesign of the whole app before the next release
It is an operation problem, so more hardware will fix it
It cannot be fixed without first choosing a new framework
It is mainly a behavior defect to fix in the code, since architecture plays a passive role in behavior
optionExplain: A single crash does not show that the shape fails the life cycle.
Extra hardware helps load, not a crash on one device.
Nothing in the argument ties a crash to a framework choice.
Right: the architecture can hardly decide such behavior, so the first move is a defect fix.
questions.explain: The author says there are few, if any, behavioral options an architecture can leave open, so most behavior defects are fixed in code, not in the shape.
questions.rule: Do not blame architecture for every defect.
questions.teaches: There are few, if any, behavioral options that the architecture of a system can leave open, which is why its role in behavior is passive.

questions.q: Three developers start a new product. Which description of early architecture work is most reasonable?
options: A light structure is enough; heavy boundaries may only slow them down
They should define separate services and interfaces for each developer
They should write detailed specifications for each component first
They should wait to start coding until the architecture is complete
optionExplain: Right: a very small team can coordinate directly.
This adds cost before the team size demands it.
Specifications do not give a tiny team what it lacks.
Waiting for a full design is the heaviest answer to a small problem.
questions.explain: A tiny team needs little structure, and many teams need more. The card next gives the book's account.
questions.rule: Choose the amount of structure for the teams that will build the system, and watch that the team split does not decide the whole shape.

questions.q: True or false: A team of five developers can work effectively on a monolith that has no well-defined components.
questions.explain: The author says such a team can do this, and may even find the strictures of an architecture an impediment in the early days.
questions.rule: Small teams need little structure.

questions.q: According to the author, what explains the large number of systems that lack good architecture?
options: Architects are rarely hired for new projects, so nobody is given the job of designing the shape
Good architecture cannot be built before the first release, so it is always postponed and then forgotten
They began with none, because a small team did not want a superstructure in its way
Frameworks make architecture unnecessary
optionExplain: The author gives a different cause: a team that began small.
Nothing in the text says it cannot be built, only that a small team skips it.
Right: the lack starts as a reasonable choice for a small team, and then it stays.
The author does not make this claim.
questions.explain: The author explains the shortage of architecture by the way systems begin: small, quick and unstructured, with the structure never added.
questions.rule: Systems that start small often stay unstructured.
questions.teaches: Many systems lack good architecture because they were begun with none: the small team did not want the impediment of a superstructure.

questions.q: A company puts five teams of seven developers on one product, with no agreed component boundaries. What does the book say they need?
options: One large shared module so that everyone sees every change made by every team
More meetings, so that the teams coordinate every change with each other in person
A single team to take over the whole code base
A division into well-defined components with reliably stable interfaces
optionExplain: Shared code is what stops teams moving on their own.
Meetings do not replace stable interfaces.
The scenario has five teams, and the book's answer is a division, not a merge.
Right: without it the teams cannot make progress.
questions.explain: Many teams cannot make progress without stable boundaries between their parts.
questions.rule: Many teams, many components.

questions.q: Five teams are driven only by their development schedule. The book predicts the system will evolve into five components, one for each ____.
questions.explain: Left to the schedule, teams carve the system along their own lines; that may not suit deployment, operation or maintenance.
questions.rule: The org chart tends to become the architecture.

questions.q: A reporting module is built by a single team of four people, who sit together and ship daily. A consultant proposes splitting it into six independently deployed components, one per developer-pair plus two for shared parts. What follows from the book's reasoning?
options: The split may cost more than it returns, since a small team can work on one unit
The split is right, because every system needs services from the first day to be ready for growth
The split is wrong only if the team grows
The split should be one component per developer
optionExplain: Right: the book's small-team case says structure can be an impediment at this size.
The book does not say every system needs services.
The cost argument already applies at this team size.
A component per person would repeat the team-driven shape the book warns about.
questions.explain: Structure has a price, and a team of this size can avoid paying it. Our reading: grow the structure when the team grows.
questions.rule: Do not buy structure the team does not need yet.
questions.teaches: A small team would likely find the strictures of an architecture something of an impediment during the early days of development, so structure has a cost that must be weighed against its benefit.

questions.q: A team picks many small services because each is easy to build separately. What risk do they run?
options: The services will not be able to talk to each other at all
The code will become impossible to read
The system may be easy to develop but painful to deploy
The team will no longer be able to use version control
optionExplain: They can talk; the trouble is in managing it.
Small services are often easy to read.
Right: many pieces mean many connections and start-up orders.
Version control does not depend on service count.
questions.explain: Easy building does not guarantee easy shipping. The card next gives the author's own story.
questions.rule: Consider the cost of deploying the whole system, ideally in a single action, while the shape is still being chosen.

questions.q: The author says a system should be deployable with a single ____.
questions.explain: A single action is the aim: deployment cost is part of what makes a system useful.
questions.rule: Aim for one-action deployment.

questions.q: In the author's story, what made the many micro-services hard at deployment time?
options: Each service was written in a different language, so no single build tool could package them all
Configuring the connections between them and the timing of their start-up caused many errors
The services could not be tested at all
The team had too few developers
optionExplain: The story does not mention languages.
Right: the interactions, more than any single service, caused the errors.
They were easy to develop; testing is not the story's point.
Team size is not the cause named.
questions.explain: The firm boundaries that helped development produced a web of connections that deployment had to configure and order correctly.
questions.rule: Count the connections, not just the pieces.
questions.teaches: With many micro-services, configuring the connections between them and the timing of their initiation can become a huge source of deployment errors.

questions.q: A team plans twelve services for a new product. Before choosing, what does the author suggest they weigh?
options: The cost of deploying twelve services, including managing their connections and start-up order
Only the build speed of each service, since the faster each builds, the faster the whole system ships
Only how many developers each service needs, since staffing decides how fast the system can be shipped
Nothing; the number can be set after launch
optionExplain: Right: the story shows these costs surfacing late.
Build speed ignores the connections the author worries about.
Team fit is a development concern; the author asks for deployment to be weighed too.
The author's point is that waiting makes the choice costly.
questions.explain: Deployment cost belongs in the decision from the start, not after the services exist.
questions.rule: Weigh deployment before you divide.

questions.q: True or false: If the team in the story had kept the same services but built an automated way to start and connect them in the right order, the deployment errors from timing and configuration would likely shrink.
questions.explain: The errors came from configuring connections and start-up timing, so managing those more integrally attacks the cause. The author mentions a more integrated way of managing the interconnections as one remedy.
questions.rule: Consider the cost of deploying the whole system, ideally in a single action, while the shape is still being chosen.

questions.q: An online shop has grown to thirty services and its releases are painful. The team still wants firm boundaries for development. Which alternative does the author's story suggest they weigh?
options: More services, so that each connection becomes simpler and each service is easier to start on its own
A single large service that holds all the code
Fewer services, or a hybrid of services and in-process components with more integrated connections
Manual checklists for each release
optionExplain: More services multiply the connections to configure.
This gives up the firm boundaries the team wants.
Right: these are the options the author says early thought about deployment might have led to.
A checklist does not remove the errors in start-up timing and configuration.
questions.explain: The firm boundaries do not have to be services; in-process components can keep them with lower deployment cost.
questions.rule: Boundaries need not all be services.
questions.teaches: Had the architects considered deployment issues early on, they might have decided on fewer services, a hybrid of services and in-process components, and a more integrated means of managing the interconnections.

questions.q: A system runs too slowly under load, and its code is poorly structured. Which fix does the book describe as often sufficient?
options: Rewrite the whole system in a faster language
Add more servers and storage
Cut the number of users
Rename the classes for readability
optionExplain: A rewrite costs people, which are the expensive resource.
Right: the author says hardware is a cheap way to resolve most operational difficulties.
This removes the problem by removing the purpose.
Readability helps developers, not throughput.
questions.explain: Hardware is cheap and people are expensive. The card next gives the book's cost reasoning.
questions.rule: Spend architectural effort on development, deployment and maintenance first, and make the shape reveal what the system does.

questions.q: The author says architectures that impede operation cost less because hardware is cheap and ____ are expensive.
questions.explain: The cost equation leans toward the people-heavy jobs: development, deployment and maintenance.
questions.rule: Hardware is cheap, people are not.

questions.q: Besides coping with load, what other role does the author give architecture for operation?
options: To hide the system's behavior behind general names, so developers cannot depend on it by accident
To keep all operational details inside one master class
To avoid any mention of operation in the code
To reveal operation, with use cases and features as visible landmarks for developers
optionExplain: This is the reverse of what is asked.
Concentration is not the same as revealing.
Revealing operation means the opposite.
Right: the author says architecture should reveal operation and elevate the use cases to first-class entities.
questions.explain: A shape that makes the use cases visible simplifies understanding, which aids development and maintenance.
questions.rule: Make the system's behavior visible in its structure.
questions.teaches: Architecture should reveal operation by elevating the use cases, features and required behaviors to first-class entities that are visible landmarks for the developers.

questions.q: An online shop is slow only during one-day sales. The team has a small budget for engineers but can rent extra servers. What does the book suggest as the first move?
options: Reorganize all the modules before the next sale, so that the load spreads across the code better
Reduce the product list until the load fits
Try renting more capacity, since operational problems can often be resolved with hardware
Write a new operating system
optionExplain: Reorganizing spends people on a problem hardware may solve.
This gives up the purpose to avoid a hardware cost.
Right: it spends the cheap resource first.
This is a far larger investment of the expensive resource.
questions.explain: Where hardware can solve it, it is the cheaper route.
questions.rule: Buy capacity before you buy a rewrite.

questions.q: True or false: If the author's cost equation changed so that hardware became very expensive and people became cheap, the argument would no longer favor setting operation behind development, deployment and maintenance.
questions.explain: The argument rests on hardware being cheap and people expensive. Reverse the costs and the lean of the cost equation reverses with it.
questions.rule: Spend architectural effort on development, deployment and maintenance first, and make the shape reveal what the system does.

questions.q: A game studio's server bill is far larger than its engineering payroll. A colleague says the book proves that tuning for operation is a waste because hardware is cheap. What does the author say about an architecture tuned to operation?
options: It is never worth the effort, since hardware solves every operational problem
It is still desirable; the cost equation only leans toward the other jobs
It is required before any feature work may start
It matters only for development and deployment
optionExplain: The author says almost any difficulty can be solved with hardware, not that tuning is a waste.
Right: the author writes that a well-tuned architecture is desirable.
No such requirement is stated.
Tuning for operation is named as desirable in itself.
questions.explain: The argument is about where the cost equation leans. Our reading: in a business where hardware is the main cost, that lean is weaker.
questions.rule: Tuned operation is still desirable.
questions.teaches: An architecture that is well tuned to the operation of the system is desirable; the cost equation only leans toward development, deployment and maintenance.

questions.q: A developer must add a small feature to a large unfamiliar system. Which cost is likely to be biggest?
options: Typing the new lines of code, since a large system has many lines to type
Buying a license for the editor and tools needed to open such a large system
Waiting for the compiler
Finding the right place and the chance of breaking something
optionExplain: Typing is small beside finding the place.
This is not a recurring cost of change.
Compile time rarely dominates.
Right: those two costs tend to dominate.
questions.explain: Finding the place and avoiding breakage are the costs the card next names.
questions.rule: Cut the cost of maintenance by dividing the system into components with stable interfaces, so features have visible homes and changes stay local.

questions.q: The author says the primary cost of maintenance lies in spelunking and ____.
questions.explain: Maintenance cost is mostly the digging for the place to change and the danger of inadvertent defects.
questions.rule: Spelunking plus risk.

questions.q: How does the author say a good architecture lowers the cost of spelunking?
options: It illuminates the pathways for future features, so developers can see where they belong
It removes the need ever to read the existing code, because the components explain themselves
It lets developers guess the right place at random
It shifts the digging to the testers
optionExplain: Right: separated components behind stable interfaces make the way visible.
Reading is reduced, not removed.
Guessing is the opposite of illuminated pathways.
The cost is cut, not passed along.
questions.explain: Components and stable interfaces show where a new feature fits, which is what spelunking tries to find out.
questions.rule: Isolation lights the way as well as protecting.
questions.teaches: Separating the system into isolated components lights up the pathways for future features, which reduces the digging as well as the risk.

questions.q: Sort each cost of a change as spelunking or risk.

items.t: Reading three modules to learn where a discount rule is applied
Fear that the new field will break the export job
Tracing which classes call an old payment function
The chance that a fix introduces a new defect in reporting
Searching a large code base for the best place to add a screen
Wondering whether a rename will fail at runtime in a distant module

questions.explain: Digging for the place or strategy is spelunking. The likelihood of creating inadvertent defects is risk.
questions.rule: Cut the cost of maintenance by dividing the system into components with stable interfaces, so features have visible homes and changes stay local.

questions.q: A system has isolated components, but each feature change also alters the interfaces between them. What does the book's reasoning predict for risk?
options: The risk drops, since there are more components and each one is smaller than before
The risk of breakage stays high, since the interfaces are not stable
The risk drops because the interfaces are documented
The risk is unrelated to the interfaces
optionExplain: Components without stable interfaces do not isolate.
Right: the benefit comes from stable interfaces, not from the mere presence of components.
Documentation does not make interfaces stable.
The author ties the reduction in risk to stable interfaces.
questions.explain: Isolation depends on stability at the boundary.
questions.rule: Unstable interfaces void the benefit.

questions.q: A legacy payroll module has no boundaries, and a team needs to add one feature each month for years. What would the book's account suggest to reduce the total cost?
options: Divide it into components behind stable interfaces, so each later feature is easier and safer
Leave it alone, since it works
Replace each monthly change with a manual process that avoids touching the legacy code at all, so it cannot break it
Freeze all features
optionExplain: Right: the saving builds up over the many changes.
Working does not lower the maintenance bill.
This moves the cost, not reduces it.
This gives up the purpose of the system.
questions.explain: Maintenance is a recurring cost, so structure that lowers each change pays back over time.
questions.rule: Pay once for structure and save on every later change.
questions.teaches: Of all the aspects of a software system, maintenance is the most costly, because the never-ending parade of new features and the inevitable trail of defects and corrections consume vast amounts of human resources.

questions.q: Which sentence best explains why software is called soft?
options: It runs on soft physical media that can be erased and rewritten at will
It never contains errors, because its behavior can be corrected at any time
It cannot damage hardware
It was invented to make a machine's behavior easy to change
optionExplain: The name has nothing to do with media.
Software has errors; softness is about change.
Not the point.
Right: softness is the ease of change.
questions.explain: Softness means ease of change. The card next ties it to structure.
questions.rule: Protect the structure that keeps software soft by leaving as many options open as possible, for as long as possible.

questions.q: The author says software has two values: the value of its behavior and the value of its ____.
questions.explain: Structure is the second value, and the author calls it the greater.
questions.rule: Structure is the greater value.

questions.q: According to the author, on what does software's flexibility depend?
options: On the language it is written in and how expressive that language is for its programmers
On how many developers are on the team and how well they communicate with each other
On the shape of the system and the arrangement and interconnection of its components
On how fast the hardware is
optionExplain: The author ties flexibility to shape, not to language.
Team size is not the claim.
Right: the flexibility is not free; it comes from the shape.
Speed of hardware is not the claim.
questions.explain: Software is soft only if its structure allows change.
questions.rule: Flexibility is a property of shape.
questions.teaches: The flexibility that makes software soft depends critically on the shape of the system, the arrangement of its components and the way those components are interconnected.

questions.q: A manager asks the team to ship a feature quickly and to skip the clean-up that would make the next three features easy. Which value is being traded away, by the author's account?
options: The value of behavior, because the feature will not be delivered to users on time
The value of the hardware budget
The value of structure, which is the greater of the two
Neither value, since both are unaffected
optionExplain: The feature is delivered; it is the later changes that suffer.
Hardware is not what is being traded.
Right: the clean-up serves structure, and the author ranks structure higher.
Structure is exactly what the skipped work protects.
questions.explain: Skipping clean-up gains this feature's behavior at the cost of structure, the greater value.
questions.rule: Do not spend structure to buy behavior.

questions.q: Sort each benefit by the value of software it belongs to.

items.t: The invoice shows the right total
A new payment method can be added in a day
The search returns matching items
A database can be swapped without touching the business rules
The report prints every order in the month
A change to one screen leaves the others alone

questions.explain: Behavior is what the system does today. Structure is what keeps it cheap to change tomorrow, which is the value the author ranks higher.
questions.rule: Behavior serves today; structure serves every later change.

questions.q: A team lead says that keeping options open means postponing every decision, including what the product should do. Which options does the author say to leave open?
options: The details that do not matter, such as the choice of database or web system
All decisions, including the use cases the system must support
The business rules, which can safely be left until the details of the system are known
Only the choice of programming team
optionExplain: Right: the options to keep open are the details that do not matter to the policy.
The use cases are the intent of the system and cannot be left open.
The policy holds the value of the system and is not an option to defer.
People are not the options discussed.
questions.explain: Only decisions that do not touch the policy can be held open.
questions.rule: Keep open what does not matter to the policy.
questions.teaches: The options we need to leave open are the details that do not matter.

questions.q: Which of these would the author most likely call details of a system? Select all that apply.
options: The rule that gives a discount on large orders
The brand of database storing the records
The procedure for approving a refund
The communication protocol used to reach the system
optionExplain: This is a business rule, so it is policy.
A database is on the author's list of details.
A procedure is part of the policy, not a detail.
A protocol is on the author's list too.
questions.explain: Rules and procedures are the policy; the means of reaching and storing them are details. The card next gives the full split.
questions.rule: Treat business rules and procedures as policy and everything that only lets others reach them as detail, and shape the system so the policy is indifferent to the details.

questions.q: Match each term with its description in the author's split.
pairs: Embodies the business rules and procedures
Let people and systems communicate with the policy without affecting it
A business rule, so part of the policy
questions.explain: Policy holds the rules; details are the means of communication, none of which changes the policy's behavior.
questions.rule: Treat business rules and procedures as policy and everything that only lets others reach them as detail, and shape the system so the policy is indifferent to the details.

questions.q: Where does the author say the true value of a system lives?
options: In the framework that connects the parts, since it decides how everything else fits together
In the database that stores the records
In the user interface that customers see
In the policy, the most essential element of the system
optionExplain: Frameworks are listed among the details.
A database is a detail that serves the policy.
The interface is one more detail, however visible.
Right: the policy is where the true value lives.
questions.explain: The author wants the shape to put the policy first and to make the details irrelevant to it.
questions.rule: Value lives in the policy.
questions.teaches: The policy is where the true value of the system lives, so the architect should treat it as the system's most essential element.

questions.q: Sort each item into policy or detail for an airline booking system.

items.t: Rule that a child cannot book an exit-row seat
The SQL dialect of the booking database
Procedure for rebooking after a cancellation
The JSON format used by the mobile app
Calculation of the baggage fee
The web framework that serves the booking page

questions.explain: Rules and procedures are policy. Formats, dialects and frameworks only help others reach it.
questions.rule: Treat business rules and procedures as policy and everything that only lets others reach them as detail, and shape the system so the policy is indifferent to the details.

questions.q: A company replaces its database vendor. If the system follows the author's split, which part should be able to stay unchanged?
options: The database access code, because it is shared by the rules and the screens alike
The policy, because the details do not affect its behavior
Nothing, because the database holds the business rules
Only the user interface
optionExplain: The access code is the detail that changes.
Right: swapping a detail should not disturb the policy.
This is the belief the author calls misguided later in the book.
The interface is a detail too and is not what makes the policy safe.
questions.explain: If the policy truly does not depend on the database, replacing the database does not touch the policy.
questions.rule: A replaced detail leaves the policy alone.

questions.q: A health clinic's scheduling app has a rule that a doctor cannot be booked for overlapping visits. A developer proposes that the rule live only in the database, as a constraint. Which statement fits the author's split?
options: The rule is a detail, because databases are built to enforce constraints
The rule is policy, so it belongs with the business rules and should not exist only in the database
The rule is a detail because it concerns scheduling
The rule must be dropped to keep the system flexible
optionExplain: Who enforces a rule does not turn the rule into a detail.
Right: policy is where the true value lives, and it should not be made to depend on a detail.
Scheduling rules are business rules.
Dropping a business rule changes the policy.
questions.explain: A detail has no effect on the policy's behavior, which is the reason it can be chosen late. A rule that exists only in the database would put policy into a detail.
questions.rule: Keep policy in the policy.
questions.teaches: Making the details irrelevant to the policy allows decisions about those details to be delayed and deferred.

questions.q: True or false: Choosing the database before writing any business rules gives a team the most information for the choice.
questions.explain: Early on the team knows little about the data the rules will need. The card next explains why waiting helps.
questions.rule: Develop the policy without committing to its details, so that each detail can be chosen as late as possible, with the most information.

questions.q: The longer you wait to decide on a detail, the more ____ you have with which to decide properly.
questions.explain: Each week of building the policy teaches the team what the details must do.
questions.rule: Wait, and learn.

questions.q: If a working part of the policy is agnostic about the database, what does the author say a team can do?
options: Switch databases at every release to avoid lock-in and to keep the vendors competing
Skip testing, since the database is irrelevant
Choose the database by a vote of the developers
Try connecting it to several databases to check applicability and performance
optionExplain: The author describes experiments before deciding, not constant switching.
Testing remains; the point is to compare options.
The author argues for evidence from experiments.
Right: deferral leaves room for experiments.
questions.explain: The same is true of web systems, web frameworks, or even the web itself.
questions.rule: Deferral makes experiments possible.
questions.teaches: A policy that is agnostic about its details lets the team run experiments, such as connecting it to several databases to check applicability and performance.

questions.q: A team starts a new booking system. According to the author's argument, which decisions can they put off? Select all that apply.
options: Which web server will deliver the pages
What the booking rules are
Whether to adopt REST for the outside interface
What the system is meant to do
optionExplain: The policy should not know it is delivered over the web.
The rules are the policy itself and cannot wait.
The policy should be agnostic about the interface to the outside world.
Its intent is the basis of the whole design.
questions.explain: Details can wait. The rules and the intent of the system cannot.
questions.rule: Develop the policy without committing to its details, so that each detail can be chosen as late as possible, with the most information.

questions.q: True or false: If the business rules import the database vendor's classes directly, the team can still defer the database decision.
questions.explain: Direct imports mean the policy now depends on the vendor, so the decision has been made in the code. Deferral needs a policy that does not know the detail.
questions.rule: Develop the policy without committing to its details, so that each detail can be chosen as late as possible, with the most information.

questions.q: A team builds an inventory tool and the manager has not decided whether it will be a web app, a desktop app or both. What does the author's argument allow?
options: They can start on the rules, since the policy need not know how the system is delivered
They must stop until the manager decides
They should choose the web, since it is the safest guess and most customers will expect it
They should build both versions in full first
optionExplain: Right: the author even says you may not have to decide if the system will be delivered over the web.
Waiting for the delivery choice is what the argument avoids.
A guess is the early commitment the author warns against.
This doubles the work and decides nothing earlier.
questions.explain: The delivery mechanism is a detail like the others, and the policy should be unaware of it.
questions.rule: Even the web is a choice.
questions.teaches: The author says that if the high-level policy is unaware of HTML, AJAX and the rest of web development, you do not even have to decide whether the system will be delivered over the web.

questions.q: Your company has standardized on one database product. How should the architect shape the new system?
options: Around the product's features, to use it fully
Without any database, since the choice might be wrong and the product might not fit
As if the choice were open, so the policy does not depend on the product
After asking the company to reverse its choice
optionExplain: This ties the policy to the detail, which the author avoids.
The product is still used; only the policy is kept apart.
Right: the author recommends pretending the decision is not made.
The author advises shaping the system, not fighting the decision.
questions.explain: A decision made elsewhere can still be kept out of the policy. The card next gives the author's phrase.
questions.rule: Treat a mandated tool as an undecided detail and keep the policy independent of it.

questions.q: True or false: When a company has already chosen a database, the author advises the architect to treat that choice as final and to design the policy around it.
questions.explain: The author advises the opposite: pretend the decision has not been made, so that the policy stays independent of the choice.
questions.rule: Do not build the policy around a mandated tool.

questions.q: What is the practical meaning of pretending, in the author's advice?
options: Tell the team the decision is not real and stop referring to it in meetings
Write documents that ignore the decision
Avoid using the chosen product entirely
Shape the system so that the decision can still be deferred or changed
optionExplain: The pretence is about the design, not about announcing anything.
Documents are not the matter; the shape is.
The product may still be used.
Right: pretending is a design stance that keeps change possible.
questions.explain: The pretence is acted out in the structure of the code.
questions.rule: Pretend in the structure.
questions.teaches: Pretending that a decision has not been made means shaping the system so that the decision can still be deferred or changed for as long as possible.

questions.q: The company mandates a particular web framework. Which design move fits the author's advice?
options: Keep the rules free of the framework's classes, and plug the framework in at the edge
Subclass the framework's base classes for every business rule, so it gets full framework support
Copy the framework's source into the project
Wait to start until the framework version is stable
optionExplain: Right: the framework is a detail that should not leak into the policy.
This puts the framework inside the policy.
This does not separate the policy from it.
The advice is to proceed, with the policy independent.
questions.explain: The mandated tool is welcome at the edge of the system and kept out of the center.
questions.rule: Mandated tools stay at the edge.

questions.q: Suppose the mandated framework is later withdrawn by its vendor. In one or two sentences, how would the author's advice change the cost of this event for the team?
questions.a: If the policy was kept independent of the framework, only the edge code that plugs the framework in has to change. If the team had built the policy on the framework, the policy itself would need rework.
questions.explain: The pretence bought a cheaper exit.
questions.rule: Independence limits the cost of change to the edge.

questions.q: A start-up must use its largest customer's required messaging system, and it has two weeks to ship. How would the author's reasoning guide the team?
options: Refuse the requirement until it is justified
Spread the messaging system's calls through the code, since two weeks leaves no time for design
Use the system behind a thin boundary, if that costs little, so the policy stays independent
Build the whole product around the messaging system's model, since the largest customer will use it
optionExplain: The commitment is a given; the advice does not call for refusal.
This builds the dependency in at once.
Right: it satisfies the commitment and keeps change possible at small cost.
This is the opposite of pretending.
questions.explain: The advice is about shaping, and shaping can be done in proportion to the time available. Our reading: weigh the cost of the boundary against the chance of change.
questions.rule: Keep a boundary where it is cheap.
questions.teaches: The author sums up the stance in one line: a good architect maximizes the number of decisions not made.

questions.q: Early programs controlled printers and card readers by their own instructions. What happened when a better medium appeared?
options: The programs ran unchanged on the new medium
The programs had to be rewritten to use the new medium
Only the operators needed new training
The old medium was converted by hardware
optionExplain: They were written for specific devices and could not.
Right: the code was bound to the device.
The programs themselves had to change.
Nothing in the story is solved by hardware.
questions.explain: Code bound to a device must change when the device does. The card next tells how the author's generation fixed this.
questions.rule: Make programs talk to an abstract device, so the real device can change without changing the program.

questions.q: By the late 1960s programmers invented device ____, so that programs no longer depended on the particular IO device.
questions.explain: The operating system presented abstract unit-record devices to the program.
questions.rule: Programs should not know the device.

questions.q: Why did the mistake of binding code to devices go unnoticed at first, according to the author?
options: The programs worked perfectly until a better medium came along
The programmers had no experience with computers, so they could not spot the flaw
The devices never changed
The operating system hid the problem
optionExplain: Right: a design can work and still carry hidden cost.
The author says they did not know it was a mistake, not that they lacked skill.
They did change: tape replaced cards.
Operating systems were what later solved it.
questions.explain: Success hides the cost until the first change arrives.
questions.rule: A design that works can still be a mistake.
questions.teaches: At first the device-bound strategy worked fine and the programs worked perfectly, so the mistake was invisible until magnetic tape offered a better medium.

questions.q: A notification service calls one SMS vendor's functions in forty places. The vendor doubles its prices. Which earlier choice would have made the switch cheap?
options: Calling the vendor from even more places, so that the vendor's name appears everywhere
Storing the vendor's key in a longer string
Having the service call an abstract messaging interface with the vendor behind it
Writing more documentation about the vendor
optionExplain: This deepens the dependency.
Keys have nothing to do with the dependency.
Right: it is device independence applied to a vendor.
Documents do not reduce the cost of switching.
questions.explain: The abstraction turns a change of vendor into a change in one place.
questions.rule: Abstract the vendor.

questions.q: Put these events from the author's story in order.
items: Programs talk directly to card readers and punches
Data integrity problems with piles of cards become serious
Magnetic tape is adopted as a better medium
Programs must be rewritten for tape
Operating systems provide device independence
questions.explain: The story runs from direct device control through the pain of change to the abstraction that removed the pain.
questions.rule: Make programs talk to an abstract device, so the real device can change without changing the program.

questions.q: A photo app saves pictures to a local folder. A year later users ask for cloud storage as well. If the app was built with the approach that device independence stands for, what changes?
options: The whole app is rewritten for the cloud, since local and cloud storage behave differently
A new storage plug-in is written, and the choice is made outside the main program
Users are told to store files by hand
The cloud service replaces the local folder permanently
optionExplain: This is the pre-independence outcome.
Right: as with operators choosing a device, the choice sits outside the policy.
This avoids the design question.
Both can coexist when the choice is made outside the program.
questions.explain: Operators told the operating system which device to connect; the program never changed.
questions.rule: Let the choice of device be made outside the program.
questions.teaches: Operators could tell the operating system whether the abstract services should be connected to card readers, magnetic tape or any other unit-record device, so the choice of device was made outside the program.

questions.q: A program prints letters on a slow printer that blocks an expensive computer. Which design lets the team move the printing elsewhere without touching the program?
options: A program that controls the printer's hardware directly, since that gives full control
A program that prints one letter at a time
A program that asks the user which printer to use
A program that writes to an abstract output chosen outside it
optionExplain: This binds the program to the printer.
Speed of printing is not the matter.
This moves the choice to a person but not outside the code's dependence.
Right: the output target can then change freely.
questions.explain: An abstract output lets the target change. The card next tells the author's version.
questions.rule: Keep the formatting policy free of the device, so the same program serves both test and production devices.

questions.q: Sort each item from the junk mail job as the policy or the detail.

items.t: Formatting of name and address records
The line printer on the 360
The magnetic tape drive
Where each element appears on the form
The offline printers that read the tapes
Which customer data is shown in the letter

questions.explain: The author says the policy was the formatting of the records and the detail was the device.
questions.rule: Formatting is policy; devices are details.

questions.q: How did writing tapes instead of printing directly help the author's company use its expensive computer better?
options: The tapes made letters print faster on the 360, because tape is quicker than a line printer
The tapes removed the need for printing
A tape took about 10 minutes to write and was printed on offline printers
The tapes allowed the 360 to be rented for less
optionExplain: The printing happened elsewhere, not faster on the 360.
The letters were still printed, on offline printers.
Right: printing moved off the costly machine.
The savings came from using it for less time.
questions.explain: The offline printers worked around the clock while the computer did other work.
questions.rule: Move the slow device off the costly machine.
questions.teaches: A full tape could be written in about ten minutes, enough for several rolls of form letters, and five offline printers then ran around the clock, so the expensive computer was freed.

questions.q: A reporting tool formats invoices and writes them straight to a screen widget. QA wants to run the same formatting to a text file for automated checks. What would the author's example advise?
options: Copy the formatting code into a second tool that writes files, and keep both in step
Keep the formatting apart and send its output to the screen or to a file
Ask QA to test only the screen by eye
Write the file by taking screenshots
optionExplain: This duplicates the policy and invites divergence.
Right: the formatting is the policy and the target is the detail.
This gives up automation instead of fixing the dependency.
This is a workaround that avoids the design.
questions.explain: The same program ran against the line printer for tests and tape for production.
questions.rule: One policy, many targets.

questions.q: True or false: If the junk mail programs had been written to control the line printer directly, switching to tape would have required no change to them.
questions.explain: Direct control binds the program to the printer, and a switch would have meant a rewrite, as in the card-to-tape story.
questions.rule: Keep the formatting policy free of the device, so the same program serves both test and production devices.

questions.q: A weather app formats forecasts for a phone screen. The team later adds a car dashboard that shows the same forecast on a small display. Which choice matches the junk mail lesson?
options: Fork the app for the dashboard
Make the dashboard imitate the phone screen exactly, so that the same display code can drive both
Drop the dashboard to avoid change
Keep forecast formatting independent of the display and add the dashboard as a device
optionExplain: Forking duplicates the policy.
This ties the new device to the old one.
The lesson is about making the change cheap, not avoiding it.
Right: the policy stays and a new device is added.
questions.explain: New devices are cheap when the policy never knew the old one. Our reading: this is the same advantage in a modern setting.
questions.rule: A new device is cheap if the policy is device-free.
questions.teaches: With the policy and the device separated, the team could test programs on the local line printer and then tell the operating system to print to tape, deferring the decision about which device would be used.

questions.q: A program stores records by the physical position on a disk. The disk is replaced by a bigger one. What is the main problem?
options: The positions stored in the data and the code are wrong for the new disk
The new disk cannot store the old records because their format is different
The program runs too fast on the new disk
The records must be renamed
optionExplain: Right: the code and the data both embed the old layout.
Capacity is not the issue; layout is.
Speed is not the issue.
Names are not the problem; addresses are.
questions.explain: Physical positions spread through code and data are costly to change. The card next shows the remedy.
questions.rule: Hide the physical layout behind one translation point, so that only that point changes when the hardware does.

questions.q: The colleague advised changing the addressing scheme to use ____ addresses.
questions.explain: Relative addresses are sequential integers; a conversion routine turns them into cylinder, head and sector.
questions.rule: Addresses should not be physical.

questions.q: What did the conversion routine do in the author's story?
options: It stored the union's business rules in one place so that the rest of the code could ask for them
It knew the disk's physical structure and translated relative addresses on the fly
It formatted the disk at start-up
It compressed the records to save space
optionExplain: Business rules stayed outside it.
Right: the knowledge of the disk lives in one place.
Formatting is not described as its role.
Compression is not mentioned.
questions.explain: Everything else saw only sequential integers.
questions.rule: One routine knows the hardware.
questions.teaches: A small conversion routine that knew the physical structure of the disk translated each relative address to a cylinder, head and sector number on the fly.

questions.q: A system stores image paths such as /mnt/disk2/2024/a.png in thousands of database rows and in its code. Storage moves to a cloud service. Which earlier design would have kept the change small?
options: Referring to images by an identifier and translating it to a location in one place
Longer path strings with more detail, so each location can be found without any lookup
A second copy of every path in a spreadsheet, so that any path can be looked up and edited
Renaming the disk
optionExplain: Right: it mirrors relative addressing.
More physical detail makes it worse.
This doubles the places to change.
The names are not the problem.
questions.explain: A single translation point turns a storage move into a one-place change.
questions.rule: Refer by identifier, translate in one place.

questions.q: True or false: After the switch to relative addresses, a new disk drive with more heads would force changes to every business rule that reads or writes records.
questions.explain: The business rules no longer know the cylinder, head and sector scheme. Only the conversion routine, which holds that knowledge, has to change.
questions.rule: Change only the translator.

questions.q: A team says their code is decoupled because every physical detail is now read from a configuration file loaded by the business rules. Using the lesson of this story, what is the better design?
options: Keep it, since a file is easier to edit than code and the values are no longer hard-wired in the source
Move the configuration into the rules themselves, so each rule can read the values it needs directly
Drop the configuration and fix the values in the code, which is faster and keeps one source of truth
Let the rules use logical addresses only, and let a separate component translate them using the configuration
optionExplain: Easier editing leaves the policy knowing the details.
This couples the rules to the details even more.
Fixed values are the hard-wiring again.
Right: the policy should have no knowledge of the details at all.
questions.explain: A configuration read by the rules still makes the rules aware of the hardware. The author asks for no knowledge at all.
questions.rule: No knowledge means none, not a parameter.
questions.teaches: The author says good architects decouple policy from details so thoroughly that the policy has no knowledge of the details and does not depend on them in any way.

questions.q: A new developer opens a code base for a shopping cart and sees folders named controllers, models and utils. What would a better structure show first?
options: More folders named after the framework, since the framework explains how the code runs
A single file containing all the code
Elements named after what the cart does, such as checking out
Folders sorted alphabetically
optionExplain: Framework names say nothing about the system's intent.
One file hides every landmark.
Right: the use cases become visible landmarks.
Order does not show intent.
questions.explain: A good structure tells what the system is for. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Make the system's use cases visible as prominent elements named for what they do at the top of its structure.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a shopping cart application with a good architecture will look like a shopping cart application.
questions.explain: The use cases are plainly visible within the structure.
questions.rule: The structure should say what the system is for.

questions.q: According to the author, what is the first concern and first priority of the architect with respect to behavior?
options: That the architecture hides the use cases from users
That every use case gets its own server
That the architecture supports the use cases
That behavior is rewritten for each release
optionExplain: Visibility to developers is the point.
Servers are not mentioned in this claim.
Right: the architecture must support the intent of the system.
Rewriting is not the author's aim.
questions.explain: Supporting the use cases is the first priority, even though the influence of architecture on behavior is small.
questions.rule: First, support the use cases.
questions.teaches: The first concern of the architect, and the first priority of the architecture, is that it supports the use cases and so the intent of the system.

questions.q: For an online library system, sort each folder name by what it shows at the top level.

items.t: BorrowBook
SpringControllers
RenewLoan
HibernateEntities
ReserveTitle
RestEndpoints

questions.explain: Names that describe functions are landmarks for the use cases. Names of tools tell the reader the technology instead.
questions.rule: Name the top level after behavior.

questions.q: A team renames its top-level folders from technical layers to use cases. What does the author's reasoning predict for a developer looking for the checkout logic?
options: They find it faster, since behaviors are first-class and visible
They find it slower, since the folders are fewer and each one now holds more files to search
They find the same time, since folders do not matter once a search tool is available
They find that the checkout logic is gone
optionExplain: Right: they no longer hunt for behaviors.
Fewer technical folders do not hide the use case.
The author argues that visibility matters.
Renaming does not remove behavior.
questions.explain: Exposing the behavior removes the hunt.
questions.rule: Visible behavior saves the hunt.

questions.q: A mobile banking app has screens, networking and storage folders. A designer says the structure should also reveal what the bank customer can do. According to the author, what is the mismatch?
options: Mobile apps cannot have use cases at the top level because screens are fixed by the platform
Screens should be removed from the app
Storage should be placed at the top
The top level shows the technology, not use cases such as transferring money
optionExplain: The author says the use cases should be prominent.
Screens are not the problem.
Technical names are what the author wants moved down.
Right: the intent of the system is not visible at the architectural level.
questions.explain: The structure speaks of tools, so a reader learns how the app is built, not what it is for.
questions.rule: Say what the system does.
questions.teaches: The use-case elements can be classes, functions or modules; what matters is that they hold prominent positions within the architecture and carry names that describe their function.

questions.q: A system's components call each other directly, assuming they live in one process. Traffic grows until one component needs its own server. What is the likely result?
options: A simple setting change in the deployment script
A costly rework, since the components assumed shared memory
No effect, because servers do not matter to code
An improvement, because direct calls are faster over a network
optionExplain: The calls themselves would have to change.
Right: the assumption has to be undone.
The code's assumptions about location do matter.
Direct calls do not cross a network.
questions.explain: A hidden assumption about where components run limits how the system can grow. The card next gives the author's rule.
questions.rule: Isolate components and do not assume how they communicate, so the system can move between monolith, threads, processes and services.

questions.q: True or false: A system that is written as a monolith and depends on being one can easily be upgraded to run as micro-services.
questions.explain: Dependence on the monolithic form makes the move hard; keeping components isolated, with no assumption about communication, is what makes it easy.
questions.rule: Do not depend on being a monolith.

questions.q: Chapter 15 says the effect of architecture on operation is less dramatic than on the other jobs. What does the author add here?
options: Architecture has no role in operation at all, since hardware can be added to fix any problem
Architecture has a substantial role where use cases demand throughput and response time
Operation can be ignored until the system fails
Operation matters only to hardware teams, who size the servers once the design is finished
optionExplain: The author says the role is more substantial and less cosmetic here.
Right: where the demand is real, the structure has to support it.
The text calls for support for each use case that demands it.
The point is about architecture.
questions.explain: The earlier claim is about cost; this claim is about what the structure must allow.
questions.rule: Where the demand is real, structure for it.
questions.teaches: Architecture plays a more substantial, less cosmetic role in operation than first thought: it must support the throughput and response time each use case demands.

questions.q: Match each operational need with a form that may suit it.
pairs: Huge request rates spread over many machines
An array of small services run in parallel
Many small tasks sharing memory on one machine
Lightweight threads in a single process
A few parts that must not share memory
A small tool with modest load
questions.explain: The author lists the forms along a spectrum. No form is best for all systems, which is why the choice is kept open.
questions.rule: Isolate components and do not assume how they communicate, so the system can move between monolith, threads, processes and services.

questions.q: True or false: A team keeps its components isolated and assumes only that they can pass messages. The load grows and one component must move to another server. This move is likely to be much easier than for a team whose components assume shared memory.
questions.explain: Because the isolated components made no assumption about the means of communication, the move needs only a change in how the messages travel.
questions.rule: No assumption, no rework.

questions.q: A small internal tool has twenty users and will stay that way. A consultant wants it split into micro-services in case of growth. What does the author's text allow?
options: The split is required for any system, because a service boundary is the only way to keep it flexible
The tool must be rewritten in a new language
The tool should have no structure at all
A simple monolith may be enough; the spectrum is an option to keep open, not a form to adopt
optionExplain: The author lists a monolith as one possible form.
Language is not part of the argument.
Isolation of components still keeps the option open.
Right: some systems can survive as simple monolithic programs.
questions.explain: The point is not to build the biggest form but to avoid being locked out of the others.
questions.rule: Keep the door open; do not walk through it early.
questions.teaches: Some systems can even survive as simple monolithic programs running in a single process, so the largest form is not required.

questions.q: Two departments that rarely talk to each other build one product. What structure is the finished system likely to have?
options: Two separate parts that mirror the two departments
One part that merges both departments' work smoothly
A structure unrelated to the departments
A structure decided only by the programming language
optionExplain: Right: the structure of the product tends to copy how the people communicate.
Smooth merging needs communication that the departments lack.
The tendency is that design follows communication.
Language does not decide the split.
questions.explain: This tendency has a name. The card next gives it.
questions.rule: Partition the system into well-isolated components that teams can develop independently.

questions.q: Conway's law says a design's structure is a copy of the organization's ____ structure.
questions.explain: The communication structure of the people shapes the structure of what they build.
questions.rule: Systems copy how people talk.

questions.q: What does the author say the architecture should do for a system developed by many teams and concerns?
options: Make all teams share one set of source files, so that everyone sees the same code and conflicts surface early
Hide the components' names from the teams
Facilitate independent actions by the teams, so they do not interfere during development
Require every team to attend the same reviews
optionExplain: Shared files cause the interference the partition avoids.
Names are not the issue.
Right: the partition is meant to let teams work independently.
Meetings do not replace the partition.
questions.explain: The point of the partition is independence in daily work.
questions.rule: Independence in daily work.
questions.teaches: A system developed by many teams and concerns needs an architecture that facilitates independent actions by those teams, so that they do not interfere with each other during development.

questions.q: Three teams will work on a travel-booking system: flights, hotels and payments. They keep editing the same booking class and breaking one another's work. What does the author's reasoning suggest?
