options: Give all three teams the same task list so that they must talk to each other every day
Add a fourth team to review the booking class
Ask the teams to edit the class at different times, using a schedule that everybody keeps
Partition the system into isolated components so each team owns one
optionExplain: Shared tasks do not remove shared code.
Review does not remove the shared class.
Scheduling avoids the symptom, not the cause.
Right: isolation is what lets teams work independently.
questions.explain: Independence needs isolation in the code, not in the calendar.
questions.rule: Isolate in code, not in time.

questions.q: True or false: If an organization changes how its teams communicate, Conway's law predicts that the structure of the systems it designs will tend to change with it.
questions.explain: The law ties design structure to communication structure; when one changes the other tends to follow.
questions.rule: Partition the system into well-isolated components that teams can develop independently.

questions.q: A company reorganizes into five feature teams. A manager proposes to cut the system into five components matching the teams exactly, and to ignore deployment. What does the book warn?
options: A component per team may suit the schedule but not deployment, operation or maintenance
Nothing; matching the teams is best because the system then follows how people communicate
Teams should be abolished
The components should be as small as possible so that every developer owns at least one
optionExplain: Right: the partition should serve all four jobs.
The book says the team-driven shape is unlikely to be the best overall.
Nothing suggests this.
Size is not the book's concern here.
questions.explain: A partition should serve the whole life cycle, and a reorganization is a reason to check it again.
questions.rule: Do not let the org chart choose the whole shape.
questions.teaches: Teams driven solely by development schedule gravitate toward one component per team, which is not likely to be the best architecture for deployment, operation and maintenance.

questions.q: After each build, a release needs a person to copy folders, edit five property files and start services in a fixed order. What does this suggest about the architecture?
options: It is a good sign of careful control
It shows deployment is none of the architect's business
It does not support easy deployment
It proves the code is correct
optionExplain: Manual steps invite error.
The author says architecture plays a huge role in deployment.
Right: the steps show deployment was not designed in.
Correctness is not what the steps show.
questions.explain: A heavy manual process points to a missing design. The card next gives the author's target.
questions.rule: Make the build produce something deployable at once, with master components that start, integrate and supervise the isolated parts.

questions.q: The goal the author names for deployment is ____ deployment.
questions.explain: A good architecture helps the system be deployable right after the build.
questions.rule: Aim for deployable after build.

questions.q: What role do the master components play, according to the author?
options: They contain all the business rules, so that the rest of the components can stay small and simple
They tie the system together and make sure each component is started, integrated and supervised
They replace the other components when a component fails and needs to be swapped out quickly
They are used only in testing
optionExplain: Business rules are the policy, not the master components' job.
Right: they are part of the partitioned design, not an afterthought.
Replacement is not their role.
The text places them in deployment.
questions.explain: Starting, integration and supervision need a place in the design.
questions.rule: Give start-up a home in the design.
questions.teaches: The master components that tie the whole system together are part of the partitioning, and they ensure each component is properly started, integrated and supervised.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it fits the goal of immediate deployment or works against it.

items.t: The build output can be started as it is
Twenty property files edited by hand after each build
A master component that starts the parts in order
A directory tree that must be created by hand
Components isolated so they can be supervised
Dozens of small scripts that must run in a set sequence

questions.explain: The author contrasts a system that is deployable after the build with one that depends on scripts and hand-made files.
questions.rule: Deployable after build.

questions.q: A team adds a new component to a system whose master component starts all parts in order. What does the book's idea predict about the work needed to deploy it?
options: Little extra work, since the master component handles starting and supervising
A full new set of manual scripts for the new part, since each part is deployed on its own
A redesign of every existing component
No work, because deployment is free
optionExplain: Right: the master component absorbs the new part.
This is the pattern the goal tries to avoid.
Isolation avoids this.
Some registration with the master component is still needed.
questions.explain: A well-placed master component makes adding parts routine.
questions.rule: New parts join through the master component.

questions.q: A mobile app is shipped as a single signed package to an app store. How does the idea of immediate deployment apply?
options: It cannot apply to mobile apps
It requires splitting the package into many services so that each module can be released alone and updated quickly
The single package already meets it; the concern is the build producing it without manual steps
It requires users to configure the app on first run
optionExplain: The goal concerns any deployed system.
More parts make it harder.
Right: a single deployable unit is near the target.
User configuration is what the goal avoids.
questions.explain: The aim is that deployment follows the build with no manual steps. Our reading: the same aim guides how the package itself is produced.
questions.rule: No manual steps after the build.
questions.teaches: A good architecture does not rely on dozens of little configuration scripts and property file tweaks, and does not require manual creation of directories or files that must be arranged just so.

questions.q: A team starts a project and does not know what the product will need in two years. Which approach is closest to the author's advice?
options: Wait until the requirements are fully known
Use inexpensive principles that isolate components
Guess the future needs and build for them in full from the first week
Avoid structure and rely on rewrites
optionExplain: They may never be, and they will change.
Right: they leave options open without needing to know the targets.
Guesses tend to be wrong, and the goals move.
Rewrites are the expensive way to change.
questions.explain: Unknown targets call for cheap flexibility. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: When the targets are unknown and moving, use inexpensive principles that isolate components and keep options open.

questions.q: The author says the goals an architecture must meet are indistinct and ____.
questions.explain: Most of the time the use cases, constraints, teams and deployment needs are unknown, and they change over the life cycle.
questions.rule: The targets move.

questions.q: What kind of principles does the author say help even when the targets are unclear?
options: Ones that need a full requirements document first, so that the architect knows what to partition
Ones that require expensive tooling, since only automation can keep so many components in step
Ones that remove all future change
Ones that are inexpensive to implement and partition the system into well-isolated components
optionExplain: The point is that they work without a clear picture.
The author stresses low cost.
The aim is easy change, not no change.
Right: low cost and isolation are the features named.
questions.explain: The principles are cheap and general, so they pay off whichever way the targets move.
questions.rule: Cheap and general.
questions.teaches: Some principles of architecture are relatively inexpensive to implement and can help balance the concerns even when you do not have a clear picture of the targets you have to hit.

questions.q: A product owner says the team cannot start designing because the requirements are not final. Which actions follow the author's advice? Select all that apply.
options: Wait for a signed specification before any design
Partition the system into well-isolated components now
Fix the design around the use case that is most likely today
Prefer inexpensive principles that leave options open
optionExplain: The goals are inconstant, so a signature may not last.
Isolation pays off whichever way the requirements move.
This spends options early on a guess.
The author names such principles as the way to balance concerns without clear targets.
questions.explain: Unknown and changing goals are the normal case, not a reason to wait.
questions.rule: When the targets are unknown and moving, use inexpensive principles that isolate components and keep options open.

questions.q: Six months later a new operational constraint appears. In which system will the change be cheapest?
options: One built tightly around the old constraint, because it was designed with that constraint in mind
One with no components, since a single block of code has fewer places to change
One built from well-isolated components that left options open
One that was never deployed, since nobody depends on it yet and it can be redone freely
optionExplain: Tight fit makes change costly.
Without components, change touches everything.
Right: the options were not yet spent.
Not deploying avoids the question.
questions.explain: Isolation turns a surprise into a local change.
questions.rule: Isolation makes surprises local.

questions.q: A start-up's product might become a mobile app, a web app or an API. Which action best follows the author's advice at this stage?
options: Pick the most popular form and fix the design around it, since popularity reduces the risk
Keep the business rules independent of the delivery form and commit to a form later
Build all three forms fully before launch
Delay all coding until the market is clear
optionExplain: The goals are inconstant, so early fixing is risky.
Right: it keeps the unknown choice open.
This pays three times for an unknown need.
The inexpensive principles allow progress now.
questions.explain: The delivery form is an unknown, and the rules can be built without it.
questions.rule: Build what you know; keep the unknown open.
questions.teaches: A good architecture makes the system easy to change, in all the ways that it must change, by leaving options open.

questions.q: Which two parts of a shopping system are most likely to change for unrelated reasons?
options: The tax rule and the discount rule, which both belong to the pricing logic
Two lines of the same tax function
The names of two variables
The look of the checkout screen and the rule for computing tax
optionExplain: Both are business rules, so they often change together.
They share one reason to change.
Names are too small to matter here.
Right: the designer's taste and the tax law have nothing to do with each other.
questions.explain: Different reasons to change suggest separate parts. The card next names the layers.
questions.rule: Separate the user interface, application-specific rules, application-independent rules and database, because each changes for its own reasons.

questions.q: Match each part of a system with the reason it changes.
pairs: Changes for reasons unrelated to business rules
An application-independent rule tied to the domain
A technical detail apart from the rules and the UI
questions.explain: These four are the layers the author names. Each has its own reasons and its own rate of change.
questions.rule: Separate the user interface, application-specific rules, application-independent rules and database, because each changes for its own reasons.

questions.q: How does the author say application-specific rules differ from application-independent rules?
options: They change at different rates and for different reasons, so they should be separated
They are the same kind of rule, so they belong together in one layer and can change together
Application-independent rules never change
Application-specific rules concern the database
optionExplain: Right: validation tracks the application while interest tracks the domain.
The author gives them different layers.
He says they change at different rates, not never.
Validation is not a database concern.
questions.explain: Input validation is tied to the application itself, while interest and inventory counting are associated more with the domain.
questions.rule: Split rules by how close they are to the application.
questions.teaches: Validation of input fields is a business rule closely tied to the application itself, whereas calculating interest on an account and counting inventory are business rules more closely associated with the domain.

questions.q: Sort each item of a payroll system into the layer it belongs to.

items.t: Formula for overtime pay
Layout of the payslip screen
Rule that gross pay is the sum of regular and overtime pay
The table schema holding timesheets
The SQL query that loads a month of hours
Calculation of statutory deductions

questions.explain: Rules about how pay works belong to the domain. Screens, tables and queries are details that serve it.
questions.rule: Separate the user interface, application-specific rules, application-independent rules and database, because each changes for its own reasons.

questions.q: True or false: If the database schema is changed and the layers have been separated as the author describes, the user interface layer will have to change as well.
questions.explain: The schema changes for reasons of its own and sits in its own layer. The layers exist so that such a change stays local.
questions.rule: Separate the user interface, application-specific rules, application-independent rules and database, because each changes for its own reasons.

questions.q: A weekend script of sixty lines reads a file, applies one rule and prints a result. A teammate asks for four layers with interfaces. Which view fits the book's reasoning?
options: Four layers are required for any program, since every program has a UI, rules and storage to keep apart
The layers are justified by different reasons to change; for a script that will not change they may cost more
A script cannot have rules
Layers are justified only by team size, so a one-person script never needs them, however often or for whatever reasons it changes
optionExplain: The author ties the split to reasons to change.
Right: the split follows real differences in what changes.
Scripts have rules; the point is how often they change.
The text justifies them by reasons to change.
questions.explain: The split is a response to different rates of change. Our reading: where nothing changes, the split buys little.
questions.rule: Split where change differs.
questions.teaches: Use cases have elements of both the UI and the business rules, so the architect separates the UI portion of a use case from the business-rule portion, so that they can change independently while the use cases stay visible and clear.

questions.q: In an order entry system, the add-order and delete-order functions share one big class. What is the main risk?
options: A change for one can break the other
The class will compile more slowly
The two functions will run at different speeds
The class will have too few methods
optionExplain: Right: they change for different reasons, yet they are tied together.
Compile time is not the main risk.
Speed is not the issue.
Method count is not the issue.
questions.explain: Functions that change for different reasons should not share their code. The card next shows how the book cuts the system.
questions.rule: Cut the system into thin vertical use cases as well as horizontal layers, and keep each use case's parts apart from the others.

questions.q: Use cases are narrow ____ slices that cut through the horizontal layers of the system.
questions.explain: Each use case uses some of each layer, so it forms a thin vertical cut.
questions.rule: Layers run across; use cases run down.

questions.q: What does the author say makes it unlikely that adding new use cases will affect older ones?
options: Having one shared database table for all use cases, so that the data stays consistent
Adding new use cases only at night
Keeping use cases in the order they were written
Giving each use case its own aspect of the UI and the database
optionExplain: Sharing is what ties the use cases together.
Timing does not matter.
Order is not a decoupling device.
Right: separate parts per use case keep the new from touching the old.
questions.explain: A use case that has its own UI and database parts cannot reach into another's.
questions.rule: Separate parts per use case.
questions.teaches: If the elements that change for different reasons are decoupled and each use case uses a different aspect of the UI and database, adding new use cases will be unlikely to affect older ones.

questions.q: For a library system, sort each statement by whether it describes a horizontal layer split or a vertical use-case split.

items.t: Screens in one place, rules in another, storage in a third
Borrow-book code kept apart from renew-loan code
One group for everything that touches the database
A separate query for reserving a title and one for returning a title
Business rules separated from the web framework
Each action has its own screen, rule and table access

questions.explain: Layers divide by kind of work. Use-case slices divide by what the user is trying to do, and they cut through all the layers.
questions.rule: Cut the system into thin vertical use cases as well as horizontal layers, and keep each use case's parts apart from the others.

questions.q: A team adds a new use case, export-orders, to a system where add-order and delete-order are decoupled slices. What does the author's reasoning predict?
options: The add-order slice must be rewritten
The delete-order slice must be deployed again at once, because it sits in the same layers
The new use case can be added without interfering with the old ones
All three slices must share one screen
optionExplain: Decoupling prevents this.
Separate slices keep the change local.
Right: each slice has its own parts.
Sharing is what the separation avoids.
questions.explain: Separation lets a new slice stand beside the old ones.
questions.rule: New slice, old slices untouched.

questions.q: In a small mobile app, the login and logout actions change together every time, since both come from the same security policy. How does the book's advice apply?
options: They must still be separated into two slices, because every use case should be a slice of its own
They must be merged with the shopping screens
They may belong together, because the aim is to separate what changes for different reasons
Neither needs a UI
optionExplain: The rule is not to separate everything.
There is no reason to merge unrelated parts.
Right: the slices follow reasons to change.
The question is about slicing, not about having a UI.
questions.explain: Slices are a tool for separating independent changes, not an end in themselves.
questions.rule: Slice by reasons to change, not by habit.
questions.teaches: The pattern is to decouple the elements of the system that change for different reasons, and to collect together those that change for the same reasons, given the intent of the system.

questions.q: A shop wants its database to run on a stronger server than its web pages. What must be true of the code?
options: The two parts must not depend on sharing one process's memory
They must be written in the same language, so that they can call each other over the network
They must use the same data format everywhere
They must be compiled together
optionExplain: Right: separate servers cannot share an address space.
Language does not decide this.
A format does not decide placement.
Compiling together binds them to one place.
questions.explain: Running apart needs communication over a network. The card next gives the author's term.
questions.rule: Decouple for the use cases, then pick the decoupling mode that the operational need requires; services are one option, not the answer.

questions.q: To run on separate servers, components cannot depend on being together in the same ____ space of a processor.
questions.explain: They must be independent services that communicate over a network.
questions.rule: Separate servers, no shared memory.

questions.q: What is the author's stated view of service-oriented architecture and micro-services?
options: Both are the best possible architectures, and every new system should adopt one from the start
Both should be avoided in every system
Both are the same as a monolith
Neither is claimed to be best; sometimes components must be separated all the way to services
optionExplain: The author says he is not telling us this.
He accepts them when separation is needed.
They are different decoupling modes.
Right: the author endorses the option, not the fashion.
questions.explain: Services are one mode among several, and the author keeps the choice open.
questions.rule: Options, not doctrine.
questions.teaches: The author does not call service-oriented architecture the best possible architecture or micro-services the wave of the future; his point is that sometimes components have to be separated all the way to the service level.

questions.q: A video site finds that the video-encoding part needs ten servers while the account page needs one. Both live in one process. What does the book's reasoning suggest about the earlier design?
options: Nothing can be done without a rewrite from scratch, because the parts already share one process and one memory
The decoupling helps, but running the parts apart needs a mode that does not assume one address space
Both parts must be merged for speed
The account page must be copied ten times
optionExplain: Decoupled parts reduce the rewrite.
Right: the decoupling is a start; the mode must match.
Merging would work against the need.
The need was for the encoding part.
questions.explain: Decoupling in the code makes the parts movable. The mode decides whether they can move apart.
questions.rule: Match the mode to the need.

questions.q: True or false: A team decouples its modules at the source level only, inside one process. Later, moving one module to its own server will need no extra work.
questions.explain: Source-level separation keeps the option open, but the module still has to be turned into a service that communicates over a network.
questions.rule: Decoupling keeps the option; it does not use it.

questions.q: A chat app on a phone has a screen part and a message-storage part. Both run in the app's one process on one device. Does the book's argument for services apply?
options: Yes: every app must use services, since the screen and the storage are separate concerns that may grow
Not in the same way: the parts need no network to run apart, so the case for services is weak
Yes: services are required for storage
No: decoupling is useless for phones
optionExplain: The author does not say so.
Right: the operational benefit applies when parts must run on different servers.
Storage can sit in the same process.
Decoupling for use cases and layers still helps.
questions.explain: The service level pays off when parts must run apart on a network. On one device the same decoupling may stay at the source level.
questions.rule: Services answer a need to run apart.
questions.teaches: Many architects call such components services or micro-services, depending on a vague notion of line count.

questions.q: The business rules of a system do not know that a user interface exists. What follows for the team working on the interface?
options: It must wait for the rules team to finish every change
It must edit the rules to add each screen
It can no longer test its screens
It cannot much affect the team working on the business rules
optionExplain: Waiting is needed when the rules depend on the interface.
Screens are added in the interface.
Testing is not ruled out.
Right: a team cannot break what does not depend on it.
questions.explain: Independence in code gives independence between teams. The card next generalizes.
questions.rule: Decouple layers and use cases well, and teams can be organized in any way and parts can be deployed on their own.

questions.q: Match each condition with what it brings.
pairs: Business rules do not know about the UI
A UI team cannot much affect a rules team
Their teams are unlikely to interfere
Layers and use cases are decoupled
The architecture supports any team organization
Layers and use cases can be hot-swapped in running systems
questions.explain: Each benefit follows from keeping the dependencies one-way and the use cases apart.
questions.rule: Decouple layers and use cases well, and teams can be organized in any way and parts can be deployed on their own.

questions.q: According to the author, which team organizations can the architecture support while the layers and use cases are decoupled?
options: Feature teams, component teams, layer teams or another variation
Only feature teams, since use cases map directly onto the teams that own them
Only a single large team
Only teams that match the layers, since a layer team owns one layer at a time
optionExplain: Right: the architecture is not tied to a single way of organizing the people.
The author lists several.
Nothing limits it to one team.
Layer teams are one possibility among several.
questions.explain: If the parts are really independent, the way people are grouped is free to change.
questions.rule: The people can be organized in many ways.
questions.teaches: So long as the layers and use cases are decoupled, the architecture of the system will support the organization of the teams, irrespective of whether they are organized as feature teams, component teams, layer teams, or some other variation.

questions.q: A company moves from layer teams to feature teams. Which conditions in the code would let the architecture support the change? Select all that apply.
options: Every feature uses the same shared class for all screens
The use cases are decoupled from one another
The database schema is edited by every team in turn
The business rules do not depend on the UI
optionExplain: Shared classes bring the interference back.
Feature teams own use cases, and they must not interfere.
A shared edit point is the opposite of decoupling.
The layers stay independent whatever the teams are.
questions.explain: The reorganization is safe where the parts are already independent.
questions.rule: Decouple layers and use cases well, and teams can be organized in any way and parts can be deployed on their own.

questions.q: True or false: If the decoupling was done well, adding a new use case to a running system might be as simple as adding a few new files or services while leaving the rest alone.
questions.explain: The book says that, if done well, layers and use cases can be hot-swapped and a new use case can be added alone.
questions.rule: Decouple layers and use cases well, and teams can be organized in any way and parts can be deployed on their own.

questions.q: A plug-in based photo editor ships each filter as a separate package. A new filter is added by dropping its package into a folder. Which part of the author's argument does this illustrate?
options: Conway's law about how the structure of a system copies the communication structure
The need for a master component to supervise all the filters as they start
Adding a new use case as a few new files while leaving the rest alone
The danger of duplicating code
optionExplain: Conway's law concerns how organizations shape designs.
The example does not depend on supervision.
Right: independent deployability in action.
Duplication is a different topic.
questions.explain: A well-decoupled system treats each new use case as an addition, not as a change to the rest.
questions.rule: A new use case should be an addition.
questions.teaches: Adding a new use case could be as simple as adding a few new jar files or services to the system while leaving the rest alone.

questions.q: Two functions in different features look the same today. Next year they may need different behavior. How should a developer treat them?
options: Merge them at once, because duplicated code is always wrong
Copy them into more places to be safe
Delete one and hope
Be careful before merging them, since they may be accidental duplicates
optionExplain: Not all similar code is truly duplicated.
More copies do not help.
Deleting breaks one feature.
Right: the future of the copies matters more than today's resemblance.
questions.explain: Look-alike code may drift apart. The card next names the two kinds.
questions.rule: Before removing duplication, ask whether the copies must always change together; if they change at different rates or for different reasons, leave them apart.

questions.q: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: Every change to one instance needs the same change to each duplicate
Similar code that changes at different rates and for different reasons
Removing duplication without checking that it is real
Copies that look very different after a few years
questions.explain: The test is whether the copies share their reasons to change, not whether they look alike.
questions.rule: Before removing duplication, ask whether the copies must always change together; if they change at different rates or for different reasons, leave them apart.

questions.q: According to the author, what should professionals do when code is truly duplicated?
options: Reduce and eliminate it, since they are honor-bound to do so
Keep both copies for safety, since removing one could break the other
Rewrite both in a new language
Leave it until the next release
optionExplain: Right: the warning is about false duplication, not about real duplication.
The author says to eliminate true duplication.
Language is not at issue.
The text calls for elimination.
questions.explain: The trap is the knee-jerk removal of duplication that is only apparent. Real duplication still deserves removal.
questions.rule: Remove what is truly the same; leave what only looks the same.
questions.teaches: When code is truly duplicated, we are honor-bound as professionals to reduce and eliminate it; the warning is aimed at knee-jerk elimination of duplication that is not real.

questions.q: Sort each case into true duplication or accidental duplication.

items.t: Two copies of the function that rounds money to the legal precision, which must always match
Two report layouts, owned by different departments, that look alike today
The same tax-rate table pasted into the billing and quoting modules
Two signup forms from different campaigns with similar fields
A checksum routine copied into two services that must agree
Two screens that happen to list items in a table today

questions.explain: Copies that must change together are true duplicates. Copies owned by different reasons to change are accidental.
questions.rule: Before removing duplication, ask whether the copies must always change together; if they change at different rates or for different reasons, leave them apart.

questions.q: Two similar screens are merged into one shared component. A year later each screen needs its own behavior. What does the author's reasoning predict?
options: Nothing: the component splits in two at no cost, since the shared part is easy to copy
The screens will converge again
Separating them will be a challenge, as the merged code has grown to serve both
The shared component will become faster
optionExplain: The author warns the split will be hard.
The reasoning says they diverge.
Right: unifying accidental duplicates makes them hard to separate later.
Speed is not the point.
questions.explain: Premature unification ties the screens together.
questions.rule: Merging accidental copies is hard to undo.

questions.q: Two services each hold an email-validation expression. Both must reject exactly the same addresses, because a mismatch causes support tickets. By the book's test, which description fits?
options: Accidental duplication, since the services are separate and owned by different teams
True duplication, since each change to one must be made to the other
Accidental duplication, since regular expressions drift apart as the rules for addresses change
Neither: duplication is never a concern
optionExplain: Being separate does not make the reasons to change different.
Right: the copies share a single reason to change.
The case states the copies must agree.
True duplication is a concern.
questions.explain: The test is about shared reasons to change, not about team or service boundaries.
questions.rule: Same reason to change means true duplication.
questions.teaches: Architects often fall into a trap that hinges on their fear of duplication, so each apparent duplicate must be checked against whether it will change for the same reasons.

questions.q: A database record has the same fields as the screen that shows it. A developer passes the record to the screen. What risk follows?
options: A change in the table can now break the screen
The screen will show data more slowly
The table will lose its indexes
The record will become read-only
optionExplain: Right: the screen depends on the record's shape.
Speed is not the main concern.
Indexes are unrelated.
Nothing like this follows.
questions.explain: Sharing a shape couples the two. The card next gives the author's remedy.
questions.rule: Create a view model and copy the fields across rather than passing a database record to the UI or merging look-alike use cases.

questions.q: Instead of passing the database record to the UI, create a separate view ____ and copy the elements across.
questions.explain: The view model decouples the screen from the shape of the record.
questions.rule: Give the screen its own data shape.

questions.q: What does the author say will happen if two similar screens are unified now?
options: They will stay identical for the life of the system, so the shared code pays for itself
They will be easier to test forever
They are likely to diverge, and separating them later will be a challenge
They will need a database
optionExplain: The author expects divergence.
The author does not claim this.
Right: the unification becomes a cost once the screens differ.
Databases are not part of the argument.
questions.explain: Screens that look alike now will most likely look different later.
questions.rule: Look-alike screens diverge.
questions.teaches: Because two similar screens will most likely diverge as time goes by, unifying them now leaves a challenge when they must be separated later.

questions.q: For a hotel system, sort each action by whether it follows the author's advice or goes against it.

items.t: Create a view model for the room list screen
Return the room database record straight to the web page
Keep the check-in and check-out screens in separate code
Merge the check-in and check-out screens because they look alike today
Copy fields from the record to a view object in a mapper
Let the web page read the table column names

questions.explain: The author prefers a little copying to a shared shape that couples the layers.
questions.rule: Create a view model and copy the fields across rather than passing a database record to the UI or merging look-alike use cases.

questions.q: True or false: A team passes database records to the UI to save effort. Six months later the table gains new columns for the billing team. This change cannot affect the screens.
questions.explain: The screens depend on the record, so a change to its shape can reach them. A view model would have absorbed the change in one mapper.
questions.rule: Create a view model and copy the fields across rather than passing a database record to the UI or merging look-alike use cases.

questions.q: A mobile app shows a list of messages. The network gives back JSON with the same fields the list needs, so the developer binds the list directly to the JSON objects. Which view fits the book's advice?
options: Binding directly is fine, because the shapes match and the copy would add code for nothing
The list would depend on the server's format; a view model keeps the layers apart
The server should never change its JSON
The list must be removed
optionExplain: Matching today does not keep them matched.
Right: the same reasoning applies to any boundary between layers.
This is not in the author's argument.
Nothing calls for this.
questions.explain: The matching shape is the temptation, and the risk is the dependence.
questions.rule: A matching shape is not a reason to couple.
questions.teaches: Creating the separate view model is not a lot of effort, and it helps keep the layers properly decoupled.

questions.q: A team compiles all its modules into one executable, and the modules call each other as plain functions. How would the author describe the way they are kept apart?
options: By separate network services
By separate jar files deployed on their own, one for each group of modules
They are not kept apart at all
By discipline in the source code, with no physical boundary at deployment
optionExplain: Services communicate over a network, which is not the case here.
Jar files would be a deployment-level boundary.
A disciplined separation can exist inside one executable.
Right: this is decoupling at the source level.
questions.explain: Source-level separation is one of three depths. The card next names all three.
questions.rule: Name the mode before choosing a boundary: source level, deployment level or service level.

questions.q: Match each decoupling mode with what it controls.
pairs: Dependencies between deployable units such as jar files
Dependencies reduced to data structures sent as network packets
questions.explain: Each mode controls a different thing, and the control gets stronger as you move from source to service.
questions.rule: Name the mode before choosing a boundary: source level, deployment level or service level.

questions.q: At the deployment level, how may the decoupled components communicate, according to the author?
options: Only through network packets, because separately deployed units cannot share an address space
Only by sharing source files, since the units must be rebuilt together whenever one of them changes
Many may share an address space and call each other, while others live in other processes and use sockets
They cannot communicate
optionExplain: That describes the service level.
That describes a lower level of separation.
Right: the key point is that they are partitioned into independently deployable units.
They do communicate.
questions.explain: Deployment-level decoupling is about what is deployed alone, not about how the calls travel.
questions.rule: Deployment level is about deployable units.
questions.teaches: At the deployment level many components may still live in the same address space and communicate through function calls, while others live in other processes on the same processor and communicate through interprocess communications, sockets or shared memory.

questions.q: Sort each requirement by the least decoupling mode that meets it.

items.t: A change in one module must not force recompiling the others
A team wants to ship a new jar without rebuilding the rest
Two parts must run on different servers
Each execution unit must stay independent of the source and binary changes of the others
Components may share an address space and call each other
Parts communicate solely through network packets

questions.explain: Source and deployment modes keep components on one machine if needed. Only the service level removes every dependency except data.
questions.rule: Name the mode before choosing a boundary: source level, deployment level or service level.

questions.q: A team decoupled at the source level and now wants to ship one module without rebuilding the others. Which mode must it add?
options: Service-level decoupling is the only choice, since shipping alone means a separate process
Deployment-level decoupling into independently deployable units
No change, source-level decoupling is enough
A new programming language
optionExplain: The deployable-unit mode is enough here.
Right: that mode controls dependencies between deployable units.
Source level does not allow shipping alone.
The language is not what is needed.
questions.explain: The need to ship alone points to the deployment level.
questions.rule: Match the mode to the need.

questions.q: A company runs its payments and its chat as separate network services. A bug fix recompiles the chat source and replaces the chat binary. What does the payments service have to do?
options: Be recompiled, since it talks to chat
Be restarted, since it shares the chat service's libraries and would otherwise keep using the old ones
Be moved into the chat process
Nothing: at the service level each unit is independent of source and binary changes to the others
optionExplain: Recompilation is what source-level and deployment-level coupling can force.
Services need not share libraries.
Moving it would remove the service boundary.
Right: only the data they exchange links them.
questions.explain: A service-level boundary leaves only data structures and network packets in common.
questions.rule: Services share data, not code.
questions.teaches: At the service level every execution unit is entirely independent of source and binary changes to the others, because the dependencies are reduced to the level of data structures.

questions.q: A new project is unsure whether it will ever need separate servers. What does the author recommend?
options: Keep components in one address space, decoupled so a service could be formed later
Make every component a service from day one, so the system is ready for any growth
Decide nothing and mix all the code
Wait for the first outage to decide
optionExplain: Right: the option stays open at low cost.
The author calls this expensive and coarse.
Without decoupling, the option is lost.
The advice is to prepare earlier.
questions.explain: Prepare for a service, but do not pay for one early. The card next gives the author's reasons.
questions.rule: According to the author, decouple as if services were possible, but keep components in one address space until a real need says otherwise.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, decoupling at the service level by default is cheap in development time and system resources.
questions.explain: He calls it expensive in both, and adds that it encourages coarse-grained decoupling.
questions.rule: Services by default are costly.

questions.q: Why does the author say that services by default encourage coarse-grained decoupling?
options: Services cannot be made small, because every service needs its own process and network stack
However micro the services get, the decoupling is not likely to be fine enough
Coarse parts are easier to name
Fine-grained parts cannot be tested
optionExplain: The text says even micro-services do not reach fine grain.
Right: a service boundary is too heavy to put around small parts.
Naming is not the argument.
Testing is not the issue.
questions.explain: The cost of a service boundary pushes teams toward a few large parts.
questions.rule: Service boundaries are heavy, so parts get big.
questions.teaches: No matter how micro the micro-services get, decoupling at the service level by default is not likely to be fine-grained enough, and dealing with service boundaries where none are needed wastes effort, memory and cycles.

questions.q: Put the author's preferred progression in order, from the starting point to the end.
items: Components separated at the source code level
Some decoupling driven to the deployment level when issues arise
Chosen deployable units turned into services as issues increase
The system gradually shifts toward services
questions.explain: The author starts with the cheapest mode and moves only as development, deployment and operational issues call for it.
questions.rule: According to the author, decouple as if services were possible, but keep components in one address space until a real need says otherwise.

questions.q: A bank knows from day one that its payment component must scale on separate servers and be owned by a separate regulated team. Does the author's preference still point to a single address space at first?
options: Not necessarily: the preference answers uncertainty, and a known need can justify a service early
Yes, since a service is not justified until the system has run in production for some time
Yes, since regulators prefer monoliths
No, since services are better for the systems of a regulated business, which need strong boundaries
optionExplain: Right: the advice rests on not knowing the best mode yet.
The author accepts separation all the way to services when it is needed.
Regulators are not part of the argument.
The author does not say so.
questions.explain: The advice fits the common case of unknown needs. Our reading: a need known in advance changes the starting point.
questions.rule: A known need beats a default.

questions.q: A colleague argues that services by default are fine because memory and processor time are cheap. How does the author reply?
options: He agrees: cheap hardware settles the cost question, so services by default are affordable for any team
He says services use no memory at all
He says hardware will soon be expensive again
Memory and cycles may be cheap, but the effort spent on unneeded service boundaries is not
optionExplain: He grants the hardware is cheap but not the effort.
The claim is that the cost lies elsewhere.
Nothing like this appears in the text.
Right: the author concedes the hardware point and holds that effort is the real cost.
questions.explain: The expensive part is the effort of working across boundaries that nothing requires.
questions.rule: Cheap hardware does not make effort cheap.
questions.teaches: The author grants that memory and cycles are cheap, but he says that the development time spent on dealing with service boundaries where none are needed is not cheap.

questions.q: True or false: Once a system has been split into services, it cannot sensibly return to a simpler form.
questions.explain: The author says a good architecture allows the move in both directions. The card next describes it.
questions.rule: Shape the code so that the decoupling mode can move up or down as needs change, without disturbing most of the source.

questions.q: A good architecture allows a system to be born as a ____, grow into services, and later slide back down.
questions.explain: The progression runs from one executable to independent services, and it can be reversed.
questions.rule: Start simple, and be free to return.

questions.q: What does the author say a good architecture protects when the mode changes?
options: The names of the services, which must stay stable for their clients
The deployment scripts only, since they are the part that moves between modes
The majority of the source code from the effects of the change
The database schema alone
optionExplain: Names are not the focus.
The code is what is protected.
Right: only a small part should be touched by a change of mode.
The text speaks of the source code.
questions.explain: Protecting the bulk of the code lets large deployments use one mode and small ones another.
questions.rule: Keep the change of mode at the edges.
questions.teaches: A good architecture protects the majority of the source code from the changes of mode, so that large deployments can use one mode whereas small deployments use another.

questions.q: Sort each change in operational needs by the direction in which the mode may move.

items.t: Load grows until one component needs its own servers
Traffic falls and the extra services cost more than they return
A second team takes over one component and ships on its own schedule
The product is cut down to a small internal tool
A component's deployments must stay isolated from the others
Two services always change together and share the same host

questions.explain: The author says the progression can run either way as needs rise or decline.
questions.rule: Shape the code so that the decoupling mode can move up or down as needs change, without disturbing most of the source.

questions.q: True or false: If a team treats the decoupling mode as fixed forever in its design, it will find a later change of mode cheap.
questions.explain: A design that assumes one mode must be reworked in many places when the mode changes. The aim is to keep the choice open.
questions.rule: Shape the code so that the decoupling mode can move up or down as needs change, without disturbing most of the source.

questions.q: A start-up built a set of micro-services for a launch whose traffic stayed far below the forecast. Running them costs more than the load needs. What does the author's reasoning say about folding them back?
options: It is impossible, since a split into services cannot be undone
It means rewriting each service from scratch as one program
It should be possible, if the architecture left the mode open
It is a configuration switch that needs no design work, so it can be done at any time
optionExplain: The author says a good architecture should allow the reversal.
The point of protecting the source code is to avoid such a rewrite.
Right: the mode can move down as well as up.
The author calls the change tricky and not a trivial option.
questions.explain: Operational needs may decline, and the mode can follow them.
questions.rule: Folding back is part of the plan.
questions.teaches: Over time the operational needs of the system may decline, and what once required decoupling at the service level may then require only deployment-level or even source-level decoupling.

questions.q: A team plans servers for the GUI, the middleware and the database, though the product will run on a single machine. What is the likely result?
options: Large extra effort for every feature, with no gain
A faster product from the start, since each tier can be tuned on its own
Lower development costs
A simpler deployment
optionExplain: Right: the structure's overhead is paid whether or not the farm exists.
Splitting across tiers adds overhead.
The reverse is likely.
More executables make deployment harder.
questions.explain: A heavy structure for an imagined need is costly. The card next gives two stories.
questions.rule: Do not build for a need that may never come; draw boundaries to defer such decisions, and adopt heavy structures only when the need is real.

questions.q: In company P, every system sold ran on a ____ server, though the architecture was built for a server farm.
questions.explain: The farm never existed, yet its overhead was paid in every feature.
questions.rule: Do not pay for a farm you do not have.

questions.q: What was wrong at company W, according to the author?
options: Services are a mistake for any small business, so adopting them at all was the whole error here
The programmers were too few to run so many services, so the work could not be finished
The domain model was too small to justify any services, so there was little for them to do
The premature adoption and enforcement of a suite of tools that promised SoA, not services themselves
optionExplain: The author rejects this reading.
Team size is not named as the cause.
The model was huge, not small.
Right: the author says nothing is intrinsically wrong with services.
questions.explain: The fault lay in adopting and enforcing the structure before the need was known.
questions.rule: Services are fine; early enforcement is the fault.
questions.teaches: There is nothing intrinsically wrong with a software system structured around services; the error at W was the premature adoption and enforcement of a suite of tools that promised SoA.

questions.q: Sort each item from the two stories by the company where it happened.

items.t: Every domain object had three instantiations
A ServiceRegistry was asked for the service ID of a ContactService
Four message protocols and eight protocol handlers for a new field
Programmers had to fake data for messages with dozens of fields
The three executables ran on one machine for years
To test, many services and a message bus had to be started one by one

questions.explain: P paid for a three-tier distribution it never needed. W paid for a full suite of domain services.
questions.rule: Do not build for a need that may never come; draw boundaries to defer such decisions, and adopt heavy structures only when the need is real.

questions.q: The programmers at P keep their design as it is. What does the story predict about the effort for each new feature?
options: It falls as the team learns the design and writes helpers for the common messages
It stays high, since the tiers, messages and handlers are paid for every time
It falls once a server farm is bought
It becomes zero
optionExplain: Learning does not remove the messages and handlers.
Right: the overhead is built into every change.
The farm never came.
Features still need the machinery.
questions.explain: A structure for an unneeded need taxes every feature.
questions.rule: The tax is on every feature.

questions.q: A small team building a to-do app is told to use an event bus, three services and a message broker because the architect expects growth. Which lesson from the two stories applies?
options: Always avoid message brokers
Adopt such structures when the need is real, and draw boundaries now so they can be added later
Follow the architect, since growth is likely and retrofitting the structure would cost much more
Write everything in one file
optionExplain: The author does not condemn the tools themselves.
Right: defer the decision without losing the option.
Likelihood is a guess, and the stories show the price.
Boundaries are still useful for deferring.
questions.explain: The lesson is about timing and enforcement, not about banning tools.
questions.rule: Draw the boundary now; adopt the tool when needed.
questions.teaches: Three-tier is not an architecture; it is a topology, and exactly the kind of decision that a good architecture strives to defer.

questions.q: A team wants to start building features before choosing a storage product. Which first step lets them do it?
options: Build a prototype database and keep it for production if the demo goes well
Write the features to call a specific vendor's library
Delay all feature work until storage is chosen
Define an interface for finding and saving data, and stub it at first
optionExplain: This makes the choice early by stealth.
This ties the features to the vendor.
This is the wait the interface avoids.
Right: features can then be built against the interface.
questions.explain: An interface lets work proceed without a choice. The card next tells how FitNesse did it.
questions.rule: Put an interface between the business rules and the data store, and start with the cheapest implementation that lets features move.

questions.q: Put the FitNesse data-access implementations in the order they were created.
items: MockWikiPage, with stubs
InMemoryPage, with a hash table in RAM
FileSystemWikiPage, with flat files
questions.explain: Each was built only when the previous one no longer let the team write the features it wanted.
questions.rule: Put an interface between the business rules and the data store, and start with the cheapest implementation that lets features move.

questions.q: What happened to the plan to use MySQL, according to the author?
options: The team judged flat files good enough and deferred the MySQL decision into nonexistence
The team moved to MySQL after a year
The team removed the interface once flat files worked, since only one implementation was left
The team replaced MySQL with a different product
optionExplain: Right: the decision was never needed.
The authors stayed with flat files.
The interface stayed, which is why a customer could add MySQL.
They decided against any database.
questions.explain: Deferring can end in never deciding at all.
questions.rule: A deferred decision may vanish.
questions.teaches: Three months after implementing flat files the team concluded they were good enough and abandoned the idea of MySQL altogether: the author says they deferred the decision into nonexistence.

questions.q: A reader summarizes the FitNesse story. Which statements are wrong? Select all that apply.
options: The team chose MySQL first, to avoid rework
An interface named WikiPage sat between the data access and the repository
The team built real persistence before writing features
An in-memory page carried the first full version of the program
optionExplain: The team purposely delayed any database decision.
This is how the story describes the design.
Features came first; stubs and an in-memory page stood in for persistence.
The hash table in RAM served for a year of features.
questions.explain: The summary should show an interface, cheap implementations and no early database.
questions.rule: Put an interface between the business rules and the data store, and start with the cheapest implementation that lets features move.

questions.q: True or false: A team following the FitNesse approach can start building the code that renders wiki text before any real storage exists.
questions.explain: The feature works against the WikiPage interface, and a mock or in-memory implementation supplies what it needs.
questions.rule: Put an interface between the business rules and the data store, and start with the cheapest implementation that lets features move.

questions.q: A team's tests are slow because every test starts a real database. In two sentences, how would the FitNesse approach change their tests, and what must be true of the code?
questions.a: The code would reach the data only through an interface, so tests can use a fast stub or in-memory implementation instead of the database. The business rules must not depend on the database's classes or schema.
questions.explain: The interface lets fast stand-ins replace slow resources.
questions.rule: Fast stand-ins need an interface.
questions.teaches: For the first three months the team worked only on translating wiki text into HTML, which needed no data storage, so the data access methods stayed stubbed.

questions.q: A customer wants an existing wiki to store its pages in MySQL, but the wiki was built with a data interface. How much work is the change likely to be?
options: Large: every feature must be rewritten for MySQL
Impossible without the original authors
Small: write another implementation of the interface
None: the wiki already supports every database
optionExplain: This is what happens without an interface.
Anyone who knows the interface can do it.
Right: the rest of the program does not change.
Nothing supports every database for free.
questions.explain: A boundary makes a new storage option cheap. The card next tells how it worked at FitNesse.
questions.rule: A boundary around the database lets you delay it, try cheaper options and still support the original choice later.

questions.q: The author's rule that users should download only one jar was called Download and ____.
questions.explain: The rule drove many early decisions, among them the web server and the database.
questions.rule: One jar to download.

questions.q: Why was it a good decision to write FitNesse's own web server, according to the author?
options: Existing web servers were not open source, so none could be bundled into one jar
Writing a server made the program faster than any other wiki, since nothing was wasted on frameworks
It removed the need for HTML
A bare-bones web server is very simple to write and let the team postpone any web framework decision
optionExplain: The author notes there were plenty of open source servers.
Speed is not the reason given.
The wiki still produced HTML.
Right: the web server was another detail deferred.
questions.explain: A simple home-made server kept the framework choice open for years.
questions.rule: A small custom part can defer a big choice.
questions.teaches: Writing their own bare-bones web server was a really good decision because it is a very simple piece of software to write and allowed the team to postpone any web framework decision until much later.

questions.q: Which problems did the FitNesse team avoid for the 18 months they had no database running? Select all that apply.
options: Problems translating wiki text into HTML
Schema issues and query issues
Password and connection-time issues
Problems deciding what the wiki's features should be
optionExplain: This work went on throughout, and needed no database.
With no database there was no schema or query language to deal with.
These come with firing up a database.
The features were still being designed.
questions.explain: The avoided problems were all those that come from running a database.
questions.rule: A boundary around the database lets you delay it, try cheaper options and still support the original choice later.

questions.q: True or false: Choosing flat files first made it harder for the customer who later wanted MySQL to add his own implementation.
questions.explain: The WikiPage interface was unaffected by flat files, and the customer added MySqlWikiPage in about a day.
questions.rule: A boundary around the database lets you delay it, try cheaper options and still support the original choice later.

questions.q: A mobile game starts with levels stored in a local file. Later, designers want to load levels from a server. The game logic reads levels through a LevelSource interface. What does the FitNesse story suggest about the cost?
options: A new LevelSource for the server should be small, and the game logic need not change
The game logic must be rewritten around network calls, since the levels now arrive over a network
The old local files must be thrown away at once
The change is easier if the interface is removed
optionExplain: Right: the same boundary logic applies.
The interface prevents this.
Both implementations can exist.
Removing it ties the logic to one source.
questions.explain: The line between logic and source keeps a later choice cheap.
questions.rule: The boundary makes the later option cheap.
questions.teaches: The MySQL derivative was bundled with FitNesse for a while, but since nobody else used it, it was eventually dropped, even by the customer who wrote it.

questions.q: A developer says, 'Our database is our business rules; the tables define everything we do.' How would the author react?
options: As correct, since the data defines the business and the tables record every rule it follows
As a sign the team uses too many tables
As misguided: the database is a tool the rules use, not the rules themselves
As correct only for small systems
optionExplain: The author separates the two.
Table count is not the issue.
Right: the author says the database does not matter to the business rules.
The text does not limit the claim to small systems.
questions.explain: The author challenges the link between database and rules. The card next gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: Draw a boundary between each part and the parts that do not matter to it, starting with the GUI, the database and the business rules.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: Match each pair with the author's judgement.
pairs: The GUI does not matter to the rules, so draw a line
The database does not matter to the GUI, so draw a line
The database does not matter to the rules, so draw a line
The idea that the database embodies the rules
questions.explain: The author draws a line between each pair, starting from what matters to what.
questions.rule: Draw a boundary between each part and the parts that do not matter to it, starting with the GUI, the database and the business rules.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: What do the business rules need to know about the database, according to the author?
options: The schema and the query language, so that the rules can ask the database exactly what they need
Only that a set of functions exists to fetch or save data
The brand of the server
The physical location of the files
optionExplain: These are details the rules should not know.
Right: they need no more than that.
This is a detail too.
Another detail the rules do not need.
questions.explain: The rules see the database as a set of functions behind an interface.
questions.rule: Rules know functions, not schemas.
questions.teaches: The business rules do not need to know about the schema, the query language or any other detail of the database; all they need is a set of functions that can fetch or save data, which lets the database sit behind an interface.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: For an online store, sort each pair by whether a boundary line is called for.

items.t: Checkout rules and the SQL tables
Checkout rules and the web page layout
The order total rule and the discount rule
The product list screen and the database driver
The refund rule and the rule for restocking after a refund
The tax rule and the choice of web framework

questions.explain: Lines go between parts that change for different reasons and matter differently. Rules that belong to the same job stay together.
questions.rule: Draw a boundary between each part and the parts that do not matter to it, starting with the GUI, the database and the business rules.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: Two proposals for where to place the tax calculation. A: inside a stored procedure in the database. B: in the business rules, calling a data interface for rates. Which fits the author's advice?
options: B, since the database does not matter to the business rules
A, since the database holds the data that tax needs and can compute it close to that data
Either, since both produce the same number
Neither, since tax is a detail
optionExplain: Right: rules stay with the rules, and the data is reached through functions.
Holding data does not make it the home of the rule.
The place matters for what depends on what.
Tax is a business rule.
questions.explain: A rule in the database ties the policy to a detail.
questions.rule: Keep rules out of the database.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: A fitness app's analytics need a data warehouse, and the data team insists the warehouse's table design is the business model. How does the author's argument apply?
options: The warehouse design should define all rules, since the data team knows what the business measures
The app should avoid warehouses
The model of what the business does belongs in the rules; the warehouse is a tool they use
The rules should be copied into the tables
optionExplain: This is the belief the author calls misguided.
The point is about dependency, not avoidance.
Right: the same reasoning holds for any store.
This binds the rules to the store.
questions.explain: The store may be vital to the product; the rules still do not depend on it.
questions.rule: A store can be vital without being the model.
questions.teaches: The author expects that some readers will reject the claim that the business rules do not care about the database, since many of us were taught that the database is inextricably connected to the business rules.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: A rules component calls a data component through an interface. In which component should the interface be defined if the rules are to stay independent of the data component?
options: In the data component
In the rules component
In a library from the database vendor, which both components import
In neither: the rules should call the data component directly
optionExplain: The rules would then depend on the data component.
Right: the rules then own what they need.
A third place is another way, but the book puts it with the rules.
This makes the rules depend on the detail.
questions.explain: Where the interface lives decides who depends on whom. The card next gives the book's answer.
questions.rule: Put the interface the rules need inside the rules' component, and let the database component depend on it.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: True or false: In the author's design, the DatabaseInterface classes live in the BusinessRules component.
questions.explain: The rules own the interface they need, and the database component implements it.
questions.rule: The rules own the interface.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: What does the direction of the arrow show about the relationship between the Database and the BusinessRules?
options: The BusinessRules cannot exist without the Database, since they need it to store their data
Neither can exist without the other
The two are independent of each other
The Database does not matter to the rules, but cannot exist without them
optionExplain: This reverses the arrow.
The relationship is one-way.
The Database depends on the rules.
Right: the Database knows the rules and the rules do not know it.
questions.explain: The arrow points from the less relevant component to the more relevant one.
questions.rule: Details depend on policy.
questions.teaches: The direction of the line shows that the Database does not matter to the BusinessRules, but the Database cannot exist without the BusinessRules.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: Put these statements about the design in order, from the rules' call down to the data.
items: The business rules call a method of the DatabaseInterface
The interface sits in the BusinessRules component
DatabaseAccess implements the interface
DatabaseAccess directs the actual Database
questions.explain: The call goes from the rules, through the interface they own, to an implementation on the far side of the line, and then to the database.
questions.rule: Put the interface the rules need inside the rules' component, and let the database component depend on it.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: True or false: If the interface were moved into the Database component, the business rules could still be built and tested without the Database component.
questions.explain: The rules would then name a type owned by the Database component, so they could not be built without it.
questions.rule: Put the interface the rules need inside the rules' component, and let the database component depend on it.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: A team's diagram shows its OrderRules importing a class named PostgresOrderStore from the Database component. They say the boundary is intact because the store implements an interface. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: an interface anywhere is enough
The rules should be moved into the Database component, so that both sit on the same side of the line
The rules still name a class of the Database component; they should use an interface they own
The store should be called by the user interface
optionExplain: The location of the dependency matters.
This reverses the intended direction.
Right: the arrow must point toward the rules.
The question is about the rules and the data.
questions.explain: The dependency arrows must point toward the business rules.
questions.rule: Name only what you own.
questions.teaches: The boundary is drawn across the inheritance relationship, so that the classes on the rules' side know nothing of the DatabaseAccess class.
questions.section: Which Lines Do You Draw, and When Do You Draw Them?

questions.q: A customer says, 'Show me the screens first, because the screens are the system.' How would the author respond?
options: The customer is right, since users only ever see screens and judge the product by them
The screens are only the IO; the system is the model of rules behind them
The screens should be built last, with no feedback
The screens are the rules and need no model
optionExplain: Seeing the screens is not the same as being the system.
Right: the author calls this confusion between GUI and system.
The point is about dependency, not about order of attention.
This is the confusion the author describes.
questions.explain: The author separates the interface from what it presents. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Treat the input and output as a replaceable layer around the business rules, and let the GUI depend on the rules, not the reverse.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the model behind a video game needs the interface in order to model the events of the game.
questions.explain: The model does not need the interface; it would execute its duties without the game ever being displayed.
questions.rule: The model does not need the screen.

questions.q: In the author's boundary between the GUI and the business rules, what do the arrows show?
options: Which component runs first at start-up, since the arrow points from the caller to the callee
Which component has more lines of code
Which component was built first
Which component knows the other and so cares about it: the GUI cares about the rules
optionExplain: The arrows show knowledge, not order.
Size is not shown.
History is not shown.
Right: the less relevant component depends on the more relevant one.
questions.explain: A dependency arrow means the source knows the target.
questions.rule: The one who knows, cares.
questions.teaches: The arrows show which component knows about the other and, therefore, which component cares about the other, so the GUI cares about the BusinessRules and not the reverse.

questions.q: A team builds a chess program. Which parts of the author's claim can they rely on? Select all that apply.
options: The rules need the board display to decide whether a move is legal
The rules of chess can be tested without any board display
The display is unimportant to players
A new graphical front end can replace the first one without changing the rules
optionExplain: The rules should not know the interface.
The model does not need the interface.
Irrelevant to the rules does not mean unimportant to users.
The GUI depends on the rules, so it can be replaced.
questions.explain: The model stands alone, and the interface plugs in to it.
questions.rule: Treat the input and output as a replaceable layer around the business rules, and let the GUI depend on the rules, not the reverse.

questions.q: True or false: A team replaces its console front end with a web front end. If the console depended on the rules and the rules did not know the console, the rules will have to change.
questions.explain: The rules never knew the console, so removing it leaves them untouched; the new front end depends on the rules in the same way.
questions.rule: Treat the input and output as a replaceable layer around the business rules, and let the GUI depend on the rules, not the reverse.

questions.q: A voice assistant receives commands as sound and answers with sound. A designer says the business rules for booking a table must listen for audio. What does the author's principle say?
options: The booking rules should not depend on the audio; the voice layer is another replaceable IO
Rules for voice systems must handle sound directly, since the commands arrive as audio and must be understood
Voice systems have no business rules
The rules should be rewritten for each device
optionExplain: Right: sound is IO like a screen.
The model does not need the interface, whatever its form.
They do have rules.
This is what the boundary avoids.
questions.explain: Any IO, however different, plugs in to the same rules.
questions.rule: Voice is IO too.
questions.teaches: Developers and customers often define a system in terms of the GUI, so they believe they should see the GUI start working immediately, and they fail to realize that the IO is irrelevant.

questions.q: A spreadsheet program lets third parties add chart types without changing the program. Which description fits this structure?
options: The core imports each chart type by name, so that it can call it when needed
The core stays independent of the chart types, which attach to it
Each chart type contains a copy of the core
The chart types never communicate with the core
optionExplain: Then the core depends on the chart types.
Right: that is a plugin arrangement.
This duplicates the core.
They must communicate with it somehow.
questions.explain: Plugins attach to a core that does not depend on them. The card next shows the book's use of the pattern.
questions.rule: Keep the core business rules independent, and attach every optional or varied component to them as a plugin.

questions.q: In a plugin architecture, the core ____ rules are kept separate from and independent of the optional components.
questions.explain: The optional or varied components, such as the UI and the database, plug in to the core.
questions.rule: Core in the middle; plugins around it.

questions.q: What does the author say about replacing a web-based UI with a client-server UI in a plugin structure?
options: It may be challenging and need some rework, but the plugin presumption makes it practical
It is trivial, since plugins are interchangeable by design and the rules would not even notice the swap
It is impossible without a rewrite of the rules
It is unnecessary, since web UIs always suffice
optionExplain: Right: replacement is made practical, not free.
The author says replacements might not be trivial.
The plugin structure at least makes it practical.
Nothing in the text supports this.
questions.explain: Rules shaped for a web UI may need rework of some communication for another kind of UI.
questions.rule: Plugins make change practical, not free.
questions.teaches: Replacing a web-based UI with a client-server UI plugin could be challenging because some of the communication between the business rules and the new UI would have to be reworked.

questions.q: For a payroll system, sort each component by whether it belongs to the core or is a plugin.

items.t: The rules for computing gross and net pay
The web user interface for HR staff
The command-line report printer
The rules for holiday accrual
The storage in a relational database
The export to a bank's file format

questions.explain: The rules that define the business stay in the core. Interfaces, storage and exports are optional or varied, so they plug in.
questions.rule: Keep the core business rules independent, and attach every optional or varied component to them as a plugin.

questions.q: True or false: A team treats its database as a plugin. Management asks to try a NoSQL store. This change can be made without touching the core business rules, at least for the main data access.
