questions.explain: The database was treated as a plugin, so another storage technology can be attached without the core knowing.
questions.rule: Keep the core business rules independent, and attach every optional or varied component to them as a plugin.

questions.q: A game company wants one set of game rules and many front ends: phone, console and a web demo. Which structure follows the author's pattern?
options: A separate set of rules inside each front end
A core that includes the phone code, with the console and web front ends added to it later
A web demo with the other two front ends added to it
One core of rules with each front end as a plugin that depends on it
optionExplain: This duplicates the rules.
The core then depends on one front end.
This makes the web demo the center.
Right: the core stays the same while the front ends vary.
questions.explain: A core with many plugins is the structure the author describes.
questions.rule: One core, many front ends.
questions.teaches: The author says the history of software development technology is the story of how to conveniently create plugins to establish a scalable and maintainable system architecture.

questions.q: Module A imports module B. If B changes its interface, which module may break?
options: B, because it is the one that changed
Both, since changes always spread both ways
A, because it depends on B
Neither, because interfaces protect both
optionExplain: B changed its own code, so nothing in B breaks.
Changes follow the direction of dependency.
Right: a change travels from the depended-on module to its dependents.
Interfaces do not remove the dependency.
questions.explain: Changes flow along dependencies. The card next gives the author's example.
questions.rule: Make the modules you want to protect not depend on the modules that change, so changes cannot propagate to them.

questions.q: In the author's example, the source code of ReSharper depends on the source code of Visual ____.
questions.explain: So the ReSharper team cannot disturb the Visual Studio team.
questions.rule: The dependent is exposed.

questions.q: What does the author say a plugin architecture creates?
options: Shared ownership of all modules, so that no team can break another team's work
A single point of failure at the core, which every plugin team has to protect
Firewalls across which changes cannot propagate
Faster compilation
optionExplain: Ownership is not the claim.
The author argues for protection, not for a single failure point.
Right: changes in the GUI cannot affect the business rules it plugs in to.
Speed is not the claim.
questions.explain: A firewall stops changes in one part from breaking another.
questions.rule: Dependency direction makes a firewall.
questions.teaches: Arranging the system into a plugin architecture creates firewalls across which changes cannot propagate: if the GUI plugs in to the business rules, then changes in the GUI cannot affect those business rules.

questions.q: For a hospital system, sort each change by whether the plugin arrangement shields the business rules from it.
groups: Not shielded: can reach the rules

items.t: The layout of a web page is redesigned
The schema of the patient table is altered
A rule about drug-dose limits is changed
A new report printer is added
The definition of what counts as an emergency is changed
The UI framework is upgraded

questions.explain: Changes to plugins stay in the plugins. Changes to the rules themselves, by definition, are not shielded.
questions.rule: Make the modules you want to protect not depend on the modules that change, so changes cannot propagate to them.

questions.q: The core team of a plugin-based product changes the format of the data it hands to plugins, without notice. What does the asymmetry predict?
options: The plugins may break, though the core is untouched by the plugin teams
The core breaks, since it depends on the plugins
Nothing breaks, because plugins are isolated
The plugin teams can refuse the change, since the plugins sit behind a firewall
optionExplain: Right: the plugins depend on the core and are exposed to its changes.
The core does not depend on the plugins.
Isolation protects the core, not the plugins.
The effect on plugins is a cost, not a design goal.
questions.explain: The relationship protects only one side.
questions.rule: Plugins carry the exposure.

questions.q: A browser vendor and an extension author work in different companies. The vendor releases a new version that changes an extension interface. Using the ReSharper example, who bears the risk?
options: The browser vendor, since it changed the interface that the extension relied on
Both equally
Neither, since the interface was published and both sides agreed to follow it
The extension author, since the extension depends on the browser
optionExplain: The vendor does not depend on the extension.
The relationship is asymmetric.
Publication does not remove the dependency.
Right: the dependent side is exposed.
questions.explain: The example repeats at any scale: the plugin is exposed to the host.
questions.rule: Dependents bear the risk of change.
questions.teaches: The ReSharper team can do nothing to disturb the Visual Studio team, but the Visual Studio team could completely disable the ReSharper team if they so desired.

questions.q: A system has a web page layer and a tax rule layer. A manager asks why there should be a boundary between them. What is the best reason?
options: They are written in different languages, which makes them hard to compile together
They change at different times and for different reasons
They have different numbers of files
They were written by different people
optionExplain: Language is not the reason the author gives.
Right: this is the sign of an axis of change.
Size does not decide a boundary.
People are not the reason.
questions.explain: Different reasons to change call for a line. The card next names the idea.
questions.rule: Draw a boundary wherever the parts on its two sides change at different times and for different reasons.

questions.q: Boundaries are drawn where there is an axis of ____.
questions.explain: On the two sides of an axis of change, the components change at different rates and for different reasons.
questions.rule: Draw lines where change differs.

questions.q: Which principle does the author say tells us where to draw our boundaries?
options: The Interface Segregation Principle, which governs how interfaces are sized
The Single Responsibility Principle
The Liskov Substitution Principle
The Open-Closed Principle
optionExplain: The author names the SRP here.
Right: reasons to change decide the lines.
It is not the one named.
It is not the one named in this passage.
questions.explain: The SRP groups what changes for the same reason and separates the rest, which is what a boundary does.
questions.rule: The SRP says where the lines go.
questions.teaches: The Single Responsibility Principle tells us where to draw our boundaries.

questions.q: Match each pair of parts with the reason a boundary between them is justified.
pairs: They change at different times and rates
Business rules and a dependency injection framework
They change at different times and for different reasons
Neither should know the other's details, and each changes for its own reasons
Two rules in the same pricing policy
questions.explain: A line is justified by different reasons to change. Parts that change together stay together.
questions.rule: Draw a boundary wherever the parts on its two sides change at different times and for different reasons.

questions.q: A team draws a boundary between two modules only because one module is big and the other is small. By the author's reasoning, what is missing?
options: A third module in the middle to take the shared code
A larger difference in size between the two modules
An interface in each module
A difference in how and why the two sides change
optionExplain: More modules do not supply the missing reason.
Size is not the criterion.
Interfaces follow the boundary, not justify it.
Right: size does not mark an axis of change.
questions.explain: A boundary needs a reason from change, not from size.
questions.rule: Size is not an axis of change.

questions.q: A company has one team that changes the invoice layout every month and a second that changes tax rules once a year after a new law. Their code is in one module. What does the author's reasoning suggest?
options: Separate them, since they change at different rates and for different reasons
Leave them together, since both concern invoices and one team can then own the whole subject
Merge the two teams into one
Put the tax rules in the layout code
optionExplain: Right: the monthly and yearly changes mark an axis of change.
The subject is shared, but the reasons to change are not.
The code reasoning does not depend on the teams.
This would couple the slow-changing rules to the fast-changing layout.
questions.explain: Rates and reasons of change decide the line, not the subject matter.
questions.rule: Separate by rate and reason of change.
questions.teaches: To draw boundary lines you first partition the system into components, some of them core business rules and others plugins, and then arrange the code so the arrows between them point toward the core business.

questions.q: A high-level client must call a lower-level service. Which design keeps the client independent of the service's source code?
options: The client imports the service class and calls it, since it needs to know what it calls
The service imports the client class and calls back, so control flows from low to high
The client calls an interface that the service implements, owned by the client's side
Both share one big class
optionExplain: Then the client depends on the service.
Then the control flow is not inverted.
Right: the service then depends on the client's side.
This couples them tightly.
questions.explain: An interface owned by the higher level inverts the dependency. The card next shows the book's version.
questions.rule: Where control flows to a lower-level service, put an interface on the higher level's side so the source dependency points up.

questions.q: True or false: At runtime, a boundary crossing is nothing more than a function on one side calling a function on the other and passing along some data.
questions.explain: That is how the author puts it. The architectural work lies in managing the source code dependencies.
questions.rule: Runtime is simple; source dependencies are the work.

questions.q: Why does the author say a changed source module matters for boundaries?
options: Only because it is slower to compile, since a large module takes longer to build
Because changed modules must be renamed so that the other modules can find them again
Because teams must meet before every edit
Other modules may need changes, recompilation and redeployment, and boundaries build firewalls against this
optionExplain: Compile time is part of it, but not the main point.
Naming is not the issue.
Meetings are not the issue.
Right: boundaries are about containing the spread of change.
questions.explain: A firewall against change is what the boundary is for.
questions.rule: Boundaries contain change.
questions.teaches: When one source code module changes, other source code modules may have to be changed or recompiled and then redeployed, and managing and building firewalls against this change is what boundaries are all about.

questions.q: Put these in the order they happen when the high-level Client uses a lower-level ServiceImpl through the interface.
items: The Client creates a Data instance
The Client calls f() on the Service interface
The call is dispatched at run time to ServiceImpl
ServiceImpl uses the Data defined on the calling side
questions.explain: Control flows from the client down to the implementation, while the source dependencies point the other way.
questions.rule: Where control flows to a lower-level service, put an interface on the higher level's side so the source dependency points up.

questions.q: In a language without objects or any other form of polymorphism, what does the author say architects fall back on?
options: Pointers to functions, which most architects find too risky for prolific use
Global variables, which are safer
Static linking, which removes all risk because everything is bound before the program runs
Generics, which fully protect against recompilation
optionExplain: Right: the fallback is risky, so many give up component partitioning.
The text names pointers to functions.
Static linking does not give the decoupling.
The author says generics cannot give that protection.
questions.explain: Dynamic polymorphism makes the inversion safe and easy; without it the options are poor.
questions.rule: Polymorphism makes inversion practical.

questions.q: A C++ team uses templates to avoid depending on a concrete logger class. A colleague says this gives the same decoupling as an interface. Using the author's footnote, what is the catch?
options: Templates cannot be used with loggers
Templates make the code run in separate processes
Templates resolve at compile time, so a change still forces recompilation and redeployment
Templates are the same as pointers to functions, which are equally safe and equally flexible in practice
optionExplain: They can be used; the issue is their reach.
They do not.
Right: static polymorphism does not protect against that need.
They are a different mechanism.
questions.explain: Static polymorphism helps manage dependencies in a monolith but not the rebuild needs.
questions.rule: Compile-time decoupling still recompiles.
questions.teaches: Static polymorphism such as generics or templates can sometimes be a viable means of dependency management in monolithic systems, but the decoupling it affords cannot protect you from the need for recompilation and redeployment the way dynamic polymorphism can.

questions.q: A Java application ships its payment code as a separate jar that can be replaced without recompiling the rest. How would the author classify the boundary?
options: A source-level boundary, since it is written in Java
A deployment-level boundary, since the unit is deployed on its own
A service boundary, since it is separate
A thread boundary, since it runs code
optionExplain: Source level means one executable.
Right: the jar is a deployable unit.
Services talk over a network.
Threads are not boundaries.
questions.explain: Independently deployable binaries are the deployment mode. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Use dynamically linked, independently deployable units for a boundary; do not treat threads as boundaries.

questions.q: Match each item with its role.
pairs: The simplest physical form of a boundary
A WAR file or a directory
A convenient gathering of deployable units
A way to organize the schedule and order of execution
Function calls, inexpensive and possibly chatty
questions.explain: Deployment-level components are close to monoliths, apart from being delivered in binary form.
questions.rule: Use dynamically linked, independently deployable units for a boundary; do not treat threads as boundaries.

questions.q: What does the author say about static polymorphism for deployment-level components?
options: It is not an option, since the components arrive in binary form without compilation
It is the best way to manage their dependencies, because it is checked at compile time
It is required to load the library
It is possible only for threads
optionExplain: Right: the strategy must rely on dynamic polymorphism.
The author says it is not an option.
Loading does not depend on it.
Threads are not part of this point.
questions.explain: Compile-time mechanisms cannot cross a boundary where there is no compilation.
questions.rule: No compile step, no static polymorphism.
questions.teaches: Static polymorphism is not an option for deployment-level components, because deployment does not involve compilation and the components arrive in binary form.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is an architectural boundary or a way of organizing execution.

items.t: A shared library deployed on its own
A pool of worker threads
A jar file for the reporting component
A thread that spans three components
A DLL loaded at run time
A scheduler that decides the order of tasks

questions.explain: Libraries and jars are units of deployment. Threads and schedulers only decide how execution is organized.
questions.rule: Use dynamically linked, independently deployable units for a boundary; do not treat threads as boundaries.

questions.q: True or false: Replacing one deployment-level component with a new binary requires the other components in the same system to be recompiled.
questions.explain: Deployment-level decoupling means a change to the source of one module does not force others to be rebuilt and redeployed.
questions.rule: Use dynamically linked, independently deployable units for a boundary; do not treat threads as boundaries.

questions.q: A music player lets users add sound effects as plug-in libraries. A reviewer says that because the effects run in separate threads, they are decoupled from the player. What is wrong with the claim?
options: Threads are boundaries only in music players
Nothing is wrong: threads are units of deployment, so each effect is isolated from the player and can be replaced
Threads organize execution and are not boundaries; the separation comes from the deployed libraries
Libraries cannot hold threads
optionExplain: The author gives no such exception.
The author says they are not.
Right: threads may span components and prove nothing about separation.
They can; the point is that threads do not make boundaries.
questions.explain: Where the code runs and where it is separated are different questions.
questions.rule: Threads are not boundaries.
questions.teaches: Both monoliths and deployment components can make use of threads, and threads may be wholly contained within a component or spread across many components.

questions.q: Two programs on the same computer run in separate address spaces and exchange messages through the operating system. What is the best name for this boundary?
options: A thread boundary
A local process boundary
A source-level boundary
A service boundary
optionExplain: Threads share an address space.
Right: separate address spaces on the same processor.
Source level shares one executable.
Services are assumed to be reachable over a network.
questions.explain: Separate address spaces on one machine form a local process boundary. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Use a local process for a stronger boundary, keep dependencies pointing to the higher level, and limit chatter across it.

questions.q: Local processes run in the same processor but in separate ____ spaces.
questions.explain: Memory protection generally prevents such processes from sharing memory.
questions.rule: Separate memory, same machine.

questions.q: What must the source code of a higher-level process not contain, according to the author?
options: Any reference to sockets, since sockets tie the higher level to one means of communication
Comments about the operating system, since such comments tie the code to a platform
Calls to library functions
The names, physical addresses or registry lookup keys of lower-level processes
optionExplain: Sockets may be used for communication.
Comments are not the issue.
Library calls are not the issue.
Right: a name or address in the higher-level source ties it to the lower-level process.
questions.explain: A name or an address is a dependency on a specific lower-level process.
questions.rule: No names of lower-level processes in higher-level source.
questions.teaches: The source code of the higher-level processes must not contain the names, physical addresses or registry lookup keys of lower-level processes, since lower-level processes are meant to be plugins to higher-level ones.

questions.q: Sort each communication cost by whether it applies to function calls inside a monolith or to calls across local process boundaries.

items.t: A plain function call
Operating system calls and interprocess context switches
Data marshaling and decoding
A call that can be repeated thousands of times cheaply
A message sent through a socket or message queue
Passing a reference to the data structure

questions.explain: Function calls are cheap and can be chatty. Crossing a process boundary has costs that should limit the number of messages.
questions.rule: Use a local process for a stronger boundary, keep dependencies pointing to the higher level, and limit chatter across it.

questions.q: A team splits a program into two local processes and keeps the same fine-grained calls between them, thousands per second. What does the author's reasoning predict?
options: The calls will be as cheap as before, since both processes run on the same machine
The calls will become free
Each crossing is moderately expensive, so the chatter will hurt
The processes will share memory automatically
optionExplain: Process crossings add cost.
Nothing makes them free.
Right: the author advises limiting chattiness.
Memory protection prevents sharing in general.
questions.explain: A strong boundary has a price in time per call.
questions.rule: Strong boundaries cost per call.

questions.q: A desktop editor runs its spell-checker as a separate process, started by the editor. Which rule from the author applies to the editor's source?
options: It should hard-code the spell-checker's file path, which is faster than looking it up at run time
It should not contain the spell-checker's name, address or registry key; the spell-checker should plug in
It should depend on the spell-checker's source code, so that changes to the checker are noticed at once
It should share memory with the spell-checker by default
optionExplain: Hard-coding is what the author prohibits.
Right: the lower-level process plugs in to the higher-level one.
Dependencies must point toward the higher level.
Memory is generally not shared.
questions.explain: The same plugin rule applies at the process level.
questions.rule: Lower-level processes plug in to higher-level ones.
questions.teaches: Think of a local process as a kind of uber-component: the process consists of lower-level components that manage their dependencies through dynamic polymorphism.

questions.q: A call between two components takes about as long as one function call inside a program. Which boundary is least likely to separate them?
options: A source-level boundary inside one executable
A jar file loaded into the same process
A thread boundary
A service reached over a network
optionExplain: Function calls inside a monolith are cheap.
Calls across it are function calls.
Threads are not boundaries, and calls between them can be fast.
Right: network calls take far longer than function calls.
questions.explain: The stronger the boundary, the slower the call. The card next gives the author's range.
questions.rule: Treat a service as the strongest and slowest boundary: keep the same dependency rule, hold no physical addresses in higher-level source, and avoid chatter.

questions.q: A service does not depend on its physical ____, and it assumes all communication takes place over the network.
questions.explain: Two communicating services may or may not run on the same processor.
questions.rule: Services assume the network.

questions.q: Why are the boundaries of most non-monolithic systems a mixture, according to the author?
options: A system with services may also have local process boundaries, since a service is often a facade for local processes
Because standards require a mix
Because services cannot talk to local processes, so each kind must be kept in a separate part of the system
Because a mix is faster in every case
optionExplain: Right: a service often contains local processes, which in turn contain monoliths or deployable units.
No such standard is mentioned.
Nothing in the text says this.
Speed is not the argument.
questions.explain: The mixture means some boundaries are chatty and local, and others are concerned with latency.
questions.rule: Boundaries come in nests.
questions.teaches: Most systems, other than monoliths, use more than one boundary strategy, so the boundaries in a system are often a mixture of local chatty boundaries and boundaries that are more concerned with latency.

questions.q: Put the boundary types in order from the cheapest crossing to the most expensive.
items: A function call across a source-level boundary
A function call across a deployment-level boundary
A message across a local process boundary
A request across a service boundary
questions.explain: Function calls in a monolith or between deployable units are cheap. Process crossings are moderately expensive. Service calls are very slow in comparison.
questions.rule: Treat a service as the strongest and slowest boundary: keep the same dependency rule, hold no physical addresses in higher-level source, and avoid chatter.

questions.q: True or false: A system moves a component from a local process to a service on another machine and keeps the same chatty calls between them. The system will probably become slower.
questions.explain: Network communication is very slow compared to function calls and local process calls, so chatting should be avoided across service boundaries.
questions.rule: Treat a service as the strongest and slowest boundary: keep the same dependency rule, hold no physical addresses in higher-level source, and avoid chatter.

questions.q: A checkout service calls a tax service at an address typed into the checkout source code. The address changes when the tax service moves to another data center. Which rule from the author is broken?
options: Services must run in the same processor, so that the address stays valid when it is typed in
The higher-level source must not hold physical knowledge, such as a URI, of a lower-level service
Services must not communicate over a network
The lower-level service must call the higher one by name, so that it can be found in the registry
optionExplain: The text says they may or may not.
Right: the address ties the higher level to the lower one.
They must, by assumption.
The dependency rule points the other way.
questions.explain: A hard-coded address is a source dependency on the lower-level service.
questions.rule: No physical addresses in higher-level source.
questions.teaches: Turnaround times for communication across service boundaries range from tens of milliseconds to seconds, so the communication must deal with high levels of latency and chatting should be avoided where possible.

questions.q: A program reads a file, applies a long set of pricing rules, and writes a report. Which policy is likely to be the highest level?
options: The pricing rules, which are farthest from the file and report
The file reading, since everything starts there
The report writing, since the user sees it
All three share one level
optionExplain: Right: farthest from input and output means highest level.
The input is the lowest level, not the highest.
The output is the lowest level.
They differ in distance from the IO.
questions.explain: Level is measured from the IO. The card next gives the definition.
questions.rule: Group policies by how they change, measure level by distance from the inputs and outputs, and make low-level components depend on high-level ones.

questions.q: A strict definition of level is the distance from the inputs and ____.
questions.explain: The farther a policy is from both the inputs and the outputs of the system, the higher its level.
questions.rule: Level is distance from IO.

questions.q: What are the edges of the directed acyclic graph the author describes?
options: The flow of data between components, since the arrows in the diagram follow the data
The order in which components start
The people who talk to each other
Compile-time source dependencies such as import, using or require statements
optionExplain: Data flow is shown separately, and may point another way.
Start order is not the dependency.
People are not the edges.
Right: they are the dependencies the compiler needs.
questions.explain: The edges connect components at different levels and are what the compiler needs to function.
questions.rule: Edges are source dependencies.
questions.teaches: The directed edges of the graph are the dependencies between components of different levels, and they are source-code, compile-time dependencies: import statements in Java, using statements in C#, require statements in Ruby.

questions.q: For a system that reads sensor data, applies safety rules and sends alarms, sort each policy by its level.

items.t: The rule that decides when a reading is dangerous
Parsing bytes from the sensor cable
The rule that decides which readings to compare
Formatting the alarm message for a pager
Reading the keyboard for configuration
The safety threshold policy

questions.explain: Policies far from input and output are higher level. Those that handle the IO are the lowest level.
questions.rule: Group policies by how they change, measure level by distance from the inputs and outputs, and make low-level components depend on high-level ones.

questions.q: True or false: In a good architecture, a low-level component such as an input reader should depend on the high-level policy it feeds.
questions.explain: The author says that in every case low-level components are designed so that they depend on high-level components.
questions.rule: Group policies by how they change, measure level by distance from the inputs and outputs, and make low-level components depend on high-level ones.

questions.q: A reviewer notes that a validation rule and a report format sit in one component because both are 'business logic.' Applying the author's grouping, what is the likely mistake?
options: Validation and reports should be in one component, since both are business logic of the same system
Business logic should not be in components
The two change for different reasons and at different times, so they sit at different levels
The report format should be a database table
optionExplain: Grouping follows change, not the label.
Components are the unit of grouping.
Right: grouping should follow how policies change.
This mixes up detail and policy.
questions.explain: A shared label does not make a shared reason to change.
questions.rule: Group by how policies change.
questions.teaches: Some policies describe how business rules are calculated, others how reports are formatted, and still others how input data are validated, and these are separated and regrouped according to the ways they change.

questions.q: A small program reads text, encrypts it and writes it out. A developer writes one function that calls readChar, then translate, then writeChar. What is the likely weakness?
options: The function will run too slowly
The function reads characters in the wrong order
The encryption logic is tied to the input and output routines
The function cannot be compiled
optionExplain: Speed is not the concern.
The order of calls is fine.
Right: the high-level function depends on the low-level ones.
It compiles; the weakness is dependency.
questions.explain: Calling the IO directly ties the logic to it. The card next shows the author's alternative.
questions.rule: Let source dependencies follow the level of the policy, not the direction of the data flow.

questions.q: In the encryption program, the ____ component is the highest level because it is the farthest from the inputs and outputs.
questions.explain: The author calls it the highest-level component.
questions.rule: Farthest from the IO is highest.

questions.q: How do higher-level policies compare with lower-level ones in how they change, according to the author?
options: Higher-level policies change less often and for more important reasons; lower-level ones change often, with urgency, for lesser reasons
Higher-level policies change more often, since they matter more and are touched by every new feature request
All policies change at the same rate
Lower-level policies change for more important reasons
optionExplain: Right: the IO devices are likelier to change than the algorithm.
The author says the reverse.
The point is that they differ.
The author says less important reasons.
questions.explain: Trivial but urgent changes at the lowest levels should have little effect on the higher, more important levels.
questions.rule: High level: stable and important. Low level: frequent and urgent.
questions.teaches: Higher-level policies tend to change less frequently and for more important reasons than lower-level policies, which change frequently and with more urgency but for less important reasons.

questions.q: Match each element of the better encryption design with its place.
pairs: Low level: implements the CharReader interface
Inside the highest-level unit, with every dependency crossing the border pointing inward
The highest-level policy: calls only the two interfaces
Low level: implements the CharWriter interface
questions.explain: The console classes sit outside and depend on the interfaces; the interfaces and Encrypt form the inner unit that depends on nothing outside it.
questions.rule: Let source dependencies follow the level of the policy, not the direction of the data flow.

questions.q: True or false: If the console input is replaced by a network input in the better design, the Encrypt policy has to change.
questions.explain: The network reader would implement CharReader, and Encrypt would not know the difference.
questions.rule: Let source dependencies follow the level of the policy, not the direction of the data flow.

questions.q: A photo app resizes pictures. Its resize routine calls the camera driver and the file saver by name. A teammate wants to reuse the resize routine in a web service. Using the encryption example, what is the better design?
options: Copy the routine into the web service and edit the calls, so that each context has its own version to change freely
Make the web service imitate the camera driver
Move the camera code into the resize routine
Let the resize policy depend on reader and writer interfaces that the camera and file code implement
optionExplain: This duplicates the policy.
This ties the new context to the old device.
This couples the policy even more.
Right: the policy becomes usable in other contexts.
questions.explain: Making the high-level policy independent of the IO makes it reusable.
questions.rule: Policy independent of IO is reusable.
questions.teaches: The component diagram shows the same arrangement at a larger scale: lower-level components should be plugins to the higher-level components, so Encryption knows nothing of IODevices and IODevices depends on Encryption.

questions.q: True or false: A bank's rule for charging interest on a loan would stop being a business rule if a clerk worked it out by hand.
questions.explain: The rule makes the bank money whether a program or a clerk applies it. The card next names this kind of rule and where it lives.
questions.rule: Put each rule that would make or save money even without a computer, together with its data, in a separate Entity that knows nothing of databases, screens or frameworks.

questions.q: Critical Business Rules and the Critical Business Data they work on are bound together in an object called an ____.
questions.explain: The author calls the object that holds a small set of critical rules and their data an Entity.
questions.rule: Put each rule that would make or save money even without a computer, together with its data, in a separate Entity that knows nothing of databases, screens or frameworks.

questions.q: A Loan class gets its interest rate by running a SQL query through a connection string it holds. What fault does the author's view point to?
options: Nothing is wrong, since an Entity must fetch its data by whatever means it needs, including queries to a database
It is wrong only in languages that are not object-oriented, where classes are optional
It mixes a storage concern into a class meant to stand apart from databases, interfaces and frameworks
It is wrong because an Entity must hold no data at all, only functions of other classes
optionExplain: The Entity holds its data or has easy access to it, but easy access does not mean it carries storage code.
The author says an Entity needs no object-oriented language, and the fault does not depend on the language.
Right: the Entity should stay unsullied by concerns about databases.
An Entity binds data and rules together, so it does hold data.
questions.explain: An Entity may have easy access to its data, but it must not carry database code, because that would tie the business rule to one storage technology.
questions.rule: Keep storage code out of the Entity.

questions.q: Which rules would the author call Critical Business Rules? Select all that apply.
options: A shop charges a late fee of 2 percent a month on unpaid invoices
A clerk may not refund more than the customer paid
The checkout page cannot continue until the address form is verified on screen
An invoice total is shown on the web page with two decimal places
A warehouse bills one pound a day for goods left unclaimed
optionExplain: Right: a clerk with a ledger could apply it, so it would exist without any computer.
Right: it would hold in a manual shop too.
This rule exists only because of the automated screen flow, so it is not an Entity rule.
This concerns how data is shown, which is neither a business rule nor critical data.
Right: a manual warehouse could charge it, so it is a critical rule.
questions.explain: A critical rule would make or save money even if executed manually. A rule about screens or formatting exists only because the system is automated.
questions.rule: Ask whether the rule would exist with no computer at all.

questions.q: A bank replaces its web app with a mobile app on the same loan terms. What happens to the Loan Entity, in the author's design?
options: It stays as it is, because it does not depend on how the system is presented or how data is stored
It needs new classes for the mobile screens, because Entities hold the screen data they work with
It needs a copy for each platform, because the interest rules differ between web and mobile
It needs a different storage method, because the Entity chooses where its own data is kept
optionExplain: Right: the Entity is pure business and could serve the business in any system.
Screens are not part of an Entity; they are concerns the Entity is kept free of.
The loan terms are the same, so the critical rules are the same on every platform.
How data is stored is a concern the Entity is separated from.
questions.explain: Because the Entity carries no concern for presentation or storage, a new delivery leaves it untouched.
questions.rule: Entities survive a change of presentation.

questions.q: A team writes in a language with no classes and asks whether it can have Entities. Which answer fits the author?
options: Only after adding a framework that imitates classes, since an Entity has to be a class in a language that has them
Yes, but only when the functions are exposed to the outside as database procedures
No: an Entity is an object, and without classes the rules must go into the use cases
Yes: data structures plus functions that bind the critical data and rules in a separate module will do
optionExplain: The author says you do not need an object-oriented language; adding a class framework is not required.
Where the data is stored does not make a module an Entity.
The author says all that is required is a single, separate module binding data and rules.
Right: the book says an Entity can be an object with methods or a set of data structures and functions.
questions.explain: What matters is the binding of critical data and rules in one separate module, not the language feature used.
questions.rule: An Entity is a module, not necessarily a class.
questions.teaches: No object-oriented language is needed for an Entity: it can be a set of data structures and functions, so long as many applications in the enterprise can use it.

questions.q: A shop's app must not offer express checkout until the delivery address is validated. Which description fits this rule best?
options: A rule that makes the shop money whether or not any computer applies it, such as a fee for late payment
A rule about how the automated system is used, which would make no sense in a manual shop
A rule about the colours and layout of the checkout page that customers see
A rule about how finished orders are stored in the database after payment
optionExplain: A manual shop has no express checkout, so the rule needs the system.
A fair guess: the rule only exists because the system is automated.
The rule is about when a step is allowed, not about appearance.
It concerns the order of steps, not storage.
questions.explain: The rule shapes how the automated system operates. The card next names where such rules live.
questions.rule: Put rules that exist only because the system is automated into use cases that describe input, output and processing steps, and leave the user interface out of them.

questions.q: A use case specifies the input from the user, the output returned to the user, and the ____ steps that produce the output.
questions.explain: The author describes a use case by its input, its output and the processing steps in between.
questions.rule: Put rules that exist only because the system is automated into use cases that describe input, output and processing steps, and leave the user interface out of them.

questions.q: Sort each rule by where the author would place it.

items.t: Interest accrues each day on a loan balance
A refund cannot exceed the price paid
Renewal is refused until the member's contact details are confirmed on screen
The returns form asks for the order number before the reason
An unclaimed parcel is charged a storage fee per day
The upload step cannot start until the photo check has passed

questions.explain: Rules that would hold in a manual business are Entity rules. Rules about the order of steps in the automated system are use case rules.
questions.rule: Ask whether the rule would exist without the computer.

questions.q: A library app has three rules. Match each to its home in the author's design.
pairs: A late fee accrues for each overdue day
Renewal is refused until the member's contact details are confirmed
The renewal page uses green buttons
Neither: it is a user interface detail
questions.explain: The fee would exist in a paper library, so it is a Critical Business Rule. The contact check is an application rule. Button colour is about presentation, which neither holds.
questions.rule: Entity, use case, or neither: ask what the rule is about.

questions.q: A use case written for a web form must now serve a command-line tool too. What must change in the use case, according to the author?
options: Its steps must be rewritten for the console, since a console asks for data one line at a time
Nothing in its rules, since it names only the data going in and out and not how the system is delivered
Its input must be rebuilt around keystrokes, since a use case holds the screen events
Its Entities must be copied, since each delivery mechanism needs its own rules
optionExplain: The use case does not describe screens, so the console's way of asking does not enter it.
Right: from a use case alone you cannot tell whether the application is on the web, a thick client, a console or a pure service.
Use cases do not describe how the system appears to the user.
Entities are shared; a delivery change does not call for a copy.
questions.explain: Because a use case describes rules and data, not appearance, a new delivery mechanism leaves it alone.
questions.rule: A use case is silent about the delivery mechanism.

questions.q: A team models a Create Loan use case as a class in a new language. Besides functions for its rules, what would the author expect it to hold?
options: Nothing more, since data belongs in the database and the class should hold only functions
HTML templates for the output page, so that results can be shown straight away
Copies of the Entity rules, so that the use case can run without the Entities
Data elements for the input, the output and the references to the Entities it works with
optionExplain: The book gives the use case data elements of its own.
A use case does not know HTML; the book says it must not.
The use case refers to Entities rather than copying their critical rules.
Right: the book says a use case is an object with functions plus input, output and Entity references.
questions.explain: A use case is an object: functions carry the application-specific rules, and data elements carry what comes in, what goes out and which Entities it uses.
questions.rule: A use case is an object with rules, data and Entity references.
questions.teaches: A use case is an object with one or more functions for the application-specific rules, plus data elements for the input data, the output data and references to the Entities it interacts with.

questions.q: True or false: An Entity should call the use cases that use it, so it can ask them for the current application context.
questions.explain: Entities are general; use cases are specific to one application. The card next shows which way the knowledge runs.
questions.rule: Use cases depend on Entities and direct them, and Entities never refer to use cases.
High level means general, not large.
questions.q: Entities are the ____-level concepts, and they know nothing of the use cases that control them.
questions.explain: Entities are generalizations usable in many applications, so they are the higher-level concepts.

questions.q: A reviewer reads: Loan.calculateInterest calls ApproveLoanUseCase.currentCutoff to find the credit score cutoff. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since Entities are objects and may call any other object that happens to help them do their work
The cutoff should come from the user interface, which knows the current screen
An Entity names a use case, so the dependency points from the high-level concept to the lower-level one
The method should be a use case, since it calls another use case
optionExplain: Entities may not just call anything; the book's direction rule forbids this call.
The interface is a lower-level concern; going to it makes it worse.
Right: Entities know nothing of the use cases that control them.
Moving it does not fix the direction; the Entity still names a use case.
questions.explain: The use case may refer to the Entity, but the Entity must not refer back. The cutoff could be passed in by the use case.
questions.rule: Entities know nothing of use cases.

questions.q: A shop has an Order Entity and an ApplyDiscount use case. Which arrangement follows the author?
options: Order holds a list of the use cases that may be run on it, so it can offer them
Order and ApplyDiscount refer to each other, so either can start the other
A screen class refers to both, and each of them refers back to the screen
ApplyDiscount refers to Order, and Order refers to no use case
optionExplain: A list of use cases would make the Entity know the use cases.
Mutual references give the Entity knowledge of the use case.
Referring back to the screen would tie both to the delivery mechanism.
Right: use cases depend on Entities and Entities do not depend on use cases.
questions.explain: One direction only: the use case knows the Entity.
questions.rule: Arrows run from use cases to Entities.
A new application reuses the Entities.
questions.q: True or false: When a shop adds a mobile app with new use cases for the same Order rules, the Order Entity must be changed to know about them.
questions.explain: Entities know nothing of use cases, so new use cases simply refer to the Entity. The Entity serves the new application unchanged.

questions.q: A bank adds a second form that officers must complete before a payment estimate. Which code does the author expect to change?
options: The Entities, since the form concerns customer data that Entities hold
Both equally, since an Entity and its use case always change together
The use case that controls the steps, and not the Entities
Neither, since the form is part of the interface adapters alone
optionExplain: The Entities embody critical rules, which do not change when an application's steps change.
The book expects use case changes not to reach the Entities.
Right: a change to how the application operates is expected to affect the use cases.
The order of steps is an application rule, which the use case holds.
questions.explain: A change to the operation of the application lands in the use cases, while the Entities stay put.
questions.rule: Operational changes land in use cases.
questions.teaches: Changes to how an application operates are expected to affect its use cases, while changes in a use case are not expected to affect the Entities.

questions.q: A use case method takes the web framework's HttpRequest object as its argument. What is the main trouble with that?
options: The use case becomes bound to the web framework through its input type
The method can then be called only once for each request it receives
The framework will refuse to compile any call to the method
The request holds too little data for the use case to do its work
optionExplain: A fair guess: the dependency is the trouble, not the amount of data.
Call counts have nothing to do with the type of the argument.
Compilers accept it; the trouble is architectural.
A request usually holds plenty of data; the trouble lies elsewhere.
questions.explain: An input type from the web makes the use case depend on the web. The card next shows the alternative.
questions.rule: Give a use case plain request and response structures that carry no framework types, so it knows nothing about how data is delivered.

questions.q: The use case class accepts simple request data structures for its input and returns simple ____ data structures as its output.
questions.explain: The two structures are the request model going in and the response model coming out.
questions.rule: Give a use case plain request and response structures that carry no framework types, so it knows nothing about how data is delivered.

questions.q: Which of these breaks the author's advice for request and response models? Select all that apply.
options: A request class that derives from HttpRequest
A response class that holds a ready-made HTML fragment
A request that is a plain object holding an amount and a term
A response that is a plain object holding a monthly payment
A request that carries the web framework's session object
optionExplain: This ties the use case to the web framework's interface.
HTML is a web concern the use case must not know about.
A plain object with the needed data depends on nothing.
A plain object with the needed value depends on nothing.
A session object belongs to the web framework and drags that dependency in.
questions.explain: The models must know nothing of the web or any user interface, so anything from a framework or in a web format breaks the advice.
questions.rule: No framework types in the models.

questions.q: A library lends e-books through a web app and soon a voice assistant. Which input design for a Renew use case fits the author?
options: A plain RenewRequest holding the member id and book id, built by each delivery mechanism
The web framework's form object, which the voice assistant will convert into later
Raw query-string text that the use case splits into fields itself, whatever the channel
A JSON string that the use case parses with the web library already in the project
optionExplain: Right: each delivery mechanism builds the same plain request.
That ties the use case to the web form type from the start.
Query strings are web concerns the use case should not parse.
Parsing with a web library brings the web into the use case.
questions.explain: Plain request models let a web app and a voice assistant share one use case.
questions.rule: Each delivery builds the plain request.

questions.q: The request model derives from HttpRequest, and a command-line front end is now added. What is the likely cost?
options: Nothing, since a derived type works wherever its base type is accepted by the caller
Only the console front end changes, since the use case ignores whatever type of request object it is given
The console must pretend to be a web request, or the use case must be changed to accept something else
The Entities must be rewritten, since they are bound to the request type
optionExplain: Working wherever the base works is exactly what ties the console to the web type.
The use case does receive the type, so it is bound to it.
Right: the web type has leaked into the use case, so every caller inherits it.
The Entities do not know requests; the use case does.
questions.explain: The dependency sits in the use case's input type, so a new front end pays for it.
questions.rule: A framework type in the model follows every caller.

questions.q: A response model has a field typed as a web framework's Cookie class. The team says the use case does not touch cookies, so it is fine. What fits the book?
options: It is fine, since only the code that actually calls Cookie methods depends on the framework in any real way
The use case is indirectly bound to whatever the response model depends on, including that framework
It is fine if only the response carries it, since the request is the one that matters
It is a problem only when the use case is compiled apart from the response
optionExplain: The book says the binding is indirect, so not calling the methods does not free the use case.
Right: if the models are not independent, the use cases that depend on them are indirectly bound.
The book makes no such split between request and response.
Compiling together or apart does not change what depends on what.
questions.explain: A use case depends on its models, and so on whatever they depend on.
questions.rule: Dependencies of the models are dependencies of the use case.
questions.teaches: A use case is indirectly bound to every dependency of the request and response models it uses, even if its own code never touches them.

questions.q: A response model and an Entity both hold a customer name and balance. A developer proposes using the Entity as the response. What is the author's view?
options: Adopt it: removing a duplicate class is the cheaper design in the long run
Adopt it if the Entity is immutable, since then nothing can go wrong with sharing
Adopt it only when no web page is involved, since pages are the only trouble
Avoid it: the two have different purposes and will change for different reasons
optionExplain: Saving a class is the temptation the author warns about.
Immutability does not change the different reasons for change.
The author's objection is not about web pages.
A fair guess: the shared data tempts, but the reasons to change differ.
questions.explain: The author says to avoid the temptation. The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: Do not let request or response models hold Entity objects: they change for different reasons, so keep them separate even when they share data.

questions.q: Models and Entities change for different ____, so tying them together violates the Single Responsibility Principle.
questions.explain: The Single Responsibility Principle in the author's sense concerns the reasons a thing changes.
questions.rule: Do not let request or response models hold Entity objects: they change for different reasons, so keep them separate even when they share data.

questions.q: Which results does the author expect from tying request and response models to Entities? Select all that apply.
options: Lots of tramp data
Lots of conditionals in your code
A violation of the Common Closure Principle
Fewer classes to maintain, so changes get cheaper
Entities that are free of any knowledge of the use cases
optionExplain: Right: the book names tramp data, meaning values carried along that the receiver does not use (our gloss).
Right: the book names lots of conditionals.
Right: tying them together violates this principle.
The book expects the opposite of cheaper change.
That is a separate rule about direction, not a result of tying the models.
questions.explain: The book lists tramp data and conditionals as the result, and the two principles as the ones violated.
questions.rule: Tying the models to Entities brings tramp data and conditionals.
questions.teaches: Tying the models to Entities leads, in the author's words, to lots of tramp data and lots of conditionals in the code.

questions.q: A ShipOrder response needs the customer name and shipping total, and a screen also wants a gift-wrap-offered flag that no business rule uses. Where does the flag go?
options: On the Order Entity, so every part of the system shares one class
On the Order Entity as a field used only when the screen sets it
In the response model only, leaving the Order Entity as it was
In both, so the two stay in step with each other
optionExplain: A single shared class is the temptation the author warns about.
A field used only sometimes is the sort of conditional the author warns about.
Right: the flag serves the exchange with the screen, not a critical rule.
Keeping them in step is tying them together.
questions.explain: A screen detail changes for screen reasons and stays out of the Entity.
questions.rule: Screen details belong in the response model.

questions.q: Product asks for another screen field, and the Entity is used as the response. What does the author's reasoning predict?
options: The Entity gains a field for a screen, and code unrelated to screens must now handle it
The change stays in the screen code, so no other code is touched by the new field
Only the database mapping changes, since fields in an Entity are stored data
Nothing is lost, since both always change together in the same way
optionExplain: Right: the Entity now changes for a reason that is not about business rules.
Sharing the class spreads the change beyond the screen.
The field is for a screen; storage is a side matter.
The two change for different reasons, so they do not move together.
questions.explain: A shared class carries every change to every user of it.
questions.rule: A shared class spreads each change.

questions.q: A team passes a whole Order Entity from its controller into a use case across an architectural boundary. Which view fits the author?
options: Pass the Entity, since it is the one type that every layer of the system already understands well
Pass a database row, since it holds the most complete form of the data
Pass the Entity only if it has no methods, since methods bring dependencies
Pass a simple data structure instead, since Entity objects and database rows should not cross
optionExplain: The author names this as the cheat to avoid.
Rows are also named as something not to pass.
An Entity stripped of methods is still an Entity object.
Right: the book says not to cheat and pass Entity objects or database rows.
questions.explain: Only isolated, simple data structures cross a boundary.
questions.rule: Entities do not cross boundaries.
questions.teaches: Across an architectural boundary the author also refuses to pass Entity objects or database rows; only simple data structures cross.

questions.q: True or false: The plans of a library reveal its purpose mainly through the rooms and their arrangement, and not through the building material.
questions.explain: Plans show entrances, reading areas and galleries, so they say what the building is for. The card next applies the same idea to software.
questions.rule: Let the top-level structure announce what the system is for, its use cases, rather than which framework it uses.
Announce the use cases.
questions.q: According to the author, the architecture of an application should scream its ____ cases.
questions.explain: The structure should support and announce the use cases, as house plans announce a house.

questions.q: A hospital system's top-level folders are rails, hibernate and tomcat. The team says this shows the architecture. Which complaint fits the author?
options: Three folders are too few to hold all the layers that an architecture needs
The names announce tools, so a reader cannot see which use cases the system supports
Folders should be named after the programming language, not the tools used
Each tool folder needs a readme file before it can count as part of the architecture
optionExplain: The number of folders is not the issue; their meaning is.
Right: the structure should tell readers about the system, not about the frameworks.
A language name also says nothing about the use cases.
A readme would not change what the names announce.
questions.explain: Tool names at the top level hide what the system is for.
questions.rule: Top-level names should describe use cases.

questions.q: A team builds a payroll system. Which top-level layout follows the author's advice?
options: Folders named after the conventions that the web framework generates by default
One folder per technical layer, each named after the library that fills it
A single folder named src, with every file listed in alphabetical order
Folders named after what the system does, such as pay-runs, timesheets and tax-filing
optionExplain: Framework conventions announce the framework.
Library names announce tools, not use cases.
A flat folder announces nothing about the purpose.
Right: a reader sees the system's use cases at once.
questions.explain: Name the structure after the use cases.
questions.rule: Name folders after what the system does.
Use-case names outlast frameworks.
questions.q: True or false: Swapping the web framework would force the renaming of top-level folders that were named after the system's use cases.
questions.explain: The names described the use cases, not the framework, so they keep their meaning.

questions.q: A newcomer to a health care repository asks where the views and controllers are. What reply does the author suggest?
options: They live in the framework's default folders, so there is no need to look for them
We will add views and controllers folders at the top level at once, for familiarity
Those are details that need not concern us now; we will decide about them later
A good architecture has none, since views and controllers belong to old systems
optionExplain: Pointing to framework folders keeps the framework in charge of the structure.
Adding them at the top level would make the structure announce the delivery.
Right: the newcomer should learn the use cases without knowing how the system is delivered.
The author does not say they do not exist, only that they are details to decide later.
questions.explain: A reader of the structure should learn all the use cases while still not knowing how the system is delivered.
questions.rule: Delivery pieces are details to decide later.
questions.teaches: A newcomer should be able to learn all the use cases from the structure and still not know how the system is delivered; views and controllers are details to decide about later.

questions.q: A house architect hands over plans that do not say whether the walls are brick or cedar. What does this say about the plans?
options: They are unfinished and cannot be used until the material is known
They assume the owner already prefers wood, which is the usual choice
They treat the outside material as a matter that needs no plan at all
They can meet the use cases while the choice of material stays open for later
optionExplain: Plans can meet the use cases without naming the material.
Nothing in the plans assumes wood.
The material is chosen later, not ignored.
A fair guess: usability comes first and the material can follow.
questions.explain: The material is a detail that can be decided later. The card next draws the software parallel.
questions.rule: Centre the architecture on use cases so that framework, database and web-server choices stay open options, to be decided late.

questions.q: A good software architecture treats frameworks as ____ to be left open.
questions.explain: The author says frameworks are options to be left open.
questions.rule: Centre the architecture on use cases so that framework, database and web-server choices stay open options, to be decided late.

questions.q: A kickoff memo says: Week one, pick Rails, Hibernate and MySQL; then plan the use cases. Which flaw would the author point to?
options: It lists too few tools for an architecture to be complete in its first week
It fixes tool choices before the use cases are known, instead of leaving them open
It plans the use cases after the tools, when they should be left out altogether
It names tools by brand, which a good architecture is not allowed to do
optionExplain: The number of tools is not the issue.
Right: the choices should wait until much later.
The author wants a use-case emphasis, not the absence of use cases.
Brand names are not the problem; the early commitment is.
questions.explain: The memo commits to tools first. The author wants those choices left open.
questions.rule: Do not commit to tools first.

questions.q: A startup is unsure whether its product will be a web app or a console tool. Which step best follows the author?
options: Pick the most popular framework now, so that hiring will be easy and training stays short
Build both front ends at once, so that no choice has to be made
Write the use cases and their rules first, and leave the delivery choice open
Choose the database first, because data outlives any front end
optionExplain: Early commitment is what the author advises against.
Building both avoids the choice by doubling the work, and does not keep options open.
Right: the delivery mechanism is a decision that can wait.
Choosing the database first still commits early.
questions.explain: Centre on the use cases and defer delivery.
questions.rule: Use cases first, delivery later.
Open options are cheap to change.
questions.q: True or false: In an architecture that follows the author, replacing a slow database stays at the edge of the system.
questions.explain: The use cases never depended on that database, so the choice was an open option and changing it is modest work.

questions.q: A mobile team built on one cloud backend, and the vendor later raises prices. Which property of the architecture mattered most, in the author's view?
options: That changing the earlier decision stayed easy, and not only that deciding had been late
That the decision was taken as early as possible, so that the team could move on
That the backend was hidden from the app's users behind the screens
That the vendor was chosen for its reputation, so that the change was unlikely
optionExplain: Right: a good architecture makes it easy to change your mind about these decisions.
Early commitment is the opposite of the advice.
Hiding it from users is not the point; hiding it from the rules is.
A reputation does not make the change easier.
questions.explain: Deferring is half the benefit; the other half is that a decision can be reversed later.
questions.rule: Make it easy to change your mind.
questions.teaches: A good architecture also makes it easy to change your mind about framework, database and server decisions later, not only to postpone them.

questions.rule: Treat the web as an IO device: a delivery detail whose choice can wait and that must not dominate the system's structure.
questions.q: True or false: The author treats the web as a delivery mechanism and not as an architecture.
questions.explain: The web is a delivery mechanism, an IO device. The card next gives the reasoning.

questions.rule: The web is an IO device.
questions.q: The author describes the web as a delivery mechanism, an ____ device.
questions.explain: The web only gets data into and out of the application, as an IO device does.

questions.q: A planning note says: Because we ship on the web, our package layout will mirror the web framework's page structure. What does the author say?
options: That is correct, since web delivery fixes the shape that a system must have
The web is a detail, and its delivery shape should not dominate the system structure
That is fine for web pages but not for web services, which have no pages
That is wrong because no system should ever be delivered over the web
optionExplain: The author says the opposite: the web does not dictate the architecture.
Right: the structure should not follow the delivery mechanism.
The author does not split pages from services in this way.
The author does not reject the web; he rejects its dominance.
questions.explain: Delivery over the web does not dictate the structure.
questions.rule: Delivery does not dictate structure.

questions.q: A clinic's booking rules are served by a website, and it also wants phone-kiosk and text-message access. What should the booking rules know about delivery?
options: Which channel each request came from, so that replies can be shaped to fit
Only the web, since it is the main channel and the others are extras
The kiosk's screen size, since kiosks have a fixed display to fill
As little as possible, so each channel is a thin layer around the same rules
optionExplain: Channel details leak delivery into the rules.
Making the web the model repeats the fault the author describes.
Screen size is a delivery detail.
Right: the rules should be as ignorant of delivery as possible.
questions.explain: Each channel is an outer piece around one set of rules.
questions.rule: Rules ignore the channel.
Delivery changes stay at the edge.
questions.q: True or false: If the website is dropped and only a kiosk remains, the fundamental architecture stays and only the delivery piece changes.
questions.explain: The web was a detail, so removing it leaves the fundamental architecture alone.

questions.q: A game engine's rule code checks isBrowser before deciding how to score. What does the author's view say about this?
options: It is a leak: the architecture should be as ignorant as possible about how it will be delivered
It is a sound habit, since rules should always know where they will run
It is acceptable, because browsers are the one place where delivery matters to rules
It is harmless, since the check is a single condition and not a framework
optionExplain: Right: the rules should not know the delivery mechanism.
The author wants the opposite of knowing where they run.
The author makes no exception for browsers.
A single condition is still knowledge of delivery in the rules.
questions.explain: The rules should work as a console, web, thick client or service app unchanged.
questions.rule: The system should be ignorant of delivery.
questions.teaches: The system architecture should be as ignorant as possible about how it will be delivered.

questions.q: A framework's tutorial tells you to let it generate all your classes. How should you read this advice?
options: As the safest route, since the people who made it know best how to use it
As proof that frameworks should be avoided in every project that you start
As a requirement of the framework, with no alternative way to use it
As the view of a true believer, to weigh against what it costs your architecture
optionExplain: Authors of a framework often take the all-encompassing position.
The author does not tell you to avoid frameworks.
Such advice is a choice, not a requirement.
A fair guess: the author tells you to read such advice with care.
questions.explain: Tutorials often assume the framework does everything. The card next says how to respond.
questions.rule: Use a framework as a tool, with skepticism, and plan how to protect a use-case architecture from it.
questions.section: Frameworks Are Tools, Not Ways of Life

questions.q: The author tells you to look at each framework with a ____ eye.
questions.explain: A jaded, skeptical eye keeps a framework from taking over.
questions.rule: Use a framework as a tool, with skepticism, and plan how to protect a use-case architecture from it.
questions.section: Frameworks Are Tools, Not Ways of Life

questions.q: Which are questions the author wants you to ask about a framework? Select all that apply.
options: How should I use it?
How should I protect myself from it?
It might help, but at what cost?
Which of its conventions should my top-level packages follow?
How can I let it do everything?
optionExplain: Right: the author asks how to use it.
Right: the author asks how to protect yourself.
Right: the author asks about the cost.
That lets the framework supply the architecture.
That is the true believer's position.
questions.explain: The author's questions are about use, protection and cost, not about handing over the structure.
questions.rule: Ask about use, protection and cost.
questions.section: Frameworks Are Tools, Not Ways of Life

questions.q: A team adopts a persistence framework. A senior developer proposes wrapping its calls behind interfaces owned by the use cases. How does this fit the author?
options: It conflicts, since a framework must be used everywhere for it to pay off
It fits: it is a strategy that stops the framework from taking over the architecture
It fits only if the framework is dropped again before the project ends
It is unneeded, since frameworks never affect the structure of a system
optionExplain: The author wants the framework kept at arm's length.
Right: the author asks for a strategy to protect the use-case emphasis.
Dropping it is not the point; keeping it from taking over is.
The author says frameworks can take over an architecture.
questions.explain: Wrapping a framework is a protective strategy of the kind the author asks for.
questions.rule: Protect the architecture from the framework.
questions.section: Frameworks Are Tools, Not Ways of Life

questions.q: A team follows a framework's tutorial in every package. What does the author's argument predict for its architecture?
options: It becomes easier to test, because the framework supplies a ready structure
It risks being based on the framework, so it cannot be based on the use cases
It gets stronger, because experts designed the framework with care
It stays as it was, because tutorials do not affect design decisions
optionExplain: The book says frameworks kept at arm's length help testing, not the reverse.
Right: if the architecture is based on frameworks, it cannot be based on the use cases.
Expertise in the framework does not make the use cases the basis.
Tutorials that hand over the structure do affect design.
questions.explain: Letting the framework lead means the use cases do not.
questions.rule: A framework-based architecture is not use-case-based.
questions.section: Frameworks Are Tools, Not Ways of Life

questions.q: A UI toolkit demands that every business class extend its base class. Which response follows the author?
options: Extend the base class everywhere, since the toolkit's authors know best what structure a system of this kind needs
Drop the toolkit and write the screens by hand, since any dependency is a danger
Extend it only in the Entities, since they are the most important classes
Keep the business rules free of the toolkit, so it stays a tool and not a limit to cram the system into
optionExplain: That puts the system into the toolkit's constraints.
The author says frameworks can be useful, so dropping is not required.
Entities are the last place for a framework dependency.
Right: independence of frameworks lets you use them as tools.
questions.explain: Independence from frameworks lets you use them as tools instead of cramming the system into their limited constraints.
questions.rule: Use frameworks as tools.
questions.teaches: Being independent of frameworks lets you use them as tools, rather than forcing you to cram your system into their limited constraints.
questions.section: Frameworks Are Tools, Not Ways of Life

questions.q: True or false: To unit-test a business rule in a well-structured system, the database must be connected first.
questions.explain: In the author's design the rules are tested without the database. The card next says why that is possible.
questions.rule: Keep Entities plain and have use cases coordinate them, so that all of them can be tested together without a web server, a database or any other framework.
Use cases coordinate Entities.
questions.q: In the author's picture, use case objects ____ the Entity objects.
questions.explain: Entities carry the critical rules, and use case objects coordinate them.

questions.q: A test of the late-fee rule starts the web server and loads a test database. What does the author's view suggest about the design?
options: That is the normal price of testing any business rule in a real system
The test is fine, since only tests that include the web layer count
The rule is probably tied to frameworks that it need not depend on
The database should be copied into the Entity so that it can be tested
optionExplain: The author says these tests should not need the frameworks.
The author says the opposite: use cases can be tested without frameworks.
Right: with a use-case architecture these tests need no server and no database.
Copying a database into an Entity makes the dependency worse.
questions.explain: A test that needs the web server and database points to frameworks in the rules.
questions.rule: Rule tests need no frameworks.

questions.q: A returns app has an Order Entity and a RefundOrder use case. Which test setup fits the author?
options: Start the app server, post a form, wait for the response and then read the refund back from the database
Replace the Order Entity with a mock, so the use case runs apart from its own rules
Test only the Order Entity, since use cases cannot run without the web
Create plain Orders, run RefundOrder on them and check the result, with no server or database
optionExplain: That is the kind of test the architecture avoids.
Mocking away the Entity hides the rules the use case coordinates.
The author says use cases can be tested without frameworks.
Right: plain objects and a use case that coordinates them can be tested directly.
questions.explain: Plain Entities and a coordinating use case make a small, direct test.
questions.rule: Test plain objects directly.
Plain Entities keep tests simple.
questions.q: True or false: If an Entity imports the persistence framework's base class, tests of that Entity still need no framework.
questions.explain: The import ties the Entity to the framework, so its tests need the framework present and the plainness is lost.

questions.q: A manager says testability is a nice extra to add after the architecture is done. Which reply fits the author?
options: It can be added later at no cost, since tests can be written for any code
It matters only for Entities, since use cases cannot be tested alone
Testability is an attribute of a good architecture, not an add-on
It matters only for systems that have a user interface to check
optionExplain: The author ties testability to the architecture itself.
The author says use cases can be tested too.
Right: it has long been known that testability is an attribute of good architectures.
The author's claim does not depend on a user interface.
questions.explain: A good architecture is testable by its structure.
questions.rule: Testability comes from structure.
questions.teaches: It has long been known that testability is an attribute of good architectures.
