questions.q: A business rule class and a database driver class are related in a layered design. Which source code dependency fits the author?
options: The driver depends on the rule's side, and the rule depends on nothing from the driver
The rule depends on the driver, since rules must call the driver to save results
Each depends on the other through a shared configuration file
Neither may depend on anything, since layers are not allowed to share code
optionExplain: A fair guess: mechanisms depend on policies, not the reverse.
Rules calling drivers directly would point the dependency outward.
Mutual dependence defeats the rule.
Dependencies are allowed, if they point inward.
questions.explain: Policies sit inside and mechanisms outside. The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: Source code dependencies point only inward, so nothing in an inner circle may mention a name or a data format declared in an outer circle.

questions.q: Source code dependencies must point only ____, toward higher-level policies.
questions.explain: Inner circles are policies and outer circles are mechanisms, so dependencies point in.
questions.rule: Source code dependencies point only inward, so nothing in an inner circle may mention a name or a data format declared in an outer circle.

questions.q: Code in the use case circle imports a serializer class declared in the outer web circle. Does that obey the rule?
options: No: inner code may not mention any name declared in an outer circle, even a class
Yes: a serializer is a formatting tool, so it counts as a policy and can sit inside
Yes: the rule covers functions only, and an imported class is not a function
Yes, if the serializer is third-party code, since third parties are always neutral
optionExplain: Right: any named entity declared outside counts.
Formatting tools in the web circle are mechanisms.
The author lists functions, classes, variables and any other named entity.
Origin does not matter; the circle in which it is declared does.
questions.explain: The rule bans naming anything declared in an outer circle.
questions.rule: No outer names in inner code.

questions.q: Which of these would break the Dependency Rule? Select all that apply.
options: A use case calls a function declared in the controller circle
An Entity declares a field of a type generated by the persistence framework
A controller calls a method on a use case
A presenter implements an interface declared in the use case circle
A use case takes a web framework's request object as its parameter
optionExplain: Right: inner code names something in an outer circle.
Right: a framework-generated type is declared outside.
This points inward, so it obeys the rule.
This also points inward: the outer presenter names the inner interface.
Right: the request object is declared in the outer web circle.
questions.explain: A dependency breaks the rule when inner code names something declared in an outer circle.
questions.rule: Arrows may only go in.

questions.q: The web framework is replaced with another. If the rule held, which parts can stay unchanged?
options: Only the Entities, because the use cases are tied to the web in any design
None, because replacing a framework changes every circle in some way
The inner circles, because they never name anything from the outer circle
Only the outer circle, because the inner circles drive the framework
optionExplain: The use cases do not name the web if the rule holds.
The rule is meant to prevent that spread.
Right: the inner circles do not know the framework.
The outer circle is where the change lands.
questions.explain: The outer circle absorbs a framework change.
questions.rule: Change lands in the outer circle.

questions.q: A mobile team passes the persistence framework's generated record class from its repository into the use case layer, because it is convenient. Which part of the rule does this break?
options: The ban on outer circles calling inner ones, since the repository is the outermost part of the design here
The ban on inner circles using data formats declared outside, especially framework-generated ones
Nothing, since the rule covers the names of functions only and not data
It breaks the rule only if the record class is mutable and can be changed
optionExplain: Outer circles calling inward is what the rule allows.
Right: the rule covers data formats too.
The author says data formats declared outside should not be used inside.
Mutability is not part of the rule.
questions.explain: Data formats count as names too, particularly when a framework generates them.
questions.rule: Data formats follow the rule too.
questions.teaches: Data formats declared in an outer circle should not be used by an inner circle either, especially if a framework in the outer circle generates them.

questions.q: Where should all SQL live in a system built to the clean architecture?
options: In the use case layer, next to the rules that need the data
In the Entities, since they own the data that SQL reads and writes
In the frameworks and drivers circle, as part of the database itself
In the interface adapters layer, in the parts that deal with the database
optionExplain: No code inward of the adapters should know about the database.
Entities must not know the database.
The database is in the outer circle, but the author restricts SQL to the adapters.
A fair guess: SQL is a detail, and a converter layer holds it.
questions.explain: SQL is kept to the adapters that deal with the database. The card next gives the whole layout.
questions.rule: Place enterprise rules in Entities, application rules in use cases, converters and SQL in interface adapters, and tools and glue in frameworks and drivers.

questions.q: Match each circle to what it holds.
pairs: Converters between inner and outer data forms
The database, the web framework and glue code
questions.explain: Each circle gathers one kind of code, from the most general rules in the middle to the tools at the edge.
questions.rule: Four circles, four kinds of code.

questions.q: Sort each piece of code into the circle where it belongs.

items.t: A controller that packages web form data
The rule that estimates are blocked until the credit score is checked
Code that turns Date objects into formatted strings for a page
SQL that loads a customer's loans
The sequence of steps that runs a loan application
A view that moves strings into an HTML page

questions.explain: Conversion between inner forms and web or database forms belongs to the adapters. The steps and rules of the application belong to the use cases.
questions.rule: Convert in the adapters, decide in the use cases.

questions.q: A design review finds SQL strings inside a use case class. Which fix does the layering imply?
options: Move the SQL into the Entities, which own the data that the statements read and write on each call
Leave it there, since use cases handle application data access directly
Move the SQL to the interface adapters layer, in the part concerned with the database
Move it to the frameworks and drivers circle as glue code
optionExplain: Entities must not know the database.
No code inward of the adapters should know anything about the database.
Right: the author restricts all SQL to the adapters layer.
Glue code lives there, but the author places SQL in the adapters.
questions.explain: Inner circles know nothing about the database, so SQL sits in the adapters.
questions.rule: SQL belongs to the adapters.

questions.q: A team finds it needs a fifth circle. What does the author say happens to the Dependency Rule?
options: It still applies, and source code dependencies still point inward
It lapses until the circles are renamed to fit the new layout
It applies to the first four circles only, which the diagram names
Dependencies in the new circle may point either way, as it is new
optionExplain: Right: the circles are schematic, and the rule always applies.
The rule does not lapse when circles are added.
The author says there is no rule that you must have just these four.
The rule applies to any number of circles.
questions.explain: The count of circles may vary; the direction may not.
questions.rule: More circles, same rule.

questions.q: A game studio redesigns its menu navigation and adds a login. Which circle is the least likely to be touched, in the author's view?
options: The use cases
The interface adapters
The frameworks and drivers
The Entities
optionExplain: Use cases hold application steps, which login and navigation touch.
Adapters convert for the web or UI, which navigation touches.
Frameworks and drivers hold the tools that the UI uses.
Right: no operational change to an application should affect the Entity layer.
questions.explain: Entities hold the most general rules and are the least likely to change when something external changes.
questions.rule: Entities change least.
questions.teaches: Entities are the code least likely to change when something external changes: a change to page navigation or security should not affect them, and no operational change to an application should touch the Entity layer.

questions.q: A use case must show its result through a presenter in an outer circle. How can it do so without breaking the Dependency Rule?
options: By calling the presenter's class directly, since a call is not a dependency
By calling an interface declared in its own circle that the presenter implements
By copying the presenter's formatting code into the use case itself
By having the presenter call the use case and then drop the output step
optionExplain: A call that names the presenter class is a dependency.
A fair guess: the call can go through something the inner circle owns.
Copying brings an outer concern inside.
That removes the output instead of delivering it.
questions.explain: An interface owned by the inner circle can be implemented by the outer one. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: When control must go from an inner circle to an outer one, have the inner circle call an interface it owns and let the outer circle implement it.

questions.q: The author uses the ____ Inversion Principle to make source code dependencies oppose the flow of control.
questions.explain: The inversion makes the source dependency point opposite to the call.
questions.rule: When control must go from an inner circle to an outer one, have the inner circle call an interface it owns and let the outer circle implement it.

questions.q: A use case has a field of type HtmlPresenter, a class from the web circle, and calls it directly. What is the flaw?
options: A use case should never produce any output at all, since output is a UI task
The inner circle names a class from an outer circle; it should call an interface it owns
The presenter should be declared inside the use case class, to keep the two always together
HtmlPresenter should extend the controller class, so that both share a parent
optionExplain: The use case does produce output data; it just hands it over through an interface.
Right: the output port interface removes the outward name.
Declaring the presenter inside the use case would pull the outer concern inward.
Extending the controller adds a dependency and does not fix the direction.
questions.explain: The fix is an interface in the inner circle.
questions.rule: Call an interface you own.

questions.q: Put the steps in the order that control flows when a user submits a form.
items: The controller receives the request and calls the use case
The use case runs its rules
The use case calls the output port interface
The presenter that implements the port formats the result
questions.explain: Control goes in through the controller, runs the rules, and goes back out through the output port to the presenter, while every source dependency points inward.
questions.rule: Control goes in and out; dependencies only in.

questions.q: What if the output port interface were declared in the presenter's circle instead of the use case's circle?
options: Nothing would change, since the presenter would still implement the interface
The presenter could no longer be tested apart from the use case
The flow of control would reverse, and the presenter would call the use case
The use case would have to name something in an outer circle, which breaks the rule
optionExplain: The owner of the interface decides the direction of the dependency.
Testability is not the issue here; the direction is.
The flow of control does not depend on where the interface is declared.
Right: the interface must belong to the inner circle.
questions.explain: Whoever owns the interface is the one depended on.
questions.rule: The inner circle owns the interface.

questions.q: A use case must load data from a database in an outer circle. Which technique does the author expect?
options: The same one: it calls an interface in its own circle that a database class implements
A different one: databases need direct calls from the use case, because the data flows inward
A global variable shared by both circles, holding the loaded data
A copy of the database driver placed inside the use case circle
optionExplain: Right: the same technique crosses all the boundaries.
The direction of data flow does not change the technique.
A shared global is a dependency the rule forbids.
A copied driver brings the outer concern inside.
questions.explain: Dynamic polymorphism turns the source dependency against the flow of control, whichever way control travels.
questions.rule: One technique for every boundary.
questions.teaches: The same technique, dynamic polymorphism used to make source code dependencies oppose the flow of control, crosses every boundary in the architecture, whichever direction control travels.

questions.q: A repository returns a framework's query result object. A developer wants the use case to take it as its input. Why does the author object?
options: Query results hold many more columns than a use case could possibly need for its work
Query results cannot be copied, so the use case could never keep them
The result type is declared in an outer circle, so the use case would depend outward
Use cases accept only numbers and text, never any structured data
optionExplain: Size is not the objection.
Copying is not the objection.
A fair guess: the type belongs to the framework outside.
Use cases accept simple data structures, not only primitives.
questions.explain: The objection is the direction of the dependency. The card next lists what may cross.
questions.rule: Pass only simple, isolated data structures across a boundary, never Entity objects or database rows.
Simple structures only.
questions.q: Isolated, simple data structures such as basic structs or simple data transfer ____ may cross a boundary.
questions.explain: Simple data transfer objects are on the author's list of acceptable forms, unlike row structures and Entity objects.

questions.rule: Pass only simple, isolated data structures across a boundary, never Entity objects or database rows.
questions.q: True or false: A hashmap holding only plain values may be passed across a boundary.
questions.explain: The author lists a hashmap among the acceptable forms. What matters is that the structure carries no dependency that breaks the rule.

questions.q: A pricing use case needs a customer's tier and country, which sit in a CRM tool's record object. What fits the author?
options: Pass the CRM record object, since the use case needs both of its values
Copy the two values into a simple structure shaped for the use case, then pass that
Pass the Customer Entity, so that the CRM type stays hidden from the use case
Give the use case the CRM client and let it fetch the record itself
optionExplain: The record object is declared in an outer tool.
Right: a simple structure carries no outer dependency.
The author names Entity objects as something not to pass.
The use case would then name the CRM client, an outer detail.
questions.explain: The adapter copies what the use case needs into a simple structure.
questions.rule: Copy into a simple structure.

questions.q: The database framework is upgraded and changes its row structure. If that structure was passed inward, where do the effects appear?
options: Only in the outer circle, since that is where the framework lives
Nowhere, since compiled code ignores changes in a field's layout
Also in the inner circle that uses it, so the change leaks inward
Only in the Entities, since they own the data that rows describe
optionExplain: That would be true only if the structure had not crossed.
Compiled code does depend on the layout of the types it uses.
Right: the inner circle now depends on the outer format.
The Entities are not named in the row structure.
questions.explain: A passed-in outer format carries outer change inward.
questions.rule: Outer formats leak change.

questions.q: A payments adapter receives a vendor's response with 40 fields, and the use case needs three. Which form does the author want crossing inward?
options: A simple structure in the form that suits the use case, filled in by the adapter
The vendor's whole response, since the outer form is the authoritative one
A raw text string for the use case to parse into the fields it needs
The vendor's client object, so the use case can ask for fields as needed
optionExplain: Right: data crossing a boundary takes the form most convenient for the inner circle.
The outer form is the one the inner circle should not use.
Parsing in the use case brings outer formats inside.
The client object is an outer detail.
questions.explain: The inner circle gets the data in the shape that suits it, not the shape the outside has.
questions.rule: Shape the data for the inner side.
questions.teaches: When data crosses a boundary it is always put in the form most convenient for the inner circle, not the form of the outer one.

questions.q: In a web request handled this way, which object first receives the user's input from the web server?
options: The Controller
The use case interactor
The Presenter
The View
optionExplain: A fair guess: the controller sits on the input side.
The interactor receives the input only after the controller has packaged it.
The Presenter works on the output side.
The View displays the output.
questions.explain: The controller starts the flow. The card next follows the request all the way.
questions.rule: The Controller passes plain input through the InputBoundary to the interactor, which passes OutputData through the OutputBoundary to the Presenter, whose ViewModel the View displays, with every dependency pointing inward.

questions.q: Put the parts in the order in which a request reaches them.
items: The Controller packages the input
The InputBoundary interface is crossed
The UseCaseInteractor runs the rules
The OutputBoundary interface is crossed
The Presenter builds the ViewModel
questions.explain: The request enters through the Controller and the input boundary, is handled by the interactor, and leaves through the output boundary to the Presenter.
questions.rule: Controller, boundary, interactor, boundary, presenter.

questions.q: Match each component to its job in the scenario.
pairs: Packages the user's input into a plain object
Controls the dance of the Entities
Moves the ViewModel data into the HTML page
questions.explain: Each component has one job, and the View has almost nothing left to do.
questions.rule: One job for each component.

questions.q: A diagram shows an arrow from the UseCaseInteractor straight to the Presenter class. What is wrong, according to the book?
options: The interactor should reach the Presenter through the Controller, to keep one entry point
Nothing is wrong, since control flows from the interactor to the Presenter anyway
The interactor should use the OutputBoundary interface, so the dependency points inward
The Presenter should be placed inside the interactor, so they are always together
optionExplain: Routing through the controller adds a detour without fixing the direction.
Control flows that way, but the source dependency must point inward.
Right: the interface lets the dependency oppose the control flow.
Putting it inside pulls an outer concern into the inner circle.
questions.explain: A direct arrow to the Presenter would make the inner circle name an outer class.
questions.rule: Go through the output boundary.

questions.q: A team's use case interactor formats a Date as a display string for the page. Which role from the scenario has been bypassed?
options: The Controller, which should format values on their way in
The Presenter, which should repackage output data into display form
The InputBoundary, which should convert dates into strings
The Entities, which should hold the display strings of their data
optionExplain: The Controller packages input; it does not format output.
Right: the Presenter turns output data into viewable form.
The InputBoundary is an interface on the input side.
Entities hold critical rules, not display strings.
questions.explain: Formatting for the screen is the Presenter's job.
questions.rule: Presenters format for display.

questions.q: The database is swapped for a cloud store. Which parts of the scenario stay as they are?
options: Only the Entities, since the interactor and the Presenter both read from the store
None of them, since the data access interface is shared by every part of the whole system
Only the View, since the user sees nothing of the store
Everything except the class behind the data access interface, which alone must change
optionExplain: The interactor does not see the store directly.
The interface is used by the interactor alone.
The View is not the only part unaffected.
Right: the interactor sees only an interface.
questions.explain: The store sits behind the data access interface, so the swap stays there.
questions.rule: A new store changes one class.

questions.q: A new report use case needs customer records held in a database. Which route fits the scenario?
options: The interactor opens a database connection itself, runs the query it needs and keeps the rows
The controller loads the records and packs them into the input data
The interactor calls a data access interface, which a database-side class implements
The presenter queries the database when it formats the report
optionExplain: That puts database code in the inner circle.
The controller only packages the user's input.
Right: the interactor uses the data access interface to bring Entity data into memory.
The presenter formats output data and does not fetch.
questions.explain: The interactor reaches the database through the data access interface.
questions.rule: The database sits behind an interface.
questions.teaches: The interactor uses a DataAccessInterface to bring the data its Entities work with into memory from the database.

questions.q: A GUI shows prices. Which part of this is hard to unit test?
options: Seeing that the right element is displayed on screen
Formatting a number with two decimal places for the price label
Choosing which items go in the list that is shown
Deciding whether a value is negative or positive
optionExplain: A fair guess: a test must see the screen.
Formatting is plain logic that a test can check.
Choosing items is plain logic.
A sign check is plain logic.
questions.explain: Seeing the screen is hard; the logic around it is easy. The card next shows the split.
questions.rule: Split hard-to-test behaviour into a humble module stripped to its barest essence, and move everything testable into a second module.

questions.q: The module that holds the hard-to-test behaviours, stripped to their barest essence, is called the ____ object.
questions.explain: The humble object keeps almost nothing of its own to test.
questions.rule: Split hard-to-test behaviour into a humble module stripped to its barest essence, and move everything testable into a second module.

questions.q: A voice assistant has two kinds of behaviour. Sort each into the module where the pattern would put it.

items.t: Sends audio bytes to the speaker hardware
Chooses the wording of the reply
Switches to shorter replies while the user is driving
Plays a prepared audio clip
Decides which reply follows a spoken request
Passes finished audio to the device driver

questions.explain: Hardware-facing steps are kept thin in the humble object. Decisions about content are testable and go in the other module.
questions.rule: Thin hardware code, testable decisions.

questions.q: A developer puts date formatting inside the View, to keep the View complete. What is the flaw, by the pattern?
options: Date formatting is hard to test, so the View is the right place for it, along with all other formatting
Views should never display dates, since dates are a business concern
Formatting is fine anywhere, since both modules are tested to the same degree
Formatting is testable, so it belongs in the other module and the View stays humble
optionExplain: Formatting is plain logic, easy to test.
Views display dates; the formatting is the issue.
The humble object is not tested to the same degree.
Right: the View should hold only the hard-to-test part.
questions.explain: Formatting can be unit tested, so it is moved out of the humble object.
questions.rule: Move testable logic out of the View.

questions.q: A ReportScreen class draws a chart and also decides which data series to include, and nothing is tested. What does the pattern suggest?
options: Leave the logic where it is and add screenshot tests for each possible series
Move the choosing logic into a separate testable class and keep the drawing code thin
Move the drawing code into the testable class, so everything can be tested together there
Merge the two into one class, so that the tests see the whole behaviour
optionExplain: Screenshot tests keep the hard-to-test part large.
Right: split the testable from the hard to test.
The drawing code is the hard-to-test part.
Merging removes the split.
questions.explain: Keep the drawing thin and test the choosing.
questions.rule: Thin drawing, tested logic.

questions.q: A team splits a sensor-driver class into a hardware-facing part and a rules part. What further conclusion does the author draw about such splits?
options: It marks a boundary only between a GUI and the data that the GUI shows to the user at run time
The line often marks an architectural boundary, and Presenter and View is only one such boundary
It never marks a boundary, because both parts stay in one program
It marks a boundary only where a database is involved in the split
optionExplain: The author says the Presenter and View boundary is one of many.
Right: the separation of testable and non-testable behaviour often defines an architectural boundary.
Staying in one program does not stop a boundary from being there.
Databases are one case among many.
questions.explain: Testability and architecture meet at the boundary.
questions.rule: The testable line is often a boundary.
questions.teaches: The separation of behaviours into testable and non-testable parts often defines an architectural boundary; the Presenter and View boundary is one of many.

questions.q: A negative balance must show in red. Where should the decision red or not be made?
options: In the View, since the View is the part that draws the colour
In the Entity, since the Entity knows the balance best
In the database query, since the sign is found when loading
In the Presenter, which sets a flag that the View only reads
optionExplain: The View is hard to test, so decisions there go unchecked.
The Entity holds critical rules, not screen colours.
The database should not decide on display.
A fair guess: decisions belong where they can be tested.
questions.explain: The View is hard to test, so decisions are made earlier. The card next shows the Presenter's job.
questions.rule: Have the Presenter turn every on-screen value into a string, boolean or enum in the View Model, so the View only moves data to the screen.

questions.q: The View Model holds only strings, booleans and ____.
questions.explain: Everything on screen that the application controls is a string, a boolean or an enum.
questions.rule: Have the Presenter turn every on-screen value into a string, boolean or enum in the View Model, so the View only moves data to the screen.

questions.q: Match each screen item to what the Presenter places in the View Model.
pairs: A formatted string and a flag for negative
A button that must be greyed out
questions.explain: The Presenter decides everything; the View Model carries only simple values.
questions.rule: The View Model holds simple values only.

questions.q: A View receives a Date object and calls a formatter itself. Which principle of the pattern is bent?
options: The View makes a formatting decision that the Presenter should have settled beforehand
The View is too simple, since it ought to hold the main logic for the page
The Date should have been an enum, since enums are the only type that the View accepts
The View should have formatted the date in the use case, which is nearer to the data
optionExplain: Right: nothing is left for the View to do except load data.
The pattern wants the View simple.
Enums are one of three simple types, and are not required for dates.
The use case should not format for display.
questions.explain: Formatting belongs to the Presenter, where it can be unit tested.
questions.rule: Format before the View.

questions.q: Marketing wants dates shown as 13 Oct instead of 13 October. Where does the change go, and how is it tested?
options: In the View, tested by screenshots of each page that shows a date
In the Entity, tested with the database that holds the dates
In the Presenter, tested by unit tests without a screen
In the use case, tested through the web server
optionExplain: That puts formatting in the hard-to-test part.
Entities do not format.
Right: formatting lives in the testable Presenter.
The use case does not format.
questions.explain: A formatting change lands in the Presenter and is checked by plain tests.
questions.rule: Formatting changes land in the Presenter.

questions.q: A reporting app shows a sales table. The View receives rows of numbers and rounds them. Which change fits the pattern?
options: Keep the rounding in the View, since a table is too large to format elsewhere
Give the View the Entity rows, so it can round them from the exact values
Move the table into the database, so it arrives already rounded
Have the Presenter produce a table of formatted strings for the View to copy
optionExplain: Size is no reason to put decisions in the hard-to-test part.
Entity rows would pull an inner object to the View.
The database should not format for display.
Right: tables of numbers are loaded by the Presenter into tables of formatted strings.
questions.explain: Tables are handled like single values: formatted strings in the View Model.
questions.rule: Even tables are strings by the time they reach the View.
questions.teaches: Tables of numbers to be shown on screen are loaded by the Presenter into tables of properly formatted strings in the View Model.

questions.q: True or false: A use case may contain SQL, as long as the SQL is well tested.
questions.explain: The author does not allow SQL in the use cases layer. The card next shows what to use instead.
questions.rule: Let use cases call gateway interfaces with one method per database operation, and put the SQL in the humble implementation in the database layer.
The implementation is humble.
questions.q: In a database gateway design, the gateway ____ is the humble object that issues the SQL.
questions.explain: The implementation just uses SQL, or whatever the database interface is, to answer each method.

questions.q: A gateway interface exposes runSql(String statement) for interactors to call. What is wrong with it?
options: Interfaces may not have text parameters, so the method cannot be declared
Gateways should be classes and not interfaces, so that they can hold the SQL
It lets SQL leak into the use cases layer; the interface should offer one method per needed operation
Nothing is wrong, since one general method is more flexible than a long list of narrow ones
optionExplain: Interfaces can take text parameters; the issue lies elsewhere.
The gateway must be a polymorphic interface so that it can be replaced.
Right: the interactor would have to write SQL.
Flexibility is bought with SQL in the wrong layer.
questions.explain: The interface should speak the application's language, not SQL.
questions.rule: Methods named for needs.

questions.q: A shop's use case needs to know which products gold members bought yesterday. What should the gateway offer?
options: A method named for that need, taking a date and returning the product ids
A generic query method that takes a table name and a condition
Direct access to the products table, for the interactor to filter
A method returning the whole orders table, for the interactor to search
optionExplain: Right: one method per need, like the book's last-names example.
A generic query pushes query writing into the use case.
Table access puts storage structure into the use case.
Returning everything pushes the data work into the use case.
questions.explain: A named method hides the query behind the application's need.
questions.rule: Name the need.
A new store changes one class.
questions.q: True or false: When a company moves from an SQL database to a document store, only the gateway implementation changes and the interactors keep calling the same methods.
questions.explain: The interface speaks the application's needs, so the humble implementation is the part that is replaced.

questions.q: A team wants to test a billing interactor but has no database in its build. What does the author suggest?
options: Make the interactor humble by moving its rules into the gateway implementation where they can be tested
Spin up an in-memory SQL database inside the interactor for the test
Replace the gateway with a stub or test double: the interactor is not humble but stays testable
Skip the test, since interactors are humble objects and need none
optionExplain: The rules belong in the interactor, which is not humble.
SQL does not belong in the interactor.
Right: gateways can be replaced with stubs and test doubles.
Interactors are not humble and are worth testing.
questions.explain: Because the interactor sees only an interface, a stand-in can take the gateway's place.
questions.rule: Stub the gateway.
questions.teaches: Interactors are not humble, since they hold application-specific rules, yet they stay testable because the gateways can be replaced with stubs and test doubles.

questions.q: In which layer should a persistence tool such as Hibernate sit?
options: In the use case layer, where the data is needed
In the database layer, behind the gateway interfaces
In the Entities, since it maps the Entities
In the presentation layer, next to the screens
optionExplain: The use cases must not know the database.
A fair guess: it is a detail of storage.
Entities must be free of storage tools.
Screens are a different concern.
questions.explain: It is a database detail. The card next gives the author's reasons.
questions.rule: Treat an ORM as a data mapper that loads relational rows into data structures, and keep it in the database layer behind the gateways.
Objects expose operations.
questions.q: From a user's point of view, an object is a set of ____.
questions.explain: Users cannot see an object's data, which is private; they see only its public methods.

questions.q: Sort each description by what it fits, from a user's point of view.

items.t: Exposes only public methods
A set of public variables with no implied behaviour
Keeps its data private
A record loaded from a relational table into fields
Users see operations and no data
Fields that anyone may read and write

questions.explain: An object hides data and offers operations. A data structure shows data and implies no behaviour.
questions.rule: Objects hide data; data structures show it.

questions.q: A teammate says Hibernate maps objects to tables, so objects keep their private data and behaviour inside the table. How does the author respond?
options: Objects and tables are the same thing, and the tool stores both of them unchanged in the database
The tool belongs in the Entities, because it works with their data
Such tools load data into data structures; users of an object cannot see its data
The name is right, since all code that stores data is an object mapper
optionExplain: Objects are not data structures from a user's view.
The tool belongs in the database layer.
Right: the author says there is no such thing as an object relational mapper.
The author says the name misleads.
questions.explain: What the tool loads are data structures, which is why data mapper is the better name.
questions.rule: It maps data, not objects.

questions.q: A team adopts a library that fills record classes from a relational table. Where does the author place it?
options: In the database layer, behind the gateway interfaces
In the use case layer, next to the interactors that need the records
In the Entities, next to the rules that apply to the records
In the controller, where the request first arrives
optionExplain: Right: such systems reside in the database layer.
Use cases must not know the database.
Entities must stay free of storage tools.
Controllers handle input, not storage.
questions.explain: The mapper is a database detail.
questions.rule: Mappers live in the database layer.

questions.q: A team places a mapping tool between its gateway interfaces and its relational database. What role does the author give that tool?
options: A use case boundary
An Entity that owns the data
A Presenter for stored data
Another Humble Object boundary
optionExplain: Use cases sit above the gateways.
Entities hold critical rules.
A Presenter prepares data for a screen.
Right: ORMs form another kind of Humble Object boundary between the gateway interfaces and the database.
questions.explain: The mapper keeps the database's quirks on its own side of the boundary.
questions.rule: A mapper is a humble boundary.
questions.teaches: ORMs form another kind of Humble Object boundary, lying between the gateway interfaces and the database.

questions.q: An application must receive messages from a payment provider in the provider's own format. What should reach the use case?
options: The provider's raw message objects, so that nothing is lost on the way
A simple data structure shaped for the application, built by a listener
A reference to the provider's client library, to read fields as needed
Entities pre-filled by the provider before they arrive
optionExplain: Raw objects carry the provider's format inward.
A fair guess: a listener converts at the edge.
A client library is an outer detail.
The provider cannot know the application's Entities.
questions.explain: Convert at the edge. The card next names the modules that do it.
questions.rule: At a service boundary, pass simple data structures across and let humble modules on the outside format and send, or listen and format.

questions.q: On the input side, service ____ receive data from the service interface and format it into a simple data structure.
questions.explain: Service listeners are the humble modules on the input side.
questions.rule: At a service boundary, pass simple data structures across and let humble modules on the outside format and send, or listen and format.

questions.q: A use case builds the exact JSON that an external shipping service expects before sending it. What is the flaw?
options: Use cases may not send anything, so the call should be removed entirely
Formatting and sending belong to an outer module; the use case should hand over simple data
JSON is not a permitted format, so the use case must use another one
The shipping service should format its own input, so nothing is needed in the application here
optionExplain: The use case does hand data to the edge; it just should not format it.
Right: the format belongs outside the application's rules.
The format is allowed, in the right place.
The sending side must still format for the service.
questions.explain: The use case passes data; a module at the edge formats and sends.
questions.rule: Format at the edge.

questions.q: A weather app provides a service to partners and calls two upstream services. Where does the code that formats outgoing messages live?
options: In the use cases, next to the rules that decide which data is to be sent to the partner
In the Entities, since they hold the data that is being sent out
In the controller of the partner-facing web page that lists services
In modules on the outer side of the service boundary, fed by simple structures
optionExplain: Use cases must not know message formats.
Entities must stay free of delivery formats.
The web page controller deals with a different boundary.
Right: humble modules format and send.
questions.explain: Formatting for each service belongs at its boundary.
questions.rule: One edge module per service.
Format changes stay outside.
questions.q: True or false: When the shipping provider changes its message format, the change is absorbed by the module at the edge that formats the data.
questions.explain: The format lives in the humble module, and the application's own structures stay the same.

questions.q: A new team lists its boundaries: the GUI, the database and an external service. Which expectation matches the author?
options: Only the GUI boundary uses a humble object; the others are covered by integration tests
Humble objects replace the need for simple data structures at the boundaries
A humble object is likely to be found near each one, and the testability of the whole system rises
Humble objects appear only where a framework is in use at the boundary
optionExplain: The author says the pattern lurks near each boundary.
Simple data structures cross as well.
Right: at each boundary the pattern is likely to be nearby.
Frameworks are not the condition.
questions.explain: Humble objects at boundaries vastly increase testability.
questions.rule: Expect a humble object near each boundary.
questions.teaches: The author expects the Humble Object pattern near almost every architectural boundary, with simple data structures crossing it, and says this vastly increases the testability of the entire system.

questions.q: A team wants to keep the option of splitting a module later but cannot afford separate releases now. What could it do?
options: Skip all interfaces for now and add them later, when the need for the split is clear
Ship two components now, to be safe, and manage both releases
Merge the sides into one and mark the line with code comments
Build the interfaces of a full boundary and its data structures, yet ship one unit
optionExplain: Adding them later is costly once code has grown together.
Two components bring the release burden the team cannot afford.
Comments do not enforce a boundary.
A fair guess: the design work can be done without the deployment cost.
questions.explain: The boundary can be built and still deployed as one. The card next names this approach.
questions.rule: To hold a place for a boundary, build every interface and structure of a full boundary but compile and deploy both sides as one component.

questions.q: Skipping the last step means compiling and deploying both sides as a single ____.
questions.explain: The components are independently deployable in design, but shipped together.
questions.rule: To hold a place for a boundary, build every interface and structure of a full boundary but compile and deploy both sides as one component.
To hold a place for a boundary, build every interface and structure of a full boundary but compile and deploy both sides as one component.
questions.q: True or false: Skipping the last step needs the same code and preparatory design work as a full boundary.
questions.explain: The same code and design work are needed. What it avoids is the administration of several components.

questions.q: A team builds the interfaces of a boundary but ships one binary. Which burden does it avoid?
options: Writing the boundary interfaces for both directions of the boundary in detail
Tracking version numbers and managing releases for several components
Designing the input and output data structures for each side
Thinking about the direction of dependencies between the sides
optionExplain: The interfaces are still written.
Right: this is the difference the author says should not be taken lightly.
The structures are still designed.
Dependency direction still has to be managed.
questions.explain: Only the administration disappears.
questions.rule: Only administration is saved.

questions.q: Years later it is clear that no second user of the component will ever appear. What is likely to happen to the separation?
options: Nothing, since the interfaces still enforce the direction of every call
The compiler blocks any new wrong-way dependency, because the sides share one component
It weakens: dependencies cross the line the wrong way and re-separating becomes a chore
The component can be split again by changing a configuration setting
optionExplain: Inside one component nothing enforces the direction.
The compiler sees one component and allows them.
Right: this happened with FitNesse.
The weakening is in the code and not a setting.
questions.explain: Without a real boundary, discipline erodes.
questions.rule: Unused boundaries erode.

questions.q: A tool must be a single download that runs with no extra steps, but its authors may one day publish the parser separately. Which strategy fits the FitNesse example?
options: Skip the last step: design the parser as separable, and ship it inside the one component
A full boundary, with the parser released as its own versioned package from the first day
Copy the parser into every product that needs it, and keep the copies in step
No boundary at all, since a single download means no separation will be wanted
optionExplain: Right: FitNesse wanted download and go, with a separable web component.
That makes users fetch and match several components.
Copies drift apart and avoid no work.
The authors may want the separation later.
questions.explain: Separable in design, single in delivery.
questions.rule: Separable design, single download.
questions.teaches: FitNesse used this strategy early because its goal was download and go: users should fetch one jar, not hunt for other jars or work out version compatibilities.

questions.q: A team puts an interface between a client and a service class, and nothing else. What will stop a developer from calling the service class directly?
options: Only the diligence and discipline of the developers
The compiler, since the interface hides the class from the client
The reciprocal interface on the other side of the boundary
The Dependency Rule, which the language enforces on its own
optionExplain: A fair guess: with one interface, nothing in the structure blocks the direct call.
The class remains visible to the client in the code.
There is no reciprocal interface in this structure.
A language does not enforce the rule by itself.
questions.explain: An interface alone does not stop a direct call. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A Strategy interface gives a one-dimensional boundary: it isolates clients from the implementation in one direction and relies on discipline for the rest.
Strategy is the one-way boundary.
questions.q: The author uses the traditional ____ pattern to illustrate a one-dimensional boundary.
questions.explain: A ServiceBoundary interface used by clients and implemented by ServiceImpl classes is the Strategy pattern.

questions.q: A diagram shows Client depending on ServiceBoundary, ServiceImpl implementing it, and also a direct arrow from Client to ServiceImpl. What does the author say?
options: It is required, so that the client can construct the implementation it needs
It is the kind of backchannel that, in this structure, only discipline can prevent
It is harmless, since the interface is still present between them
It is impossible, since dependency inversion forbids such a direct arrow
optionExplain: The book calls the arrow nasty, not required.
Right: the book says nothing prevents it other than diligence and discipline.
The interface does not protect against the direct arrow.
Nothing in the structure makes it impossible.
questions.explain: The interface does not forbid the shortcut.
questions.rule: Only discipline holds this boundary.

questions.q: A team has budget for one interface and wants to keep clients off a payment module's classes. What does the Strategy shape give it?
options: A full boundary in both directions, at about half the usual cost of such a boundary
A guarantee that no code can reach the implementation any other way
Independent deployment of the client and the implementation
The clients are isolated from the implementation, in that one direction only
optionExplain: Both directions need reciprocal interfaces.
Nothing prevents a backchannel.
Deployment is a separate step.
Right: one direction is protected.
questions.explain: One interface gives one direction of isolation.
questions.rule: One interface, one direction.
Discipline does not scale by itself.
questions.q: True or false: As a team grows, a Strategy-only boundary gets easier to keep intact, because more people watch it.
questions.explain: Only discipline holds this boundary, and discipline is harder to keep as a team grows, so backchannels become more likely.

questions.q: A team plans to extract a pricing library later. It wraps pricing in an interface now, and a colleague calls this wasted effort. Which reply follows the author?
options: The inversion needed for a future boundary is in place, though discipline is still required
It is wasted, since a boundary cannot be added later whatever is done now, however carefully the team works
It gives a full boundary at a lower cost, so nothing more is ever needed
It is wasted, since only reciprocal interfaces ever help in a split
optionExplain: Right: the structure sets the stage for a future boundary.
The point is that it helps the later work.
It is not a full boundary.
A one-direction boundary does help.
questions.explain: It is a placeholder that makes a later full boundary easier.
questions.rule: A Strategy is a placeholder.
questions.teaches: The Strategy structure sets the stage for a future architectural boundary, because the necessary dependency inversion is already in place.

questions.q: True or false: A client that only calls a Facade class has no dependency on the service classes behind it.
questions.explain: The client depends on them transitively. The card next explains the cost.
questions.rule: A Facade is the simplest partial boundary: one class lists the services, but clients still depend, transitively, on every service class behind it.
One class lists the services.
questions.q: A Facade class lists all the ____ as methods and forwards the calls to classes the client is not supposed to access.
questions.explain: The boundary is simply the Facade class that lists all the services.

questions.q: Which feature does the Strategy boundary have that the Facade lacks?
options: A class that lists all the services as methods
Dependency inversion between the client and the implementation
Isolation in both directions through reciprocal interfaces
Independent deployment of the client and the services
optionExplain: That is what the Facade has.
Right: the Facade sacrifices even the dependency inversion.
Neither partial boundary has reciprocal interfaces.
Neither is deployed apart in these forms.
questions.explain: Strategy keeps the inversion in one direction; Facade drops it.
questions.rule: Facade drops inversion.

questions.q: A statically compiled client shows long rebuilds. It calls a Facade that forwards to ten service classes. What explains the rebuilds?
options: Facades always recompile their clients, whatever the service classes do or do not undergo
The transitive dependency: a change in any service class forces the client to recompile
The Facade has too many methods, which slows the compiler down
Dependency inversion is in place but is set up wrongly
optionExplain: Facades do not recompile clients by themselves.
Right: the client depends on the service classes through the Facade.
The number of methods is not the cause.
A Facade has no inversion.
questions.explain: The Facade hides the classes without removing the dependency.
questions.rule: Transitive dependency causes rebuilds.
A Facade is a convention.
questions.q: True or false: In a Facade structure, the compiler rejects a call from the client straight to a service class behind the Facade.
questions.explain: Nothing makes the service classes inaccessible, so the Facade marks the boundary only by convention.

questions.q: A team is choosing between skip-the-last-step, Strategy and Facade as a placeholder. Which statement matches the author?
options: Each has costs and benefits, suits some contexts, and can degrade if no full boundary arrives
Facade is always the best of the three, since it is the simplest and costs the least to build
Skip the last step is the only one of the three that cannot degrade
Only a Strategy placeholder can ever grow into a full boundary
optionExplain: Right: the author offers three examples among many.
Simplicity has a price, as the Facade shows.
The FitNesse story shows that it degrades too.
The author does not limit the growth to one.
questions.explain: Choose by context, and expect decay if the boundary never comes.
questions.rule: Every placeholder has costs.
questions.teaches: Each of the three partial boundaries has its own costs and benefits, suits certain contexts as a placeholder, and can degrade if the full boundary never materializes; there are many other ways.

questions.q: A text adventure must run in several human languages and keep saves in different places. How should its rules treat these two things?
options: Know the language, since the rules produce the replies
Know the store only, since saved games are the core of the rules
Know neither, and talk to each through its own API
Know both through a single combined settings object
optionExplain: The language is a UI concern.
The store is a detail too.
A fair guess: both vary, so both can sit behind APIs.
A combined object ties the two together.
questions.explain: Each varying thing gets its own API. The card next shows the layout.
questions.rule: Give each part that varies, such as the UI language or the data store, its own component behind an API the rules define, so that many variants can reuse the same rules.

questions.q: In the example, the game rules communicate with the UI component through a language-____ API.
questions.explain: The API does not depend on any human language, so the UI translates.
questions.rule: Give each part that varies, such as the UI language or the data store, its own component behind an API the rules define, so that many variants can reuse the same rules.

questions.q: A designer places both English and Spanish text inside GameRules, to avoid an extra component. What is the flaw?
options: Rules cannot hold text, so the design cannot be built at all with the tools at hand
English and Spanish need separate rules, since they differ in grammar
The store is now unprotected, since text and saves are linked
The rules now depend on the UI language, so every new language changes the rules
optionExplain: Rules can hold text; they just should not know the language.
Rules are the same for every language.
Storage is a separate matter.
Right: the rules should neither know nor care about the language.
questions.explain: Language belongs in the UI side.
questions.rule: Rules ignore the language.

questions.q: A fitness app logs workouts in kilograms or pounds and saves them on the phone or in the cloud. Following the example, which design fits?
options: A rules component that holds the unit conversions and also the code that writes to phone storage
A rules component with one API for the display side and one for storage, each with variants
One component holding units and storage, to keep the app small
A rules component per unit, each with its own copy of the storage
optionExplain: That puts both concerns inside the rules.
Right: each varying part is behind its own API.
That mixes two things that vary independently.
Copies of the rules multiply the work.
questions.explain: Two independent changes, two APIs.
questions.rule: One API per varying part.
New variants plug in.
questions.q: True or false: Adding a third human language to the example requires changes to the game rules.
questions.explain: A new Language implementation plugs in behind the same API, and the rules neither know nor care which language is used.

questions.q: A weekend project of 150 lines gets a proposal to use full clean architecture with APIs everywhere. What fits the author's footnote?
options: Not for a trivial program; the game stands in for a much larger system
Yes: every program, however small, deserves every circle and boundary
Only if the program has a UI, since UIs are the part that varies from one market to another
Only if it uses a database, since storage is what varies the most
optionExplain: Right: the author says the approach would not be applied to something so trivial.
The author says the opposite.
Triviality, not the UI, decides here.
Triviality, not the database, decides here.
questions.explain: The example is a proxy for a larger system.
questions.rule: Do not over-build a trivial program.
questions.teaches: The author says the clean architecture would not be applied to a game this trivial, which could be written in 200 lines or less; it stands in for a much larger system with significant architectural boundaries.

questions.q: A Language component translates text, and a TextDelivery component sends it. Who should define the API between them?
options: The user of the API, Language, with TextDelivery implementing it
The delivery component, since it knows what it is able to send
A third shared package that both of them import
The rules component, for both of them at once
optionExplain: A fair guess: the user decides what it needs.
That makes the user depend on the implementer's choices.
A shared package adds a dependency both ways.
The rules do not own this boundary.
questions.explain: The user owns the API. The card next confirms it.
questions.rule: Treat each axis of change as a potential boundary with an API that the using component defines and the used component implements.

questions.q: The API between two components is defined and owned by the ____, not by the implementer.
questions.explain: The user of the API defines it, and the implementer conforms.
questions.rule: Treat each axis of change as a potential boundary with an API that the using component defines and the used component implements.

questions.q: A team's TextDelivery component publishes the interface that Language must call. What is the problem, by the author's account?
options: Nothing is wrong, since implementers know their own capabilities better than the components that use them
Components should not publish interfaces at all and should be called directly
The implementer owns the API; the user should define it, so dependencies lead toward the policy
The interface should be owned by the rules component, which is at the top
optionExplain: The author says the opposite.
Interfaces are how polymorphic boundaries work.
Right: the API is owned by the upstream component.
Each boundary is owned by its own user.
questions.explain: The user owns the API.
questions.rule: The user owns the API.

questions.q: A checkout rules component must send receipts by email today and by push message later. Who defines the receipt-sending API?
options: The email sender, since it will be the first to exist
The checkout rules, with the senders implementing it
The push sender, since it will be the most modern
A shared messaging library that both senders import
optionExplain: The implementer would own it.
Right: the user of the API defines it.
Same: the implementer would own it.
A shared library sits between them and weakens ownership.
questions.explain: The rules state what they need.
questions.rule: The using side defines the API.
Variants implement the API.
questions.q: True or false: Adding SMS delivery beside the shell window means adding a new implementation of the delivery API, with Language and the rules unchanged.
questions.explain: Variants are implementations of the abstract API, so a new channel is a new implementation.

questions.q: In a chat app, the rules call a message formatter for output, and the formatter passes parsed user commands to the rules. How are the boundary interfaces arranged?
options: One set only, defined by the rules and implemented by the formatter
One set only, defined by the formatter and implemented by the rules
Two sets: one defined by the rules and implemented by the formatter, and one the other way round
None, since the two components call each other's classes directly, which is simpler to maintain
optionExplain: That covers only one direction.
That covers only the other direction.
Right: each component uses interfaces the other implements.
Direct calls would break the rule in one direction.
questions.explain: Interfaces run in both directions between two components.
questions.rule: Interfaces run both ways.
questions.teaches: Between two components, boundary interfaces run in both directions: each component uses interfaces that the other implements, and implements interfaces that the other uses.

questions.q: In a component diagram, an arrow from Language to GameRules means what?
options: Language's source code depends on GameRules, on the API that GameRules defines
Data flows from GameRules to Language and never in the other direction through the same API
GameRules calls Language at run time and Language never calls back
Language is the more important component of the two
optionExplain: A fair guess: arrows record dependencies.
Data actually flows both ways.
Run-time calls are not what the arrow shows.
Importance is the reverse: the target is the higher-level policy.
questions.explain: Arrows show who depends on whom. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Orient dependency arrows toward the highest-level policy: each independent concern forms a stream that meets at that policy, and there can be more than two.

questions.q: In the example, the two streams of data flow meet at the ____ component.
questions.explain: GameRules is the ultimate processor of the data in both streams.
questions.rule: Orient dependency arrows toward the highest-level policy: each independent concern forms a stream that meets at that policy, and there can be more than two.

questions.q: A colleague reads an arrow from TextDelivery to Language as: data flows from TextDelivery to Language only. What correction does the author give?
options: Arrows show the order in which the components are deployed to the machines that run them
Arrows point to the component that runs first at start-up
The colleague is right, since arrows always show data flow
Arrows point in the direction of source code dependencies, not of data flow
optionExplain: Deployment order is not what arrows show.
Start-up order is not what arrows show.
Data flows both ways in the example.
Right: the book adds this as a reminder in a note.
questions.explain: Dependency arrows are not data flow arrows.
questions.rule: Arrows show dependencies.

questions.q: A ride-sharing app has components Rules, Maps, Payments and Driver Chat. Where should the highest-level policy sit?
options: At the bottom with Maps, since Maps is the component that is used most often by drivers
At the top, with the other components depending on it through APIs it defines
In Payments, since money is the centre of the whole business model
Spread evenly over all components, to avoid a single high-level one
optionExplain: Usage count does not decide level.
Right: streams meet at the highest-level policy.
The centre of the business is not the same as the highest-level policy here.
The example puts one component on top.
questions.explain: Place the rules on top.
questions.rule: Rules on top, streams below.
New concern, new stream.
questions.q: True or false: Adding a network component for multiplayer play creates a third stream of data flow, still controlled by GameRules.
questions.explain: Each new concern becomes a new stream that meets at the highest-level policy.

questions.q: In a voice assistant, speech enters through AudioInput and SpeechToIntent and reaches DialogRules. Which describes the rest of the round trip?
options: DialogRules replies directly to AudioInput, bypassing SpeechToIntent on the way back
The reply starts in SpeechToIntent, which owns the dialog state
The reply is stored in DataStorage, and the user reads it from there
DialogRules sends its reply back down the same chain, each component translating
optionExplain: That skips the translating component.
The rules hold the policy and not the translator.
Storage is a separate stream.
Right: input rises through the chain and output descends again.
questions.explain: Input rises, output descends, and each component translates.
questions.rule: Input rises, output descends.
questions.teaches: Input rises through the Language component, translated into commands for GameRules, and the output descends back through Language, which translates it into the user's human language.

questions.q: Inside a game's rules, map movement and the player's health and win conditions both appear. Which is the higher-level policy?
options: The health and win-or-lose policy, which decides what each event costs or gives
Map movement, since it runs on every turn of the game and is used by every other part
Neither, since all rules inside one component sit at the same level
Map movement, since it must be written before anything else
optionExplain: A fair guess: policy that decides outcomes sits above mechanics that report events.
Frequency of use does not set the level.
Policies in one component can differ in level.
Writing order does not set the level.
questions.explain: The player's fate is decided above the mechanics. The card next gives the example.
questions.rule: Inside one component, look for policies at different levels: the lower level declares events and the higher level decides what they mean.
Mechanics report events.
questions.q: MoveManagement declares events such as FoundFood or ____ to the higher-level policy.
questions.explain: The lower-level mechanics declare events, and the higher-level policy decides what each one means for the player.

questions.q: True or false: In the multiplayer example, the line between MoveManagement and PlayerManagement is only a partial boundary.
questions.explain: The author says a full-fledged architectural boundary exists there, because the two are deployed apart.
questions.rule: Inside one component, look for policies at different levels: the lower level declares events and the higher level decides what they mean.

questions.q: A delivery app's routing code reports events such as Delayed or Arrived to a billing policy that decides refunds. Which is the higher-level policy?
options: The routing code, since it produces the events that everything else depends on
Neither, since both parts sit inside one app and share its policy
The refund screen, since it shows the result to the customer
The billing policy, which decides what each event costs or gives
optionExplain: Producing events is the lower-level task.
Policies inside one app can differ in level.
A screen is a delivery detail.
Right: the lower level declares events and the higher level decides.
questions.explain: Billing decides; routing reports.
questions.rule: The deciding policy is higher.

questions.q: The mechanics start to report a new event, FoundTreasure. What must change?
options: The mechanics must be changed to compute the new health of the player after each event of that kind
The higher-level policy must decide what it costs or gives; the mechanics only declare it
Both policies must be merged, since they share the new event
Nothing, since events carry their own meaning to the player
optionExplain: Health belongs to the higher-level policy.
Right: the meaning of an event belongs to the higher level.
The two levels stay apart.
An event has no effect until the policy decides.
questions.explain: The higher level assigns meaning to events.
questions.rule: Meaning lives above.

questions.q: In an analytics app, per-tenant rules run locally and billing runs on a central server with an API used by all tenants. What is the line between them?
options: A partial boundary, since both parts belong to the same product
No boundary, since a single team owns both parts
A full-fledged architectural boundary, as in the multiplayer example
A Facade, since the server lists its services as methods
optionExplain: Deployed apart, it is a full boundary.
Ownership does not decide the boundary.
Right: the policy is offered as a micro-service API.
The micro-service API is a full boundary, not a Facade.
questions.explain: A policy offered as a micro-service API to many components sits behind a full boundary.
questions.rule: Separate deployment means a full boundary.
questions.teaches: When a policy is offered as a micro-service API to many connected components, as PlayerManagement is in the multiplayer example, the line between them is a full-fledged architectural boundary.

questions.q: A startup wonders whether to build every architectural boundary on day one. Which view is closest to the author's?
options: Choose which to build fully, partly or not at all, and keep reviewing as friction appears
Build them all now, since adding a boundary later is always cheap
Build none, since YAGNI settles the matter for every project
Decide once at kickoff and keep to that decision for the whole of the project, whatever happens
optionExplain: A fair guess: the author asks for weighing and watching.
The author says late additions can be very costly.
The author sees wisdom in YAGNI but not a rule.
The author says the decision is not a one-time one.
questions.explain: Weigh and review. The card next gives the author's reasoning.
questions.rule: Weigh the cost of each boundary against the cost of ignoring it, aiming to build it where building becomes cheaper than ignoring.

questions.q: The author wants a boundary implemented at the ____ point where the cost of implementing becomes less than the cost of ignoring it.
questions.explain: The inflection point is where building becomes cheaper than ignoring.
questions.rule: Weigh the cost of each boundary against the cost of ignoring it, aiming to build it where building becomes cheaper than ignoring.

questions.q: How does the author weigh YAGNI against anticipating boundaries?
options: YAGNI has wisdom, yet a missing boundary can be very costly to add later
YAGNI is wrong, so every boundary should be anticipated from the first day
YAGNI wins, since boundaries built early are only speculation
YAGNI applies to code and not to architecture, so it never matters for the decisions here
optionExplain: Right: the author sees both sides.
The author says there is wisdom in YAGNI.
The author notes the cost of missing boundaries.
The author applies it to architecture and finds a tension.
questions.explain: Both costs are real, so the answer is a judgement.
questions.rule: Both costs are real.

questions.q: Two modules keep editing each other's files, with no boundary between them. This is the first friction. What does the author advise?
options: Ignore it, since friction is normal in any growing system and tends to settle by itself
Rebuild the whole system around new boundaries at once, before work goes on
Weigh the cost of adding the boundary now against the cost of living without it
Wait until a test fails before thinking about the boundary again
optionExplain: The author tells you to watch for friction.
That would build boundaries that are not needed.
Right: the first inkling of friction is the signal to weigh the costs.
Waiting for a failure misses the first inkling.
questions.explain: Friction is the signal to weigh.
questions.rule: Friction is the signal.
Ignoring has a growing cost.
questions.q: True or false: A boundary that is ignored for years becomes cheap to add once the team has comprehensive tests.
questions.explain: The author says a boundary added late is very expensive even in the presence of comprehensive test suites and refactoring discipline.

questions.q: A mobile team ignored a sync boundary at kickoff. Six months later, bug reports show cross-module edits. What does the method say about the earlier decision?
options: It was final, and a decision once made should be followed to the end
It proves YAGNI wrong, so every boundary should now be added
It should have been put off forever, since boundaries never pay
It should be reviewed, since the decision is made again as friction shows
optionExplain: The author says it is not a one-time decision.
The author does not say YAGNI is wrong.
The author says boundaries can pay for themselves.
Right: you watch the system as it evolves and review the decision frequently.
questions.explain: Decisions about boundaries are revisited as the system evolves.
questions.rule: Review boundary decisions often.
questions.teaches: The boundary decision is not made once at the start: you watch the system as it evolves, look for the first inkling of friction from a missing boundary, and review the decision frequently.

questions.q: The first code to run in a system builds its concrete objects and starts everything. How does it relate to the high-level business rules?
options: It sits above them, because it starts everything and so the rules depend on it
It sits beside them as a shared helper that the rules call to fetch settings
It sits outside them as the most detailed code, and nothing else depends on it
It sits inside them as the opening step of the central business logic itself
optionExplain: Starting first feels like being in charge, but control passing down to the rules is not a dependency of the rules on the start-up code.
Settings lookups feel handy, but a rule that calls start-up code would depend on the lowest-level detail.
Right: start-up code is the lowest-level detail, and the rules must not depend on it.
Start-up is a step in the story of a run, but its code is detail, not policy, so it does not belong inside the rules.
questions.explain: Start-up code is the most detailed part of the system, so it belongs on the outside where nothing depends on it. The card next shows the author's name for it.
questions.rule: Start-up code is detail, so it sits outside the policy.

questions.q: The author calls the Main component the ultimate ____.
questions.explain: Main is the lowest-level policy and the initial entry point, which is why the author calls it the ultimate detail.
questions.rule: Main is the ultimate detail.

questions.q: A startup class builds a PaymentGateway, a TaxCalculator and an EmailSender, then calls OrderProcessor.run(). Which statement fits the author's view?
options: The startup class plays Main: it may know every concrete class, but OrderProcessor should not depend on it
The startup class is high-level policy, so OrderProcessor may call back into it for shared settings
The startup class should be merged into OrderProcessor so one component both builds and uses the parts
The startup class is a boundary that every business rule should import to find the concrete classes
optionExplain: Right: it creates the concrete parts and hands over control, and nothing depends on it.
It starts the run, which makes it look important, but a call back into it would make the policy depend on the lowest-level detail.
Merging avoids one class, but it mixes the lowest-level detail with the policy that must stay clean of it.
Rules importing it would make everything depend on Main, the reverse of the author's picture.
questions.explain: The startup class does the job the author gives to Main: build the parts, then hand over control. Because nothing may depend on it, OrderProcessor must not reach back into it.
questions.rule: Main knows the concrete classes; the policy does not know Main.

questions.q: A reviewer writes: Main starts the system, so it is the highest-level component and business rules may import its settings. Which part is wrong, and why?
questions.rule: Starting first does not mean ranking first.
questions.hint: Which direction may dependencies point toward Main?
questions.a: The claim that Main is the highest-level component. The author calls Main the lowest-level policy and the ultimate detail, and nothing except the operating system depends on it, so business rules must not import its settings.

questions.q: In the Hunt the Wumpus example, what does Main do with the player's typed commands?
options: It carries out each command itself, since Main holds all of the game's rules and the higher levels only draw the screen
It hands the raw text to the operating system, which turns each command into a game action for the player
It stores each command in a file, from which a higher-level component reads and carries it out later
It runs the game loop and reads commands, but defers all processing to higher-level components
optionExplain: Main does the loop, so doing everything feels natural, but the author notes it defers all processing upward.
Only the operating system may depend on Main, but it does not interpret the game's commands.
Storing commands in a file is not in the example; Main passes the commands straight on.
Right: Main creates the input stream, runs the loop that interprets simple commands, and leaves the processing to higher levels.
questions.explain: Main owns the loop and reads simple commands, but it only translates them into calls on the higher-level game. Detail work stays in Main; decisions do not.
questions.rule: Main may read input and loop, but the processing happens above it.
questions.teaches: In the Hunt the Wumpus example Main creates the input stream and runs the main loop that interprets simple commands, but defers all processing to higher-level components.

questions.q: A web app's startup script reads a config file, builds a database adapter and starts the server. A developer proposes that the order rules read the config file directly. Why does this clash with the author's picture?
options: Config files change too rarely, so the rules would end up coupled to something far too stable to be useful
The config file belongs to the outermost circle, so rules reaching for it would depend on the lowest-level detail
The rules would be tied to the web server, which is the only part of a web app that is allowed to read files
Reading files makes the rules slow, and the author asks for fast high-level policy that does no input or output
optionExplain: Stability is not the issue; the clash is the direction of the dependency, from policy to detail.
Right: Main sits in the outermost circle and loads everything up for the high-level system, so the rules should not reach into it.
No component is singled out as the only reader of files; the point is the policy-to-detail dependency.
Speed is not part of the author's argument here; dependency direction is.
questions.explain: Main belongs to the outermost circle of the clean architecture: it loads everything up for the high-level system and then hands over control. Rules that read the config file would depend on that outer detail.
questions.rule: Policy receives what Main loads; it does not go and fetch it.
