questions.teaches: Main is a dirty low-level module in the outermost circle of the clean architecture: it loads everything up for the high-level system and then hands control over.

questions.q: A team uses a dependency injection framework to build its objects. Where should the framework do its wiring?
options: In every class that needs a dependency, so that each one can ask the framework for it
In Main, which then hands the objects to the rest of the system in ordinary code
In the domain entities, because they know best which collaborators they need
In the user interface layer, because that layer sits closest to the person using it
optionExplain: Each class asking the framework spreads it everywhere, so every class depends on the framework.
Right: the framework belongs in Main, the outermost detail.
Entities hold the central rules, and tying them to a framework makes the rules depend on a detail.
The user interface layer is itself a detail that depends on the rules, not the owner of system-wide wiring.
questions.explain: The framework is a detail, and Main is the home of details. The card next shows what Main does afterwards.
questions.rule: The framework lives in Main.

questions.q: Once dependencies are injected into Main, Main passes them on normally, without using the ____.
questions.explain: Main takes the dependencies from the framework, then distributes them by ordinary means.
questions.rule: After Main, the framework is out of the picture.

questions.q: A ReportService fetches its exporter by calling a framework annotation on itself. Which change fits the author's advice?
options: Add the same annotation to every caller of ReportService so that injection looks the same everywhere in the code
Move the exporter's construction into ReportService so that the class no longer needs the framework to find it
Keep the annotation and move ReportService itself into Main so that the framework stays inside Main as well
Move the framework wiring into Main, and have Main pass the exporter to ReportService in a plain constructor call
optionExplain: More annotations spread the framework further instead of confining it.
Building the exporter inside the service ties the service to a concrete class, which is the detail Main exists to handle.
Moving the service into Main would put policy inside the lowest-level detail.
Right: the framework stays in Main, and the service gets its collaborator by ordinary passing.
questions.explain: ReportService should not know the framework. Main injects the exporter once and passes it on in the usual way.
questions.rule: Wire in Main, pass on plainly.
questions.hint: Which component is allowed to know the framework?

questions.q: True or false: When the class that Main names by a string changes, Main has to be recompiled or redeployed.
questions.rule: A name in a string is not a compile-time dependency.
questions.explain: Main refers to the class only by name, so changes inside that class do not force Main to recompile or redeploy.

questions.q: Which set-up job does the Wumpus Main do before handing over to the game?
options: It builds the cave map: picks how many caverns, names and connects them, and places the player, wumpus, bats and pits
It decides whether the player dies when meeting the wumpus, as part of the opening setup before the game starts
It works out which cavern a bat carries the player to when the player enters a bat cavern during a game
It subtracts an arrow and a hit point each time the player shoots in a direction while a game is running
optionExplain: Right: Main creates the map and the starting positions, which is initial set-up.
Whether meeting the wumpus is fatal is a game rule, which belongs to the higher-level game.
Carrying the player off is behaviour during play, handled by the higher levels.
Changing arrows and health during play is game behaviour, not set-up.
questions.explain: Main sets the stage: the map and starting positions. Rules that decide what happens as play unfolds stay in the higher-level components.
questions.rule: Main prepares the initial conditions; the game rules run above it.
questions.teaches: In the Wumpus example Main also creates the map: it chooses a random number of caverns, names and connects them, and places the player, the wumpus, the bats and the pits.

questions.q: A mobile app's launcher builds a network client and a local database from config strings, then hands both to the use cases. A teammate wants each use case to read the config file itself. How does this compare with the author's view of Main?
options: It is fine, because use cases are the best place to know where outside resources come from
It is wrong only because config files must be read once per run, not once per use case
It moves a Main job, gathering outside resources and settings, into the high-level code
It is fine, as long as the use cases read the file through a dependency injection framework
optionExplain: Use cases hold policy; knowing where resources come from would tie that policy to the outside.
The number of reads is not the author's concern; the placement of the job is.
Right: Main sets up initial conditions and configurations and gathers outside resources, so use cases should receive them.
A framework in each use case spreads the framework instead of keeping it in Main.
questions.explain: The author's closing description of Main adds a job beyond creating objects: it sets up initial conditions and configurations and gathers all the outside resources. The use cases should receive these.
questions.rule: Main gathers; policy receives.
questions.teaches: Main sets up the initial conditions and configurations and gathers all the outside resources before it hands control over; creating objects is only part of its job.

questions.q: A product ships to three countries with different tax set-ups. Which structure does the author's view of Main suggest?
options: One Main with a country switch that the high-level rules read at run time to choose behaviour
One copy of the high-level policy for each country, each with its own start-up code inside it
One Main that the high-level rules import so that they can ask which country they are running in
One Main for each country, each wiring in its own pieces and then starting the same high-level policy
optionExplain: A switch read by the rules makes the policy depend on configuration detail.
Copying the policy multiplies the part that should stay single.
Rules importing Main would depend on the lowest-level detail.
Right: a Main plugin per configuration keeps the policy unchanged.
questions.explain: Each country is a configuration, and each configuration can have its own Main. The next card shows why that works.
questions.rule: One configuration, one Main.

questions.q: The author suggests thinking of Main as a ____ to the application.
questions.explain: Main is a plugin behind an architectural boundary, which is why several of them can exist.
questions.rule: Main is a plugin.

questions.q: A loyalty app is sold to one big customer that uses its own CRM. The high-level policy is shared by all customers. What fits the author's view?
options: Add an if for that customer inside the policy, which already knows which customer it is serving
Write a new Main for that customer that wires in its CRM adapter, and leave the policy untouched
Fork the whole policy for that customer, so its CRM code sits next to its rules
Add a flag that every use case reads to decide whether to call the customer's CRM
optionExplain: A customer check inside the policy ties the policy to one customer.
Right: a new configuration gets a new Main plugin.
A fork leaves two policies to keep in step.
A flag read in every use case spreads configuration detail through the policy.
questions.explain: A customer-specific set-up is a configuration, and configurations are the job of Main plugins. The shared policy stays as it was.
questions.rule: A new configuration means a new Main, not an edited policy.

questions.q: True or false: Under the plugin view, supporting one more jurisdiction should call for changes to the high-level policy.
questions.explain: The plugin view keeps jurisdictions in Main components, so a new jurisdiction should mean a new Main.
questions.rule: New configuration, new Main; the policy is unchanged.

questions.q: According to the author, which Main plugins might a team keep for its environments?
options: One for the database and one for the user interface
One for reading and one for writing
One for Dev, one for Test and one for Production
One for each class that the high-level policy contains
optionExplain: These are details that Main wires in, not configurations of the application.
Reading and writing are operations, not configurations.
Right: the author names Dev, Test and Production as examples.
Policy classes are not configurations; Main plugins are chosen by configuration.
questions.explain: The environments a team already has, Dev, Test and Production, each become a Main plugin.
questions.rule: Each environment can have its own Main.
questions.teaches: The author's examples of Main plugins by environment are one for Dev, one for Test and one for Production.

questions.q: A firm runs one invoicing engine for a regulator in each of two states and for a key customer with special hooks. How many Mains does the author's view suggest?
options: Three: one for each state and one for the customer, each a configuration with its own Main plugin
One: the engine has one policy, so it has one Main with branches for the states and the customer
Two: states are configurations, but a single customer is part of the policy
Four: each state and the customer need a Main, plus another to start them all
optionExplain: Right: the author mentions Mains per jurisdiction and per customer.
One Main with branches mixes the configurations that separate plugins keep apart.
A customer's special set-up is a configuration just as a state's is.
A coordinating extra Main is not in the author's picture.
questions.explain: The same idea reaches beyond environments. The author mentions a Main plugin for each country, each jurisdiction or each customer.
questions.rule: Any distinct configuration can be a Main.
questions.teaches: The same approach extends to one Main plugin for each country, each jurisdiction or each customer you deploy to.

questions.q: True or false: A system built from many small services has a good architecture by that fact alone.
questions.explain: How a system is cut into services says little by itself about where policy and detail are kept apart. The card next shows what the author counts as architecture.
questions.rule: Services alone are not architecture.

questions.q: Services that only separate application behaviors are little more than expensive ____ calls.
questions.explain: The author compares such services with function calls that cost more because they cross a process or platform.
questions.rule: A service that only separates behavior is an expensive function call.

questions.q: A team splits a shop into Cart, Pricing and Shipping services that call one another. What does the author say decides whether this split is architecture?
options: Whether the split draws boundaries that keep high-level policy apart from low-level detail and follow the Dependency Rule
Whether each service runs in its own process with its own deployment pipeline, release schedule and monitoring set-up
Whether the services talk to each other over a network, instead of through calls that stay inside one process memory
Whether each service has a dedicated team that owns the code, answers the pager and runs the service in production
optionExplain: Right: architecture is defined by boundaries that follow the Dependency Rule.
Separate processes are a deployment fact, not a rule-following boundary.
A network call is a mechanism of communication, which the author says does not define architecture.
Ownership by a team is an organisation fact, not an architectural boundary.
questions.explain: The author defines architecture by boundaries between policy and detail and by the direction of dependencies across them. Process, network and team structure do not by themselves meet that test.
questions.rule: Ask where the boundary is and which way dependencies point.
questions.hint: What kinds of things does the author say separate by boundaries?

questions.q: Sort each statement: does it match the author's view of services?

items.t: Services are function calls that cross process or platform boundaries
Some services are architecturally significant and some are not
Services that only separate behaviors are not necessarily significant
Using services is by its nature an architecture
A service split is architecture because it separates processes

questions.explain: The author treats services as function calls across process or platform boundaries, some of which matter architecturally. He rejects the idea that services in themselves define an architecture.
questions.rule: Services in themselves do not define an architecture.

questions.q: Which situation does the author warn about when he says some services have no architectural significance at all?
options: A service that is a single component with an architectural boundary running all the way around it
A service built from several components that are separated by architectural boundaries inside it
Clients and services so tightly coupled that they have no architectural significance whatever
A service that runs on a different platform from the clients that call it across the network
optionExplain: A single component with a boundary around it is a significant service in his picture.
A service divided by boundaries is also a significant case.
Right: he calls these cases hopefully rare, though experience suggests otherwise.
Running on another platform is a fact of deployment, not the sign of insignificance.
questions.explain: At the far end the author puts clients and services so coupled that no boundary of any meaning exists between them. He hopes this is rare, but says experience suggests otherwise.
questions.rule: Some service splits carry no architecture at all.
questions.teaches: In rare cases, which the author fears are not rare, clients and services may be so coupled that they have no architectural significance whatever.

questions.q: A team wraps one self-contained pricing component in its own service, with a firm boundary around it. How does the author describe such a service?
options: As a service with no architecture at all, since it contains only one component that could be divided
As a service that is a single component, completely surrounded by an architectural boundary
As an expensive function call, since every service is little more than that and nothing beyond it
As a service that is architecturally significant only if it also owns a database of its own
optionExplain: Having one component does not make it architecture-free; the boundary around it counts.
Right: a service can be one component enclosed by a boundary.
Only services that merely separate behaviors fall into that description.
A database is not part of the author's test; the boundary and the Dependency Rule are.
questions.explain: The author says a service might be a single component with an architectural boundary completely around it. That kind of service is architecturally significant.
questions.rule: One component inside a real boundary can be a significant service.
questions.teaches: A service might be a single component, completely surrounded by an architectural boundary.

questions.q: In a monolithic system, which function calls define its architecture?
options: Those made most often when the system is running under heavy load
Those made between functions that sit in different source files
Those that are public, since any public call may be used by other modules
Those that cross architectural boundaries in line with the Dependency Rule
optionExplain: Frequency measures traffic, not the separation of policy from detail.
File boundaries are layout, not architectural boundaries.
Visibility is a language feature; many public calls only separate behaviors.
Right: the author says architecture is defined by calls that cross boundaries and follow the Dependency Rule.
questions.explain: Only some calls matter architecturally. The card next shows how the same reasoning applies to services.
questions.rule: Boundary-crossing calls that follow the Dependency Rule define architecture.

questions.q: A service is a function call that crosses a process or ____ boundary.
questions.explain: The author describes services as function calls across process and/or platform boundaries.
questions.rule: A service is a function call across a process or platform.

questions.q: In an order monolith, which call is most likely to be architecturally significant?
options: A call from one pricing helper to another helper in the same class, which formats the numbers shown
The call that runs most often when the profiler measures the system during a busy afternoon of orders
A call from the web adapter into a use case, where the source dependency points toward the use case
The call with the most parameters, since it moves the most information between two parts of the system
optionExplain: A helper-to-helper call only separates one behavior from another.
Frequency says nothing about boundaries.
Right: it crosses the line between detail and policy in line with the Dependency Rule.
The number of parameters is not the author's test.
questions.explain: The significant calls cross a boundary between detail and policy and point inward. Calls inside a class only separate behaviors.
questions.rule: Significance comes from the boundary crossed.

questions.q: A colleague argues: services cross process boundaries, so every service call defines our architecture. Which step is wrong?
options: A process boundary alone is not enough; the call must also cross an architectural boundary in line with the Dependency Rule
A service call is not a function call at all, so it cannot sensibly be compared with a function call in a monolith
Process boundaries matter only in monoliths, so they are irrelevant when the system is built from several services
Architecture is defined by deployment units, so a call between two services defines nothing about the architecture
optionExplain: Right: only some services are architecturally significant.
The author says services are function calls across process or platform boundaries.
Process boundaries are part of what makes a call a service call.
The author defines architecture by boundaries and dependencies, not by deployment units.
questions.explain: The colleague treats every service call as architecture. The author says some are and some are not.
questions.rule: A process boundary is not an architectural boundary by default.

questions.q: A team's services ignore the Dependency Rule but let a payment feature scale on its own servers. What does the author say about such services?
options: They are of no use, because services without the Dependency Rule have no benefits
They become significant as soon as they run on separate servers
They should be merged back into the monolith, since architecture is the only reason to split
They may still bring substantial benefits, even though they are not architecturally significant
optionExplain: He denies that: benefits can exist without architectural significance.
Running apart does not make a service significant; the boundary and rule do.
He does not tell teams to merge services; he says the benefits are real.
Right: he says services can bring substantial benefits whether they obey the Dependency Rule or not.
questions.explain: The author separates two questions: whether a service is architecture and whether it is worth having. Splitting across processes and platforms may help even when no rule is followed.
questions.rule: Worth building and architecturally significant are different questions.
questions.teaches: There are often substantial benefits to services that separate functionality across processes and platforms, whether or not they obey the Dependency Rule.

questions.q: In a hospital system, sort each call: is it likely to be architecturally significant in the author's sense?

items.t: The appointment screen calls the scheduling rules through an interface the rules own
The rules call the lab-results gateway through an interface the rules own
The scheduling rules call a helper that formats dates
A report service is called only to put patient names in capitals

questions.explain: Calls that cross a line between policy and detail in line with the Dependency Rule are the significant ones. Calls that only separate small behaviors are not, even across a process.
questions.rule: Ask whether a call crosses a policy-detail boundary.
questions.teaches: The chapter itself is interested only in the architecturally significant services; the rest are ordinary function calls separated by a process.

questions.q: True or false: Because services run in separate processes, adding a field to a record they share cannot force changes in more than one service.
questions.explain: Every service that operates on the new field has to change. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Shared data couples services across processes.

questions.q: Services are decoupled at the level of individual ____, but strongly coupled by the data they share.
questions.explain: A separate process protects a service's variables from others, but not the meaning of the records they pass around.
questions.rule: Decoupled in variables, coupled in data.

questions.q: A booking service and a billing service both read an Invoice record. The booking team changes the amount field from pre-tax to post-tax and tells only its own team. What does the author's argument predict?
options: Nothing happens, because the formally defined interfaces of the two services protect billing from the change in booking
Billing misreads the amounts: the services are coupled through the meaning of the data despite separate processes
Billing is unaffected, because it cannot reach booking's variables from inside its own process on another machine
Only a network failure could reveal the change, since the invoice data crosses a network between the two services
optionExplain: A defined interface gives the shape of the data, not agreement on what a field means.
Right: services must agree about the interpretation of shared data.
Billing cannot reach variables, but it reads the record, which is shared.
The mismatch shows up as wrong results, not as a failure of the network.
questions.explain: Both services depend on what the field means. Changing it in one place without the other breaks the agreement, whatever the process boundary.
questions.rule: Agreeing on meaning is coupling.

questions.q: Suppose the same Invoice record were passed between two classes in one process. How would the coupling to the record's meaning compare?
options: It would be weaker, because classes that live in one process cannot be coupled to each other through a shared record
It would be the same: the classes must still agree what each field means, so the service boundary did not remove it
It would disappear, because a change to the record forces no change elsewhere when everything lives inside one process
It would be stronger only because the classes would share variables in addition to the record they already pass
optionExplain: Classes can be coupled through records as services can.
Right (Our reading): the book's point is that data coupling is not removed by the process boundary.
A changed record still affects whoever operates on the changed field.
Sharing variables could add coupling but does not change the data coupling already present.
questions.explain: Our reading: the author's argument is that the process boundary leaves data coupling in place, so moving the same record into one process would not change that coupling.
questions.rule: A process boundary does not remove coupling through data.

questions.q: True or false: Service interfaces are better defined and more rigorous than function interfaces.
questions.rule: Well-defined interfaces belong to functions too.
questions.teaches: Service interfaces are no more formal, no more rigorous and no better defined than function interfaces.
questions.explain: The author says service interfaces are no more formal, rigorous or well defined than function interfaces.

questions.q: Two services share no records, but run on one server and use the same connection pool. Which coupling does the author's argument also count?
options: No coupling at all, because shared hardware is not shared data
Coupling through variables, since a shared pool is a shared variable
Coupling that the interfaces remove, because interfaces hide resources
Coupling through shared resources within a processor or on the network
optionExplain: Separate data does not make them independent; shared resources can still couple them.
The author says services are decoupled at the level of variables.
Interfaces define calls; they do not remove a shared resource.
Right: services can be coupled by shared resources in a processor or on the network.
questions.explain: Besides shared data, the author names shared resources within a processor or on the network as a way services remain coupled.
questions.rule: Shared resources couple services too.
questions.teaches: Services can still be coupled by shared resources within a processor or on the network, as well as by the data they share.

questions.q: True or false: Large enterprise systems can only be built to scale from independently deployable services.
questions.explain: History has shown monoliths and component-based systems can scale as well. The card next gives the author's two replies.
questions.rule: Services are not the only scalable option.

questions.q: History shows that large enterprise systems can also be built from monoliths and ____-based systems.
questions.explain: Monoliths and component-based systems have both been used for large systems.
questions.rule: Services are one option, not the only one.

questions.q: Two teams own an Orders service and an Inventory service. Orders needs a new field that Inventory must also interpret. What follows from the author's argument?
options: The releases have to be coordinated, because the services are coupled through the data
Each team can release alone, because every service has its own deployment pipeline
Only Orders must change, because Inventory does not own the record
The teams should be merged into one team, since coordination is a failure of independence
optionExplain: Right: to the extent services are coupled by data, the work must be coordinated.
A separate pipeline does not remove the agreement both services need on the field.
Inventory operates on the new field, so it must change too.
The author does not say teams should merge; he says work must be coordinated.
questions.explain: Both services use the field, so both must change and agree. Their independence is limited by that coupling.
questions.rule: Coupling by data limits independence.

questions.q: True or false: By the author's argument, the coordination services need depends on how far they are coupled by data or behavior, not on how many there are.
questions.rule: Coordination follows coupling, not count.
questions.explain: To the extent that services are coupled by data or behavior, development, deployment and operation must be coordinated; count alone does not decide it.

questions.q: On what working model does the independence claim rest, according to the author?
options: A central operations team deploys every service on behalf of all of the development teams in the company
A single team writes all of the services but releases each of them on its own schedule
A dedicated team writes, maintains and operates its service as part of a dev-ops strategy
A vendor team writes the service while the customer team runs it in the customer's own data centre
optionExplain: Central operations is the opposite of a team owning its own service.
A single team is not the claim; the claim is many teams.
Right: the supposed benefit is that a dedicated team owns development, maintenance and operation.
Vendor ownership is not mentioned in the claim.
questions.explain: The claim describes teams that own their services end to end. The author's two replies address whether that ownership can really be independent.
questions.rule: The claim is that each service has a team that owns it end to end.
questions.teaches: The claim rests on a dev-ops strategy in which a dedicated team writes, maintains and operates its own service.

questions.q: A logistics firm with 400 developers plans microservices so that teams can work independently. Which question does the author's argument say to ask first?
options: How many services can the platform host before the network between them becomes the limit on speed?
Which services can be assigned to the largest teams so that none of the teams is left without work?
How soon can the old monolith be switched off once the first services have been released to customers?
To what extent will these services be coupled by data or behavior, and so need coordinated work?
optionExplain: Platform capacity is not the author's concern here.
Team size does not decide independence.
Switching off the monolith does not address coupling.
Right: coupling decides how independent the work can be, in development, deployment and operation.
questions.explain: The author notes that to the extent that services are coupled by data or behavior, their development, deployment and operation must all be coordinated.
questions.rule: Ask how coupled the services are before counting on independence.
questions.teaches: Coupling forces coordination across all three activities: development, deployment and operation.

questions.q: A taxi system is a chain of four services: UI, finder, selector and dispatcher. A new rule must exclude certain drivers and vehicles from certain orders. How many services change?
options: Only the finder, because it is the service that builds the candidate list of taxis
All four, because the rule touches every step from order to dispatch
Only the selector, because it is the service that applies the customer's criteria
Two, the finder and the selector, because they are the services that handle taxi data
optionExplain: The finder builds candidates, but the UI, selector and dispatcher also need the new rule.
Right: the author says all of them have to change.
The selector applies criteria, but it cannot apply a rule the others do not carry.
Two services seem enough, but the UI and dispatcher are involved as well.
questions.explain: A rule that cuts across the chain touches every service. The card next walks through the example.
questions.rule: A cross-chain feature changes the whole chain.

questions.q: Put the four services of the taxi aggregator in the order an order flows through them.
items: TaxiUI
TaxiFinder
TaxiSelector
TaxiDispatcher
questions.explain: The UI takes the order, the finder gathers candidate taxis, the selector chooses one and the dispatcher orders it.
questions.rule: Order, find, select, dispatch.

questions.q: A restaurant app is built from Menu, Cart, Kitchen and Payment services. A new feature lets customers declare allergies, and every dish must be checked. What should the team expect?
options: Only the Menu service will change, since dishes and their descriptions are held there and nowhere else
No service will change, since every service has an interface that is formally defined and stable
Most or all of the services will change together, and their releases must be coordinated
Only the Kitchen service will change, since the cooks are the people who must act on the allergy
optionExplain: Cart, Kitchen and Payment must carry the allergy as well.
Interfaces do not make a cross-cutting feature disappear.
Right: a feature that cuts across the whole chain touches every service.
Kitchen acts on it, but the others must carry the data to Kitchen.
questions.explain: As with the kitten feature, a requirement that touches every step of the order forces change in every service that touches the order.
questions.rule: Look for features that run through the whole chain.

questions.q: True or false: Our reading: a change to how TaxiDispatcher contacts one supplier would probably need changes in all four services.
questions.rule: Only features that cut across the chain spread through it.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book's trouble comes from a feature that cuts across every service. A change that stays inside one service's job should stay inside that service.

questions.q: Which kitten rule depends on the recent history of a vehicle?
options: A vehicle that delivered kittens in the last 3 days must not be selected for customers who declare allergies
Drivers who are allergic to cats must not be selected for any kitten orders that come in to the system
Only some of the taxi suppliers have agreed to take part in the new kitten delivery service in the city
Kittens are collected from several collection points that are set up across the city for the new service
optionExplain: Right: the 3-day rule looks back at what a vehicle carried.
That rule is about a driver's attribute, not about history.
Participation is a business decision about suppliers.
Collection points are locations, not a rule about history.
questions.explain: The 3-day rule means the system must remember what each vehicle carried, which is why even the selection step needs new data.
questions.rule: Some kitten rules need new data about the past.
questions.teaches: The kitten feature adds a history rule: a vehicle that delivered kittens within the last 3 days must not be chosen for a customer who declares an allergy.

questions.q: A company has 40 programmers and splits its system into micro-services, one small team per few services. Roughly how many services does the author's footnote suggest?
options: About one per programmer, roughly 40
About one per team, roughly 10
About one per customer, roughly 100
About one per feature, roughly 400
optionExplain: Right: the footnote says the number of micro-services will be roughly equal to the number of programmers.
One per team undercounts; small teams own several services.
Customers are not what counts services.
Features are not what counts services.
questions.explain: The footnote to the taxi example says that, with small teams each owning a few services, the number of micro-services will be roughly equal to the number of programmers.
questions.rule: Many small teams mean many services.
questions.teaches: In the taxi example the number of micro-services is roughly equal to the number of programmers.

questions.q: True or false: Only service-oriented systems have to deal with features that cut across every part of the system.
questions.explain: Any system split by function can meet such a feature. The card next names the problem.
questions.rule: Cross-cutting features are not a service-only problem.

questions.q: The author calls features like kitten delivery, which touch every functional behavior, cross-____ concerns.
questions.rule: A feature across all behaviors is a cross-cutting concern.
questions.explain: The kitty problem is the problem of cross-cutting concerns.

questions.q: A bank splits its system into Accounts, Transfers, Statements and Notifications. Sort each new requirement.
questions.rule: Cross-cutting means every piece is touched.

items.t: Every operation must record an audit entry with a reason code
Every screen and message must show amounts in the customer's currency format
Statements must print in a larger font
Transfers get a new daily limit
Notifications move to a different email provider

questions.explain: Requirements that need a change in every piece cut across the split. The others touch only one piece.

questions.q: A manager says: our monolith has no services, so cross-cutting features cannot hurt it. What is wrong with this?
options: Monoliths are the only structures that cannot be split by function, so they escape the problem entirely
Cross-cutting features hurt only those systems that are built and maintained by more than one team
The author says every software system must face the problem, whether service-oriented or not
A monolith avoids cross-cutting features because it has a single deployment instead of several
optionExplain: A monolith can be split into functional modules like any other system.
The problem is in the structure, not in the number of teams.
Right: the problem is not specific to services.
A single deployment does not remove the need to change many modules.
questions.explain: The manager assumes services are the cause. The author says the problem faces every significant software system.
questions.rule: Any functional decomposition can be cut across.
questions.hint: What does the author say about systems that are not service oriented?

questions.q: A system cut up by functional behavior, like the chain of taxi services, is called a functional ____.
questions.rule: Name the structure to see its weakness.
questions.teaches: A system cut up by functional behavior, like the service chain, is called a functional decomposition, and such decompositions are very vulnerable to new cross-cutting features.
questions.explain: The author names this structure a functional decomposition and says it is very vulnerable to cross-cutting features.

questions.q: A mobile team has one module per screen. A new feature, a dark theme, must change every screen module. Which statement fits the author?
options: The feature is easy, because each screen is independent and can be changed alone
Teams that own screens must carefully coordinate the development and deployment of the feature
The feature should be dropped, because cutting across modules is a design error by the team
Only the team that owns the home screen needs to act, because it is the entry point
optionExplain: Screens are independent in structure but not for a feature that runs through all of them.
Right: the author says the kitten feature had to be developed and deployed with great care.
The author does not blame the team; he says every system faces the problem.
The entry point is not special for a feature that touches every screen.
questions.explain: As with the taxi services, a feature that touches every module forces coordinated work.
questions.rule: Cross-cutting features need coordination in a functional decomposition.
questions.teaches: Because every service changes for such a feature, its development and deployment must be very carefully coordinated.

questions.q: A new feature touches every step of a pipeline in a component-based design. Which approach keeps edits to existing classes smallest?
options: Add if-statements for the feature to every existing class that handles one of the steps of the pipeline
Copy each existing class and edit the copies so that the feature has its own separate version of each step
Move the feature into the shared database so that no class has to know about it or be changed to handle it
Put the feature in a new component whose classes override abstract base classes using Template Method or Strategy
optionExplain: If-statements edit every class and tie each to the feature.
Copies double the code to maintain.
The database can store data, but the behaviour still has to live in code.
Right: polymorphic extension leaves the existing classes alone.
questions.explain: Extending through abstract base classes lets a new component add behaviour without editing the old ones. The card next shows the author's version.
questions.rule: Extend through abstractions.

questions.q: Match each part of the author's component-based taxi design to its role.
pairs: Keep the logic common to rides and kittens
Holds the ride-specific logic taken out of the original classes
The pattern used to override the base classes
questions.explain: The base classes keep the shared logic, the two components override them for their features, and a pattern such as Template Method or Strategy is the mechanism.
questions.rule: Shared logic below, features above, patterns in between.

questions.q: A notification system must add an SMS channel that affects formatting, sending and logging. Which design follows the author's approach?
options: Add an if for SMS inside each of the formatting, sending and logging classes, using a flag set at start-up
Clone the whole email system and change the clone so that it formats, sends and logs text messages instead
Keep abstract steps for formatting, sending and logging in a core component, and add an SMS component that overrides them
Add a setting to the database that tells every class to behave differently when the channel is SMS rather than email
optionExplain: If-statements put the feature into every existing class.
A clone leaves two systems to maintain.
Right: the new feature lives in its own component and overrides abstractions.
A setting read in every class spreads the feature through the code.
questions.explain: The SMS channel is a new feature that cuts across several steps, so it goes into its own component that overrides the abstract steps.
questions.rule: A feature across steps becomes a component over abstractions.

questions.q: A sketch shows the base-class component importing the Kittens component directly. What does it break?
options: The Dependency Rule: Kittens and Rides should depend on the base classes, not the reverse
The Open-Closed Principle: base classes should never be extended by other components
The single responsibility principle: a component should have only one class
The need for factories: base classes must create their own subclasses
optionExplain: Right: dependencies must point toward the abstractions.
Extending base classes is the way the design follows the Open-Closed Principle.
That principle is about reasons to change, not the number of classes.
Base classes that create subclasses would depend on the details.
questions.explain: In the author's design the new components depend on the base classes. A base-class component that imports a feature component reverses the dependency.
questions.rule: Features depend on the abstractions, never the other way.

questions.q: In the author's design the kitten component is added as a new jar file, Gem or ____ and loaded dynamically at runtime.
questions.rule: A feature is a new loadable unit, not an edit.
questions.teaches: The kitten feature is added to the system as a new jar file, Gem or DLL, and loaded dynamically at runtime.
questions.explain: Only the user interface changes; the new component arrives as a loadable unit.

questions.q: In a plugin system for a document editor, who should create the objects that implement a new export format?
options: The core component's base classes, which pick the plugin class by name when an export is requested
The plugin classes themselves, which create each other as soon as the editor starts up for the user
The operating system, which loads whichever classes it finds in the folder where the editor is installed
Factories under the control of the user interface, so the core never names the plugin classes
optionExplain: Base classes creating plugin classes would depend on them.
Plugins creating each other leaves nobody in charge of what is created.
The operating system is not the author's chosen creator.
Right: in the author's design the classes that implement features are created by factories under the control of the UI.
questions.explain: In the taxi design, factories under the UI's control create the classes that implement Rides and Kittens, so the base classes never name them.
questions.rule: Factories, not base classes, create the feature classes.
questions.teaches: In the author's design the classes that implement the features are created by factories under the control of the user interface.

questions.q: True or false: A service has to be a small monolith, so adding a feature to it means changing and redeploying its code.
questions.explain: A service can have the same component structure as a program. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: A service can have components too.

questions.q: In Java, each new feature can be another ____ file whose classes extend the abstract classes of the service.
questions.explain: The service is a set of abstract classes in jars, and features arrive as more jars.
questions.rule: A feature is another jar.

questions.q: A pricing service must gain a seasonal discount without redeploying the service. Which design follows the author?
options: Edit the core pricing class to include the discount, then redeploy the service in the usual way after testing it
Keep abstract pricing steps in the service's core jar, and ship the discount as a separate jar that extends them
Create a second pricing service that calls the first one and then adjusts the prices it gets back for the season
Move the discount rules into the caller, which applies them after the pricing service has replied with a price
optionExplain: Editing the core class is what the structure is meant to avoid.
Right: a feature is a new component extending the service's abstractions.
A second service adds a call hop and may couple to the first by data.
Moving rules to callers spreads pricing logic outside the service.
questions.explain: A component structure lets the discount be delivered as its own unit that extends the core's abstractions.
questions.rule: Add features as components, not edits.

questions.q: True or false: A service whose rules sit in one module with no abstractions can take a new feature by adding a jar to its load path.
questions.rule: No abstractions, no extension without edits.
questions.explain: A jar can only extend abstractions the service already offers, so a service without a component structure has to be edited.

questions.q: Which principle does adding new features as derivative classes in this way satisfy?
options: The Single Responsibility Principle
The Open-Closed Principle
The Liskov Substitution Principle
The Interface Segregation Principle
optionExplain: Single responsibility concerns the reasons a class changes.
Right: the author says adding new features this way conforms to the Open-Closed Principle.
Liskov concerns substituting subtypes safely.
Interface segregation concerns clients that depend on unused methods.
questions.explain: A service open for extension through new components and closed against edits to its existing ones follows the Open-Closed Principle.
questions.rule: Extension without edits is the Open-Closed Principle.
questions.teaches: Adding new features as new derivative classes in new components conforms to the Open-Closed Principle.

questions.q: A Java service team ships the kitten rules as KittenRules.jar. How is the feature deployed under the author's design?
options: By rebuilding the service with the jar's source copied in and releasing it
By replacing the service's base jar with one that has the kitten rules merged in
By starting a new service that holds KittenRules.jar and forwards calls to the old one
By adding the jar to the service's load path; the service itself is not redeployed
optionExplain: Copying the source in changes the service itself.
Replacing the base jar redeploys the service's core.
A forwarding service adds a hop and keeps the old service unchanged but coupled by calls.
Right: deploying a feature means adding the jar to the load paths of the service.
questions.explain: The author says deploying a new feature becomes a matter of adding the new jar files to the load paths of the services.
questions.rule: Features arrive on the load path.
questions.teaches: Deploying a new feature means adding the new jar files to the load paths of the services, not redeploying the services themselves.

questions.q: According to the author, where do the architecturally meaningful boundaries of a service-based system run?
options: Through the services, dividing each into components
Between the services, along every network call
Around the whole system only, at the load balancer
Between the teams, along the lines of ownership
optionExplain: Right: the boundaries run through the services.
Network calls separate services but need not separate policy from detail.
A single outer wall tells nothing about the inside.
Team lines are organisation, not architecture.
questions.explain: The author says the boundaries do not fall between services. The card next gives his reason.
questions.rule: Boundaries inside services.

questions.q: Architectural boundaries run ____ the services, dividing them into components.
questions.explain: The boundaries cut through services rather than between them.
questions.rule: Boundaries run through services.

questions.q: An Inventory service has one codebase mixing REST controllers, stock rules and a SQL driver. To give it architecture in the author's sense, what comes next?
options: Split it into three smaller services, one each for the controllers, the rules and the driver, calling each other over HTTP
Run a second copy of the whole service behind a load balancer so that the service can scale with the number of requests
Split it into components for the rules and for the details, with dependencies pointing at the rules, behind a boundary
Give the controllers, the rules and the driver each their own team and their own deployment pipeline and release cycle
optionExplain: Three services would make the same cut between processes without a rule-following boundary.
Scaling the service does not change its internal architecture.
Right: the boundary belongs inside the service, with the Dependency Rule.
Teams and pipelines are organisation, not boundaries.
questions.explain: The service already runs as one process, so its architecture has to come from components and the direction of their dependencies.
questions.rule: Architecture is built inside the service.

questions.q: Sort each item: does it define architecture, in the author's view?

items.t: Boundaries drawn within the system
Dependencies that cross those boundaries
Components inside a service that follow the Dependency Rule
The physical mechanism by which elements communicate
Whether elements run as separate processes

questions.explain: The author defines architecture by the boundaries and the dependencies that cross them. The mechanisms of communication and execution do not define it.
questions.rule: Boundaries and dependencies define architecture; mechanisms do not.

questions.q: What does the author say about the value of services, even though they are not architecturally significant by themselves?
options: They are useful only when they follow the Dependency Rule
They are useful only for systems with fewer than ten components
They are not useful, because a monolith always does the job better
They are useful for the scalability and develop-ability of a system
optionExplain: He says services can help whether or not they follow the rule.
Component count is not a condition he gives.
He does not claim monoliths do the job better.
Right: services are useful to scalability and develop-ability.
questions.explain: The author separates value from architecture: services help a system scale and be developed, but they do not by themselves define its architecture.
questions.rule: Useful is not the same as architecturally significant.
questions.teaches: Services are useful to the scalability and develop-ability of a system, but in and of themselves they are not architecturally significant elements.

questions.q: A search service has an indexing component, a ranking component and a storage adapter, separated by boundaries that follow the Dependency Rule. How would the author describe it?
options: As a single component completely surrounded by one boundary
As a service composed of several components separated by architectural boundaries
As a service with no architectural significance because it has several parts
As three services that happen to share a process
optionExplain: That describes a service with no internal boundaries.
Right: a service can contain several components with boundaries between them.
The internal boundaries give it significance.
It is one service whose parts are components, not three services.
questions.explain: The author allows both shapes: one component inside a boundary, or several components separated by boundaries.
questions.rule: A service may have boundaries inside it.
questions.teaches: A service might be composed of several components separated by architectural boundaries.

questions.q: True or false: From an architectural point of view, a tiny TDD test and a large Cucumber acceptance test are different kinds of component.
questions.explain: The author calls all tests architecturally equivalent. The card next gives the reason.
questions.rule: All tests are architecturally equivalent.

questions.q: Tests depend ____ on the components of the system, toward the code they check.
questions.explain: Tests are detailed and concrete, so they depend toward the code being tested.
questions.rule: Tests depend inward.

questions.q: Which dependency in a shop codebase breaks the Dependency Rule for tests?
options: An order test imports the order rules in order to call them directly
An integration test imports the database adapter that it exercises
The order rules import a helper class from the folder of order tests
An acceptance test imports the web controller that it drives from outside
optionExplain: Tests depending on rules is the correct direction.
Tests depending on adapters is the correct direction.
Right: the system would depend on a test.
Tests depending on controllers is the correct direction.
questions.explain: Tests may depend on any part of the system, but nothing in the system may depend on a test.
questions.rule: Arrows run from tests to the system, never back.

questions.q: True or false: If a production class calls a utility that lives in the test code, the system now depends on its tests.
questions.rule: Nothing in the system depends on the tests.
questions.explain: The dependency points from the system to a test, reversing the rule that nothing in the system depends on the tests.

questions.q: What follows for large tool-driven tests such as FitNesse or Cucumber suites?
options: They are architecturally equivalent to tiny TDD tests: both are concrete and depend inward
They belong to the inner circles, since they check whole features of the system and not single classes
They are the only tests that need to obey the Dependency Rule, since they are so large in scope
They fall outside the system, since they use separate tools that the system itself does not use
optionExplain: Right: the author says they are architecturally equivalent.
Size does not move a test inward.
The rule applies to every test.
Using a separate tool does not take a test out of the system.
questions.explain: The equivalence covers tiny and large tests alike, so tools or size do not change a test's place.
questions.rule: Size and tooling do not change a test's place.
questions.teaches: The author names FitNesse, Cucumber, SpecFlow and JBehave tests as large tests that are architecturally equivalent to the tiny tests of TDD.

questions.q: In the author's picture of circles, where does a payroll system's test suite belong?
options: In the outermost circle, depending inward on the components it tests
In the middle circle, between the rules and the interface adapters
In the innermost circle, beside the entities, since tests protect them
Outside the circles, since tests are not part of the system
optionExplain: Right: the author calls tests the outermost circle.
Nothing in the system depends on tests, so they do not sit in the middle.
The innermost circle holds the most general policy, which tests are not.
The author says tests are part of the system.
questions.explain: Tests are very detailed and concrete, so they are the outermost circle, like Main, and depend inward.
questions.rule: Tests are the outermost circle.
questions.teaches: You can think of the tests as the outermost circle in the architecture.

questions.q: Which part of a system is most likely to be deployed on its own even when nothing else is?
options: The domain entities
The database schema
The tests
The user interface
optionExplain: Entities travel with the rest of the production code.
A schema is deployed with the database, usually alongside the code.
Right: tests are deployed in test systems, apart from production.
A user interface is usually part of the same release as the rest.
questions.explain: Tests are normally deployed to test systems and not to production. The card next explains what that makes them.
questions.rule: Tests deploy on their own.

questions.q: Tests support development, not ____.
questions.explain: Tests help the people building the system; the running system does not need them.
questions.rule: Tests support development, not operation.

questions.q: A small cafe app deploys all of its parts together. Does the author say its tests need separate packaging?
options: No: when nothing else is deployed separately, the tests ship inside the production package with the rest
Yes: tests are deployed in test systems, so they are deployed independently even where nothing else is
No: tests are deployed together with the code they test, wherever that code happens to be deployed
Yes, but only if the cafe app has more than one team that writes and looks after the tests
optionExplain: Shipping tests to production is not the author's picture.
Right: the author says tests are independently deployed even in systems where independence is not otherwise needed.
Tests are deployed to test systems, not with the production code.
The number of teams plays no role in his claim.
questions.explain: Independent deployment of tests does not depend on whether the rest of the system is split.
questions.rule: Tests are deployed independently in any system.

questions.q: A reviewer says: users do not depend on tests, so tests sit outside the system and need no design. Which step is flawed?
options: The claim that no user of the system depends on the tests in any way
The claim that tests are mostly deployed in test systems and not in production
The claim that tests have a role in supporting development of the system
Moving from not needed for operation to not part of the system
optionExplain: That claim is correct: no user depends on the tests.
That claim is correct: tests are mostly deployed in test systems.
That claim is correct: their role is to support development.
Right: the author says tests are no less a system component for being unneeded in operation.
questions.explain: The flawed step is the jump from isolation to exclusion. Tests are isolated but still components.
questions.rule: Isolated does not mean outside.
questions.hint: Which step moves from a true fact to a conclusion?

questions.q: True or false: The author considers tests, in many ways, a model that all other system components should follow.
questions.explain: He says tests are no less a system component than any other and, in many ways, the model the others should follow.
questions.rule: Tests are in many ways a model for other components.
questions.teaches: In many ways the tests represent the model that all other system components should follow.

questions.q: Payroll users do not call the test suite. Which claim about the suite follows from the author's description?
options: It is not part of the system, since no user depends on it and the running system does not need it
It is the least isolated component, since developers use it every day to check each change they make
It is the most isolated component, since no user depends on it, yet it remains a system component
It is isolated only while the build server is not running it, and part of the system when it is
optionExplain: The author says tests are part of the system.
Developers use it, but nothing in the running system does.
Right: no user depends on it, and it is still a component.
The build server does not change who depends on the suite.
questions.explain: The author notes that no user depends on tests. That makes them the most isolated component without making them any less part of the system.
questions.rule: Users do not depend on tests, yet tests belong to the system.
questions.teaches: No user depends on the tests, which is part of what makes them the most isolated system component.

questions.q: A test suite drives the GUI from the login screen to check discount rules. Marketing changes the page navigation. What happens?
options: A large share of the tests break, though no discount rule changed
Only the tests of the navigation break, since the discount tests check rules
No test breaks, since tests are outside the system and unaffected by its changes
The discount tests pass, since they were written before the navigation changed
optionExplain: Right: every test that passes through the navigation breaks.
The discount tests go through the navigation, so they break too.
Tests that go through the GUI are affected by GUI changes.
Writing order does not protect a test from later changes.
questions.explain: Tests that go through the GUI depend on the GUI. The card next names this problem.
questions.rule: Coupled tests break with what they are coupled to.

questions.q: The name for hundreds of tests breaking after one small change is the Fragile ____ Problem.
questions.explain: The book calls this the Fragile Tests Problem.
questions.rule: Fragile tests break on small changes.

questions.q: Which suite is most likely to suffer the Fragile Tests Problem?
options: 50 tests of a date-handling function that has not changed in years and is used by only two modules
200 tests that call the premium rules directly with prepared inputs and check the results returned
A handful of tests that check one report against a fixed sample of data kept in a small file
5,000 tests that log in through the web form and click through screens to check premium rules
optionExplain: A stable function rarely changes, so its tests rarely break.
Tests that call the rules directly avoid the screens.
A few tests against fixed data break rarely and in few places.
Right: all of them are coupled to the screens, which change.
questions.explain: Many tests coupled to something that changes means many tests fail at once.
questions.rule: Volatile coupling times many tests equals fragility.

questions.q: True or false: The author expects developers who know a simple change would break 1,000 tests to resist the change.
questions.rule: Fragile tests make the system rigid.
questions.explain: The cost of fixing the tests makes developers reluctant to change the system, which is how fragile tests make it rigid.

questions.q: How does the author describe the view that tests lie outside the design of the system?
options: As harmless when tests are rarely deployed
As a catastrophic point of view
As reasonable for small projects
As a matter of style
optionExplain: Rare deployment is why people hold the view, not a reason to excuse it.
Right: he uses the word catastrophic.
He makes no exception for small projects.
He treats it as a matter of consequences, not taste.
questions.explain: The author is blunt: the result is fragile tests and a rigid system.
questions.rule: Leaving tests out of the design is costly.
questions.teaches: The author calls the view that tests fall outside the design of the system a catastrophic point of view.

questions.q: A mobile team scripts taps through the UI to verify refund rules. After a redesign 40 percent of the tests fail and the team stops fixing them. Which statement fits the author?
options: The team should have written more UI tests, so that the redesign would have been covered by the suite
Tests not designed as part of the system become fragile and are often discarded as too hard to maintain
The failures show the redesign was a mistake, since good tests are written so that they do not break
The team is right to drop them, since tests should not be used to cover rules such as refund eligibility
optionExplain: More UI tests would add more coupling to the volatile part.
Right: the author says such tests end up on the maintenance room floor.
A redesign is normal; the issue is the coupling of the tests.
The author wants business rules tested; the issue is how.
questions.explain: The author's conclusion is that tests which are not designed as part of the system are fragile and hard to maintain, and often discarded.
questions.rule: Badly designed tests do not survive.
questions.teaches: Tests that are not designed as part of the system often wind up on the maintenance room floor, discarded because they are too difficult to maintain.

questions.q: A team wants tests for its tax rules to survive a user-interface redesign. What does the author recommend?
options: Write more GUI tests, so the redesign breaks only a small share of them
Freeze the GUI so that it does not change after the tests are written
Test the rules by hand after each redesign, since automated tests will break
Design so that the rules can be tested without using the GUI
optionExplain: More GUI tests mean more tests to break.
Freezing the GUI does not fit a volatile part of the system.
Manual testing gives up the tests instead of redesigning them.
Right: testing the rules without the GUI avoids the dependency.
questions.explain: The author's rule is to avoid depending on volatile things. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Test rules without the GUI.

questions.q: The first rule of software design is: do not depend on ____ things.
questions.explain: GUIs are volatile, so tests that depend on them are fragile.
questions.rule: Do not depend on volatile things.

questions.q: Which tests break for the reason the author warns about? Select all that apply.
questions.rule: Depending on layout is depending on a volatile thing.
options: One that sets a flight to full through a test-only call and checks the waiting list
One that picks a seat by clicking the third button on the seat-map page
One that asks the seat-allocation rules for the best seat for a party of four
One that reads a price from a styled label on the booking page
optionExplain: A test-only call avoids the GUI.
Right: it depends on the layout of a page, which is volatile.
Asking the rules directly does not depend on the GUI.
Right: it depends on how a page is built, which can change.
questions.explain: Tests that depend on page layout or markup break when the GUI changes. Tests that reach the rules directly do not.

questions.q: The booking site's web GUI is replaced by a mobile app. Which tests need no change?
options: The tests that exercise the seat-allocation rules without the GUI
The tests that click through the web pages to book a seat
The tests that read text from the web page to check prices
All of them, since the rules are part of the GUI
optionExplain: Right: they never touched the GUI.
Those depend on web pages, which are gone.
Those depend on the pages that were replaced.
The rules are separate from the GUI.
questions.explain: Tests that never go through the GUI do not notice that it was replaced.
questions.rule: Tests free of the GUI survive its replacement.

questions.q: True or false: The author presents the rule not to depend on volatile things as holding for any reason to design software, not only for testability.
questions.explain: He says the first rule of software design, whether for testability or for any other reason, is always the same.
questions.rule: The rule applies to design in general.
questions.teaches: The first rule of software design, whether for testability or for any other reason, is the same: do not depend on volatile things.

questions.q: A team finds its rules cannot be exercised without the GUI. Whose design must change?
options: Only the tests, which must find cleverer ways to drive the GUI and read what it shows on the screen
Only the GUI, which must be made less volatile so that tests can keep on going through it with no change
Both the system and the tests, so the rules can be reached without the GUI
Neither of them, since the rules and the GUI are bound together in the way the product was first designed
optionExplain: Cleverer driving still depends on the GUI.
The GUI is volatile by nature.
Right: the author says to design the system and the tests.
Rules and GUI do not have to be bound.
questions.explain: Testability is a property of the system as well as the tests, so the design of both must change.
questions.rule: Design the system and the tests together.
questions.teaches: Design for testability means designing both the system and the tests so that business rules can be tested without the GUI.

questions.q: Tests must check rules, but the database is slow and some actions need a login. What would help most?
options: A faster database server that is shared by all of the tests
A script that logs in before each test and records the steps
A longer time limit on each test, so slow steps still pass
A dedicated API for tests that can skip the login and the database
optionExplain: A faster database is still a database in every test.
Logging in before each test keeps the dependency and the delay.
A longer limit hides the cost instead of removing it.
Right: a testing API removes the obstacles at their source.
questions.explain: The author's solution is an API made for tests. The card next lists its powers.
questions.rule: Give tests their own door.

questions.q: Match each superpower of the testing API to what it lets a test do.
pairs: Call an operation without logging in
Put the system straight into a state such as an account being frozen
questions.explain: The three powers are avoiding security constraints, bypassing expensive resources and forcing states.
questions.rule: Skip security, skip cost, force state.

questions.q: An airline test needs a flight that is fully booked, which normally takes 180 bookings. What should the testing API offer?
options: A script that makes 180 bookings through the web pages before each test
An operation that sets the flight to full directly
A copy of last month's database with a full flight in it
A rule in production code that treats flights on a test date as full
optionExplain: Making bookings through the pages is slow and depends on the GUI.
Right: a testing API can force a state.
A copied database is an expensive resource.
A test rule in production code mixes test code into the system.
questions.explain: Forcing a testable state is one of the superpowers.
questions.rule: Force the state; do not walk to it.

questions.q: True or false: A testing API that offers only what the UI offers lets tests reach hard-to-reach states as easily as one with superpowers.
questions.rule: Superpowers shorten the way to a state.
questions.explain: Without the powers to skip security, bypass expensive resources and force states, such states must be reached the long way round.

questions.q: What does the author say to do if the testing API's superpowers might be dangerous in production?
options: Protect them with a password that only the developers know, and keep them in the production system
Leave them out of the tests, since production safety comes before test speed and convenience
Keep the testing API and its dangerous parts in a separate, independently deployable component
Rename the operations so that no one calls them by mistake while the production system is running
optionExplain: A password leaves the powers in production.
Without the powers the tests lose their purpose.
Right: the author puts them in a component that can be deployed on its own.
A name does not stop a call.
questions.explain: The same independence that tests enjoy lets the dangerous parts be left out of production.
questions.rule: Keep test-only powers in a separate component.
questions.teaches: If the superpowers could be dangerous in production, keep the testing API and the dangerous parts of its implementation in a separate, independently deployable component.

questions.q: In a command-line billing tool built along clean-architecture lines, from what is a testing API built?
options: Everything the interactors and interface adapters offer to the command line, plus the test-only powers
A separate copy of the business rules written specially for tests, so the tests cannot disturb the real ones
The command-line parser, because tests must go through the same input that the real users type in
The database layer, because tests must read the stored results to see whether a rule was applied
optionExplain: Right: the author calls it a superset of the interactors and interface adapters that the UI uses.
A copy of the rules would test the copy, not the rules.
The parser is part of the user interface that tests avoid.
The database is an expensive resource tests aim to bypass.
questions.explain: A testing API is built on the same interactors and adapters that serve the UI, with extra powers for tests.
questions.rule: A superset of what the UI uses.
questions.teaches: The testing API is a superset of the suite of interactors and interface adapters that the user interface uses.

questions.q: True or false: Having one test class per production class and one test method per production method makes a suite resilient to refactoring.
questions.explain: Mirroring ties each test to the structure it mirrors. The card next names this coupling.
questions.rule: Mirroring couples tests to structure.

questions.q: Structural coupling ties the tests to the ____ of the application.
questions.explain: A suite that mirrors classes and methods is coupled to how the application is built.
questions.rule: Structural coupling is coupling to structure.

questions.q: A team splits the class InvoiceBuilder into three classes, and 80 tests fail. What does the author trace this to?
options: Structural coupling: the tests mirrored the production classes and methods
Too few tests, since a larger suite would have caught the problem earlier
The test framework, which should have updated the tests when the classes changed
Coupling to the GUI, since the classes were part of the invoice screen
optionExplain: Right: tests that mirror structure break when structure changes.
More tests would break more.
A framework cannot know what the tests meant to check.
The classes are not part of the GUI in this case.
questions.explain: A refactoring that changes no behaviour breaks tests only when they are coupled to structure.
questions.rule: Refactoring breaks structure-coupled tests.

questions.q: A lead says: mirror every production class with a test class so the tests are well organised and easy to change. What is wrong with this?
options: Mirroring makes the suite too small to find faults in the application, because each class gets only one test class
Mirroring is wrong only because test classes must not share their names with the classes that they test
Mirroring couples the structure of the tests to the structure of the application, so a change to one breaks the other
Mirroring is wrong only because the test classes are not allowed to call production code in this kind of suite
optionExplain: Suite size is not the author's concern here.
Naming is not the issue.
Right: this is structural coupling.
Test classes depend on production code; the issue is the structure they copy.
questions.explain: The mirror feels tidy, but it makes every refactoring of the production code a change to the tests.
questions.rule: Tidy mirroring is a coupling.
questions.hint: What happens to the tests when the production classes are split?

questions.q: True or false: Over time, tests tend to become more concrete and specific while production code tends to become more abstract and general.
questions.rule: Tests grow concrete, code grows general.
questions.teaches: As time passes the tests tend to become more concrete and specific, while the production code tends to become more abstract and general.
questions.explain: Because the two move in opposite directions, tying them together blocks both. The testing API keeps them apart.

questions.q: A data science team keeps one test notebook per module and hesitates to generalise a function, because 30 notebooks would change. What does the author say about this?
options: The team is right to hesitate, since generalising a function always makes it harder to test than before
Strong structural coupling stops the production code from being as general and flexible as it could be
The hesitation is harmless, since notebooks are not part of the system and can be thrown away at any time
The team should write one notebook per function, to make the coupling between tests and code explicit
optionExplain: Generalising does not make code harder to test if the tests are not coupled to structure.
Right: the author says it prevents the code from being as general as it could be.
Tests are part of the system.
One notebook per function would add more structural coupling.
questions.explain: The team avoids a better design because of the tests that mirror it. That is the cost the author names.
questions.rule: Coupled tests hold back the design.
questions.teaches: Strong structural coupling prevents, or at least impedes, the necessary evolution and keeps the production code from being as general and flexible as it could be.

questions.q: Which description best says what makes code firmware?
options: Its storage in ROM or flash memory instead of in a file on a disk drive, which is what most definitions say
Its running on a microcontroller rather than on a desktop computer, with a small amount of memory
Its being written in C instead of in a higher-level language that hides the details of the machine
Its dependence on hardware, which makes it hard to change as the hardware evolves
optionExplain: Where code is stored is the common definition, which the author rejects.
The kind of processor does not decide whether the code depends on hardware details.
The language does not decide what the code depends on.
Right: it is defined by dependencies and difficulty of change.
questions.explain: The author defines firmware by what code depends on. The card next gives his argument.
questions.rule: Firmware is defined by dependence.

questions.q: Code is firmware because of what it depends on, not because of where it is ____.
questions.explain: The author rejects definitions based on storage in ROM or flash.
questions.rule: Not where it is stored.

questions.q: Which of these is firmware by the author's definition?
options: A stateless scheduling library with no hardware references, stored in flash
A routine that converts temperatures to modes and runs on the microcontroller
Thermostat scheduling rules compiled together with direct writes to GPIO pins
A table of temperature ranges held in ROM and read through a function
optionExplain: It is stored in flash, but depends on no hardware.
Running on the chip does not make a routine depend on it.
Right: the rules cannot move without the pins.
ROM is a storage place; the table is not tied to the hardware.
questions.explain: The first option is tied to specific pins, so it is hard to change when hardware changes. The others have no such dependency.
questions.rule: Look at the dependency, not the storage.

questions.q: Sort each item by the author's definition: software or firmware?

items.t: A call parser that knows only message formats
Name and value storage logic that uses only an interface
Call logic hard-wired to one kind of hardware interface
A message dispatcher in the same file as UART code
SQL buried in business logic
