questions.explain: Code with a long useful life depends on little about the hardware or platform. Code that carries those details has become firmware, even outside embedded systems.
questions.rule: Hardware or platform detail in the code makes it firmware.

questions.q: Which non-embedded practice does the author say amounts to writing firmware?
options: Burying SQL in business code
Using a relational database at all
Writing unit tests against a mock repository
Using Java rather than C for a server
optionExplain: Right: SQL spread through code binds it to a platform.
Using a database is fine; the issue is burying SQL throughout the code.
Mock repositories help keep code free of platform detail.
The language is not the author's issue.
questions.explain: Non-embedded developers write firmware whenever they bury SQL in code, spread platform dependencies, or mix business logic with the Android API.
questions.rule: Platform dependencies make firmware anywhere.
questions.teaches: Non-embedded developers also write firmware when they bury SQL in code, spread platform dependencies, or fail to separate business logic from the Android API.

questions.q: A bank rewrites a terminal-based system for the web. The only specification is the old code, which mixes terminal handling with rules. What does the author's story suggest about the old product?
options: The product was clean, since terminals are a stable platform
The product was software, because it ran on general-purpose computers
The product can be ported easily, because the rules are written in the same language as the terminal code
The whole product had essentially become firmware, so its code is the only spec for the new one
optionExplain: Dependence on a platform is the problem, whether or not it is stable.
Where it ran is not the test.
A shared language does not untangle the rules from the terminal.
Right: the author tells a similar story of tangled legacy code as the spec.
questions.explain: In the author's telephone example, the tangled legacy code was the specification for the new product, and the whole product had become firmware.
questions.rule: Tangled hardware dependence turns a whole product into firmware.
questions.teaches: In a communications subsystem the author helped redesign, the tangled legacy code was the spec for the new product, because nothing separated the technology from the business logic.

questions.q: A developer gets a sensor app working on the target board and ships it. Which of Beck's three steps is done?
options: The first two: make it work and make it right
Only the first: make it work
All three, since a shipped product is right and fast
Only the last, since shipping shows the code is fast enough
optionExplain: Making it right means refactoring so others can understand and evolve it.
Right: working is the first step only.
Shipping does not show that the code was refactored or tuned.
Speed was not checked by working.
questions.explain: Working code is the first of three activities. The card next gives all three.
questions.rule: Working is the first step.

questions.q: Put Kent Beck's three activities in the order he recommends.
items: Make it work
Make it right
Make it fast
questions.explain: First make it work, then refactor so that it is right, then refactor for needed performance.
questions.rule: Work, right, fast.

questions.q: A web developer puts routes, SQL and email sending into one file and the app works. What does the author's view say?
options: It is finished, since working code is the goal of the three activities
It passes the App-titude test, but the step of making it right remains
It needs micro-optimisations next, since speed is the second step
It needs a rewrite in another language, since the structure is a language problem
optionExplain: Beck puts two steps after working.
Right: the code works, and making it right is still ahead.
Making it fast is the third step.
Structure is not a language problem.
questions.explain: The file works, which passes the App-titude test. Refactoring so others can understand and evolve it is still to do.
questions.rule: Working is the start, not the finish.

questions.q: A team says: we put micro-optimisations everywhere in our firmware, so it is right. What is wrong with this?
questions.rule: Fast is not right.
questions.hint: Which step is about understanding and evolving the code?
questions.a: Making it fast is the third step. Code is right when it has been refactored so that you and others can understand and evolve it; speed does not show that.

questions.q: Fred Brooks advised: plan to ____ one away.
questions.rule: Learn what works, then do better.
questions.teaches: Fred Brooks's advice to plan to throw one away is virtually the same as Beck's: learn what works, then make a better solution.
questions.explain: Brooks's advice is virtually the same as Beck's: learn what works, then make a better solution.

questions.q: A web team ships a Rails app in a month, with the rules inside the controllers. How does the author classify the team?
options: It is exempt, since the problem described by the author applies only to embedded systems
It has made the code right, since delivering a working product in a month shows a fast schedule
It has made the code fast, since the Rails framework comes with efficient defaults for web requests
It passes the App-titude test, like an embedded team that stops at working code
optionExplain: The author says embedded software is not special in this respect.
Speed of delivery is not the second step.
Framework defaults are not the author's second or third step.
Right: embedded software is not special, and most non-embedded apps are built only to work.
questions.explain: The author says most non-embedded apps are also built just to work, with little regard for a long useful life.
questions.rule: The test applies to all programmers.
questions.teaches: Embedded software is not special when it comes to these problems: most non-embedded apps are also built only to work.

questions.q: True or false: When the hardware for a new device is not ready, a team with well-structured code can still test much of it.
questions.explain: Code separated from the hardware can be tested elsewhere. The card next names the problem the structure removes.
questions.rule: Good structure frees tests from the target.

questions.q: If the target is the only place where testing is possible, the target-hardware ____ will slow you down.
questions.explain: The author names the slowdown the target-hardware bottleneck.
questions.rule: A target-only test is a bottleneck.

questions.q: A smart-lock team has no board for three months. Which plan fits the author?
options: Separate the lock logic from hardware access, and run its tests on a development machine
Wait for the board before testing anything, since embedded code must run on the target
Write the logic with direct register access first and test it all once the board arrives
Write an emulator for every register of the board before writing any logic
optionExplain: Right: separation lets the tests run without the target.
Waiting accepts the bottleneck.
Register access in the logic ties it to the target.
An emulator for every register is a large cost that structure would avoid.
questions.explain: Separating logic from hardware access lets the team test the logic before the board exists.
questions.rule: Test off the target.

questions.q: True or false: If tests can run only on the target, defects in the hardware slow progress further.
questions.rule: Hardware delay and defects slow target-only testing.
questions.explain: The author notes that hardware defects make development slower than usual, and target-only testing inherits them.

questions.q: How does the author phrase the relation between clean embedded architecture and testing?
options: A clean embedded architecture is a faster embedded architecture
A clean embedded architecture is a smaller embedded architecture
A clean embedded architecture is a testable embedded architecture
A clean embedded architecture is a portable embedded architecture
optionExplain: Speed is not what the heading says.
Size is not what the heading says.
Right: this is a heading in the chapter.
Portability follows, but the heading names testability.
questions.explain: Testability is the point of the structure the author goes on to describe.
questions.rule: Clean means testable.
questions.teaches: The author's heading says a clean embedded architecture is a testable embedded architecture.

questions.q: A software team writes code for a device whose hardware is still being designed by another group. How does the author describe such a situation?
options: Rare: hardware is usually finished long before any of the software that runs on it is written
Harmless: simulators of the hardware always match the real hardware exactly in every respect
Impossible: code cannot be written before the hardware exists, so such projects do not start
Common: the hardware is usually developed at the same time, so you may have no place to run the code
optionExplain: He says concurrent development is typical.
He does not say simulators always match.
Teams write code in this situation; the difficulty is where to run it.
Right: he says the hardware is concurrently developed most of the time.
questions.explain: Most of the time the hardware is developed together with the software and firmware, which is why the bottleneck bites.
questions.rule: Hardware is often not ready.
questions.teaches: Most of the time the hardware is developed concurrently with the software and firmware.

questions.q: A one-line change to a function in an embedded product requires the full regression suite to be re-run. What does the author call the likely cause?
options: Too many layers, since each layer adds a new place for faults
Software and firmware intermingled, which he calls an anti-pattern
Too little firmware, since firmware catches changes before they spread
Too many tests, since the suite is larger than the code
optionExplain: Layers limit the effect of change.
Right: intermingled code makes every change risky.
More firmware would add more hardware dependence.
Tests are the symptom, not the cause.
questions.explain: Intermingling spreads hardware knowledge, so any change may break something far away. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: Intermingling makes change dangerous.

questions.q: Software and firmware intermingling is an ____.
questions.explain: The author calls it an anti-pattern.
questions.rule: Intermingling is an anti-pattern.

questions.q: In a drone controller, flight rules and I2C sensor reads sit in one source file. Which symptom should the team expect?
options: The flight rules run faster, since they sit right next to the hardware calls that they need
The sensor reads become easier to replace, since all of them are gathered in one place in the file
Even a minor change to the flight rules needs a full regression test of the whole system
The rules can be tested on a laptop, since the file compiles anywhere that has a C compiler
optionExplain: Nothing in the author's argument promises speed.
Mixing makes the reads harder to replace.
Right: the rules cannot be checked apart from the hardware.
The hardware calls tie the file to the target.
questions.explain: Mixed code needs whole-system testing for any change, which is the cost the author warns about.
questions.rule: Mixed code means whole-system tests.

questions.q: True or false: Without externally instrumented tests, the author expects tedious manual testing and then new bug reports.
questions.rule: No instrumented tests, no safety.
questions.explain: Without externally instrumented tests the team falls back on manual tests that are tedious and miss faults.

questions.q: Why will the hardware layer change, according to the author?
options: Technology advances and Moore's law make parts obsolete, and new parts use less power, perform better or cost less
Hardware vendors change their products only to force customers to rewrite their code and buy new support contracts
Software teams ask for new hardware each time they add a feature that the old hardware cannot run fast enough
Regulators require new parts every year, so that older parts become forbidden in products sold to customers
optionExplain: Right: he says parts become obsolete and new parts are better or cheaper.
He gives no such motive.
Features grow, but hardware changes for its own reasons.
Regulation is not mentioned.
questions.explain: The author expects the hardware to change and wants the software to survive it.
questions.rule: Hardware will change.
questions.teaches: Because of technology advances and Moore's law, parts become obsolete and new parts use less power, perform better or cost less, so the hardware will change.

questions.q: An Android app mixes its business logic with calls to the Android API. When does the author say such code is hard to change?
options: Not only when the platform changes, but also when users ask for changes or bugs need fixing
Only when the platform changes, since users do not touch the business logic
Only when bugs need fixing, since user requests are added in new files
Only when the app grows beyond a hundred files, since small apps are easy to change
optionExplain: Right: he says it is not just hardware change but user changes and bug fixes.
He names more triggers than the platform.
User requests also touch mixed code.
He gives no size threshold.
questions.explain: The author says the problem is not only when the hardware changes, but when the user asks for a change or a bug needs to be fixed.
questions.rule: Mixed code resists every kind of change.
questions.teaches: Code polluted with hardware knowledge is hard to change not only when the hardware changes but when the user asks for a change or a bug needs to be fixed.

questions.q: Firmware writes bytes to flash, and the application wants to save settings by name. Where should the translation live?
options: In the application, which should call the flash driver directly with its own address scheme
In the flash driver, which should learn the application's setting names
In a layer between them whose API is shaped by what the application needs
In every module that saves a setting, as a small private helper
optionExplain: The application would depend on the flash.
The driver would depend on the application's names.
Right: a layer that serves the application hides the flash.
Helpers in each module duplicate the translation.
questions.explain: The layer between software and firmware is the HAL. The card next describes it.
questions.rule: A middle layer shaped by the software's needs.

questions.q: The HAL exists for the ____ that sits on top of it, and its API should be tailored to that.
questions.explain: The HAL serves the software above it.
questions.rule: The HAL serves the software.

questions.q: A thermostat's firmware sets a PWM duty cycle on pin 3. What HAL call would the author prefer for the control logic?
options: Pwm_SetDuty(3, value), so the logic can pick the pin and the duty cycle itself
Heater_SetLevel(level), shaped around what the controller wants to do
Gpio_WritePin(3, value), so the logic can control the heater exactly
Register_Write(0x40, value), so the logic can reach every register it needs
optionExplain: It puts the pin number in the software.
Right: it speaks of heating, not of pins.
It puts a GPIO pin in the software.
It puts a register address in the software.
questions.explain: The HAL should offer services in the language of the product. Pins and registers stay below it.
questions.rule: Name the service, not the pin.

questions.q: Sort each call: is it shaped by what the software needs, or does it mirror the hardware?

items.t: Settings_Save(name, value)
Indicate_LowBattery()
Flash_WriteBytes(address, data)
Gpio_SetBit(5)
Display_ShowMessage(id)

questions.explain: Calls named for product services belong to the HAL's software-facing side. Calls named for addresses and bits mirror the hardware.
questions.rule: Services up, bits down.

questions.q: How does the author describe the layers of a design that has a HAL?
options: Exactly three layers, no more and no fewer, in every embedded product that has a HAL in it
Exactly one layer for each piece of hardware in the product, from the processor to the last sensor
A stack in which each layer may call any layer below it, so the top can reach the bottom
Layers may contain layers: it is more a repeating fractal pattern than a fixed set of layers
optionExplain: He starts with three layers but says there is no fixed set.
Layers are not counted by pieces of hardware.
He does not say layers may call any layer below.
Right: the author sees a repeating pattern.
questions.explain: Lower-level layers can sit inside higher-level ones, as when Indicate_LowBattery() is built on Led_TurnOn(5).
questions.rule: Layers repeat at different levels.
questions.teaches: Layers may contain layers; it is more of a repeating fractal pattern than a limited set of predefined layers.

questions.q: A rover team wants to test its navigation logic on a laptop. What does the author say the GPIO assignments should be?
options: Constants shared by all of the software, so that every module uses the same names for the same pins
Parameters of the navigation logic, so that each mission can choose the pins that suit its sensors
Details hidden from the software, so a laptop version of the HAL can stand in for the hardware
Comments in the code, so that engineers can see at a glance which pins are used by which routine
optionExplain: Sharing pin names spreads hardware knowledge.
Pins are not part of navigation.
Right: the GPIO assignments are details that should be hidden from the software.
Comments leave the dependency in place.
questions.explain: The author says the GPIO assignments are details that should be hidden from the software.
questions.rule: Hide pin assignments below the HAL.
questions.teaches: The GPIO assignments are details that should be hidden from the software.

questions.q: A vendor compiler adds a keyword for reading a serial buffer register. What is true of code that uses it?
options: It is no longer standard C, and it may not compile for another processor or compiler
It is standard C, since the compiler accepts it and gives no warning when it builds the code
It is portable, since the keyword stands for a serial buffer that every processor has in some form
It is portable, since the compiler vendor also supports a range of other chips with the same keyword
optionExplain: Right: the code is tied to the toolchain.
Acceptance by one compiler does not make it C.
The meaning may be common but the keyword is not.
Support for other chips does not make the keyword standard.
questions.explain: The extensions tie code to a toolchain and chip. The card next shows how to limit the damage.
questions.rule: Extensions are not C.

questions.q: You will have to limit which files are allowed to know about the C ____.
questions.explain: The author warns that vendor help becomes a hindrance if it spreads.
questions.rule: Limit who knows the extensions.

questions.q: A project includes the vendor header vendor_types.h in 300 files. What should the team do?
options: Keep including the vendor header everywhere, since the project will only ever use that vendor's chips
Copy the vendor typedefs into each file, so that the build no longer depends on the vendor's header
Switch to a C++ compiler so that the extension keywords are no longer an issue for the build
Use standard stdint.h types everywhere, and let only a small target-build header include the vendor header
optionExplain: Plans change, and the author expects hardware to evolve.
Copying spreads the dependency into every file.
A different compiler does not remove the vendor dependency.
Right: it limits the vendor knowledge to one place.
questions.explain: Standard types in the code and one target-build header confine the vendor dependency.
questions.rule: One header knows the vendor.

questions.q: True or false: Limiting which files know the vendor header makes a later port to another processor easier.
questions.rule: Porting cost follows spread.
questions.explain: Every file that names the vendor's types must be touched in a port, so limiting those files limits the work.

questions.q: Why would using acmetypes.h directly hurt testing the code off the target?
options: The header cannot be opened on a development machine, because the vendor ships it in a binary format
If the vendor type definitions are used on a development machine, the integers can have the wrong size
The header slows the tests down, since it defines far too many types for the compiler to read
The tests would pass every time on the development machine, hiding the faults that show up on the target
optionExplain: The header is plain text; the issue is the sizes.
Right: the author warns integers will be the wrong size off-target.
The number of types does not matter.
Wrong sizes can cause failures, not silent passes.
questions.explain: The vendor's definitions suit the DSP. On another machine they give different sizes, so results differ.
questions.rule: Vendor types do not travel.
questions.teaches: Using the vendor types directly and defining the vendor macros for off-target tests gives integers of the wrong size.

questions.q: Firmware code calls register-level routines through a processor abstraction layer. What does the author say about the code above the layer?
options: It must still run on the target, since the layer hides nothing
It can be tested off-target, which makes it a little less firm
It becomes software only if it is stored in ROM
It must be rewritten whenever the processor changes
optionExplain: The point of the layer is to allow off-target testing.
Right: firmware above a PAL can be tested off the target.
Storage place is not the test.
A PAL limits what must change.
questions.explain: The author says firmware above the PAL can be tested off-target, making it a little less firm.
questions.rule: A PAL loosens firmware.
questions.teaches: Firmware above the processor abstraction layer can be tested off-target, making it a little less firm.

questions.q: Embedded code calls RTOS functions directly in thousands of places. The RTOS supplier is bought and royalties rise. What is the likely cost?
options: Nothing, since an RTOS is a standard component
Changing a few include lines, since function names are the only difference
Rewriting the hardware layer, since the OS belongs to the hardware
Changing a lot of code, including semantic adaptation to the new OS's capabilities
optionExplain: RTOSes are not standardised enough to swap without change.
Differences go beyond syntax.
The OS sits between software and firmware.
Right: direct use spreads the dependency.
questions.explain: Direct use of an RTOS spreads it through the code. The card next shows a way to contain it.
questions.rule: Contain the OS behind a layer.

questions.q: The OS is isolated by an operating system ____ layer.
questions.explain: The author calls it the OSAL.
questions.rule: OSAL: operating system abstraction layer.

questions.q: A wearable moves from one RTOS to another with different task primitives. What fits the author?
options: Write a new OSAL implementation to the existing interface and leave the application code alone
Edit every task-creation call in the application to use the primitives that the new RTOS offers
Wrap the old RTOS inside the new one, so that both of them run on the board at the same time
Move the application code into the OS itself, so that it can use the new primitives directly
optionExplain: Right: the application depends on the OSAL, so only the OSAL changes.
That spreads the change.
Running two operating systems is not the author's way.
The application would depend on the OS.
questions.explain: The author asks which you would rather do: modify complex code or write new code to a defined interface.
questions.rule: Write a new OSAL.

questions.q: True or false: Implementing an OSAL can be as simple as changing the name of a function.
questions.rule: Sometimes a rename; sometimes a wrapper.
questions.explain: The author says that in some cases the layer is as simple as a rename; in others it wraps several functions together.

questions.q: How does the author answer the worry that an OSAL adds code bloat?
options: Code size does not matter in embedded systems, since memory prices fall every year as chips improve
The layer can be removed before shipping, once the tests have passed on the laptop and the target
The layer is where the duplication around using the OS is isolated, so the overhead need not be big
The layer is small because it holds only one function, which every task in the application calls
optionExplain: Embedded systems have limited memory, which the author mentions.
The layer is part of the architecture.
Right: much of the duplication is isolated there.
The layer may wrap several functions.
questions.explain: The OSAL also lets a team offer shared structures, such as message passing, instead of every thread making up its own concurrency model.
questions.rule: The OSAL collects duplication.
questions.teaches: An OSAL isolates the duplication around using the OS and can encourage a common structure, such as message passing, instead of every thread handcrafting its concurrency model.

questions.q: Audio-codec logic runs on an RTOS in the product, and the team wants to test it on a laptop. What does the author say an OSAL provides?
options: A copy of the RTOS that runs on a laptop and keeps exactly the same timing as on the board
A way to skip testing of the application, since the OS has already been tested by its vendor
A list of the OS functions that the codec must call directly, so that the tests can name them
Test points that let the valuable application code be tested off-target and off-OS
optionExplain: The OSAL is a layer in the code, not a copy of the OS.
The OSAL helps testing, not replaces it.
The codec should not call the OS directly.
Right: the OSAL provides seams for off-target and off-OS testing.
questions.explain: The author says a successful OSAL provides a seam, or a set of substitution points, for testing off the target OS.
questions.rule: OSAL gives seams for off-OS tests.
questions.teaches: A successful OSAL provides a seam, or a set of substitution points, so the application code can be tested off the target and off the target operating system.

questions.q: A header for a storage module also holds a flash page size constant and a struct for the driver's state. What is the cost?
options: The compiler refuses to build the module, since headers cannot hold constants
Callers can come to depend on those details, so they spread beyond the implementation
The module runs slower, since the constants are read at every call
Nothing, since every header should show all it contains
optionExplain: Headers can hold constants.
Right: details in the header invite dependencies.
The cost is dependency, not speed.
Exposed details bring unwanted dependencies.
questions.explain: Anything in the header may be used by callers. The card next gives the author's rule.
questions.rule: Keep details out of headers.

questions.q: A header used as an interface should hold function declarations and only the constants and struct names the ____ require.
questions.explain: Anything beyond what the functions need is implementation detail.
questions.rule: Only what the functions need.

questions.q: The header gps.h declares Gps_GetPosition() and a typedef for a ring buffer used only inside gps.c. Which item should leave the header?
options: The declaration of Gps_GetPosition()
The struct name Position that Gps_GetPosition returns
The ring-buffer typedef used only inside gps.c
The constant GPS_MAX_SATELLITES used in the signature of Gps_GetPosition()
optionExplain: It is the interface itself.
Callers need the struct name to use the function.
Right: it is an implementation detail.
Callers need the constant the signature uses.
questions.explain: Items the functions need stay; items only the implementation needs go.
questions.rule: Remove what only the implementation needs.

questions.q: Sort each item: interface header or implementation file?

items.t: A function declaration that callers use
A struct name that appears in a function signature
A typedef for a driver's private buffer
A constant used only by the driver's loops

questions.explain: Callers need declarations and the names that appear in them. Private buffers and loop constants belong in the implementation.
questions.rule: Public in the header, private in the file.

questions.q: What lets a hand-written small printf replace the standard one on the target?
options: It has the same interface as the standard version, so one can override the other
It is written in assembly, which every target supports, so it can be linked in on any board
It is shorter than the standard version, so it fits in the small memory of the target device
It calls the standard printf underneath, which keeps the old behaviour for every format string
optionExplain: Right: substitution works through the shared interface.
The language is not the point.
Size is not the author's point.
Calling the standard printf would not replace it.
questions.explain: When modules interact through an interface, a provider can be swapped for another with the same interface.
questions.rule: Same interface, swappable provider.
questions.teaches: Many engineers write their own small printf for the target; as long as its interface is the same as the standard version, they can override one service with the other.

questions.q: A team wants to test a sensor-filter module without the sensor driver. What do the interface headers give them?
options: A substitution point: a test version of the driver that implements the same header can stand in for the real one
A way to compile the filter without any driver at all, since the header already holds the filter's code
A guarantee that the real driver is correct, because the compiler checks the header against it
A way to run the real driver without the sensor, because the header hides the sensor from it
optionExplain: Right: each interface is a seam.
The filter still needs something that implements the interface.
A header guarantees nothing about the driver's correctness.
Running the driver needs the sensor.
questions.explain: The author says a clean embedded architecture is testable within its layers because modules interact through interfaces.
questions.rule: Interfaces are seams for tests.
questions.teaches: A clean embedded architecture is testable within the layers because modules interact through interfaces, and each interface provides a seam for off-target testing.

questions.q: A telecom code base tests the board version with #ifdef in thousands of places. Which principle does the author say this breaks?
options: The Open-Closed Principle
The Liskov Substitution Principle
Don't Repeat Yourself
The Single Responsibility Principle
optionExplain: Open-Closed is about extension without editing.
Liskov is about substitutable subtypes.
Right: the same test is repeated everywhere.
Single responsibility is about reasons to change.
questions.explain: The author names the principle the repetition violates. The card next gives his alternative.
questions.rule: Repetition breaks DRY.

questions.q: Repeated #ifdef BOARD_V2 statements violate the Don't Repeat ____ principle.
questions.explain: The author names DRY.
questions.rule: Don't Repeat Yourself.

questions.q: A product supports three radio chips and uses #ifdef RADIO_X at 400 places. What fits the author?
options: Keep the conditionals, and add a fourth branch to each of them when a new chip comes along
Hide the radio behind an interface, with one implementation per chip chosen at link time
Move the conditionals into one huge function that every module calls to find out about the chip
Remove the support for all but one chip, to make the code simpler and the product cheaper
optionExplain: That multiplies the repetition.
Right: the chip becomes a detail under an interface.
A huge function still holds the repetition.
Dropping chips changes the product.
questions.explain: An interface with one implementation per chip removes the repeated test.
questions.rule: Interface plus binding, not conditionals.

questions.q: A fourth board is added after the change to a HAL with link-time binding. What must be done?
options: Edit all the places in the software that mention the old boards
Rewrite the HAL's interface to include the new board's name
Add a new #ifdef to every file that touches the hardware
Write one new implementation of the interface and select it at link time
optionExplain: The software no longer mentions boards.
The interface is shaped by software needs, not boards.
That is the old approach.
Right: the software is not touched.
questions.explain: The new board is a new implementation behind the same interface.
questions.rule: A new board is a new implementation.

questions.q: True or false: The author says a single occurrence of #ifdef BOARD_V2 is a real problem.
questions.explain: He says seeing it once is not really a problem, and six thousand times is an extreme problem.
questions.rule: One conditional is fine; repetition is the problem.
questions.teaches: A single #ifdef BOARD_V2 is not really a problem; the author calls it an extreme problem when it appears thousands of times.

questions.q: A Python tool checks the platform in 200 places. Which option from the author fits a language with no linker step?
options: Conditional compilation, since it is the only way to select code for a platform in any language
Link-time binding, since every language has a linker that can pick the implementation for you
Runtime binding: choose the implementation behind an interface when the program starts
Copying the file once per platform, so that no selection is needed when the program starts
optionExplain: That is the repeated pattern the author advises against.
Python has no link step in that sense.
Right: the author names the linker or some form of runtime binding.
Copies repeat code.
questions.explain: The author mentions two ways to connect software to hardware without conditionals: the linker or some form of runtime binding.
questions.rule: Link time or run time.
questions.teaches: Instead of conditional compilation, the author names two ways to connect software to hardware: the linker or some form of runtime binding.

questions.q: True or false: Calling the database a detail does not mean that the structure of the application's data is unimportant to the architecture.
questions.explain: The author separates the two. The structure of the data matters; the software that stores it does not. The card next shows the split.
questions.rule: Data model and database are two different things.

questions.q: The author compares the database to a ____ in the architecture of a house.
questions.explain: A doorknob is useful but is not part of what makes a house the house it is.
questions.rule: Useful is not the same as architectural.

questions.q: A team spends weeks choosing a database vendor and one afternoon on how orders and customers relate in the code. Which is the author's advice?
options: Spend equal effort on both, since data and storage cannot be told apart
Keep the effort on the vendor, since every other choice in the system rests on the database
Give the structure of orders and customers the design time; the vendor is a detail
Skip both, since the structure of data is also only a mechanism
optionExplain: The author's whole point is that they can and must be told apart.
This puts the detail first. The author says it is irrelevant from the architecture's point of view.
Right: the data model is significant; the utility behind it is a mechanism.
The author calls the data structure highly significant, so it is not skipped.
questions.explain: The data model is the part with architectural weight, so it earns the design time.
questions.rule: Spend design effort on the model, not the product.
questions.hint: Which of the two does the author call highly significant?

questions.q: A project builds its whole design around one database product. According to the author, what is the result for the architecture?
options: A low-level mechanism pollutes the architecture, which a good architect avoids
The data model becomes more significant, because the product defines it
The architecture improves, because the database is the most reliable part of the system
Nothing changes, because a detail cannot affect the architecture
optionExplain: Right: the product, a detail, ends up shaping the system.
The author keeps the model significant on its own; the product does not give it that rank.
Reliability is not the author's test; the question is what belongs in the architecture.
The author warns it can pollute the architecture, which is why it is kept out.
questions.explain: Letting a mechanism shape the design is the pollution the author warns about.
questions.rule: Keep mechanisms out of the core.

questions.q: A colleague summarises the chapter. Which statements misread the author? Select all that apply.
options: The data model is architecturally significant
Because the database is a detail, the data model is a detail too
The author says databases are poorly built tools
The database is a utility that provides access to the data
optionExplain: This matches the author: the structure of the data is significant.
This merges the two things the author keeps apart.
The author has no complaint about quality; he calls the relational model elegant, disciplined and robust.
This matches the author's description of it.
questions.explain: The author's claim is about rank in the architecture, not about the model's worth or the tool's quality.
questions.rule: Separate rank in the design from quality of the tool.

questions.q: A team picks a document store because experts praise it as brilliant and mathematically sound. By the author's reasoning, what does that praise change?
options: It makes the store irrelevant, so the team can ignore how it is used
It makes the store an architectural element, since quality earns a place in the design
It moves the data model into the store, so the model is no longer the team's concern
Nothing about its rank: however brilliant, a technology is still a technology
optionExplain: A detail still has to be dealt with; the point is only where it sits.
The author denies this; quality does not lift a technology out of the detail class.
The model remains the application's own structure, whichever store holds it.
Right: the author says this of the relational model, and the reasoning carries over.
questions.explain: The author notes that relational databases became dominant by the mid-1980s and are elegant, disciplined and robust, and says that no matter how brilliant a technology is, it is still just a technology, and that makes it a detail.
questions.rule: Brilliance does not make a technology architectural.
questions.teaches: The author grants that the relational model, defined by Codd in 1970 and dominant by the mid-1980s, is elegant, disciplined and robust, yet says that being brilliant and mathematically sound does not stop it from being just a technology, and so a detail.

questions.q: True or false: A data access framework that returns rows as objects should not be called freely from business rules, because a row carries the table structure with it.
questions.explain: Rows carry the relational structure with them, so whoever receives a row learns that structure. The card next shows the cost.
questions.rule: A row is not neutral data.

questions.q: Knowledge of the tabular structure of the data should be restricted to the lowest-level ____ functions in the outer circles of the architecture.
questions.explain: These utility functions are the only place that should know about rows and tables.
questions.rule: Tables are known only at the edge.

questions.q: A use case class receives a result set from the data access framework and reads columns by name. What does the author say is wrong with it?
options: Result sets are slower than lists, so the use case is inefficient
It ties the use case to the relational structure of the data
Column names should be shorter, so the code is easier to read
Nothing, because reading columns is the use case's own job
optionExplain: Speed is not the author's concern here; the issue is coupling.
Right: the use case now depends on how the data is arranged in tables.
Naming is not the issue; the dependency on the table layout is.
The author says use cases should neither know nor care about such matters.
questions.explain: Reading columns by name means the use case knows the table layout.
questions.rule: Reading columns is the job of the outer layer.

questions.q: A table is split in two for storage reasons. Rows of the old table were passed to use cases as objects. What must now change?
options: Only the outer utility code, because inner code never saw the table structure at all
The use cases, business rules and perhaps the UI coupled to the row structure
Nothing, because rows are only data and data does not carry structure
Only the database vendor's driver, which handles table changes
optionExplain: This would be true if rows had stayed in the outer circle, which the author asks for.
Right: coupling means a change to the structure ripples to every receiver of rows.
A row carries its columns, so its receivers depend on them.
A driver does not know the use cases that depend on the old rows.
questions.explain: The error shows its cost when the structure changes: every receiver of rows has to change.
questions.rule: Coupling shows up as ripple on change.
questions.hint: Who received the old rows?

questions.q: Sort each piece of code by whether the author lets it know the tabular structure.

items.t: A lowest-level utility function in the outer circles
A use case
The business rules
The UI
The code that reads rows from the store
A function that decides an order's total

questions.explain: Only the lowest-level utilities in the outer circles may know the tables. Use cases, business rules and the UI must not.
questions.rule: Know tables only at the edge.

questions.q: A reporting module hands each row from its store to a chart screen as an object. Which change fits the author's pattern?
options: Keep the rows as they are, because a UI is allowed to know the table layout
Rename the row fields so that the screen can read them more easily
Give the screen a direct connection to the store, so it can read rows itself
Have the outer data code turn rows into the report's own structures first
optionExplain: The author names the UI among the parts that get coupled by this error.
Renaming leaves the screen still tied to the row structure.
This spreads knowledge of the tables to the UI, the opposite of the pattern.
Right: the tabular form stays in the outer utility, and the screen sees only the application's form.
questions.explain: The author names the UI as a layer that can end up coupled to the relational structure, so the screen is covered by the rule.
questions.rule: Convert at the edge, before the data moves inward.
questions.teaches: The author counts the UI among the parts that rows can couple to the relational structure, in some cases, so the UI needs protection from rows as much as business rules do.

questions.section: Why Are Database Systems So Prevalent?
questions.q: What mainly explains why database systems became so prevalent in software?
options: Disks are slow, so data needs indexes and caches
Programmers find tables the most natural shape for any data
Files cannot store data once the power is switched off
A database lookup is faster than reading data held in RAM
optionExplain: Right: the author answers in a word, disks. The card next shows how.
The author says programmers organise data otherwise once it is in RAM.
Files can; the issue is access time and searching.
RAM access takes nanoseconds, far faster than any disk.
questions.explain: The author gives a one-word answer: disks.
questions.rule: Slow disks created the need.

questions.section: Why Are Database Systems So Prevalent?
questions.q: Match each system or action to its description.
pairs: Document based: stores and fetches whole documents by name
Content based: finds records by what they contain
Move the head, wait for the sector, read it into RAM
questions.explain: File systems work by document name, databases by content, and every disk read pays the cost of head movement and rotation.
questions.rule: Name for files, content for databases.

questions.section: Why Are Database Systems So Prevalent?
questions.q: A team stores thousands of scanned contracts and retrieves each by its contract number. By the author's description, which system suits that job?
options: Neither, since scanned contracts are not stored data at all
A database, which is best at storing opaque documents
A file system, which fetches whole documents by name
Either, since both search inside documents equally well
optionExplain: Scans are stored data; the question is which system suits them.
The author says databases are rather poor at storing and retrieving opaque documents.
Right: documents fetched by name are the file system's strength.
Searching inside documents is a file system weakness.
questions.explain: Whole documents fetched by name are exactly what file systems do well.
questions.rule: Match the system to the access pattern.

questions.section: Why Are Database Systems So Prevalent?
questions.q: Suppose a disk read took nanoseconds, like RAM. According to the author's account, what would happen to the main reason for indexes and caches?
options: It would stay, since indexes are needed to represent data regularly
It would grow, since faster reads need more elaborate indexing
It would weaken, since indexes and caches exist to offset the disk delay
It would vanish together with files, since file systems depend on the delay
optionExplain: Representation is part of the need, but the delay is the stated driving force.
The author ties indexing to the delay, which is gone in this case.
Right: the author presents them as the answer to disk slowness.
File systems and databases both remain ways of arranging data.
questions.explain: This is our reading of the account: the author names slowness as the force behind the whole apparatus.
questions.rule: Remove the cause and the apparatus has less to do.

questions.section: Why Are Database Systems So Prevalent?
questions.q: A colleague explains disk delay. Which statements are wrong? Select all that apply.
options: A disk read moves the head to a track, waits for the sector, and reads it into RAM
A millisecond is about as long as one processor cycle
Reading one byte reads only that byte, and the rest of the sector stays on disk
Data in RAM can be reached in nanoseconds
optionExplain: This matches the author's description.
A millisecond is about a million times longer than the cycle time of most processors.
The whole sector, often 4K, is read into RAM, then the byte is picked out.
This matches the author's contrast with disks.
questions.explain: The cost is millisecond-scale and a whole sector is read at once.
questions.rule: Disks cost milliseconds and read whole sectors.

questions.section: Why Are Database Systems So Prevalent?
questions.q: A developer must find every source file that uses a variable named x, in a project stored as ordinary files. By the author's contrast, how does this search go?
options: It is hard and slow, since file systems help little with searching content
It is easy, because file systems index the variables inside every document
It is easy, because a file name reveals what the file contains
It is impossible, because file systems cannot open the documents
optionExplain: Right: finding every .c file with a variable named x is the author's example of this weakness.
Indexing content is what database systems do; file systems index names.
The author says a name is easy to find, but content is not.
They can; the author calls the search hard and slow, not impossible.
questions.explain: The author says it is easy to find a file named login.c but hard and slow to find every .c file that has a variable named x in it.
questions.rule: Files find by name, not by content.
questions.teaches: The author's example of the file system weakness: it is easy to find a file named login.c, but hard and slow to find every .c file with a variable named x in it.

questions.section: What If There Were No Disk?
questions.q: True or false: If all your data lived in RAM, you would most likely organise it into lists, trees and hash tables rather than tables queried with SQL.
questions.explain: In RAM you would reach for lists, trees, hash tables and similar structures. The card next gives the author's argument.
questions.rule: In RAM, structures win over tables.

questions.section: What If There Were No Disk?
questions.q: According to the author, which structures would programmers use if all data were stored in RAM?
options: Records on tape, reached by sequential reads from the start of the tape
Tables and indexes, reached by SQL statements and query plans
Files and directories, reached by path names and directory listings
Linked lists, trees, hash tables and queues, reached by pointers
optionExplain: Tape drives are named among the technologies that went away.
This is the disk-era habit the author says would not carry over.
The author asks whether you would organise data into files and gives the answer no.
Right: these are what programmers do.
questions.explain: The author's answer is the ordinary in-memory structures.
questions.rule: In RAM use ordinary data structures.

questions.section: What If There Were No Disk?
questions.q: Put the steps of the author's argument in order.
items: Disks are being replaced by RAM
With data in RAM you would use lists, trees, hash tables and similar structures
You already organise data that way today
So the form of data on the disk is not an architectural concern
questions.explain: The argument runs from a prediction to a habit that already exists, and ends in the conclusion about the disk form.
questions.rule: Premises first, conclusion last.

questions.section: What If There Were No Disk?
questions.q: A team stores orders in a database and loads them into trees for pricing. According to the argument, what does the team show by this?
options: It needs a second database, since a tree cannot be kept in a table
It already reorganises data into its own structures once in RAM
It should store the trees on disk in the same form to avoid conversion
It is misusing the database, since the data should stay in tables
optionExplain: The author's point is the reverse: structure is chosen in RAM for convenience.
Right: this is the author's observation about what programmers do.
The author does not say disk form should match the in-memory form.
The author says it is unlikely you leave the data in table form in RAM.
questions.explain: The author says you read data into RAM and reorganise it, which is exactly what the team does.
questions.rule: You already reorganise in RAM.

questions.section: What If There Were No Disk?
questions.q: True or false: The author's argument says that databases are defective products.
questions.explain: The argument concerns what is architecturally significant. A detail is not a defect.
questions.rule: A detail is not a defect.

questions.section: What If There Were No Disk?
questions.q: A team says that fast SSDs make the disk argument obsolete. By the author's own reasoning, what must the team still ask?
options: Whether tables are faster on SSDs, since speed decides the shape of the architecture
How the data would be organised in RAM, since its storage form is still a mechanism
Whether to buy more disks, since faster disks mean more data in tables
Whether the data model still matters, since SSDs change what data is
optionExplain: The author treats performance as a low-level concern, not the test.
Right: the argument is about the shape of data in use, whichever medium holds it.
This is not part of the argument.
The data model stays significant whatever medium is used.
questions.explain: The shape data takes in use is the design question, whichever medium holds it.
questions.rule: The question is the shape of data in use.
questions.teaches: The author says that even now, with data kept in a database or file system, you read it into RAM and reorganise it into lists, sets, stacks, queues or trees for your own convenience.

questions.q: True or false: In the author's view, the architecture should not even acknowledge the form the data takes on the surface of the disk.
questions.explain: He says the architecture should not even acknowledge the disk. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The disk form is not the design.

questions.q: The database is really nothing more than a big ____ of bits where we store our data on a long-term basis.
questions.explain: The author's image is a bucket: it holds bits, and nothing more is claimed.
questions.rule: The database is a bucket of bits.

questions.q: A design review finds that the core classes are laid out to match the database tables. Which advice follows from the author?
options: Rename the tables to match the classes and leave both unchanged
Keep the match, since a core that mirrors the tables is easiest to maintain over time
Move the tables into the core classes so they share one definition
Design the core for the data as the program uses it, with tables a detail at the edge
optionExplain: Renaming leaves the dependency in place.
The author wants the disk form unacknowledged by the architecture.
This pulls the mechanism into the core, which is the reverse.
Right: the stored form should not decide the shape of the core.
questions.explain: The stored form is a mechanism, so the core is designed around the data as it is used.
questions.rule: The core follows use, not storage.

questions.q: True or false: If the core ignored the disk form, replacing the storage product would leave the core unchanged.
questions.explain: This is our reading of the author's advice: a core that does not acknowledge the disk is not touched when the disk form changes.
questions.rule: Ignoring the detail makes it replaceable.

questions.q: A colleague restates the chapter. Which restatement goes wrong?
options: Since architecture ignores the disk, no code ever has to touch it
The database moves data back and forth between the surface of the disk and RAM
We seldom use the data in the form it has on the disk
The database is a place for long-term storage of bits
optionExplain: Wrong: some code must still read and write the disk. The author says the architecture should not acknowledge it, not that nothing touches it.
This follows the author.
This follows the author.
This follows the author.
questions.explain: Not acknowledging a detail in the architecture is different from not having the detail at all.
questions.rule: A detail still exists; it is only kept out of the core.

questions.q: An analyst notes that her program loads stored records and then works with them only as in-memory lists and maps. What does the author say this shows?
options: The store must be a file system, since databases do not load into lists
The program is misusing the store, since records should be used where they sit
We seldom use data in the form it has in storage, so that form stays a detail
The lists and maps must be written back as tables, to keep one form
optionExplain: Both kinds bring data into RAM, and neither is singled out.
The author expects data to be reorganised after loading, not used in place.
Right: this is the author's observation about how data is really used.
Nothing in the chapter asks for one form on disk and in memory.
questions.explain: The author says we seldom use the data in the form of the stored bucket of bits, which is why the stored form is a detail.
questions.rule: Use shapes the design, not storage.
questions.teaches: The author observes that we seldom use data in the form it has in storage: we read it into RAM and reorganise it into lists, sets, stacks, queues or trees for our own convenience.

questions.q: True or false: Although storage speed matters, the author keeps it out of the core business rules.
questions.explain: Speed matters, but the author keeps it out of the core. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Speed is handled at the edge.

questions.q: The author says the performance concern of data storage can be entirely ____ and separated from the business rules.
questions.explain: Encapsulation is how the concern is kept out of the rules.
questions.rule: Encapsulate storage speed.

questions.q: Queries on an orders table are slow. According to the author, where should the team look for the fix?
options: In the use cases, by passing rows through them faster
In the business rules, by reshaping them around the query
In low-level data access mechanisms, leaving the business rules alone
In the overall architecture, by reorganising its layers around the database
optionExplain: The use cases should not handle rows at all.
This lets the speed concern shape the rules, which the author separates.
Right: speed of storage is handled at the low level.
The author says the concern has nothing to do with the overall architecture.
questions.explain: A speed problem in storage is solved in the storage mechanisms.
questions.rule: Fix storage speed in storage code.

questions.q: A team adds a cache to the data access code to speed up reads. If the concern was encapsulated, which part of the system should need to change?
options: Only the data access mechanisms
The business rules, which must learn about the cache
The use cases, which must call the cache directly
The UI, which must wait for the cache to fill
optionExplain: Right: encapsulation confines the change to the low-level code.
This would mean the concern was not separated.
The use cases should stay unaware of how data is fetched.
Nothing in the encapsulated design leaks to the UI.
questions.explain: This is our reading of encapsulation: a change in how data is fetched stays where data is fetched.
questions.rule: Encapsulation confines the change.
questions.hint: Where does the speed concern live?

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether the author would accept it.

items.t: Storage speed can be handled by low-level mechanisms
Business rules must be written in terms of the disk's speed
Getting data in and out quickly is a low-level concern
The overall architecture should be organised around the speed of the database
The speed concern can be separated from the business rules
Slow disks mean use cases must hold data as tables

questions.explain: The author accepts that speed matters and places it in low-level code. He rejects letting it shape rules or architecture.
questions.rule: Accept the need, place it low.

questions.q: A teammate says performance is an architectural concern, so storage speed should drive the core design. How does the author answer?
options: He says performance matters only for the web, which a later chapter covers
He denies that performance matters at all to a system, whatever its type
He agrees, and concludes the core must be tuned to the disk it runs on
He agrees it is architectural, yet says storage speed can be encapsulated
optionExplain: The web is the subject of a later chapter and plays no part here.
He treats it as a real need that has to be met.
He draws the reverse conclusion for data storage.
Right: he asks the question himself and answers that it is, but that this case is separable.
questions.explain: He asks whether performance is an architectural concern, answers that of course it is, and then says that for data storage it can be encapsulated and separated.
questions.rule: Performance matters; its storage part is separable.
questions.teaches: The author does grant that performance is an architectural concern ('Of course it is'), and then argues that when it comes to data storage the concern can be entirely encapsulated and separated from the business rules.

questions.q: True or false: A customer expectation that has no engineering rationale can safely be ignored.
questions.explain: The author lost his argument because the expectation, though irrational, was real. The card next tells the story.
questions.rule: Real does not mean rational.

questions.q: Why did the author's team keep its data in random access files?
options: The T1 devices at the line endpoints could only deliver files to the system
The data had few content-based relationships and suited trees and linked lists
Relational products did not yet exist in the late 1980s, when the system was built
The company could not afford any database software at that stage of the startup
optionExplain: The text gives no such limit; the choice was the team's.
Right: the form suited how the program used the data.
They existed; they were becoming dominant by then.
Cost is not given as the reason; the data suited files.
questions.explain: He chose the form that was most convenient to load into RAM.
questions.rule: Use the form that suits use.

questions.q: A buyer will not sign without a relational database on the feature list, though the product will not query it. By the author's hindsight, how should the team treat that demand?
options: As noise to refuse, since engineering principles must come first
As a real requirement, though it has no engineering rationale
As proof that the architecture needs a database at its core
As a marketing matter that is outside the team's decisions
optionExplain: This is what the author did, and says he was wrong.
Right: the need is irrational and external but no less real.
He was still right that the core should stay free of it.
The author treats the demand as one the team has to weigh itself.
questions.explain: The demand has to be met, but its place in the design is a separate matter.
questions.rule: Meet real demands, place them well.

questions.q: True or false: If the customers had not expected a relational database, the author's reason for being wrong in the story would have disappeared.
questions.explain: He says he was wrong not for engineering reasons but because customers expected one. This is our reading of the condition he gives.
questions.rule: His error was about customers, not engineering.

questions.q: A colleague retells the anecdote. Which statements are wrong? Select all that apply.
options: The author concluded he had been wrong on engineering grounds
The author was right to resist an RDBMS in the architectural core
The customers had a realistic way of using the relational data
The hardware engineer was promoted to software manager
optionExplain: He says he was right on engineering and wrong for another reason.
He says so himself.
The text says they had no realistic way of using it.
This is part of the story as told.
questions.explain: The wrong statements reverse the author's two points: engineering was on his side, and the customers had no use for the data.
questions.rule: Right on engineering, wrong on the market.

questions.q: Where does the author say the customers' expectation of a relational database came from?
options: From a technical weakness of random access files that customers had met in use
From an industry standard that all network monitoring systems of the time follow
From legal rules that require corporate data to be held in relational tables
From vendor marketing that convinced executives their data needed protecting
optionExplain: The text says there was no engineering rationale.
The author names no such standard.
No legal rules are mentioned.
Right: the author traces the check box to vendor marketing.
questions.explain: The author says the expectation originated in the vendors' marketing campaigns.
questions.rule: Expectations can be manufactured.
questions.teaches: The author says the expectation originated in highly effective marketing campaigns by the database vendors, who convinced high-level executives that corporate data assets needed protection and that their systems were the ideal means.

questions.q: A product's core keeps data in files, but customers insist on a relational database. Which approach best serves both needs?
options: Attach the database at the edge through one narrow channel
Replace the core's files with tables so customers see what they expect
Refuse the database and risk losing sales to rival products
Let every module read and write the new database freely
optionExplain: Right: both needs are met. The card next gives the author's version.
This moves the detail into the core.
This is the choice the author later regretted.
This spreads the detail through the whole system.
questions.explain: Both needs can be met if the database stays at the side.
questions.rule: Attach at the edge.

questions.q: The author says he should have bolted an RDBMS on the ____ of the system.
questions.explain: The side, not the core.
questions.rule: Bolt it on the side.

questions.q: A reporting tool keeps its data in memory structures. A client requires a store compatible with a particular vendor. What fits the author's hindsight?
options: Let the core call the store from many places for convenience
Rebuild the core's structures as tables in that vendor's store
Add the store at the side, behind one narrow and safe channel
Decline the client, since the core does not need the store
optionExplain: This is the opposite of a narrow channel.
This moves the detail into the core.
Right: the demand is met and the core is untouched.
The demand is real; declining ignores it.
questions.explain: The store is a detail demanded from outside, so it goes at the side.
questions.rule: Satisfy the demand, protect the core.

questions.q: The bolted-on database is reached only through one narrow channel. Later its product is replaced. What would need to change?
options: Every module that touched data, since all used the product
The core, which must be rewritten around the new product
Only the code behind that channel
Nothing, since a replaced product cannot be reached
optionExplain: Only the channel did, by design.
The core never depended on it.
Right: this is our reading of what a narrow channel buys.
Replacement is possible; it is only contained.
questions.explain: A narrow channel limits the damage of a change to one place.
questions.rule: A narrow channel limits change.
questions.hint: How many places know the product?

questions.q: Match each actor in the story to what happened or what should have happened.
pairs: Put an RDBMS into the system
Bolt an RDBMS on the side behind a narrow channel
questions.explain: The author fought, the company added the database, and he says the better course was to attach it at the side.
questions.rule: Fight, give in, or attach at the side.

questions.q: A vendor says every serious company must adopt its enterprise platform built on service-oriented architecture. What does the author suggest about such terms?
options: They often have more to do with marketing than reality, so weigh the need
They name proven engineering needs that every serious system shares
They matter only to executives and can safely be ignored by architects
They are a reliable sign of a mature and well-run architecture
optionExplain: Right: the author says the same marketing pattern still occurs.
The author says they are marketing, not engineering.
The story shows that executives' beliefs can become real requirements.
The author gives no such weight to them.
questions.explain: The author says that the word enterprise and the notion of service-oriented architecture have much more to do with marketing than with reality.
questions.rule: Weigh the need behind the label.
questions.teaches: The author sees the same kind of marketing campaigns today: the word enterprise and the notion of Service-Oriented Architecture have much more to do with marketing than with reality.

questions.q: True or false: The author holds that the web should not have changed how business rules are designed.
questions.explain: He says the web changed nothing, or should not have. The card next gives his reason.
questions.rule: The web is a swing, not a new world.

questions.q: Put these browser-era swings in the order the author gives.
items: Browsers are stupid and the power sits in server farms
Applets are put into the browsers
Dynamic content moves back to the servers
Ajax and JavaScript move lots of processing back into the browser
JavaScript is pulled back onto the server with Node
questions.explain: Each step reverses the one before, which is the author's point about oscillation.
questions.rule: Each step reverses the last.

questions.q: A colleague says a new front-end framework changes everything about building apps and wants the core rewritten around it. What does the pendulum view suggest?
options: Wait for the pendulum to swing back, then rewrite the core to match
Rewrite the core, since each swing makes earlier designs obsolete
Ignore the framework, since no swing ever reaches a real product
Treat it as another swing, kept away from the core business rules
optionExplain: The core is not rewritten for either swing.
The author says earlier swings changed nothing in the core.
Swings do reach products; the answer is to contain them.
Right: swings are short-term issues to push away from the core.
questions.explain: The framework is another swing, so it should be contained.
questions.rule: Contain swings; do not follow them.

questions.q: By the author's history, what is likely to happen to today's fashion for heavy processing in the browser?
options: It will become permanent, since the browser is now the only client
It will probably be reversed later, as earlier fashions were
It will end server computing altogether within a few years
It will matter only to consumer products, not to enterprise systems
optionExplain: The history shows no permanent settlement.
Right: the author expects the oscillations to continue.
The pendulum swings back, not off the scale.
Nothing in the text limits the swings to one product type.
questions.explain: This is our reading of his remark that the oscillations will continue for some time to come.
questions.rule: Expect a swing back.

questions.q: True or false: The author says the oscillations between centralised and distributed computing began with the web.
questions.explain: He says it would be incorrect to think so; they began before most of us were born.
questions.rule: The pendulum is older than the web.

questions.q: A team lead says browser-based apps are an unprecedented style. Which precedent from the author's history undercuts this?
options: Punched cards, which he calls the first browsers of their day
Mainframes with smart terminals, which resemble modern browsers
Desktop client-server apps, which he says had no server component
Applets, which he says were abandoned before the web arrived
optionExplain: He names punched cards but not as browsers.
Right: the author draws this analogy.
Client-server had servers; the point is the split of power.
Applets came during the web era.
questions.explain: The author places mainframes with smart green-screen terminals before minicomputers with dumb terminals, and calls them very analogous to modern-day browsers.
questions.rule: The browser has a precedent.
questions.teaches: Before the web came client-server, before that central minicomputers with arrays of dumb terminals, and before that mainframes with smart green-screen terminals, which the author calls very analogous to modern-day browsers.

questions.q: A desktop app's marketing team demands that the whole UI look like a web browser. What would best protect the application?
options: A rule that marketing must approve each release before it ships
A faster database behind the business rules
A larger team able to rewrite the whole UI quickly
Business rules that are already isolated from the UI
optionExplain: This does not remove the coupling.
Speed does not help with a change of look.
This fixes the symptom, not the coupling.
Right: the new look then touches only the UI. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.explain: Isolation turns a UI redesign into a local change.
questions.rule: Isolate before it is needed.

questions.q: What did company Q do after the web arrived, as the author tells it?
options: Made its desktop GUI look like a browser, then gradually removed that feel
Moved the whole finance app onto servers and dropped the desktop version
Replaced the GUI with a text interface for speed and reliability
Sold the product to a web company that rebuilt it as a browser app
optionExplain: Right: users disliked the change, and Q backed away from it.
The text says the product returned to a regular desktop GUI.
No such step is described.
No sale is described.
questions.explain: Q changed the look, saw it fail, and reversed it.
questions.rule: A UI swing can be reversed.

questions.q: A team's order rules call GUI widgets directly, and marketing wants a new look next quarter. What does the author's advice imply?
options: Rewrite the rules in the language of the new look and its widgets
Wait for the new look and fix each rule as it breaks, one at a time
Isolate the rules from the GUI now, so only the UI changes later
Refuse the new look on engineering grounds and keep the old UI
optionExplain: This ties them even more closely to the UI.
This accepts the coupling he warns about.
Right: this is the protection he recommends.
The anecdote with the database showed the cost of refusing outside demands.
questions.explain: The coupling is what makes the change expensive, so remove it first.
questions.rule: Remove the coupling before the change.

questions.q: True or false: After a platform changes its look, an app whose UI and business rules are isolated needs work mostly in its UI.
questions.explain: Isolation confines the effect of a UI change to the UI.
questions.rule: Isolation limits the blast.

questions.q: A colleague draws lessons from Q's story. Which are weak readings of it? Select all that apply.
options: Q's architects had decoupled the rules, which saved the product
A marketing decision can reshape a UI suddenly
Users reject a browser look in every desktop product
Decoupling the UI from the rules is the protection the author recommends
optionExplain: The author does not know whether they had.
This fits the story.
The story shows one case, not a universal rule.
This fits the author's advice.
questions.explain: The story shows a risk and a remedy, but does not show what Q's architects did or prove a general taste of users.
questions.rule: A story is not a proof.

questions.q: An architect says one small direct call from the business rules to a screen class is harmless. How does the author's remark about marketing apply?
options: It applies only to company A's phone, not to desktop software like company Q's
It does not apply, since small calls are too small to matter to marketing
Each bit of coupling is something marketing can pounce on, so small ones count
It shows marketing should be kept out of design meetings entirely
optionExplain: The author uses both stories for the same lesson.
The remark is about exactly such small couplings.
Right: the author says there are always marketing geniuses waiting for the next little bit of coupling.
The author asks for isolation, not for excluding marketing.
questions.explain: The author hopes the architects at A kept UI and business rules isolated, because marketing geniuses are always ready to pounce on the next bit of coupling.
questions.rule: Each coupling is a future cost.
questions.teaches: The author says there are always marketing geniuses waiting to pounce on the next little bit of coupling you create, so even small couplings between the UI and the business rules carry risk.

questions.q: True or false: The author argues that the web's richness exempts it from being treated as a detail.
questions.explain: He grants the richness but still treats the web as a detail. The card next gives his argument.
questions.rule: Richness does not remove detail status.

questions.q: Put the three steps of the author's argument in order.
items: The GUI is a detail
The web is a GUI
So the web is a detail
questions.explain: Two premises lead to the conclusion.
questions.rule: Two premises, one conclusion.

questions.q: A team says the web front end is so special that business rules should be written in terms of browser events. What is the reply from the author's argument?
options: The web is a GUI and a GUI is a detail, so it goes behind a boundary
Browser events are fine, since the web is no ordinary GUI but a platform of its own
Business rules should avoid events by using only synchronous calls
The web should be treated as an architectural element of its own
optionExplain: Right: the premises carry over to this case.
This accepts the richness argument he sets aside.
The reply is about the boundary, not about call style.
He calls it a detail.
questions.explain: The argument applies to any GUI, so it covers the browser.
questions.rule: A rich GUI is still a GUI.

questions.q: What stops the application's exchange with the web from being abstracted the way UNIX abstracts devices, according to the author?
options: Business logic has no inputs or outputs to abstract
Browsers do not support any form of standard interface
UNIX devices are always faster than browsers
The exchange is chatty in ways specific to each GUI
optionExplain: He says it does, which is the next idea.
The author does not argue from browser standards.
Speed is not the issue he names.
Right: this is the part that cannot be generalised.
questions.explain: The obstacle is the shape of the exchange, which varies with the GUI.
questions.rule: Chatty exchanges resist abstraction.

questions.q: True or false: The author grants that part of the objection to device independence for the web is correct.
questions.explain: He says that to some extent the objection is true, because the exchange with a GUI is chatty in ways specific to the GUI. He still treats the web as a detail.
questions.rule: Accept the limit, keep the boundary.

questions.q: A team ports a desktop GUI app to the browser and finds the pattern of exchange changes. What does the author say about that difference?
options: The difference shows the web needs an architecture of its own, separate from the business rules
The browser-app dance differs from the desktop one, so abstracting it is unlikely
The difference is small and a standard abstraction removes it
The difference is a defect of browsers that will pass
optionExplain: He calls the web a detail, not an architecture.
Right: the exchange is specific to each kind of GUI.
He says abstraction here seems unlikely.
Nothing in the text treats it as temporary.
questions.explain: The author says the dance between a browser and a web application is different from the dance between a desktop GUI and its application.
questions.rule: GUIs differ in how they converse.
questions.teaches: The dance between a browser and a web application is different from the dance between a desktop GUI and its application, so trying to abstract that dance, as devices are abstracted out of UNIX, seems unlikely to be possible.

questions.q: A use case needs a customer name and a quantity from a screen. What should it receive?
options: The screen object itself, so that it can read the fields later
A plain data structure that holds the input data
A callback it can use to ask the screen for more fields as needed
