A string of markup that it parses to find the fields
optionExplain: This ties the use case to that screen.
Right: the card next shows why.
This keeps the exchange chatty and screen specific.
This ties it to the form of the UI.
questions.explain: A data structure leaves the use case free of the UI.
questions.rule: Data structures cut the tie.

questions.q: Each use case can be described by its input data, the processing performed, and the ____ data.
questions.explain: Input, processing, output.
questions.rule: Describe use cases by input and output.

questions.q: A refund use case was built behind a web form and now needs a phone app. Which design lets it stay unchanged?
options: It asks the UI for each field in turn as it runs, over many calls
It reads fields directly from the web form object of the framework
It calls the page to render its result when it finishes
It takes a request structure and returns a result structure
optionExplain: This is the chatty exchange that cannot be abstracted.
This is tied to the form.
This is tied to the web UI.
Right: either UI can fill and read the structures.
questions.explain: Plain structures at the boundary work for any UI.
questions.rule: Structures at the boundary.

questions.q: A second UI is added and fills the same input structure. What does the use case need to know about the new UI?
options: Nothing, as it only receives and returns data
Its screen layout, so the output can be formatted
Its event model, so that it can wait for input
Its name, so that it can choose a style of reply
optionExplain: Right: this is what the pattern buys.
Formatting belongs to the UI.
It runs only once input is complete.
The use case does not choose among UIs.
questions.explain: The use case sees only the structures, whichever UI made them.
questions.rule: Structures hide the UI.

questions.q: Which of these designs break the author's approach? Select all that apply.
options: The use case takes a form object from the web framework
The use case returns a structure that the UI then formats
The use case calls a method on the UI between its steps
The input is collected first and then passed in one structure
optionExplain: This ties the use case to one UI.
This is the approach.
This is the chatty exchange the approach avoids.
This is the approach.
questions.explain: Passing a framework object or calling back into the UI both leave the use case tied to that UI.
questions.rule: No UI types inside a use case.

questions.q: A wizard collects an order over five screens. When can the use case run, by the author's account?
options: Only after the UI is closed and all its screens are gone
After the first screen, using whatever data exists so far, to save time
Once the input data is complete, and the result then feeds back
In small parts, one part for each screen in the wizard
optionExplain: Results are fed back into the exchange, so the UI stays.
The author says the input must be complete.
Right: this is the point at which the use case executes.
Nothing says a use case is split to match screens.
questions.explain: The author says at some point in the exchange the input data is complete, which allows the use case to execute, and the result is then fed back.
questions.rule: Run on complete input.
questions.teaches: At some point in the dance between the UI and the application the input data can be said to be complete, which allows the use case to be executed, and its resulting data can then be fed back into the dance.

questions.q: True or false: Framework authors write their frameworks to solve the problems they know: their own and those of their coworkers and friends.
questions.explain: They write for the problems they know, not for the problems of everyone who will use them. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Authors know their own problems.

questions.q: Framework authors know their own problems, and write their frameworks to solve those problems, not ____.
questions.explain: The author says they do not know you or your problems.
questions.rule: Authors know their own problems.

questions.q: A popular framework was built to solve problems in its authors' shop. Your team has a different workload. What does the author's view predict?
options: It will not fit at all, since problems of different teams do not overlap
It will fit fully, because popular frameworks cover every need
It will fit to the extent that your problems overlap with theirs
It will fit once you rewrite your workload to match
optionExplain: The author says overlap is usually quite large.
Popularity comes from overlap, not from covering all needs.
Right: usefulness follows overlap.
The author does not advise bending your problem to the tool.
questions.explain: The author's test is overlap between your problems and the author's.
questions.rule: Fit follows overlap.

questions.q: Suppose your own team writes a framework for its own product. How would the author's concern change?
options: It would shrink, since the authors would know the problems
It would grow, since a team always misjudges its own problems
It would stay the same, since any framework is an architecture
It would vanish, since a framework made at home needs no care
optionExplain: Right: this is our reading; the concern comes from the author not knowing you.
Nothing in the text supports this.
The concern is about whose problems are known, not about size.
The author's other warnings about coupling still apply.
questions.explain: The author's worry rests on a gap in knowledge between author and user.
questions.rule: The gap in knowledge drives the concern.
questions.hint: What does the author say the authors do not know?

questions.q: A colleague summarises the author's view. Which statements misread it? Select all that apply.
options: Frameworks are generally a bad thing and should be avoided
Most framework authors offer their work free to be helpful
Authors who give their work free must have users' interests at heart
Frameworks can be very useful where problems overlap
optionExplain: He says that, generally, popularity of frameworks is a good thing.
This is his account.
He says that, whatever their motives, they cannot, because they do not know you.
This is his account.
questions.explain: He praises the motives and the usefulness and still says the authors cannot know your problems.
questions.rule: Praise the tool, doubt the fit.

questions.q: A framework's marketing calls it the architecture for your application. How does the author's opening remark about frameworks apply?
options: It applies only to web frameworks, since others lack a UI
It applies only if the framework is free, since paid ones are real architectures
It does not apply, since a popular framework has proven itself an architecture
Frameworks are not architectures, though some try to be, so the claim needs care
optionExplain: The remark is about frameworks in general.
The author does not tie the claim to price.
Popularity does not make a framework an architecture.
Right: this is how the chapter opens.
questions.explain: The author opens by saying frameworks are not architectures, though some try to be.
questions.rule: A framework is a tool, not a design.
questions.teaches: The author opens the chapter by saying that frameworks are not architectures, though some try to be.

questions.q: True or false: A framework author commits to supporting the users who couple their code tightly to the framework.
questions.explain: He commits to nothing of the kind. The card next shows the imbalance.
questions.rule: The author makes no commitment.

questions.q: The author calls the relationship a one-directional ____.
questions.explain: The image is a marriage in which only one side commits.
questions.rule: One side commits.

questions.q: A framework's guide urges you to derive your business objects from its base classes. Which description fits the author's view?
options: You and the author share the risk of changes to the framework
You take on a large commitment, and the author takes on none
The author carries the risk, since the framework is his product
Neither side carries any risk, since deriving is a small step
optionExplain: The author says the framework author takes on nothing.
Right: that is the asymmetry.
He says his coupling is no risk because he controls the framework.
He calls it a huge commitment.
questions.explain: The user binds themselves; the author remains free.
questions.rule: Risk sits with the user.

questions.q: The framework later changes in ways that do not suit your product. Who bears the cost, in the author's picture?
options: The author, who must keep every user's code working
You, who made the commitment; the author made none
Both equally, since both depend on the same code
Neither, since a framework is stable once published
optionExplain: He makes no commitment to you.
Right: that is what a one-directional marriage means.
The dependency runs one way, from you to the framework.
The author lists framework changes as a risk.
questions.explain: The party who coupled pays for the change.
questions.rule: Coupling transfers the cost to you.
questions.hint: Who committed?

questions.q: Match each party to its position in the author's picture.
pairs: Has absolute control, so coupling to the framework is no risk
Takes on all the risk and burden
Advises deriving from base classes and importing the framework into business objects
questions.explain: The author controls, the user bears, and the documentation pushes towards tight coupling.
questions.rule: Control and risk sit on opposite sides.

questions.q: How does the author describe a framework author's feeling when users derive from the framework's base classes?
options: Guilt, since tight coupling harms the users who derive from the base classes
Indifference, since the author has no stake in how users build on the framework
Worry, since each user adds to his duties
Nothing feels more validating than users who inextricably derive from them
optionExplain: The author does not say this about the framework author's feelings.
He says the author wants users coupled.
He says the author makes no commitment, so no such duty is felt.
Right: that is the author's remark.
questions.explain: The author says nothing feels more validating to a framework author than a bunch of users willing to inextricably derive from the author's base classes.
questions.rule: Tight coupling flatters the author.
questions.teaches: The author says nothing feels more validating to a framework author than a bunch of users willing to inextricably derive from the author's base classes.

questions.q: A framework helps with your early features. Which long-term problem might follow if your business objects inherit from it?
options: As the product matures, the framework may fight you
The framework becomes cheaper to use as it grows older
The business objects become easier to move to another framework
The framework automatically follows your changing needs
optionExplain: Right: the card next gives this and other risks.
The author lists no such benefit.
He says the reverse: it is very hard to break away.
The author says it may outgrow your needs, not follow them.
questions.explain: The early help hides a later cost.
questions.rule: Early help, later cost.

questions.q: Which of these does the author list as risks of coupling to a framework? Select all that apply.
options: The framework's architecture may violate the Dependency Rule
Your product may outgrow the framework's facilities
A new and better framework may come along that you wish you could switch to
Frameworks cannot be combined with any database
optionExplain: This is the first risk he lists.
This is a risk he lists.
This is a risk he lists.
The author makes no such claim.
questions.explain: Three of the listed risks are about the framework's architecture, your growth and a better alternative.
questions.rule: Know the listed risks.

questions.q: Your Entities extend a framework's base class, and a better framework appears. What do you face, by the author's account?
options: No switch is needed, since the old framework keeps on improving release after release
An easy switch, since only the outer circles depend on it
A hard switch, since the framework sits in your innermost circle
A free switch, since the author of the old one will help
optionExplain: The author says better ones may come along that you wish to adopt.
Your Entities are in the innermost circle.
Right: once in, the framework does not come out.
He says the author makes no commitment to you.
questions.explain: Inheritance in the core makes later change costly.
questions.rule: Core coupling is hard to undo.

questions.q: Your product grows beyond what the framework offers. What does the author say follows?
options: The framework drops out of the code on its own
The framework adapts to your needs through new releases
The framework fights you more and more as time passes
The growth stops, since the framework limits your design
optionExplain: He says the wedding ring stays on.
He says it may evolve in a direction you do not find helpful.
Right: that is his wording.
The text does not say growth stops.
questions.explain: Growth makes the framework's limits felt.
questions.rule: Outgrown frameworks fight back.

questions.q: True or false: Once a framework has been inherited into your business objects, the author says it is easy to remove later.
questions.explain: He says that once in, the framework is not coming back out, like a wedding ring on your finger.
questions.rule: Do not expect to remove it.

questions.q: A framework releases a new version that changes features you used. Which risk from the author's list does this show?
options: You may be stuck upgrading to versions that do not help you
The framework's own architecture may violate the Dependency Rule
A new and better framework may come along that you wish to adopt
Your product may outgrow the facilities that the framework offers
optionExplain: Right: this is a listed risk.
This is a different risk, about the framework's own structure.
This is also a different risk, about alternatives.
This is about your growth, not the framework's changes.
questions.explain: The author lists the risk that the framework may evolve in a direction you do not find helpful, so you may be stuck upgrading and may lose features you used.
questions.rule: A framework evolves on its own schedule.
questions.teaches: The framework may evolve in a direction you do not find helpful: you may be stuck upgrading to new versions that do not help you, and old features you used may disappear or change in ways that are hard to keep up with.

questions.q: A framework wants your business objects to extend its base class. What does the author tell you to do?
options: Avoid every framework in all code, including the outer circles
Agree, since every framework deserves a place in the core
Copy the framework's code into your core and modify it
Say no, and derive proxies instead, kept in plug-in components
optionExplain: He says you can use the framework; just do not couple to it.
This is the marriage the author warns against.
The author does not suggest copying.
Right: the card next gives the details.
questions.explain: The core stays free of the framework.
questions.rule: Proxies, not business objects.

questions.q: The author's advice about frameworks is: do not ____ the framework!
questions.explain: The image of the whole chapter is marriage.
questions.rule: Do not marry.

questions.q: A domain class would need persistence annotations and a base class from an ORM framework. What does the author prefer?
options: Add the base class, since the ORM is what stores the class
Keep the domain class free of them and use framework-aware proxies in a plug-in
Add only the annotations, since annotations are not inheritance and so do not couple
Drop the ORM altogether, since any framework is unacceptable
optionExplain: This puts the framework into the innermost circle.
Right: proxies in outer components carry the framework.
Annotations still couple the domain class to the framework.
He says you can use frameworks.
questions.explain: The framework serves the plug-in component, not the domain class.
questions.rule: Domain classes stay clean.

questions.q: True or false: If a framework sits in a plug-in component, replacing it forces changes in the business rules.
questions.explain: This is our reading of keeping the framework at arm's length: the rules never referred to it.
questions.rule: The rules do not notice the swap.

questions.q: A reviewer finds autowiring annotations in five business objects. What is the problem, by the author's advice?
options: The annotations make the business objects run slowly at runtime
Business objects should not know about the framework
Autowiring never works with business objects
There are too few annotations to be consistent
optionExplain: Speed is not his concern.
Right: they have been married to it.
It works; the problem is where it is used.
Consistency is not the issue.
questions.explain: He says to use the framework but not to sprinkle its annotations through business objects.
questions.rule: Keep annotations out of the core.

questions.q: A team wires a new framework only in its Main component. Why does the author consider that acceptable?
options: Main is owned by the framework author, who permits the use
Main is the largest component in the system, so it can hold more code
Main is written first, so any later code can depend on it
Main is the dirtiest, lowest-level component in the architecture
optionExplain: The text gives it no such owner.
Size is not his reason.
Order of writing is not his reason.
Right: it is the right place for such knowledge.
questions.explain: He says it is okay for Main to know about Spring since Main is the dirtiest, lowest-level component in the architecture.
questions.rule: Put knowledge of details at the lowest level.
questions.teaches: It is okay for Main to know about the framework since Main is the dirtiest, lowest-level component in the architecture.

questions.q: True or false: The author says that for some frameworks a team has no real choice but to marry them.
questions.explain: He says a team cannot always avoid depending on a framework: some you simply must marry. The card next gives the advice.
questions.rule: Some marriages are unavoidable.

questions.q: Try not to marry a framework right away; see if you can ____ it for a while first.
questions.explain: Dating is the author's name for keeping it at a distance first.
questions.rule: Date before you marry.

questions.q: A team lead wants to adopt a UI framework across all modules on day one. What does the author advise?
options: Hold off, keep the framework behind a boundary as long as possible
Adopt it at once across all modules, since delay only adds cost
Refuse it outright, since all frameworks do the same harm to a design
Let each module choose for itself whether to couple to it
optionExplain: Right: this is his advice.
He advises delay.
He says some are worth using.
This makes the commitment by drift, not by decision.
questions.explain: The commitment should be late and deliberate.
questions.rule: Delay the commitment.

questions.q: A team marries a framework. For how long must it expect to live with the choice?
options: Until a better framework appears, when it can swap freely
Until the next major release of the framework
For the rest of the application's life cycle
Only for the first year, while the code is young
optionExplain: He lists this as a risk, because swapping is hard.
Nothing says the commitment ends then.
Right: that is the author's warning.
He says the whole life cycle.
questions.explain: A marriage is for the long term.
questions.rule: Marriage is long term.

questions.q: Which readings of the author's advice are wrong? Select all that apply.
options: Coupling to a framework is forbidden in every case
Marrying a framework should be a deliberate decision
A team that has married a framework can leave it cheaply
Keep the framework behind a boundary for as long as you can
optionExplain: He says some frameworks must be married.
This is his advice.
He says you will be stuck with it.
This is his advice.
questions.explain: The advice allows marriage and warns that it is lasting.
questions.rule: Allowed, but lasting.

questions.q: A C++ team asks whether it must keep the standard template library behind a boundary. How does the author see it?
options: It is not a framework at all, so the advice about frameworks does not apply to it
It must be kept behind a boundary like any framework, with no exceptions
It is hard to avoid marrying it; that is normal, but it should be a decision
It should be avoided by writing the team's own containers
optionExplain: He includes it among frameworks you may have to marry.
He says some are unavoidable.
Right: the author uses this as an example of a marriage that is hard to avoid.
He does not suggest this.
questions.explain: He says that with C++ you will likely have to marry the STL, and with Java the standard library, and that this is normal but should still be a decision.
questions.rule: Unavoidable is still a decision.
questions.teaches: In C++ you will likely have to marry the STL, and in Java you will almost certainly have to marry the standard library; the author calls that normal.

questions.q: A site sells videos to individuals and businesses, and also has authors and administrators. How many separate sources of change would you expect from them?
options: Four, one for each actor, whether viewer, purchaser, author or admin
One, since all four kinds of actor work on the same videos and the same site
Two, one for buyers and one for the staff who run the whole site
Six, one for each use case
optionExplain: Right: the card next explains the split.
They want different things from the system.
Viewers and purchasers differ for businesses.
The Single Responsibility Principle counts actors, not use cases.
questions.explain: Each actor can ask for changes independently.
questions.rule: One source of change per actor.

questions.q: According to the Single Responsibility Principle, the four actors will be the four primary sources of ____ for the system.
questions.explain: The principle names the actor as the reason to change.
questions.rule: Actors are reasons to change.

questions.q: A new bulk-discount rule is requested, which only purchasers see. Which part of the system should change if it is partitioned by actor?
options: Only the administrators' code, since they set prices
The code of every actor, since prices are shared
The code that serves authors, since they supply the videos
Only the code that serves purchasers
optionExplain: Our reading: price setting is a different request from a purchasing rule.
This would mean the partition failed.
Authors are not affected by purchase discounts.
Right: the change belongs to one actor.
questions.explain: The point of partitioning is that one request touches one actor's code.
questions.rule: One request, one actor.

questions.q: True or false: With the system partitioned by actor, a change for one actor can still be expected to touch the code of the other actors.
questions.explain: Partitioning by actor aims to prevent exactly this.
questions.rule: One actor, one change set.

questions.q: Why are viewer and purchaser separate actors for businesses, though one person plays both for individuals?
options: Businesses may only stream while individuals may only download videos
Businesses often have buyers who differ from the people who watch
Viewers pay a higher price than purchasers
Purchasers are always administrators
optionExplain: Individuals can stream or download.
Right: the two roles can be played by different people.
Viewers do not pay in the text.
No such link is stated.
questions.explain: A role is an actor when it can change independently of the other.
questions.rule: Different people, different roles.

questions.q: A reader notes that the use-case list has no log-in or log-out. How does the author explain this?
options: They are not use cases, since every user must do them
He left them out to manage the size of the problem
They belong to the administrators only
They are covered by the abstract use case
optionExplain: He does not say this.
Right: the list is deliberately incomplete.
No such assignment is given.
The abstract use case concerns the catalog.
questions.explain: The author says the use cases shown are not a complete list, and omits log-in and log-out to manage the size of the problem.
questions.rule: A case study is a partial list.
questions.teaches: The use cases shown are not a complete list: log-in and log-out are omitted to manage the size of the problem, because including every use case would turn the chapter into a book.

questions.q: Two use cases in a system differ only in who performs them. What could the analysis do?
options: Delete one of them, since it is only a duplicate of the other
Merge them into one use case that ignores which actor performs it
Leave them separate and unrelated so they can evolve freely and independently
Capture their likeness early in a shared use case that both flesh out
optionExplain: They serve different actors.
Who performs it is what keeps the actors apart.
This hides the likeness.
Right: the card next gives the author's version.
questions.explain: A shared policy can be recorded once.
questions.rule: Unify the likeness.

questions.q: An abstract use case is one that sets a general ____ that another use case will flesh out.
questions.explain: The abstract use case holds the general policy.
questions.rule: Abstract use cases hold policy.

questions.q: A library app has Browse Books as Member and Browse Books as Librarian, which are nearly identical. What does the author's approach suggest?
options: An abstract Browse Books use case that both inherit from
A single Browse Books that both actors share and change together
No change, since actors should never share anything
A new Browse Books actor to hold the shared code
optionExplain: Right: the same move as the catalog.
This couples the actors.
The author unifies the similarity.
The sharing is between use cases, not actors.
questions.explain: The author's catalog example is the model.
questions.rule: Inherit from an abstract use case.

questions.q: A third actor later needs a similar catalog view. What does the abstract use case give the analysis?
options: A guarantee that the catalog never changes once it is drawn
A way to avoid adding the new use case for the third actor
A place to hold shared policy that the new use case inherits
A reason to merge all three actors into a single actor
optionExplain: Nothing is guaranteed.
A new actor still needs its own use case.
Right: this is our reading of the benefit.
The actors stay separate.
questions.explain: Inheritance gives the third use case the shared policy.
questions.rule: Shared policy is reusable.

questions.q: True or false: In the case study, View Catalog as Viewer and View Catalog as Purchaser each define separate, unrelated policies.
questions.explain: Both inherit from the abstract View Catalog use case, which sets the general policy.
questions.rule: They share one policy.

questions.q: A teammate says the abstract use case was needless, since removing it loses no feature. How does the author respond?
options: He says the abstraction is required by the UML standard and cannot be removed
He denies it, saying several features would be lost without it
He agrees it was not strictly necessary, but unified the likeness early
He withdraws it from the design in the later chapters
optionExplain: He calls his notation his own.
He says no feature would be compromised.
Right: he grants the point.
The abstraction stays in the case study.
questions.explain: He says it was not strictly necessary and could have been left out of the diagram without compromising any feature, but the use cases were so similar that unifying them early seemed wise.
questions.rule: Some abstractions are for clarity.
questions.teaches: The author admits the abstract use case was not strictly necessary: it could have been left out of the diagram without compromising any feature of the product.

questions.q: In a system with several actors, how might views, presenters, interactors and controllers be divided into components?
options: Each category is broken up by the actor it serves
Each category goes into one big component shared by all actors
Each class goes into its own component, whatever its actor
Everything goes into one component until it grows
optionExplain: Right: the card next shows this.
This lets one actor's change reach the others.
This ignores the actors.
This gives no partition.
questions.explain: Components follow actors.
questions.rule: Partition by actor.

questions.q: Each component in the author's partition is a potential .jar file or ____ file.
questions.explain: Jar for Java, dll for .NET and native code.
questions.rule: A component is a potential deliverable.

questions.q: Authors get a new upload feature. In this partition, where should the new view code go?
options: In the interactors, which process the upload
In the purchasers' views, which already display videos
In a new shared view component used by every actor
In the components that hold the authors' views
optionExplain: Views display; interactors process.
Purchasers are a different actor.
This would couple the actors.
Right: the change serves the author actor.
questions.explain: The feature serves authors, so its view goes in their views.
questions.rule: Code goes where its actor is.

questions.q: A change is requested only for administrators. Which actor-based groups should need to change?
options: The components of all four actors
Only the administrators' components
The authors' and the administrators' components
Only the controllers of every actor
optionExplain: This would mean the partition failed.
Right: that is the purpose of the partition.
Authors are a different actor.
Controllers are split by actor too.
questions.explain: The partition confines a change to one actor's components.
questions.rule: One actor, one change set.

questions.q: Which descriptions of the component drawing are wrong? Select all that apply.
options: Each category of code is kept in one component shared by all actors
The double lines are architectural boundaries
Every component must be shipped as its own jar file
Each component is a potential jar or dll file
optionExplain: Each category is broken up by actor, not shared.
This matches the drawing.
The author keeps the right to combine them.
This matches the drawing.
questions.explain: The partition is by actor, and the components are only potentially separate deliverables.
questions.rule: Split by actor; ship as needed.

questions.q: How does the author expect the catalog components for the shared View Catalog use case to be coded?
options: As copies of the same code in each actor's own component, kept in step
As abstract classes in special components that others extend
As interfaces that no class implements, used only in the diagrams
As a database table shared by every actor in the system
optionExplain: This repeats code and does not use the abstraction.
Right: the inheritance mirrors the use-case abstraction.
Inheriting classes are expected.
The text describes classes, not tables.
questions.explain: The author notes the special components for the Catalog View and Catalog Presenter, which he assumes hold abstract classes that inheriting components extend.
questions.rule: Abstraction in the use case becomes abstraction in code.
questions.teaches: The special Catalog View and Catalog Presenter components are assumed to hold abstract classes, and the inheriting components contain view and presenter classes that inherit from them.

questions.q: True or false: A system built from many components need not be delivered as one file per component.
questions.explain: The author keeps the right to combine them. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Build apart, ship as needed.

questions.q: The author would break the compile and build environment into components so that he could build independent ____.
questions.explain: Independent deliverables are the point of the separation.
questions.rule: Separate builds give choices.

questions.q: Views change often, and interactors rarely change. Which deployment fits the author's advice?
options: Ship the interactors with every release, since they hold the policy
Ship everything as one file so that versions always match each other
Ship one file per class, so that every class can deploy alone
Deploy the likely-to-change components apart from the stable ones
optionExplain: Policy is the part that should change least.
This gives up independence.
This is far finer than the components.
Right: independent deployment follows change.
questions.explain: The point of grouping is to ship what changes separately from what does not.
questions.rule: Group by rate of change.

questions.q: Conditions change, and the team merges five deliverables into two. What does the structure need?
options: No change to the code structure, only a new file grouping
A rewrite of the interactors, since they now share a file with others
A new set of actors, since the files changed shape
A new architectural boundary between the two files
optionExplain: Right: components stay separate in the source.
File grouping does not change the source.
Actors are unchanged.
The boundaries stay where they were.
questions.explain: Deployment grouping is a choice made on top of the structure.
questions.rule: Grouping is not structure.
questions.hint: Does the source structure change?

questions.q: True or false: If components are combined into fewer jar files, the component boundaries in the source disappear.
questions.explain: The boundaries stay in the source; only the packaging changes.
questions.rule: Packaging does not erase boundaries.

questions.q: The author describes an even more primitive grouping than five files. Which is it?
options: Three files: controllers, interactors and a shared utilities file
One file for each actor, holding all its code
Two files: views and presenters in one, the rest in the other
A single file, holding the whole system
optionExplain: This is not given.
This is not one of the groupings he describes.
Right: the primitive grouping has two jar files.
He describes two files as the most primitive.
questions.explain: He also describes putting views and presenters together in one jar and interactors, controllers and utilities in another, then a still more primitive two-jar split.
questions.rule: More groupings are possible.
questions.teaches: An even more primitive grouping is two jar files, with views and presenters in one and everything else in the other.

questions.q: In a system where controllers receive input and views display output, which way should source dependencies point?
options: Toward the views, which are what users see first and last
The same way as control flows, from input to display
Toward the components holding higher-level policy
Toward whichever component has the most code in it
optionExplain: Visibility to users does not set the direction.
This is the intuitive reading the author does not follow.
Right: the card next explains how.
Size is not the test.
questions.explain: Dependencies follow policy, not control flow.
questions.rule: Point toward policy.

questions.q: Put the flow of control in the case study in order.
items: Controllers receive the input
Interactors process the input into a result
Presenters format the result
Views display the presentation
questions.explain: Control flows from input to display.
questions.rule: Control flows input to display.

questions.q: An interactor must hand a result to a presenter, but dependencies must point toward policy. How does the case study handle this?
options: A closed arrow: inheritance runs against the flow of control
The interactor depends directly on the concrete presenter class it calls
The presenter keeps its own copy of the interactor's code to avoid a link
A shared database holds the result between them while each runs
optionExplain: Right: this is the Open-Closed Principle at work.
That would point dependency with the flow, toward the detail.
Copying is not described.
The text uses no database here.
questions.explain: Closed arrows run against the flow of control.
questions.rule: Inheritance reverses the arrow.

questions.q: A view component is redesigned. By the dependency direction, what happens to the interactors?
options: They must change if the redesign touches how output is shown
They must be rewritten, since the views depend on their results to display
They must be redeployed together with the new view
Nothing, since low-level changes do not ripple up to high-level policy
optionExplain: Output is formatted by presenters and displayed by views.
The dependency runs the other way.
Deployment is a separate choice.
Right: that is the aim of the arrows.
questions.explain: Dependencies pointing toward policy shield policy from detail.
questions.rule: Detail changes stay below policy.
questions.hint: Which side depends on which?

questions.q: Match each drawing mark used in the case study to its meaning.
pairs: A using relationship, pointing with the flow of control
An inheritance relationship, pointing against the flow of control
questions.explain: Open arrows use, closed arrows inherit, and double lines mark boundaries.
questions.rule: Read the marks.

questions.q: In the case study, what corresponds to components changing for different reasons, and what to different rates?
options: Reasons correspond to levels of policy, and rates to the actors
Reasons correspond to actors, and rates to levels of policy
Reasons correspond to jar files, and rates to the programming language
Both correspond to the actors, since actors decide everything
optionExplain: The assignment is the other way round.
Right: these are the two dimensions.
Neither is mentioned.
Rates correspond to levels of policy.
questions.explain: The author says the different reasons correspond to the actors and the different rates to the different levels of policy.
questions.rule: Reasons are actors; rates are policy levels.
questions.teaches: The different reasons to change correspond to the actors, and the different rates of change correspond to the different levels of policy.

questions.q: A code base has top-level packages named web, service and repository. What does that structure mainly tell a newcomer?
options: Which business the system serves, since the names are standard
What kind of code each package holds, not which business it serves
How the system will scale, since layers separate the load between them
Which team owns each package, since layers match teams
optionExplain: The names are technical and say nothing about the business.
Right: the card next shows this.
Scaling is not what the structure shows.
Ownership is not shown by layer names.
questions.explain: Layer names describe technique, not domain.
questions.rule: Layers say how, not what.

questions.q: Match each type in the orders example to its role.
pairs: A web controller that handles requests from the web
The implementation of the orders business logic
An interface for access to persistent order information
An implementation of the repository interface
questions.explain: The example has one type for each role at the web, business and persistence levels.
questions.rule: Know the example's types.

questions.q: In a strict layered architecture, which layer may the web layer depend on directly?
options: Any layer, including those above it
The persistence layer, since it holds the data the web needs
Any layer below it, in whichever order is handy
Only the business logic layer, the next adjacent lower layer
optionExplain: Dependencies point downward only.
This skips a layer, which strict layering forbids.
That describes the relaxed form, not the strict one.
Right: strict layering allows only the adjacent lower layer.
questions.explain: Strict layering means one step down.
questions.rule: One layer down.

questions.q: A product grows much larger under package by layer. What does the chapter's author expect?
options: Three big buckets are not enough, and the code needs splitting
The layers split on their own along the lines of the business domain
The web layer shrinks as the business layer slowly absorbs its code
The dependencies start to point upward as the layers grow
optionExplain: Right: this is the problem Fowler points out.
Nothing in the text says this.
No such effect is described.
He describes downward dependencies throughout.
questions.explain: Three buckets do not scale.
questions.rule: Big buckets need splitting.
questions.hint: Fowler's point about three buckets.

questions.q: True or false: Package by layer makes the business domain obvious from the top-level package names.
questions.explain: It names web, services and repositories, not the business.
questions.rule: Layers hide the domain.

questions.q: A bookshop system and a hospital system both use package by layer. What does the chapter's author expect when you place their packages side by side?
options: The hospital system has more layers, since it is more complex
They look very different, since each domain needs its own layers
They look eerily similar: web, services and repositories
Only the class names differ, since the packages are shared
optionExplain: Layer count is not tied to the domain.
The layers are the same.
Right: the layers do not show the domain.
The packages are not shared.
questions.explain: The author says two layered architectures from different domains side by side will likely look eerily similar.
questions.rule: Layers look alike across domains.
questions.teaches: Put the code for two layered architectures from two very different business domains side by side and they will likely look eerily similar: web, services and repositories.

questions.q: True or false: Moving from package by layer to package by feature leaves the interfaces and classes the same; only their packages change.
questions.explain: The interfaces and classes stay the same; only their packages change. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Same classes, new packages.

questions.q: Package by feature slices the code ____, based on related features or domain concepts.
questions.explain: Layers slice horizontally and features slice vertically.
questions.rule: Features slice vertically.

questions.q: The view orders use case changes. Where is its code under package by feature?
options: In a separate package for each class that the use case involves
In the web package, since the change starts from the screen the user sees
In one package named for the concept, not spread over three layers
In the repository package, since orders are stored there
optionExplain: This splits the code further.
That is where it would start under package by layer.
Right: this is the potential benefit.
The repository is only part of it.
questions.explain: The code for one concept sits together.
questions.rule: Related code lives together.

questions.q: A newcomer opens the top level of a package-by-feature code base for a bookshop. What do they see?
options: Names that reflect the business domain, such as orders
The same web, services and repositories as in any system
A single package holding every class of the system
Names of the frameworks the system uses
optionExplain: Right: the structure now says something about the domain.
That describes package by layer.
Packages are split by concept.
Frameworks are not what features name.
questions.explain: Features give the domain a voice.
questions.rule: Packages name the domain.

questions.q: Sort each description by the style it fits.

items.t: Code sliced horizontally
Top-level names say web, services and repositories
Top-level names say orders
Code sliced vertically
All the orders types sit in one package
Types are split among three packages

questions.explain: Layers slice horizontally by technique, and features slice vertically by concept.
questions.rule: Horizontal by technique, vertical by concept.

questions.q: A developer says finding all the code of a use case is easy in any layout because of their IDE. How does the chapter's author's footnote bear on this benefit of package by feature?
options: The benefit depends on the language, not on the IDE
The benefit is greater, since IDEs list packages by concept
The benefit is unchanged, because IDEs do not search packages
The benefit is much less relevant with modern IDE navigation
optionExplain: The footnote is about IDE navigation.
The footnote does not say this.
He says IDE navigation weakens the benefit.
Right: the footnote says so.
questions.explain: The footnote says this benefit is much less relevant with modern IDE navigation, although a renaissance of lightweight text editors has brought it back for some.
questions.rule: The ease of finding code depends on tools.
questions.teaches: The benefit of finding all the code in one package is much less relevant with the navigation facilities of modern IDEs.

questions.q: In a design with an inside for the domain and an outside for infrastructure, which way should source dependencies point?
options: From the inside toward the outside
From the outside toward the inside
Both ways, so that each side can call the other
Neither way, since the two sides are unrelated
optionExplain: This would tie the domain to the infrastructure.
Right: the card next gives this as the major rule.
The rule forbids the inside depending on the outside.
The outside does depend on the inside.
questions.explain: The domain is depended upon and depends on nothing technical.
questions.rule: Depend inward.

questions.q: The major rule is that the outside depends on the ____, not the other way around.
questions.explain: Dependencies point inward.
questions.rule: Depend on the inside.

questions.q: In the orders example, where do a web controller and a JDBC repository belong?
options: On the inside, since they handle orders
On the outside, depending on the domain on the inside
One on each side, the controller inside and the repository outside
In neither, since they sit between the sides
optionExplain: They handle technology, not domain concepts.
Right: both are infrastructure.
Both are infrastructure.
The two-region model has no middle.
questions.explain: UI and database code are the outside.
questions.rule: UI and database are outside.

questions.q: A developer makes a domain class import a database driver class. What does this do to the rule?
options: It is neutral, since drivers have no domain meaning
It follows the rule, since both are in one code base
It follows the rule, if the driver is part of a standard library
It breaks the rule: the inside now depends on the outside
optionExplain: The dependency is what matters.
The rule concerns direction, not location.
The driver is infrastructure.
Right: this is the direction the rule forbids.
questions.explain: The inside must not know the outside.
questions.rule: Never import outward.
questions.hint: Which side is the driver on?

questions.q: Which statements about the orders example are wrong? Select all that apply.
options: The domain package is the inside
Dependencies flow away from the inside toward the outside
The diagram is complete, including interactors
The other packages are the outside
optionExplain: This matches the example.
The dependencies flow toward the inside.
The diagram omits interactors and marshalling objects.
This matches the example.
questions.explain: The example points inward and is a simplified diagram.
questions.rule: Inward and simplified.

questions.q: Inside a ports and adapters design, a repository interface for orders is named Orders. Why?
options: Inside names use the ubiquitous domain language: we say orders
Shorter names compile faster and are easier to type
The word repository is reserved for the outside by naming convention
The framework requires the name Orders for its mapping
optionExplain: Right: this is the domain-driven design advice.
Compile speed is not the reason.
No such reservation is described.
No framework is involved in the naming.
questions.explain: The author explains that in domain-driven design everything inside is named in the ubiquitous domain language, so we say orders, not the orders repository.
questions.rule: Inside names speak the domain.
questions.teaches: Names inside follow the ubiquitous domain language of domain-driven design: in a discussion of the domain we talk about orders, not about an orders repository.

questions.q: A new developer injects a repository straight into a web controller, bypassing the service layer. All dependency arrows still point downward. What has happened?
options: The layers have become a cycle, since the controller reaches down twice
Nothing, because the arrows still point the right way down the layers
Layering was relaxed: the controller now skips the service layer
The service layer has been removed from the code base
optionExplain: The graph is still acyclic.
The direction is right, but a layer is skipped.
Right: the card next names this.
The service still exists; it is bypassed.
questions.explain: A correct direction can hide a skipped layer.
questions.rule: Direction is not the only rule.

questions.q: When layers may skip their adjacent neighbours, the result is called a relaxed ____ architecture.
questions.explain: The relaxed layered architecture allows skipping.
questions.rule: Skipping makes it relaxed.

questions.q: The business logic layer checks whether a user may see an order. What risk does a controller that reads the repository directly create?
options: It makes the business layer depend on the controller
It makes the repository run slower
It can skip the authorisation check
It forces the service interface to become private
optionExplain: The dependency arrows still point downward.
Speed is not the risk named.
Right: the check lives in the layer being bypassed.
Nothing forces that.
questions.explain: Bypassing a layer bypasses what it guards.
questions.rule: Skipping skips the guard.

questions.q: True or false: When a deadline looms, a team that relies on discipline alone becomes less likely to break its rules.
questions.explain: The chapter's author says we all know what happens when budgets and deadlines start looming.
questions.rule: Discipline is fallible.

questions.q: Which statement matches the chapter's author on code reviews and static analysis tools?
options: Both are fallible, with a longer feedback loop than is wanted
Reviews are fallible, while static analysis is a certain guard
Static analysis is fallible, while reviews are a certain guard
Both are certain guards if the team trusts its developers
optionExplain: Right: he states both problems.
He says both approaches are fallible.
He says both are.
He says trust is not enough.
questions.explain: Both approaches are fallible and slow to give feedback.
questions.rule: Both are fallible.

questions.q: When can a controller that bypasses the service be the intended design, according to the chapter's author?
options: Never, since layers may not be bypassed in any sound design
Whenever the team wants a quicker response from the controller layer
Whenever the business layer has grown too large for one team
When following CQRS, with separate paths for updating and reading
optionExplain: He says in some situations it is the intended outcome.
Speed is not given as a reason.
Size is not given as a reason.
Right: he names CQRS as an intended case.
questions.explain: He says that in some situations, such as following the CQRS pattern, bypassing is intended.
questions.rule: Skipping is sometimes intended.
questions.teaches: A relaxed layered architecture is sometimes the intended outcome, for example when following the CQRS pattern, in which updating and reading data use separate patterns.

questions.q: A team wants every part of the code that touches orders to be reachable through one entry point. Which organisation fits?
options: Spread the order code over web, service and repository packages by layer
Bundle order logic and persistence behind one interface in one package
Put all order types in a package and mark each of them public
Let the UI call the database directly for every orders operation
optionExplain: This is package by layer, with several entry points.
Right: the card next gives this as package by component.
Public types are open entry points.
This has no single entry point.
questions.explain: One interface at the front of the component.
questions.rule: One door in.

questions.q: Match each style to its description.
pairs: Groups all types of one concept in one package
Splits the domain inside from infrastructure outside
Bundles logic and persistence behind one interface, UI apart
questions.explain: Each style slices the same code in a different way.
questions.rule: Know the four slices.

questions.q: A developer needs to add order-related behaviour. Where does the chapter's author say there is only one place to go?
options: The orders controller in the web package
The orders component
The repository package for all orders
Any package that mentions orders
optionExplain: The UI is kept apart from the component.
Right: all order responsibilities are behind it.
Persistence is only part of the component.
There is one place, not several.
questions.explain: The component gathers the responsibilities.
questions.rule: One place to go.

questions.q: True or false: After the persistence code inside the orders component is rewritten, consumers of the component must learn how it is organised.
questions.explain: The separation inside is an implementation detail that consumers do not need to know.
questions.rule: Hidden parts can change freely.

questions.q: How does the chapter's author's definition of a component differ from the book's earlier one?
options: They are identical in substance, differing only in the name each author gives to the idea
The book's is a single class, while his is a whole application with a database
The book's is a layer of the system; his is a feature of the system
The book's is a deployable jar; his is functionality behind a clean interface
optionExplain: He says his is slightly different.
Neither is a class or an application.
Neither definition is a layer or feature.
Right: his is about grouping and interface.
questions.explain: He quotes the book's definition and says his own is slightly different.
questions.rule: Two definitions of component.

questions.q: The chapter's author says well-defined components in a monolith can be a stepping stone to something. To what?
options: A micro-services architecture
A strictly layered architecture
A larger and more tangled monolith
A package by feature design
optionExplain: Right: a component resembles a separate service.
This is where the monolith started.
The text says the opposite direction.
Feature packaging is a different style.
questions.explain: He says well-defined components in a monolithic application can be a stepping stone to a micro-services architecture.
questions.rule: Components prepare for services.
questions.teaches: Well-defined components in a monolithic application can be a stepping stone to a micro-services architecture.

questions.section: The Devil Is in the Implementation Details
questions.q: True or false: A team's chosen architectural style is guaranteed by how it names its packages.
questions.explain: Names do not stop code from reaching across packages. The card next shows what does.
questions.rule: Names do not enforce.

questions.section: The Devil Is in the Implementation Details
questions.q: Marking all of your types as public means you are not taking advantage of the language's facilities for ____.
questions.explain: Encapsulation is what access modifiers provide.
questions.rule: Public throws encapsulation away.

questions.section: The Devil Is in the Implementation Details
questions.q: In a layered Java code base, the repository implementation class is public. What can anyone now do?
options: Only call it through the service, since packages forbid anything else
Nothing, because the interface is the only visible type to other packages
Instantiate the concrete class directly, bypassing the structure
Only read it, because public types cannot be instantiated
optionExplain: Packages do not forbid access to public types.
The implementation class itself is visible.
Right: nothing in the language prevents it.
Public classes can be instantiated.
questions.explain: Public makes the class reachable from anywhere.
questions.rule: Public is open to all.

questions.section: The Devil Is in the Implementation Details
questions.q: A team moves from package by layer to ports and adapters but keeps every type public. What does the chapter's author expect for the intended style?
options: The new style works better, since more types are reachable from everywhere
The compiler now enforces the new style automatically for the whole team
Nothing in the language protects it; the style lives only in intentions
The style is protected, because the packages are different
optionExplain: Reach is what removes the protection.
Enforcement needs the access modifiers.
Right: the compiler cannot stop code breaking it.
Packages without modifiers protect nothing.
questions.explain: A style needs the modifiers to be real.
questions.rule: Modifiers carry the style.
questions.hint: What does public allow?

questions.section: The Devil Is in the Implementation Details
questions.q: Which statements misread the chapter's author? Select all that apply.
options: The habit of overusing public is limited to layered code bases
Overuse of public appears whatever style the code aims at
Public types are needed to make any style work
Overusing public stops the language from protecting the architecture
optionExplain: He says it appears whatever style is aimed at.
This matches his account.
He says the fewer, the better.
This matches his account.
questions.explain: The habit is not tied to one style, and it removes the language's protection.
questions.rule: Public is not a free default.

questions.section: The Devil Is in the Implementation Details
questions.q: What evidence does the chapter's author offer that developers overuse the public modifier?
options: The code samples of books, tutorials and open source frameworks
A survey of developers in his own company and its clients
The Java language specification, which requires it for most classes
Compiler warnings that appear in most builds of such code
optionExplain: Right: he invites the reader to look there.
No survey is described.
He says the keyword is used by instinct.
No compiler warnings are mentioned.
questions.explain: He says that if you do not believe him, you can look at the code samples for books, tutorials and open source frameworks on GitHub.
questions.rule: The habit is easy to find.
questions.teaches: As evidence of the public habit, the chapter's author points to the code samples for books, tutorials and open source frameworks on GitHub.

questions.q: True or false: If every type in a Java code base is public, the choice among the four packaging styles makes no difference to which code may depend on which.
questions.explain: Public types can be used from anywhere, so the packages stop mattering. The card next explains.
questions.rule: All public means all reachable.

questions.q: If all types are public, packages are only an organisation mechanism, like ____.
questions.explain: Folders group things without hiding them.
questions.rule: Folders organise, they do not hide.

questions.q: In package by layer, which types must stay public, and which can be package protected?
options: All four package protected, since packages hide everything from other packages
All four types public, since every type is used by some other type
The implementations public and the interfaces left package protected
The interfaces public, and their implementations package protected
optionExplain: The interfaces must be seen by other packages.
The implementations are used only through the interfaces.
This reverses the need.
Right: only the interfaces have inbound dependencies from other packages.
questions.explain: Make public only what other packages must see.
questions.rule: Interfaces public, implementations hidden.

questions.q: In package by component, a developer outside the package tries to use the repository implementation directly. What happens?
options: It compiles, but a later code review catches it and flags it
The compiler rejects it, as only the component interface is public
It compiles, but a static analysis tool fails the build afterwards
It compiles and runs, since packages are only folders to organise code
optionExplain: Review is not needed.
Right: the language enforces the principle.
The compiler itself rejects it.
Here the types are package protected.
questions.explain: The compiler enforces what the modifiers hide.
questions.rule: The compiler can enforce.
questions.hint: Which types are public in this style?

questions.q: Sort each type by whether it can be package protected in the orders example.

items.t: The service interface in package by layer
The repository interface in package by layer
The service implementation in package by layer
The JDBC repository implementation
The component interface in package by component
The repository in package by component

questions.explain: A type needs to be public only when a class in another package depends on it.
questions.rule: Public only when needed from outside.

questions.q: In package by feature, the controller is the sole entry point and everything else is package protected. What caveat does the chapter's author give?
options: Controllers can no longer be tested, since they hold all the order logic now
Nothing else can reach order information except through the controller
The compiler stops enforcing the style, since one type is public
Order information becomes public, since the controller exposes it
optionExplain: Testing is not mentioned.
Right: this is his caveat.
The caveat is about access, not enforcement.
The caveat is about restriction, not exposure.
questions.explain: He notes that nothing outside the package can access information related to orders unless it goes through the controller.
questions.rule: Strong hiding has a price.
questions.teaches: In package by feature the controller is the only entry point, so nothing outside the package can reach order information except through it, which may or may not be desirable.

questions.q: Besides access modifiers, how might a team stop web code from depending directly on persistence code?
options: Put the web and persistence code together in the same source tree
Name the packages so that developers know not to mix them up
Mark every class final so no one can extend it
Split web, persistence and domain into separate source trees
optionExplain: A shared tree allows the dependency.
Names do not enforce anything.
Final classes do not stop dependencies.
Right: the card next gives this as a decoupling mode.
questions.explain: Separate trees let the build tool refuse the dependency.
questions.rule: The build can refuse.

questions.q: Match each term to its description.
pairs: Distinguish public types from published types
Built as separate modules in a tool such as Maven or Gradle
Domain on the inside and infrastructure on the outside
Infrastructure in one area calls another area directly
questions.explain: Each term names one decoupling mode or its trade-off.
questions.rule: Know the modes.

questions.q: A team keeps all infrastructure in one source tree and forgets access modifiers. What can a web controller now do?
options: Call the database repository directly, skipping the domain
Nothing outside its own class, since trees forbid calls
Call the domain only, since the domain tree is separate
Call the repository only through an interface the domain defines
optionExplain: Right: this is the anti-pattern.
One tree allows calls between its types.
Both infrastructure parts are in one tree.
Nothing forces the interface.
questions.explain: A shared tree allows sideways calls.
questions.rule: One tree allows shortcuts.

questions.q: A team splits web and persistence into separate trees that depend only on the domain tree. What can the web code no longer do at compile time?
options: Be built with the same build tool, Maven
Use the domain code that it depends on
Reach the persistence code directly
Show anything to the user of the system
optionExplain: The build tool is not affected.
It still depends on the domain tree.
Right: the web tree has no dependency on it.
Output is not affected.
questions.explain: Missing dependencies cannot be compiled.
questions.rule: No dependency, no call.
questions.hint: Which trees does the web tree depend on?

questions.q: True or false: The chapter's author calls splitting every component into its own source tree a practical default for every team.
questions.explain: He calls it an idealistic solution because of performance, complexity and maintenance issues.
questions.rule: Idealistic, not default.

questions.q: Why does the chapter's author name the two-tree trade-off after a ring road in Paris?
options: The ring road joins the city to its suburbs, as the domain joins the web, so the name fits
The ring road is the busiest road in Paris, as infrastructure is the busiest code in the system
A ring road goes round the city without entering it, as infrastructure goes round the domain
The ring road was built in a hurry, as infrastructure code often is, so shortcuts are likely
optionExplain: It does not enter the city, which is the point.
Traffic is not the point.
Right: the image fits the sideways calls.
Construction is not the point.
questions.explain: He says the Boulevard Périphérique allows you to circumnavigate Paris without entering the complexities of the city.
questions.rule: The ring road bypasses the centre.
questions.teaches: The Boulevard Périphérique, a ring road, lets you go around Paris without entering the city, just as infrastructure code can go around the domain.

questions.q: True or false: A good design on paper is enough to ensure that the code keeps the intended architecture.
questions.explain: Implementation choices can undo it. The card next gives the closing advice.
questions.rule: Paper designs are not enough.

questions.q: The devil is in the ____ details.
questions.explain: The closing line of the chapter.
questions.rule: Details of implementation.

questions.q: A team has designed a ports and adapters system. What should it do next, by the closing advice?
options: Map the design onto code structures and decoupling modes
Consider the design finished and start writing features straight away
Add more layers, since layers protect the design from drift
Move the design into a document that all developers must follow
optionExplain: Right: this is the missing step.
The advice says implementation can undo the design.
Layers alone do not enforce a style.
Documents are fallible enforcement.
questions.explain: Map the design to structures that protect it.
questions.rule: Map design to code.

questions.q: True or false: The closing advice asks a team to adopt the finest possible module split whatever its size and budget.
questions.explain: The advice is to be pragmatic about team size, skill, complexity, time and budget.
questions.rule: Be pragmatic.

questions.q: Which stance toward options does the chapter's author recommend?
options: Take whichever option the framework suggests
Decide every option at the start so nothing can change
Leave every option open for as long as the project runs
Leave options open where applicable, but stay pragmatic
optionExplain: The framework is not the guide.
The advice is to leave options open.
He adds pragmatism.
Right: this is the stance.
questions.explain: Flexibility with realism.
questions.rule: Flexible but pragmatic.

questions.q: A team has fixed its package structure and access modifiers. What other area does the closing advice say to watch for coupling?
options: Colour themes
Data models
Build servers
Team names
optionExplain: Not mentioned.
Right: the chapter's author names them.
Not mentioned.
Not mentioned.
questions.explain: He asks the reader to think about using the compiler to enforce the style, and to watch out for coupling in other areas such as data models.
questions.rule: Coupling hides in data too.
questions.teaches: Watch out for coupling in other areas, such as data models.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The authors judge a design mainly by how quickly its first release shipped.
questions.explain: They judge it by what each later change costs over the system's whole life. A fast first release can sit on a structure that makes every change expensive. The card next states the measure.
questions.rule: Judge by the cost of change, not the speed of the start.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors say software has two values: behavior and ____.
questions.explain: Behavior is what the system does today. Structure is what makes that behavior easy to change, and the authors rank it higher.
questions.rule: Two values: behavior and structure.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two teams built the same reporting tool. Whose design does the authors' measure favour after a year of changes?
options: Team A: first release in two weeks, but every later change has grown to take a month of work
Team B: first release in six weeks, and each later change costs about what its size would suggest
Team C: first release in three weeks with the most features, but each change now needs agreement from five other teams
Team D: first release in one week, with plans to clean up and rewrite the design in the second year
optionExplain: It shipped fast, which is tempting, but the measure counts the cost of change over the system's life, and that cost has grown out of proportion.
Right: it paid more at the start, and the cost of a change stays in line with the size of the change.
Feature count measures behavior, the first value. The measure here is the second value, and five-team agreement shows change is expensive.
Promising a cleanup later is the overconfidence the authors warn about: the pressure that caused the mess does not go away.
questions.explain: The measure is effort per change over the whole life. Team B pays more at the start but keeps each change affordable.
questions.rule: Cost of change should track the size of the change.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each statement by the value of software it speaks to.

items.t: The checkout page renders correctly on every test phone
A new payment type needs changes in one module only
The monthly report totals match the ledger
Adding a language to the app costs about what its size suggests
Every open bug on the tracker has been closed
A new engineer can alter the tax rules without touching the screens

questions.explain: Behavior means meeting requirements and fixing bugs. Structure means that changing the behavior is cheap and local. The authors want both kept high and rank structure higher.
questions.rule: Behavior is today; structure is tomorrow's changes.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A program works perfectly but is practically impossible to change. Requirements then change. What do the authors conclude?
options: It stays useful, because it already does everything it was built to do, whatever changes later
It can be rescued by a rewrite, which the authors present as the usual cure
It becomes useless, because nobody can afford to make it meet the new requirements
It loses only its second value, which matters little once the first is met
optionExplain: It met the old requirements, but requirements move, and a program that cannot follow them stops being useful.
A rewrite without changed habits repeats the mess, so the authors do not offer it as the cure.
Right: the program works, but the cost of the change exceeds its benefit, so it cannot be kept working.
This treats structure as optional, which is the attitude the extremes argument is built to refute.
questions.explain: The authors compare two extremes. A perfect but unchangeable program fails when requirements change, while a faulty but changeable one can be fixed and kept working.
questions.rule: A system you cannot change cannot be kept working.
questions.teaches: No program is literally impossible to change, but many systems reach a point, in some features or configurations, where a change costs more than it is worth, and that is what impossible means here.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Site A is slow, but extra servers fix it. Site B is fast, but each change takes weeks. Which costs more, by the authors' reasoning?
options: Site A, because slow responses lose users faster than slow changes do
They cost about the same, because both are failures of speed in some form
Site A, because the spending on servers grows with every user who is added
Site B, because hardware is cheap and people are expensive
optionExplain: It sounds practical, but it weighs operation above change, which is the order the authors reverse.
Both involve waiting, but they differ in what fixes them: money for hardware in one case, people's time in the other.
Server costs do grow, yet the authors note that adding hardware is often the cheaper repair.
Right: inefficient operation can often be repaired by adding hardware, while an architecture that impedes change consumes costly human effort.
questions.explain: Hardware is cheap and people are expensive. An architecture that impedes operation therefore costs less than one that impedes development, deployment and maintenance.
questions.rule: Spend architectural effort on change first, operation second.
questions.teaches: Because hardware is cheap and people are expensive, an architecture that impedes operation costs less than one that impedes development, deployment and maintenance.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A rules module must show results on a screen that is redesigned often. Which source dependency would a clean design choose?
options: The screen code depends on an interface that the rules module owns
The rules module imports the screen class so that it can call it directly
The two modules import each other so that either side can start an exchange
The rules module imports the screen library so that it always matches the latest release
optionExplain: Right: the rules are the code worth protecting, and the screen is the part that changes more, so the screen depends on the rules.
Calling directly is natural, but every redesign of the screen then reaches into the rules.
Mutual imports make each side vulnerable to the other, which protects neither.
Staying current with the library ties the rules to the most volatile code around.
questions.explain: Point the dependency from the part that changes more toward the part you want to protect. The card next names this as a move that recurs through the book.
questions.rule: Volatile code depends on protected code.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In the Clean Architecture, source code dependencies point only ____.
questions.explain: The inner circles hold policy and the outer circles hold mechanisms. Dependencies cross every circle boundary pointing inward.
questions.rule: Dependencies point inward, toward policy.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: An invoicing core must send emails, and the email vendor changes its API every year. How should the source dependency run?
options: The core calls the vendor's classes directly, since that is the shortest path
The core copies the vendor's classes into its own package so that it controls them
A shared module holds both, so that neither one depends on the other
The core declares a sender interface, and an adapter for the vendor implements it
optionExplain: It is short, but each API change then edits the core, which is the code to protect.
Copying makes the core name vendor concepts and maintain them, so it still depends on the volatile side.
A shared module hides the arrow but does not point it: the vendor's churn still lands next to the rules.
Right: the vendor-facing code depends on an interface that the core owns, so vendor changes stay outside.
questions.explain: The core is the code worth protecting. It owns the interface, and the volatile vendor adapter implements it.
questions.rule: The protected side owns the interface.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Order the steps that let policy code use a detail without naming it.
items: The policy code needs a service from an outer detail
An interface for that service is declared inside the policy's component
The detail's class implements that interface
Main creates the concrete class and hands it to the policy
questions.explain: The interface lives with the policy, the detail implements it, and something must still create the concrete object. That something is Main, which sits in the outermost circle.
questions.rule: Declare inside, implement outside, wire in Main.
questions.teaches: Main is the one place that may name the concrete classes: it is a low-level module in the outermost circle that builds the concrete parts, hands control to the high-level policy, and has nothing depending on it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reviewer rejects a use case that calls a presenter, saying source dependencies must follow the call direction. What is wrong with that rule?
options: Nothing: if the use case calls the presenter at run time, it must name the presenter in its source
Control can flow outward while the dependency points inward, because the use case calls an interface that it owns
The rule is sound, which is why presenters belong inside the use case layer
Dependencies and calls are the same thing, so a use case should never call anything outside its circle
optionExplain: It sounds logical, but it treats the run-time call and the source dependency as one thing.
Right: the interface is declared inside, the presenter implements it, and the source arrow points inward even though control goes out.
Moving the presenter inward would put an output detail into the policy it is meant to be kept out of.
This repeats the confusion: calls and source dependencies can point in opposite directions.
questions.explain: Dynamic polymorphism lets the source dependency oppose the flow of control, so the Dependency Rule holds whichever way control travels.
questions.rule: Control direction and dependency direction can differ.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Many components depend on a Pricing component, so it is hard to change. What should it mostly contain, by the book's component rules?
options: Concrete classes holding the formulas, so that every caller sees working code
A mix of formula classes and database calls, so that it is self-contained
Abstract classes and interfaces, so that it can be extended
Whatever runs fastest, since stability and abstraction are unrelated
optionExplain: Concrete code is easy to read, but a stable concrete component is rigid and painful to change.
Self-containment feels safe, yet database calls tie a stable component to a volatile detail.
Right: a component that is hard to change should be abstract enough that new behavior arrives by extension.
