The book links the two: the more stable a component, the more abstract it should be.
questions.explain: A heavily depended-on component cannot change cheaply, so it should hold abstractions that others extend. Concrete volatile code belongs in components few depend on.
questions.rule: Stable components should be abstract.
questions.teaches: The stable abstractions principle says a component should be as abstract as it is stable. Together with the rule to depend toward stability, it amounts to the DIP for components, because dependencies then run toward abstraction.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Merging two identical-looking pieces of code into one shared function is safe only if the copies change together every time.
questions.explain: If different groups ask for their changes, the shared function links those groups. The card next gives the test.
questions.rule: Look-alike code is not always duplication.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each scale to the form the single-responsibility idea takes there.
pairs: An axis of change that draws a boundary
questions.explain: The same idea of grouping by reason to change appears at three scales: the module answers to one actor, the component holds classes that change together, and the architecture draws a boundary at each axis of change.
questions.rule: One idea, three scales.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Shipping labels and tax invoices both use one address-formatting routine. Finance now needs a legal change to invoice addresses. What does the card suggest?
options: Edit the shared routine, since one copy is easier to keep correct
Edit the shared routine and add a flag that the label printer never sets, so labels are unaffected
Give each user its own routine unless labels and invoices change for the same reasons
Move the routine into the database layer, where both can reach it equally
optionExplain: One copy is easier only while both users want the same thing; here finance wants a change the other does not.
A flag keeps one routine but makes it answer to two groups, so every later change risks the other group.
Right: the test is who asks for changes. Labels and invoices belong to different groups, so separate routines keep their changes apart.
Moving the routine changes where it lives, not how many groups depend on it.
questions.explain: Two groups with different reasons to change should not share a routine, even if the code looks the same today.
questions.rule: Share code only between users that change together.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: After two look-alike screens for different user groups are merged, a layout change for one group can alter what the other sees.
questions.explain: The merged code now answers to both groups, so a change made for one reaches the other. Keeping the screens apart, with a view model and copied fields, avoids this.
questions.rule: Merged code carries both groups' changes.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Under one grouping, a requirement change touches a single component. Under another, the same change touches five. What does the first grouping save?
options: Nothing, since the same number of classes is edited either way
Only compile time, since component boundaries do not affect release work
The need to write tests, since a change inside one component needs none
Releasing the four components that do not depend on the change
optionExplain: Class count may match, but the cost of releasing differs by how many components change.
Compile time may improve, but the main saving is in release work.
Any change needs checking; the saving is in how many components need it.
Right: components that do not depend on the changed one need not be revalidated or redeployed.
questions.explain: Grouping what changes together confines a change. Only the changed component, and those depending on it, need the release work.
questions.rule: Confined changes mean fewer releases.
questions.teaches: Confining a change to one component means only that component needs redeploying; components that do not depend on it need not be revalidated or redeployed.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A hospital app serves nurses, billing clerks and pharmacists, and is already layered by the Dependency Rule. Which further split does the case study suggest?
options: Split by programming language, so that each group's code uses its preferred one
Split by user group, so nurses, billing and pharmacy each get components
Split by database table, so that each table gets a component of its own, matching how the data is stored
Split by file size, so that no component grows past a fixed limit
optionExplain: Language is a technical choice and says nothing about who requests changes.
Right: each group is a different actor, a different reason to change, so each gets its own views, presenters and rules.
Tables are a storage detail; splitting by them follows the database, not the people asking for change.
Size is a convenience, not a reason to change.
questions.explain: The case study separates in two dimensions at once. Layering handles levels of policy, and splitting by actor handles the different groups that ask for change.
questions.rule: Separate by actor and by level of policy.
questions.teaches: The video-sales case study separates in two dimensions: by actor, which captures different reasons to change, and by the Dependency Rule, which captures the different rates of change at different levels of policy.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The authors advise choosing the database product first, because every other design decision depends on it.
questions.explain: They advise the opposite: the business rules do not depend on the database, so the choice can wait until more is known. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Rules first, database later.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The book treats the web as a delivery detail, much like an ____ device.
questions.explain: The web only carries information to and from the policy, as a keyboard or screen does. Like an IO device, it is a detail whose choice can wait.
questions.rule: The web is a detail, like an IO device.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A team must choose among three web frameworks before writing any pricing rules. What does the book's approach suggest?
options: Write the rules behind a boundary first, and choose the framework later
Pick the most popular framework now, so that later choices have fewer unknowns
Build the rules inside the framework, since it will provide the structure they need
Ask each vendor for a sample design, then choose the one offering the most options
optionExplain: Right: rules that do not know the framework let the choice wait, and a later choice rests on more information.
Popularity sounds safe, but it makes an early commitment with the least information.
Building inside the framework makes the rules depend on a detail, which is what the book warns against.
Samples from vendors show what each vendor sells, not what the rules need.
questions.explain: Developing the rules without committing to the framework keeps the choice open and lets you try alternatives against working code.
questions.rule: Decide details late, with more information.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each item: a detail that can wait, or a part of the architecture.

items.t: Which database product stores the orders
How orders relate to customers in the data model
Whether orders arrive through a web page or a mobile app
The rules that decide when an order earns a discount
Which web server hosts the system
How a use case turns an order request into a stored order

questions.explain: The storage product, the delivery channel and the server are details. The data model, the business rules and the use cases carry the system's value, so they belong in the design.
questions.rule: The data model matters; the database product does not.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A customer demands a relational database, though no engineering reason supports it. What does the author say he should have done?
options: Refused until the customer gave an engineering reason, since the demand is not a real requirement
Rebuilt the core around tables, since customer expectations define the architecture
Ignored the demand, since details can be postponed for as long as the project runs
Bolted the database on at the side behind a narrow channel, and kept the core as it was
optionExplain: It sounds principled, but the author learned the demand was real even without a reason.
This lets a customer's wish reshape the core, which is the harm the boundary exists to prevent.
Postponing is the default, but a demand that will not go away still has to be met.
Right: the demand is met at the edge, and the core keeps its own design.
questions.explain: The author kept the database out of the core, which was right, but refused the demand, which was wrong. A narrow side channel serves both goals.
questions.rule: Meet outside demands at the edge, not in the core.
questions.teaches: A customer's expectation is a real requirement even without an engineering reason; meet it by attaching the detail at the side of the system through a narrow, safe channel, not by moving it into the core.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A thermostat's control code calls its real-time operating system directly. The vendor drops that system. What would the book have advised earlier?
options: Write the control code in assembly, so that no operating system is involved
Put an abstraction layer between the code and the system, so a change means a new layer
Keep calling the system directly, but choose only operating systems from large vendors, which rarely drop products
Copy the operating system's source into the project, so that it can never be dropped
optionExplain: Assembly removes the system but also removes portability and testability.
Right: the control code depends on an interface it owns, and only the layer below knows the operating system.
Vendor size lowers the odds of being dropped but leaves the code tied to a detail.
Copying the source makes the project own a huge detail instead of isolating it.
questions.explain: The operating system is a detail like any other. An abstraction layer lets the valuable control code stay as it is when the system changes.
questions.rule: Isolate the operating system behind an abstraction layer.
questions.teaches: A clean embedded design isolates software from the operating system through an operating system abstraction layer (OSAL); moving to another system then means writing a new OSAL against a defined interface, not editing complex existing code.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A good architect draws every possible boundary at the start, because adding one later costs little.
questions.explain: Full boundaries are expensive to build and maintain, and ignored ones are expensive to add late. The architect has to weigh both costs. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Boundaries cost money in both directions.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Weigh the cost of building a boundary against the cost of ____ it.
questions.explain: The aim is to build the boundary at the inflection point where building costs less than going without it. The decision is reviewed as the system evolves.
questions.rule: Build where building costs less than ignoring.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A start-up might one day sell its pricing engine to partners, but has no buyer yet. What fits the book's advice?
options: Build a separate deployable component with its own release process today
Ignore the possibility entirely, because over-engineering is the main risk
Build the boundary's interfaces and data structures, but deploy both sides together
Move the engine into its own service now, so that partners can call it later on
optionExplain: This pays the full cost for a need that may never come.
Over-engineering is a real risk, but a boundary ignored where one is needed is very expensive to add later.
Right: the place is held at a modest cost, and the sides can be separated if a buyer appears.
A service is the strongest and slowest form of boundary, so it is the costliest way to hold a place.
questions.explain: A partial boundary holds a place for the likely boundary without the release overhead of a full one.
questions.rule: Hold the place cheaply when the need is possible.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each partial boundary to what it gives.
pairs: Full interfaces and data structures, with both sides deployed as one component
Isolation in one direction only, with the other direction left to discipline
One class lists the services, but clients still depend on every service behind it
questions.explain: The three forms differ in how much protection they keep. The first keeps almost all of it, the strategy interface keeps half, and the facade gives up inversion.
questions.rule: Cheaper boundaries protect less.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Compared with a full boundary, what does the skip-the-last-step form save?
options: The version tracking and release management of separate components
Most of the interfaces, since only the data structures are needed
The design work, because the two sides need not be separated on paper
Nothing, because it needs the same administration as a full boundary
optionExplain: Right: the code and design work match a full boundary, but one component means one version and one release.
The interfaces are all there; that is what makes the form a real placeholder.
The design work is the same, so the saving is not there.
The administration is exactly what is saved, and the book says the difference should not be taken lightly.
questions.explain: The form pays for the structure but not for managing several components. That is why it suits a boundary that may never be needed.
questions.rule: Same structure, less administration.
questions.teaches: Skipping the last step costs the same code and design work as a full boundary but removes the version tracking and release management burden of separate components.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A firm splits its app into five services and calls the architecture clean. A new feature still forces changes in all five. What follows?
options: The services are sound; changing all five shows they are well aligned to the feature
The firm should add a sixth service to coordinate the other five
Services are decoupled by nature, so the feature must be badly specified
The services are still coupled through the data they share
optionExplain: Alignment would mean one change, not five.
A coordinating service adds another place to change and does not remove the coupling.
Services can look decoupled while sharing the same data, so the blame cannot fall on the specification alone.
Right: shared data records tie services together, so a cross-cutting feature touches them all.
questions.explain: Separate services are decoupled only at the level of variables. If a new field must be understood by every service, they are coupled to the record and to each other.
questions.rule: Services alone do not decouple.
questions.teaches: Services are decoupled only at the level of variables; the data they share still couples them, so a feature that cuts across all of them forces every service to change.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The sales team asks for a new discount rule. What should you find out before choosing where to edit?
options: Which database table currently stores the prices and the discount tiers
Which group asks for this kind of change, and which module answers to them
Which framework version the web layer runs on, and when it was last upgraded
How many lines the pricing module has, and how many people have edited it
optionExplain: Storage is a detail and does not decide where a rule belongs.
Right: the actor behind the request points to the module or component that should absorb the change.
The framework version is a detail that should not decide where rules go.
Size says little about who the code serves.
questions.explain: Changes come from people, and code is easiest to change when it is grouped by those people. The card next gives the whole order of questions.
questions.rule: Start with who is asking.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put the card's questions in the order to ask them.
items: Who is asking for this change?
What level of policy does the change belong to?
Do dependencies run from the detail toward the rules?
Is a new boundary now cheaper to build than to ignore?
questions.explain: The actor comes first, then the level, then the direction of dependencies. The cost of a new boundary is the last question, asked when friction keeps appearing.
questions.rule: Actor, level, direction, cost.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Finance wants a new rounding rule in a price-formatting class that the web team also uses for display. What fits the card?
options: Edit the shared class and tell the web team to retest their pages
Add a finance flag to the class so that one copy serves both groups
Wait until the web team also needs a rounding change, then edit once
Separate finance's rounding from the web display before adding the rule
optionExplain: It works today, but the web team pays for a change they did not ask for.
A flag leaves one class answering to two groups, so later changes still collide.
Waiting does not resolve who the class answers to.
Right: the actors differ, so the code is separated before the new rule is added.
questions.explain: Two actors share one class, so a change for finance can reach the web team. Splitting first keeps each group's changes local.
questions.rule: Separate the actors, then change.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A developer adds low-stock warnings. Which steps break the book's advice? Select all that apply.
options: She makes the stock Entity import the warning screen class so that it can raise the alert
She adds a use case that checks stock and hands plain data to a presenter
She passes the database row object straight to the screen so that it can read the level
She asks which team wants the warnings before choosing where the code goes
optionExplain: Breaks the advice: an Entity is an inner circle and must not name anything from the screen in an outer circle.
Follows the advice: the use case coordinates, and plain data crosses toward the presenter.
Breaks the advice: database rows must not cross a boundary, because they tie the screen to the storage structure.
Follows the advice: knowing the actor is the first question.
questions.explain: The Dependency Rule forbids an inner circle naming an outer one and forbids passing database rows across a boundary. The other two steps follow the order of questions.
questions.rule: Inner circles never name outer ones.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A client in a new country needs different settings and outside resources. Where does the book put this change?
options: In the business rules, with a country flag read by each rule
In the use cases, with one branch per country
In a separate Main component for that configuration, behind a boundary
In the Entities, so that every rule can see the country
optionExplain: Flags spread the country through the rules, the code that should not know about it.
Branches make each use case answer to every country.
Right: Main is the outermost detail, so each configuration gets its own Main and the policy stays unchanged.
Entities hold the most general rules, so country settings do not belong there.
questions.explain: The change concerns configuration, which is a detail. The book treats Main as a plugin and keeps one per configuration.
questions.rule: One Main per configuration.
questions.teaches: Main is a plugin that sets up initial conditions and outside resources and then hands control to the high-level policy, so there can be one Main for each configuration, such as development, test, production, a country or a customer.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Marketing wants the order flow on mobile as well as the web. Which part needs no change if the book's advice was followed?
options: The use case, which exchanges only plain data and does not know which interface serves it
The web page, since it already holds the order logic that the mobile app will need as well
The presenter, which formats output for one particular interface such as the web page
The database schema, since mobile clients need their own different tables for the same orders
optionExplain: Right: the use case sees only plain data, so a new interface can use it unchanged.
If the page held the order logic, the book's advice would not have been followed.
A presenter prepares output for a specific interface, so a new interface needs its own.
The schema belongs to storage, which is unrelated to the delivery channel.
questions.explain: The change is to the delivery mechanism, an outer detail. A use case that uses plain data structures does not know which interface it serves.
questions.rule: Use cases exchange plain data with any interface.
questions.teaches: Each use case should receive and return plain input and output data structures, so that it does not know which user interface it serves and a new interface can reuse it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: If a program passes every test its authors wrote, the best that can be said is that it is correct enough for its purposes.
questions.explain: Tests can show that a program is wrong but cannot show that it is right. The best that can be said is that it is correct enough for its purposes. The card next shows why this shapes design.
questions.rule: Tests show bugs, not their absence.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Tests can show that a program is wrong, but cannot show that it is ____.
questions.explain: Like a scientific theory, a program can be disproved by a test but never proved by one. It earns trust by surviving attempts to break it.
questions.rule: Tests falsify; they do not prove.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A mobile app's screen is hard to test automatically, but its formatting logic is easy. Which design follows the Humble Object pattern?
options: Put the formatting logic in the screen code, so that everything stays together in one file
Test the screen by tapping through it, and leave the formatting logic untested for now
Keep the screen to showing prepared values, with formatting in a separate testable module
Move the screen code into the database layer, where automated tests already exist
optionExplain: One file is convenient but keeps the easy logic locked inside the hard-to-test screen.
Tapping through the screen is slow and fragile, and it leaves the easy part untested.
Right: the screen becomes humble, and the formatting can be tested without a screen.
The database layer does not hold screens, so this changes nothing about testability.
questions.explain: The pattern splits behavior into a humble part that is hard to test and kept as simple as possible, and a part that is easy to test and holds the logic.
questions.rule: Make the hard-to-test part humble.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Tests log in through the GUI and navigate menus to check tax rules. Marketing then changes the menu layout. What is likely?
options: Nothing breaks, because the tax rules themselves did not change in any way
Many tests break though the tax rules are unchanged, and the team may resist changes
Only the login test breaks, since that is the only screen to change, and it is quick to fix
The tests keep passing, because the GUI and the rules are tested together as one system
optionExplain: The rules are unchanged, but the tests reach them through the menus.
Right: every test that passes through the changed menus fails, and the cost can make developers refuse changes.
Each test navigates the menus, so the damage is not confined to the login.
Testing together is what makes the tests depend on the layout.
questions.explain: The tests depend on a volatile part, the GUI, so a harmless change breaks them. The rules should be testable without it.
questions.rule: Do not depend on volatile things in tests.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The book gives tests their own API. Which powers should it have? Select all that apply.
options: Bypassing security constraints so that a test need not sign in
Bypassing expensive resources such as a real database
Forcing the system into a particular testable state
Editing the business rules while a test is running
Reporting a pass whenever a test cannot finish
optionExplain: Right: security checks are not what the test is about, so the testing API can skip them.
Right: skipping slow resources keeps tests quick.
Right: some states are hard to reach by normal use, so the API can force them.
Changing rules during a test would make the result meaningless.
Hiding failures defeats the point of testing.
questions.explain: The testing API is a superset of what the UI uses, with powers that make business rules easy to check. It also hides the application's structure, so tests and code can change separately.
questions.rule: Give tests an API of their own.
questions.teaches: Tests get their own API, a superset of what the user interface uses, with powers to skip security, skip expensive resources and force states, and it hides the structure of the application so that tests and code can evolve independently.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Firmware can be tested only on the physical board, and boards are scarce. What does the book advise?
options: Buy more boards, since testing only on the target is a normal cost of embedded work
Test only the parts of the software that do not touch hardware, and skip the rest
Write the code against the chip vendor's headers throughout, so that tests match the board exactly
Separate the software from the hardware behind an interface, so that it can be tested off the board
optionExplain: It is a common response, but the book names target-only testing as a bottleneck to design away.
Skipping the rest leaves much of the logic untested.
Vendor headers throughout tie the code to one chip and make off-board testing harder.
Right: the interface is a seam where a substitute can stand in, so most of the software needs no board.
questions.explain: The same reasoning applies to hardware as to a GUI: do not let the code under test depend on the volatile or scarce thing.
questions.rule: Test behind a seam, not on the target.
questions.teaches: The target-hardware bottleneck arises when code can be tested only on the target; a hardware abstraction layer between software and firmware gives a seam for substitution, so the software can be tested off the target.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The authors say business managers are not equipped to judge how important a system's architecture is, so developers have to assert it.
questions.explain: They say managers are not equipped to judge it, which is why developers have to assert it. The card next gives the duty this creates.
questions.rule: Developers must assert architecture.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors say developers must assert the importance of architecture over the urgency of ____.
questions.explain: Features are urgent, while architecture is important. Only developers can judge the second, so the duty falls on them.
questions.rule: Important beats urgent.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A tech lead fills the sprint with urgent but minor features and postpones dependency cleanup. Which mistake does the book warn about?
options: Treating architecture as urgent, so that it crowds out feature work
Letting urgent but unimportant features push aside the important architecture
Letting managers choose the architecture without developers' input
Cleaning up too early, before the features that justify the structure exist
optionExplain: This reverses the book's concern: architecture is important but rarely urgent.
Right: the sprint puts items that are urgent but not important ahead of the important structure.
That is a related risk, but the scenario describes the tech lead's own ordering.
The book argues that postponing structure is costly, not that cleaning up early is a fault.
questions.explain: The book warns against raising urgent but unimportant features above the important architecture, since that leaves the system ever harder to change.
questions.rule: Do not let the urgent push aside the important.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A component whose distance from the main sequence is 0.3 must be redesigned.
questions.explain: The distance is a measurement against a pattern the author chose. It marks components worth examining, and the examination, not the number, decides whether to change them.
questions.rule: Metrics prompt a look, not a verdict.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Your team is told to adopt a popular framework because its documentation calls its layout the recommended architecture. How do you respond?
options: Adopt it fully, since the framework's author knows its problems best
Refuse every framework, since frameworks are details and cannot be used
Use it as a tool behind a boundary, and marry it only by deliberate decision
Derive your business objects from its classes so that the two stay in step
optionExplain: The author knows the author's problems, which may differ from yours.
Frameworks are details to keep behind a boundary, not forbidden things.
Right: the framework is a tool, and any deep commitment should be a conscious, late choice.
Deriving business objects from framework classes is the deepest form of commitment.
questions.explain: The book treats a framework as a tool used with skepticism. Commitment is acceptable only as a deliberate decision, kept behind a boundary as long as possible.
questions.rule: Use frameworks as tools; marry only deliberately.
questions.teaches: The commitment to a framework runs one way: you take on all the risk and burden, and the framework's author makes no matching commitment to you.
